Title: Drupal Commerce Core Vulnerability Exploited Against Online Stores
Context: It has also not said whether the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day, before patches became available
Full Text:
Drupal is urging online store owners to patch a highly critical access bypass vulnerability in the Commerce Core module, warning that it is being exploited in the wild.

Tracked as CVE-2026-118539, the issue affects a contributed module that adds e-commerce features to Drupal websites, including a shopping cart and checkout process. Drupal’s statistics show the module is used on more than 42,000 sites.

“The module doesn’t sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor,” Drupal explains in its advisory.

The Drupal security team gave the issue a risk score of 21 out of 25. According to the score, unauthenticated attackers can exploit the flaw no matter how the module is set up.

Drupal has confirmed the attacks but has not said how the bug is being exploited, who is behind the activity, or how many sites have been targeted. It has also not said whether the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day, before patches became available.

The vulnerability affects 3.x versions before 3.3.13 and earlier releases before 8.x-2.41. Administrators should update to one of the two fixed versions and review their store orders.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“Sites should audit their orders for inconsistencies as this vulnerability is being actively exploited,” the advisory reads.

The 38 other advisories Drupal published on October 28 address vulnerabilities in 21 contributed projects. Nearly a dozen are rated critical, including bugs that could lead to remote code execution, account takeover, or Commerce orders via Stripe being marked as paid without payment.

The CAPTCHA module also received a fix for a moderately critical bug that allows a protected form to be submitted again without solving a new challenge. Drupal’s rating indicates that exploit code for this bug exists in the wild, although the advisory doesn’t mention active exploitation.

Drupal’s ratings also indicate that proofs of concept exist for two information disclosure bugs, one in Commerce Core and one in Media Alias Display.

On October 14, Drupal announced fixes for two critical remote code execution bugs: CVE-2026-108097 in core’s Field UI module and CVE-2026-108099 in the Entity List module. Neither component exposes the flaws on its own, but certain other contributed modules or custom code make exploitation possible, in some cases without authentication.

Ahead of its October 14 security releases, Drupal cautioned that exploits might appear within hours or days. So far, however, there have been no public reports of the flaws being exploited in the wild.

CVE-2026-9082, a highly critical SQL injection issue in Drupal core’s database abstraction API that affects PostgreSQL-backed sites, did attract exploitation attempts in May.

Title: CISA Adds Actively Exploited GitLab RCE and Cisco Firewall DoS Flaws to KEV
Context: 2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert Attackers Hijacked Over 300 Tor Exit Relays to Intercept SSH Connections PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday added two security flaws impacting Cisco and GitLab software to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score: 10.0) - An integer overflow or wraparound vulnerability in GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition that could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration due to insufficient regular expression validation.

CVE-2026-76418 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An unchecked return value to NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

The development comes after Cisco said it became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability earlier this month. It has not publicly identified the attackers, the number of targeted organizations, or the actions taken by attackers after gaining initial access.

As for CVE-2026-97229, its addition relates to a security incident disclosed by Alpine Linux in which an unknown threat actor unsuccessfully attempted to exploit the flaw targeting its instance on October 20 and 21, 2026.

Specifically, the attacker probed an unpatched GitLab instance by sending crafted CI configurations, causing the GitLab worker processes to crash eight times. In four of those crashes, the exploit failed at the next step.

The threat actor also downloaded Alpine Linux's GitLab container image. Subsequent attempts by the attacker to get back in on October 25 and 26 were blocked.

"The attack came close to working," the maintainers of the security-focused Linux distribution said. "We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with."

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 1, 2026.

Title: Smart TVs can harbor unpatched security flaws and track what you watch
Context: The detections include scans stopped at routers, attempted logins and exploit patterns detected and blocked
Full Text:
Smart TVs and connected plugs accounted for a large share of recorded security weaknesses in household devices, according to Bitdefender’s 2026 IoT Security Landscape Report. The analysis covered approximately 10.4 million protected home routers between January and September.

Televisions represented 22.7% of vulnerability observations, followed by smart plugs at 22.4% linked with a known software flaw.

Top vulnerable device families (Source: Bitdefender)

Household electronics can stay in use for five to ten years, while their security support may last two to four years. Once updates stop, TVs, plugs and home storage systems can remain connected with unresolved flaws.

Automated scans dominate detected attack activity

Automated port scans accounted for 90.1% of detected attack-category events, with approximately 4.85 billion scan attempts recorded over the nine-month period.

These probes check for accessible services, including remote desktop connections, remote login services and administration interfaces. Finding an open service can provide a starting point for further attempts to gain access, but a scan does not establish that someone broke in.

Password brute-force attempts accounted for approximately 8.7% of attack-category events. Of the 466.6 million brute-force events reported, approximately 455 million targeted Remote Desktop Protocol, commonly used to access Windows computers remotely.

The detections include scans stopped at routers, attempted logins and exploit patterns detected and blocked. They do not establish how many households experienced a successful intrusion.

Free TV apps can share household connections

Citing findings from security firm Spur, the report describes software bundled into free smart-TV apps that can turn televisions into residential proxies after users accept consent terms.

The household’s broadband connection then carries a customer’s traffic for uses marketed as web scraping, advertising verification and market research. Websites receiving that traffic see the household’s public internet address.

Accepting an app’s terms authorizes the sharing, even though users may not understand how their connection will be used.

Viewing data and household profiling

Televisions can also collect information about what people watch and the devices around them.

Gamers Nexus findings cited in the report describe LG televisions collecting viewing data, voice recordings, geographical location, details of other devices on the local network and information about nearby wireless networks.

Automatic Content Recognition, or ACR, identifies material displayed on a television by matching content samples against a reference database. The technology is used to support personalized advertising.

Connected equipment can occupy several roles: an attack target, a proxy carrying outside traffic, a sensor collecting information or a foothold inside a network.

“Once inside, criminals can stay hidden and move laterally across the home network,” warned Chandan Nandakumaraiah, head of product and cybersecurity at NETGEAR.

Title: php2shell one week later: Why one exploit doesn’t work everywhere
Context: What can we learn from this Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk...
Full Text:
php2shell raised fears of mass exploitation. A week of testing by our research team found that working exploits had to be fitted to each target’s exact PHP setup. Systems that share one build, such as network appliances, are the exception: one tuned exploit can reach every device that runs it.

Key takeaways

The five vulnerable PHP sites we exposed to the internet were not compromised, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) that go beyond version checks do not reliably confirm whether a host is vulnerable. Exploitation has been confirmed elsewhere, on researcher honeypots and on some network appliances.

In realistic environments, turning php2shell into remote code execution usually takes an exploit built for the specific target. That is hard, not impossible, and it puts php2shell in a different category from Log4Shell, even though both received near-maximum severity ratings. Where many systems share one build, such as network appliances, a single calibrated exploit can work against all of them.

Patch now, starting with internet-facing management interfaces, network appliances, and end-of-life PHP branches. Tenable Nessus and Tenable One Web App Scanning have had version-based detection since October 21.

Background

On October 20, 2026, PHP announced two vulnerabilities, and on October 21 released fixes for flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Each has a CVSSv4 score of 9.2. For a full breakdown of affected versions, fixes and mitigations, see our frequently asked questions blog post.

This post covers what happened after the disclosure, based on what our team observed directly.

From disclosure to headline in under 48 hours

php2shell got big fast. Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online before the official release. Within two days, the vulnerability had a name, a logo and coverage in mainstream media.

Several websites went offline as a precaution, as described in our threat actor response blog post. Censys’s php2shell dashboard, which tracks PHP services by reported version, showed about 30.3 million PHP services still on an affected version on October 29, though a matching version does not mean a system can be exploited.

The comparison with Log4Shell came up early, but the two are very different to exploit. With Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), attackers only had to send a short piece of text to a vulnerable application, for example in a login form or a web request. If the application logged that text, the attack worked. The same text worked against almost any vulnerable target without changes, so attackers could launch it at scale within hours, and many of those attacks succeeded.

php2shell is different. Exploitation depends on the state of the heap, the process manager in use, worker reuse and how memory is laid out on a given build. php2shell drew attention quickly, but attackers can't exploit it as easily as Log4Shell.

What changed while we were testing

Several developments that matter for defenders came after our research began:

On October 24, honeypots run by Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three sensors running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, a configuration that favors the exploit.

On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Federal civilian agencies have until October 29 to remediate.

The same day, security firm Dream reported an attack chain that combined php2shell with a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw, Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300). Dream says the campaign rooted “25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.” Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 says it independently verified the same attacker’s tooling and confirmed the reported results. We have not verified these findings ourselves.

On October 28, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV catalog and noted that it can be chained with php2shell to run commands as root. By October 29, Palo Alto Networks reported active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces.

These reports are consistent with what we found. The exploit has to be calibrated to a specific build. Network appliances often run the same software across many devices, so one calibrated exploit can reach many of them. That is where we expect targeted exploitation to keep growing.

What we observed during our exploit research

Exposed targets

To measure real-world activity, we kept five vulnerable PHP sites reachable from the internet: four through the evening of October 24, and one still running in a standard, vulnerable configuration at the time of writing.

Over that period, we observed mass exploitation attempts that matched php2shell exploitation patterns. None of our targets had been compromised as of October 29.

Other organizations have reported exploitation attempts and, in the cases described above, successful exploitation. Amazon Threat Intelligence says php2shell is “now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.” Our data does not contradict these reports. It shows that attempts, even at scale, were not enough to compromise a default installation in our environment. Attempts and successful compromises are two different numbers, and in the first days after a disclosure people often treat them as the same.

Public proofs-of-concept

We collected and tested almost all public PoCs. An early lead was php2shell poc, published by researcher Daniel Púa (devploit). It let us reproduce the exposure on multiple 8.4 and 8.5 environments with specific configurations. From there, we did deeper research, including white-box testing and code and patch comparison, and achieved remote code execution on PHP 7.4.33.

What we learned from this research is that the exploit inadvertently reveals a clean discriminator: the same multipart POST that begins stage 1 produces a different allocator response on patched vs. unpatched PHP. No heap corruption, no crash, no shell, just a measurable size difference in how the server handles the request. That became signal 1: a large filename in the multipart request produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable versions than on fixed versions, because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Same request, same PHP – different memory behavior depending solely on whether the UAF patch is present.

Tenable Research identified a second signal as well: the compact amplification sequences that exercise the UAF window's existence without triggering corruption. The session upload-progress oracle watches for the crash/recover pattern that vulnerable versions exhibit under controlled amplification.

These two signals became a stateful probe that a Nessus ‘direct check’ plugin could detect. However, the probe would miss some vulnerable systems and flag some patched ones as vulnerable.

The memory corruption is real, and PHP confirms memory disclosure as one of the impacts. Turning it into code execution on a target is difficult and unique to each target. Our working RCE required an exploit tuned to the target's environment, including its PHP build, SAPI, extensions and runtime configuration. A payload that works against one lab setup does not carry over to a different distribution package or a different PHP-FPM pool configuration.

AI-accelerated research: Useful, but it needs checking

AI agents sped up our reverse engineering and testing, and they also produced at least one convincing false positive. During a multi-hour session, an agent built a working shell against our PHP-FPM lab containers and reported it as confirmation of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. It was not. The agent had used a local file inclusion weakness that we had added to the lab, a different attack class that does not exist in default PHP deployments. A researcher caught the error by checking the exploit chain against the vulnerability's mechanics.

The lesson applies to anyone reading exploitation claims this week: a real shell is not proof that a specific CVE was used. We also ran into inconsistent responses from AI tools when doing authorized exploit validation, which slowed parts of the work.

White-box testing

The GDB analysis and heap geometry research below show why: there is no universal offset. Code execution is a real exposure yet it is not as simple as portrayed. The RCE we achieved on PHP 7.4.33 worked only once the exploit matched that one setup. A profile that achieves a shell against one lab container does not carry over to a different distribution package, a different PHP-FPM pool configuration, or a different memory limit.

The chunk-relative offsets pictured in the ‘heap geometry capture method’ visuals below reference _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0, arData at chunk+0x64b80. These values illustrate the measurement method and are specific to PHP 8.3.35 built from the docker-library bookworm image on amd64. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or a PHP 8.3.35 built with different extensions, produces different chunk geometry values. We used GDB against the live worker to measure the actual values for a given target.

Our failure to show that mass exploitation is quick or easy does not make this vulnerability harmless. A well-resourced attacker who wants a specific target can build that exploit, and AI-assisted tooling shortens the time it takes. It does make mass exploitation of the Log4Shell kind much less likely. The exception is any population of systems that share one build, such as network appliances, where the cost of calibration is paid once.

Why exploitation is hard

When possible, Tenable Research releases exposure direct checks to help customers detect exploitable vulnerabilities within their environments. These direct checks depend on finding reliable and safe methods of exercising a vulnerability in a way that simulates an exploit without triggering any destructive actions. This typically involves first researching how to develop an exploit, then figuring out how to test that safely.

Our research found the php2shell exposure difficult to reproduce broadly, even with white-box testing and GDB attached to processes, and even with AI agents analyzing runtime memory and source code for weaknesses and leads in parallel. What we learned from this research helps to inform us on the practical realities of real-world exploitation:

php2shell is a multi-stage memory corruption chain. A direct check triggering an out-of-memory condition alone does not fully guarantee the asset is also exposed to remote code execution.

In-memory offsets are version and system specific. The chunk-relative structure offsets required for heap manipulation change with every PHP patch release and system/software combination. Gaps in an inventory of known offsets and platforms could make a vulnerable system look patched (false-negative).

The OOM trigger depends on application-controlled memory limits. Whether the condition fires depends on the configured memory_limit and on whether the application overrides it via ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives.

The use-after-free requires reuse of the PHP worker across consecutive requests. Under mod_php, keep-alive pins a connection to one worker; under FPM, session affinity (PHPSESSID) is required. Both depend on SAPI and process-manager settings. For example, pm.max_requests recycles workers and breaks the use-after-free chain with no visible sign, so the check returns a false negative.

The exploit crashes PHP workers. Workers appear to respawn reliably, but a direct check that intentionally degrades performance could still affect production systems.

What can we learn from this

Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk reaction is triggered that creates significant fears of mass exploitation and extreme risk. While we do not want to downplay the dangers of this vulnerability, it is valuable to understand the practicalities of exploitation in the real world versus the fear that is built around a CVE during the regular news cycle. In this case, that nuance points remediation first at internet-facing assets, especially appliances such as network infrastructure management interfaces, and anything else that runs a common, basic deployment that reduces overall complexity.

Prioritization matters more as AI finds more vulnerabilities

Calif, OpenAI and Wiz are credited with finding php2shell. Calif says AI assisted the discovery. We expect the number of disclosed vulnerabilities to keep rising as these tools improve, and many of them will come with high base scores. Patching everything rated critical at the speed of the news cycle will not be possible.

Security teams need to understand what a vulnerability takes to exploit, not only how bad the worst case is:

Is there a public exploit that works without changes, or only a crash PoC?

Does exploitation depend on a non-default configuration, a specific build or prior access?

Is the vulnerable component reachable from the internet in your environment?

Has anyone observed successful compromise, as opposed to scanning?

Exploit prediction scores such as EPSS, Tenable's Vulnerability Priority Rating (VPR) and confirmed exploitation sources such as CISA's KEV catalog help answer these questions. They work better alongside an analysis of the vulnerability itself than in place of one.

Patch anyway

Our observations do not mean php2shell should be ignored. The conditions for exploitation exist, exploit development will improve and targeted attacks against high-value PHP applications are plausible. Updating to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or applying your distribution's fixed packages, remains the recommendation. For end-of-life branches, plan an upgrade. Until then, apply the configuration mitigations described in our FAQ and limit internet exposure, starting with appliance management interfaces. For network appliances, PHP version numbers do not apply: use your vendor's fixed build or its interim mitigations.

What we are recommending is a different order of work. Patch or isolate internet-facing network appliances, management interfaces, and end-of-life PHP systems now. For the rest of your PHP estate, patch on your critical schedule, and check that less publicized vulnerabilities that are easy to exploit in your environment are not waiting behind php2shell.

Title: Researchers find bugs in 5 AI developer tools, with OpenAI and Microsoft flaws still unpatched
Context: Both Claude Desktop and VS Code allow local pages access to their respective project folders, but the researchers found that these restrictions did not apply to web workers – a...
Full Text: Multiple vulnerabilities in five popular AI developer tools could allow attackers to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof browser address bars. Researchers say flaws in OpenAI's Codex and Microsoft's VS Code remain unpatched, potentially putting developers who use affected configurations at risk. AI security startup Forever Security discovered vulnerabilities in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Codex, and disclosed four of the flaws to the affected vendors. GitHub independently fixed the Copilot vulnerability without receiving a report from Forever Security. All five share a common security weakness: embedded browsers granted capabilities beyond those available to conventional browsers. Each tool “enriched its embedded browser beyond what a normal browser allows, and those enrichments undermined the traditional threat model - as agent input, as the authority on a tab’s own address, or as reach onto the host,” Forever researcher Gal Weizman wrote in a Thursday report. Forever dubbed this class of vulnerability “Embrace,” short for EMbedded BRowser, and said the flaws led to code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot. Here’s what each of these looks like, starting with Cursor. Cursor: arbitrary code execution Typical web pages can’t run commands on the host computer because a web page’s JavaScript cannot talk to local apps. Cursor’s integrated browser, however, allows a page to call the agent’s composer. The agent reads this as instructions and follows them, but the instructions remain hidden from human users. This opens the coding agent up to prompt injection attacks that could allow an attacker to execute commands on the host machine. The researchers disclosed the vulnerability to Cursor on September 10, and the vendor silently patched the flaw on October 1. According to Forever, Cursor did not publish a security advisory about the issue or respond to the researchers' disclosure. Cursor also did not reply to The Register’s request for comment. GitHub Copilot: address bar spoofing Under normal browser operations, a webpage cannot change the content of the address bar. “Copilot’s browser preview works differently,” Weizman wrote. “Some pages change their address without loading a new page, and the app cannot always see that. So Copilot let the page tell the app its own address.” The app checked only whether the text looked like a web address, starting with http, https or file, but it didn’t check where the tab really pointed to. This can be abused to trick the embedded browser into displaying a spoofed URL - such as github.com/login - in the address bar, while loading a fraudulent website - like a phishing page - underneath. The researchers found the address-bar spoofing flaw in GitHub Copilot 1.1.27 on September 26. GitHub independently fixed the flaw in a later Copilot build (1.1.29) on October 13 without receiving a vulnerability report from Forever. We reached out to GitHub and did not receive a response. Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code: arbitrary file read All three of these vendors’ coding assistants allow local HTML files opened in the built-in browser to escape its boundaries and access other files. Both Claude Desktop and VS Code allow local pages access to their respective project folders, but the researchers found that these restrictions did not apply to web workers – a browser feature that allows JavaScript to run in a background thread, separate from the page's main thread. This means a local page can start a worker, and the worker can bypass restrictions to reach any file on the machine. Codex, however, didn’t have this same restriction, meaning a local page could read any file directly without a worker. Weizman said his team disclosed the issue to Anthropic on July 23, and the AI vendor declined the Claude Desktop bug report as invalid for a “workspace trust” gated security boundary. A day later, however, Noma Security reported the same flaw, according to Weizman, and Anthropic accepted the report as valid. Anthropic did not respond to The Register’s questions about either bug report or Forever’s timeline of events. Forever disclosed the Codex bug to OpenAI on July 27 and didn’t get a response. The flaw remains unpatched, but an OpenAI spokesperson told The Register that it's aware of the issue and working to address it. On September 10, Forever disclosed the VS Code vulnerability to Microsoft and says the vendor also labeled it as an invalid workspace trust gated security boundary issue. The researchers claim it remains unpatched. Microsoft did not respond to our request for comment.®

Title: Suspected Chinese attackers built a custom PHP2Shell exploit and rooted 25 servers
Context: REG AD The attackers rooted the first US government-affiliated firewall on October 23, but the device crashed shortly afterward, possibly due to around 900 MB of exploit traffic
Full Text: Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, according to Dream researchers. The snoops began exploiting these servers on October 23, targeting organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. The attackers also honed in on US government-affiliated firewalls. “Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign - all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet,” the Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said in a report. Plus, the attackers “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks, Dream noted. The attackers rooted the first US government-affiliated firewall on October 23, but the device crashed shortly afterward, possibly due to around 900 MB of exploit traffic. According to Dream, it remained unresponsive despite 240 automated checks over two hours. They successfully exploited the second firewall a day later, on October 24. The compromised firewalls ran vulnerable versions of Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS. Dream said it had been working with the vendor to investigate the compromises, and Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 researchers independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed Dream's reported results. To break into the firewalls, the attackers built a custom exploit chain that includes PHP2Shell and a Fragnesia kernel flaw, and ran about 40 custom post-exploitation scripts once they were inside the targeted organizations. Total attack chain in under 15 minutes PHP2Shell, comprised of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, came to light early last week, along with fears that attackers would abuse the bugs to take down most of the internet. Despite “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, the first reports of successful attacks didn’t start until Saturday. Both bugs have CVSS scores of 9.2 and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers. The PHP2Shell exploit recovered by Dream was not a copy of any known public exploit. It “appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform,” the researchers wrote. The attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), a high-severity local privilege-escalation vulnerability affecting the Linux kernel's XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added this Linux kernel bug to its catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities on Wednesday. Both CISA and the FBI declined to comment. The miscreants developed a four-stage PHP2Shell exploit that allowed them to execute commands without authentication on vulnerable Palo Alto Networks firewalls. They then used Fragnesia to escalate their privileges and gain root access. The attackers targeted PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2, which run PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enabled the exploit's memory-corruption stages. “The total chain - from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell - completes in under 15 minutes,” the Dream team wrote. 4 steps to root Here’s how it works: First, they flood the servers with crafted multipart POST requests to corrupt PHP’s memory, and force a predictable memory layout. Then a second request forges the stale session ID length from the memory corruption part of the attack, forcing an out-of-bounds read and exposing the base address of libphp.so in the running process. The attackers then exhaust PHP's memory again to force mod_data=NULL, creating a stale reference they can forge in the final stage to execute commands as the nobody user. They use Fragnesia to escalate to root and plant a web shell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall. After breaking in via the compromised firewalls, the attackers snooped around in Active Directory, stealing credentials and other sensitive information. With root access, the attackers also had the master key to decrypt the LDAP service account password, which they hardcoded into every subsequent script. They also enumerated every user and group in the domain via LDAP queries, and sprayed passwords against every user account. Attackers also tried to create backdoor AD accounts and attempted SAML signing key extraction - but Dream doesn’t know if these were successful. “The attack results - whether the password spray found valid credentials, whether the backdoor accounts were created, whether SAML keys were extracted - stayed on the management server's local filesystem and were not among the artifacts we recovered,” the researchers noted. AI tools in the attack The investigation also uncovered evidence that the attackers used AI tools, but noted that this was not a fully autonomous attack. The researchers found Anthropic's Claude Code installed, an AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan configured with Chinese models DeepSeek and Kimi, and API keys for the FOFA reconnaissance service. FOFA is a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan. The attackers used it to identify about 19,000 internet-facing Palo Alto Networks firewalls worldwide. “The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running,” Dream warned. “And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional PAN-OS versions.”®

Title: Hackers exploit Cisco SD-WAN flaw to deploy custom KeyDrift malware
Context: In a report Lumen released yesterday, researchers revealed that the Silent Train framework allowed Volt Typhoon to evade detection while conducting zero-day vulnerability attacks
Full Text:
A newly identified advanced persistent threat (APT) group tracked as UAT-11473 was observed exploiting CVE-2026-20127, an authentication-bypass flaw in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers, to deploy a custom malware framework called KeyDrift.

CVE-2026-20127 is a max-severity flaw that Cisco patched in February 2026, which allows remote attackers to gain privileged access to Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager and add rogue peers.

UAT-8616 has exploited the vulnerability as a zero-day since at least 2023, and recent research also linked its exploitation to the Chinese Volt Typhoon state-sponsored hacking group.

According to Cisco Talos researchers who reported on the activity, the UAT-11473 threat cluster appears to overlap with Volt Typhoon’s "Silent Train" covert access network, but they made no definitive links.

In a report Lumen released yesterday, researchers revealed that the Silent Train framework allowed Volt Typhoon to evade detection while conducting zero-day vulnerability attacks.

Deploying KeyDrift

The attacks Cisco researchers observed targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research organizations, using the KeyDrift malware, which is a custom malware framework designed to operate on Cisco SD-WAN controller instances.

"Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material," explained Cisco Talos.

"KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records."

KeyDrift has two primary components, PolyFlame and LittleFilch, for which Talos saw signs of ongoing development, including new anti-debugging mechanisms and varied process impersonation.

PolyFlame runs inside legitimate vdaemon processes using modified service startup scripts and an injector for deployment.

It supports command execution through a TinyShell-styled component, file uploads and downloads, and relaying communications between an attacker’s command-and-control (C2) server and multiple peers.

LittleFilch is a control-session interception module that hooks SSL_read to inspect control-plane messages after they have been decrypted inside the controller.

For predefined edge nodes, it extracts IP identifiers and a 32-byte field that Talos assesses to be AES-256 IPsec data-plane key material.

It uses RSA encryption to protect the collected information, saves it to /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, and then transmits it over UDP to the attackers.

Talos believes with high confidence that KeyDrift is designed to maintain persistent access to Cisco SD-WAN controllers, intercept control-plane traffic, extract cryptographic keys, and securely stage or exfiltrate the stolen data.

Cisco recommends that system administrators apply the available security updates for CVE-2026-20127 and also consult the vendor’s dedicated hardening guide for Catalyst SD-WAN deployments.

Title: Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes
Context: Related: GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub From Vulnerability Discovery to Chained Exploits Historically, creating such chained exploits would...
Full Text:
An unreleased version of Claude identified critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used browsers and operating systems and chained them into working exploits requiring little or no human interaction, Anthropic said this week.

The exploits included one that enabled data theft from a locked Android smartphone, another zero-click exploit allowed remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on Linux servers, and a third that could have allowed attackers to remotely crash Windows systems. In total, Anthropic said, the model generated five working exploits targeting Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. All affected vendors have addressed the vulnerabilities after Anthropic reported them.

The exploits are the latest evidence that frontier AI models are moving beyond simply identifying individual flaws to combining multiple into sophisticated working exploits. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic's Frontier Red Team said in a blog post this week.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

From Vulnerability Discovery to Chained Exploits

Historically, creating such chained exploits would have required special teams with domain expertise, the researchers wrote. "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Anthropic's report described a one-click RCE exploit chain involving Chrome on macOS. The exploit combined four vulnerabilities in Chrome's JavaScript engine, memory protections, browser process isolation, and federated sign-in functionality.

Each of the vulnerabilities that Claude discovered helped overcome a different security control and allowed the chained exploit to escape the browser's sandbox. As a proof of concept, Anthropic's exploit launched macOS Calculator from Chrome when a user loaded a malicious webpage.

Anthropic said it reported 62 vulnerabilities to Google, all of which had been assigned CVE identifiers, rated high or critical, and patched by Chrome 156.

On Safari, Claude's exploit chain allowed JavaScript on any website to bypass the same-origin policy, a security control that prevents one website from accessing another site's data. An attacker could have used the exploit to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and session data, potentially allowing an attacker to read information from authenticated websites.

"For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers," Anthropic said. The exploit chain combined four weaknesses Claude identified in Safari — a use-after-free flaw in Safari's JavaScriptCore engine, a way to bypass WebKit's Gigacage memory protection, a vulnerability in the WebContent sandbox, and a JavaScriptCore flaw.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

Apple has since fixed the issue, Anthropic said.

The Android exploit, meanwhile, targeted a locked Google Pixel 9. Claude chained three vulnerabilities in Android's device-transfer and USB-handling mechanisms, bypassing four layers of protection to extract photos and other personal information from the phone without unlocking it. Anthropic said Google has addressed the issue.

Claude's Windows exploit, which Microsoft has patched, involved a remotely exploitable denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability. The flaw was an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's implementation of the transport protocol used by HTTP/3. An attacker could send a small number of specially crafted network packets to a vulnerable server to crash it and repeatedly trigger crashes, disrupting access for users, Anthropic said.

For Linux, Claude developed a zero-click exploit against the kernel's networking stack that would have let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute commands with root-level privileges on affected servers, without requiring any user interaction. "This vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches," Anthropic said.

Related:Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

Expanding Defender Access to More Powerful Models

With AI getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, defenders need powerful models for patching them before attackers can exploit the flaws, Anthropic said. "Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do," the company said.

To that end, the company is expanding access to its most capable AI models for vetted cybersecurity professionals through its Cyber Verification Program. The program now has three access tiers that give security teams a way to apply for the level of access appropriate for their work.

"It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward," Anthropic said. "Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever."

Andrew Bolster, senior R&D manager at Black Duck, says Anthropic's results are credible where they can be verified. The Chrome, WebKit, Windows, and Linux fixes are all public, he notes, but any claims that Claude discovered them autonomously are Anthropic's own. "The report gives no success rates, cost, or human-hours per chain, which is critical context for security leaders," he says.

Some of the conditions for the exploits to work were also noteworthy, he says. For instance, the Android chain involved a stolen phone and a USB cable, and the Linux exploit required an exposed MPTCP listener. "Exploit benchmarks show model success dropping sharply once ASLR, stack canaries, and sandboxing are enabled, and VulnCheck found only 1.3% of AI-discovered vulnerabilities confirmed exploited in the wild," Bolster says. "Delivery, reliability, and target preconditions remain the attacker’s problem for now, though I'd expect that gap to narrow."

Claude's chained exploits are another indication that AI has lowered the barrier to discovering vulnerabilities and building working attacks, says Jacob Krell, senior director, secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs. But there are still substantial barriers between a proof of concept and a reliable attack in the wild. "A shell on one honeypot tells you little about the next server's worker count, build, or kernel," Krell notes. "AI has made finding the bug cheap. Getting it to work on a server it has never seen is still the expensive part."

At the same time, the gap between a proof of concept and a reliable, broadly deployable attack is increasingly becoming about time and target-specific adaptation rather than specialized expertise, he cautions.

Defenders are making a mistake if they assume this kind of vulnerability discovery always requires the most powerful AI models, adds John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security. "Local systems, including a Mac Studio with 128GB of memory or a DGX Spark, can support AI-assisted reverse engineering and vulnerability research. The target, model, tools, and operator's skill matter."

It may take attackers longer, with less capable systems, and attacks may be more practical only against smaller, less-scrutinized code bases. But defenders need to account for that capability, Strand says. "If AI can find vulnerabilities in Windows, Android, Linux, and Chrome, what does that say about code that receives a fraction of that attention? Think about your IP cameras. Think about the firmware on the router running a remote office. All of that is in play."

Title: Chinese hackers used VMware ESX zero-day; PHP2Shell and Fragnesia chained to root firewalls
Context: Attackers exploit Cisco firewall DoS flaw Cisco confirmed today that a newly disclosed vulnerability (CVE-2026-76418) affecting its “classic” and next-gen firewalls has been...
Full Text:
China-nexus threat actors have exploited a VMware ESX zero-day to hide their tracks and chained PHP2Shell flaws with the “Fragnesia” Linux kernel bug to root servers and firewalls, cybersecurity researchers claim.

Cisco has also confirmed that attackers are crashing its firewalls with a newly disclosed vulnerability.

VMware ESX zero-day helped Chinese spies cover their tracks

Chinese APT group Warp Panda has leveraged an insufficient logging vulnerability (CVE-2026-41709) in Broadcom’s VMware ESX bare-metal hypervisor as a zero-day, a new CrowdStrike report revealed.

CVE-2026-41709 was publicly disclosed and fixed by Broadcom in July 2026. Broadcom thanked CrowdStrike researcher Ian Barton for reporting the issue.

CrowdStrike now says that the latest intrusion where it saw Warp Panda exploiting CVE-2026-41709 happened in early 2026, and that the flaw uallowed the group to significantly reduce audit trail visibility.

“WARP PANDA represents a sustained and strategically focused China-nexus cyber espionage threat to U.S. entities across multiple sectors, including the legal sector. The adversary typically exploits internet-facing edge devices to gain initial access, then pivots to VMware vCenter environments to deploy custom malware such as BRICKSTORM and SharpStorm, maintaining persistent covert access for extended periods of time,” CrowdStrike explained.

“The legal sector’s concentration of client communications, merger and acquisition materials, active litigation strategy, and cross-client access makes it a high-value collection target for a state-directed adversary seeking intelligence with downstream operational utility.”

The group has also been breaking into Microsoft 365 environments by obtaining user session tokens and occasionally registering a new MFA device on a compromised account.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-41709 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 28, 2026, and has ordered US federal civilian agencies to address it by November 11.

Linux kernel flaw joins PHP2Shell exploit chain

CVE-2026-46300 (aka “Fragnesia”), a Linux Kernel local privilege escalation vulnerability disclosed in May 2026, was also added to CISA’s KEV catalog on Wednesday. That one should be addressed by October 31, CISA saya, and comes with the forensic triage requirement mandated by BOD 26-04.

“This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root,” the agency noted.

According to cybersecurity outfit Dream, that’s what a China-nexus threat actor did in an AI-assisted campaign that rooted 25 firewalls, then planted webshells and extracted credentials from the Active Directory domain controllers.

“Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts,” the company said.

“This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment.”

The attack path (Source: Dream)

Dream did not name the maker of the rooted firewalls. But, whether a coincidence or not, Palo Alto Networks updated its PHP2Shell-related advisory today to say that “active exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet”.

Security researcher Kevin Beaumont also said that he’s “aware of a ransomware group using PHP2Shell against Palo-Alto firewalls to gain initial access to [organizations],” and mentioned reports about a Chinese national state group exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to get on Palo Alto Networks firewalls for espionage against the US government.

Help Net Security has reached out to Palo Alto Networks for more information and we’ll update this article when we hear back from them. In the meantime, their customers should consult the advisory for advice on how to protect their boxes.

Attackers exploit Cisco firewall DoS flaw

Cisco confirmed today that a newly disclosed vulnerability (CVE-2026-76418) affecting its “classic” and next-gen firewalls has been exploited to crash devices.

“This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group. [An unauthenticated, remote] attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition,” the company stated, and said that its Product Security Incident Response Team became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability in October 2026.

Since there are no available workarounds, Cisco “strongly recommends” that customers upgrade to a fixed software release to remediate the flaw.

CVE-2026-76418 has yet to be added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Title: Cisco Open Sources Quarry to Catch AI Agent Attacks Hidden in Harmless Steps
Context: It is the ability of AI to separate an attack into multiple individually benign steps that defeats traditional defenses and requires this new form of neurosymbolic threat detection
Full Text:
Detecting an AI agent attack isn’t simply finding multiple small needles scattered in a large haystack; it is recognizing whether and for what purpose the needles are connected.

Traditional security controls evaluate single actions to classify whether an intent is bad or benign. This approach fails on AI agent activity when the bad intent only emerges over a series of benign actions. It only becomes apparent if and when the overall sequence of actions is viewed or actioned.

Fraud detection is an example. A bank analyzes each purchase on its own. That’s largely how traditional security operates. Fraud detection, however, needs to see patterns of apparently benign single purchases across multiple purchases, possibly in multiple locations with unlikely timing (potentially employing agent capability). “Agent security needs the same combination of pattern detection and evidence, applied to the steps an agent takes rather than to purchases,” writes Cisco in announcing the open sourcing of its Project Quarry.

Cisco describes Quarry as a neurosymbolic rule language, combining machine learning judgment with rule-based checks. “It covers single-turn and multi-turn large language model (LLM) conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs.”

Each defined rule draws on neural evidence from ML classifiers and LLM judges, and symbolic rules that check exact conditions, sequences, string matches, and tool relationships. It is designed to provide a shared policy layer rather than be a replacement for every detector or every enforcement control.

Quarry can be used to provide runtime guardrails on agents, post-hoc rule set security analytics, and incident response. It integrates with Cisco’s existing Integrated AI Security & Safety Framework. It expands the framework from describing AI risk toward detecting it in agent activity, and is positioned as the policy and evaluation layer for the framework. The framework defines AI risks while Quarry provides detection of the risks in agent activity – the framework categories also offer a roadmap for the further development of new rules.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Quarry’s detection purpose is to identify suspicious patterns that span individual permitted actions. Such patterns may only become suspicious over a period of time. In 2025, Claude Code was used by bad actors in two campaigns: one against around 30 organizations, and a second against Mexican government institutions. The former attack was split into small routine-looking tasks that told the existing defense it was part of new defense testing. It looked like an authorized pentest from its parts, but the true intent (theft of data) only became apparent when the requests came together in the right sequence.

It is the ability of AI to separate an attack into multiple individually benign steps that defeats traditional defenses and requires this new form of neurosymbolic threat detection. But it is not a ‘write once and move on’ requirement. Attackers are constantly developing new approaches to their attacks. So, whenever a new attack technique is recognized, defenders must respond immediately by writing a new Quarry rule that can be used by all organizations everywhere.

But writing new rules by hand does not scale against the attackers’ use of AI to develop new malicious agents. “We want agents, as well as security and AI engineers, to be able to write Quarry rules,” declares Cisco. A Quarry Plugin allows a coding agent to compose, compile, and refine rules from a plain-English description of an organization’s risk, and then test those rules against real conversations. A rule that passes in a coding agent should behave the same way at runtime.

By open sourcing the project, the traditional cybersecurity asymmetry of attack and defense (multiple attackers against individual defenders) is equalized (multiple global attackers now face multiple global defenders). Allowing the use of AI for development also balances the speed advantage that bad actors have enjoyed in AI-assisted attacks.

“The open-source project,” says Cisco, “gives practitioners a working foundation for detection engineering.” The Quarry starter pack includes:

a readable DSL for conversations, tool use, and event relationships;

an evaluation runtime with configurable safety and resource limits, which compiles each rule when it loads;

a command-line scanner for individual traces, directories, and datasets;

a Python SDK for application integration;

optional configured model operations for semantic signals;

the Quarry plugin for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents;

rule metadata, examples, documentation, and message-format guidance; and

a workflow for validating rules against positive and benign datasets.

Project Quarry is intended to become a common, open standard for expressing and sharing detections for AI-agent attacks, much as Snort, YARA, and Sigma became standards in other areas of cybersecurity. “Hugging Face reconstructed roughly 17,600 agent actions after the fact,” says Cisco. “Our aim with Project Quarry is to help defenders recognize sequences like that one while they are still in progress, and to preserve the evidence behind each finding for the people who have to act on it.”

Title: CVE-2026-101767: Critical Oracle EBS SQL Injection Actively Probed in the Wild
Context: CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3
Full Text:
What is CVE-2026-101767?

A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-101767, CVSS 9.8) was disclosed affecting Oracle E-Business Suite’s Application Object Library, allowing attackers to achieve full remote code execution and system takeover via an unauthenticated SQL injection in the Thin Client Framework servlet. Due to the potential for complete compromise of financial, payroll, and HR data managed by EBS, immediate patching is required.

How the Oracle EBS SQL injection leads to remote code execution

The issue originates from the Application Object Library’s TCF servlet at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, where missing authentication on a critical function combined with improper input sanitization leads to SQL injection as the privileged APPS database user. By sending specially crafted POST requests to the servlet instantiating oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer, attackers can execute arbitrary SQL commands and chain to operating system command execution as the EBS application account, potentially achieving full takeover of the EBS instance and all data it manages. No authentication is required to exploit this issue.

CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline

The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3.ai and reported to Oracle on July 24, 2026. Oracle addressed it in the October 2026 Critical Patch Update, released October 20. Within a week of the patch release, threat intelligence firm Defused observed exploratory exploitation attempts hitting Oracle EBS honeypots on October 27. EBS has historically been a target for financially motivated threat actors, including the Cl0p group’s large-scale EBS campaign the previous year.

Which Oracle E-Business Suite versions are affected?

The following components are affected: Oracle E-Business Suite Application Object Library, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. Oracle notes that earlier unsupported versions are likely also affected. The vulnerable servlet passes through the default EBS URL firewall configuration, meaning any internet-facing EBS instance with default settings is exposed. Organizations running EBS for financial, payroll, HR, and procurement operations face elevated risk due to the sensitive data accessible through the APPS database user.

How to patch and mitigate CVE-2026-101767

Users should apply the October 2026 Critical Patch Update immediately (details in My Oracle Support Note KA923), and also patch the underlying EBS Database and Fusion Middleware components, which have separate CPU entries. As interim mitigations until patching is complete, administrators should remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict network access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks only.

Is CVE-2026-101767 being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, Horizon3.ai has published technical details of the attack chain, and active probing has been confirmed in the wild by Defused. The vulnerability is not yet listed on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments.

What attackers can do with a compromised Oracle EBS instance

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary SQL and OS commands as the APPS and EBS application accounts, exfiltrate or manipulate sensitive financial, payroll, and HR data, and potentially pivot to other systems within the network, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or full infrastructure compromise.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable Oracle EBS assets

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable versions of Oracle E-Business Suite, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the newItem view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first

Title: Volt Typhoon Used Covert Silent Train Network in Four Zero-Day Exploitation Campaigns
Context: " Its main purpose is to facilitate critical attack phases like vulnerability exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration, and to maintain continued access to victim...
Full Text:
The China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Volt Typhoon has been attributed to a now-disrupted covert access network dubbed Silent Train that has been put to use for zero-day exploitation and strategic access.

"First identified in late 2023, Silent Train uses rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise infrastructure," Lumen Technologies Black Lotus Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It employs anti-forensic techniques, compartmentalized operations, and post-operation cleanup to minimize detection and attribution."

Its main purpose is to facilitate critical attack phases like vulnerability exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration, and to maintain continued access to victim environments. The activity stands out for two main reasons -

It singled out entities that could provide scalable access to downstream customers, sensitive networks, or strategic programs.

It targeted endpoint management platforms, network management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators, and control plane technologies that play a crucial role within enterprise environments.

Hundreds of victims have been identified across telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms, and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, and emergency services.

Volt Typhoon (aka Bronze Silhouette, Insidious Taurus, UNC3236, Vanguard Panda, and Voltzite) is the moniker assigned to a China-linked state-sponsored group known for its targeting of critical infrastructure networks, particularly communications, energy, transportation, and water and wastewater systems sectors.

Known to be active since at least 2021, the threat actor was previously observed exploiting a file upload vulnerability in Versa Director as a zero-day (CVE-2024-39717) to deliver a bespoke web shell called VersaMem designed to harvest credentials and enable access to downstream customers.

Silent Train session chains through multiple non-U.S. and U.S. hops

The latest findings from Black Lotus Labs show that the security flaw was one among four confirmed zero-day campaigns the threat actor has conducted through Silent Train. The remaining three vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 - A set of insecure deserialization and command injection vulnerabilities in N-able N-central

CVE-2026-20127 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller

CVE-2026-16812 - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator

Separately, Volt Typhoon is also suspected to have taken advantage of a likely zero-day vulnerability in Quest KACE before it was patched in October 2025. The campaign is estimated to have impacted more than 30 victims.

"Silent Train is built around rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise devices that are exploited on demand, used against carefully selected targets, cleaned up after each operation, and continuously refreshed," Black Lotus Labs said.

"This model has enabled Volt Typhoon to conduct exploitation and post-exploitation operations with exceptional operational security while minimizing opportunities for detection, attribution, and disruption."

A defining characteristic of these attacks is the repeated targeting of systems that can open the door to broad visibility, control, and access across large enterprise environments of strategic value to the U.S.

What's interesting is that the covert access capability began to take shape sometime around November 2023, just weeks before the first round of disruption targeting KV-botnet, an IoT botnet linked to multiple China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors, including Volt Typhoon.

Silent Train's operational activity is said to have surged in the wake of the botnet's second disruption in late January 2024, while simultaneously shifting to an ephemeral infrastructure comprising diverse device types and across geographies.

"Rather than continue using persistent infrastructure, Volt Typhoon shifted to a model using one-time-use chains of compromised devices that it could rebuild as needed," Black Lotus Labs said. "Volt Typhoon rapidly assembled and dismantled transient infrastructure, creating a resilient, secure, and compartmentalized framework that protected valuable access."

Sector distribution of organizations targeted through Silent Train

Described as a "layered, multi-hop framework," Silent Train is designed to let Volt Typhoon operators relay malicious traffic through several devices before it reaches the targets so as to obscure its origins from both victims and defenders. Each link in the chain serves a specific purpose -

Virtual private servers (VPS) that function as a temporary staging area and allow threat actors to provision and discard them after each session. The sessions begin from VPS infrastructure located outside the U.S.

Compromised non-U.S. SOHO and IoT devices located across different countries, providers, and hardware that conceal the starting point of the attack.

U.S.-based compromised devices that function as an exit node before reaching the domestic victim and help evade geofencing and IP reputation blocklists.

No less than 27 device classes, ranging from SOHO and IoT devices (e.g., TP-Link, Intelbras, Ruckus Wireless, SATO, NETGEAR, Zyxel, and Cambium) to enterprise platforms (e.g., Fortinet, Cisco, PRTG, Mirth Connect, and CyberPanel), have been exploited and enrolled into the covert network.

"Silent Train stands out for its operational discipline, focusing on short-lived, selfmanaged sessions rather than persistent relays or C2 infrastructure," Black Lotus Labs said. "To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node."

"This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and 'live off the land' utilities. At the end of operational sessions, they removed every artifact and dismantled the operational chain in their wake. Silent Train sessions lasted about four hours on average, with some lasting only minutes."

Another notable aspect is the designation of certain device types to specific positions within Silent Train. For instance, Intelbras modems have been found to only appear as relay nodes, while Netgear Orbi and Fortinet FortiGate appliances served as U.S.-based intermediary and exit points responsible for interacting with the victim.

Put differently, the infrastructure points to deliberate compartmentalization across layers, confining some device types to certain roles that remain constant while the underlying infrastructure itself changes over time so as to complicate attribution efforts.

By early 2025, however, Silent Train is believed to have evolved from a completely ephemeral relay network to a hybrid architecture that retained enterprise-grade devices for an average of one to three months instead of changing them after each engagement.

Subsequent maturation of the platform introduced reverse-tunnel variants that used open-source proxies like Chisel and FRP to send traffic from infected devices to upstream infrastructure.

Within the U.S., Hawaii, California, and Texas have emerged as the focus areas of Silent Train operations, which boils down to the fact that these states host major military installations, telecommunications infrastructure, defense contractors, satellite communications providers, and critical logistics networks.

"Victimology indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region," Black Lotus Labs said.

"The resulting picture is one of a highly structured framework built to acquire, protect, and sustain strategic access at scale. Through repeated targeting of centralized management platforms and control plane technologies, Silent Train shows how Volt Typhoon systematically pursues and preserves access to some of the most consequential networks in the United States."

Title: CVE-2026-111497: Node2Shell / HTTP2Shell Vulnerability May Allow RCE
Context: ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below
Full Text: IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project disclosed CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. The vulnerability is also known as Node2Shell and more recently as HTTP2Shell. The CVE score, filed by Google as the numbering authority, is 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. The flaw can be triggered when a vulnerable process decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. Successful exploitation may result in process crashes, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution (RCE). Imperva reported demonstrating code execution in fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with multiple attempts required in its test environment. The vulnerable Brotli decoder may be present in a range of runtimes, libraries, and software packages, including Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli bindings, .NET, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Java brotli4j, libbrotli, curl/libcurl through Brotli dependencies, and Linux distribution packages. Applications may be exposed if they decompress attacker-controlled data using a vulnerable decoder. The vulnerability may be reachable through both inbound and outbound traffic paths. A malicious client could send a crafted request with Content-Encoding: br to a vulnerable server-side component that performs Brotli request decompression. Conversely, a malicious or compromised server could return a crafted Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable client application that automatically decodes Brotli responses. ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below. RecommendationsZscaler recommends the following measures to address CVE-2026-111497 and monitor for potentially related activity:Patch vulnerable runtimes and libraries. Upgrade vulnerable runtimes, packages, and infrastructure components to the patched versions listed in the Vulnerable Versions table. Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli data, including internet-facing applications that accept compressed request bodies and services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs. Validate each vulnerable component independently. Updating the system-wide libbrotli package may not remediate applications that statically bundle Brotli or ship their own decoder copy.Rebuild and redeploy containers. Use patched base images, runtimes, and libraries, and verify the versions in running workloads. Updating a host’s libraries does not update copies bundled within container images.Disable Brotli decoding where patching is delayed. If immediate patching is not possible, disable Brotli decompression on vulnerable paths where supported, following vendor guidance and testing for application compatibility.Monitor for exploitation and post-exploitation behavior. Investigate the following: Unexpected process crashes in Node.js, Bun, Python, .NET, Envoy Proxy, or service mesh workloads.Repeated malformed Brotli payloads.Requests containing Content-Encoding: br to endpoints that normally do not receive compressed request bodies.Abnormal memory access violations or segmentation faults.Web server or application worker crashes after compressed request handling.Unexpected child processes spawned by web application runtimes.Unexpected outbound connections following crashes or the processing of malformed compressed input. Vulnerable VersionsThe following table lists vulnerable versions and corresponding fixes for selected software that incorporates the Brotli decoder. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving CVE-2026-111497 through Zscaler Deception. Within the first 24 hours following public disclosure, Zscaler Deception’s global decoy mesh observed activity from 20 source IP addresses targeting 12 customers across 402 events. Of these events, 40% involved reconnaissance and 60% involved exploitation attempts. The table below summarizes the unique payloads associated with reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497 observed through Zscaler Deception.Payload DescriptionJA4 FingerprintMalformed Brotli stream headers + valid Brotli differential check + Node.js path recont13d4312h1_c7886603b240_b26ce05bbdd6Truncated JSON Brotli + 8-byte invalid Brotli padding stream + uncompressed controlsNone22-byte & 23-byte invalid block-switch OOB-write seeds (CVE-2026-111497)t13d251100_b78ed14e2fd0_ab7e3b40a677Brotli decompression bomb / Celery stream probe + 1B controlsNoneAssetnote 1-byte malformed/valid Brotli differential checkMultiple observed3-stage Node2Shell capability, Strapi & CVE-2026-111497 JSON parser probet13d521100_b262b3658495_8e6e362c5eac14-byte Brotli {"ping":1} differential sweept13d1714h1_ab0a1bf427ad_5e078a691127Table 2: Unique payloads observed during reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497. How It WorksBrotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It is used for HTTP compression to reduce the size of web content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and API responses. Brotli-encoded HTTP content is identified by the Content-Encoding: br header.Applications may use Brotli directly or through dependencies such as runtimes, frameworks, HTTP clients, and middleware. In some configurations, these components automatically decompress Brotli-encoded content without application code explicitly calling Brotli APIs.Vulnerability detailsThe flaw occurs in Brotli’s block-decoding logic. When a stream changes block type, the decoder determines the next block type and length. In vulnerable versions, there is a macro (in the fast-path logic) that does not properly check the return value of the DecodeBlockTypeAndLength function, which can cause the decoder to continue processing an invalid state (e.g., when provided a maliciously crafted Brotli stream). This can lead to an out-of-bounds write and be used as a primitive for RCE. The upstream fix modifies the decoder so malformed block-switch conditions return a distinct error that is propagated to the caller, stopping further decoding of the malicious Brotli stream.Attack chainExploitation of CVE-2026-111497 may follow either an inbound or outbound path, depending on where Brotli decompression occurs, as shown in the figure below. Inbound attempts use crafted Brotli-compressed HTTP request bodies while outbound attempts use crafted responses returned by an attacker-controlled or compromised server. These responses may be consumed through fetch(), webhook delivery, URL previews, crawlers or scrapers, and API integrations. In either path, exploitation requires attacker-controlled Brotli data to reach a vulnerable decoder, with compressed HTTP content marked by Content-Encoding: br. Figure 1: Potential inbound and outbound exploitation paths for CVE-2026-111497. ConclusionCVE-2026-111497 affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. Exposure depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled Brotli data to a vulnerable decoder. Organizations should identify vulnerable components and apply corresponding vendor updates, including updates for applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli.Zscaler Deception has observed active reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving this vulnerability.
