Title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

Title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
Context: There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially...
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.

So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

Title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943)
Context: Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users
Full Text:
Executive Summary

A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111943.

The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported recovering the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates after discovering that the underlying cryptographic keys contained only a fraction of the expected entropy. Browser and OS vendors have since blocked the certificates, and eMudhra has revoked them. Security teams now face an immediate question: Where do certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates exist within my environment?

Qualys VMDR and Qualys Certificate View already collect the data needed to answer that. This post explains how to use them, with QQL queries you can run today.

What is eMudhra?

eMudhra, a digital trust and cybersecurity provider, offers solutions spanning Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, identity management, and secure digital transactions. Recent security concerns involving eight of its intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates highlight the importance of strong cryptographic key generation, rigorous validation, and continuous oversight of digital trust infrastructure. The incident reinforces a critical security lesson: trust in digital certificates depends not just on the technology, but on the operational controls protecting the keys behind them.

What Happened

A flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process produced a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step, and those weak keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw reduced the effective entropy of the affected P-384 keys to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute.

The weak keys came from a key generation ceremony held on April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. Anyone holding the private key of one of these intermediates could issue a certificate that impersonates any website or service, subject to each client’s validation controls. Some key points about the incident:

Six of the eight intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs.

Browsers: Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have blocked the TLS certificates, and Microsoft has blocked the two code-signing certificates.

Root distrust: Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from the Chrome Root Store, and Mozilla removed trust in the root that signed the intermediates.

eMudhra: has revoked the eight certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. It states that its root CA private keys and other intermediate CAs are not affected, and that the issue is limited to its global website-security business, not Indian DSC and eSign services.

Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users.

Who is at Most Risk?

Organizations should prioritize investigation if they:

Operate internet-facing websites, APIs, VPNs, or other TLS-enabled services.

Use publicly trusted certificates issued through eMudhra or emSign trust hierarchies.

Distribute signed software that relies on publicly trusted code-signing certificates.

Develop or run applications built on the Go programming language.

Maintain legacy systems, unmanaged endpoints, or custom trust stores that may not receive certificate distrust updates automatically.

How Can Qualys VMDR and Certificate View Help Identify eMudhra Certificates?

Use Certificate View, included with VMDR, to identify certificates issued by affected eMudhra authorities and use VMDR with Cloud Agent to identify hosts running vulnerable Go installations or software requiring vendor-issued updates.

Step 1: Make Sure Coverage Is Complete

Entitle Certificate View on your VMDR scan ranges. Confirm that the IP ranges you scan with VMDR are enabled in Certificate View.

Add external domains. For sites hosted by web or app providers, add the FQDNs or IP addresses in Certificate View. It runs a lightweight scan across standard ports to detect TLS services and analyze their certificates.

Use Cloud Agent where scans cannot reach. Agents report software and certificate data from endpoints, servers, and remote workers that network scans miss.

Step 2: Pinpoint the Eight Compromised Intermediates

To confirm whether any of the eight compromised intermediates appear in a chain, search for their SHA-256 fingerprints, serial numbers, or issuer names in Certificate View > Certificates.

Reference QQL Queries

By Issuer:

certificate:(issuer.name:[`EM EV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM EV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV CS CA – G3B`, `EM OV CS CA – G3C`])

By Serial Number:

certificate:(serialNumber:`c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1` or serialNumber:`6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568` or serialNumber:`a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214` or serialNumber:`8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109` or serialNumber:`296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504` or serialNumber:`588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321` or serialNumber:`7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a` or serialNumber:`544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6`)

The Information tab shows the fingerprints, serial number, and first and last found dates so that you can compare them with the SHA-256 values in the table.

Step 3: Find Software That Still Trusts the Affected Certificates

Certificates presented by your servers are only half of the exposure. Applications running older Go runtimes may continue to trust certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. VMDR/Cloud Agent can help you find them.

Find Go toolchains to update

Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block certificate chains that contain any of the eight compromised keys (CVE-2026-111943). Qualys has released QID 5019897 for SwCA scanning to detect affected Go versions. Before you scan, confirm your agents have the latest signatures that include this QID, so the new scan picks it up. Then open the Vulnerabilities tab and use the query below to list the impacted assets:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:5019897

Find Additional Vendor-Specific Updates

Qualys has also released QIDs to detect Go vulnerabilities associated with other vendor operating systems.

Title: Obstacles to Weaponizing PHP2Shell Likely Constrain Immediate Widespread Exploitation
Context: Many of the ones CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has analyzed are crash POCs that only prove a vulnerability exists; converting them to a reliable POC exploit capable...
Full Text:
To exploit these vulnerabilities, attackers must adapt the POC exploit for the specific PHP version and application (e.g., WordPress). This adaptation presents a meaningful barrier to would-be threat actors, as it requires the exploit developer to know and use the same versions of Docker containers, packages, and other elements used by targeted applications.

At this time, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has not observed successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities in the wild or within our honeypot environments. Additionally, we have not identified any fully weaponized exploit, or any POC exploit, sufficient to widely achieve applicable exploitation. Despite the attention PHP2Shell is receiving, only testing, probing, and unsuccessful exploitation attempts have been observed at this time.

Threat actors have several viable alternative vulnerabilities capable of achieving unauthenticated RCE against many applications that use PHP reliably and at scale. Many opportunistic threat actors may currently favor proven effective exploits and other attack vectors as they are not able to successfully leverage PHP2Shell in the near term.

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Overview

On October 21, 2026, PHP disclosed CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which affect the following versions:

Earlier than 8.2.35

Earlier than 8.3.36

Earlier than 8.4.27

Earlier than 8.5.12

Preliminary analysis by industry sources and the vendor suggests many older versions, including end-of-life PHP versions, are also impacted by these vulnerabilities and may receive limited patches to fix them.

CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations reproduced a POC exploit achieving RCE with the privileges of the running mod_php or the PHP-FPM worker processes, both of which should be unprivileged in most cases, as dictated by the least privileges principle.

Understanding PHP Workers and Request Handling

A PHP worker is a long-running process that executes PHP requests. Instead of starting a new PHP interpreter for every HTTP request, the server reuses workers to reduce startup overhead. Under normal conditions, request-specific data is initialized when a request begins and released when it ends, while process-level state persists for the worker's lifetime. Consequently, two unrelated requests may be handled sequentially by the same worker. This distinction is critical for cross-request vulnerabilities: Memory left in an inconsistent state by one request may affect a subsequent request only if the request reaches the same persistent worker.

mod_php and PHP-FPM are the two most common PHP deployment and web server integration models. They use different server APIs (SAPIs), which define how the PHP engine receives and processes web requests.

With mod_php, PHP is loaded directly into Apache as a module, and PHP code executes within Apache worker processes.

With PHP-FPM, PHP runs as a separate service composed of a master process and a pool of workers. A web server such as Apache or Nginx forwards requests to these workers using the FastCGI protocol, typically through a Unix socket or a TCP connection.

In both models, workers are reused across multiple requests. This reuse is relevant to vulnerabilities that leave a corrupted or stale state behind for subsequent requests.

During technical analysis of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations identified three distinct flaws that, if exploited, can enable RCE.

CVE-2026-109618 aligns with the partial hashTable insertion flaw, and CVE-2026-109619 aligns with the persistent serialization-context use-after-free and session-global use-after-free flaws.

CVE-2026-109618 Partial HashTable Insertion

PHP uses HashTable structures internally to store collections of key-value pairs, including arrays and HTTP request variables. Each stored entry is represented by a bucket, which contains the value together with information such as the value’s key and type. PHP uses the HashTable’s entry count to determine which buckets contain valid data and must be processed or released.

The vulnerability stems from a memory corruption during HTTP request-variable parsing. If a memory allocation fails while PHP is adding a new HashTable entry, the entry count may be updated before the corresponding bucket is fully initialized. During request shutdown, PHP may then treat this incomplete bucket as valid and attempt to access or release invalid data. This can result in an invalid memory access, memory corruption, or termination of the PHP process, potentially leading to execution of arbitrary code.

CVE-2026-109619: Persistent Serialization-Context Use-After-Free

PHP’s serialize() function converts a PHP value, such as an array or object, into an encoded string that can be stored or transmitted. The corresponding unserialize() function reconstructs the original PHP value from that string. While these operations are running, PHP maintains an internal serialization context to track objects, references, and recursive data structures.

zend_bailout(), PHP’s internal emergency mechanism for stopping execution after a fatal error, immediately transfers control to a recovery point, so normal function returns and cleanup code may be skipped unless they are handled explicitly.

PHP contains a cross-request use-after-free vulnerability in its serialization-context handling. If a fatal error causes zend_bailout() to interrupt serialize() or unserialize(), PHP may leave the internal context pointing to memory owned by the current request. That memory is released when the request ends, but the PHP worker may remain alive and retain the stale pointer. A later request handled by the same worker may then access or modify the released memory. Based on the configuration, successful exploitation may allow an attacker to disclose memory, crash the PHP worker, or execute arbitrary code.

CVE-2026-109619: Session-Global Use-After-Free

PHP’s session upload-progress feature allows an application to monitor a file upload’s progress. When enabled, PHP detects a specific field in a multipart or form-data request and creates a temporary progress record in the user’s session before the PHP script begins executing. As upload data arrives, PHP periodically opens the session, updates the number of processed bytes, writes the session data, and releases the session lock. When the upload finishes or is cancelled, PHP removes the progress record and clears the related internal state.

PHP contains a cross-request use-after-free vulnerability in the session upload-progress life cycle. If a fatal error interrupts multipart request processing before upload-progress cleanup finishes, PHP may skip the code that normally closes the session and clears its internal state. The current request’s memory is then released, but the persistent PHP worker may still retain pointers to that memory. A later request handled by the same worker may access or modify the released memory.

Depending on the configuration, successful exploitation may cause memory disclosure or corruption, crash the PHP worker, leave a session lock permanently held, or make the affected service unavailable.

Assessment

Exploit developers are unlikely to create a single universal exploit that works reliably across all affected PHP deployments. The creation of a POC exploit capable of reliable remote exploitation is feasible, however, against specific deployment profiles, such as a fixed Docker image or a known combination of PHP, libc, SAPI, and web application versions. For such cases, an attacker can calibrate exploit offsets and heap grooming in advance, producing an exploit that reliably applies to any system running that same unmodified package or image release.

In the short to long term, advanced threat actors will likely attempt to exploit this vulnerability against high-value targets where alternative exploitation methods are less feasible. However, if a public exploit overcoming the aforementioned exploitation challenges becomes available for a widely used PHP deployment, many additional threat actors will almost certainly seek to leverage it immediately.

The widespread media and industry attention surrounding this vulnerability will almost certainly incentivize both threat actors and security researchers to discover additional PHP vulnerabilities in the short to long term.

Although threat actors have not yet successfully exploited PHP2Shell, the rapid speed with which they attempted to weaponize these vulnerabilities highlights how swiftly attackers integrate new exploits into their operational capabilities, frequently aided by public research from industry sources. This trend, combined with the recurring pattern of vulnerability discovery, rediscovery, and patch circumvention, which is currently accelerated by AI-assisted vulnerability research, underscores the critical necessity for organizations to remain vigilant in patching and hardening their environments against emerging threats.

Recommendations

These recommendations can be implemented to help protect against the activity described in this report:

Patch all applications using PHP to the latest version as soon as possible, prioritizing the patching of internet-facing applications

Rebuild container images and restart all Apache and PHP-FPM workers after deployment to remove any stale process state

Disable session upload progress (via session.upload_progress.enabled = Off) unless explicitly required; this blocks the upload-progress paths associated with the serialization-context and session-global use-after-free conditions, but does not mitigate the HashTable vulnerability

Disable file uploads (via file_uploads = Off) where they are not needed; apply this per application or PHP pool whenever possible to avoid unnecessary functional impact

Limit request bodies before they reach PHP; configure Apache, NGINX, a reverse proxy, or a WAF to restrict body size, upload size, upload duration, parameter-name length, nesting depth, and the number of form fields, and eject unusually large URL-encoded keys and malformed or abnormal multipart requests

Run each PHP application under a separate, minimally privileged account and prevent PHP workers from modifying application code or accessing unrelated secrets

Title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 2: Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Cloud Context
Context: For example: SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active...
Full Text:
In Part 1, we established how to centralize your AppSec tools, correlate assets, and map scanner coverage across repositories. Establishing visibility is an essential baseline, but once your connectors start streaming data into a single location, prioritization becomes the primary focus.

As highlighted in our recent State of SDLC Security 2026 report, AI’s primary impact isn't necessarily introducing entirely new risks. It's the amplification of existing ones through faster code generation, contributing to a wider attack surface area with less time for human review.

For lean AppSec teams, the real promise of ASPM lies in how it helps prioritize application risk across their enterprise. But, as we saw with the React2Shell example, prioritization requires context across the entire application lifecycle. AppSec teams must quickly distinguish between theoretical code flaws sitting on un-deployed branches and active vulnerabilities running on internet-facing workloads.

To transform raw scanner output into actionable risk, Wiz Code executes prioritization across two distinct layers:

Finding-level prioritization: Normalizing scanner data into unified schemas, actively enriching findings with threat intelligence and network reachability, and deduplicating identical alerts across overlapping tools.

Attack path prioritization: Using the Wiz Security Graph to connect code-level findings with live cloud runtime context, elevating isolated flaws into fully validated attack paths.

Let’s look at how to operationalize both layers in your environment.

Enrich, Deduplicate, and Prioritize Individual Findings

Findings from connected scanners populate into their respective domains in the Wiz platform. For example, SAST results flow into the SAST Findings tab, SCA results populate in the Vulnerability Findings tab, and Secret results show up in the Secret Findings page. You can easily filter any table by “origin” to isolate alerts from a specific tool. In the example below, we’re filtering vulnerability findings surfaced from a Snyk SCA scan.

From this unified baseline, Wiz executes multiple layers of prioritization to help AppSec teams focus on what matters.

Enrichment

Imported findings are enriched with domain specific context, turning generic alerts into prioritized findings. For example:

SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active exploit availability, and CISA KEV status. Our Threat Research team also denotes findings with active threats and writes complete advisories, so security teams have the latest insight on zero days.

SAST: CWE findings include code snippets so security teams have visibility into the location and context of weaknesses.

DAST: Wiz independently validates network exposure for the web applications with DAST findings using the Attack Surface Management (ASM) module. The ASM engine can be configured to run other checks such as secrets or sensitive data exposure checks from the perimeter on these newly created endpoints. Private-only addresses are marked differently so teams can prioritize findings with a real external attack surface.

Secrets: Wiz runs ingested secrets through databases to see if the secret was leaked, classifies secret types for understanding its impact, and assigns severities to the detected secrets based on threat research if the originating scanner did not provide any.

Deduplication

Security teams should not waste time chasing down multiple vulnerability findings for the exact same issue. When multiple tools scan the same codebase and produce duplicative vulnerability findings, Wiz can easily reconcile them.

Wiz labels one finding as "Representative" and the duplicates as "Duplicate." Teams can apply automated Ignore Rules scoped to duplicate findings, instantly eliminating redundant noise in reporting without losing the underlying scanner audit trail. So instead of generating individual tickets for each finding, teams can create one ticket to consolidate the findings.

Prioritize Exploitable Attack Paths

Traditionally ASPM has focused on aggregating findings and prioritizing risk using simple scoring. Wiz takes a different approach by correlating findings with additional risk on the Wiz Security Graph. This is where the platform moves from managing vulnerabilities to managing exploitable attack paths.

The Wiz Security Graph correlates multiple risk factors into a single Wiz Issue (identifying toxic combinations of risk). Critically, these controls run on your third-party findings exactly the same way they run on native Wiz findings. If you connect a scanner, its data instantly becomes part of your code-to-cloud attack path analysis.

What this looks like in practice

Let's look at how this context transforms a standard alert into a prioritized Wiz Issue. Imagine your Snyk integration flags a high-severity SAST finding (such as a remote code execution or command injection flaw) on a repository branch. In a vacuum, a developer might treat this as an urgent priority, or they might ignore it if they assume it is an internal tool.

The Wiz Security Graph evaluates the entire deployment lifecycle to uncover the actual risk. A single Wiz Issue might reveal:

The Code Flaw: A SAST finding from Snyk and a native Wiz SAST finding, both originating on the same repository branch.

The Build Artifact: That specific branch was built into a container image currently running in a production Kubernetes cluster.

The Exposure: The Kubernetes cluster is exposed to the internet via a public application endpoint.

Active Validation: An Attack Surface Management (ASM) finding confirms the endpoint is actively reachable from the outside.

Instead of manually piecing together four separate alerts across three different tools, Wiz draws the connection natively. Because these findings all resolve to the same underlying resource and represent the same attack path, they are surfaced as one unified, high-priority Wiz Issue.

Conversely, if that same SAST flaw was detected on a branch that never ships to a running cloud workload, it remains a low-priority finding—sparing developers from interrupting their sprint for a non-exploitable risk.

Manage security debt at scale

Not every finding may map to an attack path. But, lower-severity findings still represent real risk if left unaddressed. In Wiz, organizations can track and govern these findings through Posture Issues.

AppSec teams can create logical groupings of findings based on several criteria such as severity, project, code repository and more to build tailored campaigns for managing security debt. Teams can also define SLAs for remediation to align with organizational policies.

Up Next: Remediation and Automation at Machine Speed

Separating signal from noise is a massive win, but prioritization without rapid remediation is only half the battle. Once critical attack paths are identified, how do you ensure the right engineering team fixes them without slowing down release cycles?

In Part 3, the final instalment of this series, we’ll explore how to remediate at machine speed. We’ll cover how to leverage the Wiz Green Agent to generate tailored remediation plans in developer workflows and how to automate response with Wiz Workflows.

Title: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
Context: The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack,...
Full Text:
The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.

Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.

But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.

AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.

“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.

Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, tells WIRED that the organization was unaware of AWS's research prior to publication and did not immediately have a comment on the findings. She added, “Although we agree that upgrading is absolutely imperative, to our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution.”

Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”

Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up, given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.

“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”

Updated 10/22/2026 at 10:10 am ET to include comment from the PHP Foundation.

Title: Two critical RCEs in PHP core
Context: Splunk Enterprise Security customers have an Enterprise Security Content Update with detections available
Full Text:
Update 10/22: Added section detailing observations of in the wild exploitation and associated IOCs.

Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed.

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359, 67360, and 67375. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Splunk Enterprise Security customers have an Enterprise Security Content Update with detections available. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information.

Details

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it.

Impact

The potential blast radius is enormous and extends across the PHP ecosystem. The vulnerability sits in PHP core, so applications running affected versions — including WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and Laravel, plus PHP sites hosted through cPanel or Plesk — may be exposed. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible.

Talos regularly investigates threat actor exploitation of vulnerabilities. State-sponsored and affiliated threat actors, as well as ransomware and other financially motivated groups, all employ tactics to exploit RCE. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life (EOL), and PHP 8.2 security support ends Dec. 31, 2026. Talos’ initial estimates based on open-source intelligence show a significant corpus of PHP systems that will not receive a patch (~50%). If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older.

Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these CVEs and has not seen them being exploited in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC/10:00 a.m. ET).

Observed Exploitation

Cisco Talos began observing exploitation attempts within hours of the vulnerabilities’ disclosure. So far, most of the activity is scanning, along with some uncoordinated attempts to deliver various payloads. This is expected: scanning or basic exploitation with public proof-of-concept (PoC) code takes far less effort than integrating a vulnerability into an actor’s own tooling. We expect exploitation volume to grow in the coming days, and campaigns to become more sophisticated and coordinated as more capable groups finish updating their tooling and begin deploying it.

Recommendations and detection guidance

Talos strongly recommends all PHP users to upgrade to the available fixed releases. There are no intermediate or temporary controls that provide comprehensive protection; however, PHP advises that the following measure may reduce exposure to specific attack paths:

CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length.

Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.

Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not help.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing, and cleanup.

This is another vulnerability that owes its discovery to AI and its associated technologies. As we move through 2026, the wave of vulnerabilities and related patches is building. Talos advises organizations to work on a triaged process for prioritizing vulnerabilities with a specific focus on public-facing systems and vulnerabilities that are under active exploitation. The glaring need to prioritize vulnerabilities along with a streamlined process for rolling out patching strongly indicates that the historic trend of “baking in” patches before deployment is not going to survive the AI era.

The true impact of this vulnerability will take time to evaluate. These types of vulnerabilities that impact core technologies tend to cascade into other platforms and applications as they evaluate impact and provide associated patching, harkening back to the waves of exploitation that we saw after Log4J.

Full Text: PHP developers have released emergency updates for two critical vulnerabilities after cybersecurity authorities warned organizations to patch immediately or consider taking exposed applications offline. PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The project's developers urged users to update immediately. All PHP installations serving web requests are potentially affected, including deployments using PHP-FPM, Apache's mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, the developers said. "We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs." Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at watchTowr, said: "As expected, watchTowr Intel is already observing in-the-wild exploitation of the latest PHP vulnerabilities, with a variety of vibecoded PoCs already hitting our sensors featuring a variety of 'php2shell' User-Agents. Whilst nobody has been successful to date, we don't expect that will last long." "Where immediate patching is not feasible, organizations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available," CERT-EU said in an advisory issued ahead of the patches. The body lists both vulnerabilities with CVSS scores of 9.2. Finnish government services and websites belonging to the Dutch parliament, cybersecurity authorities, and data protection regulator were taken offline as a precaution. Privacy campaign group noyb also temporarily withdrew its website. PHP "powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," infosec vendor Huntress noted. That makes identifying exposed installations a substantial job. "The number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast," said John Hammond, Huntress's senior principal security researcher. ®

Title: “Next Exploit Opportunities”: How a Threat Actor Used AI to Help Plan and Execute Multiple Types of Cybercrime Activities
Context: Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

“Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing [sic],” the threat actor typed. The conversation was with one of several AI assistants that the actor was using to get advice on planning and executing a variety of cybercrime activities.

Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks across multiple campaign types.

Unit 42’s investigation into the actor’s operational environment and activities makes two things clear:

The attacker used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, suggesting they didn’t have the skills these activities would have required before the advent of readily available AI tools.

Despite some apparent bumbling, the actor had an impact, attacking a number of targets in India, including universities. The actor recovered thousands of records revealing personal information and mapped multiple organizations’ attack surfaces.

The attacker’s conversations with jailbroken AI tools included getting step by step advice on how to set up a fraudulent Voice over IP (VoIP) operation. One assistant “helpfully” generated a document including a “NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES” section, outlining planned followup attacks.

Unit 42 identified and investigated this threat actor's operational environment. There, we determined that they had weaponized an AI assistant across several types of cybercrime, including:

Credential theft and data exfiltration

VoIP telecommunications fraud

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

Command-and-control (C2) operations

An actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) as a secondary tool, both with safety controls disabled. The actor ran an AI-generated brute-force campaign against an Indian university’s website. The actor also achieved a confirmed intrusion against a second university, where they exfiltrated a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students.

The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders). Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Multiple, unrelated actors are independently adopting the same Hermes + DeepSeek combination. This suggests we may be witnessing an increasingly prevalent toolchain of choice for cybercriminals adopting AI-enabled capabilities. We assess a key driver is low safety friction at low cost: DeepSeek models are inexpensive and easy to access, and readily jailbroken with a simple system-prompt override.

Technical Analysis

We identified evidence that the threat actor leveraged AI systems for a wide range of criminal activity against multiple target networks, primarily in India. The criminal activity included:

Planning for VoIP fraud

Credential theft targeting several organizations

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

C2 payloads

Credential Theft and Data Exfiltration

WordPress Brute Force

The actor used AI-generated reconnaissance to conduct a methodical attack against an Indian university's online education platform. The actor’s enumeration reports exhibit structured formatting (executive summaries, severity ratings, systematic endpoint categorization) consistent with AI-generated output. The attack progressed through four stages:

Subdomain enumeration: The actor identified 12 subdomains including the main WordPress site, a learning management system (LMS), student portal and administration dashboard

WordPress REST API enumeration: The actor extracted 13 active user IDs with real names via post author fields and author sitemaps, bypassing the Cloudflare Web Application Firewall (WAF) that blocked direct user endpoint access

Targeted brute force: A generator script produced a brute force tool with 117 usernames (derived from the enumeration) and 28 common passwords

Credential brute force: The actor’s tool flagged one WordPress login as valid

University Database Exfiltration

The actor exfiltrated a MongoDB database from a second Indian public university. The exfiltration tooling wrote a manifest alongside the dumped collections, recording the following data:

Admin credential obtained: An administrator account with a weak password

Exfiltrated records: Thousands of student records (diploma, undergraduate, postgraduate) and faculty records containing PII

Infrastructure exposed: Cloud load balancing, edge routing, database services, and a third-party cloud storage service account

E-Commerce Enumeration

The actor enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform, extracting:

A storefront API token

Three admin email addresses

Two phone numbers

Payment merchant IDs

The attack report is a suspected large language model (LLM)-generated document, including a NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES section outlining planned follow-up attacks.

VoIP Telecommunications Fraud

We also identified evidence that the actor was developing VoIP (Voice over IP) fraud infrastructure, using the alice Hermes profile as an AI-powered advisor. Evidence included:

A detailed technical knowledge base

Carrier research

However, the absence of call logs, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) traces or active call routing suggested the operation was still in a planning or early setup phase.

With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, alice provided detailed, actionable criminal methodology through conversations and a comprehensive fraud knowledge base ingested into the bot. The actor developed a planned approach following an established VoIP fraud model:

Establish a legitimate front: Register a US limited liability company (LLC) with an employer identification number (EIN) to qualify as a telecommunications provider. The knowledge base includes detailed guidance on:

Forming LLCs in Wyoming or Delaware as a non-US resident

Obtaining an EIN without a Social Security number via the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) fax

Completing Federal Communications Commission (FCC) registration

Obtain carrier access: Contract with legitimate VoIP carriers to purchase call routing capacity (SIP trunks).

Traffic mixing: Route approximately 70% legitimate call traffic alongside 30% fraudulent calls to stay below carrier compliance audit thresholds.

Bypass caller ID authentication: Circumvent STIR/SHAKEN, the FCC-mandated caller identity verification framework. In the advisory conversations, alice covers bypass techniques and Calling Line Identification (CLI) spoofing.

Monetize: Generate revenue with the 30% fraudulent traffic through toll fraud and other non-compliant routes. Least-cost routing (LCR) optimizes per-minute costs across carrier tiers.

Other Operations

Command and Control

The threat actor’s infrastructure maintained a listening port for a Python-based C2 listener supporting Windows reverse shell connections. Supporting payloads include:

A Base64-encoded PowerShell reverse shell delivered via VBScript

A QubesOS VM setup script with SSH and ncat

Multiple Windows shell variants

Wi-Fi Password Cracking

The actor developed an automated Wi-Fi password cracking process. A Linux (Kali) device the actor labeled Pi placed within range of target Wi-Fi networks captured Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) authentication material (PMKID or EAPOL handshakes) from nearby access points.

The server collected these hashes over an SSH tunnel and dispatched them to Vast.ai cloud GPU instances for cracking, with results automatically reported back to the actor via Discord webhooks. This technique requires physical proximity to the target networks, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Credential Scanning Toolkit

We also identified a large Go-based credential-scanning toolkit. This toolkit scrapes webpages and extracts exposed credentials, including:

.env values

S3 signed URLs

Google Cloud service account keys

Content delivery network (CDN) API keys

Private keys in log files

A companion Python script scrapes domain lists for scanning.

Cryptocurrency Reconnaissance

The actor scraped the top 500 ETH holders and major token holders via the DeBank API, producing intelligence files that documented 45 cryptocurrency whales with net worth figures. We assess this was likely for future targeting, but we were unable to identify any follow-on activity during this research.

Tool Design and Infrastructure

The threat actor used a single US-based server (162.243.3[.]92) to host multiple core services, including:

The Hermes Agent framework

A C2 listener

A Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) proxy

Several supporting components

Our analysis of the actor’s logs and test scripts indicates that they experimented with various LLMs, including GLM 5.2 by Zhipu AI and other models accessed through OpenRouter. Ultimately, they chose DeepSeek V4 as the backend for operations.

The actor's test scripts show repeated attempts to defeat model safety controls with a prompt-level override. Although GLM 5.2 is an open-weight model that has been reported as weakly guarded, the actor built a dedicated script to send the override to GLM 5.2 and flag refusals. This is evidence of resistance the actor worked to overcome.

The actor ultimately operationalized DeepSeek V4, consistent with the minimal safety controls observed in the Chinese-speaking activity we previously reported. Conclusion

This case illustrates how AI lowers the skill barrier for cybercrime. The actor used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, but still achieved notable impact. They recovered more than 5,200 PII records and mapped multiple organizations' attack surfaces. AI enabled a single actor to operate across diverse attack types (credential theft, VoIP fraud, Wi-Fi cracking, cryptocurrency targeting) that would traditionally require distinct skill sets.

The VoIP fraud planning demonstrates a particularly notable use of AI as a domain expert. With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, the actor's bot profiles provided detailed, actionable criminal guidance.

This guidance included specific fraud-to-clean traffic ratios, carrier audit thresholds to stay below and operational security measures to avoid detection. The model's minimal safety controls allowed it to function as an on-demand criminal advisor, enabling the actor to acquire operational expertise through conversation rather than experience.
