Title: The Science of Exploitability: Decoding BlueHammer
Context: Exploitation depends on a reachable vulnerable path, the privileges an attacker starts with, the available services and components, and the system’s current state
Full Text:
Executive Summary

BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825) is an eight-stage local privilege-escalation chain targeting the Windows Defender Antimalware Platform before 4.18.26030.3011. It does not grant initial access; an attacker needs standard-user code execution first. Still, in the lab, it reached NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, recovered domain-admin credentials from LSASS, and moved laterally via pass-the-hash. This is not memory corruption. It chains CloudFilter callbacks, batch oplocks, object-manager symlinks, Defender’s update RPC, offline SAM parsing, and SAMR. Crucially, affected is not the same as exploitable: runtime factors — pending signature update, WinDefend state, filter drivers, VSS, CloudFilter reachability decide whether the path works on a given host. That’s the gap version-based scanning can’t close. Qualys TruConfirm marks a host Exploit Validated only after environmental checks, plus a non-destructive BAS validation of the CloudFilter freeze (Stages 2–3), no SAM extraction, no password reset, no service creation, no SYSTEM shell.

Introduction and Execution Flow

A CVE tells you what could go wrong. It does not tell you whether an attacker can actually make it happen on your machine. Exploitation depends on a reachable vulnerable path, the privileges an attacker starts with, the available services and components, and the system’s current state. Exploitability analysis brings these signals together to answer a practical question: can this vulnerability be exploited on this machine right now?

BlueHammer provides a concrete case study. Windows Defender is an always-running, highly privileged component whose filter drivers, RPC interfaces, scanning engine, and update mechanisms operate with SYSTEM authority. Publicly tracked as CVE-2026-33825, BlueHammer combines these trusted components in an eight-stage local privilege-escalation chain. Microsoft identifies Defender Antimalware Platform versions earlier than 4.18.26030.3011 as affected; our reverse-engineering host ran version 4.18.2104.10.

BlueHammer does not provide initial access. An attacker must first obtain code execution as a standard user, potentially through phishing, malicious content, or abuse of valid accounts. In our lab, the exploit abused Defender’s privileged update and file-handling paths to obtain NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. From that shell, we recovered credential material for CITRIX\administrator that was already present in LSASS. Using pass-the-hash, we authenticated to the domain controller as CITRIX\administrator, and then accessed protected system locations, started services, and extracted NTDS.dit. This demonstrated the tested path from a user-level foothold to verified domain-administrator control.

The complete tested attack path, along with its potential follow-on impact, is as follows:

Initial Access → BlueHammer Execution → Local SYSTEM → LSASS Credential Access → Pass-the-Hash → Domain Controller Access as CITRIX\administrator → Domain Compromise → Potential Follow-on Activity (not performed)

BlueHammer does not depend on memory corruption. Instead, it integrates several components, including cloud files, callbacks, opportunistic locks, object-manager symbolic links, Defender’s local update RPC interface, offline registry parsing, and SAMR operations, with each stage preparing the next. We reconstructed the chain by reverse-engineering the original FunnyApp.exe binary in IDA Pro and tracing it in x64dbg. The subsequent sections explain the eight stages, the verified post-exploitation path, and how Qualys TruConfirm safely validates vulnerable customer environments before an attacker reaches the destructive stages.

Test environment used for this analysis:

PoC binary: FunnyApp.exe (SHA-256 : f4ffef4204880031a6a532ff5c1b5686e6a301c365f492071c1d462fa5b6b4a0)

Host: DESKTOP38, Windows 11 Pro 21H2, OS build 22000.2295

Defender platform: 4.18.2104.10 | Engine: 1.1.17300.4 | Security intelligence: 1.321.69.0

Real-time protection: enabled

This article discusses two distinct test contexts. Reverse engineering and end-to-end debugging were performed on DESKTOP38 using the original, unmodified FunnyApp.exe PoC whose SHA-256 is listed above. The TruConfirm’s evidence presented later was collected from the validation asset BlackHat2-CVE-2026-33825, which utilized a modified, non-destructive PoC. This validation process stops before any actions such as: SAM extraction, password modification, service creation, credential recovery, or shell execution.

Figure 1: BlueHammer’s eight-stage execution flow, from Windows Update precheck to interactive SYSTEM shell.

Exploit Reasoning

BlueHammer’s approach to determining exploitability is tailored to each host. While identifying an affected version of Defender indicates a vulnerability, it does not guarantee that the vulnerable path is reachable or that the complete exploit chain can execute successfully. The effectiveness of the exploit is influenced by runtime and environmental factors, which may vary across similar endpoints.

The analysis begins by considering the attacker’s perspective, especially their ability to execute code as a standard user. Several critical factors are assessed, including the Defender platform version, the status of WinDefend and its real-time protection, the presence of necessary filter drivers, the availability of Volume Shadow Copy, and the existence of pending updates to Defender signatures. It also checks whether the CloudFilter and Defender update paths are reachable based on the current privilege level.

In the case assessed, the Defender platform version 4.18.2104.10 was found to meet all required conditions. The original PoC demonstrated that it completed all eight stages of the exploit, gaining a SYSTEM shell, recovering domain-administrator credentials from LSASS, and authenticating to the domain controller via pass-the-hash. This confirmed not only that the host was running an affected version but also that the entire exploit process worked correctly within its actual configuration and system state.

On the other hand, TruConfirm adopts a proactive strategy in customer environments. It initiates the process by verifying that all required environmental factors are in place. Following this, it employs a modified Qualys Breach and Attack Simulation workflow to replicate only the non-destructive aspects of the exploit. This step is crucial for confirming the accessibility of the critical CloudFilter primitive. The validation process focuses on the relevant behaviors from Stages 2 and 3, ensuring the Defender freeze and a clean Defender release. It does not perform potentially harmful actions such as extracting SAM data, resetting passwords, creating a service, recovering credentials, obtaining a SYSTEM shell, or reproducing the domain-compromise path demonstrated in the original PoC. An endpoint is designated as “Exploit Validated” only when it successfully passes environmental checks and validation. This thorough approach yields stronger, host-specific evidence than relying solely on version detection, all while avoiding the execution of destructive and post-exploitation phases of the original PoC.

Stage 0 — Windows Update Precheck

The exploit begins by querying the standard Microsoft.Update.Session COM interface to determine whether a Defender signature update is pending. It specifically filters Windows Update (WU) results by the category ID E0789628-CE08-4437-BE74-2495B842F43B, which is associated with Definition Updates. This GUID serves as a distinctive identifier within the .rdata section, effectively acting as a hunting signature. If no updates are pending, the exploit will terminate without further action. For the subsequent stages to successfully hijack the update consumption process, a pending update is crucial. Additionally, this initial check serves as a soft-target filter, since systems on aggressive update schedules typically do not retain pending updates long enough for the exploit to be operational.

Stage 1 — Signed Package Download and CAB Extraction

The exploit begins by downloading Microsoft’s signed executable file, mpam-fex64.exe, from fwlink and extracting its embedded CAB payload without saving it to disk. It mimics a Chrome/141.0.0.0 User-Agent in the HTTPS request, which is atypical for a native binary, and reads the response into a buffer via InternetReadFile. Then, GetCabFileFromBuff extracts the CAB payload from the executable by locating its header and creates custom I/O callbacks to handle the file. This results in the extraction of five files: mpasbase: vdm, mpavdlta.vdm, and mpengine.dll. In the exploit, specifically, it replaces the mpasbase.vdm file with a malicious version, while keeping the other four stay byte-identical to the legitimate signed originals. This tactic helps the exploit evade detection by allowing Windows Defender’s update-engine signature checks to pass successfully.

Figure 2: Stage 1 — fwlink download of mpam-fex64.exe and in-memory CAB extraction.

Stage 2 — Oplock Signaling on RstrtMgr.dll

The exploit relies on precise timing to detect when Defender begins scanning a file it has placed on the system. Since there is no official API to achieve this, the exploit cleverly combines two documented methods. It initiates a batch oplock on RstrtMgr.dll, a system DLL frequently accessed during Defender’s scanning process, and subsequently creates an EICAR test file to trigger a scan.

To implement this, the exploit first writes the EICAR file and opens RstrtMgr.dll with the FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED flag. It then requests a batch oplock via a DeviceIoControl call with control code 0x90008. Opening the EICAR file initiates Defender’s real-time scanning. The exploit then uses GetOverlappedResult to wait for Defender’s scanning process to touch RstrtMgr.dll and release the oplock, signaling the start of the scan. In the background, a thread named ShadowCopyFinderThread monitors the NT object namespace for any VSS snapshots that Defender may create during its scans. As Defender often uses shadow copies, the exploit captures its path for later use. In the context of an exploit, when a specific condition arises, the exploit captures the path of the VSS copy, typically designated at \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopyN. This captured path is then stored for later use in Stage 6 of the exploit. During this stage, the exploit manipulates the process by redirecting Windows Defender’s file access to the system’s Security Account Manager (SAM) file, located at \??\<fullvsspath>\Windows\System32\Config\SAM on the previously captured shadow copy.

To evade detection, the EICAR string is stored in reverse within the binary’s .rdata section and is reversed again at runtime, ensuring the binary does not trigger Defender’s EICAR signature detection. Notably, the 0x90008 FSCTL code, used to establish the oplock, reappears in later stages of the exploit, indicating a strong signal: two independent batch oplocks are present in a single binary.

Figure 3: Stage 2 — TriggerWDForVS: EICAR drop, RstrtMgr.dll oplock, wait for Defender scan.

Stage 3 — Freezing MsMpEng.exe via the CloudFilter Callback

The Stage 3 exploit targets Windows Defender’s scanning engine, MsMpEng.exe, by placing it in a controlled wait state. This manipulation allows the exploit to perform file operations without interference from Defender. The technique leverages the behavior of the Cloud Files subsystem, particularly the CloudFilter minifilter (cldflt.sys), which intentionally blocks a thread in kernel mode while awaiting completion from a user-mode synchronization provider. The intentional wait in the process allows cloud providers, such as OneDrive, to perform network I/O operations necessary to retrieve and prepare a file before delivering its data to the requester. It’s important to note that there is no predefined limit to the duration of this wait.

To implement this strategy, the exploit registers itself as a CloudFilter provider for a sync-root directory it controls and drops a decoy executable named foo.exe in that directory. When the real-time scanner of MsMpEng detects the executable file foo.exe, which is prioritized for scanning by Defender, the driver cldflt.sys activates a callback to fetch placeholders within the process associated with the exploit. At this point, the exploit checks whether the caller’s process ID, CF_PROCESS_INFO, matches the WinDefend service’s process ID obtained via QueryServiceStatusEx. If they match, the callback halts the operation using an event controlled by the exploit’s worker thread. This effectively keeps MsMpEng stalled in the waiting state of cldflt.sys, enabling the exploit to proceed without detection by Windows Defender.

Figure 4: Stage 3 — the \foo.exe decoy filename hard-coded as a wide-string literal in the exploit binary.

Figure 5: Stage 3 — FreezeVSS worker thread: register CloudFilter provider, arm oplock, release callback, freeze confirmed.

The worker thread initiates a batch oplock on a designated lock file in the sync root, then signals the release event. During this process, the callback, which retains control over MsMpEng, invokes the CfExecute function using a placeholder for the lock file. The cldflt.sys component then handles the CfExecute call, accesses the lock file, and breaks the oplock, allowing MsMpEng to continue its operations. The entire cycle sequence occurs within a single CfExecute round-trip, allowing the exploit to perform its Stage 4 | Stage 6 operations without being hindered by Defender.

Figure 6: Stage 3 — CloudFilter callback body: identify MsMpEng as the calling process, then signal the worker thread to arm the release oplock.

MsMpEng.exe operates as a Protected Process Light (PPL) with PsProtectedSignerAntimalware protection, preventing any user-mode observers from attaching debuggers or inspecting its threads. Although Task Manager displays the process as “Running,” it can be misleading, as its main scan thread may be halted within cldflt.sys, and per-thread wait states are not visible to users with limited privileges. While PPL protects the process, exploits can weaponize it. The key action in this context is performed by a single SetEvent instruction, which releases the callback, as illustrated in detail in Figure 7.

Figure 7: Stage 3 — SetEvent pivot instruction (pink) and freeze-confirmation string (blue).

Microsoft has identified Defender Antimalware Platform version 4.18.26030.3011 as the threshold for addressing CVE-2026-33825. Endpoints that operate on this version or any later version are safeguarded against the vulnerable Defender path exploited by BlueHammer, effectively preventing access to Stage 4 of the attack.

Stage 4 — Staging Fake Definition Files

In Stage 4 of the exploit, the attacker prepares update files under their control by creating an NT object manager path structured as \Sessions\<N>\BaseNamedObjects\<GUID>. This path is established using the NtCreateDirectoryObjectEx function. Within this directory, a symbolic link named WDUpdateDirectory is created, pointing to a temporary filesystem location where in-memory update files from Stage 1 are stored. This approach is crucial because, in Stage 6, the attacker will replace the symbolic link without being detected after the Defender has accessed it.

The staged update files are designed to be byte-identical to Microsoft’s original signed versions, except for mpasbase.vdm, which is replaced with a malicious version. The remaining files retain their valid signatures, ensuring that Defender’s signature validation checks continue to succeed. It is important to note that these update files differ from the foo.exe decoy used in Stage 3, which was intended to entice MsMpEng into a CloudFilter callback that would freeze it. Instead, the focus here lies on the genuine signature-update files that Defender will eventually utilize.

Figure 8: Stage 4 — per-session object-manager directory + WDUpdateDirectory symlink setup.

Stage 5 — RPC to Defender’s Update Engine

In Stage 5 of the exploit process, the malicious update files are delivered to Windows Defender via its local update engine through an RPC interface. This interface, specifically the MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI, is typically used for legitimate Defender signature updates and is managed by MsMpEng.exe with assistance from MpSvc.dll.

The exploit creates a worker thread, WDCallerThread that binds to the RPC interface using a specific UUID over the ncalrpc transport. It targets the endpoint designated as IMpService77BDAF73-B396-481F-9042-AD358843EC24 and invokes procedure 42, called ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature. In the compiled exploit binary, the corresponding MIDL-generated stub for this procedure has been streamlined, with the pseudocode reflecting a direct call to the core function.

Notably, the argument provided to this procedure is not a typical filesystem path; instead, it is formatted as an NT object-manager path that leads to a staging directory set up by Stage 4 of the exploit. This path can be represented as \\?\GLOBALROOT\Sessions\<N>\BaseNamedObjects\<GUID>\WDUpdateDirectory. When Defender processes these files, it successfully validates their signatures except for the manipulated mpasbase.vdm, which is disguised as a genuine Microsoft file.

As Defender creates a new SYSTEM-owned copy of the files in a subdirectory of C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Definition Updates\, the exploit actively monitors this directory using the ReadDirectoryChangesW function. It captures the name of the new subdirectory as soon as Defender completes its copy operation, allowing the exploit to proceed with its objectives.

Figure 9: Stage 5 — WDCallerThread: MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI RPC binding and inlined Proc42 dispatch.

Stage 6 — Oplock-Timed Symlink Race

Stage 6 represents an advancement from Stage 5 by transforming the arbitrary file write as SYSTEM into a targeted file read. Specifically, it focuses on accessing the SAM registry hive from the VSS shadow copy created in Stage 2. Following Stage 5, Windows Defender creates a new directory for signature updates and populates it with SYSTEM-owned versions of the staged files. Prior to loading these new signatures, Defender reopens the mpasbase.vdm file from the WDUpdateDirectory to verify its contents. This second opening is critical, as it becomes the target of a race condition.

In this setup, a batch oplock is placed on the current mpasbase.vdm located in the exploit’s staging directory. The file is accessed with the FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE option via NtCreateFile, causing it to disappear immediately upon closing the handle, leaving no forensic trace. Subsequently, DeviceIoControl activates the batch oplock using FSCTL 0x90008, the same control code utilized in Stage 2. The process then leverages GetOverlappedResult to block until Defender’s second opening of the file interrupts the oplock.

Figure 10: Stage 6 setup — open mpasbase.vdm, arm batch oplock, wait for Defender to break it.

When an oplock is broken, Defender’s I/O operation is temporarily halted during the open process. The kernel intervenes by breaking the oplock and waits for the current handle holder to close before allowing Defender’s operation to continue. This situation creates a brief opportunity, typically lasting only a few hundred microseconds, for the exploit to execute a swap of the symbolic link.

During this narrow time frame, the exploit closes the existing WDUpdateDirectory symlink handle. It then creates a new symlink that points to the object-manager directory itself and introduces a new mpasbase.vdm symbolic link within that directory. This link directs to the SAM file located in the Windows System32 directory on the Stage 2 shadow copy.

Once the CloseHandle(FileHandle) function is called, it releases the paused state of Defender’s open process. At this point, Defender accesses the SAM hive using its SYSTEM token through the newly swapped symlink chain. Since Defender’s operation runs within a transaction established by the exploit, the exploit can call CreateFileTransacted with the same transaction handle to open the same file. Both handles recognize the SAM hive that Defender just accessed as SYSTEM, allowing the exploit’s handle to navigate the leaked SAM handle as Stage 7 progresses.

Figure 11: Stage 6 race — swap WDUpdateDirectory symlink, plant mpasbase.vdm → SAM, release Defender.

Stage 7 — SAM Parse to SYSTEM Shell

The final stage of the exploit, Stage 7, serves as the culmination of the previous stages, granting access to a crucial artifact: a leaked handle that allows access to the System’s SAM registry hive on a volume shadow copy (VSS). This process circumvents the standard registry API, which typically requires a hive to be mounted under HKLM or HKCU. Instead, the exploit relies on the offline registry API in offreg.dll, specifically the OROpenHiveByHandle function, to interact with the hive directly from its file bytes.

Furthermore, the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) encrypts each account’s NT hash using a unique per-machine syskey. This syskey is derived from a 16-byte value known as the LSA bootkey, which is distributed across four specific registry subkey class names located under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Accessing these class names requires using RegQueryInfoKey, as they are not visible via standard registry queries. A function called GetLSASecretKey navigates through these four subkeys, retrieves their class names, decodes them from hexadecimal, and applies a specific permutation to reconstruct the 16-byte bootkey.

Figure 12: Stage 7 — GetLSASecretKey: read hidden bootkey chunks from four LSA subkey class names.

The process begins with the function UnprotectPasswordEncryptionKey, which extracts the encrypted syskey blob from SAM\Domains\Account\F using the Windows CryptoAPI. This involves acquiring the “Microsoft Enhanced RSA and AES Cryptographic Provider” to import a DES-derived intermediate key and then performing a 32-byte AES-CBC decryption. This method is standard for Windows 10 and 11 and is designed to exploit the encryption chain associated with these systems while avoiding older versions that only used DES for syskeys. Once the syskey is obtained, the exploit accesses the SAM database at SAM\Domains\Account\Users\<RID>, parsing its entries to retrieve the encrypted NT hashes for each user. The function UnprotectNTHash then decrypts these hashes using the recovered syskey and the account’s RID as a salt. During testing, the administrator account with a RID of 1001 revealed a plaintext NT hash of 8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c and the corresponding MD4 hash for the password “password.”

The next phase, referred to as the “swap,” occurs in two steps. The function CalculateNTLMHash is called with the plaintext password “$PWNed666!!!WDFAIL,” resulting in an MD4 hash to replace the existing NT hash. During the execution of the CalculateNTLMHash function, the RCX register directly references a specific set of plaintext bytes. These bytes are represented as a string that also appears as a literal in the binary .rdata section. This string stands out as a significant indicator of compromise (IoC) within the entire binary.

Figure 13: Stage 7 — x64dbg at CalculateNTLMHash entry: RCX points at the plaintext bytes of “$PWNed666!!!WDFAIL” as the exploit computes its new NT hash.

When changing a user password, the ChangeUserPassword function is invoked with specific parameters: the target account name in RCX, the decrypted old NT hash in RDX, and the newly generated NT hash. At the entry point of this function, the account name “admin” is stored in RCX, while R12 holds the decrypted old NT hash from the Security Account Manager (SAM). This hash is displayed in hex format, specifically “8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c.”

Within ChangeUserPassword, the SamiChangePasswordUser function is invoked, replacing the admin account’s stored NT hash. A noteworthy aspect of this process is that SamiChangePasswordUser requires the old NT hash for authorization, rather than the plaintext password. As the exploit has already obtained the necessary old hash from the SAM decryption, it meets the authorization criteria.

However, it’s important to note that simply extracting the SAM does not grant elevated permissions, as you cannot use a raw NT hash to log on. Additionally, performing a password reset typically requires administrative rights. It is only when these two actions are executed together, in the specified order, that a local admin’s cached hash can be transformed into a functional password of the exploit’s choosing.

Figure 14: Stage 7 — x64dbg at ChangeUserPassword entry: RCX = L”admin”, R12 dump shows the decrypted old NTLM hash “8846f7ea…” about to be swapped via SAMR.

After the admin password is reset, the exploit uses the new credentials to log in as an administrator. It then retrieves the UAC-elevated linked token using the GetTokenInformation(TokenLinkedToken) function and impersonates the admin. With administrative authority now established, the exploit accesses the Service Control Manager and creates a temporary service. This service is assigned a random GUID name and has its ImagePath linked to the exploit’s own binary, allowing it to start successfully. The Service Control Manager (SCM) defaults to launching the service as LocalSystem.

When the service initiates, the exploit’s primary function (wmain) executes a second time. This new instance identifies itself as running as LocalSystem and shifts its approach to relocate its SYSTEM token from Session 0 to the caller’s interactive session. To facilitate this transition, it performs four consecutive SetPrivilege calls to enable the necessary privileges, including SeTcbPrivilege (needed by SetTokenInformation for cross-session operations), SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege (needed by CreateProcessAsUser), SeImpersonatePrivilege, and SeDebugPrivilege. Following these preparations, DuplicateTokenEx is used to create a new primary token, which is then redirected to the user’s session using SetTokenInformation with the TokenSessionId. Finally, the exploit successfully launches conhost.exe within that interactive session using CreateProcessAsUser.

Figure 15: Stage 7 — SYSTEM-to-user-session pivot: SetPrivilege chain + DuplicateTokenEx + SetTokenInformation(TokenSessionId).

In a security exploit scenario, two instances of the conhost.exe process appear on the desktop as the attack unfolds. One process runs under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account, originating from the SYSTEM-side component of the exploit, while the other runs under the compromised administrator’s account, initiated by the original process via CreateProcessWithLogonW using the altered admin credentials.

As the exploit progresses, it restores the administrator’s original NT hash to keep the account intact. However, if the exploit’s process is terminated between the reset and the restoration phases, the administrator may inadvertently be left with a residual password: $PWNed666!!!WDFAIL. This showcases the potential risk of a vulnerability on a live host, highlighting the importance of robust security measures to prevent such exploits.

Figure 16: Stage 7 payoff — SYSTEM shell (left) and admin shell (right) spawned by the FunnyApp.exe process visible in the x64dbg title bar (PID 8308).

Beyond the Shell — Turning SYSTEM into Domain Admin

In Stage 7 of the exploit process, the attacker gains an interactive shell running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, indicating a successful local privilege escalation on the isolated exploit-analysis host. This access is significant because, within an enterprise domain, the SYSTEM account can reveal the credentials of users who have logged in to the compromised workstation. In our lab setup, we used the SYSTEM shell to retrieve sensitive data from LSASS with Mimikatz. Ultimately, this led to the discovery of the domain credentials for the CITRIX\administrator account. It’s important to note that while BlueHammer did not create these credentials, it provided the necessary SYSTEM access to extract the credential information already residing on the compromised system.

Figure 17: mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords extracting a cached domain-administrator NTLM hash from LSASS memory under the SYSTEM shell.

In our process, we utilized the recovered NTLM hash with the sekurlsa::pth module of Mimikatz. This allowed us to create a process that included a domain administrator’s logon session, eliminating the need for the plaintext password. Subsequently, we authenticated the domain controller using the NTLM hash through PsExec.

Figure 18: mimikatz sekurlsa::pth module spawning a new process under a spoofed domain-administrator logon session using the captured NTLM hash.

In the pass-the-hash process conducted on Node01, the local host machine, we used PsExec to connect to the domain controller, dc60. During this process, the source shell was identified as NODE01\administrator, while the command shell on the remote dc60 operated under the CITRIX\administrator account. This setup allowed us to access protected system locations, initiate services, and extract the NTDS.dit file, successfully demonstrating full control as a domain administrator.

The analysis of the remote whoami command revealed that the command shell on the dc60 workstation was operating under the CITRIX\administrator account. This finding was further validated by accessing sensitive system locations, initiating services, and extracting the NTDS.dit file. At this stage, it was clear that the security breach extended beyond a single workstation; the attacker had gained control of the domain’s built-in Administrator account, granting them access to various credentials and administrative capabilities throughout the domain.

Figure 19: Pass-the-hash session moving from NODE01\administrator to a remote command shell on domain controller dc60 as CITRIX\administrator.

The outlined sequence illustrates the complete attack path that the exploit aims to uncover. It began with a foothold gained by a standard user, followed by successful exploitation of BlueHammer, elevation to local SYSTEM privileges, and extraction of cached domain administrator credentials. The attacker then utilized pass-the-hash authentication to gain access to the domain controller, ultimately executing commands as CITRIX\administrator. Detection and Hunting

BlueHammer operates stealthily, making it challenging to detect if each of its actions is viewed in isolation. It uses legitimate Windows subsystems and interfaces with Microsoft infrastructure rather than relying on attacker-controlled update mechanisms. Even after a successful operation, it leaves minimal enduring traces; however, some transient indicators, such as temporary files, object-manager links, RPC interactions, CloudFilter registrations, oplock activities, password alterations, and service creations, might still be noticeable. Therefore, effective detection hinges on correlating these behaviors rather than depending on a singular file hash or event.

Title: Sizing the PHP exposure window for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with VirusTotal
Context: On October 20, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, fixing two critical vulnerabilities rated CVSS v4
Full Text:
On October 20, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, fixing two critical vulnerabilities rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). Hours before the release, technical details leaked publicly. They point to the session.upload_progress feature, which has been part of PHP since 5.4.0 and is enabled by default. The community quickly converged on an interim mitigation: set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini.

That leaves defenders with two questions: how big is the exposed surface, and where should they start? We used Internet Scanning in VirusTotal to answer both.

Note: Official details, affected versions and fixed versions are published by the PHP project with the release. The figures below describe the Internet-facing PHP footprint, not confirmed vulnerable hosts.

Most PHP servers don't say they are PHP

VirusTotal fingerprints roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP (port_service_cpe:php), about 3.8 million of them with at least one port open today. Only around 1.1 million of those announce a version in an HTTP header such as X-Powered-By: PHP/8.3.35.

In other words, roughly four out of five PHP servers hide their version (expose_php = Off, stripped headers, reverse proxies). VirusTotal still identifies them as PHP through other signals: the application on top (WordPress, Laravel, Nextcloud...), PHPSESSID cookies and framework-specific headers. If you only search for a version string, you only see the fraction of the problem that volunteers it.

The version picture: the long tail of end-of-life PHP

Among the servers that do disclose their version, the split is stark:

~272K run a supported branch (8.2 to 8.5), the only branches that receive security fixes from the PHP project.

~758K run an end-of-life branch between 5.4 and 8.1. These branches have session.upload_progress enabled by default and no longer receive security fixes. PHP 7.4 alone accounts for ~187K IPs and PHP 5.4 for ~119K.

~88K run PHP 5.2 or 5.3, which predate session.upload_progress.

Being up to date doesn't buy much time either: about 85K IPs run the exact releases published on September 24 (8.3.35, 8.2.34, 8.4.26 and 8.5.11), the latest available before this fix.

What runs on top, and where

Apache (~2.9M) and nginx (~1.48M) are the web servers most often seen on PHP hosts, followed by LiteSpeed (~90K). On the application side, WordPress dominates with ~538K IPs, followed by Laravel (~141K) and Nextcloud (~107K). Webmail (Roundcube) and database admin panels (phpMyAdmin) add another ~25K high-value targets.

The geography is concentrated: the United States accounts for ~920K PHP hosts with at least one open port, and a handful of cloud and hosting providers (AWS, DigitalOcean, Alibaba, OVHcloud, Hetzner) concentrate a large share. That concentration is good news for remediation: a few providers that push a configuration change or a WAF rule can cover a lot of ground.

Going beyond the web port

PHP rarely travels alone. ~394K PHP hosts also have port 22 open (SSH by default), ~233K port 3306 (MySQL) and ~68K port 3389 (RDP). Those co-exposed services are useful for something else: identifying the exact build behind the web server.

The leaked material references LiteSpeed lsphp82 8.2.34 builds for Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04, and notes that HTTP headers alone don't tell those builds apart. The OpenSSH package on port 22 does. With the bracket syntax, every condition is pinned to its port:

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"PHP/8.2.34" port_service_version[22]:"9.6p1 Ubuntu"

Of the ~3.5K IPs whose banners show both LiteSpeed and PHP 8.2.34, about 500 also have port 22 open. Across all PHP 8.2.34 hosts, the OpenSSH package on port 22 matches Ubuntu 24.04 on 269 IPs, Ubuntu 22.04 on 112 and Debian 12 on 65. For a defender, that is the difference between "patch everything" and "these are the machines that match the leaked target profile, patch them first". Keep in mind that port 22 reveals the host operating system: PHP may still run inside a container built on a different base image.

Adversaries run PHP too

The exposed surface also includes attacker infrastructure. Around 5.7K PHP hosts with at least one open port have five or more detections in VirusTotal, 729 of them disclosing PHP 8.x. One of them is an old acquaintance: the NOX Stealer panel (rebranded as BOMBAY) on 5.175.221[.]206:8443, which we profiled in our Internet Scanning post, runs nginx 1.24.0 with PHP/8.3.33.

What the VirusTotal corpus saw

The leak left traces across VirusTotal. The archive referenced in the write-up was first submitted at 02:29 UTC on October 21, less than 15 minutes after the first submission of the write-up URL. By the time of writing, 21 crowdsourced reports covering the vulnerabilities had been ingested as collections. Following entity:collection collection_type:report "CVE-2026-109618" is the fastest way to keep up with new reporting as it appears.

What to do now

Patch. Upgrade to the fixed release of your branch (8.2, 8.3, 8.4 or 8.5) as soon as it is available on php.net or through your distribution.

Plan the EOL migration. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive security fixes. If you are on 5.4 to 8.1, upgrade the branch or check whether your distribution or vendor ships a backport.

Disable upload progress until you patch. Set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini (or the pool configuration) and reload PHP-FPM, Apache or LSAPI. It only breaks upload progress bars that rely on the feature. Community analysis suggests it may not cover every vector, so treat it as a stopgap, not a fix.

Filter multipart at the edge. Where an application doesn't need file uploads, block or inspect multipart/form-data requests before they reach PHP. Cloudflare shipped emergency rules to its Managed and Free rulesets on October 21, and its CTO stated that they cover known payloads, while stressing that only updating PHP fully protects a site.

Make sure the WAF can't be bypassed. Edge rules only help if the origin is not directly reachable. Search your own ranges in VirusTotal (for example, entity:ip port_service_cpe:php asn:<your ASN>) to find origins that expose PHP directly to the Internet.

Don't rely on hiding the version. expose_php = Off hides the header, not the vulnerability.

Executive Summary

October 19 Update

Unit 42 has observed attempted exploitation of the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 by ransomware operators, including Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc).

We’re also aware of public reporting attributing exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Fixes for this vulnerability have been available since May 2026. Palo Alto Networks has become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.

Customers can mitigate the risk of this issue by taking any of the following actions:

Use a dedicated certificate for Authentication Override cookies: Generate a new certificate exclusively for authentication override cookies and store it securely. Do not reuse the portal or gateway certificate, and do not share this certificate with other features or users.

Disable Authentication Override: Uncheck the Authentication Override options (for generating and accepting cookies) in the GlobalProtect portal and gateway configuration.

June 5, 2026

In June 2026, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 observed active exploitation of the May 2026 PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 by an unidentified threat actor attempting to access GlobalProtect. This security flaw involves an authentication bypass in the portal and gateway components of vulnerable versions of PAN-OS® software, which could allow unauthorized attackers to circumvent security controls and initiate virtual private network (VPN) connections.

This CVE was added to the Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026.

No post-access behavior or lateral movement was identified. Only a small portion of the probed devices actually established VPN sessions, resulting in gateway-connected events.

We advise organizations to proactively hunt for the indicators of the activity specified in this report and activate incident response protocols for any successful gateway-connected events linked to these indicators. Additionally, we strongly recommend reviewing the security advisory for CVE-2026-0257, following the available workarounds and mitigations or upgrading to a version that includes a fix for this issue.

For pre-proof-of-concept release (May 29, 2026) activities, search for these IP addresses in GlobalProtect logs to look for successful login connection:

As part of post-PoC release monitoring, search GlobalProtect logs for successful gateway-connected events matching the following hard-coded client configuration values from the PoC code.

endpoint_os_version : Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit

source_user_info.domain : empty

We encourage organizations to consult our official Palo Alto Networks Security Advisory for additional details about the vulnerability and configuration guidance. We also recommend reading Rapid7’s technical analysis about the exploitation activity they observed in the wild.

Palo Alto Networks Cortex Xpanse is able to identify publicly exposed PAN-OS gateways and GlobalProtect portals.

Management Interface Exposure Risk and Remediation

During incident response (IR) engagements associated with the Lunar Peak campaign, Unit 42 observed a recurring misconfiguration that led to critical, unintended exposure. Specifically, organizations frequently mapped GlobalProtect (GP) profiles to HTTP/HTTPS services on their management interfaces.

This configuration inadvertently exposes the management interface to the internet on specific ports, most notably 4443 and 3879, often without administrators' knowledge. While the risks of this exposure were previously documented, the frequency of this oversight during the Lunar Peak incidents prompted a comprehensive update to our official guidance to ensure maximum clarity.

Verification and mitigation:

Verify exposure: Defenders can rapidly verify whether their environments are affected by attempting an out-of-band HTTPS connection to their management IP address on ports 4443 and 3879 via an external web browser.

Remediate: To remediate this issue and enforce the principle of least privilege, we strongly advise administrators to review official Palo Alto Networks documentation on configuring Interface Management profiles to safely restrict access.

Update: Oct. 19, 2026

Ransomware operators exploiting the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc). Public reporting attributes exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session. Following this, the threat actors are typically:

Conducting internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools

Moving laterally via RDP and SMB

Staging additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration and ultimately, ransomware deployment

Our investigations have continued since early June 2026, and have spanned across numerous industries, including:

Financial services

High technology

Hospitality

Manufacturing

Professional and legal services

Government

Utilities and energy

Wholesale and retail

The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer. In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).

This tactic bypasses in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security controls, representing a highly sophisticated method for obtaining domain-wide credentials. We have also observed actors chaining this initial access with other exploit tools, such as those targeting Veeam backup infrastructure (CVE-2023-27532), to maximize their impact.

The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

Title: Siemens Customers Targeted by ClickFix Attackers Exploiting DLL Side-Loading Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Siemens has warned customers that attackers are actively exploiting a dynamic link library (DLL) side-loading vulnerability in its Software Center to distribute malware.

The company has attributed the activity to the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign.

Romulus is a server hosting panel that was identified by Forescout researchers on October 14. The panel allows cybercriminals to deploy ClickFix tactics into an entire ecosystem which can be repeatedly used to deliver multiple forms of malware to victims.

ClickFix is a popular attack technique among cybercriminals. It relies on social engineering to trick the victim into running attacker-supplied commands on their own machine.

The Siemens blog, published on October 19, detailed how attackers are targeting CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS 8.4) to load malicious DLL files into a directory that the Siemens Software Center searches for. They use a genuine copy of the application with a valid signature and place their own files next to it.

The attackers then attempt to distribute these files to customers by using a ClickFix lure.

Version 3.5.8.7 of Software Center loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them, the firm admitted.

If a user follows the ClickFix commands, malicious code will execute on the device with the privileges of the affected application.

“Never paste a command from a web page into Win+R, the Run box or PowerShell. A real ‘I am not a robot’ check never asks for this,” Siemens wrote.

How to Defend Against the Romulus Campaign

Siemens urged Software Center customers update to version 4.0.9.8, which contains a fix for the flaw. Existing installations update automatically the next time they start.

Customers should also look out for the following indications that their PC is affected by the campaign:

"Siemens Software Center" in the start-up apps or Task Scheduler of a PC that never had it installed

A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service inside AppData\Local\Programs is created by the malware

Files named activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe

A folder called FTSuite containing a file ftc.uml inside AppData\Local

Network connections to 96.62.218[.]59

If a PC has been found to be compromised, customers should isolate the device, stop the process first, then remove the start-up entry and task and reset passwords.

Siemens added that detection tools should focus on the folder and suspicious behavior, not on the Siemens file fingerprint as the file itself is genuine.

Customers should also ensure that they only download Siemens software from official Siemens sources and block the active IP address and domain listed in the advisory.

The Moody’s report also warned that AI agents are already capable of exploiting vulnerabilities and compromising systems within days. It documented containment failures during developer testing at OpenAI and Anthropic, although OpenAI’s case involved an internal evaluation rather than an attack by a threat actor.

The report noted that no comparable threat-actor campaign at that scale has been publicly documented.

However, the barriers to fully autonomous cyber-attacks are likely temporary, Moody’s analysts noted.

High computing costs and restricted access to frontier AI models currently limit their use in large-scale campaigns. Organizations with weak patching practices face the greatest credit risk, according to the Moody’s report.

Those with large digital networks are particularly exposed because their broader attack surfaces create more opportunities for exploitation. Smaller and mid-sized companies could also become more economically viable targets as AI reduces the cost and effort required to carry out cyber-attacks, the analysts noted.

Published on October 19, this Moody’s report uses February 2026 data from Bitsight Technologies that accounted for vulnerabilities disclosed over previous two years.

“Meaningful advances in AI's offensive cyber capabilities since then may have further reduced the average time to exploit; remediation times may also have changed,” the Moody’s report noted.

Title: Supply Chain Zero Days: Closing the Gap Between Publication and Detection
Context: By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages...
Full Text:
Modern software development depends on open source packages. Developers and AI coding agents can pull new dependencies and versions into projects at speed, helping teams build and ship faster.

But that speed creates a challenge for security teams. When a trusted package is compromised, malicious code can enter development environments and build pipelines before traditional vulnerability databases flag the threat.

Organizations cannot manually review or block every update to foundational packages without slowing development. Therefore, most organizations scan newly downloaded packages against known vulnerabilities and block if needed. But, zero-day supply chain compromises won’t show up in vulnerability databases right away; and, because popular packages are already trusted, developer workflows and build pipelines are often configured to automatically pull their latest versions. If an attacker compromises one of those packages, a malicious update can spread across the environment before a CVE is even published, leaving security teams to defend from behind.

Trusted package compromises in the wild

Our own research team is seeing this technique in practice more often than ever before. In H2 2025, notable supply chain attacks made up about 10% of significant incidents. In H1 2026, that percentage increased to 25%, and now, notable supply chain attacks account for 1 in 4 significant security incidents. During the Axios compromise, for example, an unknown threat actor compromised the npm account of an axios maintainer and published two malicious versions of the npm package (v1.14.1, v0.30.4), which introduced a dependency on plain-crypto-js, a newly created malicious package.

Although the malicious versions were removed within hours, that didn't mean that the threat disappeared. According to the Wiz Research team’s own observations, at the time, Axios was present in approximately 80% of cloud and code environments, and downloaded around 100 million times per week. The package’s popularity enabled rapid exposure, with observed execution in 3% of affected environments. This reality underlines the importance of speed in defending against supply chain attacks.

Detecting malicious packages at publication

Traditionally, security teams find out a trusted package was compromised by receiving a threat advisory or vulnerability database update. In an ideal world, teams could take a proactive approach to securing the software supply chain by knowing which packages published to npm are clean, preventing installation of those that are not, and alerting on malicious versions across all tools.

That’s why we built a dedicated supply chain detection pipeline to analyze new packages and versions as soon as they are published to npm. This allows us to flag malicious packages and add detection rules in Wiz Defend, code and cloud pipelines, all before a formal CVE is published.

Here’s how it works:

When a new package version is released, the pipeline downloads and extracts the current version and previous versions for comparison.

Static analysis techniques flag suspicious files. This analysis feeds into our AI classifier engine, which returns an initial verdict.

Suspicious versions undergo dynamic analysis to validate the verdict. This dynamic analysis involves in depth work to understand the file contents, including:

Installing the package version in a sandbox environment to monitor runtime activity.

Importing the version and exposed modules .

Running the package from the CLI (where possible).

The Wiz Sensor observes runtime behavior to monitor for malicious activity. This helps the pipeline confirm the suspicious verdict, and provides our AI classifier with additional evidence.

The AI classifier returns the final verdict, generated based on all previous analyses. Once a version is confirmed as malicious, the pipeline automatically publishes IOCs to the Wiz reputation service. This ensures that Wiz customers are alerted as soon as a package enters their environment, via:

Threat intelligence center notifications, alerting on compromised packages so teams can understand if they are impacted.

Code and cloud scanning pipelines, surfacing malicious package findings wherever detected.

Wiz Defend, with auto-updated detection rules for malicious packages and configurable runtime detection and response policies.

Combining various analysis methods and live runtime execution allows us to flag zero-day compromises at speed while keeping false positives to a minimum.

Detection in the real world

A notable example of the pipeline in action is the keyv attack, where multiple npm packages in the keyv/cacheable ecosystem were compromised following the compromise of a GitHub maintainer account. In this particular case, instead of hardcoding command-and-control (C2) domains into the package source code, where static rules could easily extract and block them, the malware dynamically retrieved its C2 domains at runtime by querying an Ethereum smart contract. Because the malicious domains never appeared in the code itself, traditional static analysis alone could not identify the C2 infrastructure.

Using the supply chain pipeline, the Wiz Research Team was able to successfully see network activity to the malicious domain, automatically detecting the malicious domain connection without human intervention. Combining static and dynamic analysis, along with AI classification and live runtime monitoring, helped the pipeline flag the package with high confidence. As soon as the package was confirmed malicious, the relevant information automatically pushed to Wiz Defend and across the Wiz platform, enabling customers to detect compromised keyv versions in their environments before a formal CVE was published.

Proactive detection of compromised packages with Wiz

Open source packages are fundamental to the modern software development ecosystem. As workflows accelerate, security teams need real-time visibility and control over third-party dependencies before malicious code can land on developer workstations or build pipelines.

By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages before traditional vulnerability signals become available. In addition, Wiz evaluates dependencies during each install or upgrade process, to help security teams detect and manage risky or compromised package versions at the exact point of ingestion.

The goal is simple: empower security and development teams to move at machine speed, with the visibility and control over what enters the software supply chain.

IntroductionOn September 27, 2026, Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-88771, a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting NetScaler Application Delivery Controller (ADC) and NetScaler Gateway. The vulnerability carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 according to NVD and a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5 according to the Citrix security bulletin CTX697096. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands on affected appliances. Exploitation requires no optional features to be enabled.Citrix confirmed exploitation on unmitigated appliances, and the US’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-88771 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following reports of active exploitation worldwide. Citrix has since disclosed another critical vulnerability affecting NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, CVE-2026-107406, which can lead to RCE or denial of service. CVE-2026-107406 affects appliances configured as SAML service provider or identity provider depending on the software version. The analysis in this blog focuses on the exploitation of CVE-2026-88771.Zscaler ThreatLabz observed a staged exploitation chain involving access-log poisoning, remote command execution before authentication, appliance fingerprinting, and attempts to deploy multiple web shells. ThreatLabz also observed delivery of a FreeBSD x64 implant from infrastructure that overlapped with activity we previously associated with exploitation of StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650), a vulnerability affecting Adobe Commerce and Magento.This overlap provides an investigative lead but does not establish threat actor attribution. Shared hosting and compromised infrastructure, malware distribution services, or payload reuse by unrelated operators could explain the connection. Fixed ReleasesCitrix recommends installing the following builds or later:Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.46 and later releasesCitrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.29 and later releases of 13.1Citrix NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.46 FIPS and later releases of 14.1-FIPSCitrix NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1.37.283 and later releases of 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP RecommendationsOrganizations running NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway should take the following actions immediately:Identify exposed appliances: Inventory every NetScaler appliance and determine its software version, build, and internet exposure.Preserve forensic evidence before updating: Capture a virtual machine snapshot, where applicable, and collect remote syslog data, the NetScaler technical support bundle, and available packet-engine core dumps. CISA warns that updating may remove or reduce forensic visibility.Isolate potentially compromised appliances: Remove potentially compromised appliances from untrusted networks while preserving evidence.Mitigation and response: If your environment includes any of the impacted appliances, it is advisable to proactively hunt for signs of compromise. The following commands, sourced from Sh3llc0de, can help identify suspicious activity.To investigate modifications within the FreeBSD shell, access the NetScaler console, enter shell, and run the commands below:#1. Inspect running processes for suspicious shells spawned by nsppe ps aux | grep -E "sh|bash|python|perl|nc|curl|wget" | grep -v "nsconmsg" # 2. Check startup script rc.netscaler for unauthorized modifications cat /flash/nsconfig/rc.netscaler # 3. Audit cron jobs for suspicious automated scripts crontab -l cat /etc/crontab # 4. Title: Irish police force has its Twitter hacked in cryptocurrency scam
Context: There are a number of ways in which malicious hackers can gain access to accounts - including through the use of phishing emails and password-stealing malware, as well as...
Full Text:
There must have been red faces in the social media department of Ireland's police headquarters after two of its accounts were hijacked this week.

The official @GardaInfo and @GardaTraffic Twitter accounts of Garda Síochána were accessed by an unauthorised third party who posted cryptocurrency-related messages on Wednesday evening, potentially reaching hundreds of thousands of users.

The messages claimed that followers were eligible to claim free cryptocurrency through an airdrop. However, victims who followed the link could potentially be tricked into handing over the keys to their cryptocurrency wallet, and end up with their savings drained.

The problem, however, is not just that a hacker found themselves with the ability to post fraudulent messages posing as the Irish police. If an unauthorised person was able to publish unauthorised posts from the accounts they may also have been able to access direct messages (DMs) which could contain sensitive personal information from members of the public.

Speaking to the Belfast Telegraph, a police spokesperson attempted to dampen fears that sensitive information could have been compromised:

"An Garda Síochána is satisfied that there is no unauthorised access with any Garda systems and that there is no loss or impact on any Garda data."

Scammers like to hijack established accounts with a large followers as they are both more likely to be trusted, and provide a rapid route to reach a significant number of potential victims. The @GardaTraffic account has over 600,000 followers, and is normally used by Irish police for traffic and road safety updates, while the @GardaInfo account has almost 300,000 followers.

The Garda says that is carrying out an internal investigation into what may have happened, and is working "with the X platform to understand how this unauthorised access has occurred."

The Garda is not the only police force to have ever suffered a security breach on its Twitter account.

For instance, in 2019 the UK's Metropolitan Police had its account hijacked (as well as part of its website) by hackers who posted explicit messages calling for the release of London-based rapper "Digga D". Two men were subsequently charged in connection with the hack.

Five years before, the social media accounts of Dubai police were hacked by an Anonymous-affiliated group calling itself HorsemenLulz, who claimed the UAE's police service was “spying on you”.

In 2022, the official Twitter account of the Philadelphia Police Department was compromised and used to post what appeared to be a series of adverts targeting businesses.

There are a number of ways in which malicious hackers can gain access to accounts - including through the use of phishing emails and password-stealing malware, as well as exploiting the common habit of users choosing non-unique passwords that they have used elsewhere.

The advice of cybersecurity experts remains to protect accounts with multi-factor authentication, to always use unique, strong passwords, and to review which third-party apps may have been granted access to accounts.

Title: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134)
Context: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134) #SMB Security #Enterprise Security #Ransomware #Threat Research By Martin Zugec / Oct 15, 2026...
Full Text:
[CRITICAL] | CVSS 10.0 (CVE-2026-105134, per VulDB) | Active exploitation confirmed, listed in CISA KEV | Patch immediately

TL;DR

Attackers are chaining two vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS, the server-side backup management platform of the Ahsay Cloud Backup Suite: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication flaw, and CVE-2026-105134, an OS command injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 by VulDB. Every AhsayCBS v7 to v10 server that an attacker can reach, and that runs a build below v10.3.4.45 (v10) or v9.15.2.70 (v7, v8, v9), is exposed. That includes servers on the earlier patches v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59, which the Ahsay announcement, October 2026 says did not fully fix the flaws. If you have already patched, you are not necessarily safe: verify the installed build, apply the new hotfix, reboot, and check for prior compromise. Patching closes the entry point but does not remove webshells or other access an attacker has already planted, and that access can sit unused for weeks before a ransomware or data theft attack. Bitdefender MDR has investigated multiple incidents at our customers through this chain since around 7 October 2026. For exact remediation steps, including how to identify affected systems and assess for prior compromise, see What To Do below.

Advisory History

15 October 2026: Initial publication, based on three Bitdefender MDR incident investigations. Vendor hotfixes are available, and both CVEs are listed in CISA KEV.

Situation

AhsayCBS is the server side of Ahsay’s backup product. It receives, stores and manages backups for the clients connected to it. Attackers are exploiting two flaws in its web-facing components in the wild. The timeline:

4 October 2026, 07:16 UTC: Both CVEs are published in the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Both entries state that a public exploit exists.

Around 7-8 October 2026: Bitdefender MDR’s first two incidents begin. They coincide with the first public reporting of exploitation and the first Ahsay advisories.

12 October 2026: Ahsay releases hotfixes (v10.3.4.45 for v10, v9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9). The same advisory states that the earlier patches, v10.3.4.0 and v9.15.2.59, did not fully address the vulnerabilities.

14 October 2026: CISA adds both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. KEV is the US government’s list of flaws with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and federal agencies must fix listed flaws by a set deadline. MDR identifies a third incident the same day.

17 October 2026: CISA’s federal remediation deadline.

Bitdefender MDR investigations and the KEV listing both confirm exploitation. Some indicators in our incidents overlap with publicly reported activity. We do not attribute this activity to any named actor.

The NVD entries still list 10.3.4 as unaffected. The vendor’s later advisory supersedes that statement, and this advisory follows the vendor.

How it’s Exploited

Backup servers are a valuable foothold. They hold credentials for the systems they protect and the storage they write to, and they control the copies an organization relies on to recover. A ransomware operator wants to steal or destroy exactly that data before encrypting anything else. AhsayCBS exposes a management web service so administrators and clients can reach it, so on many deployments the server is reachable from the internet by design.

All three incidents Bitdefender MDR investigated began the same way, through a combination of the two CVEs. One flaw breaks authentication. Improper authentication means the server can be tricked into treating an unverified request as legitimate. The other is OS command injection, where text supplied by the attacker is executed as an operating system command on the server. Both NVD entries name the same argument, random, and neither flaw needs an account or any user action. MDR saw the two used together. NVD, however, scores the command injection as needing no privileges on its own, so an attacker may not need the full chain to run commands. A public exploit exists. CISA’s Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) is the model CISA uses to prioritize fixes, and it rates exploitation of both flaws as active and automatable.

Once inside, the attackers moved to confirm and test their access. In the first incident, they validated access through JSP webshells, which are small scripts planted on a web server that let an attacker run commands through ordinary web requests. They also staged PowerShell payloads, tried to stage payloads as command files (.cmd) in the shared C:\Users\Public folder, and tried to establish persistence, meaning a way back in that survives reboots and password changes. MDR analysts detected and blocked portions of this activity early. In the second incident, the attacker deployed JSP files (Java Server Pages, which act as webshells on this Java-based server) and again tried to stage command files in C:\Users\Public. The attacker then ran reconnaissance aimed at finding stored credentials, elevated a user account to SYSTEM (the highest privilege level on Windows), and used obfuscated PowerShell commands to install and configure OpenSSH, the standard remote-login service. A working SSH service would give an attacker a way back in that does not depend on the vulnerable web service, which is why patching alone does not end the incident. The attacker tried to establish persistence before being detected. In the third, MDR blocked and remediated the activity early in initial access. MDR credits three things: it identified known clusters of attacker behavior, the customer responded promptly, and configurations were reviewed quickly.

After that shared start, the incidents diverged. File names differed, the attackers abused different system tools and binaries, and the apparent objectives did not match. The Bitdefender MDR assessment is that the exploit chain was the constant, while file names, tools, and binaries changed from one incident to the next. Some indicators did overlap between the first two incidents, and the campaign appears to share some infrastructure: the C2 address 38.60.252[.]110 was the starting point of the two first incidents. Even so, a hash or file name from one incident may not reliably find the next one. The reliable signal is how the server behaves after the exploit fires. Combined with the differences between incidents, the shared infrastructure suggests a fluid situation in which several different actors may be using the same exploits. That is an assessment, not a finding, and it may change as more incidents surface.

Exposure conditions. Your server is exposed if two things are true. It runs AhsayCBS v7, v8, v9 or v10 below v9.15.2.70 (v7 to v9) or v10.3.4.45 (v10), and the attacker can reach its management web service. Servers on the earlier patches are not safe. An administrator who patched to v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59 did the right thing at the time, but the vendor now says that fix was incomplete. The question to ask is not “did we patch?” The question is whether the server runs v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70 or later.

Amplifying factors. VulDB, the CVE Numbering Authority, scores the command injection 10.0 under CVSS 3.1, the industry’s standard severity scale. A public exploit exists, and exploitation is rated automatable. The incomplete first patch leaves administrators believing they are covered. MDR’s assessment is that several actors may be using the chain. The credential reconnaissance in the second incident fits what backup servers hold.

Limiting factors. Exploitation requires network access to the management web service, so servers reachable only from internal networks carry less realistic exposure. MDR blocked one incident early in initial access and blocked part of the activity in another. MDR saw no encryption, data exfiltration or ransomware deployment. Ransomware remains a plausible risk because of the target type, but MDR did not observe it.

Confidence. This is observed in the wild, confirmed by first-party MDR investigations and corroborated by the KEV listing. We are not hedging on severity. This is internet-exposed, unauthenticated remote code execution with a public exploit, and in MDR’s assessment several different actors may be using it. That makes it a playbook case: continued opportunistic exploitation of unpatched and earlier-patched servers is near-certain. We are deliberately restrained on everything else. Three incidents cannot establish who is behind this, how many groups are involved, or what they ultimately want.

If you have confirmed exposure, skip ahead to What To Do.

How it Works

Public disclosure of the mechanism is limited. Everything below comes from the NVD entries and Bitdefender MDR observations, and nothing here speculates on root cause. Each flaw carries a CWE classification. CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) is the standard catalog of software weakness types.

CVE-2026-105133 (improper authentication, CWE-287). The flaw is in the checkSysPwd function of the API component, in ApiStructsAction.java. Manipulating the random argument results in improper authentication. It can be exploited remotely, with no privileges and no user interaction.

CVE-2026-105134 (OS command injection, CWE-77 and CWE-78). The flaw is in the Replication Receiver component, the offsite store that synchronizes backup data from one or more AhsayCBS servers (Ahsay, “CBS v9 Replication Guide”, August 2025). The affected endpoint is /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Manipulating the same random argument leads to OS command injection, again remotely and with no privileges or user interaction.

Why is this possible? NVD classifies the two as different weaknesses: improper authentication in CVE-2026-105133 and OS command injection in CVE-2026-105134, both reached by manipulating the random argument. Ahsay has not published why the first patches fell short, and we will not guess.

Scores. VulDB assigned all scores below as the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), the organization that issued these CVE IDs. NVD reports them but has not published scores of its own.

CVE

CVSS 3.1

CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-105133

7.3 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L)

CVE-2026-105134
