Title: What’s New in GravityZone October 2026 (v 6.78)
Context: This section describes new functionality designed to elevate analysts' capabilities, offering enhanced tools for threat detection, investigation, and response
Full Text:
Bitdefender rolled out new functionality in Bitdefender GravityZone, a unified cybersecurity platform that provides prevention, protection, detection, and response capabilities for organizations of all sizes. These features, aligned with our multi-layered security strategy, are designed to reduce the workload for security analysts, administrators, and users.

What’s new for Security Analysts

As attackers increasingly blend into legitimate activity, security analysts must uncover signs of sophisticated attacks and make the invisible visible. This section describes new functionality designed to elevate analysts' capabilities, offering enhanced tools for threat detection, investigation, and response.

CLAIRE AI Assistant Enhancements (Early Access)

When an analyst opens an incident and needs to decide on containment, the assistant now starts from that page’s context instead of a blank prompt. CLAIRE, previously named GravityZone AI Assistant, is a conversational assistant built into the Control Center. It applies large language model (LLM) reasoning to Bitdefender Support Center documentation and to data from your GravityZone environment to answer questions, issue recommendations, and initiate selected response actions.

CLAIRE is available through a controlled Early Access Program (EAP). It now has its own entry in the GravityZone navigation menu, with a Chat page and an Advisor briefing page.

On the Incidents, Network, and Policies pages, a new chat opens with page-specific prompts, and coverage extends to the rest of the interface. As the conversation continues, CLAIRE suggests follow-up prompts. When asked to isolate the endpoints associated with an incident, CLAIRE builds the endpoint list for review, and isolation runs only after the analyst refines the list and clicks Isolate. Outside incident work, the Advisor briefing page lists proactive posture recommendations. Each recommendation’s details page explains why CLAIRE chose the issue, summarizes the top affected items, and suggests remediation actions.

The chat window also adds a Stop button that cancels a prompt before the response is generated. A message now appears when you reach your usage limit, and all chats now follow a 30-day retention period.

Attack Path in GravityZone Exposure Management

Attackers rarely reach a critical asset in one step. They chain a misconfiguration on one asset to an exposed account or vulnerability on the next. Attack Path is now available as part of the new GravityZone Exposure Management license. It correlates endpoint risk findings, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) data, and External Attack Surface Management (EASM) asset records to determine the most likely paths an attacker could take to compromise your assets.

Each attack path under Risk Management > Attack Path shows a graph and an asset list that mark potential entry points, exploitable vulnerabilities, and misconfigurations along the route. The graph can highlight the shortest path to the target asset, showing where a single remediation action breaks the largest portion of the chain. Risk factors such as Public exposure and Critical asset appear in both the graph and the asset table. When an asset also has a Risk Management entry, the asset details panel includes a button that opens the matching Risk Management > Resources or Risk Management > Accounts record.

Four new widgets on Monitoring > ASM Dashboard track attack paths across the environment:

New attack paths: lists newly created attack paths for Last 24 hours, Last 7 days, or Last 30 days.

Open attack paths over time: charts New and Resolved attack paths, with a trend line, for Last 7 days, Last 30 days, or Last 90 days.

Top 5 attack path destinations: lists the five assets that attack paths target most often.

Top 5 attack path entry points: lists the five assets that most often serve as attack path entry points.

For detailed information about Attack Path, see the dedicated TechZone article here.

AI Visibility and Control Enhancements

Unmanaged AI tools on endpoints are now a routine part of an organization’s attack surface, and assessing that exposure requires seeing it alongside other risk data. AI Visibility and Control (AIVC), is a discovery and risk layer that reports which AI software is installed and running on managed endpoints and assigns a risk score to each finding. This release extends AIVC data to the ASM Dashboard, the AI Services page, and Risk Management > Resources.

Monitoring > ASM Dashboard now includes a dedicated AI Visibility and Control smart view with an overview of AI usage and risk exposure across the organization. Its widgets show the overall AI risk posture, compare risk across AI categories, list the affected users and endpoints, break findings down by AI category, and list the discovered AI services. AIVC widgets can also be added to custom dashboard smart views.

On AI Visibility and Control > AI Services, each discovered AI service now shows its associated finding or finding count, in both the grid and the service details. From there, analysts can open the AI Findings page to investigate. AI-related findings also appear in Risk Management > Resources, so an endpoint’s AI exposure sits alongside its other risk data. From there, analysts can move between the affected resource, its findings, and the associated AI services.

For comprehensive insights into AIVC, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

EASM Enhancements

External Attack Surface Management builds an attacker-centric view of an organization’s internet-facing exposure. This release adds classification detail to similar domain findings, and maps discovered public IP addresses back to the managed servers that use them.

Similar domains flagged as potential brand impersonation attempts now identify the typo squatting technique used to construct them — misspellings, alternative top-level domains, and substitutions involving visually similar or keyboard-adjacent characters. EASM also highlights public IP addresses used for external communication by servers managed by Bitdefender Endpoint Security Tools (BEST), with the managed servers using each address viewable alongside it. Analysts can identify which addresses to add to the EASM scan list, giving Attack Path additional context on potential entry points into the organization’s network.

For comprehensive insights into EASM, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

EDR and XDR Enhancements

GravityZone Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) give security analysts the tools to detect, investigate, and respond to threats across managed endpoints and connected sensors, with raw event telemetry that supports historical querying and incident investigation. This release changes how search is organized and shared and adds detail to incident and alert data.

Search and investigation

Separate menu entries: Historical search and Live search now appear as separate entries in the left-side menu of GravityZone Control Center.

Shared smart views: Smart views created on the Live search page can now be shared with other users in the company, with read-only or editable permissions. Company Administrators can edit, delete, rename, or make editable for any shared smart view, regardless of who created it or what permissions it has. Other users can delete, rename, or make editable only the views they created, and can edit only those they created or have edit permissions for. Shared smart views appear in a separate section of the Queries panel. Each one has a banner showing its access rights, creator, last update date and time, and the user who last modified it. Create, edit, and delete actions are logged on the User activity page, in the Live search area.

FQDN search: Historical search now supports searching and filtering raw events and alerts by endpoint-submitted fully qualified domain name (FQDN) values. The fqdn field is available in the query editor helper under the Other category, and other.fqdn can be added as a column in the results table and viewed in the event details panel.

Incidents and alerts

Entity type filter: A new Entity type filter under More filters on the Incidents page narrows incidents by the types of entities they contain. It supports multiple selections, and its options are populated from the entity types present in your incidents.

Self Protect attribution: In alert details for Endpoint incidents, alerts generated by the Tamper Protection module now show Self Protect in the Detected By field.

MITRE ATT&CK tactics: XDR and EDR incident and alert details now also support the Resource Development, Stealth, Defense Impairment, and Reconnaissance tactics. Activity previously classified as Defense Evasion may now be reported as Stealth or Defense Impairment, depending on the detection context.

Timestamps with seconds: Timestamps throughout Incidents and Historical search now include seconds as well as hours and minutes.

For analysts reconstructing an intrusion, the new tactics and second-level timestamps work together. A sequence in which an attacker disables a security service and then clears event logs within the same minute can now be ordered precisely, with each step mapped to Defense Impairment or Stealth.

For comprehensive insights into detection and response with GravityZone EDR and XDR, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

What’s new for Administrators

With administrators constantly juggling numerous tasks and responsibilities, they appreciate tools that make their daily work easier. This section describes new functionality designed to simplify managing features responsible for prevention, protection, and detection in a defense-in-depth security architecture.

Extended Email Security Enhancements

Bitdefender Extended Email Security (EES) offers flexible deployment models (Gateway, API-based, and Unified) to provide a comprehensive defense against sophisticated spear-phishing, brand impersonation, and supply chain fraud. This release adds outbound data loss prevention rules, distributor-level console access, and a confirmation step for identity provider sign-in.

DLP rules in Extended Email Security now also cover outbound email for the Gateway and Unified deployment models, which require Outbound Smarthost. Rules inspect the subject, headers, body, attachment types, URLs, and sensitive data patterns, including credit card numbers, International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), and Social Security Numbers (SSNs). Matching outgoing messages are sent to Quarantine or deleted with Delete. You can apply enforcement globally or target specific customers, domains, or users.

Distributors and higher-level partners can now access the Extended Email Security consoles of the downstream partners they manage directly from the Extended Email Security section, across nested partner hierarchies, without Extended Email Security being provisioned for their own company. Console visibility follows the existing Your Bitdefender partner can assist you with security management settings, and the available actions are determined by Extended Email Security permissions within each accessible company. For detailed information, see the dedicated TechZone article here.

In addition, users who sign in with GravityZone credentials and open the Extended Email Security console now see a confirmation prompt. The prompt asks them to approve the automatic switch to the GravityZone identity provider (IdP) before proceeding.

For comprehensive insights into Extended Email Security, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Security Data Lake Single Sign-On

Security teams that use Security Data Lake alongside GravityZone can now sign in to both with the same corporate credentials. Bitdefender GravityZone Security Data Lake combines SIEM operations with scalable data lake storage and advanced analytics, collecting and correlating data from multiple organizational sources for proactive threat hunting.

Security Data Lake now supports single sign-on (SSO) through GravityZone IdP Proxy, so users authenticate with their organization’s identity provider. GravityZone IdP Proxy supports SSO using SAML 2.0 and System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) to manage and verify digital identities across the GravityZone ecosystem.

With Security Data Lake added, sign-in to it is now handled by the organization’s existing identity infrastructure, the same as for the other GravityZone services connected through IdP Proxy.

Network Enhancements

The GravityZone Network inventory gives administrators a consolidated view of all managed endpoints, containers, and network assets across their environment. This release adds two network identifiers to the Network page and refines one filter option:

Public IP column and filter: Displays each endpoint’s public IP address, separately from the existing IP column and filter, which show the local IP address. The filter supports text matching with starts with or contains, so partial IP addresses also return results. Endpoints imported through integrations such as Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID, VMware vCenter, or Amazon Web Services (AWS) do not display a public IP address.

MAC addresses column and filter: Displays each endpoint’s MAC address information with the same text-matching options. Devices with multiple network interfaces show all their MAC addresses in a single cell, and the filter matches any of them.

Golden Image role option: The Golden Image option in the Role filter now appears only when the feature is turned on for your company.

With public IP and MAC addresses searchable directly in the grid, administrators can locate an endpoint from a known address, match devices against data exported from external network or security tools, and narrow large endpoint inventories even when only part of an address is known.

Compliance Manager Enhancements

The Compliance Manager in GravityZone maps endpoint findings against regulatory and industry compliance standards, giving administrators a structured view of their organization’s compliance posture across managed assets.

This update adds two new compliance standards, now available across the Findings, Identity risks, and Compliance manager pages:

BNM RMIT 2025 (MY): Issued by Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM), the Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) policy document sets out requirements for financial institutions on technology risk management, covering technology governance, cybersecurity management, and operational resilience.

CSA Cyber Trust 2025 (SG): Issued by the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), Cyber Trust is a risk-based certification mark for organizations with extensive cybersecurity measures and practices. The 2025 edition extends coverage to cloud, operational technology (OT), and AI security.

In addition, a new Notes column and filter on the Compliance manager page let administrators add and view notes for individual controls, such as justifications, context, or links to external documentation. Control notes can also be included when exporting compliance reports in PDF or XLSX format.

For comprehensive insights into Compliance Manager, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Security Telemetry Enhancements

Organizations that correlate endpoint activity in their own Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platform depend on the range and naming of the events they receive. Security Telemetry forwards raw operating system events from endpoints running BEST to a third-party SIEM. Administrators configure it in the Policy under General > Security Telemetry, where they select the event types to send. This release groups all events by category, adds descriptions for every category and event, and extends coverage with additional event types.

The Security Telemetry page now lists event types under named categories. Each category and event has a description, so administrators can see what an event captures before turning it on. The following categories and event types are now available:

Service: Added, Change status, Modify.

Scheduled task: Create, Delete, Modify.

Account management and authentication: Create local account, Delete local account, Logon failed, Settings changed.

Shell and script activity: Command Prompt command, PowerShell command, PowerShell script block logging, Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) buffer.

Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) job activity: Add file, Create, Delete.

Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) activity: Execution method, New activity, New binding.

Device and driver: Driver module load, Hardware mount, Hardware unmount.

BEST agent: Agent uninstall request.

Audit policy: Change Windows audit policy.

Process: Injection.

Existing event types now sit within the new categories under shorter names:

Process: Create and Terminate, previously Process creation and Process deletion.

File: Create, Delete, Modify, Move, and Read, previously File creation, File deletion, File modification, File move, and File read.

Registry: Create key, Delete key, Modify value, and Delete value, previously Registry key creation, Registry key deletion, Registry value modification, and Registry value deletion.

Account management and authentication: Logon, and Logout (renamed from Logoff).

Network: Connection and DNS query.

With command-line, PowerShell, and AMSI buffer events added next to service, scheduled task, and WMI activity, a SIEM can now correlate script-based execution with the persistence mechanisms that commonly follow it. Examples include a PowerShell command that registers a scheduled task, or a new WMI binding created shortly after an AMSI buffer event.

Firewall for macOS

Organizations that run mixed Windows and macOS fleets can now apply the same network traffic controls across both platforms. The GravityZone Firewall gives administrators granular control over network traffic, including which services and applications can communicate. The module, previously available on Windows servers and workstations, now also supports deployment and management on macOS endpoints.

Also, macOS support for the Firewall module carries through the Control Center areas that already handle Firewall on Windows: policy settings, installation packages, Threats Xplorer, Executive summary, Network, Reports, Dashboard, Health dashboard, Notifications, User activity, and the public API. The module requires BEST for Mac version 8.26.10.2000xx or later.

Policy rules now account for the platform they target:

Platform column: The Policies > Firewall > Rules table includes a new filterable Platform column that shows which operating system each rule applies to.

Existing rules: All rules previously defined in a policy are automatically set to Windows as their default platform.

Protocol support: The complete list of macOS-supported protocols is available on Bitdefender Support Center here.

The rollout of the Firewall module on macOS endpoints will take place in phases, so availability in individual environments may follow the console update.

Service API Keys

Automated integrations such as SIEM connectors, ticketing systems, and orchestration scripts often run on API keys tied to an individual user account, so the integration’s access depends on that user’s account and permissions. GravityZone now introduces dedicated service API keys and associated service accounts that manage automated integrations and API access independently of user API keys.

Service API keys are managed from the new Accounts > Service API keys page, with options to create, edit, clone, suspend, activate, and delete keys. You can configure each key with specific API module permissions, a target company and folder scope, and an expiration period of 1 to 365 days. Access to the page is controlled by the new Manage service API keys permission, available in the user account settings under Accounts.

Key lifecycle events are recorded in the User activity log, and administrators can receive email and Control Center notifications before keys expire. This keeps integration access auditable and scoped to the companies and API modules each integration needs.

More information about service API keys can be found on the Bitdefender Support Center here.

API Enhancements

Bitdefender Control Center APIs enable developers to automate business workflows. These APIs are exposed via the JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol. You can find usage examples and documentation in our Support Center, located here.

This update introduces new methods, push events, and response parameters to support incident assignment and tracking, service API key permissions, scan task visibility, network inventory, and macOS package configuration.

Incidents: The new assignIncident method assigns and reassigns Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) incidents to eligible GravityZone users in bulk, and also removes assignees. All assignment changes are recorded in the Incident history panel and on the User activity page in GravityZone Control Center. Actions performed by Managed Detection and Response (MDR) analysts are attributed to an MDR Service account.

Event Push: Six new Event Push API events report EDR and XDR incident updates: incident-status-changed, incident-assignee-changed, incident-priority-changed, incident-note-created, incident-note-updated, and incident-note-deleted. They are turned on through the existing setPushEventSettings method. The Task Status push event payload now also includes the parentTaskId parameter for correlating parent tasks with their child subtasks.

Companies: The getCompanyDetails method now returns the status of companies undergoing migration between partners instead of a generic error.

Accounts: Accounts API methods now support the manageServiceAPIKeys permission, which corresponds to the Manage service API keys permission described in the Service API Keys section above. The createAccount, updateAccount, getAccountsList, and getAccountDetails methods now accept and return the updated role identifiers used with service API keys.

Network: The getTaskStatus response now includes the subTaskId (unique child task identifier) and scanType parameters in the subtasks object for scan tasks (Type 1). This identifies the scan type: Quick Scan, Full Scan, Custom Scan, Network Scan, Memory Scan, or YARA Scan. The getEndpointsList and getNetworkInventoryItems methods now also return the endpoint’s public IP address in the publicIp parameter.

Packages: The createPackage, updatePackage, and getPackageDetails methods now support configuring and installing the Firewall module on macOS endpoints.

For comprehensive insights into the GravityZone API, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

To learn more about the Bitdefender GravityZone platform, contact us or a Bitdefender partner for more information. You can also start a free trial by requesting a demo here.

As the digital landscape evolves, Bitdefender stays ahead, providing prevention, protection, detection, and response capabilities to help keep organizations of all sizes worldwide safe.

Title: Bitdefender Threat Debrief | October 2026
Context: Citrix NetScaler vulnerability is added to the KEV catalog: Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-88779 to crash NetScaler ADC and Gateway devices that have logon via SAML enabled
Full Text:
Operation KillSwitch Halts KillSec’s Ransomware Activity

This edition of the Bitdefender Threat Debrief covers the latest developments in the ransomware threat landscape: We have details on Operation KillSwitch, a look at how ShinyHunters’ tried to ransom a competing group, and news about which group announced the end of their ransomware operations.

As ransomware continues to evolve, our goal with this monthly Bitdefender Threat Debrief is to help you stay ahead of the curve. To do this, we combine information from openly available sources (OSINT) - things like news reports and research – with data we gather by analyzing Data Leak Sites (DLSs), websites where ransomware groups post details about their victims. We can't independently verify all these claims, but we are confident in the trends we see over time.

For this month's report, we analyzed data from September 1 to September 30 and recorded 790 claimed ransomware victims. This was a 30% increase vs. September 2025.

Featured Story: Operation KillSwitch Halts KillSec’s Ransomware Activity

What Happened?

On September 30, 2026, the international operation known as Operation KillSwitch, resulted in law enforcement’s seizure of KillSec’s data leak site which held more than 10 TB of data. Law enforcement also seized several of KillSec’s servers. Agencies from multiple regions, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Spain, Belgium, Switzerland, Romania, and Greece supported the takedown operation.

According to the recent publication by Europol, three KillSec members were arrested as a result; KillSec’s operator found in Spain was identified as young teen. Bitdefender began tracking Killsec in 2024 and contributed to Operation KillSwitch.

How Did KillSec Catch the Attention of Law Enforcement?

KillSec started operating as a Ransomware as a Service group towards the end of the second quarter in 2024. Before emerging as a RaaS group, they also ran hacking campaigns. It’s estimated that KillSec has claimed at least 500 victims and conducted more than 1000 attacks.

Notably, the group has claimed victims in the public sector based in regions that include North America, Southern Europe, and Western Europe. KillSec’s victim demographic includes a high volume of small to mid-sized organizations. Contrary to popular belief, many of the breaches the group has conducted do not involve executing ransomware; instead, the group may scan for and exploit weaknesses in cloud platforms to identify data of interest and exfiltrate it from the victim’s system.

What is a Takedown and What Does this Mean for KillSec’s Future?

A takedown is an operation intended to seize the resources criminals use and shut down their activity. The eventual prosecution of staff and connected affiliates is a huge outcome that may result from the takedown; however, this is not always likely, especially for criminals in leadership roles who may be evasive. Operation KillSec was impactful because several KillSec Staff were identified and arrested. While some ransomware groups may collapse after a takedown, it is far more common for groups to rebrand and operate under a different moniker. Organizations should remain cognizant of this fact, regardless of outcomes that may affect KillSec or other ransomware groups in the future. The seizure of the KillSec site and servers and arrest of KillSec staff is encouraging, but it is difficult to account for other factors including hidden backup infrastructure, historical affiliate growth, and other external partnerships and resources that may remain.

What Actions are Recommended for Organizations?

Takedowns are intricate, layered processes that follow large-scale joint investigations. Organizations should not wait for law enforcement agencies to investigate before seeking additional guidance on containing or recovering from an incident. The following actions are recommended:

If impacted by a ransomware attack, contact law enforcement and ensure records are maintained. Victim reporting is just one way that LE can collate information on a ransomware group’s movements.

Remain informed about regulations and current policies concerning breach notification

Ensure that the digital forensic and incident response teams deployed have exercised due diligence in collecting and analyzing data relevant to the attack

Request and review intelligence on an ongoing basis to evaluate the threat actor’s behavior and current indicators of compromise

Ensure that systems are hardened-following any recovery and lessons learned phases of the incident response process to reduce opportunities for the threat actor to compromise systems again

Watch the Live Discussion

Our expert panel will cover Operation KillSwitch and other notable ransomware developments during our monthly Ctrl-Alt-Decode debrief.

Other Notable Ransomware News

Now, let’s explore the notable news and findings since the last Threat Debrief.

The Gentlemen rises to the top rank again: The Gentlemen has been the most active ransomware group for two of the last three months, including September 2026, when the group claimed a total of 105 victims in September. The group continues to claim victims based in regions beyond North America, including Southern Europe, South America, and Western Europe. The Gentlemen have also continued to claim victims in the manufacturing, retail, construction, technology, and healthcare industries. Known for their insistence on implementing safeguards to secure their sites, the group uses GentleCloud to protect their infrastructure against attacks and minimize opportunities to crawl their site.

ShinyHunters defaces Clop’s site: ShinyHunters recently compromised Clop’s dedicated data leak site after exploiting a vulnerability that allowed them to extract server logs and private keys linked to the Tor service. Clop was encouraged to contact ShinyHunters and submit a Bitcoin payment in the millions alongside an interest fee and public apology for stealing their proof of concept for campaigns leveraging Oracle E-Business Suite exploits. As a result, Clop’s victim count saw a sharp decline in September with only 2 victims claimed.

Citrix NetScaler vulnerability is added to the KEV catalog: Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-88779 to crash NetScaler ADC and Gateway devices that have logon via SAML enabled. The NetScaler ADC and Gateway devices affected include versions released prior to 14.1-73.41 and versions released prior to 13.1-64.28. NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS, 13.1-FIPS, and 13.1-NDcPP are also affected (versions released prior to 14.1-73.41-FIPS and prior to 13.1-37.282). Organizations using Citrix NetScaler devices with SAML enabled are advised to review the vendor documentation to ensure that the flaw is mitigated.

CRPx0 announces the end of their ransomware operations: The group CRPx0 updated the landing page on their data leak site with news that their infrastructure, including their source code, blog, command and control infrastructure, and negotiation platform are now for sale. Listed at $1500, this price could let criminals entering the RaaS space access a suite of tools at a low cost. According to the same post, CRPx0’s Hacking as a Service program remains available. Whether CRPx0 intends to operate under a different brand name in the near future or has joined another entity remains unclear.

Top 10 Ransomware Families

Bitdefender's Threat Debrief analyzes data from ransomware data leak sites, where groups publicize their claimed number of compromised organizations. This approach provides valuable insights into overall RaaS market activity. However, it comes with a trade-off: while it reflects attackers' self-proclaimed success, the information comes directly from criminals and may be unreliable. Additionally, this method captures the number of victims claimed, not the actual financial impact of these attacks.

The Top 10 ransomware groups in September include The Gentlemen, Qilin, and Akira. The Gentlemen ranked first, while Qilin saw a 50% decrease in the number of victims claimed compared to the previous month.

Top 10 Most Attacked Regions

Ransomware gangs prioritize targets where they can potentially squeeze the most money out of their victims. In many cases, this means focusing on developed countries with higher projected growth rates. Threat actors may also launch strategic attacks during geopolitical conflicts or periods of social unrest.

US victims fall significantly: While the United States continues to make up the largest demographic, fewer victims were claimed in September. Other regions saw slight decreases, and Japan ranked number 10. In September, ransomware groups claimed mostly victims in the technology industry in this region.

Top 10 Most Attacked Industries

Ransomware gangs may target organizations in critical infrastructure sectors, select other organizations that offer consumer-facing services, or attack organizations that fall into both categories. Understanding the trends and ramifications associated with specific industries, and how specialized services and clientele are impacted, is crucial for assessing risk. Here are the Top 10 industries affected by ransomware attacks.

In September, the manufacturing industry saw a decrease in the total victim population. Education and research remained in the Top 10. Also, the transportation industry rose to the number 10 position during September.

More than 180 technology brands have licensed and added Bitdefender technology to their product or service offerings. This vast OEM ecosystem complements telemetry data already collected from our business and consumer solutions. Bitdefender Labs discovers 400+ new threats each minute and validates 30 billion threat queries daily. This gives us one of the industry’s most extensive real-time views of the evolving threat landscape.

Title: Malware Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) | Recorded Future
Context: An IoC can provide the first concrete lead, while TTPs can help analysts search for related activity after an attacker changes a domain or recompiles malware
Full Text:
One malware hash can turn a vague alert into a concrete investigation. Analysts can search endpoints for the exact file, trace where it appeared, and determine whether related activity exists elsewhere. But if the attacker changes the file, the hash changes too. Domains and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses can also lose relevance as attackers rotate infrastructure.

This is why malware indicators of compromise work best as evidence within a larger investigation, not as isolated entries on a blocklist. Their value grows when analysts can establish where an indicator came from, how recently it was observed, what threats are connected to it, and whether those connections matter to their organization.

Malware indicators of compromise are technical artifacts or observations that suggest malicious activity. They help security teams detect, investigate, and contain threats, but an IoC is most useful when analysts can assess its source, timing, confidence, and relationship to other threat activity.

Key takeaways

Malware indicators can include file-based artifacts, network infrastructure, and other technical evidence associated with malicious activity.

IoCs do not exclusively describe past attacks. They can point to malicious activity that may be underway or has already occurred.

Indicator types have different defensive lifespans. An IP address may quickly lose relevance, while a file hash remains an exact identifier for the same sample even if attackers create a new version.

Threat intelligence can add context that helps analysts prioritize IoCs, connect related activity, and move from an isolated match toward a wider investigation.

What are malware indicators of compromise?

An indicator of compromise (IoC) is a technical artifact or observable that suggests malicious activity. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines IoCs broadly enough to include signs that an attack may be imminent, underway, or that a compromise may already have occurred.

For a security operations center (SOC) analyst or incident responder, an IoC can help answer a practical question: Have we seen evidence associated with this threat in our environment?

Analysts can use malware IoCs to validate an alert, search logs and endpoints for related activity, or scope an incident after malicious activity is confirmed. They can also use an indicator as a starting point for investigating connected infrastructure, malware, or attacker behavior.

An IoC does not automatically prove that an organization has been compromised. Context matters. Finding a malware hash executing on an endpoint carries a different meaning from finding the same hash in an intelligence feed.

IoCs and TTPs serve different purposes

Indicators of compromise identify observable evidence associated with malicious activity. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) describe how an adversary operates.

A specific command-and-control domain is an IoC. The techniques an attacker repeatedly uses to establish persistence or move through a network are TTPs.

Atomic indicators are often easier to match against security telemetry, but attackers may be able to change them quickly. TTP-based detection can be harder to evade when it focuses on established attacker behavior, but it can also demand richer telemetry and more detection engineering.

Security teams do not need to choose one or the other. An IoC can provide the first concrete lead, while TTPs can help analysts search for related activity after an attacker changes a domain or recompiles malware.

The most common types of malware indicators

Malware indicators generally appear either in files and host activity or in network communications. Each gives analysts a different view of what the malware has done.

File-based IoCs

File hashes such as SHA-256 fingerprints allow security tools to identify an exact known file. They provide a precise match, but attackers can alter a malware sample and generate a new hash.

Other file and host artifacts can reveal how malware operates after reaching a system. Analysts may examine suspicious file names and paths along with changes malware makes to the operating system, such as registry activity or mutex creation.

These artifacts can help investigators determine whether the same malware has appeared elsewhere in the environment.

Network-based IoCs

Network indicators show where malware connects or where malicious content is hosted.

These may include IP addresses associated with command-and-control infrastructure, domains used to distribute malware, or URLs connected to malicious activity. Analysts can also examine characteristics of network traffic when those characteristics are specific enough to the threat.

Network IoCs can help teams find infected systems that contacted known malicious infrastructure. Their usefulness can change over time because infrastructure may be abandoned, reassigned, or shared with legitimate services.

Why raw IoCs have limits

The main problem with raw malware indicators is not that they are useless. It is that the indicator alone often does not tell an analyst enough to make a good decision.

Indicators can lose defensive value quickly

Threat actors can move command-and-control infrastructure, register new domains, or change malware files to avoid known indicators. This makes some IoCs highly time-sensitive.

It is more accurate to think in terms of defensive lifespan than to assume every IoC simply expires. A hash continues to identify the same file, for example, but it stops detecting new versions once an attacker changes the sample.

A malicious label does not provide organizational context

An IP address listed as malicious does not tell a SOC whether its own systems communicated with it, whether the activity is current, or what defensive action is appropriate.

This is where raw feeds can create unnecessary analyst work. Teams must investigate why an indicator was flagged and decide whether that evidence applies to their environment.

Recorded Future recommends combining external indicator context with internal network data and subjecting indicators to organizational vetting before using them for detection in its guidance on indicators of compromise.

More indicators can create more noise

Threat intelligence feeds can contain overlapping, stale, or irrelevant information. Adding feeds without a way to assess their quality can increase alert volume without giving analysts better evidence.

Volume can still matter when a source provides useful threat coverage. It should not serve as the only measure of intelligence quality. Timeliness, confidence, provenance, and relevance also affect whether an indicator deserves attention.

IoCs do not provide complete threat visibility

Threat intelligence can tell analysts a great deal about an indicator that has already been observed. It cannot provide context for infrastructure or malware that its collection sources have never seen.

Better information about known IoCs can improve interpretation, but it does not guarantee complete threat visibility.

How threat intelligence makes malware indicators more useful

Security teams can get more value from IoCs by connecting individual observations to evidence that explains why they matter.

Recorded Future malware intelligence connects malware samples with associated IoCs and threat context. It also supports automated YARA rule generation for malware hunting.

Add context before taking action

Useful context can show when an indicator was observed, what malware is associated with it, and what other infrastructure or activity is connected to it.

Recorded Future uses Risk Scores to help analysts prioritize indicators. These scores can help determine what deserves attention, but they should inform security decisions rather than replace organizational context.

Automate repetitive IoC work

Large indicator volumes make manual lookup difficult. Application programming interfaces (APIs) and security integrations can automate IoC lookup, add threat context, and bring external intelligence into existing security workflows.

Recorded Future Cyber Operations supports these workflows through threat intelligence, APIs, and integrations.

Automation does not need to mean automatic blocking. Teams can automate research and prioritization while applying stronger requirements before an indicator triggers a direct enforcement action.

Turn individual indicators into threat-hunting leads

An IoC often becomes more useful when it leads analysts to related activity.

A malware sample can point investigators toward related variants, behaviors, and infrastructure. Recorded Future malware intelligence includes Auto YARA, which analyzes malware samples for distinctive patterns and generates YARA rules that analysts can use in malware hunting.

This lets teams move beyond searching only for a known hash and look for related files that share useful characteristics. Recorded Future University's guide to malware hunting provides more detail on how threat hunters approach that work.

Best practices for an IoC-driven security program

A useful IoC program should focus on the quality of security decisions rather than the size of the indicator database.

Check context before enforcement. Establish the source, confidence, and timing of an indicator before deciding whether it should trigger blocking or containment.

Match automation to the consequence. Automating lookup and prioritization carries less operational risk than automatically blocking infrastructure. Raise the confidence requirement as the action becomes harder to reverse.

Connect external intelligence with internal evidence. External threat data can show why an indicator deserves attention. Internal telemetry shows whether that threat has reached systems that matter to your organization.

Review active indicator sets over time. An indicator that no longer belongs in an active detection or blocking rule may still have value for historical investigation. Removing it from active enforcement does not mean deleting the intelligence.

Recorded Future's research into malware and vulnerability trends provides further context on changing malware activity and the threats defenders need to watch.

The future of IoC detection

Attackers can change hashes, IP addresses, and domains to evade known indicators. Security teams, therefore, need ways to connect individual IoCs to related malware activity and attacker behavior.

Automated malware analysis and detection-rule generation can help teams move from a new observation to a broader hunt with less manual work. This does not make atomic indicators obsolete. It gives teams another way to use them alongside behavioral detections and threat context.

Recorded Future combines malware analysis with threat intelligence so security teams can investigate individual IoCs in the context of related malware, infrastructure, and behavior.

Ready to spend less time chasing stale or low-value indicators? Request a demo to see how Recorded Future can help your team add context to malware IoCs and put threat intelligence into existing security workflows.

FAQs about using malware IoCs in security operations

Are YARA rules the same as malware IoCs?

No. An IoC is an observable artifact or piece of evidence associated with malicious activity. A YARA rule is detection logic that searches files or other data for defined patterns. Analysts can create YARA rules from characteristics found during malware analysis, allowing them to search for related samples rather than relying on one exact file hash.

How are malware indicators of compromise collected and shared?

IoCs can come from malware analysis, incident investigations, security telemetry, threat research, and intelligence-sharing communities. Organizations can share structured threat information using standards such as Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX), while Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information (TAXII) supports the exchange of that information between systems.

Are indicators of attack the same as indicators of compromise?

No, although the distinction is not simply that one predicts an attack and the other describes the past. Indicators of attack (IoAs) focus on behaviors or activity associated with attacker intent or an attack in progress. IoCs identify technical evidence associated with malicious activity, which may relate to activity that is ongoing or has already occurred.

Can two intelligence sources assess the same IoC differently?

Yes. Intelligence sources may rely on different observations, collection methods, scoring systems, and timeframes. Infrastructure can also change ownership or use over time. Analysts should consider the source, supporting evidence, and observation dates rather than assuming every malicious classification carries the same meaning.

Title: Applying Security by Design and Cyber Immunity principles to protect AI systems | Kaspersky official blog
Context: Architects should always consider swapping a large, do-it-all framework for a compact, stripped-down system that has only the features a specific agent actually needs
Full Text:
AI systems are much harder to protect than traditional IT — whether from operator mistakes, malicious interference, or just plain unstable behavior. There are two main reasons for this. First, AI outputs are probabilistic, so the same prompt can give different answers each time you run it. Second, today’s LLMs can’t reliably tell commands apart from data. Despite the demonstrated security issues of AI systems that we’ve covered many times, it’s impossible to ignore the potential economic payoff of adopting them. That’s why many companies are moving beyond simple AI assistants to AI agents. These agents carry out tasks on their own and have direct access to the same tools as humans — from reading databases to changing settings in production processes. Our experts, in their new study, examine how to clearly define and minimize the resulting risks to keep potential problems to a minimum. The approach borrows and adapts the principles of Cyber Immunity and Security by Design.

The basic principles of Security by Design

All the principles of this discipline are universally applicable to the design of any computer system — AI agents included. What differs is how deeply each principle needs to be adapted and reworked for AI scenarios.

Security is a separate and important factor right from the design stage. Security goals and assumptions are set on day one and followed throughout every stage of development. For AI agents, these assumptions should include three key points: (i) the language model is treated as untrusted, (ii) external data of any kind is considered potentially malicious, and (iii) irreversible actions can’t be performed autonomously without mandatory human approval.

The system is designed on the assumption that it will be attacked.

The trusted computing base and attack surface are kept to a minimum. Agents get only the tools they actually need, limited permissions, and the smallest amount of context possible. Security policy enforcement is handled entirely by deterministic components: the policy monitor, the agent harness, and isolation mechanisms (sandboxes).

The principle of least privilege applies. Each agent has its own set of credentials and access privileges (identity), limited to the bare minimum it needs to do its job. If an agent temporarily needs elevated privileges, it gets them only after external approval, and they last exactly as long as the task that requires them.

Components are isolated. In agent-based systems, this is one of the most complex and multi-layered architecture problems. The agent harness should run in an isolated environment (sandbox or virtual machine), and agents should be kept as isolated from each other as possible. Data processing in trusted and untrusted contexts is also kept separate. For example, one agent reads a pull request and writes a draft of the code, while another reviews that work without ever seeing the potentially malicious text of the request.

Default deny is the rule. Security policies follow the rule: anything not explicitly allowed is forbidden. This includes tool calls, interactions between agents, and network traffic.

Defense in depth is in place. Different measures should work at the same time and reinforce each other. Probabilistic defenses — like AI guardrails (a “firewall” for language models) or alignment (the model’s own sense of what’s acceptable and what isn’t) — can’t offer any formal security guarantees. Nevertheless, they make the system more secure overall and serve as a valuable source of telemetry.

The supply chain is protected. Some agents can install skills, libraries, and other software components on their own, so these abilities need strict rules. Either block them completely, or limit them to a closed, pre-approved list of specific versions of specific components. Systems built on cloud LLMs face an extra risk: model updates. One day, the same API request might be answered by a different language model with different security properties.

Pitfalls of AI security

The general principles of Security by Design are well known and look simple on paper. But applying them to AI systems is tricky because agents are incredibly flexible. For example, a security team might believe that an agent on a developer’s computer runs in a sandbox and can’t change anything outside it. But an attacker, or even the agent itself, can come up with dozens of ways around this seemingly solid protection: from running commands through a local MCP server that the sandbox doesn’t restrict, to reconfiguring another AI agent installed on the system. To make things even harder, the range of attack vectors is huge: from arbitrary fields in the agent’s configuration to innocent-looking text strings in a skill file.

One serious problem that designers often underestimate is user fatigue. A busy agent can throw up dozens of requests every minute, asking the user to confirm potentially dangerous actions. Within an hour, the person is clicking Approve on autopilot without reading what they’re approving. That’s why it’s important to carefully tune both how often these requests appear and how they’re worded. Nobody will read a request description that’s too long. And one that’s too short can hide the key details the user needs in order to make the right call.

Vulnerabilities in agents and related tools are a pressing problem — and it’s made worse by how quickly these categories of software evolve and receive updates. Industry-standard platforms and apps — such as LangGraph, MS Semantic Kernel, and Claude Code — have had critical vulnerabilities patched more than once. Architects should always consider swapping a large, do-it-all framework for a compact, stripped-down system that has only the features a specific agent actually needs.

On top of that, carefully implementing standard, long-established security measures in the available tools greatly reduces the damage if an agent is attacked or behaves unexpectedly. One example is a strict allowlist of domains that the web fetch tool can open when asked by the agent. But designers rarely account for the hidden problems and overhead associated with maintaining the list. As a result, it slowly goes out of date and leaves loopholes for attackers. The most striking example is the EchoLeak attack. Microsoft 365 Copilot had a properly implemented and fairly effective allowlist for accessing external sites, but attackers circumvented it through a feature in a secondary tool and the MS Teams domain.

Practical tips for architects and security teams

AI system architects and heads of engineering and security teams should build in agent security from the design stage. They should rely primarily on verifiable, deterministic mechanisms: isolating components, controlling interactions, and keeping the trusted computing base to a minimum.

Key architectural decisions include defining acceptable autonomy for the agents, limiting access to confidential data and dangerous combinations of capabilities, and using sandboxes, separate roles for different models, and access control gateways. Restrictions added as an afterthought reduce risks, but they’re no substitute for secure architecture.

At the organizational and operational levels, companies need to keep an inventory of their agents, coordinate the efforts of security and deployment teams, protect container environments, manage the supply chain (AIBOM), and integrate multi-layered defense.

Observability requires special attention. For AI systems, this should include logging the LLM’s requests, responses, and reasoning, as well as detailed telemetry from the hosts and cloud environments where the agent harness runs.

The hardest part of designing agents is balancing security, performance, and usefulness. To learn how to strike that balance with threat modeling and clearly defined security goals, read the full version of the study.

Title: AI Agents Won’t Go Rogue, They’ll Inherit Overprivileged Access
Context: After the first block, the agent tried a workaround: The agent found no other path, stopped, and reported back: The agent, the task, and the persistence were the same
Full Text:
What you will learn

Here's how an AI agent inherits your admin rights, edits the policy that blocked it and finishes the task anyway, and how zero standing privilege and just-in-time (JIT) access limit what agents can do on your behalf.

The agent found out who it was working for.

Our core belief at Delinea is that organizations need to secure agent access alongside human access. Our teams are adding capabilities to the Delinea Platform that put this belief into practice. One of these capabilities enables runtime authorization policies to determine whether a human or an agent is acting.

To test that capability, I wrote a policy that enables a human to write to a database and stops the agent working for that human from changing anything in the same database.

The policy worked. The test also showed me how far an agent will go to finish a task.

To secure agents, you must make sure the humans behind them have zero standing privilege; meaning no one holds admin rights until a task requires them.

Why I ran the "human or agent" test

Engineering teams now give AI agents such as Claude Code access to production systems, including source code repositories, databases and cloud infrastructure.

An agent reads a repository, connects to a database and runs commands that nobody typed. Most access controls were built for people, and they make one decision: whether a user can connect. Once the connection opens, the user can run any command the database credential permits.

That model breaks down for agents. An agent that needs to read sales data does not need to change it, even when the person who launched the agent needs to do both.

Delinea runtime authorization enforces policy per action, not only per connection. A gateway sits between the user and the database, inspects each action and checks it against policy before the action reaches the database. The gateway can apply one set of rules to a human and a different set to the agent that human launched.

I wanted to see that work with Claude Code against a live Postgres database, so I set up a test environment.

The test

Before the test, I wrote a policy for the database. The policy had three rules:

Users must request just-in-time (JIT) access.

Agents can read but cannot write.

Humans can read and write.

I pointed Claude Code at a Postgres database behind the Delinea gateway and gave it a one-line task:

The agent requested access, and an approval workflow approved the request automatically. The agent then ran several SELECT statements to find the sales table and return the last five orders. The gateway checked each action against the policy. The reads worked.

Then I asked for a write:

The gateway blocked the write, as my policy required. The agent diagnosed the failure:

The database credential held full insert privilege, so Postgres would have accepted the write. The gateway blocked the write before the statement reached Postgres.

When I ran the same insert myself, outside Claude Code, the write succeeded. Postgres inserted two rows, and a follow-up query returned the new order:

The database and the gateway did not change. Only the identity changed. Delinea runtime authorization checks each action at the gateway and bases each decision on the policy defined for that identity.

The part I didn’t plan for

I also ran the same test while logged in to Delinea as an administrator. I was over-privileged, as admins tend to be.

The gateway recognized Claude Code and blocked the first write. Then the agent did what a persistent engineer would do. The agent investigated the denial, identified the responsible policy, and began editing it so the write would go through.

The agent could edit the policy because the agent acted on my behalf. As an administrator, I had the right to edit policies, so the agent had that right too. My policy limited what the agent could do in the database. Nothing limited what the agent could do as an administrator.

The agent had no hidden agenda. I had told the agent to insert an order, and the agent was trying to finish the task.

What the agent did

The agent reasoned in a straight line from “I was blocked” to “the block is a policy” to “I can edit the policy.” Each step was sensible. None of the steps was malicious. Together, the steps led the agent from the database to the policy that protects that database.

The same agent without admin rights

In the recorded run, I was not logged in as an administrator. After the first block, the agent tried a workaround:

The agent found no other path, stopped, and reported back:

The agent, the task, and the persistence were the same. Only my authority changed.

What the two runs show

1. Agents inherit your authority

An agent acting on your behalf can do what you can do. If you are an administrator, the agent is an administrator too. The agent will use the permissions needed to complete the job.

2. Persistence is the feature, and the risk

Agents are useful because they keep going. An agent diagnoses a failure and tries another way. The same behavior turns a denial into an obstacle to route around. In the recorded run, the agent rewrote its write after the first block and then searched for another access path.

3. Editing policy is a privilege

The right to edit a policy is a privilege, like the right to write to a database. If an agent acts for an identity that holds this privilege, the agent can remove the rule that blocked it.

What to do

Run agents from identities that cannot edit policy. In the test, the agent had its own identity, and the policy treated the agent differently from me. The agent still carried my admin rights because the agent acted on my behalf.

Grant admin rights only when needed. An administrator who holds policy rights all day passes those rights to every agent the administrator runs. Request admin rights just-in-time, for the task that needs them.

Keep access JIT and scoped. In the test, the agent had no standing access. The agent requested access before connecting.

Make denial the end of the road. Write policy at the action level, and give agent identities no other path to the resource. A control that works only if the agent gives up will eventually fail.

Log the attempts. Across both runs, the agent hit a denial, rewrote the write, searched for another access path and edited the policy. Each step belongs in your logs.

Secure the human behind the agent

Runtime authorization gave me what I wanted. Agents could read, humans could write, and the gateway decided each action. The admin run showed the other half of the story.

To secure agents, make sure the humans behind them have zero standing privilege

Policy-based authorization is only as strong as the weakest identity that can edit the policy. The agent didn’t break the control. The agent borrowed the most powerful credential in the room and turned it on the control.

Run the test yourself

Before you connect an agent to production, check whether the agent's identity can edit its own policy. To run this test on your own resources, request a demo.

Title: China Espionage Actor Actively Targeting Critical BeyondTrust Flaw, Google Warns
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A suspected China state-sponsored actor has exploited a newly disclosed critical vulnerability in a BeyondTrust Remote Support instance, Google has warned.

The threat actor, tracked as Armory Castle, was observed to escalate privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of the flaw, CVE-2026-102764, in August 2026.

BeyondTrust publicly disclosed the vulnerability, which has a CVSS rating of 9.3, on October 15.

A patch was released on October 8 for software-as-a-service (SaaS) and self-hosted customers. The vendor said it is withholding technical details of the vulnerability, as disclosing such information while appliances are still being patched could put customers at an increased risk.

In its blog published on October 15, Google urged affected BeyondTrust customers to apply patches immediately.

“Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as Armory Castle and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public,” the tech giant wrote.

Armory Castle is an espionage actor that has been active since October 2023. It is known for long-term intelligence collection on behalf of the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The group’s documented targets include legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology companies, and government.

Google has assessed with high confidence that Armory Castle will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective.

Armory Castle’s Post-Exploitation Techniques

Following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Armory Castle’s post-compromise tactics were designed to establish persistence and enable lateral movement in victim environments. Google noted that this approach was tailored for BeyondTrust systems.

A significant part of Armory Castle’s activity was the deployment of Sawfly, an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted command and control (C2) communication.

Armory Castle used the webshell to escalate privileges by copying the system shell executable to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd, then modified the file’s ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions.

This effectively granted the attackers a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system. They then elevated privileges from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host, providing access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset.

The threat actor attempted to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database by leveraging the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials.

Persistent access was achieved by targeting the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account.

The researchers highlighted how the actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from ‘No Access’ to ‘Administrator’. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list.

Armory Castle also utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment.

A tunneler tool called Bareclaw was deployed to move traffic through the BeyondTrust device.

Additionally, Armory Castle sought to evade detection by systematically deleting system, web server and application-level logs.

“Throughout the intrusion, Armory Castle leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing,” the Google researchers wrote.

Title: Behind the tags: How Elastic SIEM grades 1,781 detection rules on noise, speed, and threat coverage
Context: Threat: Deterministic first, AI-assisted as a fallback The Threat tag communicates the detection priorities defined by our Threat Research and Detection Engineering (TRaDE) team
Full Text:
Of Elastic's 2100+ prebuilt detection rules, 385 are tagged Profile: Recommended and 296 are tagged Aggressive. The rest (62% of the list) are deliberately left untagged. Prebuilt rule now carries tags like Noise: Low, Performance: Fast, and Profile: Recommended, recalculated every month from real fleet telemetry rather than fixed once and left alone. This post covers how the scoring actually works and how to use the tags to decide what to enable first.

Elastic SIEM rule metadata has two jobs

Most of the prebuilt rule metadata answers the question What does this rule detect? The metadata includes the MITRE ATT&CK technique and the data source, along with the platform. Together, these provide static context.

The new Noise, Performance, Threat, and Profile tags answer something different: How does this rule behave in production? We now have the answer to this question that users have been asking. This operational context changes over time as environments grow, adoption shifts, and detection patterns evolve. A rule that's quiet today might become noisy after a platform update. A rule tagged Noise: Unknown when it first ships will eventually accumulate enough fleet signal to get a real label.

Updated monthly using real-world usage data, these tags stay fresh and deliver actionable insights, and that’s why they’re so valuable.

How Elastic SIEM's monthly tag refresh works

We love data and automation. Once a month, an automated pipeline reads a 30-day window of telemetry across Elastic deployments and scores every prebuilt rule across four dimensions: Noise, Performance, Threat, and Profile.

The inputs are:

Analytics telemetry. Alert volume, distinct cluster counts, and firing density per rule.

Execution metrics. Average, 95th-percentile, and maximum execution times.

The rule's own TOML. Severity, age, platform, and existing tags.

The scoring is entirely deterministic. We do use large language models (LLMs) in one place, but only as a fallback for Threat classification on rules where our heuristic catalog has nothing to say. We cover more on that below.

Every month, the pipeline automatically opens a draft pull request (PR) on elastic/detection-rules with the proposed updates. Our Elastic Security Labs Threat Command team reviews that PR before anything merges: which rules moved between Recommended and Aggressive, which changed Noise or Performance buckets, and which gained or lost Threat tags. The pipeline generates the proposal, and the team makes the call.

Noise: How Elastic SIEM measures alert volume across the fleet

We make a decision on Noise tag based on the total alert volume that a rule generates across the fleet over 30 days. The core metric we use internally is global_noise, which is roughly the mean number of alerts per distinct environment on days that the rule actually fired. This smooths out the difference between a rule that hammers one customer and one that fires occasionally across many.

We classify rules into four buckets:

Noise: Low. Around the 25th percentile for its platform, or fewer than 100 total alerts in the window, or six-months-or-older with essentially no signal (we treat long-lived quiet rules as low noise rather than broken).

Noise: High. At or above the 85th percentile, or extreme alert density relative to the number of distinct environments, or a new rule that came out loud in its first 60 days.

Noise: Medium. Everything between Low and High.

Noise: Unknown. Less than 60 days old with too little signal to tell "quiet" from "not yet widely enabled."

That last bucket is worth a bit more explanation. A new rule that barely generates any alerts isn't necessarily low noise; it might just not be enabled in many places yet. We deliberately hold back the Noise: Low label for the first 60 days to avoid misleading you.

For platforms with enough rules in the fleet, such as Windows, Linux, macOS, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Okta, and GitHub, we calculate percentile cuts per platform. Everything else uses a shared fleet fallback, because what counts as "noisy" is genuinely different across environments.

Performance: How expensive is this rule to run?

The Performance tag tracks how long a rule takes to run across different clusters, measured in milliseconds. We use absolute thresholds rather than percentile-based buckets because execution times tend to cluster tightly enough that relative buckets would mislead.

Performance: Very Slow. Average of five seconds or more, or p95 at 15 seconds or more, or 25+ environments with at least one 30-second-plus execution.

Performance: Slow. Average of two seconds or more, or p95 at five seconds or more, or 10+ environments with a 30-second-plus execution.

Performance: Fast. Average of 400ms or less and p95 under one second and no 30-second executions and at least five environments sampled.

Performance: Normal. Enough data to classify, but not Fast, Slow, or Very Slow.

Performance: Unknown. Fewer than 50 total executions or fewer than three sampled environments.

We evaluate in this order: Unknown first (no judgment on insufficient data) and then Very Slow, Slow, Fast, and Normal as the default for everything in the middle. Fast is intentionally strict; it requires clean p95 numbers and enough sampling to be confident, not just a good average.

Threat: Deterministic first, AI-assisted as a fallback

The Threat tag communicates the detection priorities defined by our Threat Research and Detection Engineering (TRaDE) team. These priorities are informed by confirmed true positives observed in our own telemetry, as well as attack techniques and behaviors trending publicly. Examples include Supply Chain attacks, ClickFix, Phishing Kits, remote monitoring and management (RMM) abuse, and similar emerging or high-priority threats. This gives readers a clear view into the threat areas where our detection engineering efforts are currently focused.

We maintain a managed catalog of these Threat categories and use heuristics to match rules to them. Where the heuristic finds a clear match, the tag is applied deterministically. Where it doesn't, we can optionally use LLMs to review the rule and suggest a Threat category, gated by human reviews. The model receives a compact description of the rule and returns candidates, which we then filter against our managed catalog and cap at five tags per rule. The model cannot invent categories outside the approved list.

This keeps AI in a supporting role. Noise, Performance, and Profile are all scored by code. AI helps fill classification gaps for Threat tags, where identifying the appropriate category often depends more on understanding the rule's behavior and context than on threshold math.

Another important detail is that we don't overwrite manually curated tags. If a rule already has Threat: Cobalt Strike or another malware-family label, the pipeline leaves it alone. The same applies to Profile: Beta and other Profile tags set manually. The automated refresh only updates the categories it owns.

Profile: Elastic SIEM's summary score

The Profile tag is where everything comes together. It synthesizes severity, noise, performance, and threat coverage into a single deployment posture recommendation.

Profile: Recommended requires a score of 7 or higher, with two hard gates on top of that: any rule with Noise: High becomes Aggressive, regardless of score, and low-severity rules are never Recommended, regardless of score.

Threat coverage carries the highest weight (+4) because the tags in our managed catalog represent mechanics that we actively track and prioritize. A medium-severity rule with no Threat match typically can't reach a score of 7 without either low noise or fast performance to make up the gap. A high-severity rule with low noise and fast performance hits exactly 7 without any Threat tag (2 + 3 + 2).

Profile: Aggressive applies when a rule is High noise (the hard gate, regardless of score) or when the score falls below 2, except for low-severity rules, which get no Profile tag at all.

If a rule doesn't quite fit Recommended or Aggressive, we simply leave it without a Profile tag. This isn't a gap in our classification; it's intentional. Those rules are worth evaluating on their own terms, and we didn't want to force them into a bucket that oversimplifies the tradeoff.

Currently, 385 of our 1,781 out-of-the-box detection rules (21.6%) are tagged Profile: Recommended, while 296 (16.6%) are tagged Profile: Aggressive. The remaining 1,100 rules (61.8%) are intentionally untagged, reflecting rules that don't currently meet the criteria for either profile. That 1,781 total covers only rules that we can tune through Elastic SIEM rule artifacts. It excludes building block rules, machine learning detections, deprecated rules, promotion rules, threat intelligence rules, and the guided-onboarding test rule.

The snapshot below shows how those profiles are distributed across severity and platform, along with the Threat categories currently represented in the ruleset:

Which Elastic SIEM rules should I enable first?

If you're setting up detection coverage for the first time, start with Profile: Recommended.

Profile: Recommended. These are the rules that we believe are safe to enable broadly: high enough signal quality and low enough operational cost that you won't immediately be buried in noise or slow down your cluster.

Profile: Aggressive. Check the individual Noise: and Performance: tags before enabling. A rule that's Noise: High but Performance: Fast and maps to a tracked Threat might still be worth enabling with a suppression set. The profile score tells you whether a rule is broadly safe to enable; the individual tags tell you which specific tradeoff you're looking at.

Mid-band rules (no Profile tag). Don't ignore these. Some of our most targeted detections sit there, but they require more environment-specific evaluation before a broad rollout.

Noise: Unknown. Treat this as a watch item, not a veto. New rules need time to accumulate fleet signals. Give it a release cycle or two (two to four weeks).

For all of our existing uses, you’ll also notice other tags added to further align toward a predictable and standardized Elastic XDR/Elastic SIEM taxonomy for prebuilt tags. This taxonomy includes tags for:

Domain. The visibility plane the behavior lives in.

Platform. The ecosystem that the rule applies to.

Data Source. The log stream or integration.

Service. Optional specific component.

Vuln. Vulnerabilities and Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs).

Resources. Investigation guides and LLM consumption, among others.

In the coming release, we’ll also include MITRE ATLAS tags to accompany MITRE ATT&CK.

With additional ways to splice your rule search categories, near future search features will allow for more granular questions about coverage, such as Show me recommended (Profile) rules for identity (Domain) coverage related to ConsentFix (Threat) for Entra ID Sign-In Logs (Data Source). Check out our docs, for a catalog of tags now available. In the futuree, we’ll begin removing old tags that no longer align to the taxonomy, reducing duplicate tags and providing a better search experience.

How to give feedback on Elastic SIEM rule tags

Telemetry is voluntarily shared by our users, and it's what makes this whole system work. If you've turned on telemetry sharing, you're directly contributing to more accurate tags for everyone.

If you have feedback on how we're doing this, including rules that you think are miscategorized, thresholds that don't match your reality, or edge cases that we haven't thought about, reach out via our Slack Community or the Discuss forum. The scoring model is something we'll keep iterating on, and your experience in production is exactly the kind of input we want.
