Title: Arctic Wolf Labs: Finding, Prioritizing, and Patching PHP2Shell Exposure
Context: On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race...
Full Text:
On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race between defenders and attackers. The flaws are tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together they’re known as PHP2Shell. Both carry a 9.2 rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 scale. For both vulnerabilities, Arctic Wolf’s Aurora® Agentic SOC helps organizations rapidly identify affected assets, correlate exploitation signals across the environment, and accelerate investigation and response before attackers can establish persistence.

An unauthenticated attacker can use either flaw to run code on a vulnerable server. On Wednesday, October 21, the PHP project released patched versions. PHP2Shell shows how AI is changing the threat landscape. Attackers can now find and weaponize old flaws in widely used technology faster than ever before. Arctic Wolf recommends treating every PHP installation that serves web requests as at-risk presently. Internet-facing Linux web servers without endpoint monitoring carry the highest risk of quiet compromise.

Patching remains the recommended remediation. Security teams should assess exposure immediately, identify likely attack paths, and segment critical systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment. If attackers exploit PHP2Shell, Aurora Agentic SOC is designed to detect the activity that follows, including webshell deployment, unauthorized command execution, persistence attempts, and lateral movement, enabling rapid investigation and response before attacks can escalate.

Overview and Impact

All PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk. That includes PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates the risk highest for mod_php. In PHP’s demonstrated exploit, an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, and control panels like cPanel and Plesk. Many vendor applications bundle PHP without saying so, which makes the affected assets hard to find. Bundled standalone binaries such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe on Windows are easy to miss.

Understanding the Root Cause

CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. PHP can stop while internal request data is only partly set up. Request cleanup may then treat that invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale state flaw. Request-owned internal state can survive after its memory is freed. A later request on the same worker may use that stale state before normal setup resets it. The PHP session upload progress feature is one confirmed path to this flaw, and it’s enabled by default.

Guidance for Arctic Wolf Customers

Inventory every system that runs PHP. Include package-based installs, containers, appliances, and hosting panels. Include vendor software that bundles PHP. Include continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) images.

Identify the PHP branch and package source on each system.

Update to the patched version or confirm your vendor has backported both fixes. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Restart every affected service. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache, NGINX upstream pools, application workers, and containers.

Rebuild container images from patched upstream bases. Patching only the running containers leaves the image exposed.

Move end-of-life PHP to a supported branch.

Record the patched version, vendor advisory, restart time, and validation evidence for each host or image. If a workload can’t be patched right away, document compensating controls and an approved exception with an expiry date.

The PHP project no longer releases updates for 8.1 or older. Some distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes, so check with your vendor.

Audit commands

Use these commands to find PHP packages and confirm that your vendor backported both fixes.

Use stopgaps to reduce exposure while you patch

Configuration changes such as memory_limit or session.upload_progress.enabled are not remediation. PHP states that only an update is a complete solution. The required fix is a patched PHP runtime or a vendor package that explicitly backports both fixes.

If you can’t update right away, PHP lists measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths. These measures do not make an installation safe.

For CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration.

Set a low post_max_size. PHP suggests 8M for applications without uploads and 32M for those with uploads. Keep upload_max_filesize below it.

Enforce request size, field count, and header limits at the web server or proxy.

Skip RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA because they can trigger the vulnerable allocation failure.

For CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or in an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Then restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts.

How Arctic Wolf Labs turns telemetry into outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global SOC telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base. Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This means customers gain coverage against PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance

As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments. Arctic Wolf Labs’ initial investigation has identified numerous scanning efforts as well as malicious exploitation attempts, including passing wget requests to retrieve both ELF and Golang binaries associated with commodity malware.

How the Aurora Superintelligence Platform keeps customers protected

The Aurora Superintelligence Platform helps organizations reduce PHP2Shell risk before and after exploitation. Aurora Vulnerability Management identifies and prioritizes affected assets using live exploit activity and threat intelligence, helping security teams focus remediation efforts where risk is highest.

PHP2Shell vulnerability detections in Aurora Vulnerability Management

The Aurora Agentic SOC monitors the behaviors attackers rely on after exploitation, including webshell deployment, suspicious processes spawned by PHP or web servers, malicious command execution, persistence activity, and lateral movement.

Together, these capabilities help organizations quickly identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation, detect malicious activity, investigate potential compromise, and contain threats while vulnerable systems are being patched. As the threat evolves, Arctic Wolf continuously incorporates new intelligence across the platform to strengthen proactive cyber risk remediation and detection and response capabilities for all customers.

Title: Inside Arctic Wolf and Anthropic’s Trust-First Approach to the Agentic SOC
Context: Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a...
Full Text:
In the recently released 2026 SANS AI in Cybersecurity Survey, nearly two out of three security professionals said they have been given AI-generated guidance that later turned out to be wrong. Not from an experimental tool off in a sandbox, but from systems built into the security stack they were told to rely on. Security teams should not have to live with that. They need to trust the systems that protect them, which is why trust had to be engineered into the foundation of our security operations platform and agentic security operations center (SOC), not bolted on afterward.

Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection

In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a pace human-led security teams were never built to match. Speed doesn’t favor both sides equally. If an attacker’s tool fails, or an AI-generated exploit produces an incorrect result, the cost to the attacker is close to zero. They try again. Defenders do not get that luxury. An AI agent that makes the wrong call inside an organization’s environment, missing a real threat or acting on a false one, can mean damage to that business, and a win for the attacker. An agentic SOC that moves fast but gets it wrong only benefits attackers.

Meeting frontline threats like these takes more than speed. It takes frontier protection, defenses built on AI capable enough to match the attacker and trustworthy enough to be allowed to act.

Why We Chose to Collaborate with Anthropic

That asymmetry is exactly why trust has to be core to what we build, and why we made the decision to collaborate with Anthropic to help us achieve that. Their mission is to ensure the world safely navigates the transition through transformative AI, and for us here at Arctic Wolf, safety and trustworthy AI are inseparable. That alignment, more than any single feature, is why working together made sense from the start.

The first result of that collaboration was the Aurora Security Assistant, which we unveiled at the RSA Conference in 2025. Built in part with Claude models, it gives customers natural language access to security insight uncovered by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, helping them get faster answers to complex security questions via a simple, chat-based interface.

Delivering Trust and Safety from the World’s Largest Commercial Agentic SOC

Over the last 18 months, our collaboration has only deepened. Anthropic’s Claude models now run throughout the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, including the agents within the Swarm of Experts, the agentic framework that executes key functions of our SOC. That framework now supports thousands of organizations worldwide and performs more than 200,000 security investigations a week, a scale that makes the Aurora Agentic SOC the largest commercial agentic SOC in the world.

This week, at Arctic Wolf’s annual Security Operations Summit, Arctic Wolf shared the stage with Ash Alhashim, Head of Enterprise Cybersecurity GTM, Anthropic, who spoke to just how far this collaboration has come.

“Arctic Wolf’s team knows security operations deeply, and that shows in how they’ve put Claude to work,” he said from the stage. “We’ve learned a lot from working with them and we’re glad to keep building together.”

Today, the Swarm of Experts in the Aurora Agentic SOC resolves more than 60% of its investigations autonomously, with high confidence. That level of unassisted resolution comes from technology we’ve built, leveraging Anthropic’s models as part of the foundation. Title: Unboxing Phishing Kits: Huntress Examines 3 Real Kits
Context: More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time
Full Text:
Teach a noob to phish and they'll be scamming for a lifetime. It has never been easier to steal credentials, thanks to a growing number of phishing kits that give aspiring attackers everything they need in one convenient interface.

Huntress Staff Threat Intelligence Analyst Andrea Hatcher and Staff Product Manager Rich Mozeleski stopped by our monthly Tradecraft Tuesday series in October to unpack some recently staged phishing kits and walk through what the resulting malicious activity looks like from the defenders' point of view.

Watch the full video below, and keep reading for clips and other highlights.

Example phishing kits

A phishing kit is a pre-packaged resource with code, templates, and instructions for how to launch a phishing campaign and use the stolen credentials for further malicious activity. Basic kits are often made up of simple HTML and script files that can spin up a single fake login page.

More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time.

Here are three of the many phishing kits that Huntress has analyzed in the last few months, all targeting Microsoft 365 tokens:

EvilTokens

Knight Office

Kali365

EvilTokens hops off the Railway

Just a few weeks before this broadcast, a collaboration between Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit and the FBI led to the arrest of one of the alleged operators of EvilTokens, a device-code phishing campaign that abused the Railway PaaS as a token-harvesting and token-replay engine.

For more on the EvilTokens takedown, watch Rich's conversation with Microsoft's Principal Corporate Counsel Carlton Gammons and Huntress' Chief Legal Officer Lauren Zajac on-demand.

As Rich put it, discovering the EvilTokens campaign in February "opened the dam" for our researchers diving into phishing kits. He noted the kit's professional aesthetic and 24/7 support as akin to a software-as-a-service (SaaS) operation.

Moving beyond passwords

Andrea walked through how the Kali365 control panel is an entire criminal ecosystem in a box, including AI features: "It's not just someone standing up a convincing login page, it's a whole ecosystem that helps an operator acquire infrastructure, collect authentication material, retain access, and even scale it up."

>

With these additional capabilities, phishing kits can help attackers get their hands on a lot more than usernames and passwords. We asked the audience what they thought attackers found most desirable these days, and most of those polled answered an authenticated session token or a persistent foothold.

Modern phishing kids can provide low-skilled attackers with a usable authenticated session with any of the following tactics:

Device-code phishing

Adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing

Token theft and replay

Device-code phishing

Device-code phishing refers to when the user authenticates directly with the identity provider, but the attacker captures the resulting authorization. Device-code flows can reduce friction for attackers because they do not require the victim to surrender a password directly.

Rich shared that an estimated one in six incidents investigated by Huntress' ITDR team involved a rogue device being registered, and 36 percent of the audience members polled had seen device-code phishing in the wild. He points to Conditional Access Policies as a key prevention measure: "The vast majority of Microsoft environments do not need device code flow."

Adversary-in-the-middle attacks

AitM attacks reveal the limitations of MFA; the threat actor relays the authentication flow in real time, either with a fake login page or by intercepting an exchange within the legitimate app. The victim completes the MFA prompt while the attacker captures the resulting session information. This is why successfully completed MFA does not make the session trustworthy on its own.

Token theft and replay

As Andrea put it, "the session can be way more powerful than the password." After an attacker gets their hands on a sign-in token, a phishing kit can help them "replay" it into an active session, where they can access cloud resources and victim email accounts.

If you suspect token replay in your environment, your investigation should move beyond the original phishing page and examine how the token was used. Polled audience members voted sign-in address and new device registration as the top two signals to investigate first if token theft is suspected.

What defenders see, and what to do about it

Andrea emphasized the importance of detecting signals across the chain. One signal is weak; the sequence is strong. Correlate the progression of lure, authentication, token issuance or theft, device registration, mailbox activity.

Andrea drove the point home: "Join the telemetry across the identity provider, the endpoint, the browser context, the network, and the mailbox. We shouldn't just be looking at one signal in the network or one signal in the mailbox. We really need to have that holistic view."

Detection opportunities

Investigate successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure.

Hunt for device-code authentication and automated token refresh.

Review new devices, authentication methods, and mailbox activity.

Response priorities

Containment must address identity artifacts, not just the original lure.

Revoke refresh tokens.

Remove unauthorized devices and Windows Hello credentials.

Restrict or block device-code authentication where possible.

Investigate mailbox access, forwarding rules, and outbound phishing.

Continue hunting after the original phishing domain disappears.

Continuous response loop

Detect correlated identity and endpoint activity.

Revoke or remove persistence mechanisms.

Investigate downstream mailbox and outbound-phishing activity.

Continue monitoring for replay or re-entry after containment.

Title: Attack Reduction in Huntress Managed ESPM: Disrupting ClickFix
Context: Introducing Attack Reduction Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on,...
Full Text:
Mandy was stuck at an airport with a few hours to kill. She decided to get her nails done, so she found a spa listed on the airport's website and clicked through. It looked like the spa's real website, on a normal domain with HTTPS, and Chrome showed no warnings.

Then a CAPTCHA popped up. Nothing too unusual there. It asked for a few "verification steps" to ensure she was a human user:

Press and hold Windows key + R

In the verification window, press Ctrl + V

Press Enter

An example ClickFix attack where a user is told to press "Windows Key + R" and paste a command into the Run dialog that opens.

But this simple sequence of hotkeys actually opens the Windows Run dialog, and in this case, would have pasted a malicious PowerShell command that the webpage quietly copied to the clipboard. (The Windows Run dialog is a small box that lets you type a command or program name and run it right away.)

If Mandy pressed Enter, the command would have downloaded and run a file from the internet. That file sets up persistence through a registry key, installs a remote access trojan, and steals the browser's saved passwords, cookies, and credit card details.

This is not a hypothetical example. This actually happened to a Huntress employee (name changed for privacy). Thankfully, she realized what was going on and didn't get pwned. A LOT of people aren't so lucky. So, this post is about one simple idea: what if "Windows key + R" didn't open anything at all?

What is ClickFix, and why is it everywhere?

ClickFix is a simple social engineering attack that tricks users into running malicious commands they don't understand. It often employs messaging related to fixing a problem, hence the name "ClickFix."

It also works very well. Our 2026 Cyber Threat Report linked ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA scams to over half of all malware loader activity. In our own SOC, ClickFix-style Run dialog attacks now account for 31% of EDR SOC signals.

The lures keep changing: fake Windows Update screens, fake Docker ads, compromised small-business websites, and now malicious AI chatbots. But the classic version almost always ends the same way, with Windows key + R.

Most of your users should never open the Run dialog

Here's what makes this so frustrating. The Run dialog is a power-user shortcut. IT folks love it. Most employees have never opened it on purpose and wouldn't know what to type into it if they did.

We've seen this play out in the data. Across organizations in ESPM Early Access, it's common to see 90% or more of users who never use the Run dialog at all. Which is why they don't recognize the commands they are pasting in as being a problem.

Run dialog box on Windows in which a user has pasted a malicious command, unwittingly copied from a ClickFix attack.

That's a big gap. A feature almost nobody needs is the starting point for nearly a third of what our EDR SOC investigates. Detection still matters, and Huntress Managed EDR's Attack Disruption engine can kill many ClickFix chains in under a second. But when the attack depends on a feature your users don't need, the simplest fix is to turn that feature off. If only there was an easy way to do that…Oh, wait, now there is!

Introducing Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on, starting with "Windows key + R". That fits what ESPM is built to do: harden your endpoints before an attack ever starts.

ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard

We're starting with the Run dialog, because that's where ClickFix starts. More controls are coming:

Available now: Blocking the Run dialog for users who don't need it to disrupt "Windows key + R" attacks.

Planned: Command Prompt restrictions for users who don't use cmd.exe.

Planned: Interactive PowerShell restrictions for users who don't use it.

Planned: Windows Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that stop Office, script, and email apps from launching or injecting payloads.

Planned: Blocking HTML applications (mshta) for users who don't use them.

How Attack Reduction works

The hard part of turning off a Windows feature isn't flipping the switch. It's knowing who will be affected and not breaking legitimate workflows. Attack Reduction is designed with the following in mind.

1. See who actually uses the Run dialog

Once ESPM is on, Attack Reduction collects each user's Run dialog history and builds a baseline. On the Attack Reduction dashboard, you can see which users rely on the Run dialog and which never touch it, across your whole account or one organization at a time. You'll know exactly who would be affected before anything changes.

The dashboard also flags commands in a user's Run history that look like ClickFix. Windows doesn't record when those commands ran, so treat them as a reason to investigate rather than proof of an active attack.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and how many users are utilizing the Run dialog per week.

2. Turn on blocking

When you're ready, turn on blocking at the account or organization level. Attack Reduction then turns off the "Windows key + R" shortcut for users who don't need it. Users who rely on the Run dialog can keep it, and you can switch any user between allowed and blocked at any time.

3. Users get a clear message, not a mystery

If a blocked user presses Windows key + R, nothing runs. Instead, they see a pop-up explaining that the action was blocked for security reasons and asking them to contact their IT support team or take Security Awareness Training. Either way, the attack stops, and a confused user gets a quick security lesson.

4. You get a record of what they almost ran

When a blocked user presses Windows key + R, Attack Reduction also captures what was on their clipboard. If someone was about to paste a malicious command, you'll have it on record, which helps you spot users who are being targeted and follow up.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and a list of blocked attempts by users to utilize the Run dialog.

What Attack Reduction doesn't do

We want to be clear about the limits here, because ClickFix is a moving target.

Blocking the Run dialog disrupts the most common version of ClickFix. It doesn't stop every one. Attackers can, and already do, tell users to paste commands into File Explorer's address bar, Windows Terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell instead.

That's why the Run dialog is the first step, not the last one. Every path we close makes the attack harder to pull off, and the planned Command Prompt and PowerShell controls are aimed at exactly those next moves. Attack Reduction also works best alongside the rest of your defenses: Managed EDR to catch what gets through, and Managed SAT so users know a real CAPTCHA will never ask them to paste a command.

Get started with Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is available now as part of Huntress Managed ESPM Early Access for existing Huntress partners and customers.

Not in ESPM Early Access yet? Click the ESPM icon in the left-hand menu of your Huntress portal to enroll. Then let Attack Reduction collect a baseline so you can see which users actually need the Run dialog before flipping on Blocking.

As Early Access partners put this capability to work, their feedback will decide which Windows features we tackle next and how we build those controls.

Have ideas or requests? Share them at feedback.huntress.com/espm. And stay tuned. There's a lot more coming to Managed ESPM.

Title: Huntress + AlgaPSA Integration: Built in Days by Nine Minds
Context: Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server
Full Text:
Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server. For partners, that means Huntress data can show up wherever they already work, not just in our portal. It also means software vendors can build their own Huntress integrations on their own schedule, without having to wait on us.

Nine Minds is a great example. Their team built a Huntress integration for AlgaPSA, their professional services automation (PSA) platform, using our public API documentation. No technical support or special access needed. They just read the docs and, a few days later, had a working integration. This post covers what they built, what the experience was like, and what it shows about how you can use the Huntress API.

Meet Nine Minds and AlgaPSA

Nine Minds was founded by Robert Isaacs and Arnie Bellini, who both spent over a decade at ConnectWise. AlgaPSA is their answer to a problem they saw in the industry for years: PSA tools that are too expensive, too complicated, and primarily built for mature organizations.

AlgaPSA brings ticketing, projects, time tracking, billing, and client operations into one platform, and it was designed with the smallest MSPs in mind. As Robert told ChannelE2E, "The small MSP doesn't want to sign a three-year contract." But as they've progressed, larger MSPs have started taking notice, too.

AlgaPSA gives MSPs control over how they run the software with hosted, self-hosted, and open-source options. Over a hundred MSPs now rely on AlgaPSA for day-to-day operations, with more signing up every week.

Why Build a Huntress Integration?

For Nine Minds, the decision came down to two things. Mutual customers were asking for it, and their team spends a lot of time in the MSP community, including at IT Nation, and Huntress is one of the names they see everywhere.

When your users already rely on Huntress to catch threats, the next question is simple: how do those incidents get to the technicians who need to act on them? The AlgaPSA <> Huntress integration provides an answer.

How the Integration Works

The integration is built around the premise that a security incident should never go without a ticket. When the Huntress SOC publishes an incident report, it appears in AlgaPSA as a ticket on a dedicated security board, with the incident summary and a priority based on its severity.

Technicians work it like any other ticket, and the time they log flows into AlgaPSA's billing and invoicing. That means security responses get tracked and billed like the rest of their work, instead of living in a separate console. When the SOC closes the incident, the ticket can close automatically, too. And if an incident comes from a client that hasn't been mapped yet, it still lands on a triage board, so nothing slips through.

Setup takes a few steps:

Connect your Huntress API credentials

Map Huntress organizations to AlgaPSA clients

Choose where tickets land and how severities translate to priorities.

Nine Minds walks through each step in the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs.

A few things to know before you start:

Use a dedicated API key. Huntress API keys are tied to a user and mirror that user's permissions, so it's a good idea to create a separate key just for this integration.

You need AlgaPSA's paid tier. The Huntress integration is part of AlgaPSA's Enterprise Edition (also offered as AlgaPSA Pro). It isn't included in the open-source Community Edition.

Finish routing first. AlgaPSA won't start pulling incidents until the security board, the fallback client and board, and priorities for all three Huntress severities (Critical, High, and Low) are set.

Expect tickets on a schedule, not instantly. AlgaPSA checks Huntress for new incident reports at an interval you choose between one and 60 minutes, so tickets show up at the next check.

What Was It Like to Build on the Huntress API?

This is the part we're most excited about. Nine Minds went from idea to a shipped integration in just a few days.

They built it using our public documentation, without reaching out to us first. After a short period working out which data they needed, Robert said things went smoothly: no confusing fields, no missing endpoints, no documentation gaps that slowed them down. Their team also uses AI coding tools, and pointing those tools at the Huntress API docs was enough to get the job done.

"Integrating Huntress into AlgaPSA was easy enough that we almost felt as if we had missed something... [Then] our customers started thanking us for the integration. Working with Huntress could not have been easier."

– Robert IsaacsFounder / CEO, Nine Minds

Nine Minds also built a Huntress emulator so they could test the integration without depending on live incidents. They told us a dedicated sandbox environment would make that easier, and we've shared that feedback with our team.

What Else Can You Build?

AlgaPSA's integration shows one common pattern: pull incidents from Huntress and turn them into tickets. But the API supports a lot more.

A few examples:

Get incidents in real time. Instead of polling, Huntress Webhooks push incidents and escalations to your PSA, Slack, or SIEM as they happen.

Act on incidents. Approve or reject remediations through the Incident Report response API, and isolate or release hosts through the Agents API.

Automate onboarding. Create, update, and delete organizations programmatically. For example, when a new client is added in your RMM, automation can create the matching Huntress organization and start EDR deployment.

Reconcile billing and build reports. Pull billing reports and per-product organization stats, like agent counts, SIEM storage, and ITDR identity counts, into your dashboards, QBRs, or PSA contracts.

Bring Huntress into AI workflows. The Huntress MCP server connects your AI assistant to your incidents, agents, billing data, and more.

Prefer to see how this works? Watch our video below to see inside the Huntress API, Webooks, and MCP server:

Ready to Learn More?

AlgaPSA's integration started with a customer request and ended with a shipped feature just a few days later. That's the kind of experience we want every developer to have with the Huntress API. If you've been thinking about connecting Huntress to your own tools, the docs are a good place to start.

Build on the Huntress API: Start with the Huntress API docs.

Use Huntress with AlgaPSA: See the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs for setup steps.

Share feedback: Have an idea for an endpoint, webhook, or integration? Add it to our Integrations, Webhooks, and APIs feedback board.

Title: What Does the Dark Web Look Like? Pulling Back the Curtain | Huntress
Context: Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal...
Full Text:
In today’s always-connected world, the line between dark and light is blurring.

Well, actually, you’re still protected from finding out what the dark web looks like because you need to download a special browser to access it. But the drama of the dark web can be intriguing. And it’s not all wicked criminal activity either.

Curious about what’s lurking in the shadows of the internet? Keep reading to learn more about the state of the dark web, what it is, and how to access it (safely, of course!).

What is the dark web?

Everyone has their own preconceived notion of what the dark web is. (Of course, with a name as ominous as dark web, it kind of sets the mood, right?) For the sake of this blog, we focused on finding a credible definition that isn’t muddied with preconceptions.

The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that you can only reach with special tools. Merriam-Webster describes it as a set of sites that search engines don't index and that regular browsers can't open. Reaching them takes specialized software or a specific network setup, and encryption keeps both site owners and visitors anonymous.

(If you were expecting a more sinister-sounding definition for the term dark web, you’re not alone. 😅)

The web, as a whole, can be divided into three parts: the surface web vs. deep web vs. dark web:

Dark web: This is where things get…different. As we said, dark web activity isn't indexed and requires special software or network configuration to access. While it can be a place where people broker illegal activities, it can also be used for legal activities, like anonymously sourcing information.

Surface web: The surface web is everything that’s automatically indexed by search engines. It’s everything that pops up when you Google something (or Bing or whatever search engine), and you don’t need any sort of special software or login to access it.

Deep web: The deep web is sites that are not indexed, but are accessible to the average person, usually through encryption or password protection (or both, both is good!). This includes things like online banking and cloud storage.

Surface web

Deep web

Dark web

Indexing

Accessibility

Standard browser

.com, .org, .net, .gov

Primary content

Private, secured, and dynamic data (e.g., email accounts, online banking, cloud storage, medical records, private company intranets)

Legality

What does the dark web look like?

The dark web often looks surprisingly ordinary—with familiar features like About Us sections, pricing pages, and even customer reviews. You’ll see, though, in the screenshots below, that a lot of sites are basic or outdated, often tricky to navigate.

Many of these sites still work like any other ecommerce website. Threat actors advertise, highlight their skills, and market themselves, their expertise, and their services just like any salesperson.

How does the dark web work?

Frankly, the dark web has earned a bad reputation—and unfairly so. At its core, the dark web isn’t inherently evil or mysterious. (Okay, it's a little mysterious.)

It’s simply a collection of websites that require a specific, anonymity-powered web browser to access. Usually, these sites use a .onion domain and are only accessed through the anonymous Tor Browser.

The dark web isn't all crime and chaos—detectives and journalists sometimes access the dark web to do research while maintaining their anonymity. You can play chess on the dark web. At one point in time, you could even navigate to a Tor website and watch a slideshow of cats and kittens submitted by other users.

The dark web isn't any one thing—it's shaped entirely by how people choose to use it.

How to safely access the dark web

Because there are so many different reasons that you might be interested in the dark web, it’s important to know how to access it safely. Here are some tips:

Use a dark web browser: Use the official Tor browser to access the dark web. This is the essential tool for "onion routing" that provides anonymity.

Use a VPN: While Tor provides encryption, using a high-quality virtual private network (VPN) before launching adds an extra layer of privacy by hiding the fact that you are even connecting to the Tor network from your internet service provider (ISP).

Never use personal information: Don’t log into any personal accounts—email, social media, or bank accounts—while using Tor because it immediately de-anonymizes you.

Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal your identity or install malware.

Know what’s legal: Accessing the dark web is completely legal in the US, but engaging in illegal activities (such as buying/selling drugs, weapons, or accessing child pornography) is a serious felony, regardless of anonymity.

Our journey into the dark web

We’re firm believers in the buddy system when it comes to doing scary things like journeying through the dark web. Don't worry, though— we’ve suited up, strapped on our protective gear, and done the risky part for you.

How did we suit up?

First, we booted up our virtual machine (VM) to add an extra layer of security while browsing. Then, we fired up our anonymous Tor Browser. Finally, we disabled JavaScript—a quick but important safeguard against websites that run malicious code.

With these precautions in place, we were ready to access the dark web. We began our journey by navigating to a few .onion directories to find some ~shady~ websites to peruse.

One of the first things we found? A Tor scam list, complete with "safe" browsing recommendations. How… thoughtful.

Who is using the dark web?

There are About Us pages to answer that question.

Chances are, you wouldn’t hire a plumber without doing some research. You’d want to make sure she’s got the experience and skills to leave your pipes in better shape than she found them. So why would anyone hire a hacker without seeing a well-written About Us page?

You might think this requirement would narrow the pool of hackers to choose from, because are hackers really spending their time writing About Us pages? Yes. Yes, they are.

You’ve got to hand it to them: These hackers did a great job at flexing their hacking skills while staying anonymous. It's not exactly LinkedIn, but the info they share gives these folks some credibility (in a strange way).

If you’ve never browsed the dark web before, you probably weren’t expecting to see several websites with About Us pages. It’s eye-opening to see these hackers flaunting their skills and competing with one another to earn new business.

One site was even gracious enough to list the team’s favorite well-known hackers:

It’s kind of sweet, in a weird sort of way.

The takeaway: Threat actors are just like any other entrepreneurs out to make a profit. The difference? They skip the red tape and regulations that everyone else has to follow. This leaves the door wide open for them to advertise whatever services they please—as long as they abide by the Hacker’s Code of Conduct. (More on that later.)

What’s on the dark web?

Product pages, packaged deals, and more.

Now that we know our threat actors, let’s investigate what they can do for us.

Like any good businessperson, hackers aren’t shy about broadcasting what they can do if the price is right. In fact, some are so business-savvy that they provide packages and tiered solutions:

Others simply prefer to put all their services out there for people to pick and choose from:

But then, we stumbled across two different websites that made us raise an eyebrow. Here’s the first site:

And here's the second site:

These two sites look eerily similar to each other except for one thing: on the latter site, the prices for each service are noticeably higher. That’s weird, wouldn’t you say?

The takeaway: Just like any other website where you can purchase products or services, threat actors also have tiered options, promotional packages, and detailed descriptions of their offerings.

One key difference that seems to be standard across dark web websites is that hackers request that their payments be made in cryptocurrencies. Why? Because it’s anonymous.

Our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, nicely sums up why cryptocurrencies are a hacker’s best friend:

"No other technology offers a bad actor the perfect crime: anonymous threats without borders, blackmail and extortion without a financial oversight or governing authority. [...] Unless the bad actors make any unintentional mistake, the inherent design of cryptocurrency makes for a perfect getaway car."

Dark web customer experience and reviews

Threat actors are actually quite concerned with creating a positive customer experience, with features like customer reviews and FAQ on many of the pages we visited.

The takeaway: Just like any other website selling goods and services, threat actors also want to show that they have happy customers and give potential customers all the info they need to make an informed purchase.

Bottom line: The dark web is a business

If a business owner feels she’s been wronged, there are courts for that. The same can be said for hackers. That’s right—threat actors have their very own court system, along with codes of conduct to follow to minimize the chances of landing there themselves.

What happens in “hacker’s court”? The same thing that happens in any other court: Plaintiffs and defendants get together to tell their respective stories in front of a jury before a ruling is made.

We can't stress this enough: Most bad actors today don’t just hack into websites and devices for the fun of it. These are professionals who become experts in their trade and master their skills to earn a paycheck.

They build websites to sell their services, cut their customers special deals, and ask for reviews from satisfied customers. If they’re wronged, they handle it in a civilized manner in hacker’s court. These are organized operations that function just like any other business.

Don’t be afraid of the dark (web)

We hope that this field trip to the dark web has been enlightening. It’s incredible to see just how many parallels exist between anyone with a “normal” day job and dark web threat actors. Many different careers, from marketing and sales to cybersecurity and infosec, have dark-mirror versions of themselves—hackers and scammers running the same playbooks in reverse—on the dark web.

If nothing else, we hope this blog will make you more vigilant against cyberattacks. Hackers are in it for the money. What could destroy your personal records or your business’s reputation is just another payday for a hacker. Think twice before clicking on an email from an unfamiliar sender. Keep your devices updated and install patches as soon as they become available.

Threats can seem overwhelming, but with our in-depth understanding of how threat actors think, we know what to look for. Huntress gives you fully managed endpoint detection and response (EDR), so you've got 24/7 support from security experts ready to respond to threats.

* Special thanks to our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, for his help with writing this blog.

FAQ

Is it legal to look at the dark web?

Yes, exploring the dark web is legal—as long as you aren’t breaking any laws. If you’re just browsing or doing legitimate research, accessing the dark web is fine. If you engage in any criminal act, you’ll be subject to prosecution.

What is the dark web actually used for?

The dark web is a mixed bag. Some people use it for both legitimate purposes, like preserving privacy and free speech, especially in restrictive countries, and, unfortunately, others for shady activities like selling stolen data or illegal goods.

How do I know if I’m on the dark web?

If you're using a specialized browser like Tor to access websites ending with .onion that aren't reachable through regular browsers or search engines, congrats (or maybe not)—you're on the dark web!

Can you be tracked on the dark web?

The dark web offers more anonymity, but it's not exactly an invisibility cloak. With sophisticated methods and one careless click, determined parties can still track your activities, so anonymity isn't guaranteed.

What is a crime on the dark web?

Crimes on the dark web include activities like selling illegal substances, hacking services, and trafficking stolen data. Basically, if it's illegal in the real world, it's illegal on the dark web too—no free passes.

Title: 7 Key Manufacturing Cybersecurity Trends for 2027 | Huntress
Context: According to our recent cyber threat report, manufacturing made up about 17% of cyber attacks in 2025—a notable jump from 9% in 2024
Full Text:
In manufacturing, a hacked computer is like a wrench in the gears, halting production and losing money—fast.

According to our recent cyber threat report, manufacturing made up about 17% of cyber attacks in 2025—a notable jump from 9% in 2024. It’s one of the slightly startling manufacturing cybersecurity trends that we’re seeing in 2026: an increase in attacks. It’s not all bad, though; other trends are showing that manufacturers are playing quick catch-up by implementing new technologies and protections.

Keep reading to discover the top cybersecurity trends in manufacturing that the Huntress team has uncovered for 2026 and beyond.

Trend #1: Ransomware is targeting your uptime, not just your data

Threat actors have figured out that while you might be able to live without your data for a few days, you can’t survive with a dead assembly line. They’re moving past the office network to disrupt the operational technology (OT) systems that keep your machines running.

While the exact cost changes based on what you’re making, the ripple effects are the same across the board:

Missed shipments: Late deliveries trigger contract penalties and upset your biggest partners.

Idle labor: You’re still paying for staff and overhead, even if no one can do their job.

Restart pains: Getting an OT system back online safely takes much longer than a standard IT reboot.

Safety risks: Sudden shutdowns can damage sensitive equipment or create hazardous conditions for people on the floor or in the plants.

Trend #2: OT, ICS, and IIoT are now in the blast radius

The push for smart factories has removed air gaps in manufacturing, where many industrial control systems (ICS) weren’t connected to the corporate network or directly to the Internet. Between remote access for maintenance, Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensors, and cloud-based performance dashboards, the line between the office network and the shop floor may be gone.

Now, a threat actor doesn't need to walk into your plant with a USB drive; they just need to find one weak point in your corporate network. Once they’re in, those once-isolated systems are suddenly reachable, and because many of them weren't built with modern security in mind, they’re often sitting ducks.

Here is a common path threat actors take to get from a simple email to your control systems:

The foothold: It starts with a successful phishing email to someone in another department, say Sales or Finance. Now, the attacker has a foot in the door on a standard corporate laptop.

The bridge: They use that laptop to scan the network, looking for direct access or bridges—like a jump server or a vendor's VPN appliance —to get access to the manufacturing systems.

The hop: If there aren't strict boundaries (or segmentation) between the office and the plant, they use those stolen credentials to hop into the OT environment. Think of it like a master key—if the door between the finance office and the factory floor isn't strictly guarded, a thief who steals an office key suddenly has total access to the heavy machinery.

Control: Once they’re in the OT network, they look for MES, Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) or Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs). From here, they can change recipe values, stop belts, or even disable safety sensors.

Trend #3: Zero Trust finally hits the factory floor

The old way of thinking was like a castle: once you cleared the moat and got past the front gate, you had the run of the place. But in a modern plant, that’s a massive risk. Zero Trust assumes that every connection—whether it’s a laptop, a vendor, or a sensor—could be a potential invader until proven otherwise.

It sounds intense, but for manufacturing, it’s about being practical. You aren't trying to make life harder for your team; you're just making sure that a breach in the breakroom doesn’t lead to a shutdown on the assembly line. That means having multiple moats and multiple gates to defend your castle.

“Zero Trust architecture can feel like a lot to ask of an organization and its employees,” says Brian Milbier, Senior Director, Security and IT, Deputy CISO at Huntress. “But, what it’s really about is ensuring that every system at every level is protected and that no one is able to gain unauthorized access.”

Here are a few clear-cut ways businesses are making Zero Trust happen right now:

Tighter vendor access: Instead of giving OT manufacturers wide-open access to systems via VPN, you give them access only to the specific systems they need to fix and only for the time they need to fix it.

Segmenting the floor: You wouldn't put your office printer and your $5M CNC machine on the same segment. Creating digital walls between these areas keeps a small problem from becoming a plant-wide disaster.

Verifying every time: Using multi-factor authentication (MFA) for every login, such as at VPN gateways—especially for remote workers or people accessing control systems—is a simple way to stop stolen passwords in their tracks.

Checking device health: Before a device is allowed to talk to your ICS, Network Access Controls (NACs) or Zero Trust gateways check to see if it has the latest security patches or if it’s showing signs of being compromised.

Continuous network monitoring: Look for anomalous behavior by first creating a baseline of network traffic and then monitoring for things like unexpected network connections after hours, spikes in traffic, etc.

Trend #4: Legacy systems are still the soft underbelly

While legacy systems are the backbone of many plants, they’re also a massive target. Whether it's an old HMI running Windows 7 (or even XP!) or a PLC that hasn't seen an update in a decade, these devices are often the easiest way for an attacker to access your operation.

The main problem is that you often can’t patch them. Sometimes the original manufacturer is out of business, or a simple software update might break the very thing that keeps the machine running. This leaves you with outdated systems that are essentially open doors for anyone who knows how to knock.

Legacy systems are threat actors’ favorite endpoint vulnerabilities for a few simple reasons:

They’re predictable: Old software has well-known vulnerabilities that have been documented for years. Attackers don’t have to guess how to get in—they can just Google it.

They’re dark assets: Because these machines are so old, they often don't play nice with modern security tools. This means a threat actor could be hanging out on an execution system for weeks without anyone noticing.

Shared passwords: Back in the day, common passwords like “password” or “1234” were the standard. Many of these systems still use those hard-coded credentials that are used across the devices on the entire floor.

Unnecessary open services: Legacy PLCs and HMIs often have “set-and-forget” management ports active by default. Keeping insecure services like Telnet, unencrypted HTTP, or FTP open allows threat actors to intercept credentials or move laterally between machines without hitting a single security hurdle.

Trend #5: Cloud and AI create bigger attack surfaces

While great for streamlining operations, every new cloud dashboard or remote management tool also adds another endpoint for an attacker to get into your environment. When you move your data and controls to the cloud, you’re essentially trading a locked door at your facility for a digital one that’s being knocked on 24/7.

The same AI tools that help you speed up the line are also helping threat actors. They use AI to write better phishing emails and find holes in your network faster than any person could. The good news is that those same technologies, partnered with a human expert, can help keep you safe. Here’s how Huntress does it:

Weeding out the noise: Our AI-assisted human-led SOC uses automation to sift through millions of events, instantly clearing out the false positives that usually bury IT teams in alerts.

Catching quiet threats: While AI is great at spotting big spikes in data, our SOC analysts look for the subtle tradecraft—like a persistent foothold—that automated tools often miss.

Practical response: When a real threat is found, we don't just send you a generic notification. You get clear, step-by-step instructions from a real person on how to fix the problem and get back to work.

Trend #6: Supply chain and third-party access are weak links

Just like no man is an island, no plant is an island, either. You rely on a chain of vendors, equipment integrators, and partners to keep your machines calibrated and your software updated.

To do their jobs, these third parties often have total access to your network through remote management tools or permanent VPN tunnels. The problem is that while your security might be tight, you can’t always vouch for theirs. Here’s how these supply chain attacks happen:

The soft target: An attacker breaches a small HVAC contractor (like with the 2014 Target breach) or a specialized machine integrator who has a remote connection to your floor.

The stolen key: They find the saved credentials or the “always-on” VPN link the partner uses to monitor your equipment.

The silent entry: The attacker logs into your network. To your system, it looks like a routine maintenance check from a trusted friend.

The payload: Once inside, they use that high-level access to deploy ransomware across your servers or directly manipulate the control systems the partner was hired to manage.

This is why practical security means keeping a close eye on who is coming and going. You don't have to stop working with partners; you just need to make sure their access is limited to exactly what they need, exactly when they need it.

Trend #7: Controls and governance lead to rising regulatory pressure

Between government programs and directives like CMMC 2.0 and NIS2, and big customers demanding proof of security before they sign a contract, the pressure is on.

Governance is about making sure that cybersecurity programs are fit-for-purpose, well-managed, and compliant, so that if a threat actor does find a way in, you have a practical plan to stop them. Regulators and partners want to see that you aren’t just guessing—they want to see that you have a handle on who has access to your systems, apps, and data, and what’s running on your floor.

To stay compliant and keep your contracts, you’ll likely need to show:

Documented policies, procedures, and responsibilities: Clear documentation needs to show how cybersecurity is governed, operated, and who is in charge of security tasks, so nothing falls through the cracks during a crisis.

Asset inventories: You can't protect what you don't know you have. You need a live list of every laptop, PLC, and IIoT sensor on your network.

Access reviews: Regularly checking who has the "keys" to your systems—and kicking out former employees or vendors who don't need access anymore.

Incident response plans: A written, tested playbook that tells everyone exactly what to do (and who to call) the second a machine starts acting weird.

What these trends really mean for manufacturers

Cybersecurity in manufacturing directly impacts your ability to do work. A system failure often triggers a production stoppage that hits your revenue, your reputation, and your delivery dates. Viewing security as production continuity helps you see it as a necessary part of keeping the lights on.

Safety also plays a massive role here. A breach on the shop floor can lead to physical consequences for your equipment and your people. Implementing these manufacturing cybersecurity trends creates a practical safety net to ensure your machines—and the team running them—stay out of harm's way.

Make security a normal part of your operations with Huntress

Staying ahead of these shifts in manufacturing cybersecurity trends helps you do more than just check a compliance box. You’re building a business resilient enough to handle a bad day without it becoming a business-ending event.

Huntress aims to bring this level of protection to businesses of all sizes so you can keep the line moving. Threats can seem overwhelming, but with our in-depth understanding of how threat actors think, we know what to look for.

Huntress gives you fully Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), so you've got 24/7 support from security experts ready to respond to threats.

FAQs

Why are bad threat actors so focused on manufacturing now?

Threat actors attack manufacturing because they know that manufacturers have a very low tolerance for downtime. Because a stalled assembly line costs so much every hour, threat actors have more leverage to demand a quick payout. They’re also taking advantage of the fact that many plants are currently connecting old, unprotected machinery to the internet for the first time.

How is ransomware in manufacturing different from other industries?

In manufacturing, ransomware is about physical disruption. Attackers now use double extortion, where they both steal your proprietary designs and shut down your operational technology (OT). This puts your intellectual property and your physical production at risk at the same time.

How should smaller manufacturers prioritize cybersecurity investments?

Smaller manufacturers can invest in cybersecurity by reducing access to only critical systems, implementing MFA wherever possible, and making sure that they have a clear inventory of assets to keep track of what they have.

Is it realistic to prevent every cyber incident in manufacturing?

Unfortunately, it’s not realistic in any industry to prevent 100% of cyber incidents, let alone in manufacturing. The focus should be on quick threat detection, identification, and containment.

Title: ClickFix to BEC in 24 Hours: Tragic Quadrant | Huntress
Context: Threats like AI platform abuse and ClickFix-style attacks on their own can feel like small problems
Full Text:
Most cyber threats start out small and unassuming before they turn into the OH $#!T moments that put your whole business at risk. They can creep up fast during a normal day with a website you trust and a habit you don't question. You ask your favorite AI platform for help, follow "fix it" instructions when it hits a snag, and get back to work without thinking twice.

Nothing feels risky on the surface. But underneath, the "normal" AI search result you clicked and the "fix it" instructions you followed just helped an attacker gain access to your Microsoft 365 account. While you move on to the next task in your day, they walk straight into your inbox without a password or MFA prompt, looking just like you. They read through your messages and create hidden inbox rules that hide their tracks. That stealthy intrusion is mailbox manipulation, and in this case, it can escalate into full-blown business email compromise (BEC) within hours.

Threats like AI platform abuse and ClickFix-style attacks on their own can feel like small problems. Chained together, they give an attacker everything they need to set up an OH $#!T moment that no one sees coming until it's too late.

Meet Doris and her ClickFix problem

Principal Product Researcher Truman Kain shows what this looks like in practice and how easily it blends into a normal workflow.

Meet Doris Stewart, a fictional finance employee at a company called Speedway Laundry, owned by Speedway Industries. Doris wants help responding to an email, so she goes to Google and searches for ChatGPT. She clicks what appears to be a normal sponsored result and, unknowingly, lands on a custom attacker-built GPT. But there are no obvious tells that this custom GPT is malicious. And Doris trusts ChatGPT, which is what the attacker was banking on.

Here's where things start to get sketchy. The custom GPT tells her there's a service issue and sends her to a fake verification page. Doris is prompted to press Command+Space, paste a command into Terminal, and press Enter. She doesn't recognize that this is a ClickFix scam, and by following those steps, the attacker has tricked her into compromising her own machine.

Now, the attacker runs a script to retrieve cookies and spots Doris' Microsoft session cookie, the one that keeps her logged in to Outlook without entering a password or MFA code each time she needs access. By dropping that cookie into a fresh browser using a free extension and refreshing the page, the attacker is now sitting in Doris' inbox with full control. There was no password and no MFA prompt to get past. The session was already authenticated, so the stolen cookie did the work.

This is where the attacker turns access into cash. In Doris' inbox, the attacker finds an invoice awaiting approval, creates an inbox rule named ".." so it gets easily overlooked, and sets it to archive any message containing the invoice number. Then the attacker replies to Treasury as Doris, asking them to send the payment to a new routing number, deletes the sent message to hide the evidence, and empties the trash. Doris never sees any of it, and the whole thing unfolds in about 24 hours.

This attack didn't require lots of time, money, or technical know-how. But it worked fast, and Doris will be left cleaning up a financial mess that she didn't even know existed.

How Doris could have avoided trouble

The good news is that knowing where to break links in the attack chain can stop a bigger business disruption from happening. In this case, on the endpoint side, the initial access shows up as a Mac shell running curl output with the attacker's IP address Base64-encoded inside it, the exact command Doris walked through pasting into Terminal a few minutes earlier. That pattern is worth flagging as suspicious on endpoints until proven otherwise.

On the identity side, the tells are just as suspicious. Two browsers are active in one session; there are two different operating systems tied to the same login; traffic is routed through a VPN with no business reason to be there; and that sketchy, almost invisible inbox rule ("..").

This isn't new tradecraft, but it's effective and convenient for attackers to slip in unnoticed without dropping noisy tooling that'll get flagged by managed security tools.

Getting ahead of OH $#!T moments with the Tragic Quadrant

The Huntress Tragic Quadrant plots threats on two axes, including the ones in this exact attack chain. The x-axis (prevalence) shows how often we see them in the environments we monitor, and the y-axis, or as we all call it, "pucker factor" (which, if you've ever been on the receiving end of these attacks, makes perfect sense), shows how much damage they cause when they land. That view helps you tackle the riskiest gaps first, so you don't end up in an OH $#!T moment like Doris.

On the lower quadrants, you see tactics like AI platform abuse and ClickFix that aren't usually catastrophic on their own, even if we see them often in our telemetry. The real risk happens when attackers chain them together, and the arrows move up and to the right into the OH $#!T quadrant, where a hidden inbox rule can turn into much bigger problems like BEC or ransomware.

When you know which corner a tactic falls into, it gets easier to see which threats deserve your focus right now and how to spot them in your environment.
