Title: CMMC Level 2 Non-Negotiable Requirements Explained | Huntress
Context: This means your only real flexibility when achieving CMMC Level 2 is deciding which 24 (of the remaining 46) one-point requirements you'll implement to reach a minimum score of...
Full Text:
Differences between legacy self-assessments (DFARS 252.204-7019) and CMMC Level 2 self-assessments (DFARS 252.204-7021) are leading defense contractors to a rude awakening: they no longer dictate the requirements they can implement or defer during a NIST 800-171 implementation. Identifying the “non-negotiable” requirements dictated by the CMMC program avoids future scenarios where a single missing requirement voids contract award eligibility or exposes the organization to the False Claims Act.

Old vs. New CMMC Level 2 Requirements

Self-assessments performed under the DFARS 252.204-7019 (Notice of NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Requirements) and DFARS 252.204-7020 allowed contractors to report any score, ranging from a "haven't even started" score of -203 to a perfect 110 points, using the DoD Assessment Methodology (DoDAM).

CMMC Level 2 self-assessments are scored using the DOD CMMC scoring methodology, and DFARS 252.204-7997 (which replaces both 252.204-7019 and 252.204-7020 under the DFARS overhaul) now points government DIBCAC assessments at that same methodology.

The real difficulty emerges when you pair CMMC point values with self-assessment requirements from the DFARS 252.204-7021 CMMC clause. Now your CMMC self-assessment has a minimum score that isn't evident in the contract clause language itself.

The New Bare Minimum

Completing a CMMC Level 2 self-assessment uses the same assessment objectives and point values as previous self-assessment procedures, but there are some tough mandates buried in 32 CFR 170.21, which sets the bar for a Conditional Level 2 (Self) status:

Your self-assessment score must be at least 80% of the 110 requirements in the model, or 88

You must implement all requirements worth three (3) or five (5) points

Additionally, a short list of one point requirements must also be implemented

These non-negotiable requirements from NIST 800-171 yield a self-assessment score of 64, and represent 85% of all possible points in the scoring methodology. This means your only real flexibility when achieving CMMC Level 2 is deciding which 24 (of the remaining 46) one-point requirements you'll implement to reach a minimum score of 88 on your first self-assessment submitted to the Department's Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS).

A Ticking Clock

With 32 CFR 170.21 putting a new floor on minimum compliance, it's important to understand how quickly the "ceiling" approaches because of how "POA&M closeout" works in the CMMC rules. Under CMMC self-assessment requirements, submitting a CMMC Level 2 self-assessment with any unmet requirements kickstarts a 180-day period to close out those remaining items. Failing to complete those items and update CMMC Status in SPRS will cause that Conditional status to expire after 180 days.

Any contractor submitting a less-than-perfect Level 2 self-assessment should be aware of this mechanism, since it causes self-assessments to expire earlier than normal. Don't end up in a situation where your affirming official logs into SPRS to submit their annual affirmation, only to find your self-assessment has expired, silently disqualifying the company for bids they may have submitted during that timeframe.

How Huntress Helps

Some NIST 800-171 requirements call for specialized capabilities—not just written policies—including ongoing system monitoring, security-event logging and review, threat detection, and incident handling. Huntress brings together endpoint and identity detection and response, security-event collection and retention, and 24/7 SOC monitoring to help organizations operationalize requirements across audit and accountability, incident response, security-control monitoring, and system integrity. We also map our products to applicable CMMC controls and provide assessor-ready documentation, but each organization must still configure these capabilities for its environment, integrate them into its response processes, and maintain evidence that each in-scope requirement is met.

Of the 55 requirements currently documented in Huntress CMMC resources: 32 are non-negotiable. Overall, the requirements addressed in the Huntress Shared Responsibility Matrix (SRM) add up to 164 points in the Level 2 scoring methodology, or 52 percent of all possible points.

As we launch new capabilities, expect Huntress to contribute towards more 800-171 requirements and yield more possible points.

Conclusion

When a solicitation or contract requires CMMC Level 2 (Self), a current Level 2 (Self) status and an affirmation in SPRS are a condition of contract award, and that status will require an implementation score of at least 88 with every non-POA&M-able requirement met. Contractors should respond to this heightened requirement quickly, completing NIST 800-171 implementations and submitting new CMMC Level 2 (Self) assessment in SPRS before the lack of an assessment entry costs them a contract award or contract option.

Title: SMB1001: How Huntress Maps to Each Tier
Context: Affordable, verifiable, cascading certification is the only version of this that works
Full Text:
The cybersecurity industry failed SMBs. SMB1001 is the apology.

Let's be uncomfortable for a minute. For two decades, cybersecurity failed small- and medium-sized businesses (SMBs). Not maliciously. We built genuinely good technology, wrapped it in a vocabulary nobody outside the industry speaks, priced it for organisations with an internal IT team and a procurement team and then told the local accounting firm with 14 staff members to get serious about their security posture.

So the 14-person firm goes looking. What it finds is "EDR," "XDR," "MDR," "ITDR," "ISPM," "SIEM," "SOAR," "ZTNA" and a vendor at a trade show explaining their platform is "AI-native, agentic and consolidates 17 point solutions." Meanwhile, all the owner is doing is quietly wondering if anyone's backing up the file server. None of those categories is fake. Plenty are ours. The failure was deciding that the buyer had to learn our vocabulary before they were allowed to be safe.

Then someone hands them a framework built for an organisation 200 times their size. Telling them, "Just do ISO 27001," is a bit like telling someone who wants to get fitter to run a marathon on Saturday. Technically correct. But in reality, they read the phrase "information security management system," close the laptop and go back to running their business.

Every day across APAC, it's not resistance but paralysis. SMBs aren't refusing to do security. They simply don't know where to start. They've been burned by shiny things before, and every framework they open assumes they have resourcing they'll never have. We made security expensive and secretive, then acted surprised when SMBs became the softest target in the supply chain.

What if a security standard actually has a finish line?

This is where SMB1001 comes in. I've spent the last few months in the trenches with Sales Engineer Luca Gennai mapping it against Huntress.

SMB1001 is a tiered cybersecurity certification standard built specifically for SMBs. It's published by Dynamic Standards International (formerly Cyber Security Certification Australia), a not-for-profit standards body with an office in Canberra. It launched in 2023 and went international in January 2025. The current edition, SMB1001:2026, became certifiable on 1 January 2026.

It's broken into five tiers: Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Diamond. Bronze covers around seven fundamental controls, mainly the things everyone already knows they should do.

Each tier layers controls across five areas: technology management, access management, backup and recovery, policies and procedures and education and training. Bronze through Gold rest on a director's attestation. Platinum and Diamond bring in independent verification.

Here's why SMB1001 beats a binder:

It's non-subjective. Controls are implemented or they're not. No scoring rubric, no partial credit and no creative interpretation, which makes one business' certificate comparable to another's.

You can start and finish it. A small business can achieve Bronze and have something real to show for it. No 18-month programme that stalls out halfway.

It scales to capacity, not ambition. Most businesses don't need Diamond, and the standard doesn't pretend otherwise.

It updates annually. It's "dynamic." Less a certificate on the wall and more a yearly service.

The certificate is publicly verifiable. A trust conversation becomes a 10-second check.

"Community-led" is usually marketing. Here it's structural.

The standard is written by the people who have to deliver it. DSI runs SMB1001 through a steering committee stacked with MSP industry bodies and practitioner organisations, all of whom revisit it every year rather than every five. When the people working at the coalface get a vote on what the controls say, you get requirements that survive contact with a real 20-person business.

The standard setter isn't the certifier. DSI writes SMB1001, but CyberCert certifies against it, with independent verification organisations involved at the audited tiers. Keeping those roles apart is deliberate, and it's the same separation the big schemes use.

The funding model is the clever part. MSPs and technology partners deliver it, and the SMB pays for its own certification. An enterprise worried about its supply chain can write "all suppliers must hold Silver or above" into a contract, verify it in seconds and pay nothing per supplier. Then a Tier 1 supplier can require the same of its own Tier 2s.

That's the piece questionnaires never solved. Most supply chain assurance today is a spreadsheet emailed to hundreds of suppliers who self-report once, after which everyone files it and moves on. That's paperwork, not assurance, and it doesn't scale. Regulatory pressure keeps landing on the big end of town (SOCI here, NIS2 in Europe, prime flow-down in the US) while the actual weak point sits three tiers down, in a business that was never in scope. Affordable, verifiable, cascading certification is the only version of this that works.

So, where does Huntress actually sit on the tier map?

Luca Gennai and I worked through SMB1001:2026 tier by tier, control by control, asking: where does Huntress directly meet a control, where do we materially support one and does the right answer live somewhere else in the stack?

Bronze and Silver mostly ask whether controls exist. This means firewalls, patching, backups, device password policy, individual accounts and MFA on email. Prevention is the floor, and much of that floor sits with the MSP and with Microsoft-native tooling, which is exactly where it should sit. What changes the outcome is whether anyone is watching those controls hold up in production, which is where we come in.

Managed SAT is a direct hit here, because SMB1001 wants training with proof it happened, and completion reporting that becomes your evidence. Managed EDR does the evidentiary half of the antivirus control, reporting the AV status on every managed endpoint with richer detail and managed policy for Microsoft Defender and anything else surfaced as "Other AV." When an assessor asks you to prove AV is running everywhere, that should be a dashboard, not a stocktake. The same agent reports Windows firewall status for the firewall control.

From Silver up, identity is the real story. Managed ISPM defines the target configuration across Entra ID, Exchange, SharePoint and Teams and manages Conditional Access with pre-deployment impact analysis. From there, it keeps watching, catching drift within minutes and rolling settings back if a change causes trouble. Managed ITDR sits on top of the attacks that beat the correct configuration.

Something worth knowing before you assume this is handled: Huntress data shows more than 60% of tenants are missing over half of our recommended identity controls, even when other tooling is already in place.

Here's the honest version of that pitch: turning on MFA is Microsoft's job. Knowing it got bypassed is ours.

Gold is where the framework gets loud, and so do we. Control 1.12.0.0 names EDR, explicitly. Managed EDR plus our 24/7 SOC meets it directly. This is the strongest single mapping in the framework. The ongoing awareness campaign requirement is another direct hit for SAT.

Gold also asks for an incident response plan. The plan is the customer's document, in the customer's language, with the customer's sign-off. Then a real intrusion hits at 2:40am on a Sunday morning, and the gap between a certificate and an outcome is whether anyone is awake to run it. Our 24/7 SOC is. A plan nobody is staffed to execute is a PDF.

Platinum shifts the question from "do you have it" to "can you prove it runs." Independent verification enters the model, and always-on detection is the rare control that generates evidence simply by operating. Managed SIEM retains the log trail an assessor actually wants to examine.

Diamond names the service, not just the tool. Read control 1.12.1.0 slowly and it describes an operating model: endpoint detection, humans who respond to it, defined response timeframes. Managed EDR is the endpoint half, and our human-led 24/7 SOC is the MDR half. The response timeframes are contractual rather than aspirational. CyberCert still awards the certificate, but this is the tier where what we do stops being a nice-to-have.

No single vendor owns this list, and pretending otherwise is how trust breaks again

SMB1001 isn't product-shaped. It's business-shaped. It asks about firewalls and backups and DMARC records and visitor registers. That means no single vendor owns the whole thing, and pretending otherwise may help make the sale, but it costs trust later.

So here's the division of responsibility, out loud, before somebody's assessor asks for it.

Microsoft enforces. Huntress makes sure it holds. Entra is the enforcement plane for identity. Managed ISPM decides what good looks like, deploys it and then keeps it that way with continuous enforcement across Entra ID, Exchange, SharePoint and Teams. It also manages Conditional Access and catches drift in minutes, rather than at the next quarterly review.

Managed ITDR handles the attacks that beat correct configuration: token theft, session hijack, the login that's technically valid and completely wrong. "Configured" is a Tuesday. "Still configured" in March, and monitored when someone works around it, is the control.

Your RMM deploys. Huntress tells you where it mattered. Patch delivery belongs with Intune, Windows Update for Business or your RMM. What we bring is the other half of the vulnerability conversation: exposure that's actually present on actual-live endpoints, prioritised by what attackers are using this week rather than by CVSS in descending order.

The customer owns the policy. Our SOC owns the 3am. IR plans, invoice fraud procedures, cyber security and AI use policies are customer documents and customer decisions. Our job starts the moment one of them is needed, which is the entire reason the Gold and Diamond name a service and not a tool.

And a lot of SMB1001 is just the rest of the business. Backups, TLS certificates, SPF and DKIM and DMARC, encryption at rest, macro hardening, penetration testing, credential storage, visitor registers and cyber insurance. That work lives across the managed stack, the customer's documentation and their broker. An MSP that can walk a client up these tiers is selling something considerably more durable than a licence.

One guardrail to remember is that deploying a tool, ours included, doesn't confer a certificate. CyberCert assesses and awards it independently. Telling an SMB that installing an agent makes them Gold sets that business up for an awkward conversation with an assessor, and sets the whole standard back.

Three questions to ask on your next client call

You don't need a certification programme by Friday. You need better questions.

Are their customers already asking? Supplier security clauses are showing up in contracts well below the regulatory threshold. If a client lost a tender over a security questionnaire, they're ready for this conversation.

What are they already paying for? Most SMBs running a decent managed stack are closer to Bronze or Silver than they think. Count what's deployed before you quote what's missing.

Which rung do they actually need? Silver is the tier insurers tend to care about. Gold is where detection and response get named. Diamond is for a small minority, and selling Diamond to a bakery is exactly the behaviour that broke SMB trust in the first place.

Keep it simple…then keep it simple

SMBs were never the problem. Packaging was. SMB1001 works because it does the unglamorous thing of breaking security into rungs a small business can climb, in an order that makes sense, with something real to hand a customer at the end. Prevention is the floor and the framework stages the climb above it. Gold names EDR. Diamond names EDR plus a managed service. And identity is where everything from Silver up is won or lost.

Want the full tier-by-tier mapping, boundaries included? Book a Huntress demo and watch the SOC do the part that used to require a binder.

Running an MSP and want to turn this into a service line? Start with the Huntress partner page on CyberCert.

Questions on the mapping itself? Find me on LinkedIn. I'd be happy to walk through it with you.

SMB1001 is published by Dynamic Standards International. Certification is assessed and awarded independently by CyberCert. Huntress, DSI and CyberCert are independent companies.

The coverage described here reflects how individual Huntress capabilities meet or support specific SMB1001:2026 requirements. It is not a claim of complete framework coverage, and it does not confer certification, insurance eligibility or regulatory compliance. It isn't legal advice either.

Title: New Huntress View for Security Incident Investigations
Context: You might see that our Security Operations Center (SOC) looked at something and decided it was not a threat, but not much about why
Full Text:
For a long time, partners have told us the same thing: when an investigation was closed as benign, it was hard to know what actually happened behind the scenes. You might see that our Security Operations Center (SOC) looked at something and decided it was not a threat, but not much about why.

That lack of visibility made a few things harder than they needed to be:

Explaining to end customers what Huntress actually did or didn't do

Showing the value of investigations that feel like a black box

Answering reasonable questions like, "What did your analysts find?"

The new Investigations View is our answer. It's a single place where you can see every investigation, what triggered it, and exactly how it was handled. Including those "closed benign."

Prefer to watch? Robert Knapp, Director of the Huntress Security Operations Center, walks through the Investigations View, including the timeline of every step an attacker took and every step the SOC took in response, even for investigations closed as benign.

New: Chronological timeline of security incident investigations

Let's jump to the most exciting part first: you can now drill into any investigation to see a detailed, chronological timeline of everything that took place from first signal to final resolution. And you can easily export this information as a PDF to share with stakeholders.

The investigation timeline includes:

Signals that led to the investigation

Analyst notes and context

Incident reports, if one was generated

Recommended and completed remediations

Final resolution and status

The investigation details view shows a full, ordered timeline of every signal, analyst action, and decision.

This view turns what used to be a black box into a glass box: partners can see not just the outcome, but the work the Huntress SOC performed to get there. Even for investigations that determine activity is benign.

Redesigned: A dashboard for every investigation

Ok, let's zoom out from the details a little. Where do you find these delightful investigation timelines? When malicious activity is detected, they are now included by default in all Incident Reports. But you can also see the full list of investigation summaries in one place if you head over to the redesigned Investigations Dashboard. Here's how:

Sign in to the Huntress portal

Navigate to the Investigations tab in the top navigation

Use the search and filters to find the investigations you care about most

At the top of the dashboard, you'll find some high-level KPIs, including how many investigations were closed or reported, the organizations within your account that saw the most investigations, top signal types, and more.

Below that, you'll also find a row-by-row view of everything our SOC has investigated across your tenants. Review the summary to get a quick overview of each investigation, including:

When the investigation began

Which customer and which endpoint, identity, or other asset was involved

Which signal types were investigated (EDR, ITDR, etc)

How many signals contributed to the investigation

Status, including investigations closed as benign or reported

The Investigations dashboard gives partners a single view of every Huntress investigation, including those closed as benign.

From here, partners can quickly search, filter, and jump into the details that matter most for an organization or endpoint.

How to use security incident investigations in your organization

The goal of this experience is simple: help you tell a clearer story about how Huntress is protecting your organization or customers.

With the Investigations View, you can:

Show the volume of investigations our SOC handles on behalf of each organization

Walk through specific investigations during QBRs or security reviews

Answer tough questions from security teams about why something was considered benign

Demonstrate that Huntress is continuously watching, investigating, and documenting work, even when there is no incident to report

We want your feedback

This is an important step in making the Huntress platform more transparent and more useful during stakeholder conversations. But it's not the last one.

If you have requests, ideas, or feedback on the Investigations View, please let us know at https://feedback.huntress.io/.

We are listening, and we will continue evolving the Huntress portal based on your input.

Title: Integrate Aquasec and Prometheus for Greater Visibility Into Runtime Security Operations
Context: Platform Aqua Platform Runtime Powered Cloud Security Monitor behavior, detect exploitable risk, enforce policy and contain threats across the application lifecycle
Full Text:
How does the Aquasec and Prometheus integration work?

The integration uses two separate configurations to make diagnostic metrics available to Prometheus.

Aquasec Platform monitoring

Administrators enable Prometheus under Administration, Integrations, Monitoring Systems in the Aquasec Platform.

The configuration supports an optional bearer token and a configurable data collection interval. Aquasec makes diagnostic metrics available at the specified interval, including the number of connected Enforcers and Gateways, images waiting to be scanned, images being scanned and images that failed scanning.

The integration also provides metrics for successful and failed user logins, defined Image Assurance Policies, Runtime Policies and Firewall Policies.

These metrics help teams understand the operational state of their Aquasec environment and identify patterns that may require attention.

Aquasec Enforcer monitoring

For more detailed runtime monitoring, Aquasec provides a Prometheus Metrics Exporter for Aquasec Enforcers and VM Enforcers.

Administrators enable the exporter under Settings, Enforcer, Prometheus Metrics Exporter. The exporter uses port 8995 by default, although this can be changed. The Metrics Exporter advanced setting must also be enabled for the relevant Enforcer groups.

The exporter exposes several categories of metrics, including:

Resource utilization: CPU and memory usage at the host and Enforcer levels, helping teams monitor the resources consumed by runtime protection.

Enforcer health: Enforcer version and type, active container counts, enabled functions and Gateway connection status.

Runtime security activity: File related events detected or blocked by runtime controls, malware scanning activity and behavioral detection event counts.

Security operations: Audit activity, event processing errors and host or image scanning results.

For Kubernetes deployments, Aquasec’s documentation provides an example using a local Prometheus server with service discovery to collect metrics within a cluster. A remote Prometheus server can use federation to collect metrics across clusters. Standalone Aquasec Enforcers and VM Enforcers do not require the local cluster deployment step.

This architecture allows organizations to monitor Aquasec metrics across distributed environments while maintaining the runtime enforcement capabilities that operate inside protected workloads.

Title: Snyk UNFILTERED: Inside Our First-Ever Customer Summit
Context: Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job Detection is no longer the bottleneck
Full Text:
What happens when you bring security leaders from some of the world's most forward-thinking organizations into one room, close the doors, and invite them to speak candidly about what's working, what's breaking, and what they’re still working out?

That’s what we set out to find with Snyk UNFILTERED, our inaugural Customer Summit. Held in San Francisco ahead of the launch of Evo Agentic AppSec and the AI Security Summit, Snyk UNFILTERED was designed to feel nothing like a conference.

We brought together a small group of security leaders from our customer community for an afternoon of candid discussions, interactive debates, and peer-to-peer exchanges. With no traditional presentations, product demos, or carefully rehearsed talking points, the summit gave attendees the freedom to share their experiences without attribution. What followed was an open exchange of ideas about the challenges and opportunities shaping the future of AI security. Leaders compared notes on real rollouts, real roadblocks, and real questions they have not yet figured out, with a level of transparency that is hard to find at traditional industry events.

From the growing backlog of vulnerabilities to the governance of autonomous agents, attendees challenged assumptions, compared real-world experiences, and explored questions the industry is still answering. And that's where the most valuable conversations began.

Five key takeaways that stuck with us

Five themes kept resurfacing over the afternoon, across every table and every discussion:

1. When AI writes the code, who owns the risk?

If an engineer prompts an AI tool to build an agent skill and that skill causes an issue later, who is at fault? The room kept coming back to the importance of guardrails: clear controls and ownership that hold up even when no human typed the line.

2. The AI conversation has grown up

Just a few months ago, the questions were about cost and token usage. Now leadership wants to know the return on investment, what AI is really costing, and where to set budget caps. AI has moved from experiment to line item with scrutiny to match.

3. Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job

Detection is no longer the bottleneck. The questions have moved to how teams fix issues, how fast they can fix them, and how they reduce human error within the loop. Fixes that stall in review, testing, and merge were a shared frustration.

4. Risk can come from anywhere

When everyone on a team has access to AI, vulnerabilities can come from anywhere. Democratizing AI also spreads responsibility, and attendees talked about how to keep everyone accountable without slowing anyone down.

5. Humans can only do so much

Teams are limited by how much people can review and approve. Leaders are open to trusting agents, but only with controls that an agent cannot bypass, and with governance designed for machines rather than adapted from processes built for people.

From UNFILTERED conversations to the future of AI Security

Snyk UNFILTERED was just the beginning of an important week in San Francisco. The challenges discussed behind closed doors at UNFILTERED reflected a broader shift happening across the industry: security teams are moving beyond simply identifying risk toward enabling organizations to build, innovate, and operate safely at AI speed.

The next morning, we launched Evo Agentic AppSec, and the AI Security Summit brought builders, researchers, investors, and CISOs into the same building. The questions from the customer room about fixing at speed and governing agents were carried straight into those conversations. Hearing those challenges directly from customers shapes what we build next.

The best conversations don't end when the event does

The leaders in the room are navigating enormous change. They’re balancing innovation with accountability and securing technologies that evolve faster than the processes designed to govern them. What made the afternoon valuable was their willingness to talk openly about what they haven’t solved yet. Spaces like that are rare, and we plan to keep creating them.

Snyk Unfiltered is part of our commitment to bringing our customer community together through candid conversations and shared learning, and this was the first of many.

Full Text:
Learn how to use Tenable solutions to find vulnerable PHP versions, prioritize remediation, and patch the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) faster.

Key takeaways

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) put security teams in a race against attackers. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, so organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

Tenable helps you find PHP2Shell across your attack surface. Tenable One Attack Surface Management discovers externally facing PHP assets. Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center provide detections, including local checks for Linux distribution packages. Tenable One Web App Scanning assesses web applications, and Tenable One Cloud Exposure covers cloud workloads.

Tenable accelerates remediation. Tenable Patch Management matches exposures to the right patches, launches patch workflows, and validates fixes with post-scan checks. Tenable One with Tenable Hexa AI lets you find vulnerable assets, create exposure initiatives, and generate remediation tickets with simple prompts.

Respond faster with Tenable solutions

The recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have put security teams in a race against attackers to remediate or mitigate exposure before their systems are targeted. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, and many of those sites run unsupported, legacy branches that no longer receive upstream support. Organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

To help cybersecurity teams accelerate emergency response, this blog outlines tips for using the Tenable solutions to identify vulnerable versions of PHP, prioritize remediation decisions, and implement patches as quickly as possible.

External Attack Surface Management

Tenable One Attack Surface Management (ASM) helps you discover externally facing assets running PHP. ASM continuously scans public data sources, such as DNS records, IP addresses, Autonomous System Numbers (ASN), WHOIS registrations, and neighboring IP ranges, to discover forgotten, rogue, or shadow IT assets that might be vulnerable to PHP2Shell. This is one of the first steps to take. It shows your digital footprint from the attacker’s perspective and identifies potential entry points into your organization.

Important ASM tips include:

Use ASM to find additional top-level domains related to your organization. Suggested Domains helps you identify additional domains you may own based on ASN, brand, domain name, IP range, subdomain, or nameserver. You can also adjust the suggestion rules to prioritize domain names based on the likelihood of ownership.

Search the inventory for PHP deployments. Create a query in ASM to identify PHP as a programming language filter. This gives you a quick starting point to assess locations, asset details, and software versions for further analysis.

Continuously monitor for changes in your attack surface. Use Subscriptions in ASM to receive event-driven notifications and understand important changes in your attack surface that may create new exposure. Choose from hundreds of pre-built event categories or create a customized subscription. Two subscriptions apply to PHP: PHP in applications and PHP end-of-life installs.

Explore the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Attack Surface Management.

How to Identify and Tag PHP Assets in Tenable One Attack Surface Management. This demo shows how to get a view of the external attack surface and identify where php2shell creates exposure. In Explore > Asset Inventory, review the inventory of assets facing the outside world. To add another inventory source, click '+' and choose an option from the drop-down menu, such as 'Add Hostnames or Domains.' In the pop-up menu, enter a new hostname, for example 'tenable.com.' To narrow the results to assets running PHP, use the query bar to set 'Programming Language' equal to 'PHP.' The results show 265 assets with PHP listed as their Programming Language. Create a 'PHP2Shell' tag and apply it to the selected assets so they can be grouped and prioritized. The Tags column then displays the 'PHP2Shell' tag. Subscriptions can be used to view and assess PHP. Subscriptions provide a growing list of events, including predefined lists and categories. Search for 'PHP' and add the 'PHP - v1' subscription. After subscribing, create an alert for the subscription. The subscription is set to 'Programming Language' contains php, so it filters assets and sends an alert when a new asset meeting this criteria is identified.

Vulnerability Management

Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center both help you find PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with detections for PHP, including local checks for PHP packages from Linux distributions. Tenable will release additional detections as vendors publish fixes in their security advisories.

Both solutions help you create out-of-band, tactical scans based on your preferred scan policy. Additional tips include:

Update plugin feeds before running a scan. Tenable One Vulnerability Management automatically manages and updates plugin feeds through cloud synchronization by default. In offline or air-gapped environments, Tenable Security Center may require manual plugin feed updates.

Use thorough testing to discover more vulnerabilities. Enabling thorough testing and paranoia mode in your scan policy conducts deeper assessments of your attack surface using multiple methods to discover risk. This is very important when you need to scan software across all system drives or investigate deep component-level software vulnerabilities where default settings may result in false negatives.

Assign tags to indicate exposure. Use dynamic tagging to identify PHP2Shell on existing and newly discovered assets.

Actively manage open remediations. Use Exposure Response in Tenable One Vulnerability Management to create Jira tickets or ServiceNow incidents and monitor remediation progress.

Check out these solution walk-throughs to learn more about Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center:

How to Identify and Address PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities in Tenable Security Center. This demo shows how to assess and remediate disclosed PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Start the investigation by searching the complete asset inventory for potential vulnerabilities. Construct an advanced query to filter for specific known PHP-related CVEs affecting the environment. Review the IP Summary to understand the overall vulnerability posture of affected hosts with known CVEs. Use specific Tenable Plugin IDs for PHP-related vulnerabilities to uncover detailed findings across all assets. Next steps: set up a pre-configured or custom report and/or dashboard to assess the impact of PHP-related vulnerabilities across the environment.

Web App Scanning

Tenable One Web App Scanning (WAS) can help you assess your web applications for the presence of PHP2Shell, especially where PHP is embedded in content management systems (CMS), databases, and session management platforms. WAS crawls across modern web applications and APIs to identify OWASP Top 10 risks and web app component vulnerabilities. It inspects components, HTTP headers, server signatures, and cookies looking for PHP versions and associated vulnerabilities.

Tips for using WAS include:

Standard WAS scan policies will discover PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. No need to create a customized policy as long as you select all plugin groups in your scan setup. WAS assessments take longer than traditional vulnerability management scans because WAS analyzes web frameworks and responses in more depth.

Incorporate ASM results into new WAS assessments. WAS scans need known web app targets to point the scanner to assess risk. Use ASM findings to discover previously unknown web apps so that you can add them into your assessment scope.

Filter on CVEs to find results. In the Findings page, you can apply filters to see where you are exposed. Generate reports and export results to easily send to application owners and remediation teams to fix.

See the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Web App Scanning.

Patch Management

Tenable Patch Management can help you accelerate patching by matching asset and exposure findings to the patches you need to apply. You can launch patch workflows directly from Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center to define the right patch strategy based on your organization’s requirements. Tenable Patch Management enables autonomous patching, safety controls and rollbacks, and automated post-scan validation to ensure exposures have been closed.

Important Tenable Patch Management tips include:

Customize your patching strategy to address emergency vulnerabilities. Define patching schedules, deployment plans, and automation levels to address PHP2Shell and other critical out-of-band remediations.

Verify patch implementation with remediation scans. Use remediation scans to confirm patches are installed and PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are marked as fixed, or trigger an agent scan after a patch deployment finishes. You can also see the latest patch information in the plugin output.

Automatically correlate patches to vulnerable versions of PHP. Mapping patches to vulnerabilities by hand is time-consuming and error-prone. Tenable Patch Management finds the right patches for you automatically, pulling updates from official OS and third-party vendor repositories within 48 hours of release. We’ve compiled a list of vendor patches mapped to our library here.

Browse the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable Patch Management.

Cloud Security

Tenable One Cloud Exposure can help you find PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in cloud workloads using agent and agentless scanning, configuration auditing, and container inspection. Just as you would use of Tenable One Vulnerability Management, Tenable Security Center, and Tenable One Web App Scanning to address vulnerabilities in on-premises and self-managed hosts, Tenable One Cloud Exposure helps you manage and remediate vulnerabilities in Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform environments.

Tips for using Tenable One Cloud Exposure include:

Detect PHP2Shell in the Emerging Threats view. Click on the Risk tab to see the Emerging Threats page that shows all PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in one view. Toggle between virtual machines, virtual machine images, and container images to see impacted resources. This shows which resources are affected, so you can triage issues and accelerate remediation workflows.

Create a policy to detect and respond to PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Create a response playbook based on you business rules and preferences. Custom policies enable you to define rules, schedule reports, and create step-by-step remediation guides to fix issues immediately.

Leverage integrated remediation workflows. For Infrastructure as Code (IaC) environments, use auto-generated IaC snippets supporting Terraform, CloudFormation, and JSON to push code-level corrections straight to your repositories. Otherwise, you can route service tickets into your existing IT and DevOps workflows to automate processes.

View the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Cloud Exposure.

How to address PHP2Shell in Tenable One Cloud Exposure. This demo covers using Hexa, the PHP2Shell Emerging Threats dashboard, Explorer queries, custom policies, custom dashboards, scheduled reports, and risk automations to identify, track, and remediate PHP2Shell exposures. Orientation with Hexa: Ask Hexa orientation questions such as "how can PHP2Shell be exploited in my infrastructure?" Hexa returns a summary of what PHP2Shell does, how an attacker might attempt to exploit it, and recommended next steps for exposures found in the environment. Exploitation paths vary. PHP2Shell Dashboard: Navigate to Risk in the left navigation, then Emerging Threats, then PHP2Shell. The dashboard gives an end-to-end view of resources affected by PHP2Shell. Filter by infrastructure type, such as Container Images, Virtual Machines, and Virtual Machine Images. Use filters and Group By options to organize the data to fit how a team operates. To drill down, click the Vulnerability column for the first affected container image under the Container Registry account. Its properties can be reviewed to prioritize remediation and close exposures before exploitation. Under the Overview tab, the Plugins section lists Plugin ID 369483, which contains CVE-2026-109618. Clicking the plugin ID shows plugin details for the container image carrying the critical PHP2Shell CVE, along with remediation instructions. Remediation through Cloud Findings: Click the affected container image, open the Cloud Findings tab, and select a finding. Open the Remediation tab for instructions on remediating the container image. Instructions vary by finding; in this example the operating system needs to be updated. Explorer queries: Go to Explore in the left navigation, then Explorer. A custom query finds two CVEs related to PHP2Shell. Clicking a resource shows an overview, cloud findings, threat detections, vulnerabilities, and more. Save the query with the button in the upper right to turn on tracking for later use, additional dashboards, and reporting. The saved query is named "PHP2Shell - tracking." Complex queries: Queries can find different forms of Toxic Combinations or identify old VMs and images, which can prompt shutting down or isolating old systems. The example query asks which systems with PHP2Shell share the same toxic combination as "X public workloads" with critical vulnerabilities and high privileges. Custom policy: A custom policy simplifies administration of PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It lets a team ignore or close individual instances, add automations, notes, time boundaries, and more. Navigate to Policies, then Cloud Policies, select Custom, and click Create Custom Policy. Select Query, choose the saved query "PHP2Shell - tracking," and click Create in the bottom right. Custom dashboard: To show PHP2Shell data on login to Tenable One Cloud Exposure, go to Dashboards, then All Dashboards, then click Create Dashboard. Select the saved query "PHP2Shell - tracking," drag and drop widgets onto the dashboard, and click Save for a quick snapshot on opening Tenable One Cloud Exposure. Recurring daily report: In Explorer, select the "PHP2Shell - tracking" query, click Add in the right corner, and select Report. Schedule a daily PHP2Shell report to be sent, in this example through Microsoft Teams to members of the General channel every morning. Automation for new findings: To trigger notifications when new PHP2Shell resources appear, create an automated workflow based on the saved query. Navigate to Operations in the main navigation, then Risk Automations, then Create Automation. Select the PHP2Shell tracker query from the drop-down and click Create in the bottom right.

Exposure Management with Tenable Hexa AI

Tenable One includes all of the capabilities mentioned above and more. One important capability that’s only available in Tenable One is Tenable Hexa AI, the agentic AI engine that can answer questions, automate tasks, execute workflows, and more. Tenable Hexa AI can speed up your response to critical vulnerabilities like PHP2Shell.

Key Tenable One with Tenable Hexa AI tips include:

Find all PHP2Shell vulnerable assets and PHP installations. Simply click on Tenable Hexa AI and type “find all open vulnerabilities for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619” or “find all instances of PHP and create a new tag based on version number,” and Tenable Hexa AI will complete the request in minutes.

Create new remediation initiatives and track status. Prompting Tenable Hexa AI to “create an exposure initiative for PHP2Shell,” will automatically define the initiative, create SLAs and provide the description and vulnerability filters. You can see the latest status of your PHP2Shell initiative in Exposure Response to help communicate progress to stakeholders.

Automatically generate remediation tickets to address PHP2Shell. Use Tenable Hexa AI to create remediation tickets with a simple prompt such as “create remediation tickets for all systems vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Assign the severity level as Critical and the due date as Immediate.”

Title: How Tenable brought multi-language support to security detectors with agentic translation
Context: AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection
Full Text:
AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection. Here’s how Tenable trained our threat detectors to process nine additional languages and understand thousands more, without the need for a translation model, which increases costs and slows down processing.

Key takeaways

Tenable One AI Exposure’s detectors, covering AI threats, harmful content, and other policy risks, were originally English-centric. To assess threats written in other languages, our product translated them into English, a slow, expensive, and often imprecise approach.

Tenable built an agentic translation pipeline that generates high-fidelity, label-preserving training and benchmark data across nine languages, guarded by a multi-judge quality gate, a refinement loop, and a model-refusal handling fallback.

This single multilingual model detects threats natively in all 10 supported languages. Compared with our previous process of translating threats into English, this model is roughly 20-800 times faster per item and is less expensive by an order of magnitude, bearing a one-time cost that does not grow with usage traffic from our customers.

Why your AI security tool should support multiple languages

A prompt attack against an AI model written in Spanish, Arabic, or Hindi is every bit as dangerous as one written in English, which is why an English-only AI security detector will leave your organization at risk from non-English attacks.

To address this issue in our product, Tenable first adopted a “translate-then-detect” process:

Identify the language.

Translate the input to English with a large translation model.

Then run the English detector.

This process works, but it has four downsides:

Latency. A large, autoregressive translation model that runs before every non-English detection needs hundreds of milliseconds for short inputs, and seconds to tens of seconds for long ones.

Cost. Every non-English request pays for a full translation pass.

Operational overhead. You have to serve, scale, and maintain another heavyweight model.

Lost signal. Meaning and intent blur in naive translation, which degrades the tool’s ability to detect threats.

How Tenable turned our AI security tool into a polyglot

To make our AI security product natively multilingual, we discovered that we didn’t need to use a translator LLM in production. Instead, we found that we needed high-quality multilingual data in two places:

A training set to teach the model the target languages.

A test set we could trust to benchmark performance honestly in each language.

Both must preserve the labels of the data, ensuring that the label survives the translation process. Translation can quietly flip a label (a malicious data sample rendered as a benign one) or defang it (the security-relevant language “bite” softened so that what’s a clear positive in the original language instead reads as a borderline threat). Either way, the data sample is now mislabeled and poisons the data.

Tenable concluded that the following methods are not ideal:

Human-expert translation. It is slow and needs a fluent reviewer for every language, so it does not scale.

Machine translation. Standard translation methods distort dataset quality in two distinct ways: native machine translation prioritizes smooth phrasing over security context, potentially stripping out malicious intent (e.g., turning a toxin synthesis request into a benign chemistry query), while direct, word-for-word translation creates awkward, unnaturally phrased text that degrades training signal, such as an English phishing lure translated literally into Japanese.

Off-the-shelf LLMs. They may refuse to translate material they flag as inappropriate, such as prompts about weapons synthesis or self-harm topics, so the text that represents a likely threat gets left out of the dataset.

Always-on (online) translators. Relying on online translation pipelines introduces per-request latency, operational complexity, and costs that scale with hundreds of millions of items, making it impractical for production environments.

The translation process has to be cost-effective and repeatable across many languages.

The Tenable solution: An agentic pipeline plus a multilingual model

1. The agentic pipeline overview

The agentic translation pipeline. Each English item is transcreated by a frontier LLM, scored by a panel of independent judges, and either accepted or sent back to refine. On a refusal, a controlled open-source model takes over, via the same gate.

In Tenable’s data translation process, every item flows through three stages in our agentic pipeline.

Translate. A frontier LLM produces a transcreation, a translation that we fine-tune by specifying the task, the item’s label, and the target language, as opposed to a blind word-for-word rendering. This fine-tuning is precisely what keeps the security-relevant meaning, and the label, intact.

Estimate. A panel of independent judges scores each translation for fluency, meaning integrity, and whether the original data label still holds.

Gate. Only translations that clear every check are kept.

Two recovery loops keep the hard cases from being lost:

Refusal handling. When the frontier translator refuses a sensitive item, the pipeline hands the same transcreation job to a controlled, open-source small-language model that does not refuse, and its output goes through the same quality gate, so legitimate-but-sensitive security data is not silently dropped.

Refinement. When a translation fails the quality gate, it is sent back for another attempt rather than thrown away.

Because the task and labels are parameters, the pipeline can serve any future detection task requiring multilingual support.

2. A pretrained multilingual model

Instead of training a language model from scratch, we fine-tuned a compact model that was already pretrained on many languages, which yielded two benefits:

It consumes far less data per language. The model has already learned useful cross-lingual representations, so we only taught it our task.

It transfers knowledge between languages. We measured this before spending a dollar on translation. For some tasks, the model successfully generalized to other languages using only English training data, eliminating the need for translation. For harder tasks, we used the agentic translation framework to translate only to the languages in which the model underperformed. Even in those cases, training the model on a handful of languages lifted the model’s translation performance in other languages at no additional cost.

Impact and results

By replacing our legacy translate-then-detect architecture with a single native model, Tenable transformed our pipeline into an enterprise-grade solution that delivers near-instantaneous global coverage. This shift drastically reduced latency and infrastructure costs while maintaining top-tier quality and unlocking broader language support. Below are the key results achieved by this upgraded architecture:

One fast model, no translator in the path. Detection now runs natively in every supported language in tens of milliseconds, whereas it took seconds with the translate-then-detect process, roughly 20-800× faster per item. In addition, the memory footprint is about 12-14× smaller: under 1 GB versus 12-14 GB.

A one-time cost, under $10,000. We generated the multilingual training and benchmark data once. That cost does not grow with client’s production traffic, unlike an always-on translator, whose bill scales with every request.

Budget-tunable by design. We set the budget, and the pipeline adjusts the tier of LLM it uses and how much refinement each item receives.

Quality you can prove. A neutral LLM-as-a-judge from a third-party model family, outside our translation and grading stack, preferred Tenable transcreations over those from a commercial machine translation model and over those from a strong open translation model in the large majority of head-to-head comparisons.

No English regression. Every Tenable One AI Exposure detector gained the ability to understand and translate from nine languages (Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, and Hindi) while English performance held or improved, and latency stayed near real-time.

Reach beyond the languages we trained. Because the model was pretrained on a very broad set of languages, the same model can read and flag attacks in thousands of languages we never explicitly trained it on. We have only formally validated the 10 languages we support, so this wider reach is promising but needs further testing before it can be relied on.

AI-threat detection, recall @ 0.005% false positive rate. (The recall metric measures how good a system is at finding every single relevant item without missing any.) Our multilingual model matches or beats translate-then-detect on 9 of 10 languages and overall (0.93 vs 0.88).

Harmful-content detection, recall @ 0.02% false positive rate. On the harder task, the gap widens: our multilingual model leads on every language and overall (0.65 vs 0.50).

How Tenable One AI Exposure protects multilingual users

Threat actors do not limit themselves to English, and neither should your defenses. With this work, Tenable One AI Exposure extends the same detection quality (for jailbreaks, prompt injection, harmful content, and data exposure) natively across 10 languages, at production speed and without a translation bottleneck in the request path. As customers adopt AI in more markets and more languages, that multilingual coverage extends with them.

Title: Unmasking the robots: Why it’s critical to discover AI agent identities and how Tenable helps you secure them
Context: Because AI agents are becoming a new class of identity with real permissions, you must understand how an attacker could compromise and abuse them
Full Text:
Discover how to secure AI agents in your cloud environment with Tenable One Cloud Exposure. We explore Microsoft Entra Agent ID and provide essential best practices for robust agentic AI identity security.

Key takeaways

Understand your current maturity level and then build an appropriate action plan to secure your agent identities.

Use your cloud providers’ native tools or Tenable One Cloud Exposure to locate and catalog every AI agent operating in your environment.

Do not assign human identities or over-privileged service accounts to the AI agents your vendors deploy in your environment. Instead, require that vendors adopt official models like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for their AI agents’ identities.

As AI agents move from experimental toys to tools that make autonomous decisions, interact with databases, and call external APIs, organizations need to be clear on who — or what — is executing these actions in their cloud environments.

Why non-human identities (NHIs) aren’t secure enough for AI agents

Security teams categorize identities into two buckets: human identities and non-human identities (NHIs), such as service accounts, secrets, and automated scripts.

Treating AI agents as standard NHIs is a recipe for disaster. AI agents combine their non-deterministic nature with their ability to execute flexible, outcome-oriented actions, rather than following strict, prescribed instructions.

Unlike classic, predictable scripts that follow rigid code paths, AI agents:

Make creative, runtime decisions using LLMs.

Interact with dynamic external tools, memory caches, and knowledge bases.

Constantly adapt to solve problems, making it difficult for a security team to establish AI agents’ baseline behavior.

To address this challenge, major cloud providers have introduced dedicated, specialized agentic AI identity models. Let’s break down one major model: Microsoft Entra Agent ID.

Identity and cloud providers' native identity management tools present only basic information about agentic identities, without providing context about their security flaws and how they extend your attack surface. Because AI agents are becoming a new class of identity with real permissions, you must understand how an attacker could compromise and abuse them. At Tenable, we believe visibility is the foundation of security. You can’t secure assets that you do not know exist.

As organization-wide adoption of agentic AI accelerates, the immediate challenge for security teams is first and foremost finding them. Because these identities are brand new, conventional identity and access management (IAM) systems may not recognize or monitor them, which creates security blind spots.

To help our customers address this issue, Tenable One Cloud Exposure now brings Microsoft Entra agentic AI identities directly into your unified asset and identity inventory.

The Microsoft Entra Agent ID framework functions through a four-tiered structural model:

Agent identity blueprints serve as the master templates for shared attributes. Residing exclusively within the agent provider’s home tenant, they establish cross-tenant links that heighten exposure to potential supply-chain attacks.

Agent identity blueprint principals are the localized instantiation of a blueprint within every specific tenant where the AI agent is deployed and active.

Agent identities represent the functional identities utilized for routine tasks. To maintain oversight of agent behavior, these are the primary entities your security team must monitor.

Agent users offer an optional layer for each agent identity requiring human-centric features — like Microsoft Teams access or a personal mailbox — to function effectively as integrated “digital colleagues.”

Title: Hackers leak personnel data of 41,000+ Homeland Security staff, including ICE and border agents
Context: More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings
Full Text:
More than 41,000 people working for the US Department of Homeland Security, including ICE agents, have had their details published online by a group of hacktivists.

As TechCrunch reports, the leaked records include the names, job titles, work email addresses, phone numbers, abd office locations.

More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings. Around 10,000 ICE employees have had their records breached, and almost 1,000 members of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

WIRED reports that the massive leak includes staff who work undercover, as well as in other sensitive areas such as those engaged in wiretapping and the interception of communications.

A hacktivist group calling itself "Department of Peace" says that the data was taken from an Okta single sign-on system that staff use to log onto the central network of the US Department of Homeland Security. Okta for its part says that it has not seen any evidence that its own systems have been compromised.

The data reveals which tools and services particularly individuals can access. Alongside everyday office software, these include Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, the phone and social media analysis tool PenLink, and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition app used by immigration agents.

Explaining its justification for the data breach, "Department of Peace" wrote:

"They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs."

The leaked data has been published online, under the title "Icepick", and can be either downloaded via a torrent or accessed via a web interface - making it significantly easier for curious parties to search.

One threat intelligence expert told WIRED that, if authentic, the leaked data was "an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS," and could help adversaries identify vulnerable personnel or compromise ongoing investigations.

An obvious concern is that the leaked contact details could be used in phishing attacks that target employees, or could potentially put agents in physical danger. Clearly anyone whose details have been exposed through the incident would be wise to treat unexpected emails, texts, and phone calls with caution - and be particularly wary of any communications that claim to come from IT support or ask for a login to be approved.

Earlier this year the same group of hacktivists claimed to have breached the US Department of Homeland Security and accessed contracts between DHS, ICE, and more than 6000 firms including the likes of L3Harris, Raytheon, Palantir, Microsoft, and Oracle.

Explaining their motivation for that breach, the hackers referred to the killings of Alex Pretti and Renée Good by federal agents in Minneapolis.

"Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I'm releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they're working on."

There has been a long string of cybersecurity incidents affecting US government personnel. For instance, in September the notorious ShinyHunters hacking group claimed to have stolen personal details related to nearly every employee of the FBI, and the records of millions of serving and former US military personnel were reportedly stolen from the Pentagon's human resources unit.

Title: $2 Million+ Drained From Polymarket Traders in New Supply Chain Attack
Context: According to the prediction market’s status page, the exchange was first switched to cancel-only mode, with relayer actions suspended
Full Text:
Polymarket halted trading on its international platform on October 29 after users reported unauthorized withdrawals.

According to the prediction market’s status page, the exchange was first switched to cancel-only mode, with relayer actions suspended.

“We’ve identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole,” the company said.

Trading resumed about an hour later, and Polymarket pledged to reimburse all affected traders. It has not named the vendor or disclosed losses.

Researchers have linked the theft to malicious code served from DebugBear, a UK-based website performance monitoring firm. Polymarket’s US platform was reportedly unaffected.

DebugBear confirmed being “impacted by an ongoing security incident” and urged users of its real user monitoring (RUM) product to pull its snippet from their websites. It also said it brought in specialist incident responders.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Hudson Rock obtained a copy of the malicious JavaScript from a DebugBear address used by Polymarket. The code hunted for a logged-in user’s trading tools and portfolio. Depending on the account type, it then tried either to sell positions and move the proceeds, or to send position tokens straight to an attacker-set address.

“The sample reads credential-related material, but our review did not identify a routine that sends the credential map, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to its reporting endpoint. Its central approach is to reuse authority already available in the authenticated application,” Hudson Rock said.

The firm also spotted a Polymarket production build, timestamped 17:59 UTC, with a change note about removing the DebugBear script.

Loss figures vary. A screenshot reviewed by Hudson Rock showed about $2.19 million at the script’s hard-coded fallback address, though the firm said this is not a verified tally.

Blockchain security firm GoPlus, which also attributed the attack to a supply chain compromise of DebugBear’s RUM script, puts losses at roughly $2.71 million. According to its on-chain analysis, the main attack path ran through 710 deposit wallets and 731 addresses, though the address count does not equal the number of victims.

Arkham data showed a suspected attacker wallet holding approximately $2.65 million. That is the same address hardcoded in the script as its fallback recipient.

Hudson Rock has not determined how the script was tampered with or how many users were hit. Its findings do not indicate that other DebugBear customers were targeted.

The attack came the same day Binance was hit by a roughly $6 billion hack that blockchain intelligence firms have attributed to North Korea. In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, with losses reported at around $3 million.

Title: Open-weight AI model GLM-5.3 cheated its way to correct answers
Context: 3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an LLM’s ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic...
Full Text:
Irregular evaluated Zhipu AI’s open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an LLM’s ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic constraints.

The model refused none of the tasks and completed three scenarios at least once each, carrying attacks through dependent stages to reach objectives in simulated networks. Irregular said this was the strongest result it had recorded for an open-weight model.

Offensive cyber capabilities

Researchers used the officially released checkpoint. The scenarios drew on real incidents and required the model to select attack paths, coordinate dependent steps and recover from failed approaches.

Across the three completed scenarios, GLM-5.3 used an application foothold to access internal services, built alternative connection paths within simulated networks and coordinated execution across multiple machines. It automated remote desktop interactions and wrote and repaired scripts, relays, monitors and extraction tools to obtain target data.

The results followed a progression the company had previously observed in closed frontier models, beginning with GPT-5.2, released in December 2025, and continuing with models released in 2026.

Memorized code and instruction adherence

Researchers also examined how GLM-5.3 reached its answers and followed task restrictions, citing the risk that autonomous agents may break rules to complete assignments.

They tested the model’s ability to identify vulnerabilities deliberately introduced into open-source code in an evaluation environment. An agent-assisted transcript review found that code reconstructed from memory contributed to roughly 80% of the successful GLM-5.3 runs examined. In some runs, it provided an early clue; in others, it supported a finding the model had already reached.

Using memorized code violated no instructions in those tests. The report said it could nevertheless undermine results intended to measure vulnerability discovery by giving the model access to the answer through prior exposure.

Irregular had observed this behavior in closed models as well. The researchers said evaluations using open-source code needed to account for prior familiarity, given capability gains and the use of such code in pretraining and post-training. Restricting internet access does not remove that familiarity.

Reward hacking and deployment risks

In separate instruction-adherence tests, GLM-5.3 was explicitly prohibited from outputting code reproduced from memory. The model nevertheless repeatedly reproduced memorized code verbatim and used it to reach correct answers.

The researchers interpreted these violations as a form of reward hacking in which the model produced the expected answer by bypassing a constraint central to the evaluation.

They warned that judging answers solely on correctness could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions. Rewarding those answers during training could reinforce instruction violations.

The report advised operators to monitor the model’s reasoning alongside its actions and outcomes, assessing compliance with instructions as well as answer accuracy.

“Organizations adopting these models should test how reliably they follow task restrictions before granting them broader access or autonomy. The more capable a model is in offensive cyber operations, the more caution any misaligned behavior it shows calls for,” the company concluded.

Title: Binance links $6.3 billion crypto theft to compromised DevOps laptop
Context: 4 million installs caught hijacking searches Hackers exploit Cisco SD-WAN flaw to deploy custom KeyDrift malware CISA warns of Fragnesia Linux flaw chained in PHP2Shell attacks...
Full Text:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has linked the theft of about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency to a DevOps engineer's compromised laptop.

The crypto exchange said the access let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions after they accessed a service container, and it hasn't yet found evidence of a leaked wallet private key.

"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual," Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said.

Binance also said it "uncovered additional points of breach" but was "still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."

The company confirmed the breach in a statement shared with BleepingComputer on Thursday and reassured customers that their funds were safe.

"Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company's funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete," it said.

Since the attack, Binance has suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks, revoked authorizations for the affected address, and is working with blockchain intelligence partners and law enforcement to trace and recover the stolen funds.

Crypto theft linked to North Korean hackers

Although the company didn't link the incident to a hacking group or threat actor, blockchain analysis firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38.

"On October 29, 2026, an attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC. That makes this the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the USD 1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025," TRM said.

Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis confirmed TRM Labs' findings, stating with "a high degree of confidence" that TraderTraitor is responsible for the Binance $6.4 billion hack.

While stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle, Ripple, and others have frozen roughly $2.7 billion since the incident, the attackers still have control of about $2.4 billion that can't be frozen.

"Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about USD 2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly USD 2.7 billion," TRM added.

"The attacker raced the freezes by selling USDT to market makers and borrowing ETH against USDT on Aave. It now holds more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about USD 2.4 billion in assets beyond any issuer's reach."

The TraderTraitor hackers were previously linked to many other major crypto theft incidents, including the theft of $1.5 billion in the February 2025 Bybit hack. At $6.36 billion, the Binance attack is now the largest recorded crypto heist.
