Title: IR trends Q3 2026: Actors impersonate IT help desks in vishing attacks as ransomware activity increases
Context: Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control...
Full Text:
Phishing remained the leading initial access technique, appearing in slightly over one-third of all Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) engagements — a decrease from over 50 percent last quarter. In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials.

Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents made up 27 percent of engagements in Q3 2026, an increase from a maximum of 20 percent seen in the previous four quarters. Talos responded to attacks involving prolific, technologically advanced, and well-established ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) variants such as The Gentlemen, Qilin, and Rhysida, as well as Interlock, which operates as a closed group. Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Additionally, we observed the emerging ransomware variant VYPR, whose operator(s) tested a range of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) instead of following a standard attack method or affiliate playbook.

Salt Typhoon-affiliated threat actors exploit public-facing application vulnerabilities for cyber espionage

Talos IR continues to see prolonged cyber espionage intrusions targeting the telecommunications sector. Talos attributed most of these intrusions with high confidence to China state-sponsored threat actors, including Salt Typhoon. The attackers in these intrusions routinely gain initial access by leveraging valid credentials and exploiting a known vulnerability (CVE-2023-20198) in publicly accessible web-based management interfaces—two of the most frequently observed initial access vectors this quarter. In one campaign, the threat actor deployed BadCandy, a malicious web shell implant known to be leveraged by Salt Typhoon, to maintain persistent and stealthy remote access.

The adversaries continue to employ living-off-the-land (LOTL) tactics, leveraging legitimate network infrastructure features — such as VPN access, traffic mirroring, and management protocols — to establish backdoors, exfiltrate data, and conduct reconnaissance. Exploiting a vulnerability in the web-based management interface, they created privileged accounts, disabled logging to conceal their activity, and altered configurations to maintain persistence, blending their actions with normal administrative operations to evade detection.

These intrusions revealed several security weaknesses in the victim environment, including reliance on password-only authentication without evidence of multi-factor authentication (MFA), use of legacy and weak management protocols (such as plaintext SNMP and outdated VPN encryption), and inadequate credential management practices. Attackers were able to create and abuse privileged accounts, disable logging, and manipulate configuration settings without encountering effective security barriers, enabling persistent and stealthy access. The absence of strong MFA and robust credential management are two of the most frequently observed security weaknesses this quarter.

AI exploited as a weapon and a target

Recent Talos IR investigations highlight the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybercriminal activity, both as a tool and a target. In one case, an internal threat actor who was hired under false credentials abused their privileged access to install AI-powered development tools, such as GitHub Copilot CLI and Anthropic Claude Code. While the investigation did not find evidence of malicious activity or data theft, the employee’s developer-level access — including cloning repositories, configuring plugins, and connecting to databases — could have enabled them to use AI tools to automate malicious actions within the organization.

A second investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant. This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities.

These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools.

Ransomware trends

Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents increased from a little over 20 percent last quarter to 27 percent in Q3, involving well-known threat groups like Interlock and the emerging ransomware VYPR. Frequently observed techniques involved deleting EDR systems and socially engineering victims into initiating remote management sessions.

Emerging ransomware variant: VYPR

During a Talos IR engagement, we observed a ransomware variant called “VYPR” that we assess is relatively new and still operationally immature. This assessment is supported by the absence of an established data leak site (DLS), as none was referenced in the ransom note and associated DLS infrastructure was not created until after the engagement. The group also appeared to rely on older leaked Conti-derived source code with only minimal modifications, reflecting a relatively unsophisticated technical approach. Their operations further suggested experimentation rather than a refined playbook, as they took an unusually long time to exfiltrate and encrypt data while testing different exfiltration parameters and deploying multiple vulnerable drivers to disable EDR protections.

The actor gained initial access through voice phishing (vishing); they tricked a user into initiating a Microsoft Quick Assist session, allowing remote access to the endpoint. While the exact social engineering technique was not confirmed in this case, threat actors frequently impersonate IT help desks during vishing calls to manipulate victims into establishing remote connections — a tactic observed in several other Q3 engagements.

The actor was then able to utilize existing RMM software, which subsequently executed PowerShell commands to download and install a Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) package from a remote IP address. During the attack, the actor leveraged tools that are commonly observed during ransomware investigations, including MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, IP scan, and Microsoft Terminal Services Client (MSTSC). Notably, we saw exfiltration over multiple days, which is not commonly observed during ransomware investigations.

EDR killers: Why evade detection when you can destroy it?

We observed several instances where ransomware operators disabled EDR systems, prioritizing direct disruption of security controls. We observed Interlock ransomware actors making multiple attempts to impair endpoint detection EDR capabilities by trying to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint (CSE) on compromised systems and used tools such as PsExec.exe and taskkill.exe to terminate security services and integrity checkers, including cscm.exe and sfc.exe. Additionally, the adversary disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared various event logs to reduce visibility and hinder forensic analysis. This is in line with previously observed Interlock activity, where they deployed a malicious WDAC policy to terminate EDR solutions.

In the previously mentioned VYPR ransomware incident, the threat actor disabled EDR and antivirus (AV) by using Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) techniques to evade detection and execute the ransomware. BYOVD attacks take advantage of trusted but flawed drivers to gain kernel-level access, enabling threat actors to disable EDR mechanisms and carry out their operations unimpeded. While this technique is commonly observed in ransomware attacks, this actor deployed an unusually large number of vulnerable drivers in the environment, possibly to create redundancies and maximize their chances of success.

Targeting

Targeting of the financial industry increased from last quarter to comprise 18 percent of all engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector. Although the financial industry remains a valuable target, Talos has not ranked it among the top three most impacted sectors since 2024. One possible reason is that organizations in finance can typically invest more in cybersecurity, unlike sectors such as public administration, which has consistently been among the top-targeted industries over the past year. Meanwhile, health care fell to third place after ranking as the most targeted industry for the previous two consecutive quarters.

Initial access

While the number of engagements involving phishing as an initial access vector declined from last quarter, it remained the most common technique, appearing in 37 percent of Talos IR engagements. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the second most common initial access vector, accounting for 33 percent of engagements.

Recommendations for addressing top security weaknesses

The most common security weaknesses observed this quarter were insufficient logging, improper credential and secret management, and absent or improperly implemented authentication and MFA. These trends closely mirror last quarter, when insufficient logging and authentication weaknesses were also prevalent.

Centralize logging and set retention requirements

The leading security weakness was insufficient logging leading to visibility gaps, seen in over 40 percent of engagements this quarter. These gaps were in part due to the common threat actor practice of deleting logs, and in part due to insufficient log retention or configuration implemented by the customer. Talos IR recommends implementing a SIEM or centralized logging platform with a minimum of 90 days of retention, forwarding logs from servers, workstations, network infrastructure, cloud identity providers, and security appliances off-device so they survive log tampering and host rebuilds, and enabling process-creation, command-line, and cloud API (e.g., Microsoft Graph) auditing. Talos IR's Log Architecture Assessment service can identify gaps and provide a roadmap to a complete view of the environment.

Tighten authentication and MFA controls

Missing or insufficient authentication and MFA controls were the third most common security weakness this quarter, observed in 33 percent of engagements. The most prevalent issue was reliance on single-factor authentication, which allowed unauthorized access in several incidents. In many cases, legacy authentication protocols were still enabled, enabling adversaries to log in without any MFA requirements, and some environments failed to enforce MFA for high-privilege accounts. To reduce this risk, Talos IR recommends transitioning from push- and SMS-based MFA to phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and hardware security keys. Organizations should also restrict self-service MFA enrollment by requiring helpdesk verification, block legacy authentication through Conditional Access, enforce number matching or verified push where phishing-resistant methods are not yet feasible, and condition access on device compliance and trusted infrastructure rather than geographic location alone.

Safeguard credentials and secrets

Improper credential and secret management was the second most common security weakness seen in 33 percent of engagements this quarter, reinforcing the importance of security awareness training and consistent security hygiene for every user. Observed security issues included unsafe storage and handling of credentials, such as saving passwords in browser stores, poor control mechanisms like permitting autofill for browser-stored credentials, and credential reuse and sharing. Effective secret management begins with a formal process that covers passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, and other sensitive credentials. By requiring unique passwords for every account and encouraging the use of password managers, organizations reduce the risks associated with credential reuse and sharing. Storing secrets securely, with encryption and access restricted to only those who need them, further strengthens protection. When credentials are no longer necessary or are suspected to be compromised, they should be promptly revoked and replaced. Regular reviews of access to privileged credentials, combined with thorough logging, help detect unusual activity. Equipping staff with training on safe handling and clear reporting procedures ensures that accidental disclosures are addressed quickly and effectively.

Title: Reports of SIEM's Death Have Been Greatly Exaggerated
Context: Lean on a partner for the threats that look bad anywhere, and build your own detections for the things only your team would know are off
Full Text:
There's a phrase I keep hearing in cyber circles lately, at in-person conferences, on LinkedIn, pretty much everywhere:

"SIEM is dead."

I get why it's catchy. But SIEM has died more times than a soap opera villain, and it keeps showing up for next season. Before SIEM, it was the perimeter that was dead. Then antivirus. Then passwords. (Passkeys are coming for them, but plenty are still living on sticky notes under keyboards.)

Here's where I land: the way a lot of companies have been buying and feeding their SIEM deserves to go away. SIEM itself doesn't. So before anyone orders flowers, let's look at what's actually changing.

Follow the money (and the marketing)

There's so much cybersecurity marketing out there that it's hard to tell which tools and controls matter against today's threats. Every booth on the expo floor has "AI" printed on it somewhere. Some of it is impressive. Some of it is a chatbot wearing a trench coat.

"X is dead" is about the oldest trick in the marketing book. If the old category is dead, you'd better buy the new one. It makes for a great keynote slide. It also skips the question I'd want answered first: what was the old thing doing for us, and do we still need that done?

For SIEM, the job was visibility across the environment, catching attackers, running investigations, and keeping records for compliance. Attackers are still here. So are auditors. The open question is whether there's a smarter way to do it.

The "send it all" era

For years, the big legacy players (think Splunk and QRadar) priced on how much data you ingested and how much you stored. That model let them charge what they charged.

And the advice that came with it was always the same: send everything. Firewall logs, DNS queries, DHCP renewals, every time a printer had feelings. Get it all in, and figure out what's useful later.

Later almost never came. What came instead was a giant bill, a pile of alerts nobody had time for, and a very expensive junk drawer.

If your vendor makes more money every time you send another log, of course they'll tell you to send more.

The market has caught on. Cisco bought Splunk, and IBM sold its QRadar SaaS business to Palo Alto Networks. When the biggest names in a category start changing hands, something is shifting.

Enter the AI-native challengers

That market shake-up opened the door for a wave of AI-native SIEMs and security data lakes. The newest pitch I keep hearing goes something like:

"Why store everything yourself? Leave the logs where they are. Our AI will call your sources' APIs, pull what it needs on demand, and only keep the signals that matter."

I'll be fair. That sounds great, and some of the thinking behind it is smart. Nobody enjoys paying to store terabytes of noise, and using AI to pick out signal is a useful idea.

The problem is the bill.

You swapped a storage bill for a token bill

When AI is querying everything on demand, you're still paying. You've just moved the cost from storage to compute, specifically the tokens it takes to pull, parse, and reason over that data each time. During an active incident, when you're firing off question after question, that meter moves fast. It's like cutting the cable bill and then signing up for nine streaming services.

Also, tokens right now are about as cheap and subsidized as they'll ever be. AI providers are pricing to win market share, and that won't last.

We've been here before: Moving everything to the cloud was going to save us all a fortune, remember? For plenty of companies it did, right up until the egress fees and surprise invoices showed up and someone had to go hire a FinOps team. Prices settled at their real level. I expect AI inference to follow a similar path.

Cost isn't the only catch, either:

Retention: If the source system only keeps 30 days of logs, then so do you, which hurts when you find out about a breach on day 45.

Availability: Your investigations depend on someone else's API being up and free of rate limits, usually at the exact moment you need answers.

Compliance: Telling an auditor or your cyber insurance carrier "we can go fetch it if we need it" makes for a tough conversation.

A better approach: store what matters, keep what you're required to keep

In my opinion, the best way to get real security value out of logs sits somewhere between hoarding everything and storing nothing. Only store the logs that matter.

That's how we approach it at Huntress. Our smart filtering removes logs that aren't security relevant before they ever hit storage, so you're paying for signal and not chatter. The logs that drive detections and investigations stick around.

Filtering doesn't mean ignoring compliance. If HIPAA, PCI DSS, CMMC, or your cyber insurance policy says you need certain records for a certain amount of time, keep them. Those logs might not catch an attacker in real time, but after an incident they're how you show you did things right.

When I talk with teams about this, I usually suggest running every log source through a simple filter:

Detect: Does this help us spot or investigate a threat? Keep it.

Prove: Does a regulation, auditor, or insurer require it? Keep it.

Drop: Neither? Drop it. Nobody's going to miss the printer logs.

The bill shrinks, sure. The bigger win is fewer false positives, faster investigations, and analysts who spend their day hunting threats rather than scrolling past junk.

So where does AI belong?

AI isn't the bad guy here. It absolutely has a place in a modern SIEM. What I care about is whether it's running on every log, all the time, with the meter spinning, or whether someone decided where it actually helps.

Once you've filtered down to security-relevant data, AI gets a lot more useful and a lot cheaper, because it has far less to dig through.

Correlation is where I think it shines most. A VPN login from a country the user has never been to is interesting on its own. Now add an encoded PowerShell command running on a server that same account touched ten minutes later, and then a new inbox rule in their Microsoft 365 account forwarding mail to an outside address. Separately those are three data points. Together they're an incident. Pulling EDR and ITDR telemetry together with the logs coming in from across the rest of IT, and lining it all up into one timeline, is a great job for AI.

It also helps with the grunt work of an investigation, like summarizing what a user did in the last 24 hours instead of handing an analyst 4,000 raw log lines. It can add context during triage, such as whether an IP has a bad reputation or whether this process normally runs on this host. And it can write up findings in plain English for the people who don't speak fluent ES|QL, which is most of leadership and every auditor I've met.

In every one of those cases, AI shows up after the filtering, at a specific point where it helps someone make a better call. Detections and real SOC analysts still decide whether something is malicious. That control is what keeps things predictable. You know where AI is being used, so you have a decent idea what it'll cost, and it isn't dreaming up alerts out of nowhere, which keeps false positives down.

Who owns what? The shared responsibility nobody puts on the sales slide

SIEM is one piece of the bigger SecOps picture, alongside EDR, identity threat detection, security awareness training, backups, and an incident response plan you've hopefully tested at least once. So when you're figuring out what to run in house and what to hand to a partner, keep in mind that even with a managed SIEM, some of the work stays with you.

Cloud providers figured this out years ago. AWS will lock down the data center, but if you leave an S3 bucket open to the internet, that one's on you. Managed SIEM works the same way.

What your partner should handle

Some activity looks malicious in pretty much any network. Credential stuffing. A user getting hammered with MFA prompts until they finally tap "approve." Shadow copies getting wiped. Someone dumping credentials out of memory with Mimikatz.

This is where you should be able to fully lean on a partner like Huntress. Our SOC sees attacker tradecraft across hundreds of thousands of environments, so when a new technique or IOC pops up in one place, we go looking for it everywhere else. One internal team can't get that view on its own. Detection engineering, tuning, 24/7 triage, and active remediation (isolating hosts, killing sessions, locking accounts, cleaning up persistence) are all things we own, across endpoint, identity, and SIEM. We don't just hand you a pile of alerts.

What only you can catch

Then there's the stuff that could be totally fine or a huge red flag, and the only way to know is whether your team expected it.

A remote access tool you didn't approve. ScreenConnect showing up on a workstation could be your help desk. It could also be an attacker, or a "helpful" vendor, setting up shop. Only you know which RMM tools are sanctioned in your environment.

A new admin account. Was that new domain admin part of a change ticket, or did it just appear on a Friday afternoon?

An off-hours login to a critical system. For one company that's the overnight batch job. For another it's the first sign someone has the keys to the ERP.

A service account wandering off its usual path. Service accounts are supposed to run in the background, not log into the VPN from a laptop. If one shows up in your VPN logs, someone may be using its credentials as a side door.

Firewall rule or group policy changes outside a maintenance window. If nobody on your team made the change, someone else did.

Your approved software list, your change calendar, and your maintenance windows live with your team. We can tell you a service account just logged into the VPN. Only you can say whether Jim from IT set that up as a "temporary" workaround three years ago.

That's where your own saved queries and custom detections come in. You know what "weird for us" looks like, so you write the logic, and you decide what to do when it fires. The SIEM gives you the data in one place to do it.

Response is a team sport, too

A partner like Huntress can stop the bleeding and clean up after it. But some calls only you can make. Do you take the production line offline? Notify customers? Loop in legal, the insurer, or HR? Which servers can be isolated on a Tuesday afternoon, and which ones need a phone call first?

Get your own leadership, IT, legal, and HR on the same page before an incident. Decide who owns which calls, who gets the phone call, and which actions are pre-approved. With Huntress, you choose where and how we respond in your environment, so those decisions carry straight through to how we act. Revisit them after every incident. Trust me, you don't want to be figuring out who's allowed to disable the CEO's account at 2 a.m.

The partnerships I've seen work best aren't "set it and forget it." It's more like "set it, tell us what matters, and we'll both sleep better."

So, is SIEM dead?

Nope. If there's one thing I'd want you to take away, it's to be intentional.

Be intentional about what you store. Keep the logs that help you detect and the ones that help you prove, and drop the rest. Be intentional about where you use AI. Point it at the spots where it sharpens the picture, like tying endpoint, identity, and log data together, instead of running it everywhere because you can. And be intentional about who's watching for what. Lean on a partner for the threats that look bad anywhere, and build your own detections for the things only your team would know are off.

The question I'd ask isn't whether SIEM is dead. It's whether yours is earning its keep.

Title: CREST Urges Whole-Ecosystem Approach to Financial Cyber Resilience
Context: CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and...
Full Text:
Cyber resilience in financial services should be built across the wider ecosystem of institutions, supervisors and specialist providers rather than treated solely as each institution's own responsibility, a new framework has argued.

CREST, the global non-profit accreditation body for the cybersecurity industry, said its whitepaper, Cyber Resilience in Financial Services: A Whole Ecosystem Approach, provides a maturity pathway for jurisdictions to assess their capabilities and coordinate improvements across three domains.

The paper, published on October 29, argued that weaknesses in shared infrastructure, technology providers, cyber firms or public authorities can undermine resilience across the wider financial system.

CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience

Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and demonstrating their controls work under pressure.

Financial supervisors are tasked with setting proportionate expectations, overseeing individual firms and understanding systemic risk, while cyber service providers are expected to deliver specialist advice, assessment, threat intelligence, testing and response capabilities.

The framework maps each domain through five stages of cyber maturity, with the three pathways planned together. Institutions progress from incomplete basic hygiene to advanced, threat-led assurance and continuous improvement. Supervisors move from mapping their sectors and establishing mandates to adaptive, cross-sector oversight, while providers progress from unvalidated services to specialist financial-sector capabilities.

CREST said the pathways are illustrative, not a new compliance standard. Its three priorities were ecosystem-wide measurement of maturity, a common language across the three domains and faster development wherever one part of the ecosystem lags.

Read more on financial-sector cyber regulation: FCA Updates Cyber Incident and Third-Party Reporting Rules

Framework Calls For Multi-Year Cyber Maturity Programs

CREST suggested supervisors or other market participants set out multi-year programs so the three domains develop in parallel, warning that requirements outpacing readiness can produce limited assurance. Its roadmap begins in years one and two with institutions mapping critical services and closing urgent hygiene gaps while supervisors publish a baseline and strategy.

Years three to five would bring independent assessment and risk-based testing for institutions, tiered requirements from supervisors and independent accreditation for providers. Years five to 10 would focus on threat-led penetration testing where proportionate, system-wide exercises and a diverse community of accredited specialist providers.

The whitepaper also warned that moving prematurely to mandate the highest international accreditations could shut out local providers where no route to accreditation exists. It pointed to measures including mentoring, partnerships, training and CREST's Cyber Accelerated Maturity Programme (CREST CAMP).

"Financial institutions, supervisors and cyber service providers each have a distinct role, and the strength of the system depends on their capability developing together," said CREST CEO Nick Benson.

Title: Adobe, Veeam, Juniper Networks Patch Critical Vulnerabilities
Context: (Etay Maor) AI Has Changed Attack Speed, Not Security Fundamentals As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation, so-called virtual patching still comes down to...
Full Text:
Adobe, Veeam, and Juniper Networks have released patches for over three dozen vulnerabilities across their products, including multiple critical-severity code execution flaws.

This week, Adobe fixed 12 vulnerabilities in Campaign Classic, Connect, Creative Cloud, and Substance 3D Painter.

The Campaign Classic update resolves eight critical-severity bugs, including code/command injection, incorrect authorization, and XSS issues.

Successful exploitation could lead to arbitrary code execution, security feature bypass, and privilege escalation, Adobe warns in a priority 2 advisory.

Another critical-severity defect leading to arbitrary code execution was addressed in Adobe Connect for desktop and mobile.

The security updates for Creative Cloud and Substance 3D Painter resolve high- and medium-severity security holes leading to code execution, privilege escalation, and memory leaks.

Adobe says it is not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

Veeam rolled out fixes for nine security defects in Backup for Microsoft 365, Backup & Replication, Veeam ONE, and Veeam Agent for Linux.

In Backup for Microsoft 365, Veeam fixed four flaws, including a critical issue that could have allowed attackers to read/write configuration data cross-tenant and achieve remote code execution.

It also resolved a critical-severity bug in Backup & Replication that could have allowed unauthenticated attackers to bypass authorization.

Veeam’s updates also resolved high- and medium-severity weaknesses leading to REST API authentication bypass, arbitrary file read or write, local privilege escalation, and multi-factor authentication bypass.

The company makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild.

Juniper Networks patched 18 vulnerabilities in Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor, including two critical-severity flaws leading to unauthenticated arbitrary command execution and privilege escalation.

High-severity flaws leading to arbitrary file read/write/deletion, code execution, privilege escalation, command execution, information disclosure, and denial-of-service (DoS) were also resolved.

Juniper Networks discovered the bugs internally and is not aware of any of them being exploited in the wild.

In a separate advisory covering the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, the company noted that CVE-2026-109618 affects Junos OS, but not in an exploitable way. It also investigated roughly a dozen other products and found none to be vulnerable.

Title: Zero Standing Privilege: Give the Next CVE Nothing to Inherit
Context: On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why new CVEs outpace patching, how a foothold inherits standing privilege, and how just-in-time access and secrets management limit what one exploit can reach. Includes five questions to test your environment.

On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites.

The PHP maintainers shipped fixes four days later, on October 21. Any vulnerable server that an attacker exploited before the server was patched could have given up the database passwords, API keys and cloud tokens the server held.

New vulnerabilities now arrive faster than organizations can patch them. Zero standing privilege limits what each exploit can reach

On October 23, Delinea published “PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks,” which covers which secrets to rotate first and how to prepare for the attacks that follow.

This blog covers the pattern behind PHP2Shell. New exploits now arrive faster than patching programs can absorb them, so organizations need a defense that does not depend on knowing which flaw comes next. Zero standing privilege (ZSP) gives an attacker nothing standing to inheritno matter which system the attacker breaks into first.

PHP2Shell was one of three vulnerabilities in the news during the week of October 19. On October 21, CISA added Plex2Shell, a chain of four vulnerabilities that gives attackers code execution on Plex Media Server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Plex had fixed the flaws in early August, yet the Shadowserver Foundation counted more than 36,000 exposed servers still unpatched in early September. Researchers also published a working proof-of-concept exploit for a critical, unauthenticated flaw in Fortinet FortiSIEM about a week after Fortinet shipped the fix.

More exploits are likely to follow before the month ends. The pattern matters more than any single bug. New exploits arrive at a rising pace; defenders get less time to respond to each one, and some systems go months without a patch.

Vulnerabilities now arrive continuously

The 2026 data show the same acceleration. CISA added 247 vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog between January 1 and October 1, more than the 245 it added in all of 2025. Since June 10, CISA has given federal agencies three days to remediate most new KEV entries, down from 21 days for most 2025 entries. Even under the longer deadlines, organizations took a median of 43 days to fully remediate KEV vulnerabilities in 2025, according to the Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group recorded an average of 11 zero-days a month from January through August, up from 8 a month in 2025. The October Microsoft Patch Tuesday release fixed more than 1,400 CVEs, the largest release since the program began. Only a fraction of those CVEs will be exploited, but an attacker needs only one.

AI now speeds up both the discovery of flaws and the development of exploits. In June, Microsoft Vice President of Engineering Tom Gallagher said AI-assisted vulnerability discovery was enabling bug hunting “at a speed and scale previously unseen.” Amazon Threat Intelligence wrote that AI-assisted analysis “makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit.”

The pace of new vulnerabilities is likely to keep climbing. No patching program, however well run, closes the gap between disclosure and deployment to zero. Patching remains essential, and organizations should fix KEV entries first. A strategy that depends on patching faster than attackers can find and weaponize flaws will lose over a long enough timeline.

A foothold inherits whatever privilege is standing

Each of the three exploits gives an attacker the same thing: code running on a system the organization trusts. Security teams call that position a foothold. What happens next depends less on the vulnerability than on what the compromised system can reach. Field Effect made the same point about Plex2Shell, noting that further impact “depends on the permissions assigned to the [Plex Media Server] service account and the resources accessible from the host.”

A web server running PHP often holds database credentials, API keys and cloud tokens in its configuration or environment. A SIEM collects logs from across the environment and often stores the credentials it uses to access monitored systems, making an unauthenticated SIEM flaw a high-value target. Management consoles and orchestrators often hold administrative rights over the systems they manage.

Standing privilege is access that an identity holds at all times, whether or not anyone is using it. The vulnerability gets the attacker in the door. Standing privilege decides how far the attacker gets.

An AI agent ran the full attack chain in July

A July incident at Hugging Face showed what happens when exploitation no longer needs a human at the keyboard. An AI agent running in an internal evaluation at a frontier AI lab escaped its sandbox and ran a four-and-a-half-day campaign, roughly two and a half days of which it spent inside Hugging Face production infrastructure. Hugging Face reconstructed the campaign from roughly 17,600 recovered agent actions.

The agent got in through two flaws in a dataset-processing pipeline. One flaw handed the agent the secrets and tokens stored in the environment of a production pod. Nearly every escalation after that ran on standing credentials: a shared broker credential bound to cluster-admin, a VPN key built for automation and tokens for source control. The agent went from code execution in a single pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under 13 hours. None of the escalations Hugging Face describes involved a human login, so stronger authentication for people would not have stopped them.

Hugging Face named “short-lived credentials” among its defensive priorities. After the incident, Hugging Face rotated credentials across its infrastructure and rebuilt the broker with a separate credential for each cluster.

Machine-speed attackers are likely to chain together the weaknesses that PHP2Shell, Plex2Shell and the FortiSIEM flaw expose: find a foothold, harvest what is standing and move. The foothold is the part defenders can’t always prevent. The standing privilege is the part defenders can remove.

ZSP works whichever CVE lands next

ZSP means no identity, whether AI agent, human or machine s, holds privilege it isn’t actively using. Just-in-time (JIT) access puts ZSP into practice. An identity requests access for a specific task, and an access platform grants that access for a limited time and revokes the access when the time ends. ZSP doesn’t depend on knowing which vulnerability attackers will exploit next, which is why ZSP fits an era in which new vulnerabilities arrive continuously.

The graphic below compares the same foothold in three scenarios: with standing privilege, with JIT Admin and JIT Access added, and with short-lived secrets added.

The model is illustrative, and the entry point is identical in each scenario.

Layer 1: JIT Admin removes standing root from hosts

An exploit usually runs with the permissions of the process it compromises. Researchers ran the Plex2Shell exploit, for example, as the Plex Media Server service account. The attacker’s next move is to escalate to root, the account with full control of a Linux or Unix server, or to local administrator on a Windows server. Standing root and local administrator rights turn one compromised server into many, because an attacker with those rights can read the SSH keys, service-account passwords and other credentials stored on the server.

JIT Admin replaces standing admin rights with elevation on demand. An administrator requests privilege for a task, the system checks the request against policy and grants the privilege for a limited time and records the elevation. Delinea Privilege Control for Servers (PCS) replaces standing root and local administrator rights with just-in-time elevation for specific commands.

PCS also enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA) at server login and again at privilege elevation. On a host that PCS protects, an exploit finds no standing admin rights to inherit, and PCS records each failed escalation attempt.

Layer 2: JIT Access limits spread across infrastructure

Once an attacker holds a foothold, the attacker’s next move is lateral movement: using credentials found on the first system to reach other servers, databases and clusters. In the Hugging Face incident, one shared broker credential gave the agent cluster-admin on two Kubernetes clusters within one second.

Delinea Runtime Authorization grants access to servers, Kubernetes clusters and databases per identity, per resource and for a limited time, so an attacker with a stolen credential reaches one resource for a limited time. The Runtime Authorization proxy injects credentials into each connection, so the client does not hold the credential and a compromised host has no stored credential to steal. Network access alone no longer grants access to a resource. A compromised application host or management server does not inherit access to every resource the host can reach on the network, and Runtime Authorization logs each connection it brokers.

Layer 3: Delinea Secret Server shrinks what an attacker can steal

PCS and Runtime Authorization limit where an attacker can go. Delinea Secret Server limits what the attacker finds on arrival. Secret Server brings privileged-account vaulting and workload secrets management together, so workloads (the applications and services that run without a person at the keyboard) retrieve credentials at runtime instead of carrying static values in environment variables and config files.

Secret Server rotates service-account and database passwords, API keys and other secrets on a schedule or after each use. Secret Server also issues dynamic credentials. Secret Server creates each dynamic credential on demand for a single workload, and the credential expires after a set time.

Secret Server doesn’t make a compromised host blind. An attacker with code execution can still read whatever credentials are present on the host at that moment, which is why the earlier Delinea blog—PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks—advises treating each secret a compromised server could read as stolen. What Secret Server changes is the value and lifespan of what the attacker reads.

Continuous CVE discovery demands continuous identity discovery

Vulnerability management identifies which systems are exposed. Identity security identifies what an attacker can reach from a compromised system. Security teams cannot reduce standing privilege they haven’t found. Machine and service identities are often the hardest to find. Hugging Face wrote that it had “wrongly provisioned” its broker with one credential shared across clusters and bound to cluster-admin. An inventory of privileged machine identities is the kind of check that surfaces a credential like that before an attacker does.

Delinea Continuous Identity Discovery uses AI to find human, machine and AI identities across the environment and flag the identities that hold standing privilege.

What ZSP doesn't fix

ZSP doesn’t patch a vulnerability. The flaw is still there, the exploited process still runs and an attacker with code execution can still do whatever that process is permitted to do. Patching, configuration hardening, network restrictions and detection all remain necessary. After the incident, Hugging Face closed both code-execution paths, blocked pod access to cloud metadata and added detection, in addition to rotating credentials.

ZSP does a different job. ZSP shrinks what the exploited process is permitted to do and how long the process holds that permission, so the window between disclosure and patch carries less risk.

Five security questions to ask about your environment

If an attacker compromised one of your internet-facing or management systems today, such as a web server, a SIEM or an orchestrator, what admin rights and credentials could the attacker reach from that system?

How many human, machine and AI identities hold standing privileged access, and when did your team last inventory those identities?

Does any single credential grant admin rights across more than one system, cluster or environment?

How long would a stolen service-account password, API key or token stay valid?

When the next exploited CVE lands on a product you run, how quickly can you tell which privileged identities and secrets the affected system holds or can reach?

Each question your team cannot answer points to standing privilege that an attacker could inherit.

Plan for the exploit that arrives before the patch

Prevention will sometimes fail, and sometimes the patch will arrive after the exploit. The organizations that fare best are likely to be the ones that removed standing privilege, not the ones that patched fastest every time.

Privilege Control for Servers keeps a foothold from escalating to root on hosts. Runtime Authorization limits how far the attacker can move across infrastructure. Secret Server shortens the life of each credential the attacker steals. Together, the three products apply ZSP across human, machine and AI identities, which helps one compromised system stay one compromised system.

See how Delinea applies Zero Standing Privilege and just-in-time access.

The next CVE is already being found. Make sure it finds nothing standing.

Title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
Context: 5B+ valuation for entire firm, though portion sold not specified Malware Month Ten years since the first corp ransomware, Mikko Hyppönen sees no end in sight On the plus side,...
Full Text: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither. BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet. "The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all." 'Circumvention inevitable' Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented. It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks. Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout, committing to implementing more robust measures that promote the ban’s aims. It said it has identified some mitigations that could be taken to counter circumvention, such as making it easier for users to report suspected underage social media users, and “using age inference models.” The regulator said it will closely monitor circumvention for the first 12 months after the ban is enforced to understand possible methods to prevent children from finding ways around the age checks. In May, nearly a year after the OSA’s age verification requirements kicked in, researchers found that the existing age checks proved largely ineffective at keeping under-18s away from adult content online. Some reported beating age checks with just a drawn-on moustache. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said recently that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children’s ability to access potentially harmful online content. Commenting on today’s announcement, Ofcom chief exec Dame Melanie Dawes said that when the social media ban takes effect, it will take a whole-of-society approach to ensure the ban is upheld. ?This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right," she said. "It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply. "We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play." The UK government is expected to outline the first set of regulations related to the under-16 social media ban by the end of the year, and Ofcom is in the process of developing draft guidance for platforms. ®

Title: Windows 11 KB5127936 update released with 41 changes and fixes
Context: 4 million installs caught hijacking searches Hackers exploit Cisco SD-WAN flaw to deploy custom KeyDrift malware CISA warns of Fragnesia Linux flaw chained in PHP2Shell attacks...
Full Text:
Microsoft released the KB5127936 preview cumulative update for Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 26H2, with 41 changes, including File Explorer and Cloud rebuild improvements.

KB5127936 is a preview update that adds new features and fixes at the end of each month, letting IT admins and users test them before they roll out to the entire user base during next month's Patch Tuesday.

However, unlike regular Patch Tuesday cumulative updates, monthly preview updates are optional and don't include security patches.

The October 2026 preview update makes the File Explorer context menu faster and easier to customize, letting users choose which app extensions and commands appear and how they're organized.

After you install KB5127936, Cloud rebuild can also reinstall Windows without USB media or a custom image, using an image and drivers downloaded directly from Windows Update, even when Windows won't start.

Microsoft also updated XBOX mode to include a refreshed Gaming Task View with quick access to key system actions like Power Options and Exit to Desktop while gaming via a new navigation bar.

​You can install the KB5127936 preview update by downloading it from the Microsoft Update Catalog or by opening Settings, going to Windows Update, and selecting "Check for Updates."

Because this is an optional update, you will need to click the "Download and install" link unless you have "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" enabled (which prompts the OS to install it automatically).

Windows 11 KB5127936 highlights

Once installed, this optional non-security update will upgrade Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2 devices to builds 26200.9818 and 26300.9818, respectively.

The October 2026 preview update adds further changes and improvements, some of the more important ones highlighted below:

New! This update improves the Privacy & security page in Windows Settings by grouping related Camera, Microphone, and Location privacy controls and elevating usage information from linked pages onto the main page.

New! This update enables Windows recovery (WinRE) to automatically reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles already saved in Windows, including supported certificate-based networks. Devices can now get online automatically during recovery scenarios such as quick machine recovery or cloud rebuild, without preconfiguring Wi-Fi credentials in WinRE. This capability is on by default, and IT admins can disable it. Microsoft disclosed this feature last month, and it is now beginning to roll out.

New! This update introduces a Restore Summary that appears after you restore a backup profile to a new device. The summary clearly shows what was restored, including Windows settings and the list of Microsoft Store apps. This improves transparency during device transitions, helps you validate your restore results, and lets you continue setup on your new device with confidence.

New! This update improves the adaptive hibernate policy to provide faster Modern Standby instant-on resumes while helping preserve battery life when the charge is low. Noticeable changes include less hibernation when the battery is above 80% and earlier hibernation below 10%.

This month, Microsoft also reminded users that updated Secure Boot certificates are rolling out to replace the original 2011 certificates, which will expire in late June 2027.

Microsoft first announced plans to refresh expiring Secure Boot certificates on eligible Windows 11 systems in January, after warning users and IT admins in November 2025 to update them before they expire.

The company also warned customers they may need to reboot one more time after installing the October 2026 optional update and updates rolling out over the next several months.

"With recent and upcoming Windows updates over the next few months, a limited number of consumer and business devices might experience one additional restart during installation," Microsoft noted in a message center update. "This one‑time restart occurs after a Secure Boot certificate update is applied as part of the Secure Boot update process."

Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked

Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

Title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
Context: A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain...
Full Text: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register. Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register. Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register. A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.” Which repos were affected? As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects. The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular. Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K). “These projects are used by thousands of organizations," Babo said. The researchers disclosed their findings to all of the projects’ maintainers, and most of the repositories were closed or fixed, but they can’t confirm that all of them were. This campaign follows several earlier supply chain attacks against open source security and dev tools as attackers increasingly look for new methods to steal credentials and other secrets. “There is no way to stop the attackers from attempting,” Nakibly said. “The only way is to make sure that the workflow code is resilient, and not vulnerable to such attacks." The researchers recommend applying least-privilege access to CI/CD workflows, and separating as much as possible workflows triggered by external events from jobs with elevated permissions. “Developers should treat external content as untrusted, and also limit the secrets and environment variables that are available to the workflow,” Babo said. ®

Title: Webinar: How to Build AI Threat Readiness Into Your Security Operations

Security teams have spent years trying to detect threats faster. AI is changing the harder part: how much time defenders have left to act.

Advanced AI models can now help attackers discover vulnerabilities, generate exploit code, and move through weaknesses faster than traditional security processes were built to handle.

The challenge is no longer just finding another vulnerability or generating another alert. It is knowing which exposures matter, what an attacker can reach, and which issues need to be fixed first.

That is the focus of next week's webinar, How to Build AI Threat Readiness Across Your Security Operations, featuring an expert from Wiz. The session will show how security teams can improve visibility, prioritize real risk, and shorten the path from detection to remediation.

Most security teams already have plenty of data. They have vulnerability findings, cloud alerts, identity signals, application telemetry, and threat detections. The harder problem is connecting those signals quickly enough to answer the questions that drive action.

Is this vulnerability reachable? Does the exposed asset contain sensitive data? Can an attacker move from it to something more important? Who owns the affected system? What should be fixed first?

When those answers live across different tools and teams, investigations slow down. That delay matters more when attackers can automate parts of the discovery and exploitation process.

For SOC teams, that can mean less time spent manually assembling context. For vulnerability management, it means knowing which findings deserve immediate attention. For cloud and security engineering teams, it means connecting risk to the people and systems that can actually fix it.

The goal is not to automate every security decision. It is to remove delays caused by fragmented tools, repetitive investigation, and unclear ownership.

Attendees will leave with a framework for assessing whether their current security operations are ready for faster, AI-assisted attacks. Title: Telegram Android Flaw Lets Attackers Run Code When Users Answer Voice Calls
Context: 2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert Attackers Hijacked Over 300 Tor Exit Relays to Intercept SSH Connections PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as...
Full Text:
A flaw in Telegram for Android could be chained with two other bugs to take full control of a victim's phone through a voice call, once the victim answered, according to security startup NebuSec.

The attacker needed only an ordinary Telegram account. Telegram fixed the flaw in version 12.10.4 of the app, released in late September, and NebuSec disclosed it on October 29.

Combined with an information-leak bug, the flaw gives the attacker an escape from the Telegram app to Android, NebuSec co-founder and chief executive Eten Zou told The Hacker News. Adding an Android root exploit then gives full control of the phone, including its messages, microphone and camera.

The flaw can be triggered in every version from 8.6.2 through 12.10.3, Zou said. Those versions came out between March 2022 and September 2026.

The company confirmed it in private voice calls on ARM64-based phones and has no evidence so far that it directly affects Telegram's iOS and desktop apps or group calls.

Anyone using Telegram for Android should make sure the app is on version 12.10.4 or later. The version number appears at the bottom of the app's Settings page. The flaw had no CVE identifier as of October 29.

The attack needs the victim to be called and to answer, Zou said, so setting Telegram's call privacy option to "Nobody" blocks it, and so does declining the call.

NebuSec has not seen the flaw used in real attacks, and believes no one else had realized it could be turned into remote code execution.

NebuSec reported the flaw to Telegram on September 26, after version 12.10.4 had shipped. Telegram acknowledged the report but did not believe the flaw could be turned into remote code execution, so no CVE was assigned and no bug bounty was paid, Zou said. The Hacker News has asked Telegram for comment.

During a Telegram call, the two apps send each other short messages to set up the call and report its state. One type, called MediaState, reports whether the microphone is muted, whether the camera is on, and how the video is rotated.

The flaw was in the code that reads MediaState messages. That code did not handle missing fields correctly and accessed memory it should not, according to NebuSec.

Telegram's published source code for version 12.10.3 contains a flaw that matches that description, a review by The Hacker News found. When a MediaState message included a rotation value, the code checked that value. It then read a different field, the video state, even if the message had no such field.

Version 12.10.4 reads the rotation value from the right field. The calling code that uses this message was switched on in version 8.6.2, the first version NebuSec names.

Telegram's Android, iOS, and desktop apps use one shared library, called tgcalls, for calls. A change labeled "Fix camera rotation" made the same correction in tgcalls on April 21, 2026.

Telegram's iOS source code included that change from version 12.7, released in May, and the desktop app's code from version 7.0.1, released in July. Telegram for Android received it in version 12.10.4 in September.

Whether the earlier code could be exploited in those apps has not been shown.

NebuSec's video shows two phones, one marked as the attacker and one as the victim. The victim accepts a Telegram call. About half a minute into the call, the victim's phone switches to its home screen, the app icons fall down the screen, and a "HACKED BY NEBUSEC" logo appears.

The video does not show which Telegram or Android version the victim's phone was running. No technical write-up of the flaw was on NebuSec's website as of October 29, so the attack chain, including the two other bugs, depends on the video and on what the company says.

NebuSec, a startup backed by Y Combinator, says its Code Security product, which runs on OpenAI's GPT-5.4 model, found the flaw. In July, the company described an Android exploit chain that started with a Firefox flaw and reached the kernel of an ARM64 device running Android 17.

Separately, the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) published an advisory on October 15 about an unpatched flaw in rlottie, the library Telegram apps have used to draw animated stickers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111105 (CVSS score: 7.0), can let an attacker run code if a user opens a malicious file or page, ZDI said.

Telegram had told ZDI in March that checks on its servers mitigated the flaw, and in April asked ZDI for a full remote code execution chain.

Those checks could be bypassed, researcher Saifeldeen Aziz says in the abstract for his OffensiveCon talk in Tokyo. The research used AI-guided fuzzing, which feeds code with large amounts of broken or unexpected input, to find memory-corruption bugs in rlottie across Telegram's iOS, Android, and desktop apps. It then chained those bugs with flaws in how stickers are delivered and checked to run code on Telegram for iOS.

The Android app replaced rlottie with tlottie, a library written in Rust, between versions 12.8.1 in June and 12.10.0 in August, according to Telegram's published source code. The desktop app's code made the same switch in September, and the iOS code added tlottie in version 13.0 in October while still including rlottie.

Title: 26,400 Valid Cloud and AI Credentials Found Exposed in Public Gitee Repositories
Context: 2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert Attackers Hijacked Over 300 Tor Exit Relays to Intercept SSH Connections PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as...
Full Text:
26,400 credentials that developers left in public code on Gitee, a Chinese code-hosting service, still worked when a researcher tested them. Anyone who copied one from that code could have used it.

Independent researcher Ben Zimmermann found them by scanning 7.25 million public Gitee repositories and reported the results on October 28. Most were keys for cloud and AI services, led by 9,473 Alibaba Cloud AccessKey pairs.

Zimmermann sent the vendors with the most exposed keys a list of their credentials, but he did not contact the developers who leaked them. When he published, he had not confirmed that any of the reported credentials had been revoked. So anyone who has pushed a key to a public Gitee repository cannot assume it has been revoked.

The scan ran for about a month, but Zimmermann did not provide the dates, so it is unclear how long ago the credentials were tested. He also did not say whether anyone else had used them.

He ran two secret scanners, TruffleHog and Kingfisher, over every repository. Both tried each credential against the service that issued it and kept only those that worked, he wrote.

The scanners read each repository's full commit history. A key that a developer later removed from the code could still be found and counted there.

The 26,400 figure counts each credential once, regardless of how many repositories it appeared in. By commit date, 12,242 of the credentials came from 2025, nearly half the total. Some dated to the late 2000s.

What Was Exposed

After the Alibaba Cloud keys, the largest groups were 3,805 YouTube API keys, 3,170 DeepSeek keys, 1,489 keys for Zhipu's BigModel AI platform, and 1,348 OpenAI keys. Smaller numbers were found for GitHub, AWS, Google Cloud and Google's Gemini.

One of the credentials was "an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform," Zimmermann wrote. He did not name the platform or say what the credential could reach.

What a working key lets someone do depends on the service. OpenAI says that a compromised key allows another person to use the account's quota without the owner's consent. That can cause "data loss, unexpected charges," a used-up monthly quota, and interrupted API access.

A YouTube API key is a Google Cloud API key that identifies a project, Google says. Without API restrictions, such a key can be used with every API that accepts Google Cloud keys.

What to Do If You Committed Keys

Treat any key that has ever been in a public Gitee repository as exposed, and revoke it at the provider. Deleting a key from the code or rewriting the repository's history does not revoke it, as noted by TruffleHog's maker, Truffle Security.

Alibaba Cloud: create a new AccessKey pair, switch your apps to it, then disable and delete the old pair. Check for unexpected charges and for resources created or deleted that you did not need, Alibaba Cloud's leak response plan says. ActionTrail shows the key's API calls for the last 90 days, but data operations in services such as OSS and SLS have to be checked in each service's own logs.

Google and YouTube API keys: rotate the key, which creates a new key with the same restrictions, update your apps to use it, then delete the old key. Add API restrictions so the key works only with the APIs you need.

OpenAI: rotate the key immediately from the API Keys page, as OpenAI advises, and set spend limits to help limit charges from a leaked key.

Two Scanners, Different Results

MongoDB makes Kingfisher, and Zimmermann's post was developed with its Kingfisher team.

In this scan, TruffleHog found 12,737 credentials that worked, and Kingfisher found 14,664, but only 1,001 were found by both. Each tool alone found about half of the total.

TruffleHog found almost all of the Alibaba Cloud keys. Kingfisher found all 1,489 BigModel keys, because TruffleHog has no detector for Zhipu's keys, Zimmermann wrote.

Teams that rely on a single scanner should verify its detectors against the services they use.

Gitee and Other Code Hosts

China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology chose Gitee in 2020 as the base for a national open-source code-hosting platform.

Gitee's public API is limited, and a 2021 attempt to study leaked credentials on the site gave up because of it.

Gitee's rate, 3.64 working credentials per 1,000 repositories scanned, is higher than the rates from earlier scans of GitLab (3.11) and Bitbucket (2.39). Those scans used only TruffleHog, Zimmermann wrote.

Based on TruffleHog's results alone, Gitee's rate is 1.76, but that count excludes services TruffleHog does not cover, such as Zhipu. So neither figure shows which platform leaks more.

Title: Online Scam Volumes Double to Overtake Phishing
Context: The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time
Full Text:
Detections of online scams doubled between July 2025 and June 2026, as cybercriminals focused on more direct ways to generate revenue from victims, according to Akamai.

The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time.

It recorded around 6.4 million online scams in the period April-June 2026, versus 3.2 million in July-September 2025.

This category typically includes fake stores, investment scams, tech support scams and payment fraud, it said.

“The fight against fraud is no longer just an isolated financial function; it is a critical, cross-functional cybersecurity imperative,” said Patrick Sullivan, CTO, security strategy at Akamai. “As autonomous AI agents and synthetic identities redefine how customers interact with brands, threat actors are exploiting these same vectors to conduct business logic abuse and zero-click data exfiltration.”

Read more on digital scams: Social Media Platforms Earn Billions from Scam Ads.

However, phishing – which Akamai defines as attempts to steal credentials, authentication info and data via brand impersonation – also rose during the period.

Phishing detections increased by 61%, driven by reusable phishing kits, industrialized infrastructure, and AI.

The latter has helped to decrease the average phishing attack lifespan by more than 50%, dropping from 48 days (Q4 2025) to 22 days (Q2 2026), the report claimed.

“Adversaries leverage AI to generate dynamic templates, produce multilingual lures at scale, and deploy condition-aware evasion – drastically lowering costs while bypassing legacy defenses,” it explained.

“Conversely, security teams use AI to compress investigation and reduce workflows from days to less than an hour through automated indicator analysis, infrastructure clustering, and evidence collection, disrupting attacks before victims are impacted.”

The Human Impact of Scams

Over 80% of scam victims in the US reported suicidal thoughts following the crime, according to new data from the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) published on October 28.

A large part of this is down to the self-blame and social stigma attached to scams, the ITRC claimed. It also blamed “institutional ghosting" for the mental anguish that victims often feel.

“When general consumer scam victims overcame their shame to seek help, institutions frequently compounded the injury,” it explained. “Nearly nine in 10 general consumer scam victims asked an organization for help and were never contacted, and 67.2% reported that the organizations they contacted ‘made me feel it was my own fault.’”

A lack of support can also leave victims exposed to recovery scams.

“Abandoned by legitimate institutions and desperate to undo the damage, 78.9% of general consumer scam victims (and 90.9% of those experiencing suicidal ideation) paid a fee to a third party who promised to recover their stolen money, fix their credit or catch the scammer – compared to just 6.5% of scam victims who connected with the ITRC,” the report said.
