ZDI-CAN-33367

Fix status

A small patch, “net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()”, is on netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet and tagged for stable. It has not been merged.

How the bug works: Dirty Frag again

Earlier this year, Dirty Frag (CVE-2026-43284) showed defenders how an unprivileged user could get the kernel's IPsec ESP code to decrypt in place over pages that belong to the page cache. Those pages back a file the user can only read, and decryption writes the attacker's bytes into the cached copy of that file. Targeting a setuid binary or /etc/passwd this way gives the attacker root without ever opening the file for writing.

The Dirty Frag fix marked those shared pages with a flag and taught ESP to copy before decrypting when it sees the flag. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a gap in that fix.

skb_zerocopy() moves the same pages into a new socket buffer but does not carry the flag across. ESP never sees the flag, decrypts in place, and the write lands in the page cache. According to TuxCare and Safeguard, the code path dates to kernel 3.14.

Not the first gap

The Dirty Frag fix only works if every piece of networking code that moves those pages around carries the flag along. Since May, the kernel's CVE team has published six follow-up CVEs where some other path lost it:

Frag-copy and shift helpers: CVE-2026-43503

Coalescing: CVE-2026-46300

IPTFS: CVE-2026-53363, CVE-2026-64566

An error-handling helper: CVE-2026-80977

Another error path inside skb_zerocopy() itself: CVE-2026-90049

CVE-2026-90049 is a different bug in the same function, so a kernel carrying its fix is not fixed for ZDI-CAN-33367.

Exploitation

The PoC needs unprivileged user namespaces and a handful of networking modules: nlmon, nft_queue, nfnetlink_queue, cls_u32, act_pedit, act_mirred, and esp4. It does not need a Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) leak, or any capability the user doesn't already get inside their own namespace.

Each step of exploitation is a system call that can be made by an ordinary user process:

Unshare into new user and network namespaces, then write sysctls.

Bring up an nlmon interface.

Install XFRM state over netlink.

Add an nftables NFQUEUE rule.

Attach a tc pedit action with a redirect.

splice() into a socket on 127.0.0.1, which triggers the in-place decryption over the page cache.

Impact

TuxCare reproduced a root shell on AlmaLinux 8–10, CloudLinux 9–10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. AlmaLinux was rooted with the Dirty Frag fix installed. CentOS 6 and 7 kernels are not vulnerable. The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Both CVSS 9.0 reports are in ksmbd, the in-kernel Server Message Block (SMB) server. Samba is not ksmbd.

If your file servers run smbd, neither report applies to you. To check whether ksmbd is running anywhere, look for the ksmbd kernel module, the ksmbd.mountd userspace daemon, and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445.

ZDI-CAN-33774: The dispatch race

ksmbd decides per request whether it is handling SMB1 or SMB2. If an attacker packs a burst of short SMB1 packets and an SMB2 packet into the same TCP write, the worker threads can run an SMB2 handler over SMB1 data and read past the end of the shorter buffer. This works before authentication. The public PoC leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel. ZDI describes a write-past-buffer path that needs share access and labels the bug as remote code execution (RCE), but nothing public shows code execution as of this blog’s publication.

Maintainer Namjae Jeon says the bug is already fixed, and his tree bears that out. Commit 68f410faedaf ("ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU") was written on September 30, credited to a different reporter, and describes exactly this race. It is queued in ksmbd's ksmbd-for-next branch and has not reached a released kernel.

ZDI-CAN-33549: SMB Direct

An integer underflow in the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) transport turns a crafted buffer descriptor into a heap overflow of up to eight KB. The bar is higher than for 33774. The host needs an RDMA-capable interface (hardware, or the rxe software driver), a client that negotiates SMB Direct, and a writable share. The public PoC crashes the kernel.

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher believes a fix already in his branch for Linux 7.5 covers it. As of this writing, that hasn't been confirmed. Ubuntu builds SMB Direct support; Debian does not.

ZDI-CAN-34068

ZDI-CAN-34068 is an out-of-bounds write in vmwgfx, the kernel driver for VMware's virtual GPU, rated as LPE (CVSS 8.8). Only the title is public. Kroah-Hartman's reply on dri-devel points to the dirty-tracking code. There is no patch.

The exposure is narrow. vmwgfx only binds to VMware's SVGA virtual display adapter, so the bug only matters on VMware guests: vSphere and Workstation VMs, and VMware-based virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI). In Sysdig TRT testing, it does not reproduce on Lima or EC2 instances, which don't present that device.

ZDI-CAN-34076 and ZDI-CAN-32005

ZDI-CAN-34076 (nvmet) is an uninitialized-memory information leak in the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target's Get Log Page handling. Only the title is public, and the kernel team has said nothing can be done until details arrive.

ZDI-CAN-32005 (ConnMan) is a stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager's DNS proxy. It is a userspace bug, not a kernel bug, and is outside the scope of this post.

Detection

The four bugs that are the most impactful right now differ in what a syscall-level runtime sensor can observe:

ZDI-CAN-33367. The sequence of the exploitation is distinctive. The process unshares into new user and network namespaces, writes sysctls, brings up an nlmon interface, installs XFRM state over netlink, adds an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attaches a tc pedit action with a redirect, and then splice()s into a socket on 127.0.0.1. Nothing legitimate does all of that from a single unprivileged process. Of the four, this is the easiest one to detect.

ksmbd (33774 and 33549). A sensor can see that ksmbd is exposed: the module loads, ksmbd.mountd starts, and 445 is listening. It can see what an attacker does after code execution, once something spawns a process or touches files. It cannot see the race or the overflow itself. Runtime detection is the backstop.

ZDI-CAN-34068. The trigger is DRM ioctl() calls on the vmwgfx device node, made by a local process. That narrows where to look, but GPU ioctls are noisy on any desktop or VDI guest, so treat them as context for an investigation, not as a signal on their own.

Sysdig Secure customers are covered by a new runtime rule in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, Page Cache Poisoning via Spliced File Pages to Loopback, which matches the syscall patterns as seen for ZDI-CAN-33367. Work on exploits for the other flaws in this disclosure continues, and the Sysdig TRT is writing detection rules for them as the techniques become clear.

Independently of the entry point, customers also keep post-exploitation coverage, which detects the effects of a successful exploit rather than the route in.

Recommendations

ZDI-CAN-33367

Patch as soon as your distribution ships the skb_zerocopy() fix. A kernel carrying only the CVE-2026-90049 fix is not covered.

Restrict unprivileged user namespaces. Setting user.max_user_namespaces=0 (or kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 on Debian) should block the public PoC, though TuxCare notes it has not yet validated this against the PoC. The cost is real: rootless containers, some browser sandboxes and some build tooling depend on user namespaces, so scope it to hosts that don't need them.

Avoid relying on Ubuntu's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. The PoC got past it through the AppArmor profile of a container launcher package.

Block the nlmon and act_pedit modules where you can. Denying them breaks this PoC, although TuxCare cautions it may not close every path to the bug.

Enforce seccomp RuntimeDefault on Kubernetes pods. The exploit starts by creating a user namespace, so containers that can call unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) are in play. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks that call, but Kubernetes pods run Unconfined unless you set RuntimeDefault per pod or cluster-wide using the kubelet --seccomp-default option. This is a good week to make it the cluster default.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Inventory where ksmbd runs. Samba users are unaffected.

Unload ksmbd and block the module on hosts that don't need it.

Restrict TCP 445 to trusted networks where ksmbd must stay.

Disable SMB Direct unless your storage network depends on RDMA.

ZDI-CAN-34068

Inventory Linux guests running on VMware, and watch for the vmwgfx patch.

Disable 3D acceleration, or keep the vmwgfx module from loading, on guests that have no use for it.

Across all Linux flaws

Track the reports by ZDI ID and component name until CVEs are assigned.

‍

Conclusion

ZDI's decision to copy public lists put reproduction details for six bugs in front of attackers before several of them had fixes. As defenders know, a lack of an assigned CVE ID does not mean a lack of exposure. Only one of the six, ZDI-CAN-33367, combines a public root exploit, broad distribution exposure, and a fix that hasn't yet merged. It is the seventh path found to drop the Dirty Frag flag, reopening a bug class whose protection has already leaked six times since May 2026. The two ksmbd reports carry the highest scores, but they only matter where ksmbd — not Samba — is running.

For defenders, the practical takeaway is that this week's work is about exposure, not scanners. It’s also important to note that the bugs differ in what defenders should actually watch. The ZDI-CAN-33367 exploit runs as an ordinary user process through a distinctive sequence of systems calls, so teams can catch it in motion. The ksmbd bugs run inside the kernel worker threads with no attacker process on the host, so controlling exposure is key.

Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix.

Title: 3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability
Context: Related:Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots Framework 2: Record the Board's Decision Source: David Garrie, Law and Forensics Creating a paper...
Full Text:
ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — Many chief information security officers (CISOs) currently find themselves in the deep weeds of AI governance. But the question they might not be asking is: How do you defend decisions around AI deployments when litigators, regulators, and customers come looking for someone to assume liability for a compromise?

Cyber legal expert Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, is striving to answer that question with distinct frameworks that both help CISOs determine whether a specific AI feature is sufficiently safe to run, as well as generate an evidentiary trail of paperwork that can be used to defend their actions, should something go horribly awry down the road.

While the need for such frameworks is particularly in the limelight in the age of agentic AI, the work began back in June 2024, when JAMS AI Rules were established to create a framework arbitrators can use to settle AI disputes between parties. The rules themselves don't explain liability or apply to every litigator. But Garrie, who helped write the rules, says they are helpful for establishing guidelines for technical evidence handling.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Speaking from the stage at ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 this week, he stressed the importance of addressing incident-response needs at the contract stage and outlined frameworks for three best practices in particular that are useful for quantifying AI liability: calculating an AI deployment risk score; documenting board decisions around risk appetites; and determining which data specific should be preserved from an incident.

CISOs Should Negotiate for Evidence in Vendor Contracts

In the aftermath of an AI compromise, the basic forensic evidence as to what happened can be difficult to get. Garrie stresses that baking these considerations in at the contract stage with AI vendors is crucial, as is having cybersecurity leadership involved as early as possible during those negotiations, with an eye to creating provisions that allow CISOs to establish precisely what happened in an incident, including access to logs and preservation requests.

“Can the AI vendor provide you with a snapshot of the model at the time of an incident?” Garrie suggested CISOs ask. “And how fast can that be made available?”

He added that important considerations for contracts also include risk allocation that needs to be established as well, and urged CISOs to have a clear picture of vendor AI use permissions, data restrictions, warranties, insurance, and liability caps. Cyber leaders should also have a handle on the vendor's operational controls, access, and security responsibilities. Finally, an understanding of how disputes will be handled is necessary for CISOs, including ensuring compliance with governing laws, the forum for disputes, emergency relief scope, and more.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

Getting a handle on contract negotiations with AI vendors early could be the difference between getting the evidence you need to prove your company wasn't negligent and not, Gerrie stressed.

"Once the contract is signed, that's it," Garrie warned. "They aren't going to give you anything that isn't specifically outlined. You'll have to wait for a renewal."

Framework 1: AI Deployment Risk Score

Source: David Garrie, Law and Forensics

Garrie has developed a simple five-factor rubric that helps CISOs determine the risks and exposures related to the deployment of any given AI tool. Across five dimensions, including "potential harm," "data and rights," "autonomy," "evidence gap," and "vendor dependence," the framework helps provide a score that, according to Garrie, "makes assumptions visible."

The final score determines whether the AI tool falls within "standard review," "conditional approval," "restricted pilot," or "hold release" thresholds, each of which indicates a specific level of risk.

Related:Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots

Framework 2: Record the Board's Decision

Source: David Garrie, Law and Forensics

Creating a paper trail of specific board decisions can be a critical piece of evidence in disputing liability, Garrie explained. Weak or vague reporting isn't the CISO's friend.

Garrie's framework for preserving board decisions includes granular details like the scope and time frame of the board decision; the exposure associated with the deployment (and evidence provided of that risk); the conditions of the deployment and the requirements for human approval; the accountable parties who authorize the work and review evidence (and a record of oversight including the final decision; challenges that were raised during the decision-making process; as well as the owner of the tool and associated due dates.

This one is about not just creating a static record of the decision, but about generating ongoing records that are defensible against AI liability, he added.

Framework 3: AI Incident Response Checklist

Source: David Garrie, Law and Forensics

The purpose of this tool, Garrie said, is not just to contain the compromise, but to work to preserve the state of the AI system at the time of the incident. He also advised CISOs to get legal involved immediately.

The tool helps identify and preserve this kind of data, beyond the basic security logs. Garrie's framework requires evidence on the system state at the time of the incident, the interaction records, data and access information, and a governance record, as well as data integrity and chain of custody details.

What CISOs Can Do in the Next 30 Days

Over the next month, Garrie challenged CISOs to put his frameworks to the test on one AI deployment, improve one board report, and run one AI tabletop to practice coordinating actions around vendor evidence preservation and notifications.

The bottom line, according to Garrie, is that regulators, litigators, and customers ultimately are only going to care about the evidence you can produce to prove the organization considered all the risks and acted responsibly to mitigate them.

"They don't care that you're using the NIST guidelines," he warned. Determination of liability is going to come down to what the CISO and the organization can prove they did to protect their systems against AI compromise.

Title: External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery
Context: Сloud Security Application Security Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Insider Threats News External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery Mail bombing is getting a new look...
Full Text:
Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams' external chat functionality at scale, using IT-support impersonation and email bombing tactics to trick employees into granting remote access. Attackers target multiple users within short, five-minute windows of time, and once the victim bites, the attack chain reaches payload execution in under 15 minutes.

In a blog post on Oct. 26, Arctic Wolf detailed the campaign and what it described as a "recurring social engineering pattern" across more than 400 incidents in the wild. Threat actors use Microsoft Teams' external chat creation capability, which enables outside parties to contact employees.

"A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same 'IT Support (Internal)' display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains," Arctic Wolf's Shubham Dubey wrote in the blog post.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

In a typical example of the attack, the victim is "mail bombed," or inundated with a flood of email subscriptions or newsletters, to establish a sense of urgency. Then, an external Teams user claiming to be IT support contacts the victim and offers to address the issue. The impersonator persuades the employee to launch a remote-access session via legitimate tooling like Quick Assist (most common), AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn.

Once the victim grants access, the attacker conducts follow-on activity such as executing malware, stealing credentials, performing reconnaissance, or possibly deploying ransomware. Dubey explained that a typical order for this is a whoami/systeminfo-based recon, a PowerShell-based payload, a command-and-control (2) beacon, lateral movement to gain access to credentials through Kerberos abuse methods like Kerberoasting and GoldenPAC, and a second, commercial-grade remote access tool, "which provides an independent control channel that survives remediation of the original implant."

Email Bombing Evolves to Deploy at Scale

Spam or mail bombing is not a new tactic. Threat actors have been flooding inboxes as a pretense for social engineering for some time now. Microsoft researchers identified the use of this technique by Black Basta in mid-2024, with later examples seen in 3AM, Cactus, Chaos, and the GoGRPC campaigns. But what stands out about Arctic Wolf's research is that it shows this technique operating at scale, with recurring infrastructure, naming conventions, and attacker behavior seen across hundreds of incidents.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading roughly 15% of cases progressed beyond the initial stage into a successful compromise, which, given the volume of the campaign, constitutes a success.

As for who is behind recent attack waves, Moore could not make definitive attributions but says, "Black Basta-associated activity remains one of the most significant drivers of Teams chat abuse."

On the infrastructure front, Arctic Wolf noted a move from throwaway onmicrosoft.com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, especially ".top" domains, and provided data on their prevalence. The vendor stated that approximately half of observed cases involving paid domains used .top domains.

For naming, attackers would reach out with "(Internal)" appended to the display name to trick the victim that a message is coming from within the company, even though Teams labels the sender as "external" simultaneously. The names will also frequently use friendly sounding names (Arctic Wolf offered Liam, Scott McGhee, and Matthew as examples) after labels like "IT Support" and "IT Service Desk."

Other markers observed included naming conventions specific to the target's locale ("Supporte TI" for French- and Spanish-speaking organizations), and the use of 100 different emojis in attacker display names.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Get Ahead of Email Bombing Social Engineering Attacks

Arctic Wolf noted that prior to engaging with victims, the attackers initiate a one-on-one chat to avoid group conversations, which Microsoft records in its telemetry as the ChatCreated event. Arctic Wolf assesses this to be the primary detection point for defenders setting alerts.

The vendor also recommended setting an allowlist for trusted external organizations, blocking chats with unmanaged or Teams consumer accounts, disabling the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users, blocking federation with trial-only tenants, and hardening your remote access path.

In a nod to Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Arctic Wolf pointed out that it may also be wise to alert staff to the social engineering aspects behind these campaigns, including outlining exactly how IT reaches out, what these contacts look like (and what they do not look like), and to train users how to read the external sender tag in Teams to identify possible red flags. Microsoft Teams also includes end-user reporting in the application itself.

That said, the technique could yet progress further.

"We have also recently observed campaigns combining Teams chat abuse with ClickFix-style social engineering, suggesting that the technique continues to evolve and is being integrated with other intrusion methods," Moore says.

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading that the company helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through layered, built-in protections that, for example, can let administrators block external Teams users. The spokesperson adds that, next month, "Teams is introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users."

Title: AI 'hacker' finds 4 severe bugs in popular industrial control software in under 4 hours
Context: Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack...
Full Text: An autonomous AI agent discovered four vulnerabilities in the decades-old, widely used EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) open source software toolkit, including a critical flaw that could allow remote attackers to execute code on systems used to control particle accelerators and fusion experiments. The bugs include a critical, 9.8-rated under CVSS v3.1 integer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-114595), leading to an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write and potentially remote code execution; an 8.2-rated, high-severity, improper message-length validation flaw (CVE-2026-114596), causing an out-of-bounds memory write and controller-process crash; a 7.5-rated, high-severity insufficient bounds checking bug (CVE-2026-114597) that allows out-of-bounds memory reads and process crashes; and a 7.5-rated, high-severity type confusion flaw (CVE-2026-114598) that can lead to denial of service and could expose adjacent memory contents. All four affect EPICS Base, which is used to operate some of the world's largest scientific research projects and facilities, and organizations should update to version 7.0.11, which includes the fixes. “Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, disclose sensitive information, or potentially execute arbitrary code,” the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned in a Tuesday advisory. An AI agent called Cipher independently found all four previously unknown security holes - investigating and testing the unfamiliar EPICS system, and validating the four exploits - in three hours and 49 minutes, Causal Security co-founder Shubham Raj told The Register. “The initial investigation required no human intervention, followed by one instruction authorizing deeper exploitability testing in a secure environment,” Raj said. Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack paths in power-grid systems used across North America and Europe, prompting an October 8 security advisory from CISA. EPICS, originally developed by Los Alamos National Laboratory and Argonne National Laboratory, is used to build and remotely control distributed Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, connecting operators to physical devices. It’s used in around 90 major scientific, university, and industrial projects and facilities globally including Argonne National Laboratory's Advanced Photon Source and ITER's fusion reactor control system. All four of these flaws illustrate how AI agents are really good at finding vulnerabilities in industrial and operational technologies - systems and equipment that used to be able to rely on obscurity to protect them from hackers - and add to defenders' concerns that it's only a matter of time until an autonomous cyberattack shuts down critical services, like power grids or water systems. These are the types of digital intrusions that can cause physical harm. Raj points to CVE-2026-114595, the critical integer-overflow vulnerability, as an example. “It allows attacker-controlled network data to cause an out-of-bounds heap memory write, with potential for remote code execution,” he told us. “EPICS controllers sit between operators and physical equipment, handling measurements, commands, and control functions,” he continued. “Operationally: Imagine a particle accelerator in the middle of an expensive experiment. An attacker could potentially crash a controller, interrupt critical measurements or control functions, and force operators to halt the experiment. That could mean lost experimental work, significant downtime, and expensive recovery.” Plus, if an attacker was able to develop an RCE exploit, this could allow them to “take control of the affected process, manipulate readings, interfere with control functions, or disrupt the equipment connected to it,” Raj said. The prerequisite for exploiting these vulns in a real scientific facility is being able to reach the vulnerable EPICS services on a facility's control network. But this could occur if the networks weren’t sufficiently segmented, or another system had access to the vulnerable EPICS network. “Once an attacker is able to find a network, which is either misconfigured or they are able to reach, it’s pretty easy to carry out the attacks,” Raj said, adding that exploitation wouldn’t require deep OT knowledge, or understanding of how particle accelerators or fusion reactors work. “Someone with conventional exploitation skills could investigate them, and increasingly capable AI systems could help develop exploits without requiring specialized OT expertise.” Manipulating specific physical processes does require additional knowledge, he added. “But an attacker doesn't need to understand the physics of a particle accelerator to disrupt the software controlling it. Crashing critical processes or interrupting monitoring and control can already have serious operational consequences. What's changing is that attackers may no longer need years of specialized expertise just to discover these weaknesses.” ®

Title: CyberStrikeAI Uses 44 AI Agents to Automate Hacking Operations Against Japan Targets
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of three cyber attacks targeting organizations in Japan in which artificial intelligence (AI) was a key element, either in the driving seat or to assist a human operator.

TrendAI, which analyzed three exposed server environments used by threat actors to conduct the malicious cyber operations, described them as distinct from previously published attacks that have leveraged ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration testing framework, to single out entities in South Korea and Japan.

"These environments held reconnaissance and attack tools, scripts, target lists, results, logs, and command histories," security researchers Bakuei Matsukawa and Joseph C Chen said. "They ranged from workspaces used largely by hand by skilled operators to AI-agent platforms that automated the entire workflow, including command and control."

The first of the three attacks has been found to abuse CyberStrikeAI, another open-source penetration testing tool that was previously put to use in an attack campaign targeting Fortinet FortiGate appliances. The activity was concentrated in a short period in October 2026.

The AI-driven activity leverages the offensive security tool to automate various aspects of the attack lifecycle into a repeatable workflow, beginning with reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery and validation, and exploitation, to command-and-control (C2), persistence, data exfiltration, and automated reporting.

This involves delegating the work among 44 agents to handle various aspects of the attack, while also enabling the generation of forms and fake login pages in the Japanese language.

"In a short period, at least 19 identifiable organizations, including at least 16 in Japan, were subjected to validation activity," Trend Micro's enterprise security division said. "Each had a report in the same format and an index of evidence. These were outputs of a structured process run by the platform, rather than ad hoc notes left by an operator."

The second case has been characterized as a human-led attack with assistance from a large language model (LLM) to accelerate planning and tool development. Analysis of the infrastructure and artifacts indicates that the campaign is also designed to target AI workflow platforms and inference services with an aim to obtain large amounts of inference capacity at low cost.

One of the intrusions is said to have targeted a geographic information system (GIS) server exposed with default credentials, resulting in the theft of cadastral and commercial records, Windows credentials, and email data. The entire campaign lasted for 24 days in August and September 2026.

The third instance is where the AI's role has been found to be confined to developing the operator's tools and scripts, suggesting a limited role played by the technology in a series of campaigns designed to target edge devices from Cisco, Citrix, F5, and Yamaha using published vulnerabilities, management functions, or credentials present in configuration files.

The threat actor is estimated to have run at least six campaigns from January to October 2026, opportunistically striking exposed VPN devices and WebLogic servers. "The operator was experienced, with established practices for automation and evidence management," the researchers said.

There is currently no evidence at this stage that suggests these three incidents share an operator. It's also unknown if the attacks have targeted other regions and what AI models are being used to pull off the attacks.

That said, the attacks involving these threat actors are not restricted to Japan and neighboring countries like South Korea. The operator behind the first case has targeted organizations in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while the third case featured organizations in the U.K., France, Italy, Qatar, and Colombia in its WebLogic discovery lists.

"AI has increased the attackers' workforce, but the work still consists of looking for unlocked doors," TrendAI said. "The types of doors and the weaknesses that leave them open have not changed. What has changed is the ability to try thousands at once, adapt to the target country's language, and continue without fatigue."

The development coincides with the discovery of multiple campaigns in which threat actors of varied motivations have integrated agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows, allowing them to speed up research, malware development, social engineering, and other parts of an attack.

To make matters worse, AI is being increasingly used to accelerate reconnaissance, automate decision-making, and industrialize social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation of security flaws. According to Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, AI has collapsed the median time from vulnerability discovery to weaponization to well below 24 hours.

The adoption of AI by bad actors is reducing the time, expertise, and cost required to discover and exploit weaknesses, at the same allowing attackers and defenders alike to operate with greater speed, scale, and autonomy, the Windows maker added.

"The key issue is not simply whether an actor has frontier AI," Trend Micro said. "Access to capable models can already produce meaningful operational gains. Ecosystem depth, however, determines how reliably, independently, and at what scale those capabilities can be sustained."

"AI is no longer an experimental capability for APT groups; it is an operational component embedded directly into campaigns."

The growing demand for AI tools by threat actors has also opened up a new monetization avenue that peddles stolen AI provider session tokens and offensive AI tools APEX AI, MessiahGPT, and DarkGPT, further commoditizing cybercrime and lowering the barrier to entry for carrying out advanced, persistent, and evasive attacks.

Last week, Microsoft revealed that a China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used ARTEX to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. The activity has been attributed to Storm-0940, which it said has used the framework since as early as September 2026 to automate password-spraying attacks on hundreds of organizations.

"While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," Microsoft said. "Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations."

According to local media reports from South Korea, authorities have identified seven suspects linked to a cybercrime operation that broke into more than 90 organizations in the country, most of which involved ARTEX. The 32-year-old mastermind behind the activity is alleged to have worked at a cybersecurity company between 2019 and 2022, gaining expertise in penetration testing.

In 38 of the incidents, the threat actors demanded ransom payments of 360 million won ($270,000) in exchange for not leaking the stolen data. More than 8.2 million records are believed to have been siphoned from compromised organizations.

Some of the other AI-oriented campaigns that have been documented in recent weeks are listed below -

A financially-motivated threat actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor as a secondary tool (both with safety controls disabled) to run a WordPress brute-force campaign against an Indian university's website and generate a REST API enumeration report.

The attacker also breached a second Indian public university, exfiltrating a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students. A third attack enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform to extract a storefront API token, admin email addresses, phone numbers, and payment merchant IDs.

"The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders)," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations."

An e-crime group named CyberCartel has been observed using a multi-agent system called CARLIY0S to coordinate attacks against banks and payment providers across Latin America. The framework employs a cognitive swarm comprising four role-specialized Claude models that "debate each target and defer to one arbiter" before the main orchestrator acts. "The group assigned different roles to commercial AI models to analyze targets, develop attacks, and coordinate operations," Straiker said.

Threat actors have developed an offensive AI agent designed to hijack exposed AI endpoints to run autonomous attacks, with instructions allowing it to carry out up to 100,000 steps without human approval while the legitimate owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. The system features a malicious loop called Skynet mode that employs a set of 74 tools to scan for targets, infect them, deploy cryptocurrency miners, and reinfect compromised hosts.

An affiliate for the The Gentlemen ransomware operation has used Anthropic Claude Code during intrusions into at least six organizations in late June 2026, including to generate and execute reconnaissance and exploitation commands, write malicious scripts, modify firewall policies, and identify high-value business systems.

A credential-harvesting operation codenamed Zerofot built a scanner named "auto_scan" that integrated OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to harvest thousands of API keys and tokens from thousands of exposed hosts across the internet.

An AI-generated Python framework called RAGE has been used to scan internet-facing services (e.g., Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, Apache Tomcat, Jenkins, Hadoop YARN, Confluence, and Supervisord), exploit vulnerable deployments, capture credentials, and deploy cryptocurrency miners.

A human operator employed frontier AI models to breach an enterprise network autonomously over a 10-hour period. "The actor breached a publicly accessible web service to tunnel into the network, deploying an automated recon agent to map internal microservices," Unit 42 said. "Sub-agents combed enterprise code repositories, extracting hard-coded tokens and service passwords." The attacker then harvested master administrative credentials and hijacked an enterprise code application to exfiltrate cloud access keys. The stolen cloud keys were then used to turn the victim's AI endpoints into post-compromise infrastructure.

A suspected Russian-speaking cyber actor used an AI-assisted workflow to exploit PaperCut NG/MF servers and compromise hundreds of instances. "The campaign extended beyond initial exploitation into a structured post-exploitation pipeline covering Windows credential collection, service-credential harvesting, internal network pivoting, Metasploit automation, and victim packaging," Hunt.io said.

A Chinese-speaking threat actor has breached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, using an autonomous penetration testing engine called Cairn, tasking it to probe targets, search for security weaknesses that could lead to code execution or account takeover, attempt to break in, and steal sensitive data.

"AI is serving as a force multiplier and an expanding attack surface at the same time," Rapid7 said. "Generative AI is accelerating established attack methods by reducing the time, skill, and coordination previously required to execute them at scale."

"Rather than introducing entirely new categories of exploitation, threat actors are integrating AI into existing workflows to industrialize phishing, automate reconnaissance, and refine malicious scripts with greater speed and precision."

Title: Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills
Context: Get Your Recap Today December 3, 2026 | VIRTUAL Cybersecurity Outlook 2027 Secure Your Spot Keep up with the latest cybersecurity threats, newly discovered vulnerabilities, data...
Full Text:
Black Hat India — Bengaluru — The use of AI as a tool to enhance cybersecurity operations is emerging as a double-edged knife for security professionals. While it can make them more capable, it could also spell the demise of the very skills they need to use it effectively.

That's the concern of Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, who has made a case for how evolving technology can erode technical skills since well before the generative AI boom. Now, that concern is getting much louder.

Speaking to Dark Reading recently, he says he began noticing the problem around 2005 and 2006, when he encountered cybersecurity professionals who lacked a firm grasp of the fundamentals of their work. At that time, he warned about the dangers of relying too heavily on various types of technical tools, declaring to cybersecurity professionals that "your tools are killing you," and warning that practitioners are moving away from being "hands-on" operators who investigate problems directly, and toward "hands-off" monitors who oversee results presented through tools, interfaces, and dashboards.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

It's a shift that's being exacerbated now by AI-driven automation, he says, and organizations need to move quickly to optimize the use of AI without the expense of cybersecurity skill-building.

AI Tools Can Simplify Things Too Much

While automation can simplify complex tasks and allow professionals to accomplish more, it can also distance them from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a solid understanding of the fundamentals, practitioners may struggle to recognize when a tool produces an incorrect result or when its findings require further investigation, Hamiel says.

"We need to keep these skills and not let them degrade because those skills are important to making the tools work in the best way possible," he tells Dark Reading from this week's Black Hat India conference, where he's giving a keynote entitled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems."

"What AI adds to somebody with knowledge and experience is some additional capabilities," Hamiel elaborates. "A domain expert wielding AI is going to be able to gain benefits from using that tool that a novice with no domain experience isn't going to be able to get."

This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into cybersecurity workflows. It also raises questions about how the industry will develop its next generation of experts if automation removes some of the hands-on tasks that junior professionals traditionally learn.

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

AI Hype vs. Cybersecurity Reality

The current discussion around AI often falls into extremes, Hamiel says. Some predict that the technology can go a long way toward solving major problems facing not only cybersecurity but also humanity, while others warn that it will bring the industry — and some even the world — to an end.

"You have the doomers," he says, "and you have people who say this is a big nothingburger. The truth is somewhere in the middle."

For Hamiel, understanding AI's impact requires separating what the technology can demonstrate in a controlled environment from what it can reliably accomplish in the real world. Impressive capabilities do not necessarily translate into the wholesale replacement of jobs or the disappearance of entire industries, he says.

The same distinction applies to cybersecurity, Hamiel says. Although AI can help identify vulnerabilities, generate code and support security investigations, those capabilities do not mean that the complex problems facing security teams have suddenly become easy to solve.

In fact, some recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity — such as OpenAI models autonomously hacking the Hugging Face framework, among others — may reveal a more familiar and persistent cybersecurity problem: organizations failing to address basic security weaknesses.

Related:AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost

"If you read some of the incident reports, these are organizations that weren't exercising basic security hygiene," Hamiel says.

In these cases, he argues, the weaknesses were already there, waiting to be discovered. "This wasn't just low-hanging fruit; this was fruit lying on the ground where anybody who looked for it would have found it," he says.

Rather than signaling an impending cybersecurity apocalypse, such incidents could prompt what Hamiel calls a "cybersecurity correction."

"It's not that there is this huge apocalypse happening; it's that many people weren't doing the right thing for a very long time," he explains.

In other words, AI may make it easier to discover and exploit existing weaknesses, exposing the consequences of inadequate security practices. The challenge for organizations is not simply to adopt new tools but to address the underlying problems those tools bring to light.

The Shift From Operators to Monitors

Indeed, the potential erosion of technical skills is not a problem that began with generative AI. Hamiel sees it as part of a longer trend in which technology increasingly mediates the relationship between professionals and the problems they are responsible for solving.

Hamiel's concern reflects what is often called the irony of automation: As systems take on more responsibility, the humans overseeing them can lose opportunities to practice the skills needed when those systems fail.

The consequences could extend beyond the skills of today's practitioners to the way the cybersecurity industry develops future experts, he says, especially in how lower-level work that AI can eliminate helps helping junior professionals learn.

Tasks that might appear repetitive or straightforward can provide essential experience, allowing new practitioners to understand how systems work before progressing to more complex investigations. "If you automate that, there isn't room for them to learn," Hamiel warns.

This creates a potential long-term problem for employers. AI may allow teams to complete certain tasks more efficiently today, but organizations still need experienced professionals who can investigate unfamiliar problems, evaluate automated findings, and respond when systems behave unexpectedly.

Using AI Without Losing Expertise

For cybersecurity pros to use generative AI effectively, then, it's simply a matter of applying it to tasks where it offers meaningful benefits while remaining aware of the skills that might be weakened if pros rely too much on these tools to do their jobs effectively.

"The goal here is to maximize the benefits and minimize the drawbacks," Hamiel says, something that is true for the use of any technology. "That's the framing that should be placed around this," he says.

Thus, the only way that organizations can adopt AI without losing essential cybersecurity expertise is to "apply them to the right types of activities," he says.

For cybersecurity pros, this means using generative AI for tasks such as threat hunting and threat intelligence, where preliminary analysis can help professionals work through information more efficiently, Hamiel notes. AI-powered penetration-testing tools are another area of promising development, extending beyond traditional vulnerability scanning to perform more complex tasks, he says.

Ultimately, the question is not whether AI will change cybersecurity, Hamiel says. That genie is most certainly already out of that bottle. Ultimately, the real challenge is ensuring that the industry does not become so dependent on increasingly capable tools that it loses the human expertise required to use them effectively, he says.

"Skills and expertise make your AI use more effective," Hamiel concludes. "If you have two professionals, and both use AI, the one with more knowledge of the task is going to make better use of the AI."

Title: 'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants
Context: Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things,...
Full Text:
A novel infostealer that specifically targets AI applications and development tools is changing the narrative on illicit data monetization, opening up fresh revenue streams through extortion and other abuses of the stolen data.

Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things, they said in a recent report. It targets Windows-based machines and the browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications running on them — among other apps and services — with data theft.

However, Aokigahara is notable in that it has a particular focus on emerging AI-driven assets, collecting authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools, according to Check Point. This sets it apart from many of the infostealers currently active in the wild.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

"This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software," according to Check Point.

Different Targets for Cybercrime, Different Financial Opportunities

The AI data offers unique opportunities for threat actors to benefit financially from the stealer's activities by using credentials or session tokens to "enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts," according to the report.

The malicious activity can also extend to developer and cloud environments, and thus threaten enterprises. Indeed, threat actors have already demonstrated how they use stolen credentials for GitHub accounts, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files to infiltrate cloud environments of enterprise targets.

This may also pave the way for extortion of organizations by holding stolen data for ransom, according to Check Point.

"Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services," according to the post. "If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment."

Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of security firm Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that "stolen AI credentials can yield a heavy harvest for an attacker. A paid AI subscription is a resellable asset, and the conversation history behind it is often full of proprietary code, which means these stolen sessions now carry extortion value alongside their resale value."

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

Aokigahara Infostealer Malware In Action

Once an Aokigahara infection begins, it scans a computer for sensitive data, including browser passwords, session cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, and credentials stored by AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. It also searches local application files for authentication tokens, API keys, and other potentially valuable information.

Other targeted data the malware looks for are developer and cloud credentials, including Git access data, SSH keys, and configuration files for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This data is valuable to give attackers access to private code repositories or cloud resources if the stolen credentials remain valid and have sufficient permissions, according to Check Point.

Indeed, "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring," Calderone observes, and some of those keys ultimately could give attackers access to the kingdom.

"The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run," he says.

Related:BragJack Attack Can Turn a Browser's Agentic AI Against It

Aokigahara also has built-in anti-detection mechanisms. It checks for analysis environments such as virtual machines and sandboxes, and packages stolen data into zip archives and then encrypts it before sending it to attacker-controlled servers.

Modern Defense as Attackers Expand Objectives

Aokigahara's targeting of AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook, potentially exposing AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint. The theft of this data then opens new pathways for financial gain for attackers and thus may provide an incentive for others to do the same, according to Check Point.

This means that defenders should start treating AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, with protections comparable to those applied to cloud credentials and developer keys. To that end, security teams should hunt for AI-session theft by investigating suspicious access to local application storage and authentication-related files belonging to AI assistants, coding agents, and developer IDEs.

Organizations also should more closely protect developer and cloud credentials by reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets on endpoints, using managed identity and short-lived credentials where feasible, and restricting access to cloud resources and source-code repositories.

Further, organizations can protect assets across exposed apps and tools by revoking exposed sessions and rotating secrets. If an endpoint is suspected of compromise, according to Check Point, they should assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens, not just browser passwords.

Title: Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Scanner-Evading Code
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Attackers have infected 953 online stores, mostly running Magento, with a JavaScript loader that has evolved to tell security scanners apart from real shoppers.

The campaign has been active since July 2025 and has cycled through five loader domains, according to research from Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec. Its latest domain, registered October 6, was found in the content management system (CMS) blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which had carried an earlier version of the loader.

The loader is stored in Magento's cms_block database table and has visitors' browsers fetch instructions from the attackers. Sansec said the server first works out whether a request comes from a genuine customer or a security scanner, and gives scanners nothing.

Latest Loader Filters Security Scanners

Before October, the operator relied on the Keitaro traffic distribution system to choose, for each visitor, between delivering a payload, redirecting the browser and returning nothing.

The loader Sansec first found on October 7 instead called the new domain directly and replayed code saved in the browser, so anyone served the payload would rerun it on later page loads, even with the domain down or blocked.

An October 23 rewrite added browser fingerprinting, checking for signs of browser automation and collecting hardware details, screen size, time zone and language before the server chose its response.

When scanning service urlscan.io loaded an infected store in an automated browser, Sansec found no injected content. The company has yet to obtain the final payload, so the campaign's ultimate purpose remains unclear.

Read more on malicious JavaScript in online stores: Global Magecart Campaign Targets Six Card Networks

Patches Did Not Always Stop Reinfection

Sansec said a March wave planted the loader on 471 stores within an hour, using webshells placed through PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356). Among 169 infected Magento 2 installations lacking at least one core patch, 102 showed evidence of file uploads via PolyShell or SessionReaper (CVE-2025-54236).

Patching alone did not prevent reinfection. A fully patched store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 picked up the newest loader on October 23, an hour after passing a clean scan. Sansec had spotted a rogue admin account and a GSocket backdoor on the store in September.

Sansec advised merchants to look for the loader in CMS content, review admin accounts and hunt for backdoors, rotate database, admin and integration credentials once the store is clean and apply the latest Magento and Adobe Commerce security updates.

It warned that removing the script leaves an attacker's write access to the database intact, so a compromised store can be reinfected while the original way in remains.

Title: OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.
