Title: Lazarus Abuses South Korean Security Software to Deploy Malware Using Post-Quantum Encryption
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The North Korea-linked Lazarus Group has been attributed to a cyber espionage campaign dubbed Operation FlashHole targeting at least three organizations in South Korea spanning the construction, software, and wire-communication equipment manufacturing sectors.

According to Russian cybersecurity company Kaspersky, the campaign has been active since at least July 2025. It's assessed to pick up from where Operation SyncHole left off.

"The group targeted victims more selectively, sending spear‑phishing emails with links to fabricated but relevant sites, such as portfolio and résumé pages tailored to each target," Sojun Ryu, senior security researcher at Kaspersky GReAT, said in an exhaustive analysis.

Operation SyncHole was first documented by Kaspersky in April 2025, detailing the state-sponsored adversary's targeting of South Korea's software, IT, financial, semiconductor manufacturing, and telecommunications industries since November 2024 to deliver malware such as ThreatNeedle, AGAMEMNON, wAgent, SIGNBT, and COPPERHEDGE.

The attacks were characterized by the exploitation of a security flaw in iniLINE Cross EX for malware delivery. Cross EX is a mandatory financial security software program installed by South Korean internet users on their computers to support security software across various browser environments when accessing online banking and government services.

The exploit was designed to launch the legitimate "SyncHost.exe" process and inject shellcode into it to load the ThreatNeedle backdoor. The attack chain also incorporated a one-day vulnerability in the Innorix Agent file transfer solution version 9.2.18.496 for lateral movement.

Operation FlashHole continues the prior wave's targeting of South Korea-focused software to breach targets. Where SyncHole exploited Cross EX, FlashHole has been found to abuse Initech's INISAFE CrossWeb EX, another mandatory financial security solution necessary to access online banking and government portals in the country.

According to iniLINE's website, the company entered into a strategic alliance with Initech as far back as 2010 to develop CrossWeb. It's currently marketed by Initech as a certificate-based authentication and electronic-signature solution.

That said, the Lazarus Group has a long history of abusing this software to meet its goals. In Q3 2021, it was used to deploy a downloader named Racket in connection with a long-running campaign called DeathNote.

Operation FlashHole attack flow during initial compromise

Between 2022 and 2023, AhnLab also disclosed attacks in which the threat actor exploited a security flaw in the software to distribute DLL malware ("SCSKAppLink.dll") via watering hole attacks, with the DLL payload retrieved from IIS web servers compromised by the threat actor.

"The group first hacks Korean websites and modifies the content provided from the site," AhnLab noted in a July 2023 report. "When a system using a vulnerable version of INISAFE CrossWeb EX V6 visits this website via a web browser, the Lazarus malware (SCSKAppLink.dll) is installed from the distribution site through the INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe vulnerability."

Initial infection chain

The findings also come against the backdrop of a joint July 2026 advisory published by the Korea Internet and Security Agency (KISA) and domestic cybersecurity vendors, highlighting the Lazarus Group's exploitation of vulnerabilities in such financial security programs like AnySign4PC to distribute backdoors like Struggle (aka SIGNBT 3.0) and Brandoor (aka COPPERHEDGE) after tricking victims into visiting malicious URLs through spear-phishing and watering hole techniques.

"The attackers induced targets to access malicious URLs through various methods, including watering hole and spear-phishing attacks, and then exploited the vulnerabilities to ultimately install backdoor malware," AhnLab said, calling the campaign Operation Double Barrel.

The precise initial access vector for FlashHole is unclear, but signs point to malicious websites hosted on GitHub pages, one version of which hosted the résumé of a senior network appliance developer along with a profile photo likely generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Expanded infection chain after gaining persistence

It's suspected that targets are sent spear-phishing emails containing links to the malicious site, visiting which triggers an infection sequence involving CrossWeb EX to launch the legitimate Windows binary "fsquirt.exe," which is then used to launch a malicious DLL called TechHub via DLL sideloading.

"The infection chain is rather complex and reveals the Lazarus Group's advanced operational techniques on targeted hosts," Kaspersky said. "These techniques conceal their malicious payloads, intent, and their sophisticated malware delivery framework."

"Significantly, the execution chain below exists only in memory during the initial infiltration, highlighting the attackers' considerable efforts to hide the initial compromise."

TechHub, for its part, downloads from GitHub a malware called TouchHub, which leverages a DLL sideloading a second to launch a rogue DLL payload dubbed TOUCHSHIFT ("mscoree.dll") for setting up persistence by kicking off the in‑memory execution of another TechHub instance.

Overlaps between Lazarus Group Attacks

This second TechHub instance retrieves another malware family known as ClientHub to download and load LPEClient into memory. LPEClient serves as a conduit for Cubridge, the orchestration component of the malware framework designed to fetch various plugins, modules, and tools.

Additional details about the malware toolset is as follows -

TechHub, an advanced version of the CLOUDBURST and NickelLoader downloader that communicates with GitHub to fetch additional payloads like TouchHub and ClientHub, as well as collect information about the device and its running processes.

Cubridge, an improved version of SIDESHOW and LightlessCan capable of communicating with a command-and-control (C2) server and downloading reusable plugins, DLL utilities for one-off tasks, and additional modules to expand its functionality, thereby allowing it to gather comprehensive system information, run commands, and steal files and web browser data. It's also assessed to be an advanced version of CookiePlus.

TouchHub, a parent installer for TouchShift.

TouchShift, a malware dropper capable of delivering keyloggers, screenshot utilities, and backdoors.

ClientHub, a previously undocumented backdoor that comes in two versions: one that communicates with an attacker controlled server, using HTTPS and another that interacts with the Dropbox API. The end goal of the malware is to deploy additional plugins and DLLs. The plugins allow the malware to create ZIP archives, collect files matching a search pattern, delete specific files, and monitor local drive changes and return the collected status information.

LPEClient, a longstanding victim profiling and payload delivery tool used since 2019.

In August 2026, Check Point revealed that LPEClient was deployed following the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-68820, a privilege escalation flaw affecting Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock, to deploy the FudModule rootkit.

What's notable about the latest version of the malware is that it uses ML-KEM-1024, a post-quantum cryptographic algorithm, to establish an encrypted connection with the attackers' server before downloading and running additional malware directly in memory.

"Operation FlashHole is the latest wave in the broader Cascade Hole campaign, which involves the use of South Korean software as a potential entry point to deliver malware targeting the country," Kaspersky said.

The cybersecurity company said the emergence of Operation FlashHole coincided with a fresh wave of attacks targeting various South Korean organizations using the COPPERHEDGE backdoor. In at least one case, the backdoor infection is said to have resulted in the exfiltration of data to a dark web leak site named ULOSE, in a manner similar to Gunra ransomware attacks directed against South Korean entities around the same time.

"Lazarus continues to expand its operations, launches new campaigns while introducing new tools and reworking familiar ones to meet its needs," Ryu said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"What deserves closer attention is Lazarus’s adoption of cryptography designed to withstand future quantum threats. Our findings trace its use back to at least September 2024, showing that these capabilities were already protecting the group’s malware communications more than a year before this disclosure."

Context: We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting...
Full Text:
Hiding Capabilities in AI Models

Interesting research: “AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities”

Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

The preliminary phase of the certification benefitted from the input of 10,000 volunteer professionals worldwide through Job Task Analysis surveys.

From October 26, ISC2 is opening a pilot exam phase, giving cybersecurity professionals, employers and the global cybersecurity community insight into the domains and topics the exam is designed to assess.

The nonprofit is now looking for 3000 volunteers to enrol in a beta version of the exam in December 2026. Volunteers have until November 4 to submit their interest.

Six Key Domains to Shape the AI Security Exam

The pilot exam will assess candidates’ knowledge, skills and abilities across the following areas of professional practice needed to secure AI-enabled environments:

AI concepts and security fundamentals

AI governance, ethics, risk and compliance

AI data management, privacy and model security

Secure AI architecture, engineering and identity and access management (IAM)

Secure AI operations and incident response (IR)

AI threats, testing and lifecycle management

Each domain includes topics and subtopics to help candidates understand the AI security expertise the exam is designed to evaluate.

In a public statement, Casey Marks, COO of ISC2, said this pilot phase aims to provide “critical evidence to evaluate whether the examination measures AI security competence reliably, fairly and defensibly, which are all key facets of the rigor essential to certification integrity and to employers’ and professionals’ trust in what earning the credential represents.”

If the pilot exam phase is successful, the certification will be available to take from the first quarter of 2027, and maybe even as early as January, Beale estimated.

Eligibility Requirements for the New AI Security Certification

This new AI security credential will be available to both ISC2 members and non-members. It will be open to professionals who hold existing ISC2 credentials as well as those who do not.

It is primarily intended for professionals responsible for securing the design, deployment and maintenance of AI and machine learning (ML) systems throughout the AI lifecycle.

This includes managing cybersecurity risks associated with AI-enabled services and extending beyond technical defense to governance, ethics, risk-based guidance and enterprise collaboration.

In addition, candidates who wish to pass this certification must meet certain criteria, including having a minimum of four years of cumulative, paid full-time experience in cybersecurity or AI-related fields, with two years in cybersecurity and one year in two or more of the domains of the AI security certification exam outline.

Candidates holding active CISSP, ISSAP, ISSEP, ISSMP, CCSP or CSSLP credential may be substituted for the entire AI security certification experience requirement.

In his Security Congress opening speech, ISC2’s CEO Beale also said that AI questions are currently being “incorporated across all other ISC2 current certifications.”

“We’ve significantly increased the amount of certificates, webinars, events and professional development capabilities in the AI safety and security space over the past six months,” he told Infosecurity.

One example is the launch of the Cyber AI Workforce Coalition, announced on October 20.

Title: From federal SOCs to Talos: Ryan Fetterman on practical security research
Context: He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses
Full Text:
What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos. He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses.Beyond the technical grind, Ryan shares his philosophy on building a career in security without burning out. From the value of project-based learning to the importance of finding time to step away from the keyboard, here's Ryan's take on what it really means to navigate today's cybersecurity industry.

Amy Ciminnisi: Tell me a little bit about the journey that has taken you to Talos, from early on in your career through to now. How did you get here? I actually don't know that much about it.

Ryan Fetterman: I've been doing security about 15 years now, and my career was largely shaped by where I started in the DC area. I spent about a decade there. I started out in consulting and then pivoted over to research, but that was a great place to get started.

I got a lot of great experience in federal agencies and government consulting, continued my education down there, got trained up, got certifications and things like that. And that was where I got my first exposure to doing actual security operations, which is what I really stuck with. It was my first exposure to Splunk.

Querying lots of log data and building visualizations and analytics in Splunk was the first time in my career that I felt it was kind of my natural inclination. It seems like it should have been more obvious to me looking back on it, but it's something that I try to explain to people a lot. When you first get into security, there's a desire to kind of find your specialization and start working towards it. But in my experience, it's just not something that you can rush.

I met the people connected with that space, which eventually led to me going to work for Splunk. I worked on the Splunk research team, SURGe. And then after the Cisco acquisition of Splunk, I ultimately became reorganized into Talos.

AC: I'm sure there have been so many challenges, so many obstacles in your way as you're trying to do this research. Can you share one that you've faced and how it shaped your perspective on cybersecurity?

RF: Something that stuck with me was actually my first advanced persistent threat (APT) incident. Now, you can look this up. It's called Pandora Song if you search for the C2. I was in the DC area working in a federal SOC, and I was doing some of the first host-based analytics at the time, which have now become kind of the concentration of a lot of detection. Engineering and analytics are host-based, so this was kind of pioneering at the time.

I was looking at a lot of host-based sensors and writing analytics in Splunk, actually, and we had been tipped off to this incident by a third party. I was looking through the details of the incident and how the attacker was carrying out the progression of their attack...

Title: Watchdog Urges Police and Fire Service to Improve Cybersecurity

Full Text:
The cyber threat to UK police forces and fire and rescue services is growing rapidly and demands a more urgent response, an independent assessment has warned.

The Cybersecurity in Police Forces and Fire and Rescue Services report from His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) was published on October 27.

It was compiled from a three-phase inspection carried out between January and May 2026, and involved dozens of interviews, “reality testing,” and scrutiny of over 260 police service and fire and rescue service documents.

“While there have been gradual improvements, many forces and services still need to urgently redouble their efforts to respond to the increased risk of cyber-attacks,” warned Michelle Skeer, His Majesty’s inspector of constabulary.

“Cybersecurity should be viewed as a core organizational priority and not solely a technical risk. Leaders need to prioritize and invest in their cybersecurity arrangements to improve their organization’s ability to prevent, detect, respond to and recover from attacks.”

Read more on threats to policing infrastructure: Government Updates UK’s National Risk Register with Cyber Warnings

The report highlighted multiple areas of weakness:

Legacy ICT systems identified as a “strategic risk” due to difficulties with patching and integration

Exposure to third-party risk, especially ICT suppliers that manage sensitive police data, and human error when using external services

Underdeveloped preparedness and resilience, including backups and incident response

Basic control issues, including access management, authentication and provisioning/deprovisioning

A lack of accountability at a senior level, with several police and fire leaders claiming cybersecurity isn’t part of daily operational decision-making

Poor coordination at a national level, leading to uneven levels of cyber maturity across the various forces and fire/rescue services

A Plan for Improvement

HMICFRS made 13 recommendations for improving the cybersecurity posture of the nation’s police forces and fire and rescue services.

These include:

Introducing baseline cybersecurity standards to improve maturity across the board (ie Cyber Assessment Framework)

Third-party assessment of cybersecurity capabilities

Improving procurement and contract management of third-party ICT suppliers (including mandatory Cyber Essentials certification)

Enhancing collaboration between government and policing cybersecurity leads

Promoting the use of the Police Digital Service’s National Management Centre, and creating a similar national capability for fire and rescue services

Improving the preparedness of services to respond to an attack (eg backup and restore and incident response exercises)

Improving learning and development for senior leaders and cybersecurity staff

“The government’s program of police reform and local government reorganization could offer both sectors opportunities to improve and better co-ordinate the approach to cybersecurity,” said Skeer. “These opportunities to strengthen cybersecurity cannot be missed. Protecting systems and data is essential to protecting the public.”

Title: Your Attack Surface Is Growing Faster Than Your Team Can Respond
Context: As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place
Full Text:
Security teams cannot keep responding faster forever. As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place.

That requires a pivot toward prevention and a broader view of exposure. An unpatched application matters, but so do unnecessary administrative privileges, forgotten internet-facing services, or legitimate tools available to someone who never needs them. Individually, these weaknesses may attract little attention. Connected, they can create an attacker pathway to the systems and data the business depends on.

An exposure management strategy helps organizations understand these connections and act before an attacker does. For lean IT and security teams, it also offers a practical way to reduce workload: fewer opportunities for attackers can mean fewer alerts to investigate and respond to.

Why Is Exposure Management Crucial Now?

AI is putting pressure on security from multiple directions. Attackers can use it to accelerate their operations, while employees’ adoption of AI applications, assistants, and agents introduces additional access and interactions to secure.

Detection and response remain essential. However, making them carry most of the defensive burden leaves teams dependent on quickly identifying and interrupting every intrusion.

Meanwhile, many attack opportunities involve capabilities organizations already have. Bitdefender Labs’ analysis of 700,000 security incidents found that living-off-the-land techniques, which abuse legitimate tools, appeared in 84% of major attacks. Patching alone cannot address the unnecessary access that makes those techniques possible.

The challenge is operational, too. In the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 38% of security professionals cited the overhead of maintaining hardening rules and exceptions as a barrier to shrinking their attack surface.

Organizations need prevention that adapts as their environment changes and fits the capacity of the people responsible for securing it.

What Is an Exposure Management Strategy?

Exposure management is the ongoing practice of identifying, prioritizing, and reducing weaknesses attackers could exploit across an organization’s attack surface.

It extends beyond vulnerability management. Software vulnerabilities are part of the picture, alongside misconfigurations, exposed services, identity risks, and unnecessary access to powerful tools.

An effective strategy connects three activities.

First, establish visibility into relevant exposures.

Second, prioritize them using context, including the assets an attacker could reach.

Third, reduce those exposures and reassess the environment.

This is continuous work because exposure changes whenever accounts gain privileges, services become publicly accessible, or business requirements evolve. Threat Exposure Management provides a framework for organizing that repeatable process. Technology supports the program; ownership and follow-through make it effective.

How Does GravityZone Turn Visibility Into Prevention?

Bitdefender GravityZone Exposure Management combines visibility, prioritization, and adaptive hardening to help teams remove attack opportunities.

Endpoint Risk Management identifies vulnerabilities and risky configurations. External Attack Surface Management adds an attacker’s outside view of internet-facing assets and services. User risk insights and Unified Identities help teams understand accounts, behaviors, and privileges that contribute to exposure.

There is also Attack Path Analysis, which connects findings into potential routes toward critical assets. That context can change the remediation order. A medium-severity vulnerability on a privileged user’s workstation may deserve attention ahead of a higher-severity finding on an isolated system.

It also helps teams identify shared points across multiple routes, where one change could interrupt several potential paths. The analysis models connections from available findings; teams still need to assess and implement the appropriate fixes.

However, teams can add automated action through GravityZone PHASR (Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction). It learns how each machine-user combination operates and restricts unnecessary access to tools and behaviors attackers like to abuse. Hardening can adapt as legitimate usage changes.

What Outcomes Should Organizations Expect?

The primary outcome of continuous exposure management is reduced opportunity for compromise. Closing an exposed service, addressing a dangerous configuration, or restricting unnecessary tool access can remove an opening or constrain an attacker’s next move.

Better prioritization helps teams direct limited resources to the most consequential work. For example, what if an administrator account connects to several potential attack paths? Removing unnecessary access may reduce exposure across multiple systems, giving the team a clearer reason to prioritize the change.

Dynamic hardening can also reduce the manual effort of policy maintenance. PHASR allows teams to review recommendations or use Autopilot to apply them. Changes are audited and reversible, and teams can grant access when legitimate work requires it. These safeguards help teams reduce risk while managing operational disruption.

A further outcome is clearer evidence of progress. Leaders can track changes in risk posture and new or resolved attack paths, connecting security work to the routes toward important assets that have been closed.

Reducing attack opportunities can ease pressure on teams of all sizes and especially lean teams.

How Can Lean Teams Put an Exposure Management Strategy Into Practice?

Start with business priorities: the systems, identities, and services whose compromise would cause the greatest harm. Establish visibility, identify high-risk exposures, and assign responsibility for reducing them. Reassess after changes to confirm progress and identify what needs attention next.

GravityZone Exposure Management supports and simplifies this approach within GravityZone or alongside third-party endpoint protection and EDR. Organizations can build on existing investments and extend their program with separately licensed capabilities, including automated patching, cloud security posture management, and GravityZone AI Visibility and Control.

The strategic goal is to make prevention, through continuous risk reduction, part of everyday security operations. This helps close attack opportunities before they become an incident.

Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines
Context: With all the different types of deduplication, we get this final picture: Again, looking at just the actionable vulnerability reports (likely the best measure), we see an...
Full Text:
Summary

Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users.

Introduction

Fuzzing has long been successfully applied to software projects such as Chrome or V8 (Chrome’s JavaScript engine) to detect bugs. Recently, the arrival of powerful LLMs able to read, reason about, and write code is causing a transformative change to software development and software security. With hundreds, sometimes thousands of new bugs and vulnerabilities having been discovered in well-fuzzed targets, a natural question arises: how do new LLMs compare to “traditional” fuzzers? Are they starting to replace them or do the two approaches complement each other? To help answer this, we look at three key questions:

How many bugs does each approach find in the real world?

What is the overlap between the two approaches?

What is the “shape” of bugs discovered by one system but not the other?

For this blog post, we will limit ourselves to two concrete systems: Fuzzilli, a JavaScript engine fuzzer, and BigSleep, an agentic bug finding system. Both of these systems run in production and automatically look for bugs in newly added code, which makes them fairly directly comparable. Specifically, Fuzzilli runs continuously across many instances, with the first ones usually picking up new changes within a few hours, while BigSleep currently runs once per day and is prompted to review new commits and write proof-of-concept testcases for any bugs it discovers. Both systems report bugs through Clusterfuzz, which will do basic crash triaging, then file bug reports in Chrome’s issue tracker.

We also limit ourselves to V8 as a target, a high-performance JavaScript and WebAssembly engine with a sophisticated and mature testing and fuzzing setup. In particular, Fuzzilli is a special-purpose fuzzing tool designed to find bugs in these engines. The usually complicated nature of these bugs makes for an interesting “playground” to compare the two approaches’ ability to find deep and complex bugs in well-tested software. We leave it to future work to perform similar analysis on a broader set of targets, fuzzers, and agentic bug finding systems.

We will now look into each of the three main questions in a dedicated section. Each section will first summarize the general approach, then describe the methodology in detail (often as bullet points, so you can skip those blocks if you don’t care too much about the details) before exploring the results. We conclude with an attempt at interpreting the results to get a picture of the current state of fuzzing vs. AI.

Part 1: Production Statistics

This is the simplest part to analyze, although with some caveats we’ll see in a bit. The basic idea is to query issues from Chromium’s bugtracker (where V8 bugs are tracked) and extract various statistics from there. This is especially easy since there’s a dedicated hotlist for each of the two systems. We limit our analysis to the six months from April to September 2026 as the automatic BigSleep pipeline only became active in April this year. As such, our raw data comes from the following two bug tracker queries:

Fuzzilli: hotlistid:5433121 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30

BigSleep: hotlistid:8067258 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30

From there, the raw numbers of bug reports are:

Fuzzilli: 316

BigSleep: 441

Small win for BigSleep. However, this includes all types of bugs, and BigSleep initially also found a lot of configuration and integration issues in V8, for example crbug.com/503869331 where the unsafe flag blocking mechanism didn’t work properly yet. These are legitimate issues, but less relevant for our comparison since there’s little real-world security impact. One easy way to get rid of these is to look specifically at vulnerabilities by limiting the results to type:vulnerability:

Fuzzilli: 178

BigSleep: 95

Suddenly a clear win for the fuzzers? Not quite. There are still some problems with this data, notably duplicates and unactionable reports (e.g. bugs closed as WAI). At first, this seems like a simple thing to fix: just include another constraint such as status:(fixed | verified). Unfortunately, things are a bit more complicated. Take for example Fuzzilli bug crbug.com/511935486. The events on this bug are basically:

The bug is filed by Clusterfuzz on May 11 and assigned to an engineer

The bug is closed by Clusterfuzz as the testcase no longer reproduces later that same day

As such, this bug received zero developer interactions. Most likely what happened here is that this bug was a duplicate of another bug, crbug.com/511210507, but Clusterfuzz didn’t realize it as the crash signature (derived from the stack trace) was slightly different. When the other bug received a fix, the testcase stopped reproducing on Clusterfuzz, which closed the issue.

Maybe the best thing we can do is to look at “actionable” bugs, defined as those that are not marked as duplicates or WAI and that received at least one fix commit referencing them. Then, looking at only Type-Vuln bugs filters out a lot of the less-relevant BigSleep bugs, even though these were “actionable”. With that, the final picture looks like this:

So in terms of vulnerabilities, it’s roughly a tie (small advantage BigSleep) at the moment: 45 vs. 37.

This naturally raises the question of cost: how expensive is each of the two approaches and what does that mean in terms of cost-per-bug? Unfortunately, it’s challenging to make a comparison at this stage in the research. While some effort has been dedicated to making Clusterfuzz more efficient, similar effort has not been expended for Big Sleep and neither system is particularly calibrated for an optimal cost-per-bug ratio.

Part 2: Overlap

The next question is how much these approaches overlap each other. For this, our approach is twofold: we first attempt to find an answer in the bugtracker, by trying to identify bugs discovered by both systems. Next, we run a dedicated experiment in which we let BigSleep try to rediscover old Fuzzilli bugs.

Bugtracker Overlap

The basic idea is to see which bugs were found by both systems, so we’re effectively looking for duplicate bug reports. Similar to part 1, there are a few steps we need to take to ensure we get a somewhat accurate picture:

First, we look for bugs filed by one system that get deduplicated into a bug filed by the other. For example crbug.com/522410841 which is a duplicate of crbug.com/522860268. This is a clear overlap.

Next, we need to take into account that many “unactionable” reports (those with zero associated fixes) are often duplicates. For those reports, we need to find the commit that fixed them, then look at the bug associated with that commit, and treat these two bugs as duplicates. This can be a multi-prong relationship: both bug X found by BigSleep and bug Y found by Fuzzilli might be a duplicate of bug Z reported by someone/something else. In that case, that bug still counts as overlap.

Then, we need to realize that many duplicates never receive a bugtracker entry since they are already deduplicated at the Clusterfuzz level (since both Fuzzilli and BigSleep rely on Clusterfuzz for basic triage and bug filing). As such, we need to query Clusterfuzz’s underlying database to find more duplicates.

Finally, we need to decide what to do with separate bugs that get fixed by the same CL, for example the four bugs fixed by crrev.com/c/7965120. While this can legitimately happen for distinct bugs, it’s probably more likely for the bugs to be duplicates (such as in this case), and so we count them as such.

With all the different types of deduplication, we get this final picture:

Again, looking at just the actionable vulnerability reports (likely the best measure), we see an overlap of roughly 25% (20 out of a total of 81), with a slight majority of these found first by Fuzzilli and later by BigSleep.

Overlap Experiment

The second way to measure the overlap is to run a dedicated experiment in which we try to re-discover bugs found by one system in the past using the other. Specifically, here we try to re-discover old Fuzzilli bugs using a BigSleep setup that’s as close to the production configuration as possible. For each bug we collect the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, and ask the agent to review those changes just as in the production CI environment. Note that the other direction, trying to rediscover past BigSleep bugs with Fuzzilli is more difficult to set up, since fuzzers cannot easily be given a similar “starting point”. Moreover, for many of these bugs we already know the outcome of such an experiment: the majority of “historic” BigSleep bugs (e.g. those from 2025) were found after fuzzers like Fuzzilli had already been fuzzing vulnerable builds for months, sometimes years. So they would most likely also not rediscover them in an experiment (except perhaps in a few cases where Fuzzilli was since updated to support new language features). Similarly, in production, BigSleep only reports crashes with a delay of 1-2 days (as there’s currently only one run per day). As such, fuzzers also get a head-start there.

In more detail, here is how the experiment is set up:

We start with a list of historic Fuzzilli bugs (from early 2023 until mid-2026) by querying the bug tracker hotlist. This gives us around 1150 raw bugs.

We restrict this to only type:vulnerability as these are the types of bugs we care most about and will remove some “noise” as above. We are left with roughly 600 vulnerabilities.

Next, we filter this list down to bugs that reproduce in the environment used by the agent. This involves two parts:

Bugs that reproduce on an x64 debug+asan build of the d8 shell as provided by Chrome’s public build infrastructure. This is important because many bugs only reproduce in special builds, for example because they are architecture-specific or need certain compile-time features.

Bugs that can be reproduced without special flags. The problem here is that fuzzers often set custom flags, either to enable in-development features (e.g. --experimental-wasm-jspi in crbug.com/361123483) or to turn on different fuzzing modes that make certain types of bugs easier to discover (e.g. --deopt-every-n-times in crbug.com/362784006). However, we can’t let the agent set arbitrary flags on historic V8 builds as these didn’t have a “safe-flags only” mode (leading to many false-positive crashes), and we also don’t want to tell the agent which flags it should use for a given challenge as that would be a hint. As such, for simplicity we limit ourselves to bugs that can reproduce with a standard set of flags (--fuzzing, --jit-fuzzing, --expose-gc) and only allow the agent to set those.

We end up with 132 historic bugs.

We now perform some deduplication similar to what we did above to identify implicit duplicates, which we remove. This leaves us with a final number of 112 bugs.

For a realistic comparison, we then convert these bugs into “code review challenges” similar to the ones used by the production BigSleep pipeline. For that, we try to identify the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, for example based on bisection. We note that this skews the comparison against BigSleep for two reasons:

We likely sometimes identify the wrong commit that is unrelated to the bug in question, making the task harder or even impossible.

We only have one commit per bug, while in the real world, the agent might discover the bug from another, subsequent commit that touches a similar part of the codebase.

We now run the agent for 25 attempts on each commit. The agent is asked to find bugs related to the commit and prove their existence by writing a testcase that crashes the vulnerable build. The attempt is terminated once a crash is found, so each attempt can report at most one bug. We use essentially the same configuration that was used in production BigSleep at that time, including the same underlying model: Gemini 3.6 flash.

Finally, we run some post-processing on the results to check if the agent found the “right” bug or an unrelated one. For that, we check that the testcase crashes the pre-fix revision but not the post-fix revision. This is imperfect but fairly easy to implement.

Here are the results from the experiment:

Starting from just the commits that (likely) introduced the bugs, BigSleep was able to re-discover ~62% of the original bugs, while finding a different (but by now fixed) bug for another ~12% of commits. On around 26% of the commits it failed to find any bugs.

Memorization

One thing to worry about with experiments such as this one is memorization: the LLM remembering specific bugs from its (pre-)training data and as such having an easier time “re-discovering” them during evaluation. We can try to get some idea of the effect of this by looking at the success rates for bugs from different time spans, e.g. every half-year period for which we have bugs in the data set. If there was memorization, we’d expect higher success rates (both for a single attempt and for the combined run) on bugs prior to the learning data cutoff of the model. Here are the results for our experiment:

For the model used in this experiment (Gemini 3.6 flash), the knowledge cutoff date is March 2026. Combining that with the fact that in early 2026, Chrome bugs would only become publicly visible after ~3 months, the effective knowledge cutoff for Fuzzilli bugs should be around Jan 2026. Looking at the data, there seems to be no statistically significant amount of memorization pre-2026. We note, however, that this may be different for other models or future model generations and as such recommend that this be re-evaluated for similar experiments in the future.

Difficulty

A follow-up question we might ask is how the overlap compares with “difficulty”. For example, in the best case a system like BigSleep would easily find issues that fuzzers struggle with and vice versa. In that case, budget that was previously spent on long fuzzing sessions may now be re-allocated and put to different uses. Here are the results of analysing this, where “bug difficulty” is measured by the time it took Fuzzilli to discover the bug:

While we do get a statistically significant result here (although not of particularly great magnitude), it actually points in the other direction! Bugs that are hard to find for a fuzzer are likely also hard to find for an AI agent. As such, those fuzzers should probably be kept running for now.

Components

Another thing we can look at is a per-component breakdown of the bugs and their rediscovery rates:

Interestingly, the overlap is significantly smaller for compiler bugs. This is the area where Fuzzilli probably specializes most in, which may explain the results. Later on (in part 3), we’ll also develop another hypothesis for why (some) bugs in the compilers may be more difficult to rediscover for BigSleep.

Prompting

A final question is how much the specific prompting played a role in the performance of the AI agent. For that, we run two quick follow-up experiments, only on the bugs that weren’t previously re-discovered and with different prompts:

Instead of starting from commits, we start from the vulnerable file or function. This may be an easier starting point but is still a fairly realistic setup since both can for example be obtained by extracting modified files and functions from a given commit.

Instead of asking the agent to find memory corruption vulnerabilities (what we care most about), we specifically tell it that assertion failures and similar crashes are also desirable.

Running these two experiments with only 5 attempts per bug (instead of the 25 used in the main experiment), the agent re-discovered 10 additional bugs in total: 8 from the different starting points and 7 with the rephrased prompt (with 5 found in both runs).

In total, combining these results with our original experiment, we get the following picture:

So the share of “correct” bugs found climbs to ~70%, and we find some kind of bug for ~84% of starting points. However, for fairness it should be noted that equivalent tweaks to a fuzzer could likely also result in higher discovery rates for certain bugs, so the results of this follow-up experiment should be treated with some caution.

Summary

The main results from our two angles are:

In production, the overlap is noticeable but not substantial at around 25%.

In our experiment, overlap was around 60% of historic Fuzzilli bugs (70% with additional runs that used different prompts).

The overlap is not uniformly distributed:

Bugs that are difficult for a fuzzer to find are more likely to also be difficult to find for an agent, so there’s more overlap on “easy” bugs.

The overlap seems to be smaller in the JIT Compilers and higher in the rest of the engine.

From just the experiment, we might expect a higher overlap in production. However, there are probably a few factors that prevent(ed) this:

There’s a limited time window for overlaps: once a bug reported by either system is fixed, the other system no longer has a chance to rediscover it (as the bug won’t reproduce on Clusterfuzz and will therefore be discarded).

Our experiment only looked at a subset of Fuzzilli bugs that reproduce on a standard x64 d8 fuzzer build and without special flags. In production, each system has access to slightly different and specialized builds, as well as different runtime flag constraints, and there the overlap is potentially smaller.

Pipeline hiccups such as overloaded servers or bugs in the automation likely prevented a number of commits from being reviewed by BigSleep in the last months, so bugs introduced by them may have been missed.

Since its introduction in April, the model underlying the BigSleep pipeline has been upgraded multiple times. Earlier models likely performed worse, and we expect future models to perform better.

Part 3: Shape of Bugs

In this section, we will first look at three case studies of bugs found by one system but not the other, then attempt to draw conclusions from these and other bugs.

BigSleep: Chrome Bug 449760249 (October 2025)

This bug is a nice example of BigSleep benefiting from the underlying model’s reasoning capabilities to discover a variant that was (likely) too complex to trigger by a fuzzer in a reasonable amount of time. It’s also a good example to show the general working of an agentic bug finding system.

Background: TDZ and Hole Check Elision

Before diving into the bug specifics, we first need to look at some JavaScript internals, specifically variable initialization. In JavaScript, variables declared with the let or const keywords cannot be used before they are initialized, and attempting to do so will lead to an exception (”ReferenceError: Cannot access 'foobar' before initialization”). In V8’s terminology, these variables reside in a “temporal dead zone” (TDZ) until they are initialized. Internally, V8 sets variables in the TDZ to a special sentinel value, the_hole, and then checks for this value when accessing the variable’s content.

To limit the performance impact of these hole-checks, V8’s bytecode compiler implements an optimization (behind the default-enabled --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks flag) to identify redundant checks and subsequently remove them. The idea here is to identify “dominating” checks where it can then be guaranteed that a hole-check has already been performed for a given variable on all possible paths leading to the current position.

This is a security-relevant optimization as an incorrectly removed hole-check would result in the internal the_hole value leaking to JavaScript code, a condition that has historically been exploitable (although new mitigations for this bug class have since shipped).

The Original Vulnerability

The original bug (issue 40071027 - discovered two years earlier by Fuzzilli!) involved do-while loops containing a break statement. In a do-while loop, the loop condition evaluates after the body. If the condition contains an assignment to a variable, the bytecode compiler will mark the variable as initialized. However, if a break statement executes in the loop body in the first iteration, then the condition will never execute. The bytecode compiler originally failed to account for this, leading to an incorrectly omitted hole check and subsequent leak of the_hole value.

To fix this, the implementation of BytecodeGenerator::VisitDoWhileStatement was modified in the following way:

- VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + if (!loop_builder.break_labels()->empty()) { + HoleCheckElisionScope elider(this); + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + } else { + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + }

Specifically, the patch works by creating a HoleCheckElisionScope for processing the condition code in case the loop contains break statements. This means that any updates to the TDZ state of variables will be discarded once the scope object is destroyed. As such, code after the loop will see the previous TDZ state (which is the correct behavior in this case).

Discovery of the Variant

The BigSleep agent began its analysis by examining the patch to VisitDoWhileStatement, realizing that the fix relied on loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() to decide if a protective HoleCheckElisionScope was required. It then began creating and testing various hypotheses for scenarios in which no break statement was registered with a given loop but the condition would still be skipped at runtime. For example, it hypothesized that a try-catch in combination with a throw inside the loop might confuse the hole-check elision logic. It then investigated how try-catch was implemented in the bytecode compiler and concluded that this was handled correctly.

Eventually, the agent started investigating labeled breaks, which allow directly breaking out of inner loops. It hypothesized that these might not be handled correctly and continued to investigate how these were being processed, for example by studying the logic in BytecodeGenerator::VisitBreakStatement. This time, it seemed to have identified a real flaw: in the case of nested breaks, the inner loop was apparently not being informed of the existence of a break statement! It therefore formulated the following vulnerability hypothesis:

If a labeled break inside a do-while loop targets an outer scope, the inner do-while loop’s LoopBuilder is not notified.

Consequently, loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() remains true.

Therefore, when generating the code for the loop condition, the HoleCheckElisionScope introduced by the patch is not used.

The condition is bypassed at runtime, but the bytecode compiler erroneously removed a later hole-check, leading to a leak of the_hole to JavaScript.

The agent then began writing a testcase to prove the existence of this bug. The initial attempt with simply two nested loops and a label failed, however, as the bytecode compiler would add another protective scope object for the labeled block. To work around this, the agent decided to use a switch statement. When handling a switch statement, the bytecode compiler uses a HoleCheckElisionMergeScope to compute the intersection of initialization states across all branches. By ensuring that the variable was initialized in a default case, the merge logic then concluded that the variable was correctly initialized on all paths.

Proof of Concept

With that, the agent had everything in place to produce a testcase to demonstrate the vulnerability. Below is the agent’s PoC:

// Flags: --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks function trigger(cond) { { target: switch(1) { case 1: do { // Labeled break targeting the switch. The do-while LoopBuilder remains unaware. if (cond) break target; } while((x=1) && false); // Condition performs a check/assignment on x. break; default: x=1; // Ensure x is considered initialized across all switch branches for merging. } // Generator incorrectly believes x is checked/initialized. Elides TDZ check. x + 1; let x; } } trigger(true);

Here is how this testcase works:

trigger(true) executes, entering case 1 of the switch.

The do-while loop executes break target.

Control flow jumps to the end of the switch, bypassing the do-while condition where x is assigned.

At runtime, x remains uninitialized (holding the_hole).

Because the TDZ check was elided at compile time, the engine leaks the internal the_hole value to JavaScript code in the x + 1 expression, leading to a potentially exploitable condition.

We can see how this bug would be difficult for a fuzzer to find since the testcase is quite complex. While a coverage-guided fuzzer would have received rewards for triggering individual code paths (such as the handling of labeled break, the switch statement, the do-while loop, etc. in the parser), there is no additional reward for putting these together “in the right way” and so ending up with a testcase like this is quite difficult.

BigSleep: Chrome Bug 443765373 (September 2025)

This bug is an example of a relatively simple bug type that is challenging to discover with standard fuzzing approaches.

Background: Exception handling in V8

To understand this bug, it is necessary to briefly look into exception handling in V8. Take the following example JavaScript code:

function simple() { try { throw 42; } catch (e) { return e; } }

Here, we have a function consisting of a try-catch block in which an exception is raised. Running this in d8 with --print-bytecode, we can see the internal bytecode that the engine generates to execute the JavaScript code:

[generated bytecode for function: simple] 0x2ad5001000e4 @ 0 : 1b ff f9 Mov <context>, r0 0x2ad5001000e7 @ 3 : 0d 2a LdaSmi [42] 0x2ad5001000e9 @ 5 : b5 Throw 0x2ad5001000ea @ 6 : d1 Star1 0x2ad5001000eb @ 7 : 8d f8 00 CreateCatchContext r1, [0] 0x2ad5001000ee @ 10 : d2 ... ... 0x2ad5001000f7 @ 19 : b7 Return Handler Table (size = 16) from to hdlr (prediction, data) ( 3, 6) -> 6 (prediction=1, data=0)

For the purpose of this bug, the relevant part is mostly the last line of the output. Here, the bytecode essentially says “if there is an exception while the PC is between offset 3 and 6 in this bytecode, then execution should continue at offset 6 (the start of the exception handler)”.

The Bug

The agent spotted the bug while looking at the following function, responsible for writing the handler table data structure in memory:

void HandlerTable::SetRangeHandler(int index, int handler_offset, CatchPrediction prediction) { int value = HandlerOffsetField::encode(handler_offset) | HandlerWasUsedField::encode(false) | HandlerPredictionField::encode(prediction); int offset = index * kRangeEntrySize + kRangeHandlerIndex; Memory<int32_t>(raw_encoded_data_ + offset * sizeof(int32_t)) = value; }

Here, the int offset is being combined with a few other bits of data into a new int value. As such, the handler_offset cannot have the full integer range in the new field, possibly leading to integer truncation issues. The agent then investigated the specific bounds of these values and realized that the HandlerOffsetField had only 28 bits (allowing for 256MB) while the maximum bytecode size was 512MB! From there it was relatively simple to craft a testcase that crashes, simply by creating a huge function (resulting in >256MB of bytecode) with an exception handler at the end, then triggering an exception inside of it. The result is a jump to a wrong bytecode offset, a primitive that’s easily exploited. Here is the relevant part of the testcase:

// yield statements turn into a large chunk of bytecode let kNumYields = 500000; let body = ` if ("foo" === "bar") { ${"yield* 42;".repeat(kNumYields)} } try { throw 42; } catch (e) { // Will never get here } `;

Such a testcase would again be difficult to craft by a fuzzer as the fuzzer isn’t rewarded for creating large code (at least not with generic coverage feedback). In fact, the fuzzer is likely even actively discouraged from finding this bug since generating and executing large bytecode takes some time (in debug builds, the testcase generated by the agent needs a few seconds to trigger) and would therefore probably have led to timeouts during fuzzing.

Fuzzilli: Chrome Bug 40076141 (November 2023)

This bug is a good example of a type of bug that is likely difficult to find just by looking at (one part) of the source code. It was originally discovered by Fuzzilli and not rediscovered by any of the experiments from part 2.

Background: Value Representation in V8

Consider the following piece of JavaScript code:

let i = 42; let f = 13.37; let s = "foobar" i = s;

Here we create multiple variables holding values of different types. Note, however, that we never declare the type of a variable, and that variables can hold values of different types throughout their lifetime (i first contains an integer, later a string). What we see here is that JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, and so variables (and also object fields, etc.) have no fixed type. However, the actual runtime values still need to have a type: the engine somehow needs to know that foobar is a string value and that certain operations (e.g. substring search) can therefore be performed on it. Conceptually, this is possible by representing runtime values with a struct such as

enum JSType { JS_TYPE_INT, JS_TYPE_FLOAT, JS_TYPE_STRING, ... }; struct JSValue { JSType type; // Either the raw value or a pointer to another object, e.g a JSString. uintptr_t value; };

However, this is somewhat inefficient since we now need something like 16 bytes to represent a simple 4-byte integer at runtime. As such, modern JS engines use clever tagging schemas, which rely on unused pointer bits to encode type information. Specifically, in V8 the JSValue type is a tagged pointer (or just tagged for short) which stores one bit of type information in the least-significant bit:

If the bit is one, then the value minus 1 is a pointer to another object. This works because objects are aligned and so cannot start at an uneven address.

If the bit is zero, then the next 31 bits contain a raw integer value (also called a small integer - Smi)

As such, to figure out the type of a value at runtime, the engine first looks at the least-significant bit. If that is zero, the value can be “untagged” to obtain the integer value by right-shifting by one. On the other hand, if the bit is one, the value is a valid pointer to an object that contains further type information. For more details on V8’s pointer tagging scheme see also this blog post.

The Testcase

Let’s start by looking at the testcase produced by the fuzzer, which isn’t overly long:

function f0() { let v2 = 1; for (let i3 = v2; i3 >= v2; i3 += v2) { v2 = v2 && i3; } } f0();

The bug is caused during optimization of the loop by the Maglev compiler, specifically due to a conflict between two stages of the compiler pipeline: the initial graph builder and the later MaglevPhiRepresentationSelector. [truncated for CSV - full text is in the JSON export]

Title: Attackers Hijack Dahua IP Cameras in Ukraine Using P2P Access and Auth Weaknesses
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) has issued an alert warning of unauthorized remote access to video surveillance systems manufactured by Dahua.

"Cases of compromising IP cameras and DVRs with access to the video stream, changing the device configuration and creating third-party accounts have been recorded," the State Special Communications Service of Ukraine (SSSCIP) said in an alert issued last week.

The primary initial access vector used in the attacks is via Easy4IP, a peer-to-peer (P2P) platform that allows users to remotely monitor homes or small businesses by connecting their Dahua IP cameras, NVRs, and DVRs via a smartphone app or web browser by scanning a QR code or entering the hardware Serial Number (SN).

The agency has warned that the serial numbers have a predictable structure containing a 10-character model prefix that's identical for all units of the same device family and a five-character hexadecimal counter that's incremented almost sequentially (e.g., 7K01F36PCA003E8).

This, in turn, allows attackers to guess them at scale through a brute-force attack and identify if they are connected to the cloud without hitting rate limits or lockouts. As a result, all devices with active P2P functionality are at risk even if they cannot be accessed directly via the internet.

"The assumption that the serial number is unknown to anyone is not a reason to consider the device secure," CERT-UA said.

Authentication barriers are overcome by leveraging weak or known passwords, or by exploiting authentication bypass vulnerabilities in outdated firmware versions, such as CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045. CERT-UA has shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the activity -

Presence of unknown accounts

Unauthorized configuration changes

Audit logs containing authentication events using the manufacturer's native protocol (DVRIP) and from a local address (127.0.0.1), a sign of P2P access.

To counter the threat, it's advised to disable the P2P feature if not required, avoid exposing them directly to the internet, and keep the software up-to-date.

The agency has not disclosed who was targeted, when these infections occurred, how many devices had been infected, or who was responsible for the activity. However, the findings share similarities with two clusters of activity that Hunt.io disclosed as targeting IP cameras in Ukraine and Russia.

One of the campaigns, attributed to a Russian-speaking operator, singled out internet-exposed cameras in Ukraine using known Dahua and Hikvision vulnerabilities, ultimately compromising 58 devices. The activity involved the exploitation of the following flaws by integrating Ingram, a publicly available webcam vulnerability scanner -

CVE-2017-7921 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Hikvision

CVE-2020-25078 - A credential disclosure vulnerability in D-Link

CVE-2020-25169 - An unauthenticated information disclosure vulnerability in Reolink

CVE-2021-33044 / CVE-2021-33045 - Authentication bypass vulnerabilities in Dahua that allow passwordless login

CVE-2021-36260 - An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Hikvision.

In parallel, the threat actor is also said to have undertaken scanning and exploitation of TP-Link and MikroTik routers and cameras using vulnerabilities like CVE-2024-53375 and CVE-2024-57049 across 15 European countries, including Ukraine, Poland, Romania, Moldova, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, the U.K., and Austria.

The second campaign, codenamed Operation CameraSwarm and attributed to a lone threat actor, is believed to have compromised over 14,530 Dahua IP cameras between June 17 and July 22, 2026, using a combination of credential brute-force attacks and the exploitation of the CVE-2021-33044-CVE-2021-33045 chain.

The attack scans for TCP port 37777, which is the default proprietary management and video streaming port used by Dahua, followed by collecting serial numbers, breaking into those devices by employing the aforementioned two exploitation methods, and then deploying a persistent backdoor account ("p2pwn / p2password") on nearly 2,000 cameras in a manner that can survive password change and a factory reset.

"1,923 cameras carry a persistent backdoor account (p2pwn / p2password), installed over RPC after either bypass," Hunt.io noted at the time. "It is stored independently of the admin password and survives a password change and, on most firmware, a factory reset. 283 cameras were reached by serial number alone through Dahua's cloud relay, with no device address and, in most cases, no credentials."

In some instances, the attackers have been found to abuse Dahua's cloud relay to reach cameras behind NATs using only their serial numbers.

Earlier this year, Dutch intelligence agencies warned that Russian actors are compromising IP cameras across the E.U., NATO states, and Ukraine to conduct systematic digital espionage operations and acquire military intelligence.

"This actor performs automated analysis of imagery through image recognition software to conduct targeted searches for military vehicles and the military cargo they are transporting," the July 2026 bulletin said.

"This provides the actor with, among other things, relevant military data, such as E.U. and NATO military transport routes, weapon deliveries to Ukraine, and the locations of Ukrainian military personnel. The information from IP cameras in Ukraine is used in attempts to neutralize Ukrainian military personnel and to destroy their military material."

Title: Japanese virtual desktop cloud hacked so hard it asks to be banned
Context: ” “However, while we proceeded cautiously, considering the impact on service availability and prioritizing other issues, our response lacked sufficient depth and speed, allowing...
Full Text: Japanese ISP GMO Internet has warned customers the cloudy desktop service it offers as an ideal foreign exchange trading environment was compromised by an attacker, and that it had been slow to improve the service's security. GMO runs a service called Onamae.com Desktop Cloud and last week admitted “a third party had installed malicious programs in the server environments of some customers.” That’s never welcome news but is an especially poor outcome because the servers host cloudy Windows desktops that GMO recommends customers use to host foreign exchange trading applications. In later updates the company revealed that some customers reported “unauthorized operations were performed on their trading accounts” and advised that third parties had probably seen users’ passwords for trading services. The next day, the company advised users to immediately change passwords for their trading accounts, and to do so using a device that they don’t use for trading. The company has since admitted that its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service’s “systems had security vulnerabilities, that its environment was accessed without authorization, and that customer information was taken outside the Company.” “Some customers have also reported transactions in their trading accounts that they do not recognize.” Those transactions have GMO sufficiently worried that it contacted major trading services, asked them to forcibly terminate all active sessions, monitor for unauthorized transactions, and to block trade requests coming from the Onamae.com Desktop Cloud. Not paying, or complaining GMO said it has “received a demand for money from a person believed to be the attacker. We have also been told that, if we refuse, the attacker will take actions such as publishing information about the Company and our customers.” The attacker wants $50 million. The company won’t pay because it feels “complying would not guarantee that the obtained information is deleted or that its misuse is prevented.” Investigations into the incident continue, with GMO warning that 26,739 VDI servers may have been hit by the attack, and that users’ personal devices may be at risk. The company is offering all users a ¥5,000 ($32) condolence payment and promised to make good on any trading losses caused by the attack. This incident may have quite a blast radius, as GMO has warned that some trading apps may keep sessions alive even after passwords change. “Check your securities or FX company's guidance or your account page, and either disconnect all active sessions or ask the company's support desk to disconnect them,” GMO advised. That ¥5,000 isn’t going to get anywhere near paying for the work customers will do to sort this out. GMO CEO Masatoshi Kumagai acknowledged that in a blog post in which he described the payment as “a token of our initial sincerity towards our customers who have experienced inconvenience and worry.” “We will dedicate the full resources of our group to providing a free alternative environment for six months, fundamentally overhauling our system infrastructure, and conducting a thorough investigation into the cause and preventing recurrence with the help of external experts,” he added. But he also admitted that GMO knew the service’s security could be improved. “Our in-house white-hat hackers had previously pointed out areas for improvement to the team,” he wrote. “The team took these points to heart and was working on countermeasures.” “However, while we proceeded cautiously, considering the impact on service availability and prioritizing other issues, our response lacked sufficient depth and speed, allowing the attackers to exploit the vulnerability. I deeply regret that, despite having professionals on staff, we failed to fully translate their expertise into effective defenses as an organization.” The CEO also said GMO can’t secure itself without government help. “I've been involved in this world for 31 years, since the dawn of the internet industry,” he wrote. “The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues, believing it would bring smiles to people's faces, is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors.” “The ease with which open weight AI models can be combined and spread into countless attack tools has transformed cyberattacks, which once required advanced skills, into an era where anyone can easily carry them out,” he added, before claiming that GMO Group’s cybersecurity operation “has confirmed that the source of an unauthorized access attack targeting approximately 20 Japanese companies was the misuse of ‘ARTEX,’ an autonomous AI penetration testing tool originally intended for defense.” Kumagai thinks public/private partnerships are needed to improve infosec across Japan. “Yesterday, we submitted a proposal to the government to ‘apply proactive cyber defense,’” he wrote. “We are by no means trying to shift the blame for our company's actions onto the government and beg for a bailout,” he wrote, but argued that unless Japan implements national-level defenses, more such incidents are unavoidable. ®
