Title: AI Model Risk Depends on What the Model Can Reach
Context: Nearly half of AI model inventories contain a critical-scoring reference How the scores work: Snyk tests each model against 29 attacker goals, such as extracting personal data...
Full Text:
New Snyk research across thousands of scanned enterprise environments shows why a high model-risk score marks where triage begins, and how security teams should respond.

Imagine two applications that reference the same AI model. One summarizes meeting notes, and the other uses an agent to query customer records and trigger business workflows. The model might carry the same adversarial test scores into both applications. But the consequences of a failure could be very different, and so could the failure that matters. A meeting summarizer needs to know whether the model can be pushed into misleading output. A customer records agent needs to know whether it can be made to leak data or take unauthorized actions. That’s why a model score for each type of attack is more useful than one average across all of them.

That distinction is at the heart of Snyk’s 2026 State of Agentic AI Adoption, Volume III. The first two volumes established that enterprise AI is a connected software estate, not just a collection of models. This new analysis adds risk scores for identifiable models and asks the question security leaders actually need answered: Which findings require action, and what action will reduce the risk?

Nearly half of AI model inventories contain a critical-scoring reference

How the scores work: Snyk tests each model against 29 attacker goals, such as extracting personal data or executing commands, and scores each from 0 to 1,000. The score combines how often an attack succeeded with how much damage that goal could do. 500 and above is high, 750 and above is critical. Models are tested behind a basic guardrail, so the scores describe a defended model, not an undefended one.

Of 1,693 environments with at least one detected model identifier, 74.5% reference a model that scored high (500+) on at least one attacker goal, and 49.2% reference one that scored critical (750+). PII extraction and command execution account for the critical-band findings observed in this sample.

Those numbers should prompt investigation, not panic. The research matches model identifiers found in code to adversarial test results. It does not establish that every model is active in production, that a particular tool or dataset is accessible, or that an attack has succeeded in an organization's application.

Coverage is another reason to be precise: only 37.5% of detected model occurrences have a matched risk score. About 17% of model-bearing environments have no scored model at all. Treat unscored and versionless references as unknowns that still need review.

Inventory size changes the count of findings but not the mix. The chance of finding at least one high-scoring model rises from 34.6% of the smallest model estates to 100% of the largest, yet the share of model occurrences linked to high-scoring models stays between 21% and 25% at every size, and between 18.9% and 25.5% across eight industries. Use the count to size the review backlog and the share to benchmark model choices against peers. Neither number shows what an active application permits a model to do.

For every high-scoring model, the first questions are: Is it active, what can it reach, and what happens if it fails?

Agents and MCP servers make the deployment context impossible to ignore

A model can produce an unsafe answer on its own. Connected to tools, data, and workflows, it may also be able to act on that answer. That's the difference between a model's tested exposure and the reach of the system around it.

Of the 1,051 US accounts with an MCP reference, 744 (70.8%) show evidence of building an MCP server with an SDK. The rest show only client connections or configuration references. Building a server, configuring one, and operating one are three different signals, and only runtime verification confirms the last.

Among environments with no detected agent or MCP signal, 49.1% reference a high-scoring model, compared with 96.6% of those with both an agent indicator and MCP server-building code.

The latter group also runs a much larger median model inventory: 104 models versus 4. Comparing environments with 5–19 models narrows the gap from 47 points to 26 (62.1% versus 87.8%). The pattern is an association. What agents and MCP servers change is how far a model’s score can reach, which is why they’re the place to look first.

For security teams, the next step is verification: confirm which agents and MCP servers are active, which tools they expose, what data they can retrieve, and what approvals stand between a model's output and a consequential action. A model score cannot answer those questions.

Don’t prescribe the same fix for every AI weakness

Once you know what a model can reach, the next question is which fix fits the failure. A useful model-risk program doesn't stop at severity bands. It asks which attacker goal matters for the application and whether another model performs meaningfully better on that goal. The answer splits two ways:

Where switching models can help. For command execution, 77% of the tested models scored zero, while the worst reached 834. For code backdoors, 57% scored zero, while the worst reached 695.

Where application controls do the work. On misinformation, the median model reached the maximum possible score. On race bias, no tested model scored zero.

A zero means no attack succeeded in that test, and a model that performs well on one goal can perform poorly on another, so validate any replacement against every goal the workload depends on. Where results cluster, the defense sits in the application: limit access, validate outputs, require approvals, monitor use, and scan generated code and dependencies before they enter a build.

Alert thresholds also tell only part of the story: 18 of the 29 attacker goals can never reach the default alert threshold of 500, because the damage each one can do caps its maximum score below it. Those failures still matter when the alert queue is quiet.

When models differ, test a replacement. When they don’t, reduce the application's access and authority.

Which goals can switching models actually fix, and which will never raise an alert? See all 29 charted. Download the full report.

Your approved model list may need a second look

Familiarity, license, and price are poor substitutes for examining the specific model.

Lower-capability models deserve review first

In the scored group, lower-capability models performed worse on personal data leakage, decision override, and insecure code generation. On decision override, the average fell from 501 for models below 130 on the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) to 45 for models at 150 ECI or above. Those lowest-capability models account for roughly one-third of model occurrences in the scored comparison, so the finding reaches well beyond an edge case.

Capability is a separate measure from security, and a stronger model still needs to be tested against the task it will perform. Revisit lower-capability approved versions and test alternatives from the provider you already use, since the pattern also appears within individual providers’ lineups.

Provider is a useful first signal, though it tells you less at the frontier. Among mid-range models, provider averages range from 113 to 356; among the most capable, three leading providers land within 22 points of one another. If your approved list leans on one provider, the full report shows where its models lead and where they lag. Six providers are compared side by side across seven attack types, from data exfiltration to output manipulation. Premium price tiers showed no consistent security advantage in this sample, largely because the high-price tier is mostly older, lower-capability models.

Open-weight models and training-data lineage

The report also finds higher personal data leakage scores among the 16 scored open-weight models than among proprietary models: 562 versus 274, on average. It’s a small sample size, so treat the difference as a signal worth investigating for workloads that handle personal data.

Lineage visibility follows the same split. In 904 of 1,693 model-bearing environments, scans found no training-data lineage, largely because proprietary model providers do not publish their training datasets. The evidence therefore depends on the model type: ask proprietary vendors for documented assurances, and inspect the dataset lineage that open-weight models publish.

Four actions for security leaders

1. Inventory and qualify the unknowns: Track model identifiers, versions, owners, active uses, agents, tools, MCP servers, and available lineage. Keep unmatched models visible; do not silently treat them as low risk.

2. Verify the reach: Confirm the runtime path from each active model to sensitive data, credentials, tools, and downstream actions. Distinguish server-building code from configuration and actual connections.

3. Make remediation goal-specific: Rank failures by their business consequences. Test named replacement models where adversarial results vary; use least privilege, output checks, approvals, and code scanning where they do not.

4. Turn the decision into governance: Record the model and version, test evidence, owner, approved controls, rationale, and review date. Reassess when models, permissions, fine-tuning data, or applications change.

The takeaway from Volume III: a model’s score shows its exposure, and the system around it decides its reach. Act on both, switch models where they differ, and tighten controls where they don’t

Methodology: Anonymized, aggregated AI bill of materials (AI-BOM) scan data from organizations that use Snyk, beginning September 2026: 3,023 environments, including 1,693 with at least one model identifier. Model-level findings cover US accounts.

Security leaders need to know which failures could matter to their business and which control changes the outcome. Which agent and MCP pattern describes your environment, and how does your provider compare across seven attack types? Full Text: Title: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 - command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 build 1178, the closed-source incremental backup and file-replication server from Synametrics Technologies, Inc. (United States), written in Java and served by an embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 through the vendor's in-house sradef framework whose single front controller routes every request as /app?operation=<op>&st=<step> to a handler registered in WorkerMappings.xml, contains a path traversal (CWE-22 primary, CWE-269 and CWE-78 contributing for the deployment shape that converts the write into an execution) in the chunked-upload branch of its PublicLink handler. That branch, operation=pb with st=u, reads a length-prefixed binary frame straight from request.getInputStream() rather than through any parameter parser: four big-endian int32 fields for protocol, chunkNumber, totalChunks and size, then a four-byte length prefix followed by UTF-8 filename bytes, then exactly size body bytes. At PublicLink.java:70-110 the decompiled method evaluates new File(base, filename) on that client-supplied filename with no rejection of "..", no rejection of path separators, no base-name extraction and no canonical containment check, creates missing parent directories with target.getParentFile().mkdirs(), opens the result with new FileOutputStream(target, true) in append mode, writes the size bytes it read and returns 0, which the caller at PublicLink.java:127 turns into the client reply code="1" with <payload>0</payload>. base is the authenticated user's own folder at /opt/Syncrify/PublicLinks/<user>/<generated-folder>, five components below the filesystem root, so a chunk name of ../../../../../etc/cron.d/<name> leaves it and lands a cron fragment anywhere the service identity can write. Because the documented Linux deployment shape runs the server process at uid 0 and a cron daemon was active on the verified instance, the host scheduler then reads that fragment as a root-authored job definition and runs its command field through a shell on the next minute boundary. The application never constructs, quotes or invokes a command line and every execution site in the product uses an argument vector with no shell, so the execution happens one component later and argument hygiene at the application layer would not have prevented it. The chain was verified end to end and the identity capture the cron job produced was uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root), established twice over: the fragment landed as -rw-r--r-- 1 root root at mode 0644, a file's owner after creation being the effective uid of its creator, and the scheduled job's own output reported uid 0 because the fragment names root in its user field and a scheduler will not honour that for a job file it does not already trust. The principal required is the product's lowest-trust account type. The gate on operation=pb is a secLevel=0 registration, meaning no administrator session, and the handler's own authentication call validates a credential from the backup-user store at config/UserMappings.xml via syncrify.users.DefaultUserManager rather than from the web-administrator store at config/umap.dat; the two stores are independent and must not be conflated. A backup user's entire legitimate job is to move bytes into its own repository, so the privilege boundary that fails here is inside the product, not a misconfiguration of the host. The defect is an omission rather than an absent control: three sibling families in the same tree, written against the same client protocol, do filter the same kind of field, the profile-upload, profile-fetch and file-splitter handlers rejecting separators with indexOf(47) and indexOf(92), the multipart upload path collapsing the name through getName(), and the download path testing indexOf("..") and answering 404 on a match. The chunk-upload branch calls none of them. There is no decoding step between the socket and the constructor, so no encoding trick is involved or needed. The product does ship a factory administration password of letmein in its first-run install wizard, but the first administrator login is forced through a password change through ChangePassword.jsp, the credential belongs to a different user store than the one gating this sink, and it is documented as a contributing fact only: it appears in no vector, raises no metric, and no conditional reading assumes it has not been rotated. No unauthenticated path to this sink was found and none is claimed. CVSS: 7.5 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding. That is the primary reading, and the two metrics that carry its nuance are AV:N and AC:H: the vulnerable component is an HTTP handler on a network-bound servlet connector and the credential it accepts exists so that remote backup clients can use it, so AV:N is the faithful classification of the component, while the deployment-dependent exposure of the listener carrying the route is priced in attack complexity rather than smuggled into the attack vector. AC:H is High for two reasons outside the attacker's control, that the listener carrying /app?operation= be reachable from the attacker's position and that the host run a scheduler which scans /etc/cron.d. Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.620146) = Roundup(7.493265) = 7.5, from ISS = 0.914816 and Impact at S:U = 5.873119. Conditional reading: 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), applying only where the listener carrying the /app?operation= surface is reachable from the attacker's network position, which is the normal operating mode for a backup server whose clients push data to it remotely, and computed as Roundup(5.873119 + 2.835255) = Roundup(8.708374) = 8.8. The conditional is labelled conditional everywhere it appears, is never the headline, and the published score is 7.5 rather than 8.8. Two further readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic. The changed-scope variant of the same metrics, 8.6 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected because the identity reached is the same root identity the server process already holds on the same host, so no component authority boundary is crossed by the outcome; the privilege gain is carried by PR:L and by C:H/I:H/A:H, which are the metrics meant to express it. The local-vector reading, 7.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected for an evidential reason and it is worth being explicit that this rejection lowers our own number rather than raising it: that reading is what follows if you treat the loopback binding observed in the testbed as the shipped default, and 7.8 is higher than the 7.5 this submission publishes at AV:N. The loopback binding was applied by us in the configuration before any testing began, so the host carried no public exposure while research was in progress, and there is no shipped artifact, no configuration template, no installer script excerpt and no documentation quotation, establishing the factory value of that binding in either direction, not that it binds publicly by default and not that it binds loopback by default. That unestablished reachable-listener premise is the reason AC is High and the reason the 8.8 figure is conditional, and a reader who disagrees with us about the factory default ends up with a larger score than ours, not a smaller one. No version-range claim is made: only 6.2 build 1178 was decompiled and exercised. Impact: arbitrary file write with an attacker-chosen path and attacker-chosen bytes, escalating to command execution as uid 0 on the verified deployment shape. The chunk branch writes exactly the bytes it reads to whatever path the chunk name resolves to, in append mode, creating missing parent directories via mkdirs(), so /etc/cron.d is the demonstrated escalation path and not the limit of the primitive. On this product the weight comes from what the host is for: it is a backup and file-replication server, and root on it means read access to the entire repository tree, every backup belonging to every configured client, which on a multi-tenant server is a confidentiality breach across all tenants rather than within one account, plus the server's own configuration holding administrator and backup-user credential material and transport secrets, the backup-user store comparing passwords in plaintext or storing them under a reversible permutation transform so a read of it hands over credentials directly. It also means integrity control over the replication path itself: repository contents, version and retention metadata and the server's own binaries can be altered in place, and because that path is how clients back up and restore, a modified backup set becomes a distribution channel whose corruption stays invisible until the moment the data is needed. Persistence is structural rather than incidental, a cron fragment running on every minute boundary until it is deleted and surviving restarts of both the service and the host. Availability follows the same authority: the backup service can be stopped, the host rebooted or hung, repositories deleted or truncated, and the scheduler used to keep doing so after the application alone is remediated, which destroys the recoverability that is the entire reason the product exists. All of that beyond the executed identity capture is argued from the identity reached and the deployment layout and was not performed; no repository data was read and no product file was modified or deleted during verification. Verification boundary: static reversal of the decompiled handler tree, then a live run against a single deployed instance of Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 installed from the distributed Linux tarball archive into /opt/Syncrify and started with ./run.sh, behind the embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 announcing itself as Synametrics Web Server v7. Two properties of that instance were the researchers' rather than the product's and both are carried as boundaries. The portal listener was bound to the loopback address by an explicit configuration edit made before testing, so remote reachability of the route is argued from the product's own design and binding configuration, from the front controller being the same listener that serves the client-protocol operations backup clients use, and from the structural fact that a backup server whose clients push across a network must have that listener reachable from them or it cannot perform its function; it is not a measurement from a separate host, and no shipped artifact establishes the factory binding in either direction. The backup-user store did not exist after installation, so the verification account was written into config/UserMappings.xml by hand with plaintext password comparison rather than provisioned through the administrator's user-management operation, which is licence-gated and was blocked by a zero licence count; the encrypted-entry and directory-authentication branches were examined statically and not exercised. The chain was driven from the target host itself over the loopback interface because that is how the listener was bound, so the same chain arriving from across a network segment was not verified and is not claimed. Four controls were exercised: a non-traversing chunk name through identical authentication, framing and routing in the same session, landing inside the user's own PublicLinks folder with an assertion that neither the fragment nor the marker existed, which isolates the traversal as the cause of the outcome and of nothing else; a Java-level confirmation that the multipart family's getName() collapse keeps a traversing name inside the PublicLinks root; a dispatch control against st=f, which reached a different void E() overload that parses an ed parameter as a Long and performed no write anywhere, fixing the sink to the st=u branch rather than to the handler in general after an initial static reading had attributed the upload to the wrong overload; and the four-way authentication reply table showing code="1" for a correct pair, code="-2" for a wrong password so the comparison is live, and code="-1" for an absent password and an absent user so the parameter-presence gate fired before the credential lookup was entered, which is what makes the lookup's no-comparison branch unreachable from this surface. Root execution was observed rather than inferred, and a non-root service deployment was not tested, so no claim is made about what the primitive achieves under an unprivileged service identity, where the escalation demonstrated here would not follow while the file write itself survived. Exactly one payload shape was executed, an identity capture into a marker file, and only that shape is claimed; the advisory reproduces the identity string and the frame field lengths derived from the field values but not the run's own byte capture, which was not preserved, not the generated PublicLinks folder name, which embeds the run's timestamp, not the credential pair, which are mandatory tool arguments with no default, and not the per-run fragment name or marker path. The unauthenticated surface was exhausted first with negative results: thirteen operations answer anonymous requests with real content and no credential check and all thirteen are sink-free; the remaining level-0 operations are not anonymous and answer code="-2" without valid credentials; seventeen Runtime.exec and ProcessBuilder sites exist and none is reachable anonymously; eight deserialization candidates have no network caller and the classpath carries no gadget library, no commons-collections, Jackson, XStream, Kryo or Hessian; and no template engine or naming-service lookup exists in the tree. That enumeration is not a proof the unauthenticated surface is safe, and it surfaced weaknesses deliberately not claimed here and not folded into any metric, being a manualOverride filter-block bypass exposing debug pages with a directory listing and an environment-variable dump, a password-recovery account-enumeration weakness, globally disabled CSRF prevention that is irrelevant to a chain needing credentials the attacker holds, vendor-default credentials for an embedded database that is configured but disabled and was not listening, and a default trial licence serial whose effect was left unresolved. Only Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 is claimed; the same sradef framework underpins the vendor's sibling products and this build's own web.xml still carries the display-name SynaMan, which is recorded to say where else the same construction is worth auditing, and no sibling product was tested. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/synametrics-syncrify-publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/synametrics/syncrify-6.2/publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce/exploit/synametrics_syncrify_publiclink_chunk_upload_traversal_cron_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target. It takes host, port, scheme, front-controller route, operation and upload step; a mandatory backup-user credential pair with no default; and the command, marker path, fragment path, fragment user field, fragment schedule, traversal depth, scheduler wait and per-request timeout as arguments, defaulting to the loopback interface, port 5800, a depth of five and an identity capture. It offers an --insecure flag for self-signed TLS on the https scheme, a --control mode that performs the identical authenticated upload with a non-traversing chunk name and then asserts that neither the fragment path nor the marker path exists, a --proof-command argument that reads proof from a local command's standard output for an operator who already holds a shell channel to the host, an --expect-root flag that exits non-zero unless the recovered proof reports uid=0, and a --cleanup mode that removes only the two paths the script created. Nothing destructive is performed and no product file is overwritten or deleted. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

The registration websFormDefine("setWAN", ...) at 0x478484, handler at 0x441cec, name string at 0x4a6250, publishes POST /goform/setWAN. Inside the handler the WAN mode is taken from the request and dispatched: websGetVar(wp, "wanMode", "") at 0x441d3c, atoi at 0x441d44, apmib_set(0x102, &wanMode) at 0x441d54, then addiu v1, zero, 2 at 0x441d60 and beq v0, v1, 0x441e74 at 0x441d6c. That single-character scan is the entire sanitisation on the path. The value is then formatted by sprintf at 0x441ee8 with the format string at 0x49a510, echo %s > /tmp/UserName, and passed to system(buf2) at 0x441f1c through the PLT slot at 0x4c6d60, which hands the line to /bin/sh -c. A pipe, an ampersand, a backtick, a dollar sign with parentheses and an embedded newline are never inspected, so a username containing no semicolon reaches the shell untouched: the payload |id > /tmp/marker # builds the command line "echo |id > /tmp/marker # > /tmp/UserName", in which the shell treats the hash as a comment swallowing the sink's own redirect and runs id as the right-hand side of a pipeline. An escape loop replacing a hash with a backslash-escaped hash does exist between 0x441f4c and 0x441fb0, but the instruction order places it after system() at 0x441f1c with no branch back to it, and it writes the configuration buffer at sp+0x18 that apmib_set(0x6d, ...) stores at 0x44200c rather than the buffer handed to the shell, so the hash character is escaped for storage and for nowhere near execution. Between websGetVar and system there is no regex call, no inet_aton, no isdigit, no isalnum, no strchr, no strcspn, no vendor validation helper and no custom validator; the inet_aton calls that do exist in the function, at 0x441dd0 and 0x441e14, belong to the static-IP branch, wanMode 1, reached via the branch at 0x441d8c, which the wanMode 2 comparison never enters, so a quick read of the decompilation misleads a reviewer into thinking this function validates addresses. The same construction appears three times in this handler and one root cause yields three reachable parameters: pppUserName on wanMode 2 with sink region 0x441e74 to 0x441f1c and configuration object 0x6d written after the sink, pptpUserName on wanMode 3 from 0x4420d0 onward with configuration object 0xf3, and L2TPUserName on wanMode 6 from 0x44246c onward with configuration object 0x128, each selected by a value the request supplies and each using the same immediate-0x3b scan, the same echo format string and the same system() call shape, so a patch confined to the PPP path leaves the PPTP and L2TP paths injectable. Reaching the handler requires a valid administrative session: the gate auth_authorize at 0x404d00 reads configuration object 0x1bc, the setup-wizard flag, through apmib_get, and once past setup the security store at 0x4c7004, a single / entry of type Basic registered from the directive Auth / /etc/boa/boa.passwd, covers every /goform/ path with HTTP Basic authentication. The product has no second lower-privileged role, so Privileges Required is High: one realm entry, one password file, one account, an Allow directive handler at 0x407688 that is a stub answering "This version of Boa doesn't support access controls", a type-None string at 0x49070c never passed to auth_add, and a shipped configuration carrying one Auth directive and no Allow directive. The route is not one of the four carrying a post-boot uptime gate, /mp.asp, /goform/mp, /advanced_management.asp and /goform/formAdvManagement, which redirect to /index.asp once /proc/uptime exceeds 600 seconds, so it is reachable at any time the device is up. The calling process is root because etc/boa/boa.conf declares User root, the server performs no setuid, chroot, namespace or capability drop and writes /var/run/webs.pid, which requires root on this filesystem, so the landing identity is uid=0(root) with no escalation step in the chain. This handler is one instance of a broad construction: a count of the shipped registration table found 91 /goform/form* handlers of which roughly 85 reach a system() or popen() call. Two adjacent observations are reported without a score: the strcpy at 0x441e94 copies attacker-controlled bytes with no length argument into a fixed stack buffer, for which no overflow was developed and no exploitability claim is made, and because the semicolon scan writes a NUL at the first semicolon a legitimate username containing one is silently truncated before storage, a correctness defect independent of the injection. The firmware image ships a populated /etc/boa/boa.passwd for the single realm and the model's published factory login is admin:1234; that is reported separately as CWE-798, carries no score, is never described as the vector for this injection, and no cryptographic match against the shipped MD5-crypt digest is claimed because the digest string captured during analysis was recorded incompletely. One detail is left unresolved rather than smoothed over: the single account entry in the image is recorded under the name root while the model's published management login is admin, and because no device was ever authenticated against, which user name the realm accepts was not established. Absence of privilege separation is likewise reported separately as CWE-250. A static comparison against a second firmware image, BR-6208AC_V2_1.03, whose webs is a different build, ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS-I, 816568 bytes, SHA256 3ad10a41d11c8cd59185eab6c9ce67b18cd2118942eb2201f48540d7846a0328, found a setWAN implementation matching instruction for instruction, handler at 0x448710, websGetVar for pppUserName at 0x4488b8, strcpy at 0x4488bc, the same inline immediate-0x3b scan at 0x4488dc to 0x4488fc, the same sprintf at 0x448920 with format string 0x4a6954, system() at 0x448940, the same three parameters on the same three wanMode values and the same single-realm Basic authentication behind the same configuration flag, which points to a shared source component in the vendor's router software base; that model was not tested, nothing was executed from that image, no score covers it and it is not an exploited finding on it. A second independent command injection on the same image, in the formWlanMP manufacturing-test handler reaching sprintf at 0x462fd0 and system() at 0x46308c through POST /goform/formWlanMP with no sanitisation across thirty radio-calibration fields, is published as a companion advisory; it is a different handler, format string, sink address and sanitiser, so one patch point does not close both. No prior public record was found whose root cause is command injection in this setWAN handler. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, from ISS = 1 - 0.44^3 = 0.914816, Impact at S:U = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119, Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708 and Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.234708) = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. The provenance of that figure is disclosed because it is a correction: the research notes carried 8.8 next to a PR:H vector, and 8.8 is the arithmetic of PR:L, so the score was recomputed from the vector and published at 7.2, lowering the researchers' own number by 1.6 points. Four further readings are printed with their arithmetic in the public analysis. Privileges Required Low is rejected at 8.8 High, Exploitability 2.835255 and Base Roundup(8.708373), because the product has no basic-user role. Scope Changed is rejected at 9.1 High, Impact at S:C 6.128026, Exploitability 2.286496 and Base Roundup(1.08 x 8.414522), because webs is root before the attack and root after it. Attack Complexity High is rejected at 6.6 High, Exploitability 0.705547 and Base Roundup(6.578666), because success depends on no condition outside the attacker's control, the only branch to satisfy, wanMode, being attacker-supplied. An adjacent-vector reading is published as a labelled alternative at 6.8 High, Exploitability 0.900610 and Base Roundup(6.773729), and is the honest description of a stock device whose WAN-side input policy drops new connections, the shipped firewall script dropping WAN-originated SYN at firewall.sh:180, installing a default DROP input policy at firewall.sh:187 and accepting input on other interfaces at firewall.sh:189; AV:N is retained because the service is bound to the device's own network stack and addressable over IP by every host on the segment the router serves, including guest wireless clients and anything bridged or compromised behind it, and because remote management on the WAN side or forwarding port 80 are ordinary documented features. Default internet exposure is not claimed. Two readings at 9.8 Critical, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H from Exploitability 3.887043 and Base Roundup(9.760161), are published only as explicitly labelled conditionals and never as the headline: the first applies where a deployment still accepts the factory credential and is reasoned rather than demonstrated, since no device was authenticated against; the second applies to a device still in its pre-configuration setup state, where auth_authorize returns success without a challenge for paths outside /mp.asp, /index.asp and / at 0x4052d0 while /generate_204 answers 204, and that branch is structural inference only, read from the binary and never exercised, with three shipped artefacts identifying the state as the setup wizard rather than normal operation, namely formwizResetDefault at 0x44cdbc displaying Resettowizard, formWizSetup printing NO - LOGIN-WEB when the flag is 1, and pages such as web/inter_wan.asp:214 and web/admin_timezone.asp:95 reading the same flag. That conditional's Scope Changed variant computes to 10.0 and is deliberately not published, and if the setup window has to be contested rather than found open the reading is 8.1 High from Exploitability 2.221167 and Base 8.094286. No version range is claimed: only firmware BR6478AC_v2.20.bin was examined, and only the wanMode 2 path was replicated, so no claim is made for other BR6478AC builds, for the separately marketed BR-6478AC V2 hardware revision whose firmware line is a different little-endian MIPS-II build of webs, for the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances beyond the structural reading of the same handler, or for any other model. Impact: arbitrary operating-system command execution as root on the router from a single authenticated POST indistinguishable from a legitimate WAN settings submission, since the payload travels in the PPP username field of the form the product's own wan.asp page posts. Root on this device exposes every stored secret, including precisely the PPP, PPTP and L2TP credentials this handler writes into configuration objects 0x6d, 0xf3 and 0x128, so an attacker who reaches the device can read the ISP or VPN account details the owner entered, together with the administrator password file, wireless pre-shared keys and per-station key material, VPN parameters and any certificate or key on the filesystem. It grants control of the configuration and routing plane: firewall and NAT rules, the DNS resolver handed out to clients, DHCP leases and a malicious default gateway, port forwards, wireless SSIDs and the WAN uplink itself, including rewriting the WAN mode, which is exactly the configuration path this handler owns. It grants firmware-level persistence, since root can write the flash-backed configuration area and install a boot-time startup mechanism, so a compromise survives reboots and can survive a partial configuration reset, with recovery requiring a full reflash of a known-good image. It grants availability at will over wireless, routing, DHCP, DNS and the management service. There is no rate limit on the handler and no lockout in the Basic realm, so the route is repeatable and leaves no alert behind. Detection is poor by construction but this sink leaves one usable anomaly: a submitted WAN configuration produces ordinary behaviour and the sink's visible effect, a username written into /tmp/UserName and then into the configuration store, is what a legitimate submission does, so the indicator is the absence of the expected /tmp/UserName destination on a submission that should have created it. An injection also corrupts stored configuration in a way the owner may not notice, the semicolon scan truncating at the first semicolon and a pipe-and-hash payload storing a username the WAN link cannot authenticate with, a self-inflicted availability event that doubles as a fingerprint. One operational caution: the injection is not side-effect free. A successful submission overwrites the stored WAN username and can break the uplink, which is what the handler does on any successful submission, so any demonstration must record and restore the device's original WAN configuration. Verification boundary: no physical device was powered on and no end-to-end HTTP request was ever accepted by the product. The HTTP leg, being request parsing, the authentication gate, form registration, mode dispatch and PPP branch selection, is evidenced at instruction level from the shipped binary, its configuration and its boot scripts. The execution leg is evidenced dynamically by replication of the sink's semantics rather than by detonation, because a MIPS big-endian uClibc userspace with a board-specific bootloader could not be booted end to end in the research environment: the extracted binaries faulted with SIGBUS under the available user-mode translator and full-system emulation of the board was not brought up. The question under test is not the device but whether a shell evaluates a pipeline and honours a trailing comment in a string built by the vendor's own sprintf and handed to /bin/sh -c, which is a question about POSIX shell semantics that are architecture independent, combined with the exact format string read out of the binary. The string sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 was reconstructed byte for byte for a request whose pppUserName field is |id > /tmp/marker_sw # and handed to /bin/sh -c in an isolated POSIX sandbox whose invoking shell ran as root, producing a 39-byte marker file owned by root:root containing uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) with shell exit status 0, while the sink's own /tmp/UserName destination was not created, that absence being the proof that the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment rather than being escaped, since a protected sink would have left the file behind. A benign control submitting an ordinary username created its destination containing that username and produced no marker. The same replication was repeated on a workstation under an ordinary unprivileged user account and reproduced the semantics at that identity, ruling out the alternative explanation that running as root caused the marker to appear. The harness removes any pre-existing marker and destination before each run and deletes its scratch files afterwards. Consequently the on-device landing identity of uid=0(root) is inferred from the shipped User root directive plus the root-identity replication and is not an observation from hardware; AV:N is argued from the product's transport and authentication model rather than measured across a network; the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances are a structural reading of the same handler rather than a demonstrated result; the sibling-model comparison is static only with nothing executed from that image and no score covering it; no setup-state request was sent; no dictionary or credential attack was attempted; and no overflow was developed against the unbounded stack copy. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-setwan-command-injection-root-rce Companion advisory, same product and image, different handler: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-formwlanmp-command-injection-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/edimax/br-6478ac-v2.20/setwan-command-injection-root-rce/exploit/edimax_br6478ac_setwan_command_injection_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target, and it is built so that it cannot be used accidentally against a live network. Its default mode is replication: it reconstructs the exact string the device's sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 and hands it to /bin/sh -c locally, asserting both that the injected pipeline ran and that the sink's own redirect target was not created, which is what proves the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment, then running a benign username as a negative control and asserting the opposite. That replication mode, not a device run, produced the evidence above. Arguments cover target host, Basic realm username and password, the WAN mode to select, which of the three username fields carries the payload, an option to iterate all three modes, a single non-destructive command defaulting to id, the marker path, the submit-url field value defaulting to /wan.asp, a user agent and a per-request timeout. A send mode additionally POSTs the request to the target and is refused for any non-loopback target unless an explicit allow-remote flag is given, and a print-request mode emits the exact HTTP request that would be transmitted while making no connection at all. Safety rails are loopback-only by default, one non-destructive marker command, no callback listener, no reverse shell, no persistence, and removal of every local file the run created. The tool's own documentation carries the warning that sending against a real device does change stored WAN configuration, because that is what the handler does on any successful submission, so the device's WAN settings must be restored afterwards. The model's published factory password appears in the tool only as a placeholder default so the request shape is self-documenting; the injection does not depend on it and the credential is reported as a separate weakness. Use only against systems you own or are authorised to test. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Full Text: Title: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce CVE: pending Description: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E, version v2.2.44, the industrial wireless radio from ProSoft Technology, Inc. (United States) whose research designation is RLX-IH 24E, installs and executes code submitted over its management interface without performing any signature, hash or CRC check on it. The appliance is a closed-source embedded device and an OEM build of the MicroHard Systems IPx21 platform on the MHX-910 board design: an Intel IXP425 XScale processor, ARM big-endian, Linux 2.4.24-uc0, with static management pages under /usr/web and 57 ARM big-endian CGI programs under /usr/lib/cgi-bin/ served by boa over HTTP and boa_ssl over HTTPS. The classification is CWE-494, download of code without integrity check, with CWE-345 and CWE-347 co-equal, because the only authenticity check in the path is a non-cryptographic string equality and no signature is verified anywhere. CWE-434, CWE-73, CWE-250 and CWE-269 contribute. It is explicitly not CWE-78 and a command-injection remediation would not fix it: the shared platform helper SubProgram_Start at offset 0xbd5c splits its argument string on spaces with strtok into at most eight tokens and then calls vfork and execvp directly, so no shell is ever invoked and shell metacharacters are inert here. The upload hop is in usr/lib/cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi, routine HandleSubmit at offset 0x8d1c, with its formatting string at rodata offset 0x2b1c. On the file1 part of a multipart/form-data POST to /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi it calls cgiFormFileName and cgiFormTempFileName, builds the move argument with sprintf(buf, "%s /upgrade/upgrade/%s", tempfile, origfilename), runs SubProgram_Start("/bin/mv", buf), which must succeed, and then runs SubProgram_Start("/sbin/upgrade", origfilename). The client-supplied original filename is therefore used unmodified twice, once as the destination of the move and once as the installer's only argument, which makes the file extension and so the installer branch entirely the requester's choice. The handler applies no extension whitelist, no digest comparison and no path canonicalisation. The install hop is /sbin/upgrade, a short POSIX shell script shipped in the same package, running with the CGI's own privileges, which are root. It dispatches on ${FILE##*.} and its three consequential branches are: ".pkg", which tests gzip stream integrity with gunzip -t, unpacks with tar -xf into a staging tree, compares the appliance's PRODUCT_NAME read from /etc/MHX_CONFIG against a LOCK_NAME read from a lockfile inside the package itself, prints "Match image." on equality, executes ./pre, applies the inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C /, executes ./post, prints "Upgrade Successful" and then reboots unconditionally; ".passwd", which copies the upload over both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original; and ".factory", which copies the upload over /etc/db1, the configuration store holding the management interface's own transport flags, accounts and radio behaviour. The equality test is the only gate before code execution and both of its operands are available to the requester: the expected value is the compile-time platform constant IPx21PROSOFT recoverable by reading the shipped firmware once, and the asserted value is carried inside the package being installed. A package whose identity is validated against data carried inside that same package cannot be a source of assurance about it. The defect is the absence of an authenticity step, not a weak one, and strengthening the compatibility check would change nothing while both operands come from the same side. Impact: root command execution on the appliance from a single multipart/form-data POST followed by the product's own documented install sequence, with requester-authored shell code running both before and after an unconstrained archive extraction into the root of the filesystem. Attacker code reading the pre-execution state, an arbitrary rootfs write through the inner archive whose entry names are constrained in no way, and attacker code running post-write are all present in one request. The .passwd branch reaches the same privilege ceiling without executing anything, replacing both the live account database and its backup copy so that the device's own recovery path restores the modified database rather than the shipped one; since the factory admin entry is uid 0 with the restricted shell /bin/txtUI, an added uid-0 entry with /bin/sh converts an administratively restricted login into a general root shell at the next interactive login. The .factory branch lets a requester rewrite the device's security configuration, widening or narrowing the exposure of the surface they arrived through and surviving a later reconfiguration by the operator. Persistence is native to the product rather than improvised, because the install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. Availability is controlled at will, both by that reboot and by installing content that stops the device serving traffic, which for a radio carrying traffic between a process network and its field instruments is also a position on the path that traffic takes. Detection is weak by construction: every step is documented product behaviour, the request is an ordinary firmware upload, the response is the vendor's own success page, and a legitimate upgrade prints exactly the same "Match image." and "Upgrade Successful", so the usable indicators are post-hoc and filesystem-level, namely an installed package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair corresponds to no release the operator obtained, an unexpected file under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid-0 account whose shell is not the vendor's restricted interface. Verification boundary, stated exactly because it is narrower than the headline suggests, and because the classification above depends on it. The installer half of the chain was measured and the upload half was not. No HTTP request was ever issued at this product and no physical appliance was used at any point, so nothing here is an exploit run against a live device and it is not presented as one. What was executed is the firmware's own /sbin/upgrade, byte-for-byte unmodified, inside an isolated chroot sandbox built on a copy of the upgrade package's own root filesystem. A crafted .pkg printed "Match image." then "Upgrade Successful" and exited 0; the pre script left a marker proving it executed and wrote PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0 into a second marker, the post script left its own marker, and the inner archive applied an entry to the root of the filesystem. The uid marker is the load-bearing evidence: the payload wrote that value at runtime rather than having it read from a configuration file, so it is the executing identity and not an inference about it. The recorded landing identity is uid=0(root). A .passwd run replaced both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original with the uploaded text, proven by a pre-run digest of the pre-seeded database that no longer matched afterwards and by a marker line present in both copies. A negative control was run to establish that none of this came from the harness: a structurally identical package, same outer tar layout, same metadata files, same inner archive, same marker-writing scripts, with exactly one deliberate difference, LOCK_NAME=WRONGPRODUCT, was refused with "This unit doesn't support the image." and produced no markers anywhere. That control also isolates the product-string comparison as the single cause of refusal and makes the positive and negative runs mutually exclusive. Four substitutions existed in the harness and none in the code under test: an x86 busybox build supplied /bin/sh, tar, gunzip, mv and cp because the firmware's own copies are ARM big-endian and the host is not; a stub replaced the platform mhx utility; /etc/MHX_CONFIG was populated with the product identity the firmware itself ships; and /etc/passwd was pre-seeded with three factory-style entries for comparison. Two transcript lines, "logger: not found" and "mhx: not found", are absent helpers in the sandbox PATH and are not product behaviour. The run count is one positive .pkg run, one positive .passwd run and one negative control, in one sandbox on one host, each effect observed once, never repeated across sandbox builds and never performed on hardware. Not measured, and not claimed: the web server and its access control, because /bin/boa lives in the device base flash and is not contained in the system upgrade package, so the access control gating this CGI could be neither proved nor disproved from the artefacts available; the CGI binaries and the firmware's ARM helpers, for the architecture reason; the closing reboot, since the sandbox is a directory tree with no init, though the path up to it was observed; any privilege escalation, the chain starting from the administrative identity the product's own account database already grants uid 0; any reach into the radio baseband image RLX-IFH24E_v5089.mhx, identified but not exercised; and any impact on an attached control system, PLC or historian. Consequently the Type field above reflects the documented delivery vector, a network POST to a CGI on the management listener, and the Platform field reflects a firmware and hardware target; the part that was actually executed was the vendor's own installer acting on a supplied file, and a reader should weight the two halves of this chain differently. That is what the published advisory is written to allow. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, computed from first principles rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - (0.44 x 0.44 x 0.44) = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708; Base = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. AV:N because the entry point is a network service and the firmware's own default configuration record inside the shipped package enables the web interface on both transports, UI_Access_HTTP=B and HTTPS=B, with non-default values for the Telnet and SSH entries; that shipped record is the evidence for a default, and the Network classification comes from the transport the artefact establishes rather than from a reach we observed. AC:L because the chain is deterministic, with no race, no timing window, no memory-layout dependency and no on-path position, and the single piece of environment knowledge it needs is a platform string published inside the shipped firmware. PR:H because installing firmware is an administrative function, the handler is a maintenance CGI linked directly from the interface's own menu pages, and the only account model the package documents for that interface is a uid-0 admin entry with a password-change page and a configurable RADIUS mode; no lower-privileged principal was demonstrated reaching the handler. UI:N because once a session holds that privilege the move, the install, both script executions and the reboot all follow from one request with no operator action and no confirmation step in the recovered handler path. Scope Unchanged because the vulnerable component and the impacted component are the same appliance operating system, the CGI already running as root, the installer already running as root and the rootfs extracted by that same root process, so no authority boundary is crossed. Three readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: low privilege (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 8.8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach the maintenance handler, which was not tested; Scope Changed (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 9.1 and is rejected because an unproven boundary crossing may not raise a published score; high attack complexity (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 6.6 and is rejected because the control run isolates a wrong product string as the sole cause of refusal. Two of those rejected readings score higher than the number published, and the advisory says so itself. Two further readings are labelled conditionals and neither is the headline. An unauthenticated HTTP layer (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) would compute to 9.8 and was NOT demonstrated; it is a structural inference that applies only if the management listener does not gate the handler, and the binary that would answer that question is not in the package analysed. The supporting observation about the package is narrower and is weaker than that reading: none of the 57 shipped CGIs imports crypt, none parses or sets a session cookie and no login CGI exists in the directory, so the handler layer adds no authentication of its own, which says nothing about what the web server does before it forks a CGI. A factory credential still in place on a deployed unit would remove the need to discover any secret, but it was not demonstrated either, no authentication was performed against any appliance and no first-login behaviour was tested; under CVSS the metric prices the privilege level of the account used rather than whether its secret was public, so that reading leaves the vector unchanged at 7.2 and is published as a deployment amplifier for operators to assess. The factory password hash is deliberately not reproduced in this submission or in the advisory. No version-range claim is made: only the system upgrade package RLX-IFH24E_v2244.pkg was analysed, no other build of this model, no other version of the OEM IPx21 platform and no other product of either company is claimed as affected, although the upgrade path is a shared platform component rather than a per-product script, so a wider population of devices built on the same OEM platform plausibly shares the root cause, and that is stated as a likelihood rather than scored. Adjacent structural observations recorded in the analysis and deliberately excluded from this finding are a startup configuration that symlink-exposes /etc/MHX_CONFIG, /var/log/messages and /etc/system.debug into the web document root as configuration, syslog and debug views; a legacy debug CGI named request.cgi whose first-argument dispatch includes sending AT commands to the radio module, which was never executed and to which no AT command was sent; and SNMP community strings public and private shipped on the platform, which belong to the configuration plane. Public records were searched by product designation, by the RLX-IH name, by the OEM platform name and by the vendor name with no result describing this appliance and this root cause; the one record associated with the vendor's RadioLinx engineering-software line concerns a pseudo-random number generator in that software family, a different product and a different defect class, and records naming the platform manufacturer's own product families concern different platforms and different chains. Proof of concept, published unconditionally. The shipped script is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target: the target address, port, scheme, credentials, command, lock name, product name, uploaded filename, marker token and output path are all command-line arguments and default to inert values, the default target being loopback and the default payload command being true. It builds a gzip-compressed tar containing the file and lockfile metadata the installer reads, the pre and post scripts at mode 0755 and extract/upgradepkg.tar, and can either write that package to disk for inspection or carry it in a multipart/form-data POST under the part name file1. Title: AI Is Calling In Every Risk You've Accepted: Seven Insights From The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered
Context: The AISS first launched in San Francisco last year (2025) and completely sold out
Full Text:
On October 14th, the afternoon before the AI Security Summit (AISS) flagship event in San Francisco, Snyk hosted The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered. Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa moderated four people who see AI security from very different seats:

Manoj Nair, CTO and Chief Innovation Officer, Snyk

Michael D'Angelo, Technical Lead, Cyber, OpenAI

John Hultquist, Chief Analyst, Google Threat Intelligence Group

Ed Sim, Founder and General Partner, boldstart ventures

While they may have disagreed on how to regulate AI, how to supervise agents, and how far to trust them, on the core diagnosis, they lined up pretty well: AI has made attacks cheap, fast, and available to almost anyone, which calls in every risk an organization has ever accepted. Finding vulnerabilities gets easier every month, but being able to fix them is theactual constraint. Defenders won't close that gap until machines do most of the fixing, inside real identity, permission, and intent controls.

Where did this panel sit in AISS 2026?

The AISS first launched in San Francisco last year (2025) and completely sold out. This year's flagship event ran October 15th, and was just as packed as last year’s.

As the event’s tagline says, it was one full day, in one room, with one track, for the people who own AI risk at the org level, which will be followed up by “satellite”, regional editions in Copenhagen and Sydney on November 25th. AISS is a Snyk and AI Engineer initiative, and its main house rules are that no one resorts to platitudes and that it’ll host no panels where everyone just agrees. Hence, why the disagreement mentioned above is so important. We learned, anyway, that there’s more that binds us together than stuff that separates us.

This panel was the curtain-raiser for the event, held the afternoon before, and hosted by Snyk. Its main promise was to discuss four main issues: the threat now, the threat to come, who owns it, and what to do come Monday morning. The event itself went deep in each session. The panel took the wide shot, with a frontier lab, a threat intelligence team, an investor, and a security company that works where code and agents get created.

From the lively and deep conversation, seven insights stood out:

1. Why is AI a margin call on the risk you already carry?

Most of the risk AI exploits were already on the books, but what changed was the price of cashing it in.

Manoj borrowed his framing from a Snyk customer: "AI is something that attackers are using. AI is a new attack surface, and it's also an insider." Then he named the consequence.

"It's all of your existing risks. It's the margin call on that."

Manoj Nair, Snyk

John Hultquist then laid out the mechanics: attackers have used autonomous technology for about eight years, moving from fake images and spear-phishing emails to deepfake calls to whole operations. North Korean IT workers now run their operations on models from start to finish. Models also make attackers better at the work itself: troubleshooting mid-attack, moving through a network faster, and turning a fresh patch into a working exploit before most defenders have applied it. And it scales, too: "The tools are just now available to so many more people."

Ed Sim pointed to the South Korean bank breaches. CrowdStrike believes the operator was likely one China-based 26-year-old using an open-source AI penetration testing agent as well as a commercial coding agent, and at least nine banks have been reported as targets. The case,CrowdStrike's Adam Meyers told reporters, "allows one human to target many customers in a very short period of time using the power of AI." Ed's conclusion? "You can't fight hackers that are all over the world who have machines with humans."

Hultquist named the asymmetry underneath, with attackers experimenting at very low cost. If he tried a new way to rob a bank and it failed, "chances are I would be in jail or worse." Online, "they don't face the same consequences."

2. What makes AI agents a different kind of attack surface?

This new attack surface acts on its own: agents, the skills they load, and the access they garner and accumulate.

Development has indeed (or finally?) become a software factory where agents write the code and reach for whatever they need, and everything they reach for ends up becoming an attack surface. Agent skills are the sharpest case there, because they're written in plain English and, as Manoj put it, "three lines of English can become malware." Snyk's ToxicSkills research found at least one security flaw in 36.82% of the 3,984 skills it scanned, plus 76 confirmed malicious payloads. Publishing one on ClawHub took but a Markdown file and a week-old GitHub account.

Hultquist added the attacker's view. Threat actors have mostly preferred using autonomous systems rather than attacking them, with one exception: when people handed personal agents access to everything in their lives, attackers "honed in at that moment because they recognized all the sort of aggregating opportunity." Deployed systems are next, and attackers haven't moved on them en masse, "but they will," and defending them will take "an entirely new security regime."

The Hugging Face incident showed the view from the inside. In July, OpenAI models in an internal cybersecurity evaluation got around the controls meant to isolate them and breached Hugging Face. OpenAI's own report calls it a "warning shot." Michael D'Angelo put the cause in two sentences: "Go do this task, and you will be rewarded. So they went and did the task."

Manoj went to the unglamorous root of "secrets sitting in the open that a 14-year-old with a few tools without AI can attack," and the report bears out his starting point: an agent found publicly exposed Hugging Face credentials and shared them with the other agents.

Ed Sim's answer is to govern agents like the insiders they are, each with its own identity, an audit trail, and access granted for the job that disappears when the job is done. The unsolved part is intent:

"If my goal is to reduce the cost of my compute, what happens along the way if I decide to kill a couple production databases because Ifigured out that was a good way to reduce compute costs? Well, I did my job, didn't I?"

Ed Sim, boldstart ventures

And as AI moves into chips, devices, and robots, Ed asked, "Who's going to secure the firmware, the chip stuff, the whole embedded intelligence?"

3. Why did fixing become the bottleneck?

Finding vulnerabilities keeps getting cheaper, and fixing them hasn't kept up in terms of speed. A frontier lab, a threat intelligence team, and Snyk see the same gap, but from different sides.

Michael traced finding through one revolution after another, from fuzzers to dynamic testing to agent harnesses. The hard part comes after, and it's often "a political problem": teams find more than they can route, and the result is patch ping pong, a Slack thread about "who does what, when, how," where "if it breaks, it's you."

Hultquist learned it at Google with Big Sleep, a vulnerability-finding project built around an AI harness, which drew fire on social media for handing bugs to people who maintain open source on their weekends. "It's not enough to just find this stuff," he said. Hand a company a zero-day that an attacker is already using, and the answer is often "it's going to be a while." Finding and fixing are two sides of the same coin, he said, and “if you don’t do both sides, you can’t keep up.”

Manoj pointed to Project Glasswing, where Anthropic's own update says progress on software security "used to be limited by how quickly we could find new vulnerabilities. Now it's limited by how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch the large numbers of vulnerabilities found by AI."

It names human capacity to triage and patch as the bottleneck. As of May 22, early in the 90-day disclosure window, open source maintainers had patched 75 of the 530 high or critical-severity bugs Anthropic had reported.

The measure that matters, Manoj said, is "fixes that make it to production." Snyk's VulnBump research, published yesterday as well, on October 15th, starts from the same gap: over six months in 2026, Snyk Open Source recorded 459 million vulnerability findings across about 300,000 organizations, and while 94% had a known fixed version, only about 10% had been resolved. The benchmark counts a fix only if the vulnerability is gone and the project still installs, builds, and passes its tests. (Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent cleared that bar on 90.2% of 307 real dependency upgrades.)

His bigger point was where to break the loop. "The whole game has changed to the point of creation," where "agents are the actors," and developers supply the intent. Prevent there and remediate with that context, or stay in "this dead loop of find, fix, find, fix."

4. Does prioritization still work when AI can chain the long tail?

Prioritization is a workaround for human bandwidth, and AI is learning to exploit it.

The piece of standard advice Manoj disagrees with is contextual prioritization: reading signals to pick the 10 issues worth fixing out of 100 is how the industry works, but that only exists to fit the work to the people available. An autonomous attacker keeps no such budget.

"We should be looking at all 100. Get to the point where you can fix everything. Because those 10 things are going to become 100 things before you know it."

Manoj Nair, Snyk

The long tail matters because AI chains it: AI reasons across steps, Manoj said, so it can chain five or six vulnerabilities from the 99th percentile of your list, the ones "you said you would never get to because you don't have enough humans to patch it," into one severe incident. In the essay Michael cited, Greg Brockman describes the Hugging Face breach the same way: an agentic collective "chaining together vulnerabilities ranging from previously-unknown security flaws to using credentials to user accounts that had been leaked onto the internet."

The other half of Manoj's argument is cultural. For his whole career, the trade-off has run one way: operational risk is unacceptable, so security waits. In a room with hundreds of CISOs the week before, he heard it start to flip, toward leaders willing to take an application down briefly to remove a security risk. "Hey, something might be offline for a little bit, but it'll come back. That's better than super safely fixing this and taking a year."

5. What does machine-speed defense look like, and where do humans fit?

Defense has to move at the same speed as the attack, which means agents do most of the work and people do the judging.

Hultquist separated two kinds of attackers. There are your espionage crews that stay "low and slow," living off the land for years. And on the other hand, you have your criminals running extortion, so speed is of the essence: "There's a race between you and me for me to get whatever I need to extort you before you can stop me."

"The average SOC with a human in the loop is not going to be able to keep up with that. The SOC is going to have to take actions on its own, or you're just going to get a call."

John Hultquist, Google Threat Intelligence Group

Ed Sim wants defenders to build "a software defense factory the way that coders build coding factories," and most haven't started: for all the talk of autonomous defense, "99% of the companies don't do it at all." OpenAI is further along, as it says almost all of its initial security alerts are already triaged by AI before a human is looped in. "We don't have the 5 years that we thought we had. We have like 5 days," Ed said. CISOs don't want to give agents authority, "but they're going to have to at some point in time." Hultquist expects incidents to force the issue: "the money doesn't flow until there's a wake-up call in a lot of cases."

People should stay in the loop where it really counts. Manoj framed their job as intent, experience, and judgment call. His one thing is the ratio of issues found to issues fixed: "If that ratio is not fixed, all this other is moot conversation." The bottleneck is the process, because a human has to approve every pull request. You should automate the safe approvals and let people decide the exceptions. Then take the initiative back: "When an autonomous attacker is going to attack you, why don't you attack yourself?"

Michael D'Angelo put a clock on the opportunity. Open models trail the frontier "by a few months", a gap Greg Brockman calls the defender's window: use frontier intelligence now to scan your assets and patch what it finds before someone with a comparable model, "in, say, their bedroom," gets there first. That's the one move every single CISO should make before a frontier-class open model ships.

6. How do you supervise a system that never behaves the same way twice?

This is still an open question, and here’s where the panel's answers split.

Michael’s starting point: “How do you secure a non-deterministic system? Usually, there’s 2 ways: one, you control what it has access to; the other way is generally you use another non-deterministic system.” He took the pattern from his military background:

“When you give 18-year-olds access to extremely dangerous things, the way you do that is, one, you only give certain people certain accesses. And the other thing is you put a sergeant near them. Make sure that they’re doing what they’re supposed to do.”

Michael D’Angelo, OpenAI

He expects fleets of models, with very cheap ones overseeing the rest.

Ed Sim put a deterministic layer in the picture. "It's going to take a village", he said: frontier intelligence for the first scan, then systems built on years of data about real vulnerabilities and how people patch them, because "you need some determinism."The open-versus-closed question, which Manoj said has reached CIOs in the last few months, gets the same use-case logic: hosting a model somewhere you control is "one layer, but that's not sufficient because what is the behavior by use case?" Some open models are well aligned and still leak personal information badly, so "don't use it for that use case." Nor would he "just assume that frontier is secure."

7. Who is accountable when an agent does damage?

Accountability is being decided in practice while the policy debate keeps running in the background.

Ed Sim framed the question nobody has answered yet: "Is it the model provider? Is it the enterprise that deploys an agent that goes and attacks someone else's place?" OpenAI tests its own releases with internal teams and external testers documented in system cards, and Michael was candid that the field is "still figuring it out."

The panel split on who should settle it. Ed favors self-regulation, warning that rules sized for the largest companies would choke the next “$100 billion company,” and that if we “regulate ourselves to death,” China pulls ahead. Deirdre pushed back:

“When people make this China argument, though, you actually look at China, they are regulating AI in ways that are much more substantial than even America is.”

Deirdre Bosa, Yahoo Finance

She also asked whether self-regulation by the biggest companies invites regulatory capture. Manoj's answer was layered and urgent: "We don't have the luxury of time." Standards first, then visibility, self-regulation, and broader regulation that requires responsibility and disclosure, arriving "much more rapidly than in the past." His sharper point was about attention: "We spend a lot of time fixated on the labs," while agents spread through every enterprise as "very capable agents or potential insiders."

Banks are already acting. Ed pointed to JPMorgan Chase's earnings call that week, where the bank said that, to the extent it can, it is blocking services that rely on customers sharing their banking credentials. CFO Jeremy Barnum's warning, as reported by American Banker: "if they give up their credentials to the agent, and the agent does something that they don't want, that's going to be on them."

What should security leaders do on Monday morning?

The actions that came out of the hour, in the order we'd take them:

Use the defender's window. Point frontier models at your own code, infrastructure and backlog now, before open models with the same capability reach attackers (Michael D'Angelo).

Attack yourself first. An autonomous attacker is coming, anyway (Manoj Nair).

Fix the found-to-fixed ratio. Automate the safe fixes and keep people on the exceptions and judgment calls (Manoj Nair).

Let the SOC act on its own. A human in every loop can't keep up with an extortion crew (John Hultquist).

Give every agent an identity. It should have its own credentials, an audit trail, and access scoped to the job that expires when the job ends (Ed Sim). Start by auditing what your agents can already do.

Turn on strong multi-factor authentication everywhere (Manoj Nair).

Ask the board question out loud. “Why can't we fix everything?” If the answer is that uptime always wins, that's a trade-off that needs revisiting.

So, who pays the margin call?

For a panel built to disagree, the agreement ended up being the headline. A frontier lab, a threat intelligence team, an investor, and Snyk all landed in the same place: the risk you accepted when attacks were slow and expensive is now due, and attackers are the ones collecting.

The way out is the somewhat unglamorous one: fix at the speed you find, let machines do most of the fixing, keep people on the calls that need judgment, and give every agent an identity and a leash before it gets the keys.

Ed Sim’s bet for the next year is on the defenders, precisely because they’re “not using it enough” yet. That’s the optimistic read, and also the uncomfortable one: the gap is ours to close, and the clock started before the panel did.

The next morning, Manoj gave the flagship’s first keynote: The AI Hurricane Is Here: Build for the Storm. The panel had already made the case for the second half of that title.

Want to know what your own agents can reach? Download the 2026 State of Agentic AI Adoption, Volume III for Snyk’s analysis of model risk across thousands of enterprise environments.
