Executive Summary

Cyble has continued tracking GhostBat RAT activity targeting Android users in India since its initial identification in October 2025. Recent investigations into malicious mParivahan and eChallan-themed applications revealed a broader operator-controlled ecosystem that we track as GhostX.

Analysis of the exposed GhostX backend identified administrative and user-management structures, device-control records, SMS-delivery instructions, call-forwarding activity, and continuously changing phishing content, indicating active campaign management.

Impressions

The latest GhostBat RAT variant represents a significant evolution in both delivery and post-compromise capabilities. The malware now abuses the Android Accessibility Service to support Ghost Overlay and broader PIN/key-input capture targeting financial applications used across India.

Ghost Overlay transparently intercepts PIN keypad interactions in Google Pay and MobiKwik. It replays the same touches into the legitimate application, allowing the malware to capture PIN information without presenting a conventional phishing interface. The variant also targets 60 banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and payment applications for broader PIN capture.

Modus Operandi

GhostBat RAT has diversified its loader architecture, with at least six observed delivery mechanisms, while the latest build uses libnetbridge.so and multiple cryptographic and custom container stages. Firebase Remote Config further enables operators to dynamically modify C&C infrastructure and malware functionality after installation.

Figure 1 – GhostBat RAT Infection Chain

Key Takeaways

GhostBat RAT continues to target Android users in India via mParivahan- and eChallan-themed smishing campaigns, using phishing pages and public hosting platforms to distribute malicious APKs.

Our investigation uncovered GhostX, a broader operator-controlled ecosystem that supports phishing, device management, backend configuration, and the distribution of the GhostBat RAT.

The latest GhostBat RAT variant abuses the Android Accessibility Service, including the Ghost Overlay technique to intercept PIN entry in legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik applications.

The malware also implements broader PIN/key-input capture targeting 60 Android applications associated with India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem.

GhostBat RAT’s delivery layer has evolved through multiple loader and dropper implementations, with the latest libnetbridge.so loader employing several transformations, including encryption, compression, and custom container stages, before recovering the final payload.

Firebase Remote Config enables dynamic C&C and feature management, allowing operators to modify backend infrastructure and selected malware capabilities without rebuilding or redistributing the APK.

Overview

In October 2025, Cyble identified GhostBat RAT being distributed through MiningDropper and targeting Android users in India.

We have since continued to track related activity and investigate malicious applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan services. This research uncovered a broader Android threat ecosystem that we track as GhostX, along with significantly evolved variants of GhostBat RAT.

The most recent GhostBat RAT variant demonstrates a notable increase in capability and operational flexibility. It uses Firebase Remote Config to dynamically manage command-and-control (C&C) infrastructure and to enable or disable individual malware modules without requiring APK redistribution.

This variant also implements a sophisticated Ghost Overlay technique targeting legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik PIN-entry interfaces. Instead of displaying a conventional fake login page, the malware places transparent accessibility overlays over the legitimate application’s keypad, records the victim’s touch selections, and replays the same interaction into the genuine application.

Additionally, the malware implements a PIN-capture capability through keylogging, targeting 60 Android applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital payment ecosystem.

The malware’s delivery and packing mechanisms have evolved considerably across the samples analyzed. We identified at least six distinct loader or dropper implementations, including:

Native AES-CBC-protected APK containers

Custom SPKZ/SPK1 payload formats

Java-based in-memory DEX loaders

Remote APK downloaders

Multi-stage XOR/AES loaders

A newer native libnetbridge.so loader using multiple cryptographic, transformation, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final payload

This diversification suggests continued investment in defeating static detection and complicating automated malware extraction.

GhostBat RAT is primarily distributed via smishing messages that contain malicious links. When victims follow these links, they are redirected to phishing pages that impersonate either the legitimate Parivahan service or a Google Play-style application download page and are encouraged to install a fraudulent mParivahan APK (see Figures 2 and 3).

During our investigation, we also repeatedly observed GitHub repositories and GitHub-hosted assets being used to distribute malicious APKs, providing attackers with readily available public hosting infrastructure.

Figure 2 – Fake Google Play Store-style mParivahan installation website

Figure 3 – Fake mParivahan website prompting to download APK file

Discovery of the GhostX Ecosystem

The GhostX investigation began with the discovery of multiple Android applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan ecosystem.

Samples were collected from phishing infrastructure and public GitHub repositories containing APKs named or presented as mParivahan, vehicle-challan, traffic-enforcement, or other related government applications.

Initial static analysis revealed that many of these APKs were only first-stage loaders. Their visible DEX code offered limited functionality, while the actual malware payload was either concealed within encrypted assets or retrieved later.

After unpacking the applications to their final payloads, we identified multiple custom C&C infrastructures, Firebase projects, and overlapping Android surveillance and financial-fraud capabilities.

A major breakthrough came from the analysis of a NextGen mParivahan sample whose unpacked payload contained the Firebase project identifier:

ghostx-panel

The exposed Firebase backend provided significantly greater visibility into the operator’s infrastructure and control workflow. The database contained structures including:

clients

bot_users

admins

admin_logins

settings

All_Users

Verify_Device

Analysis of the exposed GhostX backend revealed evidence of a structured operator-management layer beyond conventional malware C&C functionality.

The database contained administrator and user records with role and account-status fields, a global session identifier, bot-user mappings, and dedicated admin_logins records containing device fingerprints, timestamps, and online status (see Figure 4).

These artifacts indicate that GhostX incorporates an authentication and session management framework for operator-side access and management of compromised devices.

The presence of distinct user, administrator, and bot-user roles suggests a multi-operator, service-oriented architecture. It raises the possibility that GhostX could support a Malware-as-a-Service-style operating model.

Figure 4 – Exposed administrative records.

During continued monitoring of the exposed infrastructure, we observed that SMS lure content, phishing URLs, vehicle registration numbers, and recipient phone numbers were repeatedly changing, indicating active operator-side campaign management rather than a static or abandoned database (see Figure 5).

Similar eChallan-themed messages were also observed being received by users in the wild, further supporting the campaign's operational nature (see Figure 6).

Figure 5 – Exposed SMS message configured to be sent to victims

Figure 6 – Same SMSs are being received by the victims (Source – Twitter Post)

One of the phishing URLs exposed through the GhostX infrastructure subsequently led us to a previously unseen GhostBat RAT variant, providing a direct investigative link among the backend control ecosystem, active phishing operations, and the malware's continued evolution.

These findings led us to assess that GhostX is not a single Android malware family or standalone application. Instead, GhostX represents a broader operator-controlled ecosystem encompassing phishing infrastructure, backend services, Firebase-based configuration and command mechanisms, device-management functionality, and malware distribution.

GhostBat RAT represents the Android implant operating within this ecosystem, with individual variants continuing to evolve across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities.

Technical Analysis

Evolution of Droppers and Loaders

GhostBat RAT has undergone continuous changes in its delivery and payload-protection mechanisms.

Across the samples analyzed during the GhostX investigation, we identified multiple loader and dropper implementations designed to conceal the underlying malware payload, complicate static analysis, and reduce the effectiveness of hash- and signature-based detection.

Although the recovered payloads demonstrate overlapping capabilities for surveillance, financial theft, and device control, the mechanisms used to deliver and recover them vary considerably across samples.

Earlier variants relied on comparatively straightforward native loaders that decrypted embedded APK payloads using AES-CBC. Subsequent variants of Ghostbat RAT introduced XOR-encrypted custom containers, SPKZ/SPK1 packaging, split-APK delivery, dynamically loaded DEX components, and Java-based in-memory loaders.

One variant moved away from embedded payload delivery entirely. It operated as a remote downloader, retrieving a second-stage APK from remote infrastructure, validating its SHA-256 hash, and installing it through Android's package installation framework.

The most recent variant analyzed introduces a substantially more complex native loader implemented in libnetbridge.so. This loader combines multiple transformations, encryption, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final GhostBat RAT payload.

This diversification indicates continued modification of the delivery layer while broadly retaining the malware's post-compromise objectives. Consequently, detections that focus only on the outer APK, the encrypted asset name, or a single unpacking routine are unlikely to provide durable coverage.

The GhostBat RAT loaders/droppers variants we observed are listed below:

Figure 7 – GhostBat RAT Loader variants

The most recent GhostBat RAT sample introduced a significantly more complex native unpacking mechanism.

Unlike earlier variants that relied primarily on Java-based loaders or comparatively straightforward XOR/AES routines, this variant stores the encrypted payload inside an opaque application asset, assets/isti52q4, while most of the unpacking logic is implemented in the native library libnetbridge.so.

The visible application code does not directly expose the final malicious functionality. Instead, execution transitions to the native loader, which processes the embedded asset through several sequential stages of transformation and decryption (see Figure 8).

Figure 8 – Latest native dropper unpacking chain

The first stage processes content within the encrypted asset file and derives values required for subsequent decoding. The resulting data is then passed through an RC4-like transformation before being processed through AES-256-GCM. This layered approach prevents the encrypted asset from being recovered using simple XOR or direct AES key extraction techniques that worked against earlier GhostBat RAT loaders.

Following successful decryption, the loader recovers an MSZ1-formatted intermediate object that is decompressed using zlib. The decompressed data contains an MSP1 container that packages the final Android application components.

The recovered payload consists of a split-APK application, including base.apk and split_config.dex.apk.

The executable malware code is primarily contained within the recovered split configuration DEX.

Unlike earlier samples, where the encrypted payload could be identified directly from ZIP headers or standard APK structures, the latest loader hides the final application behind several custom transformations before any recognizable Android package becomes available.

This significantly increases the effort required for automated unpacking and reduces the effectiveness of simple asset-scanning techniques.

Advanced GhostBat RAT Payload

GhostBat RAT has evolved from an Android SMS and information stealer into a modular remote-access and Banking Trojan.

Across the analyzed variants, the malware demonstrates capabilities for device profiling, SMS interception, remote SMS transmission, call-forwarding manipulation, payment-data theft, accessibility-based PIN capture, Firebase-driven command delivery, dynamic C&C configuration, and remote tunnelling.

In the new GhostBat RAT variant, we observed the introduction of Android Accessibility Service abuse, a technique commonly associated with modern Android Banking Trojans.

Earlier GhostBat RAT variants that we analyzed did not possess these capabilities during this investigation. The new variant uses Accessibility Service to monitor foreground applications, identify PIN-entry contexts, interact with application interfaces, and support two distinct credential-theft mechanisms: Ghost Overlay and targeted PIN/key-input capture.

Once Accessibility Services access is granted, the malware monitors the foreground application and compares it against configured target lists. These targets can be managed through Firebase Remote Config, allowing operators to selectively activate credential-capture functionality when a targeted banking, UPI, wallet, or payment application is in use.

Ghost Overlay

The most notable capability introduced in this variant is the Ghost Overlay technique.

Figure 9.1 – Ghost Overlay Attack Flow

Unlike conventional Android overlay attacks that display a fake login or payment page over the legitimate application, GhostBat RAT does not need to replace the victim's banking interface. Instead, it places transparent accessibility overlay regions directly over the real PIN keypad displayed by the targeted application.

The feature is controlled through Firebase Remote Config using:

ghost_overlay_enabled

ghost_overlay_packages

Figure 9.2 – Ghost overlay initialization activity

The default Ghost Overlay configuration targets the following Android packages:

com.mobikwik_new

com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa

com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa.user

Figure 10 – Target package list of Ghost Overlay activity

When the malware detects one of these applications in the foreground and identifies a PIN-related activity, it creates a transparent keypad grid using Android’s TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY. The overlay contains 12 touch regions matching the layout of a typical numeric PIN pad (see Figures 11 and 12):

Figure 11 – Ghost PIN pad structure

Figure 12 – Ghost overlay activity

When the victim taps a digit on the legitimate Google Pay or MobiKwik PIN keypad, the transparent Ghost Overlay intercepts the touch event before it reaches the underlying application.

The malware maps the touch coordinates to the corresponding keypad value and appends the resulting digit to an internal buffer used to reconstruct the PIN.

To avoid interrupting the payment flow or alerting the victim, GhostBat RAT temporarily releases the affected overlay region and uses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to reproduce the same tap at the corresponding screen coordinates (see Figure 13).

As a result, the legitimate application receives the expected input and continues operating normally, while the malware records the victim's PIN in parallel.

The same mechanism handles DEL and OK interactions, allowing the GhostBat RAT to update the captured digit sequence and detect when the PIN entry process has completed. This intercept-and-replay behavior enables the malware to observe PIN entry without presenting a fake Google Pay or MobiKwik interface.

Figure 13 – dispatchGesture activity

Once collected, the PIN is stored with metadata identifying the capture source as ghost_overlay and is subsequently queued for exfiltration over C&C “hxxps://api.cloudsettle[.]org/pin-data” (see Figure 14).

Figure 14 – Storing captured Ghost PIN

This technique is considerably stealthier than a conventional phishing overlay because the victim remains within the genuine financial application's interface throughout the interaction. GhostBat RAT effectively operates as an invisible intermediary, intercepting the victim's keypad interaction, recording the selected digits, and replaying those same touches into the legitimate application in near real time.

Targeted Keylogging and PIN Capture

In addition to the Ghost Overlay capability, the new GhostBat RAT variant implements a broader accessibility-based PIN/key-input capture mechanism targeting applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem.

Unlike the Ghost Overlay feature, which is specifically designed to intercept keypad touches in Google Pay and MobiKwik via transparent overlay regions, this functionality relies on Android Accessibility Service events to monitor user interactions across a much larger set of targeted applications.

The default pin_target_packages configuration includes 60 Android package identifiers for financial applications used across India (see Figure 15).

The target set includes applications associated with Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, MobiKwik, BHIM, SBI UPI, Axis Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Freecharge, PayZapp, Groww, Navi, Jupiter, OneCard, JioFinance, Samsung Pay, and several other banking and payment services. The complete list of targeted Android packages is provided in the Targeted Application List section.

Once Accessibility Service is granted, GhostBat RAT monitors foreground activity and determines whether the currently running application(s) match an entry in pin_target_packages. The malware then evaluates the surrounding application and screen context before treating observed numeric input as potentially sensitive PIN information.

Figure 15 – PIN target package list

The malware also uses configurable PIN-length boundaries, pin_min_digits, and pin_min_digits to determine whether the reconstructed numeric sequence is consistent with an expected PIN.

Unlike Ghost Overlay, the broader keylogging mechanism does not rely on a transparent keypad overlay. Instead, GhostBat RAT uses Accessibility Service events and UI context to identify and reconstruct PIN-like input across a wider set of targeted financial applications, giving the malware substantially broader coverage within India’s banking and digital payment ecosystem.

The analyzed variant contains a dedicated worker responsible for handling captured PIN information, “PinUploadWorker”. Captured PINS are locally queued before being transmitted to the endpoint “/pin-data”.

Figure 16 – Captured PIN upload activity

The introduction of this capability substantially expands the financial targeting of GhostBat RAT. Earlier variants primarily relied on SMS interception, OTP theft, phishing interfaces, and call-forwarding manipulation.

The new variant can also monitor user interactions within legitimate financial applications and capture PIN-like input via Accessibility Service abuse.

Command and Control Infrastructure

The latest GhostBat RAT variant uses a multi-channel command-and-control architecture that combines a conventional HTTPS backend with Firebase services and a configurable WebSocket tunnel.

Compared with earlier variants, which relied more heavily on hardcoded infrastructure, the new implementation provides greater operational flexibility by allowing the attacker to modify backend addresses and enable or disable selected malware capabilities remotely.

In the analyzed sample, the default C&C infrastructure was configured as hxxps://api[.]cloudsettle[.]org. The malware communicates with this backend via multiple REST API endpoints that handle device registration, SMS collection, call log collection, command acknowledgement, PIN data submission, service state reporting, and other post-compromise functionality.

Uploads batches of SMS messages collected from the infected device

Sends newly received SMS messages to the C&C in near real time

One of the major changes in the latest GhostBat RAT variant is the use of Firebase Remote Config as an additional control layer. The analyzed payload is associated with the Firebase project andromeda-d389d and retrieves remotely managed configuration values that control both infrastructure and malware functionality.

Of particular interest is the base_url parameter, which allows the operator to replace the active REST backend without modifying or redistributing the APK. Therefore, api.cloudsettle.org represents the observed/default backend for this sample rather than a permanently fixed C&C address.

Figure 17 – Dynamic C&C implementation

A similar dynamic C&C approach was observed during the GhostX investigation. An earlier NextGen mParivahan sample associated with the ghostx-panel Firebase project retrieved its backend configuration from Firestore using the app_config/network document and the baseUrl field.

In addition to the newly introduced Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, targeted PIN capture, and dynamically configurable C&C functionality, GhostBat RAT continues to exhibit several core behaviors documented in our earlier research.

These include collecting SMS messages from compromised devices, monitoring newly received messages for banking- and OTP-related content, stealing UPI credentials through fraudulent mParivahan payment interfaces, and registering compromised devices with attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Earlier GhostBat RAT variants also used Telegram bots for device registration and operator notification, while selected dropper chains contained cryptocurrency-mining functionality alongside the information-stealing payload.

These previously documented capabilities remain important to the overall GhostBat RAT operation; however, the latest variants significantly expand the malware's financial-theft and remote-control functionality.

Rather than repeating the earlier functionality in detail, this analysis focuses on newly observed capabilities and architectural changes, particularly Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay PIN interception, broader targeting of financial applications, dynamic Firebase-based configuration, and evolving loader and C2 mechanisms.

Conclusion

The latest GhostBat RAT activity highlights continued evolution across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities. The investigation into mParivahan- and eChallan-themed malware exposed the broader GhostX ecosystem, linking phishing infrastructure, backend control, and evolving GhostBat RAT payloads.

The introduction of Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, broader PIN capture, and Firebase-driven dynamic configuration significantly expands the malware’s financial-theft capabilities while making the operation more adaptable. Combined with continuously evolving loaders and active phishing activity, GhostBat RAT remains a threat to Android users, particularly across India’s banking, UPI, and digital payment ecosystem.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

CRIL’s analysis of this campaign has been selected for the upcoming Association of Anti-Virus Asia Researchers (AVAR) conference, where these findings will be showcased.

Our Recommendations

We have listed essential cybersecurity best practices that form the first line of defense against attackers. We recommend that our readers follow the best practices given below:

Install Apps Only from Trusted Sources:Download apps exclusively from official platforms like the Google Play Store. Avoid third-party app stores or links received via SMS, social media, or email.

Be Cautious with Permissions and Installs:Never grant permissions and install an application unless you're certain of an app's legitimacy.

Watch for Phishing Pages:Always verify the URL and avoid suspicious links and websites that ask for sensitive information.

Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):Use MFA for banking and financial apps to add an extra layer of protection, even if credentials are compromised.

Report Suspicious Activity:If you suspect you've been targeted or infected, report the incident to your bank and local authorities immediately. If necessary, reset your credentials and perform a factory reset.

Use Mobile Security Solutions:Install a mobile security application that includes real-time scanning.

Keep Your Device Updated: Ensure your Android OS and apps are updated regularly. Security patches often address vulnerabilities that malware exploits.

Full Text:
The UK’s data protection regulator has issued a reprimand and enforcement notice to the capital’s police force after a string of governance failings related to its use of a third-party platform.

The investigation by the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) was focused on Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) use of the Auror retail crime intelligence-sharing platform, which it used in a crackdown on shoplifting.

The watchdog found that, between March 2023 and September 2024, MPS officers and staff used the platform despite it not being formally approved. Some 500 MPS accounts were created, of which 375 were active, it said in its writeup of the case.

Auror provides high-level summaries of incidents, case management, data visualisation and reporting, and a “Connect the Dots” module, which uses image matching and manual suggestions to identify links between events and individuals. It has been lauded as quadrupling the number of shoplifters brought to justice in London.

However, the ICO said that between January and September 2024 personal information including names, dates of birth and home addresses relating to 179 people – three of whom were under 18 – was uploaded to the unvetted platform.

Read more on MPS privacy woes: ICO Reprimands Metropolitan Police for Data Snafu

Two “security incident reports” were raised internally at the time. In the first, an officer uploaded the full names of suspects they recognized in CCTV images shared by a retailer. In the second, officers were flagged as using the platform to collect CCTV images from retailers despite Auror not having been approved by the MPS cybersecurity team.

The ICO found four infringements. It said the MPS:

Unlawfully processed personal information without the individual’s consent and where sharing wasn’t necessary for law enforcement purposes

Failed to implement “appropriate technical and organizational measures” to protect personal information and follow proper assessment and approval processes for third-party technologies

Failed to complete a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before undertaking high-risk processing

Continues to fail to implement appropriate measures to ensure only approved third-party technologies are used to process personal information

David Doodson, ICO head of investigations, said police forces must have robust safeguards in place to protect the large volumes of sensitive personal information they handle.

“Organizations cannot allow innovation to outpace their data protection responsibilities. Before introducing new systems or platforms, they must properly assess the risks, put appropriate safeguards in place and ensure effective oversight,” he added.

“This action should send a message across the policing sector, and beyond: if you are using new technology to process people's information you must do so lawfully, transparently and with appropriate governance from the outset.”

Title: Who’s Watching AI? The Visibility Gap Security Teams Need to Close
Context: 8% of IT and cybersecurity professionals have only partial visibility into employee AI use
Full Text:
AI adoption isn't waiting for security teams.

Employees are experimenting with new tools. Business leaders are pushing teams to use AI to work faster. Applications are adding AI functionality. AI agents are accessing files, connecting to tools, and taking action as if they were employees.

This has tremendous potential.

But there's also a fundamental cybersecurity problem: Do you know what AI is doing inside your organization, or is it a growing blind spot?

That's the question at the center of a new episode of Cybercrime: From the Frontline, Who’s Watching AI? Managing Innovation Without Losing Control.

Watch or listen to the full conversation to hear Bitdefender experts explore how organizations can embrace AI innovation while managing its risks.

How Many Organizations Lack Full AI Visibility?

The 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment reveals that 44.8% of IT and cybersecurity professionals have only partial visibility into employee AI use. Another roughly 3% report having no visibility at all.

The independent research surveyed 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals across six countries and shows how widespread the lack of AI visibility and control has become. And the challenge is growing because employees have powerful incentives to experiment. AI can accelerate development, automate repetitive work, analyze information, and help meet increasingly aggressive productivity expectations.

Has Shadow IT Become Shadow AI?

Shadow AI introduces similar challenges to Shadow IT, but with potentially greater consequences.

With Shadow IT, an employee installs an unauthorized application. A department adopts a cloud service without consulting IT. Someone stores corporate information in a personal file-sharing account.

With Shadow AI, an employee might use a personal AI account instead of an approved enterprise platform. Someone could paste confidential information into a free AI service. An approved application might gain new AI capabilities through an update.

In each case, sensitive information could move somewhere security teams didn't anticipate. That's particularly concerning given that data leakage into large language models ranks among the leading AI-related concerns identified in the 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment.

According to experts on the podcast episode, AI adoption often happens without IT or security oversight, making visibility an enterprise-wide responsibility.

Why Is AI Becoming an Identity Problem?

Traditional generative AI responds to requests. Agentic AI can interact with tools, access files, connect to services, write code, and take actions. During the podcast, our experts suggest thinking about these agents as non-human identities operating inside the organization.

That raises important questions:

Which agents are operating in your environment?

What data can they access?

Which tools can they use?

What actions are they permitted to take?

And what happens if an agent is manipulated?

The podcast also explores prompt injection, where malicious instructions embedded within content can influence an AI system into performing unintended actions. If an agent has access to corporate systems, the question isn't simply whether you trust the AI.

What Does AI Visibility Look Like Today?

A simple inventory isn't enough. To achieve AI visibility, organizations must be able to identify the AI services and agents operating across their environments. Security teams need context on those tools, including their capabilities, permissions, connections, potential risks, and the endpoints they affect.

They also need to distinguish sanctioned AI use from unknown or potentially dangerous activity. Without that understanding, organizations risk applying blanket restrictions that frustrate employees or overlooking exposures that genuinely threaten the business.

Visibility provides the foundation for prioritizing risk and applying appropriate controls.

What Kinds of Tools Create AI Visibility and Control?

Organizations increasingly need specialized capabilities that discover AI usage, assess exposure, and translate security policies into action. One example is Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control, which helps security teams identify more than 700 AI tools, including chatbots, coding assistants, local LLMs, agents, MCP servers, and AI-enabled applications. It creates a centralized inventory and helps prioritize findings based on risk and business context.

Importantly, GravityZone goes beyond discovery. Security teams can review and investigate findings, then use integrated controls to allow, restrict, or block AI activity. For existing GravityZone customers, these capabilities operate through the same agent and console, helping organizations manage AI exposure without adding another disconnected security tool.

How Can AI Governance Keep Pace With AI Adoption?

Technology is part of the answer, but AI governance must also become part of acceptable-use policies, employee education, procurement reviews, third-party risk assessments, and conversations between security and business leaders.

Some organizations are establishing dedicated AI steering committees. Others are incorporating AI into existing security and risk governance. The structure matters less than the outcome: security needs to participate in AI adoption decisions before deploying new tools.

Can Organizations Innovate Without Losing Control?

According to the podcast episode's experts, organizations can continue AI innovation without losing control, but only with a sound strategy. Instead of putting the brakes on AI adoption, organizations should make approved AI easier to use safely, educate employees about the risks of unsanctioned tools, use technology to track where sensitive information moves, and establish controls based on actual usage.

As AI agents become more capable, organizations must also understand and constrain agent permissions, just as they would for human identities.

Together, these measures can help make AI innovation sustainable.

Title: VulnBump: Can AI Agents Fix Vulnerable Dependencies Without Breaking the Build?
Context: What's new: to our knowledge, VulnBump is the first benchmark for AI agents built around security-driven upgrades: every task starts from real vulnerabilities that Snyk found in...
Full Text:
Can AI agents fix vulnerable dependencies without breaking the build? The fix itself is rarely the mystery. Over six months in 2026, Snyk Open Source recorded 459 million vulnerability findings across ~300,000 organizations. 94% of these vulnerabilities had a known fixed version, yet only about 10% had been resolved.

That happens because the hard part is upgrading safely: most vulnerable packages are transitively imported, about a quarter of fixes require a major version bump, and even minor and patch releases, which are supposed to be backward compatible, often contain breaking changes.

VulnBump, new research we published at Snyk, puts AI agents to the test on 307 real upgrades of vulnerable dependencies. An upgrade counts as a PASS only if the vulnerabilities are gone and the project still installs, builds, and passes its tests.

What's new: to our knowledge, VulnBump is the first benchmark for AI agents built around security-driven upgrades: every task starts from real vulnerabilities that Snyk found in a real project, across six package managers. Earlier upgrade benchmarks check only for breakage, not whether the vulnerability is gone.

So, can AI agents fix vulnerable dependencies without breaking the build? Mostly, yes, but the model alone doesn't decide it. On the same model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passed 90.2% of upgrades. Anthropic's Claude Code passed 77.5% when given Snyk's recommended upgrade and scan (Claude Code + Snyk scan), and 59.6% with no Snyk data (Claude Code unaided). That's a gap of more than 30 percentage points. For reference, the package manager bump, a baseline with no AI that only applies Snyk's recommended version, already passed 46.9%.

Key results on VulnBump

Keeping the build green wasn't the hard part: all three agents did that about 93% of the time. Removing the vulnerability was. In 70 of its 124 failures, Claude Code, unaided, said it had fixed vulnerabilities that a rescan still found.

Our findings echo VulnBench, our June benchmark of AI security review, which found that Claude and Snyk Code miss different vulnerabilities and concluded that the two work best combined. VulnBump tests a different task, upgrading vulnerable open source dependencies, and points the same way: with Snyk's recommended version and scan, Claude Code's PASS rate rose by 17.9 points. Evo Remediation Agent shows how much further a purpose-built agent can go: 12.7 points beyond Claude Code with the same Snyk scan. VulnBump also follows up on the remediation results we shared in May, now with a newer model and six package managers.

How we built VulnBump

We started from real projects, matched to production. We collected 767 candidate projects from GitHub, including popular open source projects and repositories that pin known-vulnerable packages. Each had to install, build, and pass more than 85% of its tests before any change, and Snyk had to find at least one vulnerability. From the 99 that qualified, we picked 43 that match Snyk production data for ecosystem, vulnerability severity, direct vs transitive dependencies, and size of version jump.

VulnBump dataset comparison with Snyk Open Source production data

We turned each recommended upgrade into a task. Each task asks the agent to apply one upgrade that Snyk recommends: one package, moved to a version that fixes its vulnerabilities. Every task starts from a fresh copy of the project and is scored on its own. The 43 repositories yield 307 tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities, across Maven, Gradle, npm, Yarn, pip, and Poetry, the six package managers behind about 92% of production findings.

We added a verifier that didn't trust the agent. When the agent finished, we copied its changes into a clean container and checked them from scratch. There, an attempt counted as a PASS only if it cleared all four gates:

The dependencies install with the command CI would run.

A new Snyk scan confirms the vulnerabilities are gone.

The project builds.

Every test that passed before still passes.

The VulnBump pipeline

The harnesses we tested. All three agents ran on Claude Sonnet 5.5, with a limit of 110 turns per upgrade, in the same container for each language:

Evo Remediation Agent is Snyk’s agentic remediation engine. It uses Snyk intelligence and can run its own scan, build, and tests, and repair errors before finishing. We ran it in auto-approve mode, so it applied every fix, including upgrades Snyk rates as likely to break the build.

Claude Code Snyk scan is Anthropic's general-purpose coding agent, given Snyk's recommendation for the upgrade: the package to upgrade, the target version to move to, and the vulnerabilities it fixes. It can also run a Snyk Open Source scan itself to check its work.

Claude Code unaided gets the same task without the target version or any Snyk access. It has to determine which version fixes the vulnerabilities on its own, for example, by searching vulnerability databases on the web.

The package manager bump is the non-agentic baseline: it applies Snyk's recommended version with the project's own package manager and changes nothing else.

How the repositories were chosen, the exact prompts and tools each agent had, and the leakage controls are all in the research paper: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green, along with the limitations: we tested one model, ran each upgrade once, and used Snyk Open Source as the judge, which can only count against Claude Code unaided, since the other two agents work from the same Snyk findings. We also didn't penalize new vulnerabilities that an upgrade pulled in.

Result 1: The same model, with three different outcomes

Evo Remediation Agent passed every gate on 90.2% of upgrades (and fixed 95.9% of the 2,066 vulnerability instances). That's 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan, roughly one more working fix in every eight upgrades, and 30.6 more than Claude Code unaided.

And the ranking doesn't just hinge on a few large repositories: averaged per repository, PASS rates were 93.1% for Evo Remediation Agent, 80.1% for Claude Code + Snyk scan, 68.0% for Claude Code unaided, and 51.3% for the package manager bump.

Key finding:

Evo Remediation Agent fixes 9 in 10 vulnerability-driven upgrades end-to-end.

Result 2: Agents need to know which version is actually safe

On the same model, giving Claude Code Snyk's scan and recommended upgrade raised its PASS rate by 17.9 points, from 59.6% to 77.5%.

The clearest difference is which version it picks. Unaided, Claude Code settled on a version Snyk still flags 64 times. With Snyk's scan, that dropped to 13. Vulnerability databases don't always agree on which version fixes a vulnerability, so a version that looks safe in one source can still be flagged in another.

Snyk's guidance matters most for transitive vulnerabilities, in packages the project doesn't declare directly. Counting only upgrades that passed every gate, it more than doubled the share Claude Code fixed, from 28% to 59%.

Key finding:

Snyk's scan and target version raised Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 points and more than doubled the transitive vulnerabilities it fixed.

Result 3: Snyk's advice alone solves about half, and then the agents separate on the rest

The package manager bump splits the 307 upgrades in two: On the 144 it passes, Snyk's recommended version is all it takes, and an agent can only keep or lose an easy fix. The other 163 need more than a version bump, such as adapting code to breaking changes or resolving dependency conflicts.

Agents on the 144 upgrades Snyk's advice solves, and on the other 163

With Snyk's guidance, agents rarely break what the bump solves, while Claude Code unaided regressed on 20 of the 144, in 15 of them by picking a version Snyk still flags. The real difference becomes evident on the hard half: with the other 163 upgrades, Evo Remediation Agent passed 82.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan passed 61.3%, and Claude Code by itself passed 36.2%.

Key finding:

Of the 163 upgrades that need more than a version bump, Evo Remediation Agent passed 82.2%, against 61.3% for Claude Code + Snyk scan and 36.2% for Claude Code unaided.

Result 4: A green build can hide an unfixed vulnerability

The easiest way to keep a build green is to leave the vulnerability in place, and that's mostly where we saw Claude Code failing. The rescan was the first gate to fail in 107 of Claude Code’s unaided 124 failures, 48 of Claude Code + Snyk scan's 69 failures, against 9 of Evo Remediation Agent's 30.

First failed verification gate for every failed attempt

Evo Remediation Agent's failures are visible (and that's not a bad thing). 21 of its 30 failures broke the build or tests, mostly on major upgrades that other agents often avoided. A loud failure is much safer than a silent one: when one upgrade does go wrong, the project's own build and tests show it, where a developer can actually see it, and eventually act upon it.

Key finding:

General-purpose agents fail silently; Evo Remediation Agent fails where CI catches it.

Result 5: Knowing the target version isn't enough

Snyk's scan gets Claude Code a long way, but getting the upgrade right takes more than that: with identical findings and targets, Evo Remediation Agent passed 39 more upgrades than Claude Code Snyk scan, 23 of them major jumps.

Evo Remediation Agent combines Snyk's intelligence with a loop in which it builds, tests, and repairs the project before it finishes. While our setup can't isolate which component makes the difference, it does show how far the system around a model can impact the result, which is consistent with DepBench, where changing only the harness changed results by up to 16.3 points.

Key finding:

Same model, same Snyk findings: Evo Remediation Agent still passes 12.7 points more.

Result 6: Major jumps and transitive dependencies remain the hardest tasks

All agents still struggle with major framework migrations: 23 upgrades, mostly Spring, Spring Boot, and Dropwizard migrations, defeated all three agents.

PASS rates fell to 81% from 96% for Evo Remediation Agent, to 61% from 88% for Claude Code + Snyk scan, and to 42% from 70% for Claude Code unaided, respectively, on major vs non-major upgrades. Major upgrades are also where code has to change: about half of Evo Remediation Agent's major version PASSes edited the application source, compared to 5% of its non-major PASSes.

Upgrades passing every gate, by the size of the version jump

Transitive vulnerabilities, where the vulnerable package isn't declared in the manifest, make up 70% of fixable instances and are harder for every harness tested. Counting only fixes from attempts that passed every gate, Evo Remediation Agent fixed 73% of transitive instances, Claude Code + Snyk scan 59%, and Claude Code unaided 28%, against 91%, 71%, and 62% respectively of direct ones.

PASS rate by dependency type (direct vs transitive)

Key finding:

Evo Remediation Agent leads on the hardest upgrades, majors, and transitive dependencies, but major framework migrations still beat every agent.

How does VulnBump fit with VulnBench?

VulnBench evaluates how AI coding agents find vulnerabilities in the code you write: how consistently they detect the same issues across repeated runs, and how closely their findings match a deterministic SAST baseline. VulnBump benchmarks whether they can fix vulnerabilities in the code you depend on: upgrading vulnerable open-source dependencies without breaking the build or tests.

When you read the two together, they point the same way: models bring reasoning that deterministic tools just don't have. On their own, they report different findings across runs and often stop short of a fix. Across the platform, we put the shared lesson more simply: the generator cannot be the validator.

What does this mean for teams handing security work to agents?

Judge a fix by the evidence the agent didn't produce: An agent's report of its own fix is a claim, while a rescan, a build, and a test run become evidence. If an agent is fixing your backlog, hold it to the same checks.

Score the vulnerability and the build together: Either one alone hides a failure. Breakage-only checks miss fixes that never happened, while vulnerability-only checks miss the fix that broke the project.

Give the agent the security data: Snyk's scan and recommended upgrade were worth 17.9 points to a general-purpose agent, on the same model.

Evo Remediation Agent is Snyk's agentic remediation engine, available through the Snyk CLI and as a cloud service. It's one of the agents in Evo Agentic AppSec, which launches today.

Run your agent through VulnBump

The VulnBump harness and all 43 evaluation cases are open-sourced at github.com/snyk-labs/snyk-vulnbump.

The full methodology, failure analysis, and limits are in the research paper. If you're building a remediation agent yourself, run it through VulnBump and let us know what you find.

VulnBump was built by Gabija Pasiunaite, Ryan McMorrow, Brian Clark, Liran Tal, and Luke Tu.

Title: Introducing Evo Agentic AppSec: Security That Keeps Up With AI Development
Context: Attackers are using AI to identify weaknesses, combine lower-severity issues into more serious exploits, and accelerate attacks
Full Text:
AI is changing how software gets built. Coding agents produce more code than teams can review, and current models introduce several times more vulnerabilities per line than human developers. Many of those flaws involve business logic, access control, and authentication, areas where pattern-based scanners have limited visibility.

Most security teams were already behind before any of this started. They are flooded with findings, many of which are noise, while managing a backlog of latent risk. Attackers are using AI to identify weaknesses, combine lower-severity issues into more serious exploits, and accelerate attacks. As of October 2026, Snyk’s data showed roughly eight new vulnerabilities introduced for every one remediated. AI-driven development adds further pressure to that imbalance. And the in-depth security reviews that catch business logic flaws take so much time and context that most teams run them once, for a handful of critical apps.

Software supply chain attacks compound the problem. Malicious packages now account for most open source zero-days, with more than 20 high-profile attacks in 2026 and growth on track to exceed 600% year over year. A malicious package can steal credentials during installation, before a pull request or CI scan runs, and coding agents can introduce these packages without assessing whether they are safe.

Security needs to keep pace with how software is now built and address risks before code reaches review.

The pull request scan is no longer enough on its own

Pull request scanning remains an important control. On its own, however, it cannot address every risk, particularly when code is generated continuously, and malicious dependencies can cause harm before a scan begins.

Application security has to run in three places: checks inside the coding workflow, fast deterministic scans on every change in CI, and deeper analysis of the full application at regular intervals. That analysis must also account for business logic and application context alongside known vulnerability patterns.

Finding more issues is only useful if teams can act on them. Prevention and remediation need to scale too, with clear policies governing what gets blocked, what gets fixed, and what requires human review. Proposed fixes need independent validation before teams accept them.

The answer is not another scanner. It’s the program, run by agents and owned by your team.

The agents work across new code during development, helping to prevent new issues and block the install of malicious packages, and across the applications you have already shipped, so the backlog actually goes down.

Snyk’s security intelligence provides the context behind this work. It combines ten years of deterministic assessments with signals such as reachability, exploitability, breakability, and fix outcomes. That context helps teams separate the issues that matter from the noise, and turns a proposed change into a fix a team can use.

Independent verification is central to this approach. Deterministic engines check proposed fixes rather than relying solely on the model that generated them. Teams define the policies and acceptance criteria that govern the process.

How it works

Evo Agentic AppSec brings together a team of agents with specific roles:

Together, these capabilities help teams expand security coverage and handle more remediation work, while keeping a human on the loop, retaining control over policies, priorities, and approvals.

Giving teams more capacity

Developers can spend more time reviewing proposed changes. AppSec teams can focus on security policy, exceptions, and the risks that require their judgment. CISOs gain visibility into a continuously running program, with adversarial testing and an audit trail of automated decisions.

The culture

But, with every conversation, the same theme comes back and resonates with Boston Futurists: the sense of community. Beyond our global monthly newsletters and our fun Slack channels, we insist on making time and space to come together for in-office gatherings and celebrations.

“Even with all the change, people still show up for one another,” said Lisa Cefalo. “The office may have grown, but that sense of community has stayed with us.”

Title: Russia Is Tightening Internet Controls, Leading to Operational Risks
Context: The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since mid-2025, the Kremlin has intensified restrictions on digital communications and infrastructure, very likely to suppress the organization of domestic political dissent and conduct digital surveillance within Russia. Increasingly strict measures targeting virtual private networks (VPNs), state-managed internet shutdowns, limitations on civilian communications platforms, and monitoring of domestic and foreign entities very likely represent an escalation from the approaches to censorship and surveillance pursued prior to 2024.

However, despite intensifying internet restrictions, technical and political limitations will likely prevent the Kremlin from achieving its long-held objective of a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term. The most likely scenario is that Moscow exerts extensive censorship and monitoring of online activity with increasingly strict –– though not absolute –– controls on circumvention and anonymizing tools.

Insikt Group assesses that the Kremlin’s primary objectives regarding internet restrictions are twofold: facilitating extensive surveillance of online activity to support control over the domestic information space while maintaining connectivity to the global internet, and developing national internet infrastructure under Kremlin control, enabling isolation from the global internet if the Kremlin so chooses. Efforts in support of these objectives have almost certainly provided the Kremlin with enhanced ability to control and monitor domestic online discourse.

In this environment, individuals and organizations operating in Russia are subject to increasing operational risks, including surveillance and exposure of sensitive data, challenges in conducting emergency communications, disruptions to corporate tools and digital applications, and legal risks. Entities with indirect exposure to Russia face an increased likelihood of supply-chain disruptions and sanctions violations and, over the longer term, face challenges in assessing the political and economic situation in Russia, as restrictions limit the availability of high-quality open sources.

Key Findings

The Kremlin is very likely using managed internet shutdowns across Russia to test and improve its ability to isolate the Russian internet, though technical and political limitations make it unlikely that it will achieve its objective of establishing a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term.

In the near- to medium-term, a combination of falling approval ratings for Russian President Vladimir Putin, declining public opinion amid economic strain, and ongoing Ukrainian drone strikes very likely incentivize Moscow to impose further internet restrictions, regardless of reported public dissatisfaction with some of these measures.

The Kremlin will very likely continue to pursue strategies to deter VPN use by forcing platforms to support VPN blocks and making VPN use more expensive and inconvenient, though likely avoiding direct punitive measures against individual users.

Kremlin Systematically Tightening Internet Restrictions

Since July 2025, the Kremlin has systematically tightened access to widely used civilian communications applications and VPNs, caused regular mobile internet outages across Russia, and instituted requirements that place Russian and foreign individuals and firms under increased government surveillance. The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government to launch drone strikes against Russian critical infrastructure.

Restrictions Represent Marked Escalation in Control Over Russian Internet

Insikt Group assesses that, since 2012, Russians have seen their ability to operate without restriction on the internet decline in several waves, primarily driven by the Kremlin's calculation that Russians were using the internet to organize anti-government political actions.

2000–2012: Little Government Oversight

Laissez-Faire State Policy

During this period, the Kremlin generally viewed the internet as politically non-threatening, in part due to low internet penetration rates in Russia (from 1.8% in 2000 to 58% in 2011).

Thriving Media and Social Platforms

Individual expression on the internet was relatively free, with independent news sites such as Lenta, Novaya Gazeta, Ekho Moskvy, and Gazeta able to operate largely without government interference.

In addition, platforms such as LiveJournal and VKontakte (VK) –– Russia’s Facebook mirror –– operated largely without government control.

Minimal Government Regulation

Russian state telecommunications regulator Roskomnadzor was founded in 2008, but primarily handled telecommunications licensing rather than censorship or content filtering.

2012–2015: Blocklists and Platform Takeovers Following Mass Protests

Laws Passed Creating Blocklists of Websites

In 2012, following the largest protests in Russia since the fall of the Soviet Union, the Kremlin passed law No. 139-FZ, titled “On Introducing Amendments to the Law on Protection of Children from Information Harmful to Their Health and Development,” which created the Unified Register of Banned Websites. This introduced internet service provider (ISP)-level technical infrastructure, enabling the Russian government to block domains and IP addresses through domain name system (DNS) tampering.In 2014, the Kremlin passed the Lugovoy Law (No. 398-FZ), allowing for extrajudicial blocking of websites the government considered “extreme” or which called for unauthorized protests.

Platform Takeovers by the Kremlin

The Russian Government started taking over platforms it considered politically threatening. For example, VKontakte founder Pavel Durov was forced out of Russia in 2014 after refusing to hand over data to the Federal Security Service (FSB). The Kremlin facilitated the transfer of control of VK to state-aligned businessmen, including Vladimir Kiriyenko, who is currently VK's CEO.

Data Localization Targeting Foreign Internet Companies

In 2014, the Russian government passed the Data Localization Law (No. 242-FZ), mandating that foreign internet companies store Russian citizens’ personal data on physical servers inside Russia, likely to make it easier for the Kremlin to access that data for surveillance purposes.

2016–2021: Surveillance Mandates and Attempts to Block Platforms

Laws Passed to Mandate Data Sharing, Restrict VPNs, and Pursue Sovereign Internet

In 2016, the Kremlin passed the Yarovaya Law (No. 374-FZ and No. 375-FZ), which forced ISPs and communication providers to retain metadata for up to three years and message and audio content for six months, and to provide that information to Russian security services without a warrant.In 2017, the Kremlin passed the Anonymizers Law (No. 276-FZ), formally prohibiting the use of VPNs to circumvent blocked websites.In 2019, the Kremlin passed the Sovereign Internet Law (No. 90-FZ), which required Russian ISPs to install TSPU (technical means of counteracting threats, технические средства противодействия угрозам) controlled by Roskomnadzor, thereby giving the state the power to throttle or sever external traffic to a platform.

Attempts to Block Platforms Have Mixed Results

In 2018, Roskomnadzor attempted to block Telegram by IP-banning millions of cloud servers. The attempt failed, disrupting banking and retail systems without shutting down Telegram.In 2021, the Kremlin launched its first large-scale deployment of TSPU –– deep packet inspection (DPI) hardware –– to throttle a mainstream social media platform, thereby demonstrating technical maturity in the Kremlin’s ability to throttle platforms.

2022–2024: Crackdown on Independent Media, VPN Blocks

Mass Blocking and Shutdown of Independent Media

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin blocked hundreds of independent news outlets (including Meduza, BBC, Radio Free Europe, and Ekho Moskvy) by pushing DNS and SNI (Server Name Indication)-level blocks to TSPU devices across all ISPs simultaneously. In addition, the Kremlin throttled, before outright blocking access to, social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram. This was accomplished via TSPU's packet-dropping mechanism before full blocks were applied in March 2022.

In 2024, Roskomnadzor began throttling YouTube to near-unusable levels, likely to force users onto state-controlled video platforms.

Anti-VPN Actions

In 2023–2024, Roskomnadzor began blocking underlying VPN protocols, including OpenVPN, WireGuard, and Shadowsocks, via DPI hardware.

In 2024, the VPN Advertising Ban (No. 406-FZ) took effect, prohibiting the advertising of VPNs and other tools that circumvent blocks on certain websites and platforms.

Title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 1: Unified Visibility Across Your Stack
Context: A process that once allowed teams time to manually review scanner alerts, track down code owners, and assign tickets is no longer viable in an era of machine-speed detection and...
Full Text:
Frontier AI models and agentic development have fundamentally changed the demands on application security.

On one hand, AI models can autonomously discover vulnerabilities and generate working exploits, shrinking the window from discovery to exploitation from days to minutes. On the other, AI-assisted development is helping teams ship code faster than ever, amplifying existing risks and expanding the attack surface.

This dual acceleration breaks traditional AppSec workflows. A process that once allowed teams time to manually review scanner alerts, track down code owners, and assign tickets is no longer viable in an era of machine-speed detection and exploitation.

It’s why Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) is even more important today than it was in the past. But, it can’t just be a layer that aggregates risk signals. To drive real security outcomes, ASPM needs to help teams prioritize exploitable risks by drawing on context across the entire application lifecycle.

In this blog series, we’re taking a deep dive into how organizations can operationalize ASPM with Wiz Code. Over the next few weeks, we will cover:

Part 1: Visibility and Coverage: How to connect your existing scanners, correlate and deduplicate your resources, and identify coverage gaps across your codebases.

Part 2: Context and Prioritization: How Wiz enriches third-party findings, removes duplicate alerts, and uses the Security Graph to identify true attack paths.

Part 3: Remediation and Automation: How to systematically group findings for developers using Posture Policies and leverage the Green Agent for AI-generated fixes.

Why Context is the Foundation of ASPM

To drive security outcomes, ASPM needs a strong foundation of context.

Let’s take a practical example with React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182), the critical remote code execution vulnerability impacting Next.js applications from late last year. For an enterprise heavily invested in Next.js, a flaw in a core component does not just trigger one alert. It cascades across micro-frontends, internal tools, and public applications, instantly generating thousands of isolated findings across hundreds of repositories and container images.

Without context, AppSec teams would be left staring at a massive backlog of vulnerable packages, with no way to tell which instances were actually exploitable.

With the right context, organizations could detect every instance of the vulnerable component and immediately prioritize the ones tied to internet-facing applications or workloads with access to sensitive data.

Wiz Code delivers this exact capability by connecting your existing AppSec scanner findings with cloud exposure, runtime insights, and even adversarial testing to prioritize critical risks. The foundation of context is also what enables security teams to achieve broad visibility into application risk across their enterprise footprint and empower developers to remediate at machine speed.

Let’s dive into how organizations can get set up with ASPM in Wiz.

Maximize the Investment on your Existing Scanners

The first step is bringing your existing AppSec tools into Wiz. Whether you standardize entirely on Wiz Code’s native scanners (for SAST, SCA, IaC, and Secrets) or operate a hybrid ecosystem, Wiz provides the flexibility to ingest and contextualize all your application security findings without forcing a rip-and-replace.

Traditionally, building a unified risk dashboard across multiple third-party tools requires massive integration overhead. But with the Wiz Integration Network (WIN) we provide out of the box support for popular AppSec solutions like Snyk, Checkmarx, GitHub Advanced Security, and more.

You can deploy these Wiz-managed connectors with read-only API access and configure them to automatically fetch relevant findings. Wiz handles the API connection, data normalization, and enrichment. This gives your team immediate visibility into SAST, SCA, DAST, and Secret risks without writing or maintaining custom integration scripts.

Custom Integrations

If you use a homegrown scanner or a tool without a native connector, you can still bring that data into Wiz via SARIF file ingestion. Static Analysis Results Interchange Format, or SARIF for short, is a standard, JSON-based file format used to store and share the output of static code analysis tools in a normalized structure. So if your security team is running a custom solution for code analysis, they can still benefit from the enrichment, prioritization, and lifecycle management in Wiz.

Correlate Application Security with Cloud Resources

Once your connectors are active, Wiz begins ingesting the data your scanners generate. You can review this on the Imported Assets page in your inventory.

Each row in this table represents your third-party scanner's perspective of an asset. For example a repository branch scanned by Semgrep or Checkmarx, or Container Image scanned by Snyk. The table shows the asset name, origin scanner, classification, and correlation status.

Crucially, AppSec tools often use completely different naming conventions for the same repository. This is where Wiz asset correlation comes in to serve as your first layer of deduplication. Instead of creating disparate resources for each branch for each scanner, Wiz automatically correlates them to existing resources in Wiz, and adds the third party information as an enrichment on the existing graph entity. If Wiz does not already know of the resource, a new graph resource is created from the scanner’s asset. This cleans up your inventory and prevents unnecessary noise, while allowing you to take your normal action on graph resources such as putting them in Wiz Projects or running Workflows.

This mechanism is the foundation for true code-to-cloud analysis. Traditional AppSec scanners focus on the code. They cannot tell you if a vulnerable repository generates a container image deployed in your environment and is exposed to the internet.

Wiz advances this model. It takes an isolated finding on a repository branch, regardless of the scanner source, traces it to the container image it was built into, linking it to the exact workload where the finding is currently running. Security teams gain immediate context on where vulnerable code lives in reality without any manual searching.

Crucially, this correlation is the engine that allows Wiz to enrich external findings with live cloud context. It sets the stage for the automated prioritization and finding-level deduplication we cover in Part 2 of this series.

Map Coverage and Eliminate Blindspots in Coverage

Enterprise AppSec teams often struggle to answer a fundamental question: Are all of our repositories actually being scanned? In complex environments with multiple development teams, blind spots lead to unmitigated risk, while redundant scanning creates unnecessary noise and wastes resources.

Once your connectors are active and assets are correlated, the Code Repositories inventory gives you a unified view of scanner coverage.

Instead of guessing, you get a clear, per-repository view of exactly what is happening across your codebase.

For each repository, you can see:

Active Scanning Tools: Which AppSec tools are actively scanning each repo (such as Snyk, SonarQube, Checkmarx, Wiz Code native scanners, or VCS-native tools).

Coverage & Gaps: Which finding types are covered (SAST, SCA, Secrets, IaC) and where critical gaps exist.

Finding Volume: The exact number of open findings per category from each scanner.

You can use this view to surface repositories where no SAST scanning is active or where secret scanning exists from one tool but is missing elsewhere. By mapping your coverage, your team can eliminate blind spots, identify redundant tools on the same repository, and ensure consistent security standards across every development project.

Up Next: Prioritizing Critical Risk with Context

Getting your existing AppSec data into one platform and mapping your coverage is the crucial first step. However, visibility alone does not solve the vulnerability fatigue caused by AI-accelerated development. Security teams need context to know what to fix first.

In Part 2 of this series, we will dive into how Wiz enriches your third-party findings, automatically removes duplicate alerts across different scanners, and uses the Security Graph to trace isolated flaws into true, exploitable attack paths.
