IOCs for this research can be found at our GitHub repository here.

Title: ROMULUS Malware Server Leverages ClickFix to Deliver Multiple Payloads
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Cybercriminals have started to adapt campaigns that deploy ClickFix tactics into an entire ecosystem which can be repeatedly used to deliver multiple forms of malware to victims, cybersecurity researchers have warned.

As detailed in a blog post published on October 14, security analysts at Vedere Labs, a part of Forescout Research, discovered the server hosting panel ROMULUS while investigating an incident.

They found that the exact same malware delivered by a separate ClickFix campaign was also connected to another server linked to the incident being investigated.

The new server was discovered to be hosting a panel called ROMULUS. Further analysis revealed this to be a new multi-payload shared ClickFix delivery platform.

ClickFix is a popular attack technique among cybercriminals. It relies on social engineering to trick the victim into running attacker-supplied commands on their own machine.

And because ClickFix relies on the real, trusted user of the machine to run the commands, action often bypasses any security protections that may be in place to stop unauthorized action.

ClickFix Able to be Deployed at Scale

The newly uncovered ROMULUS platform appears to be capable of deploying a range of attack routes to deliver different forms of malware. Researchers also note that ROMULUS is a reusable delivery backend rather than a single hard-coded malware server, suggesting it is being used at scale.

In total, Forescout analysts identified a total of six different servers running ROMULUS, something they said could indicate that this infrastructure is being run as a toolkit for a wide-range of cybercriminals to use to distribute their attacks.

ROMULUS is also notable for using an unusual method to help disguise its operations. One delivery route was observed to distribute LegionLoader, a multi-pronged malware delivery platform, through encrypted archives containing an executable artificially inflated to approximately 842 MiB, potentially exceeding file-size limits imposed by security scanning and analysis tools.

Researchers believe that this operation shows how ClickFix is evolving beyond a simple social engineering technique into an entry point for malware operations, while attackers are also diversifying their delivery infrastructure, disguising malicious activity and making threats harder to detect.

The identity of the operator behind the platform and common ownership of the final malware families are unknown. But it is noted that this ROMULUS platform is separate to RomulusLoader, a form of malware identified by researchers at Proofpoint earlier in 2026.

Title: The Week in Vulnerabilities: Toptech, Lantronix, Langflow, and CISA Malcolm Flaws
Context: This Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) weekly vulnerability report covers two views of risk: what attackers tried against Cyble's global honeypot sensors, and what the...
Full Text:
This Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) weekly vulnerability report covers two views of risk: what attackers tried against Cyble's global honeypot sensors, and what the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) disclosed for industrial control systems (ICS).

The Cyble Global Sensor Intelligence (CGSI) network observed exploitation attempts against about 20 known vulnerabilities. They range from newly disclosed flaws in WordPress, Apache Solr, and Langflow to years-old bugs in GPON home routers and embedded TCP/IP stacks.

On the industrial side, CISA issued 14 ICS advisories covering 54 vulnerabilities. Of these, 13 were rated critical, 18 high, 18 medium, and five low.

Affected vendors include Toptech Systems, Lantronix, VIVOTEK, MikroTik, Armatura, Monta, Anjvision, and, unusually, CISA itself.

Cyble sensors also recorded active malware campaigns, phishing emails, and brute-force attacks against internet-exposed services.

Real-World Attacks Observed by Cyble Sensors

Attackers moved quickly against newly disclosed flaws in web platforms and AI tooling, while older IoT and embedded-device bugs continued to draw steady traffic.

Source: Cyble sensor intelligence. The 24 CVEs named in this post, counted by CVE ID year

CVE-2026-63030 — WordPress REST API

CVE-2026-63030 is a route-confusion flaw in a WordPress REST API batch endpoint. It affects WordPress 6.9.x before 6.9.5 and 7.0.x before 7.0.2.

Attackers can chain it with CVE-2026-60137 to achieve SQL injection and potentially remote code execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-44825 — Apache Solr

CVE-2026-44825 is a hardcoded credential in the Basic Authentication setup tool of Apache Solr 9.4.0 through 9.10.1 and 10.0.0.

Remote attackers can use it to access a Solr cluster with administrative privileges.

CVE-2026-9198 — Langflow

CVE-2026-9198 affects IBM Langflow OSS 1.0.0 through 1.10.0. Unauthenticated attackers can chain two API endpoints to obtain superuser tokens and execute arbitrary code.

Sensors also caught attempts against an older Langflow code injection flaw, CVE-2025-3248. Repeated targeting of the same AI workflow platform signals sustained attacker interest.

CVE-2025-68613 — n8n

CVE-2025-68613 is a critical RCE flaw in the n8n workflow automation platform. Expressions supplied by authenticated users can run in an insufficiently isolated context, enabling full system compromise.

Fixes are available in versions 1.120.4, 1.121.1, and 1.122.0.

CVE-2026-4020 — Gravity SMTP

CVE-2026-4020 affects the Gravity SMTP WordPress plugin, versions 2.1.4 and earlier. An exposed REST API endpoint lets unauthenticated users pull system reports containing server details, database metadata, and configured API keys or tokens.

CVE-2024-6587 — LiteLLM

CVE-2024-6587 is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw in LiteLLM. Exploitation can expose OpenAI API keys.

Older Flaws Still in Rotation

Cyble sensors also logged exploitation attempts against:

CVE-2025-58360, an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in GeoServer's GetMap operation

CVE-2024-7591, an OS command injection flaw in Progress LoadMaster

CVE-2024-4577, a critical PHP-CGI argument injection flaw

CVE-2024-25600, a code injection flaw in Bricks Builder 1.9.6 and earlier

CVE-2025-2010, an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in the JobWP WordPress plugin

CVE-2025-46565, a file access control bypass in the Vite development server

Command injection flaws in QNAP QTS firmware

Scanning for the Cisco Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) WebVPN login page

A Mirai variant is also targeting Dasan GPON home routers by chaining CVE-2018-10561 and CVE-2018-10562. Together, the two flaws let an unauthenticated remote attacker run commands on the device.

Most-Attempted CVEs

CVE-2020-11899, an IPv6 out-of-bounds read in the Treck TCP/IP stack, drew far more exploitation attempts than any other CVE this week. The rest of the top five, in order:

A group of four Wind River VxWorks TCP buffer overflows: CVE-2019-12255, CVE-2019-12260, CVE-2019-12261, and CVE-2019-12263

CVE-2020-11900, an IPv4 tunneling double-free in the Treck TCP/IP stack

CVE-2019-0708, a critical unauthenticated RCE in Microsoft Remote Desktop Services

CVE-2020-11910, an ICMPv4 out-of-bounds read in the Treck TCP/IP stack

Most of these flaws sit in networking code embedded in IoT and industrial devices, which often go unpatched for years.

Malware Families Observed

Files collected from Cyble sensors were linked to several malware families:

CoinMiner: Linux cryptominers that hijack CPU and GPU resources

WannaCry: Ransomware that spreads through the EternalBlue exploit, targeting CVE-2017-0147

Mirai: A botnet that turns IoT devices and Linux servers into remotely controlled bots

IRCBot: Linux malware that uses IRC connections as a backdoor

CRIL also observed Hajime, Gafgyt, and Wacatac activity.

MacSync Infostealer Targets Crypto Users

CRIL is also tracking a new version of MacSync, a macOS infostealer sold as malware-as-a-service. Kaspersky's Securelist reported that the latest campaign targets cryptocurrency users and developers.

According to Securelist, attackers distribute MacSync through malicious disk images posing as a fake crypto wallet app. In one case, they abused a public iCloud calendar event to deliver commands.

The malware steals browser data, saved credentials, crypto wallet data, Keychain files, and SSH, AWS, Kubernetes, and Git configurations. It also installs a backdoor disguised as Finder that persists through a LaunchAgent, shell profile changes, and Git hooks.

Security teams should watch macOS endpoints for unexpected disk-image apps, removal of quarantine attributes, and new LaunchAgents.

Phishing and Advance-Fee Scams

Phishing emails captured by Cyble sensors relied on emotional appeals and promises of money. Common lures this week:

Subject line

Scam type

Re: DONATION FOR less-privileged

Charity or donation scam

GOD BLESS YOU....

Emotional appeal, advance-fee scam

Re. Compensation funds for your past effort

Compensation fund scam

MY PROPOSAL

Business proposal, advance-fee scam

Investment Inquiry, Funding for Your Project

Investment or project funding scam

Dear Sir/Madam

Advance-fee scam

Many of these emails use look-alike domains or impersonate known organizations to appear credible.

Brute-Force Attacks

Brute-force traffic focused on remote access and database ports, including VNC (5900), RDP (3389), SSH (22), Telnet (23), HTTP (80), Microsoft SQL Server (1433), and PPTP (1723).

Targets included Elasticsearch, Hadoop, Oracle, GitLab, MySQL, and PostgreSQL. Attackers leaned on default and weak credentials such as "sa," "root," "password," and "123456."

The largest share of attack traffic, 39%, came from sources with a known bad reputation.

Critical ICS Vulnerabilities

CISA's 14 ICS advisories covered 54 vulnerabilities, two-thirds of them rated high or medium. Toptech Systems and CISA itself disclosed the most flaws this week.

Source: CISA ICS advisories analyzed by CRIL, Sept. 29–Oct. 5, 2026 · 54 vulnerabilities by vendor and severity

Toptech Systems TMS7 and TopHAT (Critical)

Toptech Systems' TMS7 and TopHAT version 7.6.3 carried more critical-rated ICS vulnerabilities than any other product this week. They include multiple SQL injection flaws (such as CVE-2026-72510 and CVE-2026-63713), an unrestricted file upload flaw (CVE-2026-70356), and files exposed to external parties (CVE-2026-71379).

TMS7 is a terminal management system that controls liquid fuel and chemical distribution in the Energy, Chemical, and Transportation Systems sectors. In a product that governs fuel terminal operations, these flaws could enable interference with physical processes, not just data theft. Toptech has published security update information.

CVE-2026-91191 and CVE-2026-84409 — Lantronix G520 Series (High)

Two flaws affect Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateways running 2.6.0.4R6_stable. CVE-2026-91191 is an improper cryptographic signature verification flaw, and CVE-2026-84409 is a cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw.

The signature flaw could let attackers bypass firmware integrity checks and push unauthorized firmware to remote field devices. Combined with the XSS bug, it creates a realistic multistage attack path against devices that may be hard to inspect physically. Lantronix has published remediation details.

CVE-2026-84411 — MikroTik RouterOS (Critical)

CVE-2026-84411 is a critical integer underflow vulnerability in MikroTik RouterOS versions before 7.24. Updated versions are available from MikroTik's download page.

CVE-2026-22755 — VIVOTEK Cameras (Critical)

CVE-2026-22755 is a critical command injection flaw affecting 37 VIVOTEK camera models across its V, C, S, Dome, Bullet, and Panoramic series. VIVOTEK has posted an update package.

CVE-2026-95102 — Monta (Critical)

CVE-2026-95102 is a missing-authentication flaw for a critical function in all versions of monta.app. Three other Monta flaws involve excessive authentication attempts, session expiration, and credential protection. The advisory data referenced no vendor fix.

Anjvision, Viidure, and Armatura One

Anjvision's YSSD-RTMP-H5 firmware has nine vulnerabilities, led by CVE-2026-100291, a critical insecure default setting. Others include OS command injection, hardcoded credentials, and improper signature verification.

The Viidure Dashcam Android app, version 3.3.1.260403 and earlier, contains hardcoded credentials (CVE-2026-96587, critical). Armatura One is affected by CVE-2023-46604, a critical deserialization flaw, plus hardcoded key and credential issues.

No vendor fixes were referenced for these products, so compensating controls such as network isolation are the main option for now.

CISA Malcolm (15 Vulnerabilities)

In an unusual disclosure, CISA reported 15 vulnerabilities in Malcolm, its own open-source network traffic analysis and threat-hunting platform. The flaws affect versions before 26.06.0.

They span authentication bypass, missing authorization, default credentials, OS command injection, path traversal, and SSRF. Most are rated medium, and two are rated high. Users should update through the Malcolm releases page.

The remaining advisories covered Baicells Technologies, Meari, and Johnson Controls products.

Impacted Critical Infrastructure Sectors

Energy was the most exposed sector this week, followed by Transportation Systems and Commercial Facilities.

Source: CISA ICS advisories analyzed by CRIL, Sept. 29–Oct. 5, 2026 · share of 54 vulnerabilities touching each sector

The largest single combination, Energy, Information Technology, and Water and Wastewater, accounted for 27.8% of vulnerabilities. Energy, Chemical, and Transportation Systems made up another 18.5%, driven largely by the Toptech disclosures.

These disclosures cut across traditional infrastructure boundaries rather than clustering in one domain. A single flaw in a shared product can create risk for fuel, water, and transportation operators at once.

Conclusion

This weekly vulnerability report highlights several trends:

Fast exploitation of newly disclosed flaws in WordPress, Apache Solr, and AI workflow tools such as Langflow and n8n

Persistent attacks on years-old embedded-device and router vulnerabilities

Critical ICS flaws in fuel distribution, cellular gateway, and camera products

Several ICS products with no vendor fix referenced, leaving compensating controls as the main defense

Ongoing phishing and brute-force activity that relies on weak and default credentials

With 13 critical ICS vulnerabilities and active exploitation attempts against both new and legacy flaws, organizations face risk across enterprise IT and operational technology (OT) environments.

Key Recommendations From This Weekly Vulnerability Report

Patch internet-exposed web platforms, plugins, and AI workflow tools first, starting with the flaws under active exploitation above

Replace default usernames and passwords, and enforce strong, unique credentials on servers and devices

Restrict or block exposed remote access and database ports, including VNC, RDP, SSH, Telnet, and SQL Server

Segment IT and OT networks with firewalls and demilitarized zones (DMZs) to limit lateral movement

Apply compensating controls, such as network isolation, for ICS products without available fixes

Verify firmware integrity on remote field devices and cellular gateways

Monitor macOS endpoints for unexpected disk-image apps and new LaunchAgents

Track CISA advisories and the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, and prioritize by exploitability and operational impact

Conduct regular vulnerability assessments and penetration testing

Cyble's attack surface management and vulnerability intelligence solutions help organizations identify exposed assets, prioritize remediation, and detect early signs of compromise. Combined with real-time sensor intelligence, they help security teams stay ahead of threats across enterprise and critical infrastructure environments. To see these capabilities in action, schedule a demo with Cyble.

Title: How the Aurora® Superintelligence Platform and Aurora Agentic SOC Help You Understand and Secure AI
Context: Curated by the world’s largest commercial SOC based on real-world attacks, emerging threats, and observed adversary behavior
Full Text:
AI now plays a central role in defending organizations from the modern threat landscape. It triages alerts, investigates security events, and recommends what to do next. AI is critical to defending at machine speed, but security leaders can’t see how it is making decisions on their behalf. This visibility challenge creates multiple downstream problems for security leaders that need to justify AI decisions that they can’t fully explain to their board, regulatory bodies, and insurance partners.

The challenge reaches beyond defense. Employees are also adopting AI tools faster than your team can inventory them. Governing those tools and assessing their risks only adds to the workload.

According to the Arctic Wolf® 2026 AI & Cybersecurity Trends Report, 94% of organizations say AI capabilities influence their cybersecurity purchasing decisions. Yet only 53% trust AI to perform even narrowly defined security actions on its own.

We’re working to close that trust gap by providing more transparency into agentic security operations and AI activity across your organization. With the Aurora® Superintelligence Platform, you can see how the Aurora® Agentic SOC makes decisions. You can identify the AI services in use across your environment. You can also get critical security intelligence fast through natural language conversations.

SwarmView: See the Why Behind Every AI Security Decision

To trust a recommendation, you need to know what influenced it. The Aurora Superintelligence Platform is powered by the Swarm of Experts™, Arctic Wolf’s proprietary network of 300+ AI agents that work alongside human security experts to help identify and respond to threats, evaluate findings, and support security decisions.

SwarmView™, available in November in the Arctic Wolf Portal, shows you the work behind the scenes. It highlights which agents contributed to a security event, how findings were evaluated, and what information shaped the outcome. It also lets you follow a security event from the first indicator to the conclusion.

When an agent can’t reach a clear conclusion, a human security expert steps in. SwarmView makes it clear when human expertise contributed to the decision, helping you see how Arctic Wolf reached a recommendation.

Figure 1: SwarmView provides visibility into how decisions are made and the experts contributing to each security event.

Shadow AI Discovery: Find the AI Usage You Didn’t Know About

You can’t manage AI-related risk if you don’t know how employees are using AI in your organization.

To address this challenge, we’re introducing a new Shadow AI Discovery capability in November to Aurora® Managed Detection and Response (MDR) customers. This feature shows how your organization uses AI, identifies unknown AI usage that may need further review, and supports long-term AI governance decisions and policies. It uses network, identity, and endpoint data, so you don’t need to deploy anything new.

You can review the findings through a standalone report or as part of a Security Posture In-depth Review (SPiDR).

Figure 2: Shadow AI Discovery shows AI use and flags areas that may need further review.

Train Employees on AI Best Practices

Discovering AI use is important, but employees also need guidance on how to use AI safely. When Shadow AI Discovery identifies areas that need attention, AI training in Aurora® Security Awareness and Training Plus helps employees learn AI best practices and recognize potential risks. It also teaches employees how to identify AI-powered threats, including phishing attacks and other forms of AI-generated fraud.

You can assign AI training modules to help employees make better decisions and reduce human risk related to AI usage.

Aurora Security Assistant: Get the Answers You Need Fast

Sometimes you need answers quickly. Aurora® Security Assistant gives you answers in plain language using data from the Aurora Superintelligence Platform. It now helps answer questions across more areas of your environment, including SPiDRs, Security Journey, threat intelligence, vulnerabilities, patch management, and asset risk.

Instead of searching through reports and tools, you can ask questions in natural language and quickly get the information you need. You can review critical vulnerabilities, check patch status, learn more about threats affecting your environment, and identify what requires your attention.

Aurora Security Assistant also lets you continue previous conversations, making it easier to pick up where you left off and continue investigations.

Figure 3: Aurora Security Assistant can now answer questions about vulnerabilities, assets, patch status, SPiDRs, Security Journey, and threat intelligence.

Once you have an answer, you may want to dig deeper. Searching through numerous fields and dropdown menus can make it difficult to find the information you need. Recent enhancements to the Arctic Wolf Portal let you search in natural language, so you can describe what you’re looking for in plain English instead of building complex queries.

Whether you’re investigating a security event or exploring your data, Natural Language Query helps you find answers faster and spend less time navigating the platform.

Figure 4: Use Natural Language Query to create searches without navigating complex fields.

Natural Language Query is available in the Arctic Wolf Portal, which you can access directly from your current Arctic Wolf experience.

Arctic Wolf Mobile App: Stay Connected Wherever You Work

Security work doesn’t stop when you’re away from your desk. The Arctic Wolf Mobile App helps you stay connected to important security activity wherever you are.

Available on iOS and Android, the app provides access to alerts, investigations, and other security information from your mobile device. Whether you’re reviewing activity, checking the status of a case, or keeping up with important notifications, you can stay connected when you’re away from the portal.

Expand Security Visibility with New Integrations

AI tools add more activity, more data, and more risk to evaluate, so a complete view of your environment and the ability to take a response action matters more than ever. No one tool sees everything. Identities, cloud services, business applications, networks, and critical infrastructure create their own signals.

Our platform turns raw data from your existing tools into useful security signals as well as active response, so you get greater value from the tools you already have. That’s why we’ve expanded our integrations across endpoint, identity, cloud, network, healthcare, backup, and observability technologies.

Recent additions cover several areas of your environment.

Endpoint: Aurora® Adaptive Threat Protection, Aurora® mEDR, Trend Vision One Endpoint Security, and Palo Alto Cortex

Identity: 1Password

Cloud and applications: Datadog, Cloudflare WAF, and Imperva WAF

Email and collaboration: Proofpoint Essentials and Google Workspace

Network and critical infrastructure: ExtraHop Reveal(x) 360, Veeam Data Platform, and Claroty xDome Industrial

Healthcare: Epic Systems, Claroty xDome Healthcare, and Imprivata ITDR

One highlight is our new integration with Veeam Data Platform, which extends visibility into backup infrastructure that attackers target to disrupt recovery.

We’ve also expanded visibility into healthcare environments through Epic Systems, Imprivata ITDR, and Claroty xDome Healthcare. New support for Cloudflare WAF and Imperva WAF enables detection and active response for threats targeting web applications and services.

Get the Full Picture of What AI Is Doing and Why

AI is changing how organizations detect threats, investigate activity, and make decisions. To keep up, you need visibility into how Arctic Wolf arrives at recommendations, how employees use AI across your organization, and where to focus your attention.

SwarmView lays out how the agents make decisions. Shadow AI Discovery tells you how your organization uses AI. Aurora Security Assistant gives you context to act.

In the portal, our Natural Language Query helps you find information faster. Title: How Aurora® Adaptive Threat Protection Spots Attacker Intent Early
Context: The malware arrives only after the attacker is in control
Full Text:
Imagine this: There’s an active attack but no alert. Nothing looks wrong. Every login is valid. Every tool is trusted. Every command is one your team has run before. This invisible attack chain is how many attackers work today, and they can take control of a domain in minutes and encrypt an environment while evading traditional detections.

It’s what happens between the login and the ransom note that’s the modern cyber battlefield. Attackers work in the open, scouting the network, raising their privileges, and moving between systems to weaken defenses and remove recovery options. Each action uses tools and permissions that look like normal administration. The malware arrives only after the attacker is in control.

At Arctic Wolf, we see this pattern in our incident response (IR) work time and time again. Abuse of external remote access tools drove 65% of our non-business email compromise (BEC) cases, up from 24% a few years ago. Ransomware drove 44% of the incident response cases as reported in the 2026 Arctic Wolf Threat Report, which means defensive measures didn’t stop the payload from executing in those cases.

The window to detect an attacker between login and payload is closing fast, with the time between initial access and handoff to a ransomware group happening in a matter of minutes. With AI speeding up attacks and timelines shrinking, security teams need to catch attackers earlier.

Today we’re introducing Aurora® Adaptive Threat Protection, a next-generation endpoint solution built to disrupt attacks mid-flight with AI-powered intent detection.

Why Earlier Matters

The Arctic Wolf VP of Incident Response Kerri Shafer-Page puts it plainly: “In cases where defenders interrupt the attack before detonation, the difference in cost, downtime, and recovery complexity is dramatic.” That seems straightforward, but knowing an earlier response leads to a better outcome is different from being able to achieve it.

The first minutes of an attack tend to decide everything that follows. What happens in those first minutes after initial access can determine whether an incident becomes a breach. Yet many organizations alert on everything and lack the capacity to watch or respond to those alerts.

Recovery also gets harder as time passes. Ransomware operators now target backup infrastructure and identity services directly. Once those are gone, organizations face a choice between paying and rebuilding.

Endpoint detection and response (EDR) is a well-established technology that delivers rich detection. As we respond to AI-driven attacks, we need a way to bring that capability forward in the attack chain.

We’re aligned with Gartner’s recent observation that “to stay ahead of AI-augmented attacks, enterprises are increasingly moving beyond reactive monitoring toward preemptive controls, specifically capabilities that can deny, deceive, and disrupt adversaries.”1

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is designed to help organizations make that shift. It identifies malicious intent early in the attack lifecycle and works to disrupt attacks automatically before they cause significant damage. It strengthens what your endpoint tools already do without relying on static policies.

It also runs alongside your existing endpoint protection platform (EPP) and EDR tools, including third-party platforms and Aurora® Endpoint Security. You keep what you have and add a layer that reads intent.

How Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection Predicts the Attack Story

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is powered by a custom-trained small language model that predicts and maps endpoint activity through a causal graph. That lets it detect intent as soon as a process or file begins to behave unexpectedly.

Because the causal graph keeps context over time, it can spot intent even when individual actions look benign. Consider a sequence like this: a user pastes a command from a web page into a terminal, remote access software your IT team might also use gets installed, a script bundles files into an archive, and then the archive uploads to cloud storage. Each step has a legitimate twin, but together they tell a clear story.

We don’t raise an alert on any one of those steps. Each activity is a chapter in a larger story, and Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection evaluates how each chapter relates to the others as it predicts how the whole story will end.

The small language model and agentic workflows do that evaluation. They separate legitimate business operations from emerging threats. When Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection confirms malicious intent, it’s designed to disrupt the activity and reverse the entire attack chain rather than just the final step.

The Activities That Define the Story

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection also graphs the low-level events that generate too much noise for other tools, which helps surface early signals of malicious intent. It groups those signals by how attacks actually unfold rather than by a generic framework.

Getting in. Attackers start with tricks that persuade a user to run something or with tools that look like normal IT work. It watches for the signs of both.

Staying hidden. Attackers work to slip past execution controls and weaken the defenses around them. It tracks those moves as they happen.

Taking what matters. Attackers collect credentials and data on the way to a payoff. It follows that activity from first touch to exit.

Doing damage. Encryption and destruction come last, along with efforts to block recovery. It’s built to interrupt before they land.

Credential theft keeps growing. Credential-harvesting malware now siphons stolen logins from infected devices at enormous scale. A stolen login lets an attacker skip the exploit. Spotting information stealers early shuts that door.

Rolling Back to a Pre-attack State

Stopping an attack is half the job. Cleanup is the other half. When Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection confirms malicious intent, it reverses the attack chain and returns the endpoint to a pre-attack state. That reduces manual remediation and saves your team time, all with minimal impact on endpoint performance.

Title: Passkey Authentications Double but Adoption Remains Slow
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Passkeys are an increasingly common feature on log-in screens but widespread adoption remains relatively low, according to new data from Dashlane.

The credential security specialist analyzed millions of aggregated, anonymized passkey authentications that it managed between July 2025 and June 2026 to compile its third annual Passkey Power 20 report.

It revealed that passkey authentications by Dashlane users have nearly doubled year on year, reaching 2.5 million per month in 2026.

Additionally, over half (57%) of its users now store at least one passkey, compared with 40% last year.

However, the phishing-resistant authentication technology still accounts for a minority of logins on major sites like Google (28%), PayPal (18%), Amazon (17%) and eBay (8%).

Read more on passkeys: Half of Cybersecurity Pros Still Rely on Passwords Despite Security Concerns.

Passkeys are much harder for scammers to crack as there’s no password to guess or steal: the user logs in via a device PIN or biometric such as a face scan.

They are cryptographically tied to legitimate websites, and even if the latter were breached, the hacker wouldn’t have access to the user’s private key, which stays on their device.

That’s why institutions like Report Fraud recommend passkeys as one of the most effective ways to mitigate account takeover attacks.

Closing the Gap to Passkey Adoption

For businesses, passkeys can keep sensitive corporate data and systems safe and reduce the password-reset workload for IT support.

In this space, Dashlane noted an expansion in the number of applications supporting the login mechanism.

HubSpot and Cisco Duo led the way in terms of volume of authentications, but there were also new entrants to the top 20 in the form of HR and payroll platforms like isolved HCM and BambooHR, as well as AWS and Dropbox.

The key will be closing the gap between passkey support and adoption, Dashlane argued.

It pointed to four approaches:

Making passkeys highly visible and easy to use within existing workflows

Promoting passkeys as a faster alternative to passwords, with higher completion rates

Starting to remove alternatives like one-time passcodes and passwords

Setting a deadline for mandatory passkey use

Application developers forcing users to adopt passkeys are few and far between, although Japanese internet company LY Corporation has announced a spring 2027 deadline for Yahoo Japan users, the report noted.

More should at least make the system their default method for user logins, argued Dashlane CPO, Christophe Frenet.

“Despite sustained growth, we’re not on the other side yet,” he said. “There’s still more work to be done to make passkeys easier to use, and more companies need to go from soft adoption to enforcing the change, so that passkeys become the main authentication method rather than a secondary one, as they still are today.”

Title: French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
While many supermarkets in France are still grappling with food stock disruptions due to a cyber-attack that targeted refrigeration controllers on October 11, the scope of the incident could be larger than previously observed.

Recent developments suggest that the incident does not only impact Danfoss refrigeration controllers, but also temperature regulation devices from Dixell Electronics, an Italian brand owned by American heating and cooling equipment provider Copeland.

Notably, French local media France 3 reported that an E. Leclerc supermarket in the Tarn region, in the south-west of France, experienced disruptions to its refrigeration systems, despite using Dixell equipment instead of Danfoss.

French national newspaper Le Monde also reported a supermarket near Bordeaux, where attackers reportedly changed freezer settings from −22°C to 150°C. A technician observed several settings being altered per second, suggesting automation.

A security advisory published by the French national Computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) on October 12 specifically named Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series as well as Dixell xweb and Copeland xweb as “affected systems.”

Fears of Deliberate Industrial Sabotage

Speaking to Infosecurity, Amir Preminger, CTO of industrial security provider Claroty, said refrigeration controllers are a prime target, not just for supermarkets but also cold-storage facilities, warehouses, pharmaceuticals, chemical manufacturing and more, that often go overlooked by security teams.

“Industrial control systems such as refrigeration controllers are often assumed to be on safely isolated networks, however, our research found many of these devices are directly exposed to the public internet. While this convenience significantly reduces maintenance costs by allowing engineers to troubleshoot issues remotely, it also lowers the barrier to entry for attackers,” he said.

Preminger assessed that while the attack did not necessarily require sophisticated skills, the targeting was a clear deliberate attempt to cause damage.

“I don’t think it’s sophisticated,” he said. “However, you cannot cause a defrost by mistake by typing the wrong parameter. You need to initiate the defrost. Somebody needed to guide the exploit, the campaign to have that impact.”

He compared the apparent tactic with an incident at a food-processing facility in Israelin 2025. In that case, an attacker inside the facility’s network manipulated a refrigeration compressor and caused it to defrost. While the impact was similar, Preminger did not claim the incidents involved the same group.

He argued that the broader concern was that refrigeration controllers were exposed to the internet. Preminger said such exposed Danfoss devices could be found outside of France too, including in Israel and the US, but he did not know what software versions those devices were running or whether they were vulnerable.

He also cautioned that patching alone does not make internet exposure safe. His advice was to keep critical devices off the public internet and restrict access through measures such as corporate virtual private networks (VPNs) or even access point name (APN) gateways.

He also urged operators to segment their networks, inventory their equipment, and know who can access each device. “Gate your devices, segment your devices. That’s the first frontier,” he said.

Why Supermarket Fridges Are Connected to the Internet

Supermarket fridges are generally connected to the internet to comply with legislation, which, in Europe, requires them to maintain timestamped monitoring of temperatures to strengthen food safety and to install an alarm system in case of an abnormal rise in temperature.

This connection also allows for remote maintenance.

“This is an essential system for the proper preservation of food products,” emphasized Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Coopérative U, in a post on X.

Title: Medicare scam calls, texts and ads: What to watch for this Open Enrollment
Context: And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity
Full Text:
Scammers love a pretext. And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity. From October 15 to December 7 beneficiaries are able to review and amend various parts of their plan. There’ll be ads, emails, messages and calls from genuine insurers at this time. Some might even ask for personal and health details.

That provides great cover for fraudsters, and enough plausibility for even skeptical consumers to drop their guard. Here’s what to look out for.

How do these Medicare scams work?

There are various ways scammers could approach you. They could call, message, email, or send a note on social media. They might also place an ad on Google, mocking up a website with official-looking logos and language to appear as if it’s a legitimate insurer, a specialist agency, or even Medicare itself.

The pretext for getting in touch, or posting the ad, could vary. Common ones include:

You should compare/change your plan by the December 7 deadline

Your Medicare card needs updating or replacing

You could qualify for additional benefits or lower premiums

Your existing coverage (or specific prescription coverage) is changing

You could be eligible for a new plan

They need to verify your account details

Your account has been linked to fraudulent activity

All seem plausible. But the scammer will usually employ some tried-and-tested social engineering techniques to pull you into their deceit. Urgency is a common tactic. It fires our synapses in specific ways that make us stressed and less likely to think logically, while possibly also triggering a fear of missing out. The real deadline of December 7 adds an element of truth to the lie that makes it more plausible still.

If you were told by an official-sounding representative that you could lose your benefits if you don’t act, or that you have just days to claim a lower premium offer, would you stop and think?

If they’re successful, the scammer will move on to the next stage: harvesting your personal, financial and/or medical information. They might ask for your:

Medicare number

Social Security number

Date of birth

Phone number

Email and home address

Account passwords

Health information such as doctors, prescriptions and medical records

Insurance information including provider, plan, member ID and policy details

Bank details and/or credit card information

Once you’ve handed some or all of the above over, you’re unlikely to ever hear from the scammers again. But in the background, they’ll be working hard to monetize your information for their own gain.

What do they want with your data?

There are various ways they might do this, depending on what data they’ve tricked you into handing over. They might want to commit various forms of identity fraud, using your personal and financial details to access your bank and personal accounts, or take out new credit lines in your name.

Alternatively, they may try to use your information to submit fraudulent Medicare claims in your name, for services, equipment or prescriptions that you never received. Or to actually obtain these goods and services. Scammers might even try to manipulate your Medicare enrollment in order to generate fraudulent commissions or compensation.

In September 2026, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) identified around $17.5 billion in suspicious financial activity that may be linked to healthcare fraud like this.

Depending on exactly what avenue the scammers explore, an incident could leave you out of pocket, impact your coverage, impair your medical records, and plunge you into a bureaucratic nightmare that leaves you in severe emotional and mental distress.

How to spot and avoid Medicare scams

All of which makes it more important than ever that you’re able to spot the tell-tale signs of a Medicare scam at this time of year. You should be extremely dubious of any unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true.

Yes, genuine insurers might get in touch seemingly out of the blue. But this will usually not be without your prior consent. And they should never try to strong-arm you into handing over details.

The best approach to steering clear of Medicare scams during Open Enrollment season is to:

Spot the warning signs listed above, and if in doubt, put down the phone or don’t reply to the message. You can always verify separately with the caller/sender to check if they are legitimate (using contact details sourced separately from the inbound contact).

Be very careful about online searches. Don’t click through on any Google ads, and if you’re looking for official Medicare sites be sure the address has a .gov ending.

Type the name of the site you want to visit directly into the search/address bar. Medicare is at Medicare.gov (800-633-4227), while HealthCare.gov (800-318-2596) is where to check if you qualify for savings. Help is also available from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), or local Senior Medicare Patrol.

Report any suspicious contact.

What a real call looks like

Some insurers and other third parties may pick up the phone to get in touch during the Open Enrollment period. But you should be able to tell them apart from fraudsters because they will clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straight off the bat.

They should be courteous and provide you with ways to verify who they say they are, even if it means hanging up. And they’ll often be calling because you initiated contact with their organization.

What to do if you’ve already been scammed

If you feel like you’ve fallen victim to a Medicare scammer, don’t panic. Work through the following steps:

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general

If you have handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card

If you’ve handed over other identity-related information, consider reporting the incident to IdentityTheft.gov

Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges

Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity

Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on

Don’t fall for recovery fraud. If anyone gets in touch after an incident promising to get your money back or sort everything out on your account for a fee, it’s another scam

Your health is important. But so is your personal information. So slow down this Open Enrollment season and verify every request for personal and medical details.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

When is Medicare Open Enrollment?

It runs from October 15 to December 7 each year, during which time you can make some changes to your coverage.

Would Medicare or my insurer ever call me during Open Enrollment?

A representative from Medicare, your insurer or a third party may call. But put the phone down if they start pressuring you into handing over your details, asking for financial information, or promising too-good-to-be-true benefits. Call them directly to double check, eg 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

What are the main red flags for a Medicare scam?

Watch out for unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true. Contact could come via email, phone, social media, or text. Scammers might also buy Google ads to lure you.

What do Medicare scammers want?

They want your medical, financial, personal and possibly your insurance details. They might want this to commit identity fraud, access your bank account, submit fraudulent Medicare claims or obtain goods and services in your name, or manipulate your enrollment.

Can a Medicare scam affect my healthcare?

Yes. Fraudulent claims or misuse of your medical identity could impact your insurance coverage, medical records, prescriptions and access to healthcare. It may also land you with plenty of distressing administrative work to clear your name.

How do I know if a phone call is a Medicare scam or not?

They should clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straightaway. They should allow you to hang up and verify their identity. Usually they’ll only call because you have requested it.

What should I do after falling for a Medicare scam?

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general. If you’ve handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card. Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges. Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity. Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on. Don’t fall for recovery fraud scammers who promise to get your money back.

Title: The Sovereign Advantage: Why MSPs Who Move First Will Control the Board
Context: Sovereignty is achieved only when all three are in place
Full Text:
In chess, the first player to move gains more than a step. They shape how the board develops from that point on. Digital sovereignty works the same way. MSPs that make their sovereign move now build an advantage that could decide who leads the market.

That is the idea behind our webinar, The Sovereign Advantage: Move First to Control the Board, where Alina Drăgănescu (Deputy GM of the Business Solutions Group and SVP of Business Operations, Bitdefender) and Nadine Pilote (Managing Director, Septeo IT Solutions) join Mia Thompson (Senior Product Marketing Manager, Bitdefender) to discuss what it takes to build a sovereign, compliance-ready security practice.

Key webinar takeaways to expect

Understand the difference between data residency and data sovereignty.

Explore why cybersecurity sovereignty requires three forms of control working together: data, technical, and operational.

See how Bitdefender takes a unified approach that is European-built, European-operated, and EU-governed.

Learn how MSPs can add a sovereign service tier for regulated customers without changing their operating model.

Gain clarity on the ways Bitdefender EU Sovereign MDR brings sovereignty into security operations, with monitoring, investigation, and response delivered within the EU.

Why Does a Cybersecurity Platform Hold More Than Security Data?

A modern cybersecurity platform collects signals from across the organization, so it holds one of a client's richest operational datasets, not just security events.

Twenty years ago, security tools had a narrow view. Today, a cybersecurity platform brings together signals from endpoints, servers, identities, email, cloud workloads, networks, SaaS applications, and increasingly AI-powered tools. It does not just see security events. It sees how an organization operates.

That changes the questions buyers ask. They no longer stop at "can this platform protect us?" They want to know where the information is stored, who governs access to it, which laws apply, and who ultimately controls it?

What Are the Three Dimensions of Cybersecurity Sovereignty?

Cybersecurity sovereignty requires three forms of control that work together: data sovereignty (control over security data), technical sovereignty (control over the technology), and operational sovereignty (control over operations). Sovereignty is achieved only when all three are in place.

1. Data sovereignty: control over security data

Security telemetry, logs, and incident data stay protected under European governance, with EU-based storage and processing, controlled access, and trusted, certified sovereign European cloud infrastructure.

2. Technical sovereignty: control over the technology

The cybersecurity platform itself is governed under European jurisdiction, built on European-designed technology and the EU legal framework, with reduced exposure to non-EU legal authority.

3. Operational sovereignty: control over operations

Security services are delivered from the EU, with monitoring, investigation, and response staying within it.

A provider can store data in Europe, but without technical and operational sovereignty, jurisdictional risk may remain.

How Does Bitdefender Approach Cybersecurity Sovereignty?

Bitdefender takes a unified approach that combines data, technical, and operational control, delivered as European-built, European-operated, and EU-governed cybersecurity.

The outcome is not simply European data residency. It combines data, technical, and operational control, backed by European infrastructure, governance, and cybersecurity technology.

Bitdefender is headquartered and governed in the EU, and it develops its technology under EU jurisdiction. GravityZone is available through sovereign cloud deployments with European partners, including OVHcloud in France, Secunet in Germany, and Aruba in Italy.

How Can MSPs Add a Sovereign Service Tier Without Changing Their Operating Model

MSPs can keep their scalable operating model and add a sovereign service tier for regulated or sensitive customers, all on the same unified GravityZone platform. Sovereignty does not have to be an all-or-nothing infrastructure decision.

A strong approach is to start by understanding your customers:

Identify which industries, clients, datasets, and workloads carry the highest jurisdictional risk.

Define the level of sovereignty each one needs.

Introduce a sovereign tier where it creates genuine customer and commercial value.

What Is Bitdefender EU Sovereign MDR?

EU Sovereign MDR is AI-enabled, human-led 24/7 Managed Detection and Response delivered entirely within the EU sovereign operating model. It brings sovereignty into security operations, which matters because customers increasingly ask who can access their data during an investigation, and where the team doing that work sits. This is where Bitdefender MDR becomes a leading solution for sovereign-ready service delivery.

What makes it sovereign:

24/7/365 MDR delivered by EU experts from an EU-based SOC

All monitoring, investigations, and incident response remain within the EU

No follow-the-sun handoffs or case escalations outside the EU

Threat research, malware analysis, and detection engineering remain within the EU

AI-assisted investigations use sovereign-hosted LLMs, so customer data is never processed by public AI services

People, processes, tooling, and service delivery stay under EU control, even during incident response. For MSPs, it also means growing a security service without building a full security operations center themselves.

What Does "Moving First" Mean for MSPs?

Moving first means making the sovereignty choice before you are forced to, and acting before sovereignty becomes a mandatory line in every customer tender.

Both speakers close on this idea. For Alina, moving first looks like this:

Focus on the customers for whom jurisdiction matters most.

Build a sovereign-ready service option.

Train your commercial and technical teams to explain it.

Put processes in place to deliver it consistently.

The advantage is not simply saying you offer sovereign cybersecurity. It is being able to demonstrate how it works, where the data is processed, who governs the technology, and how customers stay protected without sacrificing operational effectiveness.

What Will You Learn in the Webinar?

The Sovereign Advantage: Move First to Control the Board is designed for MSPs and MSSPs. Watch it live or on demand to hear a practical discussion of:

How Bitdefender approaches sovereign-ready deployment, and what it delivers for MSPs in practice

The three dimensions of cybersecurity sovereignty: data, technical, and operational

How EU Sovereign MDR extends sovereignty into security operations

How to build a staged, defensible path to sovereignty without an all-or-nothing migration

Join us, October 27, 4:00 PM CET. Available on demand after the live session.

It goes beyond where data is stored and covers who governs the technology, which legal jurisdiction applies, who can access the data, and who runs the security operations.

Is data residency enough to be sovereign?No. Data residency only answers where data is stored. Sovereignty also depends on legal jurisdiction, governance, and who can access, process, or compel access to the data. A provider can store data in Europe, but without technical and operational sovereignty, jurisdictional risk may remain.

What are the three dimensions of cybersecurity sovereignty?They are data sovereignty (control over security data), technical sovereignty (control over the technology), and operational sovereignty (control over operations). Sovereignty is achieved only when all three work together.

Monitoring, investigations, and incident response stay within the EU, with no follow-the-sun handoffs or case escalations outside it.

Do MSPs need to rebuild their operating model to offer sovereign services?No. An MSP can keep its scalable operating model and add a sovereign service tier for regulated or sensitive customers on the same unified GravityZone platform.

Why is sovereignty becoming a buying criterion for European organizations?Regulated buyers increasingly ask who can be compelled to access their data and under whose laws, not only where it is stored. In 2026, NIS2, DORA, and the Cyber Resilience Act move from awareness to active enforcement, which makes the question a live one.

Several TAG-193 intrusions identified through Recorded Future® Network Intelligence occurred around diplomatic developments involving Kazakhstan. Following Kazakhstan’s parliamentary consideration of a treaty on allied relations with Tajikistan, we noted communications between a Tajik government entity responsible for economic development and TAG-193 infrastructure. In Kazakhstan, water security is closely tied to economic stability and national security. Dependence on cross-border water supplies leaves the country exposed to upstream decisions about water use, storage, and diversion. Climate change, glacier loss, and inefficient irrigation place additional pressure on water availability, with implications for agriculture, industry, and domestic supplies. Title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
Context: At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an...
Full Text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

Title: An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
Context: OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office
Full Text:
An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, whom federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room.

He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing.

OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office.

Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US District Court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest.

FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but neither prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.”

OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep.

Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview, Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations.

The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment.

Title: The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk
Context: Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code...
Full Text:
When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

Internal Reconnaissance: A High-Volume, Noisy Campaign

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.

The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.

Authentication Abuse and Documentation Browsing

The pattern continued with credential testing. Over a period of a few months, the threat actor launched multiple password-guessing campaigns. They hammered at internal systems with brute-force authentication attempts, focusing on administrator accounts.

While doing this, they systematically targeted internal documentation and data shares. Using automated web requests, they scraped individual pages and attachments from internal systems and enumerated various operational and network shares.

The activity observed did not match the behavior typically associated with a sophisticated threat actor. The noise behind the scanning and login attempts, along with using common system identifiers, pointed to an opportunistic attacker attempting to compromise multiple systems. Their actions showed little effort to remain hidden or avoid detection.

Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation

In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code execution vulnerability on the central configuration management server. This server handled software distribution across the bank, making it a prime target for privilege escalation and long-term persistence.

However, the attacker's luck ran out. The moment they attempted to execute unauthorized code, Cortex XDR identified the activity and contained the threat before it could escalate. The attacker was prevented from gaining a persistent foothold or moving laterally throughout the network.

When Unit 42 engaged, our team initiated a comprehensive threat-hunting effort. We performed a deep forensic review of endpoint telemetry across approximately thousands of systems, alongside logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. Ultimately, no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors were found. Bank leadership acted quickly to review the exposed documentation and rotate all compromised credentials, completely neutralizing the threat.

What This Investigation Revealed

This case serves as a critical reminder that not every cyber threat is advanced and multifaceted. Opportunistic actors will gladly take advantage of simple oversight, such as missing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a VPN or an unpatched edge device, to compromise and break into an environment. That being said, an attacker's lack of sophistication doesn't make them harmless.

Defending against this type of intrusion relies on foundational security hygiene and swift response. This includes:

Enforcing strict identity access controls

Ensuring timely patching

Using endpoint detection to stop lateral movement

By pairing timely containment with thorough threat hunting, the organization prevented the intrusion from turning into a catastrophic event.

Outcomes

Unit 42 independently validated the incident to confirm the root cause, restoring leadership confidence through strategic guidance and complete incident management. Beyond resolving the immediate threat, we delivered specific, prioritized recommendations to harden the bank's security posture. To ensure enhanced protection, the organization expanded its defensive coverage by deploying additional Cortex XSIAM and Cortex XDR licenses and broadening its incident response retainer service.

Interested in learning more about the latest attack trends? If so, take a look at our Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report, which distills the most critical findings based on our direct experience responding to over 750 real-world cyberattacks across the globe.
